n5-54:
The idea in one line
These three patterns put actions in order, and they're as easy to grasp as their English equivalents:
〜てから＝"do ~ first, then ~"
〜たあとで＝"after ~"
〜まえに＝"before ~"
Think of telling a friend about your day: brush your teeth, then go to bed; watch TV after dinner; check the weather before heading out.
How to form it
~ first, then ~Verb te-form + から.
磨く → 磨いて → 磨いてから食べる → 食べてからする → してから
・歯を磨いてから、寝ます。(I brush my teeth, then go to bed.)
・手を洗ってから、食べてください。(Please wash your hands first, then eat.)
after ~Verb ta-form + あとで. The ta-form is just the te-form with 「て」 changed to 「た」 and 「で」 changed to 「だ」.
見て → 見た → 見たあとで飲んで → 飲んだあとで
After a noun, add 「の」 in between: 仕事 → 仕事のあとで
・映画を見たあとで、ご飯を食べました。(After watching the movie, I ate.)
・仕事のあとで、ビールを飲みます。(After work, I have a beer.)
before ~Verb dictionary form (the base form you find in a dictionary) + まえに.
寝る → 寝るまえに行く → 行くまえに
After a noun, add 「の」 in the same way: 食事 → 食事のまえに
・寝るまえに、シャワーを浴びます。(I take a shower before going to bed.)
・食事のまえに、手を洗います。(I wash my hands before eating.)
Common mistakes
・Before まえに, the verb is always in dictionary form, even when you're talking about the past: 日本へ来るまえに、英語を勉強しました。 (I studied English before coming to Japan.) You can't say 「来たまえに」.
・Before あとで, the verb is always in ta-form, even when the event hasn't happened yet: 食べたあとで、歯を磨きます。 (I'll brush my teeth after eating.) You can't say 「食べるあとで」.
・Whether the whole sentence is past or present is decided by the end of the sentence (磨きます／磨きました). The first half doesn't change with it.
・With nouns, it's easy to drop 「の」: say 授業のあとで, not 「授業あとで」.
・When あとで stands alone with nothing before it, it means "later": あとで電話します。 (I'll call you later.)
Telling similar patterns apart
てから and あとで both mean "B happens after A is done," and often either one works. The difference is in the nuance:
お風呂に入ってから、ご飯を食べます。 (First I take a bath, and then I eat. This stresses the order: I don't eat until I've bathed.)
お風呂に入ったあとで、ご飯を食べます。 (I eat after my bath. This just places the meal later in time.)
When you want the other person to be sure to do A first, てから sounds the most natural:
電話してから来てください。 (Please call first, then come over.)
Quick rule of thumb: for "do ~ first, then ~" use てから; for simply "after ~" use たあとで; for "before ~" use まえに, always with the dictionary form in front.
What to learn next
When てから is followed by a length of time, it means "it's been ~ since ...": 日本に来てから、もう三年です。 (It's already been three years since I came to Japan.)
n5-58:
The idea in one line
「〜ながら」 means "while doing ~, ...". Japanese has one habit, though: the more important action goes last. In "studying while listening to music," studying is what you're really doing and the music is just background, so Japanese says 音楽を聞きながら勉強します。
How to form it
Put the verb in ます-form, drop 「ます」, and add 「ながら」. It works the same for all three verb groups.
聞きます → drop ます → 聞きながら
食べます → 食べながら見ます → 見ながら運転します → 運転しながら
Then add the main action. 「ながら」 itself never changes. Tense, negation and politeness are all left to the final verb.
・歌を歌いながら、料理しました。(I cooked while singing.)
When to use it
Two things at the same momentYou're doing this and that at the same time.
・テレビを見ながら、ご飯を食べます。(I eat while watching TV.)
・歩きながらスマホを見るのは危ないです。(Looking at your phone while walking is dangerous.)
Both going on over a period of timeIt doesn't have to be the same second. It can also mean two things running in parallel during this stretch of your life, like working while studying.
・アルバイトをしながら、日本語を勉強しています。(I'm studying Japanese while working a part-time job.)
Common mistakes
・Attach it to the ます-form minus ます, not the dictionary form: 聞きながら is right, and you can't say 「聞くながら」; 食べながら is right, and you can't say 「食べるながら」.
・Both actions must be done by the same person. "I was watching TV while Mom was cooking" involves two people, so you can't use ながら. Use 「とき」 instead: 母が料理をしているとき、私はテレビを見ていました。
・Don't swap the two halves freely like you can in English. In Japanese, the second action is the main one. 勉強しながら音楽を聞きます sounds like "I'm mainly listening to music and studying on the side."
・Past tense and politeness change only the final verb. Don't put ました before ながら: you can't say 「聞きましたながら」. Say 聞きながら勉強しました.
Telling similar patterns apart
Te-form linking = finish one thing, then do the next, so there's an order.
ながら = two things happen at the same time.
・ご飯を食べて、テレビを見ます。(I eat, then watch TV.)
・ご飯を食べながら、テレビを見ます。(I watch TV while eating.)
〜たり〜たりします = giving examples of things you do. They aren't done at the same time.
・週末は本を読んだり、映画を見たりします。(On weekends I do things like reading books and watching movies.)
Quick rule of thumb: doing both at once is ながら, finishing one and then doing the next is te-form, and listing a few example activities is たり〜たり.
n5-62:
The idea in one line
In English, “the door opened” and “I opened the door” use the same verb, “open”. Japanese switches to a different verb: for “the door opens” you use 開く, and for “someone opens the door” you use 開ける. The first kind is an intransitive verb, the second is a transitive verb, and the particle in front has to change with them.
Get the two names straight
Intransitive + がIt only says what state something changes into, without caring who caused it. The particle before it is が.
・ドアが開きます。(The doors are about to open: an announcement you often hear on trains)
Transitive + をIt says someone does something to a thing, and the thing being acted on takes を.
・ドアを開けます。(I open the door)
A simple test: is there a doer acting on the thing? “I open the door” has a doer and an object, so use transitive + を. “The door opens” just happens by itself, with nobody acting on it, so use intransitive + が.
The most common pairs
・電気がつきました。(The light came on)
・電気をつけてください。(Please turn on the light)
・授業が始まります。(Class is about to start)
・授業を始めます。(Let's start the class)
・財布が落ちました。(The wallet fell)
・財布を落としました。(I dropped my wallet)
Here are a few more pairs. The left one is intransitive and the right one is transitive:
閉まる／閉める (close)
消える／消す (go out / turn off)
入る／入れる (go in / put in)
出る／出す (go out / take out)
No single rule tells you which is which in every case, so it's best to memorize them pair by pair with example sentences.
Easy places to slip
・Match the particle with the verb: 電気を消します and 電気が消えます are both correct, but 「電気を消えます」 is wrong.
・When you ask someone to do something, use the transitive verb: 窓を閉めてください. You can't say 「窓が閉まってください」.
・Here 開く is read あく. The same kanji also has the reading 「ひらく」, which is used differently, so don't mix them up for now.
・入る and 出る often appear with places: 部屋に入ります (enter a room) uses に. In 家を出ます (leave the house), the を marks the “place you leave”, not a “thing being acted on”, so 出る is still intransitive.
・Intransitive verbs aren't only for things that “happen naturally”: 行く and 寝る are also intransitive, and they are actions people do themselves. What matters is whether there is an object being acted on.
Tell it apart from look-alikes
Adding 「〜ています」 to each kind of verb gives very different meanings:
窓が開いています。 (The window is open) → just describes what you see
夏はいつも窓を開けています。 (In summer I always keep the window open) → talks about an action a person does, a habit
Quick tip: if you're only seeing a state like “open, on, closed”, use 「が＋intransitive ています」.
What to learn next
A transitive verb plus 「〜てあります」 means “someone did it on purpose and left it that way”: 窓が開けてあります。 (The window has been opened on purpose)
n5-15:
The idea in one line
「は」 works like English “as for ~, …”. You put the thing you want to talk about at the front of the sentence, as if to say “this is what we're talking about now”, and then say what it's like. 私は学生です。 is “as for me, I'm a student”, which is just “I'm a student”.
How to attach it
Just add は after a noun:
私 → 私は伊藤さん → 伊藤さんは今日 → 今日は
The pronunciation matters: as a particle it's written は but pronounced wa, the same sound as わ.
When to use it
Introducing and explainingThis is the most basic use: say “who / what” first, then say what it's like.
・伊藤さんは建築家です。(Mr. Ito is an architect)
・今日は暑いですね。(It's hot today, isn't it?)
Topic first, details afterBefore は you put “what this sentence is about”, and another subject can appear afterward.
・象は鼻が長いです。(An elephant's trunk is long)
・そのケーキは姉が焼きました。(That cake, my older sister baked it)
Many people get stuck on the second sentence: the one who baked is the sister, not the cake. So what comes before は isn't always “the person doing the action”. It only says “this is what the sentence is about”. Here the topic is the cake, and then you add “my sister baked it”.
Comparing two thingsIf you use は on both sides, it gives a contrast: “this one is like this, but that one is different”.
・コーヒーは好きですが、お茶はあまり飲みません。(Coffee, I like, but tea, I don't drink much)
Easy places to slip
・The particle は is read wa. The final は in the greetings こんにちは and こんばんは is also read wa. The は in other words is still read ha, like in はい and 花.
・When a question word like 「誰」 or 「どれ」 is the subject of the question, it takes が, not は. 誰は来ましたか is wrong; say 誰が来ましたか (Who came?).
・Once the topic has been stated, you can leave it out afterward. English needs “I” in nearly every sentence, but in Japanese, after you've said 私は once, you usually don't repeat it, and repeating it sounds wordy: 私は陳です。台湾から来ました。 (I'm Chen. I came from Taiwan.)
Tell it apart from look-alikes
は and が are the easiest to mix up. Look at the same scene: a new coworker arrives at the office.
Nobody knows you yet, so you introduce yourself: 私は陳です。 (I'm Chen) → what people want to know is the part after, “Chen”.
Someone is looking for you: 陳さんはどちらですか。 (Which one is Mr. Chen?) You raise your hand and say: 私が陳です。 (I'm Chen) → now the focus is the part before, “I”.
Also, something you've just seen or that has just happened uses が too: あ、バスが来ました。 (Oh, the bus has come)
Quick tip: with は, the focus is on what comes after は; with が, the focus is on what comes before が. Use が for the answer to “who? which one?” and for things you've just noticed.
What to learn next
Replace は with も and it becomes “also”: 私も学生です。 (I'm a student too). Note that it replaces は rather than stacking with it, so there's no such thing as 「私はも」.
n5-56:
The idea in one line
「〜たり〜たりします」 is like English "I do things like reading, watching movies, and so on". You pick two or three activities from a bigger set as examples, which signals "these are just examples; I do other things too." It has a second use: "sometimes this, sometimes that", like "it's hot one minute and cold the next" or "on and off."
When to use it
Giving examplesWhen someone asks what you usually do, you don't have to list everything. Just pick a few representative things.
・休みの日は、本を読んだり映画を見たりします。(On days off, I do things like read books and watch movies.)
・週末は掃除したり、買い物に行ったりします。(On weekends, I clean up, go shopping, that sort of thing.)
Back and forthTwo opposite actions or states alternate.
・最近、暑かったり寒かったりします。(Lately it's been hot one day and cold the next.)
・今日は雨が降ったりやんだりしています。(Today the rain keeps starting and stopping.)
How to form it
Three steps: change the verb to the た form → add り → finish with します.
読む → 読んだ → 読んだり
行く → 行った → 行ったり
見る → 見た → 見たり
する → した → したり
来る → 来た → 来たり
If the た form still feels shaky, think of it as swapping the 「て」 of the て form for 「た」, and 「で」 for 「だ」:
書いて → 書いた読んで → 読んだ食べて → 食べた
い-adjectives: drop the 「い」 and add 「かったり」.
暑い → 暑かったり高い → 高かったり (いい becomes よかったり)
Nouns and な-adjectives: add 「だったり」.
・朝ごはんはパンだったりご飯だったりします。(For breakfast I have bread some days and rice on others.)
Tense and politeness are all handled by the final する:
・昨日は友達と話したり、ゲームをしたりしました。(Yesterday I chatted with friends, played games, and so on.)
・週末は家で寝たり、テレビを見たりする。(On weekends I sleep at home, watch TV, and so on. This is the casual form, for talking with friends.)
Common mistakes
・Attach it to the た form, not the ます form: it's 行ったり, not 行きたり; it's 読んだり, not 読みたり。
・Don't forget the します (or する) at the end of the sentence. Without it, the sentence sounds unfinished.
・For the past tense, only the very end changes: 行ったりしました is correct; you never say 行きましたり。
・With two or more actions, put たり after every one. In casual speech you'll occasionally hear the second たり dropped, but on exams and in writing, spell it out. Using it with just one action is fine too, e.g. 映画を見たりします (I watch movies and the like).
・たり does not indicate order. To say "do A, then B," use the て form.
Telling similar patterns apart
All of these talk about "what I did yesterday":
て = in order, and these are exactly the things that happened: 昨日は本を読んで、映画を見ました。(Yesterday I read a book, and then I watched a movie.)
たり = a few examples, with more not mentioned, and order doesn't matter: 昨日は本を読んだり、映画を見たりしました。(Yesterday I read a book, watched a movie, and so on.)
や = also examples, but it connects things (nouns): 昨日は本や漫画を読みました。(Yesterday I read books, manga, and so on.)
Quick test: to tell what happened in order, use 「て」; to give a few actions as examples, use 「たり」; to give a few things as examples, use 「や」.
n5-1:
The idea in one line
「Noun＋です」is the English "is / am / are ~", and 「Noun＋じゃありません」is "is not / am not / are not ~". 私は学生です。 means "I'm a student." This is the most basic Japanese sentence, and you'll use it in the very first line of a self-introduction.
How to form it
It's simple: just add it directly after the noun. The noun itself doesn't change at all.
学生 → 学生です (is a student)
学生 → 学生じゃありません (is not a student)
The sentence pattern is 「AはBです」 = A is B.
・林です。よろしくお願いします。(I'm Lin. Nice to meet you.)
・これは私の傘です。(This is my umbrella.)
・田中さんは先生じゃありません。(Mr. Tanaka is not a teacher.)
・明日は休みじゃありません。(Tomorrow is not a day off.)
Add か at the end to make a question: 学生ですか。 (Are you a student?)
Ways to say "is not"
They all mean the same thing; the difference is the setting:
Most common学生じゃありません: everyday polite speech.
More formal学生ではありません: writing and formal situations. 「じゃ」 is just 「では」 said quickly.
More relaxed学生じゃないです: still polite, but softer in tone, and very common in everyday Japanese today.
Talking with friends
With family and close friends, drop です and use だ／じゃない:
学生です → 学生だ学生じゃありません → 学生じゃない
In actual conversation, though, 「だ」 is often dropped, or 「よ」 is added to sound more natural; otherwise it can sound a bit blunt:
・うん、学生だよ。(Yeah, I'm a student.)
Common mistakes
・The は in 「AはB」 is pronounced wa, not ha.
・The final 「す」 of です is usually very light, so it sounds like "des."
・です doesn't always translate as "is": 今日は雨です。 means "It's rainy today," and you wouldn't say "Today is rain" in English.
・You can't add です after a verb: 食べます is enough; you can't say 「食べるです」.
・You don't need to say 私は in every sentence. When it's clear you're talking about yourself, Japanese speakers usually leave it out.
Telling similar patterns apart
Nouns and な-adjectives both use じゃありません to negate, but い-adjectives are different, and that's the easiest place to get confused.
Noun: ここは駅じゃありません。(This is not a station.)
な-adjective: ここは静かじゃありません。(It's not quiet here.)
い-adjective: ここは高くないです。(It's not expensive here.)
You can't say 「高いじゃありません」; replace い with くない.
Quick test: nouns and な-adjectives take 「じゃありません」 directly; for い-adjectives, replace い with 「くないです」. Note that きれい ends in い but is actually a な-adjective, so you say きれいじゃありません.
What to learn next
The past tense: 学生でした (used to be a student), 学生じゃありませんでした (wasn't a student).
n5-34:
The idea in one line
「が」 is like pointing a finger and saying "It's this one!". When you want to single out who did something or what happened, put が right after that star of the sentence.
For example, someone asks "Who came?" and you answer "Mr. Tanaka came." "Mr. Tanaka" is the answer you're pointing at, so you say 田中さんが来ました.
How to form it
Just add が right after the noun. Nothing changes.
私が、雨が、田中さんが、誰が、何が
When to use it
Asking who or whatWhen "who" or "what" is the subject of the sentence, use が in the question, and use が in the answer too.
・誰が来ましたか。(Who came?)
・田中さんが来ました。(Mr. Tanaka came.)
・何が一番おいしいですか。(What tastes best?)
・このラーメンが一番おいしいです。(This ramen tastes best.)
Something right in front of youWhen you've just seen something or it has just happened, you simply describe the scene.
・あ、バスが来ました。(Oh, the bus is here.)
・雪が降っています。(It's snowing.)
Mentioning something for the first timeYou bring in a person or thing the listener doesn't know about yet.
・昨日、友達が家に来ました。(A friend came to my house yesterday.)
Easy mistakes
・Question words like "who," "what" and "where" can't be followed by は. 誰は来ましたか is wrong; say 誰が来ましたか. The other question words work the same way, for example どこが痛いですか (Where does it hurt?).
・If the question uses が, answer with が. If someone asks 誰が作りましたか (Who made it?), answer 私が作りました (I made it). If you answer 「私は作りました」, it turns into "Me? Well, I did make it," which sounds odd.
・It's tempting to put は on the subject of every sentence, since it feels like the default "subject" marker. But if you suddenly see rain outside the window, say あ、雨が降っています. For sentences that just describe what's in front of you, が sounds natural.
・日本語が好きです and ピアノができます also use が, but that's the "liking something / being able to do something" usage. It's covered in another card, 「助詞が（能力・好惡）」, so don't mix it in yet.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
は means "as for ~," so you set out the topic first and the point comes after it.
が means "it's ~ that...," so the point is the noun right before it.

Both of these are about you being Tanaka:
When introducing yourself, you say 私は田中です。 (I'm Tanaka.) Here everyone is listening for who you are.
If someone asks 田中さんはどの人ですか。 (Which one is Mr. Tanaka?), you say 私が田中です。 (I'm Tanaka.) Here you're picking Tanaka out from a group.

Both of these are about Tanaka coming:
田中さんが来ました。 (Mr. Tanaka came.) This simply reports who came.
田中さんは来ました。 (Mr. Tanaka did come.) Here Tanaka is the topic, with a hint of "as for the others, who knows."
Quick test: if you're answering "who is it?" or "what is it?", use が. If you're saying what this person or thing is like, use は. When a question word is the subject, always use が after it.
What to learn next
"There is something somewhere" also uses が: あそこに猫がいます。 (There's a cat over there.) Next, try the existence expressions, plus the が pattern for "like" and "can."
n5-31:
The idea in one line
「から」 means "because ~, so ~." The difference is that English puts "because" in front of the reason, while Japanese puts 「から」 at the very end of the reason. You give the reason first, then the result.
・時間がないから、急ぎましょう。(We're out of time, so let's hurry.)
The order is: reason + から, result.
How to form it
Put a complete clause before 「から」. It can be in plain form or in the polite です・ます form.
Verbs: 行く → 行くから行きます → 行きますから
い-adjectives: 寒い → 寒いから寒いです → 寒いですから
な-adjectives: add 「だ」 or 「です」 first. 静か → 静かだから静か → 静かですから
Nouns: again, add 「だ」 or 「です」. 雨 → 雨だから雨 → 雨ですから
It also works for past events: 寝なかった → 寝なかったから
Plain form before から and ます at the end of the sentence is very common in daily speech. If you want to sound more polite, use です・ます in both parts.
How you'll hear it most
Giving a reasonSay the cause first, then the result.
・この店は安いから、よく来ます。(This shop is cheap, so I come here often.)
・今日は日曜日だから、学校は休みです。(Today is Sunday, so school is closed.)
Requests, reminders, invitationsIt's also natural to follow it with a request or an invitation.
・危ないですから、触らないでください。(It's dangerous, so please don't touch it.)
Giving only the reasonWhen someone asks "why?" and the result is already obvious, just say the reason plus から.
・「どうして食べないの？」「辛いから。」("Why aren't you eating?" "Because it's spicy.")
Easy mistakes
・After nouns and な-adjectives, you can't attach から directly. Say 雨だから, not 「雨から」; say 静かだから, not 「静かから」.
・い-adjectives are the opposite: you can't add だ. Say 高いから, not 「高いだから」.
・Don't follow English word order and put から at the start of the sentence. "Because it's raining" is 雨だから, with から at the end.
・だから on its own at the start of a sentence means "so": 雨です。だから、行きません。 (It's raining. So I won't go.)
・When explaining your situation to a teacher or boss (for example, why you were late), から sounds rather direct and can come across like an excuse. In everyday conversation, から is perfectly fine.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
You've already learned 「から」 for a starting point (from ~). The two look exactly the same.
Starting point: 9時から働きます。 (I work from 9 o'clock.)
Reason: 雨だから、働きません。 (It's raining, so I won't work.)
The difference is what comes before it. For a starting point, から follows a time or place noun directly. For a reason, から follows the end of a full clause, such as a verb, an adjective, or 「だ」「です」.
Quick test: if only a noun like 9時 or 駅 comes before から, it means "from." If a complete clause like 雨だ, 寒い or あります comes before it, it means "because."
What to learn next
Put the reason at the end of the sentence as 「〜からです」 to answer "why?": 熱があるからです。 (Because I have a fever.) Later you'll also learn 「〜ので」, which also means "because" but sounds softer than から. It's more common when asking your boss for time off or apologizing.
n5-51:
The idea in one line
English uses "give" no matter who gives to whom, but Japanese looks at which direction the thing is moving. When it goes out from my side, use あげます. When it comes in from someone else to my side, use くれます. When you speak from the receiver's side and say "I got it," use もらいます.
When to use it
あげますI (or someone on my side) give to another person, so the thing goes outward. It's also used when one other person gives to another other person.
・友達に誕生日プレゼントをあげました。(I gave my friend a birthday present.)
・田中さんは山田さんに花をあげました。(Mr. Tanaka gave Ms. Yamada flowers.)
くれますSomeone gives to me or to my family, so the thing comes in toward my side. You usually don't need to say "to me" out loud, because Japanese listeners already understand it.
・母が時計をくれました。(My mom gave me a watch.)
・友達が妹にお菓子をくれました。(A friend gave my little sister some sweets.)
もらいますYou speak from the receiver's side: "I got it, I received it."
・先生から手紙をもらいました。(I received a letter from my teacher.)
How to build it
All three sentences are "who, to whom, what," and the difference is who the subject is:
あげます: giver は　receiver に　thing を　あげます
くれます: giver が　(me に)　thing を　くれます
もらいます: me は　giver に／から　thing を　もらいます
For the past tense, just swap ます for ました: くれます → くれました
Telling similar ones apart
Same situation: a friend gives me a book.
・友達が本をくれました。(A friend gave me a book.) The friend is the subject, and the book comes toward me.
・友達に本をもらいました。(I got a book from a friend.) I am the subject, and I receive it.
These two mean the same thing, and you can say either.
・友達が私に本をあげました。　This one is wrong, because あげます can't be used for "gives to me."

Conversely, if I give a friend a book, you can only say:
・友達に本をあげました。(I gave my friend a book.)
Quick check: ask yourself, "Is the thing coming toward me?" If yes, use くれます or もらいます. If it's going outward, use あげます.
Common mistakes
・Since English just says "give," many learners write 母があげました for "Mom gave it to me." That's wrong. Giving to me or to my family is always くれます.
・The subject of くれます is never "I": 私が友達にくれました is wrong. Say 友達にあげました instead.
・The に before もらいます means "from," not "to": 友達にもらいました means "I got it from a friend," not "I gave it to a friend." If that confuses you, switch to から, which means the same thing.
・Family counts as "my side," so when a friend gives something to your little sister, you also use くれます.
・When giving something to a teacher or a boss, saying あげます outright can sound a bit condescending. You'll learn more polite forms later.
・You may also hear 花に水をやります (watering the flowers). やります is used for animals and plants. Saying it about people sounds rough, so as a beginner just stick with あげます.
What to learn next
At N4, these three verbs attach after the て-form to mean doing something for someone: 友達が駅まで送ってくれました。(A friend took me to the station.) The direction logic is exactly the same as here, so if you get it straight now, that step will be easy.
n5-38:
The idea in one line
「だけ」 and 「しか」 both mean "only." だけ is like a plain "only ~" that just states the range. しか〜ません is more like "just ~" or "nothing but ~," with a feeling of "that's so little, not enough." Its biggest feature: しか must always be followed by a negative.
How to build it
だけ: put it directly after a noun or a quantity.
水 → 水だけ一つ → 一つだけ
It also attaches to verbs, in the dictionary form (the form you'd look up in a dictionary): 見る → 見るだけ (just looking)
しか: put it after a noun or a quantity, and the verb at the end of the sentence must become negative.
水を飲みます → 水しか飲みません (I only drink water)
Drop the original 「を」 and 「が」: 水を becomes 水だけ or 水しか. (You can keep を after だけ, but most of the time people just drop it.)
Particles like 「に」「で」「へ」 stay, and go before しか:
・友達にしか言いませんでした。(I only told my friends.)
When to use it
だけ: just stating the rangeYou don't feel it's particularly much or little. You're simply saying "it's only this."
・サラダだけ注文します。(I'll order just a salad.)
・見ているだけです。(I'm just looking.)
The second sentence is very handy when shopping in Japan. When a shop assistant comes over to greet you, you can simply reply with it.
しか: feeling it's little, not enoughIn your mind it's "too little" or "less than I expected."
・10分しか残っていません。(There are only 10 minutes left.)
・昨日は3時間しか寝ませんでした。(I slept only three hours yesterday.)
Common mistakes
・しか is always followed by a negative: you say 千円しかありません, and you can't say 「千円しかあります」.
・The negative can fool you: when you see 「ません」, don't assume it means "not." 千円しかありません means "I only have 1,000 yen," not "I don't have 1,000 yen." 肉しか食べません means "I only eat meat," not "I don't eat meat." Think of it as "apart from 1,000 yen, I have nothing."
・Don't keep を or が before しか: you can't say 「水をしか」. Say 水しか.
・だけ doesn't mean "enough": だけ is just a neutral "only" and carries no sense of being sufficient.
Telling similar ones apart
For the same situation, だけ is a report, while しか is an exclamation of "so little."
・パーティーに一人だけ来ました。(Only one person came to the party: a plain report.)
・パーティーに一人しか来ませんでした。(Just one person came to the party: so few people.)
・日本語が少しだけ分かります。(I understand a little Japanese: a modest way of saying you know some.)
・日本語が少ししか分かりません。(I only understand a little Japanese: stressing that you don't know much, and asking the other person not to speak too difficultly.)
Quick check: when you want to say "just ~" or "only ~" and you feel it's little, use しか＋ません. If you're only stating the range, use だけ. Remember that しか always goes with ません.
n5-2:
The idea in one line
「〜ます」 is the polite form of Japanese. Use it with teachers, shop staff and people you've just met. With family and close friends you'd use the plain form without ます. To say "don't / doesn't (do)", swap ます for ません. While you're starting out, ます is the safest choice for everything, since it's never rude.
One form for both present and future
Japanese has no separate future tense. Habits and things you're about to do both use 「〜ます」, and time words like 「毎日」「明日」「来週」 tell the listener when.
・毎日コーヒーを飲みます。(I drink coffee every day: habit)
・来週、京都へ行きます。(I'm going to Kyoto next week: future)
・田村先生はお酒を飲みません。(Mr. Tamura doesn't drink alcohol)
How to form it: first, which group is the verb?
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the final sound to the 「い」-row sound of the same row, then add ます.
飲む → む becomes み → 飲みます
行く → 行きます買う → 買います帰る → 帰ります
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop the final 「る」 and add ます.
食べる → 食べます見る → 見ます起きる → 起きます
Group 3 (only two, just memorize them): する → します来る → 来ます（きます）
Words made of a noun plus する, like 「勉強する」「出張する」, work the same way: 勉強する → 勉強します
For the negative, just swap ます for ません. It's the same for all three groups: 食べます → 食べません
Easy mistakes
・帰る, 入る, 走る and 知る look like Group 2 but are actually Group 1. It's 帰ります, not 帰ます.
・「ません」 means "don't / doesn't (do)", not "can't". お酒を飲みません means "I don't drink alcohol", not "I'm unable to drink".
・ます attaches only to verbs. To say "I'm a student" you need 学生です, not 学生ます.
・The 「す」 in ます is usually barely pronounced, so it sounds like "mas". Don't doubt your ears when you hear it.
Don't confuse it with similar forms
English speakers often want to use ます for "I'm ~ing". But ます describes a habit or something you're about to do. For "in the middle of doing", use ています.
今、ご飯を食べます。(I'm going to eat now: I haven't started yet)
今、ご飯を食べています。(I'm eating right now: already underway)
Quick test: if it hasn't started yet, or you do it every day, use ます. If you're in the middle of it, use ています.
What to learn next
Talking about the past: 飲みます → 飲みました (drank), 飲みません → 飲みませんでした (didn't drink).
To invite someone, learn 〜ませんか and 〜ましょう next.
n5-3:
The idea in one line
Adjectives like 静か (quiet), きれい (pretty, clean) and 親切 are called な-adjectives in Japanese. To say "it's quiet" you use 静かです, and for "it's not quiet" you use 静かじゃありません. They work almost exactly like noun sentences, with just one extra rule: when the adjective comes directly before a noun, you add 「な」.
What are な-adjectives?
They're words that describe states and impressions, like "quiet", "pretty" or "famous". They're called 「な-adjectives」 because they gain a な before a noun. The 「語幹」 (stem) on the card is the basic form you see in the word list, such as 静か, with nothing added.
Start with these common ones:
静か (quiet), きれい (pretty, clean), 元気 (energetic, well), 有名 (famous), 便利 (convenient), 暇 (free, not busy), 大変 (tough), 好き (like), 嫌い (dislike), 上手 (good at)
How to use them
AffirmativeAdd です directly to the basic form.
静か → 静かです
・この喫茶店は静かです。(This café is quiet)
・駅の近くは便利です。(Near the station is convenient)
NegativeAdd じゃありません directly to the basic form. The word in front doesn't change at all.
暇 → 暇じゃありません
・今日は暇じゃありません。(I'm not free today)
・この町は有名じゃありません。(This town isn't very famous)
There are two other ways to make the negative, with the same meaning: ではありません is more formal and common in textbooks and writing. じゃないです is more conversational but still polite.
QuestionsJust add か at the end.
・仕事は大変ですか。(Is work tough?)
Before a noun: add な
To say "a quiet town" or "a kind person", put a な in between. Think of it as a small connector that links the adjective to the noun.
静か＋町 → 静かな町
・静かな町です。(It's a quiet town)
・京都はきれいな所です。(Kyoto is a beautiful place)
・親切な人ですね。(What a kind person, isn't he/she?)
An easy way to remember: before です, no な; before a noun, add な.
Easy mistakes
・きれい and 嫌い end in 「い」 and look like い-adjectives, but they're actually な-adjectives. The negative is きれいじゃありません, not 「きれくないです」.
・Don't put な before です: it's 静かです, not 「静かなです」.
・Don't leave out な before a noun, and don't use の as a link either: it's 静かな町, not 「静か町」 and not 「静かの町」.
・The object of 好き and 嫌い takes が: 猫が好きです (I like cats). In English "like cats" looks like a verb plus an object, so many learners write 「猫を好きです」. For now, just remember to use が.
・Saying 「嫌いです」 outright is a bit harsh. Japanese people often say あまり好きじゃありません (I don't like it very much), which sounds much softer.
Don't confuse it with similar forms
Even when you're talking about the same "this shop", the negative looks different for each type of word:
い-adjectives: the final い changes to くない.
・この店は安くないです。(This shop isn't cheap)
な-adjectives: the word itself stays the same, then add じゃありません.
・この店はきれいじゃありません。(This shop isn't clean)
Nouns: same as な-adjectives, add じゃありません.
・ここは銀行じゃありません。(This isn't a bank)
Quick test: when you memorize vocabulary, learn the な along with it, like きれいな and 静かな. If a word takes 「～な＋noun」, its negative is simply じゃありません. Only い-adjectives change い to くない.
What to learn next
For the past tense, swap です for でした: 昨日は暇でした。 (I was free yesterday)
n5-10:
The idea in one line
「〜なります」means "become ~" or "get ~". The weather goes from hot to cold, a room goes from messy to clean, a kid grows into an adult. Whenever something changes from one state to another, Japanese uses なります.
How to form it: check the word before it
い-adjectives: replace the final「い」with「く」, then add なります.
寒い → replace い with く → 寒くなります
大きい → 大きくなります安い → 安くなります
な-adjectives: add「に」, then なります.
きれい → きれいになります元気 → 元気になります好き → 好きになります
Nouns: just like な-adjectives, add「に」.
春 → 春になります医者 → 医者になります
・寒くなりましたね。(It's gotten cold, hasn't it?)
・部屋がきれいになりました。(The room has become clean.)
・日本が好きになりました。(I've come to like Japan.)
・来月、二十歳になります。(I turn twenty next month.)
Choosing between なります and なりました
When you'd say "it has gotten cold" in English, Japanese uses なりました: the change has already happened, and this is how things are now.
なります means "will become ~" or "is about to ~". It describes something that hasn't happened yet, or something that happens every time.
・もうすぐ夏になります。(It will be summer soon.)
・薬を飲んで、よくなりました。(I took medicine and got better.)
Common mistakes
・いい is an exception: say よくなります, not いくなります. Use よくなりました both for getting better after an illness and for the weather improving.
・きれい, きらい and 有名 end in an "i" sound, but they are な-adjectives: it's きれいになります, not きれくなります.
・Don't drop the「に」after nouns and な-adjectives: 先生になりました, not 先生なりました.
・Many learners just say 寒いです for "it's gotten cold." That only means "it's cold now" and has no sense of change. To stress that it became cold, say 寒くなりました.
・The thing that changes is marked with が (or は), not を: 部屋がきれいになりました.
Telling it apart from a look-alike
The next lesson's「〜くします・〜にします」differs by just one word, but the meaning is different. Take a room getting clean:
なります = says that something becomes a certain way. The focus is on the result: 部屋がきれいになりました。(The room became clean.)
します = says that someone makes something a certain way. The focus is on who did it: 部屋をきれいにしました。(I cleaned the room.)
One more pair: 音が大きくなりました。(The sound got louder.) / 音を小さくしてください。(Please turn the sound down.)
Quick test: if English says "become ~" or "get ~", use が + なります. If it says "make ~ …" or "turn ~ …", use を + します.
What to learn next
Verbs can't attach directly to なります. To say "I've become able to ~", use the N4 pattern「〜ようになります」: 日本語が話せるようになりました。(I've become able to speak Japanese.)
n5-11:
The idea in one line
「〜くします／〜にします」means "make ~ …" or "turn ~ …", as in "turn the sound down" or "tidy the room." The point is that someone does something to change it; it doesn't change by itself.
How to form it
い-adjectives: drop the final「い」, replace it with「く」, then add します.
短い → replace い with く → 短くします
小さい → 小さくします暖かい → 暖かくします
な-adjectives: just add「にします」.
きれい → きれいにします静か → 静かにします
Nouns: also just add「にします」.
子どもの部屋 → 子どもの部屋にします
The thing being changed takes を, as the object of the action:
・音を小さくしてください。(Please turn the sound down.)
・机の上をきれいにします。(I'll tidy up the desk.)
・この部屋を子どもの部屋にします。(We're going to make this room the kids' room.)
How you'll hear it most
Asking someone to change somethingAdd「てください」to ask the other person to make something a certain way.
・静かにしてください。(Please be quiet.)
・もう少し安くしてください。(Please make it a little cheaper.)
Ordering and choosingNoun + にします is also very common for "I'll go with ~" or "I've decided on ~". You'll hear it all the time when ordering at restaurants.
・私はコーヒーにします。(I'll have coffee.)
・旅行は京都にしました。(I decided on Kyoto for the trip.)
Common mistakes
・Always drop the「い」of い-adjectives first: it's 短くします, not「短いくします」or「短いにします」.
・きれい ends in い but is a な-adjective: it's きれいにします, not「きれくします」.
・いい becomes よく: この町をよくしたいです。(I want to make this town a better place.) Not「いくします」.
・The thing you change takes を, not が.
Telling it apart from a look-alike
くなります／になります = the thing changes by itself, with が:
部屋が暖かくなりました。(The room got warm; maybe the sun came out.)
くします／にします = someone does something to make it that way, with を:
部屋を暖かくしました。(I warmed up the room; for example, I turned on the heater.)
Quick test: if you can say "make ~ …" or "turn ~ …" in English, use を + します. If it's only "~ gets …" or "~ becomes …", use が + なります.
What to learn next
Noun + にします can mean "decide on ~". When what you decide is to do something, you'll later learn verb + ことにします: 日本へ行くことにしました。(I've decided to go to Japan.)
n5-4:
The idea in one line
Words that describe things, like "cold," "expensive," and "delicious," are called い-adjectives in Japanese, because they all end in 「い」. For example: 寒い, 高い, おいしい.
To say "it's cold" politely, just add です. To say "it's not cold," change the final い to く and add ないです.
How to form it
AffirmativeAdd です to the plain form. Leave the final い alone.
寒い → 寒いです高い → 高いです
NegativeChange the final い to く, then add ないです.
寒い → change い to く → 寒く → 寒くないです
高い → 高くないですおいしい → おいしくないです大きい → 大きくないです
In textbooks you'll also see 寒くありません. It means the same thing but sounds a little more formal. For everyday speech, 「くないです」 is plenty.
Try saying it
・このラーメンはおいしいです。(This ramen is delicious.)
・この部屋は広くないです。(This room isn't big.)
・今日はあまり寒くないです。(It's not very cold today.)
In English you just say "it's cold," with no "very" needed. 寒いです already means exactly that, so there's no need to force in とても. Only say とても寒いです when it's really cold and you want to stress it.
Also, あまり followed by a negative means "not very ~." It's softer than a flat "not ~," and Japanese people use it all the time.
Common mistakes
・いい is an exception: its negative is よくないです, not いくないです. That's because いい comes from よい, so it uses よ when it changes form. かっこいい works the same way, and its negative is かっこよくないです.
・To say "it's not cold," you can't say 寒いじゃないです. The negative of an い-adjective is always formed by changing い to く, never with じゃない.
・Don't add an extra だ in the middle: 寒いだです is wrong. To be polite, say 寒いです. With friends, just say 寒い.
・きれい, 嫌い, and 有名 also sound like they end in 「い」, but they're な-adjectives. Their negative is きれいじゃないです, not きれくないです.
Telling look-alikes apart
Even for the same "this room isn't ~," the negative is formed differently depending on the type of word before it:
い-adjective: change い to く and add ないです
・この部屋は明るくないです。(This room isn't bright.)
な-adjective: add じゃないです
・この部屋は静かじゃないです。(This room isn't quiet.)
Noun: also add じゃないです
・ここは私の部屋じゃないです。(This isn't my room.)
Quick tip: if the word originally ends in 「い」, change い to く and add ないです. な-adjectives and nouns just take じゃないです. Be extra careful with きれい, 嫌い, and 有名, because they're な-adjectives.
What to learn next
Past tense: 寒いです → 寒かったです (it was cold)
Expressing change: 寒くなります (it will get cold). The 「く」 you used in the negative shows up again here.
n5-5:
The idea in one line
「〜です」 means "is ~," and 「〜でした」 means "was ~." Just like English changes "is" to "was," when you talk about the past, you swap です for でした. Adding a word like "yesterday" isn't enough on its own.
How to form it
WasAdd でした directly after a noun.
学生です → 学生でした休みです → 休みでした
Wasn'tStart with the present-tense 「じゃありません」, then add でした.
学生じゃありません → 学生じゃありませんでした
In writing, the more formal form is ではありませんでした. It means the same thing.
・昨日は雨でした。(Yesterday was rainy.)
・先週の月曜日は祝日でした。(Last Monday was a national holiday.)
・昨日は休みじゃありませんでした。(Yesterday wasn't a day off.)
How you'll hear it most
Asking about the pastAdd か at the end to make it a question.
・昨日は休みでしたか。(Did you have yesterday off?)
・はい、休みでした。(Yes, I did.)
・いいえ、休みじゃありませんでした。(No, I didn't.)
Casual versionWith close friends, replace でした with だった and じゃありませんでした with じゃなかった.
雨でした → 雨だった休みじゃありませんでした → 休みじゃなかった
Common mistakes
・It's tempting to think that having 「昨日」 in the sentence is enough, and to say 昨日は休みです. In Japanese you need to change it to 休みでした, just as English needs "was," not "is."
・The past of "is not" is the easiest one to get wrong: 学生じゃないでした and 学生じゃでした are both wrong. Say 学生じゃありませんでした.
・In everyday speech you'll also often hear 学生じゃなかったです. It's just as polite and also correct, so don't be thrown when you hear it.
・でした can only follow nouns (and な-adjectives). い-adjectives like 寒い and 高い can't take でした directly: 寒いでした is wrong. Say 寒かったです.
Telling look-alikes apart
When you talk about "yesterday," the ending changes depending on the word before it:
Noun + でした: 昨日は雨でした。(Yesterday was rainy.)
Verb: change ます to ました: 昨日は雨が降りました。(It rained yesterday.)
い-adjective: change い to かったです: 昨日は寒かったです。(It was cold yesterday.)
な-adjective: add でした, just like a noun: 昨日は静かでした。(It was quiet yesterday.)
Quick tip: after a noun or な-adjective, use でした. After a verb, use ました. After an い-adjective (like 寒い or 高い), use かったです.
Note: きれい, 有名, and 嫌い end in い but are な-adjectives, so they take でした, as in きれいでした, not きれかったです.
What to learn next
The past of verbs, 〜ました・〜ませんでした, and the past of い-adjectives, 〜かったです. Learn all three together and you won't get stuck when talking about the past.
n5-6:
The idea in one line
「〜ました」is the past form of「〜ます」, and「〜ませんでした」is the past form of「〜ません」. English changes the verb itself (go → went); Japanese changes the ending: 行きます (go) → 行きました (went). Like ます, it's polite speech, so it's safe to use with teachers and shop staff.
How to form it: start from the ます form
Here are all four forms of "drink" side by side:
Present, does it: 飲みます (drink)
Present, doesn't: 飲みません (don't drink)
Past, did it: 飲みました (drank)
Past, didn't: 飲みませんでした (didn't drink)

There are only two rules: change ます to ました; add でした after ません.
Since you always start from the ます form, the rule is exactly the same for all three verb groups:
Group 1 (godan verbs): 行きます → 行きました
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): 食べます → 食べました
Group 3 (する・来る): します → しました来ます → 来ました (きました)
When to use it
Did itTalk about something that already happened.
・先月、札幌へ行きました。 (I went to Sapporo last month.)
・昨日、映画を見ました。 (I watched a movie yesterday.)
Didn't do itTalk about something you didn't do during a past period.
・今朝は朝ご飯を食べませんでした。 (I didn't eat breakfast this morning.)
・宿題をしませんでした。 (I didn't do my homework.)
Asking someoneAdd か to make it a question.
・週末、何をしましたか。 (What did you do on the weekend?)
Easy mistakes
・The past negative is「ません＋でした」. Many learners say「食べませんました」, which is wrong.
・来ました is read きました, not こました.
・The「し」in「ました」is often very light, so it sounds like "ma-shta". Don't think you missed a sound when you hear it.
・Don't use ませんでした for "not yet". If a friend asks もう食べましたか。 (Have you eaten yet?) and you haven't eaten but will soon, answer いいえ、まだです。 (No, not yet.) 食べませんでした means "I didn't eat then", and the moment has already passed.
・分かりました means "I understand / Got it". It describes your state right now, not something in the past. When a shop clerk or coworker says this to you, it means "understood".
Telling it apart from look-alikes
When you learn the past tense, it's easy to mix up「ました」and「でした」. Using "yesterday's party" as the example, here they are all at once:
・昨日、パーティーに行きました。 (I went to a party yesterday: verbs take ました)
・料理は和食でした。 (The food was Japanese cuisine: nouns take でした)
・会場はきれいでした。 (The venue was beautiful: な-adjectives take でした)
・とても楽しかったです。 (It was a lot of fun: い-adjectives take かったです)
Common mistakes:
「学生ました」→ say 学生でした
「行きでした」→ say 行きました
「おいしいでした」→ say おいしかったです
Quick rule: after a verb, use ました; after a noun or a な-adjective, use でした; after an い-adjective, use かったです.
What to learn next
When talking with friends, the past tense switches to a form without ます, called the た-form / なかった-form: 行きました → 行った行きませんでした → 行かなかった.
n5-7:
The idea in one line
静かです means "it's quiet right now". To say it used to be quiet, swap です for でした: 静かでした. It's like English changing "is" to "was": Japanese changes the ending into its past form. This pattern is exactly the same as for nouns (学生でした), so learning one means learning both.
How to attach it
な-adjectives are the ones that need「な」before a noun, like 静かな部屋 and きれいな花.
Step 1: Drop「な」. What's left is called the "stem" (the core of the word).
静かな → drop な → 静か
Step 2: Attach the ending you need.
Present: 静かです (it's quiet) / 静かじゃありません (it's not quiet)
Past: 静かでした (it was quiet) / 静かじゃありませんでした (it wasn't quiet)
Past affirmativeIt was like that back then.
・昨日は暇でした。 (I was free yesterday.)
・テストは簡単でした。 (The test was easy.)
・子どものとき、野菜が嫌いでした。 (I hated vegetables when I was a kid.)
Past negativeIt wasn't like that back then. Often used with あまり (not very).
・部屋はあまりきれいじゃありませんでした。 (The room wasn't very clean.)
・あまり有名じゃありませんでした。 (It wasn't very famous back then.)
Other forms you'll hear
More formalChange じゃ to では: 静かではありませんでした, used in writing and formal situations.
Polite, spoken静かじゃなかったです means the same thing and is very common in everyday conversation.
Between friendsChange でした to だった, and use じゃなかった for the negative.
・昨日、暇だった。 (I was free yesterday.)
・全然大変じゃなかった。 (It wasn't hard at all.)
Easy mistakes
・Drop「な」: say 静かでした, not「静かなでした」.
・きれい, 嫌い and 有名 end in「い」, but they are な-adjectives: it's きれいでした, not「きれいかったです」.
・Don't build the past negative yourself as「静かじゃないでした」. The correct forms are 静かじゃありませんでした or 静かじゃなかったです.
・あまり must be followed by a negative: あまり暇じゃありませんでした. You can't say「あまり暇でした」.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
The past of い-adjectives works completely differently: change い to かった and add です. Take the hotel you stayed at yesterday:
ホテルは静かでした。 (The hotel was quiet: な-adjective)
ホテルは高かったです。 (The hotel was expensive: い-adjective)
Likewise, you can't put でした after an い-adjective: you can't say「高いでした」.
になりました means "has become ~". It talks about a change, not just a past state:
町は静かでした。 (The town was quiet back then.)
町は静かになりました。 (The town has become quiet: it wasn't before.)
Quick rule: first check whether it's a な-adjective; if so, "drop な + でした". When you mean "has become ~", use になりました.
What to learn next
Next, look at the い-adjective past 〜かったです. Practice the two together and you won't mix them up anymore.
n5-8:
The idea in one sentence
This is the pattern you use for "how something was": 「It was cold yesterday」「The ramen was delicious」. In English you just change "is" to "was". In Japanese, an い-adjective (an adjective ending in 「い」, like 暑い or おいしい) has to change its own form: 暑いです → 暑かったです.
How to conjugate
Past · affirmativeDrop the final 「い」 and add 「かったです」.
暑い → drop い → 暑かったです
おいしい → おいしかったです楽しい → 楽しかったです
・昨日は寒かったです。(It was cold yesterday.)
・このラーメンはおいしかったです。(This ramen was delicious.)
Past · negativeChange 「い」 to 「く」 and add 「なかったです」.
難しい → change い to く → 難しくなかったです
・テストは難しくなかったです。(The test wasn't difficult.)
The alternative 難しくありませんでした means the same thing and sounds a little more formal. Both are correct.
The special oneいい (good) has to go back to よい before it conjugates. Just memorize these:
いい → よかったです (it was good), いい → よくなかったです (it wasn't good)
・天気はよくなかったです。(The weather wasn't very good.)
How you'll hear it most
A friend comes back from a trip and you ask how it was. It goes like this:
・旅行はどうでしたか。(How was the trip?)
・とても楽しかったです。(It was a lot of fun.)
The question uses でした, but the answer is 楽しかったです. Don't let the question pull you into saying 「楽しいでした」.
Common mistakes
・You can't say 暑いでした. The past of an い-adjective relies on 「かった」, not on adding でした.
・Don't say 暑かったでした either. 「かった」 is already past. The です after it only makes the sentence polite, so it doesn't need to become でした.
・There's a small っ in the middle of 「かった」, so pause for one beat: あつかった. Saying 「あつかた」 sounds odd.
・いい can't become 「いかったです」 or 「いくなかったです」. Always conjugate from よ.
・きれい and 有名 end in the sound 「い」, but they're な-adjectives. You can't say 「きれかったです」. Say きれいでした.
Don't mix it up with look-alikes
Talking about "last week's trip" in three ways:
い-adjective: ホテルは高かったです。 (The hotel was expensive.)
な-adjective: ホテルはきれいでした。 (The hotel was beautiful.)
Noun: 天気は雨でした。 (The weather was rainy.)
An い-adjective changes itself into 「かった」. な-adjectives and nouns just swap です for でした.
Quick test: look up the word in a dictionary. If it's an い-adjective ending in 「い」, use 「〜かったです」. If it isn't (like きれい, 元気, 雨), use 「〜でした」.
What to learn next
Drop です and you get the casual way friends talk: 昨日、寒かった。 (It was so cold yesterday.) You can also go on to 「〜くなります」, which means "become ~": 寒くなりました。 (It's gotten cold.)
n5-9:
The idea in one sentence
「〜ませんか」 is the Japanese way of saying "Would you like to ~ with me?" or "Want to ~?". Literally it looks like "Won't you ~?", and that's the idea: Japanese people use it to politely ask "Would you be willing to ~?" The choice is left to the other person, which makes it easy for them to decline, so it sounds courteous.
When to use it
InvitationsAsking someone to go somewhere or do something with you.
・今度の日曜日、山登りに行きませんか。(Would you like to go hiking this Sunday?)
・一緒に昼ご飯を食べませんか。(Would you like to have lunch together?)
Offering food or drink, making suggestionsIt's also very common for offering someone something to eat or drink, or for suggesting they do something.
・このケーキ、食べませんか。(Would you like some of this cake?)
・少し休みませんか。(How about taking a short break?)
How to form it
Put the verb in ます form, then swap 「ます」 for 「ませんか」. That's it.
行きます → 行きませんか食べます → 食べませんか
します → しませんか来ます → 来ませんか（きませんか）
It's really just 「ません」 (the negative) plus the question marker 「か」, a bit like English "Won't you join me?"
How you'll hear it most
〜でも〜ませんかAdding 「でも」 after a noun means "something like ~", which makes the invitation more casual and puts less pressure on the other person.
・コーヒーでも飲みませんか。(How about a coffee or something?)
How to answerAccepting: いいですね。 (Sounds good.), ぜひ。 (Definitely!)
Declining: すみません、その日はちょっと…。 (Sorry, that day is a bit...)
Common mistakes
・Don't trust your English instinct here. In an invitation, 行きませんか means "Would you like to go?", not "Aren't you going?"
・When declining, saying いいえ、行きません。 (No, I won't go.) sounds blunt and can hurt. Japanese people usually say 「ちょっと…」 and leave the sentence unfinished. The other person understands.
・To offer "Shall I do ~ for you?" you can't use ませんか. 持ちませんか asks the other person to carry something. For "Shall I carry it for you?" say 持ちましょうか.
・With close friends you don't need to be this polite. Use the plain form with rising intonation: 行かない？ (Wanna go?)
Don't mix it up with look-alikes
Same situation, an invitation to the movies:
ませんか = nothing is decided yet, so you ask what the other person wants: 一緒に映画を見ませんか。 (Would you like to watch a movie together?)
ましょう = it's already agreed, or you both want to do it, and you give it a push: いいですね。見ましょう。 (Sounds good. Let's watch it.)
ましょうか = you offer to help with "Shall I ~?": チケット、買いましょうか。 (Shall I buy the tickets?)
So the most common order is: invite with 「ませんか」 first, and once the other person says yes, decide together with 「ましょう」. Opening with 「ましょう」 feels a bit like deciding for them without asking.
Quick test: still asking "would you like to?" → ませんか. Already agreed on "let's do it" → ましょう. Offering "let me help you" → ましょうか.
n5-12:
The idea in one line
「〜ましょう」 means "Let's ～." When you say "Let's go" or "Let's take a break" to a classmate, the Japanese is 行きましょう and 休みましょう. It's polite, so you can use it with teachers, coworkers, and people you've just met.
How to form it
First put the verb in 「〜ます」 form, then just swap ます for ましょう. You don't need to worry about which verb group it belongs to.
行きます → 行きましょう食べます → 食べましょう
します → しましょう来ます → 来ましょう
When to use it
Inviting someone to join youUse it when everyone does something together. It often pairs with 一緒に (together).
・一緒に帰りましょう。(Let's go home together.)
・ちょっと休みましょう。(Let's take a short break.)
Kicking things offTeachers and meeting leaders say this a lot.
・じゃあ、始めましょう。(Okay, let's begin.)
Adding か: ましょうか
"Shall I help you?"You offer to do something for the other person. It's a very considerate way to say it.
・荷物を持ちましょうか。(Shall I carry your bags?)
Working it out togetherYou've already decided to do something together and now you're asking about the details. A question word like 「何」「どこ」「何時」 often comes first.
・何時に会いましょうか。(What time shall we meet?)
Common mistakes
・ます gets replaced, not followed by something extra. It's 行きましょう, not 「行きますましょう」.
・Say 「ましょう」 with a long vowel, ましょー. Don't clip it to a short 「ましょ」.
・The meaning includes you. It doesn't tell the other person to go do it alone. To say "please go ～", use 「〜てください」. Public signs like ゴミは持ち帰りましょう (Please take your trash home) are a softer, special use. Don't use it that way in your own speech for now.
・When you're inviting someone for the first time and don't know if they want to come, saying 「行きましょう」 outright sounds as if you've already decided for them. It's more polite to ask with 「〜ませんか」 first.
Telling similar forms apart
Take the same "invite someone to a movie" situation. These three often show up one after another:
ませんか = first asking whether the other person wants to: 映画を見ませんか。 (Would you like to watch a movie?)
ましょう = they said yes, and you move forward together: ええ、見ましょう。 (Sure, let's watch one.)
ましょうか = asking for their opinion: 何を見ましょうか。 (What shall we watch?)
Quick rule of thumb: if the other person hasn't agreed yet, use 「ませんか」. If it's settled and you're doing it together, use 「ましょう」. If you want their opinion or you're offering to help, use 「ましょうか」.
What to learn next
With close friends you don't need to be this formal. You can switch to a more casual form: 行きましょう → 行こう. You'll learn this at N4 as the volitional form.
n5-13:
The idea in one line
Japanese has two ways to say the same thing. Polite style is the polite version with 「です・ます」, and plain style is the friend version with です・ます removed. The meaning is exactly the same; only the tone differs. It's like texting your boss “Certainly, I'll be there tomorrow” but just replying “Yep, be there tomorrow” to a friend.
When to use it
Polite styleUse it with teachers, bosses, shop staff, customers, people you're meeting for the first time, and older people you don't know well. When you're unsure which to use, polite style is never rude.
Plain styleUse it with family, close friends, classmates, and people younger than you. It's also used for diaries, talking to yourself, and your own notes, since there's no one you need to be polite to.
One sentence, two ways to say it
Say you want to ask, “Are you going tomorrow?”
・明日、行きますか。(Will you be going tomorrow? — to a teacher)
・はい、行きます。(Yes, I'll go.)
・明日、行く？(Going tomorrow? — to a friend)
・うん、行く。(Yeah, I'm going.)
Notice the friend-version question: the final か disappears and your voice rises at the end instead. The answer 「はい」 also becomes 「うん」.
How to convert: polite to plain
Nouns and な-adjectives: replace です with だ.
学生です → 学生だ静かです → 静かだ
Negative and past forms change too:
学生じゃありません → 学生じゃない学生でした → 学生だった
い-adjectives: just drop です, and don't add だ.
高いです → 高い高くないです → 高くない高かったです → 高かった
Verbs: change the ます form back to the dictionary form, the form you'd find in a dictionary.
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the sound before ます to the う-row sound in the same row.
行きます → change き to く → 行く飲みます → 飲む
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop ます and add る.
食べます → 食べる見ます → 見る
Group 3 (する・来る): just memorize them.
します → する来ます → 来る（くる）
Other common ones: 行きません → 行かない行きました → 行った読んでいます → 読んでいる
The details of how negative and past forms change will be taught step by step in the lessons on the dictionary form / ない form and the た form.
Common mistakes
・Don't add だ to い-adjectives. Just say 高い; 「高いだ」 is wrong.
・In casual chat, a bare 「雨だ。」 sounds blunt, like talking to yourself or announcing something. People usually add よ or ね: 明日、雨だよ。 (It's going to rain tomorrow, you know.)
・In plain-style questions with nouns and な-adjectives, drop だ: 学生？ (Are you a student?), not 「学生だ？」.
・Plain style isn't "rude"; it means "close." Using it with a teacher is impolite. Conversely, if you keep using です・ます with a good friend, they'll find you distant, as if you were upset with them.
・When talking to one person, beginners should stick to one style. Don't mix ます in one sentence and plain style in the next, because it sounds confusing.
・In speech, 読んでいる is often shortened to 読んでる. When you hear it, know that it means the same thing.
What to learn next
Plain style isn't only for chatting. Many grammar patterns must follow plain style, even when the whole sentence is polite: 明日は雨だと思います。 (I think it will rain tomorrow.)
Next, you can look at the plain-form summary, which lays out the present, past, affirmative, and negative of each word type in one place.
n5-17:
The idea in one line
「の」 works like English "'s" or "of". It links two nouns, and the first one describes the second: 私の本 = my book. The order is like "'s": first you say whose it is or where it's from, then the thing itself.
How to attach it
Noun A + の + Noun B = "B of A" or "A's B". B is the main noun, and A adds detail about which B you mean.
弟＋車 → 弟の車 (my younger brother's car)
数学＋教科書 → 数学の教科書 (math textbook)
When to use it
WhoseSays who something belongs to.
・これは私の本です。 (This is my book.)
Belonging toSays which company or school a person belongs to. It's very common in self-introductions and on the phone.
・さくら銀行の山田です。 (This is Yamada from Sakura Bank.)
What it's aboutSays what a thing is about or what kind of thing it is.
・数学の教科書を忘れました。 (I forgot my math textbook.)
Where fromSays where a thing or person comes from or is located.
・台湾のお茶はおいしいです。 (Taiwanese tea is delicious.)
The second noun can be dropped
When everyone already knows what you're talking about, you can leave out B and just say 「A の」. 私の simply means "mine".
・「これは誰の傘ですか。」「私のです。」 ("Whose umbrella is this?" "It's mine.")
Common mistakes
・English often has no "'s" or "of" where Japanese needs の. In English you say "my mother", "my friend" and "Japanese teacher" with nothing linking the words. In Japanese you must say 私の母, 私の友達 and 日本語の先生. Saying 「私母」 or 「日本語先生」 is wrong.
・Chains of の are fine. "My friend's car" has only one "'s" in English, but Japanese needs two の: 私の友達の車.
・"This book" is この本, not 「これの本」. この already means "this", so attach the noun directly. Don't add another の.
Don't confuse it with look-alikes
In English, an adjective just goes in front of the noun: "a Japanese car", "a new car", "a pretty car". Japanese changes depending on the type of word in front:
Nouns (people, things, places) take の: 日本の車 (a Japanese car, a car from Japan)
い-adjectives (like 新しい and おいしい) attach directly, with no の: 新しい車 (a new car), not 「新しいの車」
な-adjectives (like きれい and 静か) take な: きれいな車 (a pretty car), not 「きれいの車」
Quick test: use の when what comes before it is a noun (who, what thing, where). Don't use の when it's an adjective describing "what it's like".
What to learn next
「の」 has another job. After a verb, it turns an action into "the thing of doing it", as in 本を読むのが好きです。 (I like reading books.) You'll meet this in the lesson on the nominalizing 「の」. It's a different use from the "'s" meaning here.
n5-18:
The idea in one line
「か」 is Japanese's question marker. Add か to the end of a sentence and a statement becomes a question: 学生です → 学生ですか, "I'm a student" becomes "Are you a student?"
How to attach it
The polite form is easy. When the sentence ends in です or ます, just add か. Nothing else changes.
日本人です → 日本人ですか
高いです → 高いですか
静かです → 静かですか
行きます → 行きますか
食べました → 食べましたか
When to use it
Yes/no questionsQuestions the other person can answer with 「はい」 or 「いいえ」.
・これは日本の本ですか。 (Is this a Japanese book?)
・このラーメン、おいしいですか。 (Is this ramen good?)
・明日、学校へ行きますか。 (Are you going to school tomorrow?)
To answer a noun question, you often say はい、そうです。 (Yes, that's right.) or いいえ、違います。 (No, it isn't.) For verbs and adjectives, repeat the original word: はい、行きます。 (Yes, I'll go.) / いいえ、行きません。 (No, I won't go.)
With question wordsWhen the sentence has a word like "what", "where" or "when", you still add か.
・すみません、駅はどこですか。 (Excuse me, where is the station?)
・昨日、何を食べましたか。 (What did you eat yesterday?)
Common mistakes
・Add か even with a question word. In English, "What is that?" needs nothing extra beyond the question word and word order, so many learners forget か. In polite Japanese you still need it: say 何ですか, not 「何です」.
・Raise your intonation. The か in 「ですか」 goes up. Take そうですか: said with a rising tone it means "Is that so?" With a falling tone it becomes "Oh, I see," showing you understood. The meaning is different.
・With friends, you usually drop か. Use the plain form without です or ます and raise your tone at the end to make it a question: 明日、行く？ (Going tomorrow?), これ、おいしい？ (Is this good?) Adding か directly to the plain form (like 「行くか」) sounds blunt and rough, so beginners should avoid it.
・With friends, a noun question is 学生？. Don't say 「学生だか」, which isn't a question.
・Punctuation: Textbooks and formal writing usually put 「。」 after か, since か already marks the question. In LINE messages and manga you'll often see 「？」. You'll see both.
Don't confuse it with look-alikes
ますか = simply asks whether the other person will or wants to do something:
・明日、パーティーに行きますか。 (Are you going to the party tomorrow?)
ませんか = invites the other person to do something with you:
・明日、一緒にパーティーに行きませんか。 (Would you like to go to the party together tomorrow?)
The two sentences differ by only a little, but the first asks about the other person's plans, while the second invites them along.
Quick test: if you just want to know whether they'll do it, use 「ますか」. If you want to ask them to do it with you, use 「ませんか」.
What to learn next
Learn question words like 「何、どこ、いつ、だれ」 and you can ask all kinds of questions. Then learn 「〜ませんか」 and you can start inviting people.
n5-21:
The idea in one line
Put 「で」 after a vehicle and it means "by ~", or "take / ride / drive ~". English changes the verb depending on the vehicle (take the train, ride a bike, drive a car). Japanese doesn't care what you travel in. It's always "vehicle + で", followed by 行きます, 来ます or 帰ります.
How to build it
Vehicle + で + 行きます／来ます／帰ります. Put the noun right in front, with no changes to its form.
・電車で会社に行きます。(I go to the office by train.)
・自転車で学校へ行きます。(I go to school by bike.)
・バスで帰ります。(I go home by bus.)
・飛行機で来ました。(I came by plane.)
Notice that English uses "take," "ride" and "drive", but Japanese uses the same 「で」 for all of them. 車で行きます works the same way. You might be driving yourself or riding in someone else's car, and Japanese doesn't distinguish.
Asking "How did you get here?"
Just replace the vehicle with 「何」:
・何で来ましたか。(How did you come here?)
・タクシーで来ました。(I came by taxi.)
Here 「何で」 is read なにで. If you say なんで, it's easily heard as "Why did you come?"
Common mistakes
・No で for walking. Don't say 「足で行きます」. Say 歩いて行きます (I walk there). Just memorize this as a whole phrase for now.
・The action of getting on a bus takes 「に」: バスに乗ります (I get on the bus). Many learners say 「バスで乗ります」, which is wrong.
・The order can change: 電車で東京へ行きます and 東京へ電車で行きます are both correct. Just keep 「で」 right after the vehicle.
Don't mix up the look-alikes
で (vehicle) = what you "travel" by: バスで駅へ行きます。 (I go to the station by bus.)
に + 乗ります = which vehicle you "get on": 駅でバスに乗ります。 (I get on the bus at the station.)
で (place of action) = where you do something: the 駅で in the sentence above means "at the station". What comes before it is a place, not a vehicle.
Quick test: if what follows is "go, come, return", then で after a vehicle is right. If what follows is 「乗ります」, use に. If what comes before is a place rather than a vehicle, that で means "at ~".
What to learn next
This 「で」 really means "using ~", and it isn't limited to vehicles. Eating with chopsticks or speaking in Japanese use it too: はしで食べます。 (I eat with chopsticks.) That's the next card, "Particle で (means / tools)".
n5-22:
The idea in one line
「と」 means "with ~". To say "I watch a movie with a friend", add と after 「友達」: 友達と映画を見ます. What comes before と is the person doing this with you.
How to build it
It's simple: person + と + what you do. To stress "together", you can add 一緒に (together) after と. The meaning is the same, but the "together" feeling is stronger.
友達と → 友達と一緒に
・友達と映画を見ました。(I watched a movie with a friend.)
・母と一緒に料理を作ります。(I cook together with my mom.)
・毎朝、犬と散歩します。(I take a walk with my dog every morning.)
To ask "with whom", use 誰と. You can answer simply with "person + とです".
・誰と行きますか。(Who are you going with?)
・友達とです。(With a friend.)
If you want to say "I" too, mark the main person with は and the companion with と: 私は友達と京都へ行きます。 (I'm going to Kyoto with a friend.)
Common mistakes
・When you do something alone, say 一人で, not 一人と. Numbers of people and whole groups also take で: 二人で, 家族で, みんなで.
・一緒に is an optional extra. と alone already means "together with someone". Conversely, when you say only 一緒に without naming who, it's because everyone already knows who: 一緒に帰りましょう。 (Let's go home together.)
・Things that need two people, like 結婚する, also use と, and usually without 一緒に: 田中さんと結婚しました。 (I married Mr. Tanaka.)
Don't mix up the look-alikes
と has another use: connecting two things, like "A and B" (a list). Compare these two sentences:
母とケーキを食べました。 (I ate cake with my mom.) → Mom is the person eating with you
パンとケーキを食べました。 (I ate bread and cake.) → Bread and cake are both things that were eaten
Quick test: if what comes before と is a person who does the action with you, it's "with someone", which is what you're learning here. If と sits between two things side by side, it's "A and B".
What to learn next
Combine it with 「〜ませんか」 to invite someone: 週末、私と映画を見ませんか。 (Would you like to see a movie with me this weekend?)
n5-14:
The idea in one line
There are two polite ways to say "don't/doesn't ~": 食べません and 食べないです. Both mean "don't eat." The difference is a bit like wearing a suit versus a shirt: ません is more formal and ないです is more relaxed. Both are polite, so you can safely use either with a teacher or a shop clerk.
How to form it: first check the verb group
The ません version is easy. Just replace ます with ません: 飲みます → 飲みません
The ないです version takes the ない form (the casual "don't ~" form of a verb) and adds です after it:
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the あ-row sound of the same column, add ない, then add です.
飲む → change む to ま → 飲まないです
行く → 行かないです帰る → 帰らないです
If the last sound is 「う」, change it to 「わ」: 買う → 買わないです
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop 「る」 and add ないです.
食べる → 食べないです見る → 見ないです
Group 3 (only two verbs, just memorize them): する → しないです来る → 来ないです（こないです）
Adjectives and nouns also have two versions
い-adjectives: change the final 「い」 to 「く」, then add ないです or ありません.
寒い → 寒くないです＝寒くありません
な-adjectives and nouns: add じゃないです or じゃありません directly.
静か → 静かじゃないです＝静かじゃありません
学生 → 学生じゃないです＝学生じゃありません
To make it even more formal, change じゃ to では: 学生ではありません.
The past negative ("didn't ~") also has two versions: 食べませんでした＝食べなかったです, 寒くありませんでした＝寒くなかったです.
When to use which
Formal situationsFor emails, work, interviews, and talking to your elders, ません is the safer choice.
・明日は会社に行きません。 (I'm not going to the office tomorrow.)
・私は学生ではありません。 (I'm not a student.)
Everyday conversationWhen chatting with shop clerks, neighbors, or classmates you don't know well, you'll hear ないです a lot. With adjectives, くないです and じゃないです are often even more common than ありません in everyday speech.
・肉はあまり食べないです。 (I don't eat meat much.)
・この店、高くないですよ。 (This shop isn't expensive, you know.)
・今日はそんなに寒くないですね。 (It's not that cold today, is it?)
Common mistakes
・Don't mix the two: there is no 食べないません and no 食べませんです.
・The negative of ある is special. It becomes ない directly, and there is no あらない: 時間がありません＝時間がないです (I have no time).
・いい becomes よくないです, not いくないです.
・買う becomes 買わない, not 買あない.
・来ない is read こない, not きない.
・The two forms aren't interchangeable everywhere: すみません is a fixed apology and never becomes すまないです. Likewise, when inviting someone, 一緒に行きませんか (Shall we go together?) is the most natural and polite with ません.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
After learning ないです, many learners start dropping です in the middle of a conversation. Here are three ways to say "I'm not going today":
To a teacher: 今日は行きません。／今日は行かないです。 (both are fine)
To a friend: 今日は行かない。 (the casual version, too blunt for a teacher)
Quick test: if the sentence ends with ます (ません) or です, it's polite. If it has neither, it's casual.
What to learn next
To find out when you can drop です and just say 行かない, check out the lessons "丁寧体與普通体" and "辞書形・ない形".
n5-16:
The idea in one line
「も」 means "also" or "too". The position works differently from English, though. English can say "I also drink" (before the verb), but Japanese 「も」 attaches directly after the thing that is "also" (私も = me too).
How to attach it
は・が・をThese three are removed and replaced by も.
私は → 私も猫が → 猫もコーヒーを → コーヒーも
に・で・へ・とThese are kept, and も is added after them.
大阪に → 大阪にも家で → 家でも
・大阪にも行きました。 (I went to Osaka too.)
When to use it
AlsoYou've already mentioned one thing, and now you add another that's the same.
・A：私は学生です。B：私も学生です。 (A: I'm a student. B: I'm a student too.)
・A：コーヒーが好きです。B：私も。 (A: I like coffee. B: Me too.)
AもBもBoth are the same: "both A and B ~". With a negative ending, it means "neither A nor B".
・パンもケーキも好きです。 (I like both bread and cake.)
・肉も魚も食べません。 (I eat neither meat nor fish.)
Question word + も + negative"Nothing," "no one," "nowhere". A negative must always follow.
・今朝は何も食べませんでした。 (I didn't eat anything this morning.)
・教室には誰もいません。 (There's no one in the classroom.)
・週末はどこにも行きませんでした。 (I didn't go anywhere this weekend.)
Common mistakes
・There is no はも, がも, or をも. は, が, and を are simply replaced by も.
・Whatever も attaches to is the thing that is "also," so the meaning can change a lot:
私もコーヒーを飲みます。 (Other people drink coffee, and I drink it too.)
私はコーヒーも飲みます。 (I drink tea, and I drink coffee too.)
English can say "I drink coffee too" for both, but in Japanese you need to decide first whether the "also" is the person or the coffee.
・何も and 誰も are followed by a negative. To say "I like everything," you can't say 何も好きです. You need a different expression (like 何でも好きです, which you'll learn later).
・To say "didn't go anywhere," use どこにも. Don't leave out に.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
AとB = simply listing two things: パンとケーキが好きです。 (I like bread and cake.)
AもBも = stressing "both": パンもケーキも好きです。 (Bread, cake, I like both.)
The way you attach them is different too: と goes only once, in the middle, but も goes after every item.
Quick test: use と to simply list things, and use 〜も〜も when you want to stress "both ~".
n5-19:
The idea in one line
「に」 goes after a time word and works like English at 7 or in March. It pins an event to a specific point in time. Whenever the time has a number, Japanese requires に: 7時に起きます。 (I get up at 7.)
How to attach it
Just add に right after the time word.
7時 → 7時に3月 → 3月に2025年 → 2025年に
When to add it and when not to
This is the part of the grammar you really need to remember. Time words fall into three groups:
Always add itTimes with a number: hour, minute, month, year, date.
・朝6時に散歩します。 (I go for a walk at 6 in the morning.)
・3月に日本へ行きます。 (I'm going to Japan in March.)
Clearly specific days without a number also take it, such as 誕生日, クリスマス and 夏休み.
・誕生日にケーキを食べます。 (I eat cake on my birthday.)
OptionalDays of the week. Adding it is a bit clearer, so as a beginner, adding it is the safest choice.
・金曜日に歓迎会があります。 (There's a welcome party on Friday.)
・日曜日に休みます。 (I rest on Sunday.)
Never add it① Times measured from "now": 今日, 明日, 昨日, 今週, 来年, 今.
How to tell: these words point to a different day depending on when you say them. They move along with "now", so no に. (English works the same way: we don't say "at tomorrow".)
② "Every ～" times: 毎日, 毎朝, 毎週. These describe a repeating pattern, how often something happens, not one point in time, so no に either.
・明日、映画を見ます。 (I'm going to watch a movie tomorrow.)
・毎朝コーヒーを飲みます。 (I drink coffee every morning.)
It's also very common to combine the two kinds:
・毎朝7時に起きます。 (I get up at 7 every morning.)
・明日の3時に会いましょう。 (Let's meet at 3 tomorrow.)
When one sentence has both kinds, just apply the rule to each one separately. Times based on now (明日…) and "every ～" times (毎朝…) get no に; times with a number (7時, 3時…) do.
Common mistakes
・Dropping に: "7時起きます" is wrong. Say 7時に起きます.
・Adding too much: "明日に行きます" and "毎日に勉強します" are both wrong. After 明日 and 毎日, just continue the sentence.
・When asking about time, 何時 takes に but いつ doesn't: 何時に起きますか。 (What time do you get up?) and いつ日本へ行きますか。 (When are you going to Japan?)
・「時」 and 「時間」 are different: 2時に勉強します means "I study at 2 o'clock", while 2時間勉強します means "I study for two hours". A length of time takes no に.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
With the same "7 o'clock", a different particle changes the meaning:
に = at that exact point: 7時に起きます。 (I get up at 7.)
から = starting from that time and continuing: 7時から勉強します。 (I study from 7.)
まで = up until that time: 7時まで寝ます。 (I sleep until 7.)
Quick tip: English "at 7" is に, "from 7" is から, and "until 7" is まで.
What to learn next
に does more than mark time. It can also mark where something is (n5-33, location of existence): 部屋に猫がいます。 (There's a cat in the room.) It's the same に; just check whether the word before it is a time or a place.
n5-20:
The idea in one line
「へ」 means "toward ～". Placed after a place, it tells the listener where you're moving: 日本へ行きます is literally "go toward Japan", that is, "go to Japan". It's written へ, but as a particle it's pronounced "e", not "he".
How to attach it
Place + へ + a verb of movement (such as 行きます, 来ます, 帰ります).
学校 → 学校へ行きます (go to school)
・明日、京都へ行きます。 (I'm going to Kyoto tomorrow.)
・田中さんは去年日本へ来ました。 (Mr. Tanaka came to Japan last year.)
・6時にうちへ帰ります。 (I go home at six.)
To ask where someone is going, swap the place for どこ:
・週末、どこへ行きますか。 (Where are you going this weekend?)
Common mistakes
・Pronunciation: the particle へ is read "e", just like the particle は is read "wa". But when writing, always write へ, never え.
・It must be followed by a verb of movement. "Go to the library to study" sounds natural in English, but the place where you do the action ("study at the library") takes で: 図書館で勉強します. You can't say 図書館へ勉強します.
・Times can't take へ. "Go tomorrow" is 明日、行きます, not 明日へ.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
へ vs にWhen talking about going, coming or returning somewhere, the two are mostly interchangeable and mean the same thing.
・東京へ行きます。 (I'm going to Tokyo.)
・東京に行きます。 (I'm going to Tokyo.)
If you insist on a difference: へ feels like "in that direction", while に feels like "arriving at that point". In everyday conversation に is used more. When the focus is on arrival, as with 着きます (arrive), に is the normal choice:
・駅に着きました。 (I arrived at the station.)
へ vs でへ is "going to a place"; で is "doing something at a place".
・図書館へ行きます。 (I'm going to the library.)
・図書館で勉強します。 (I study at the library.)
Quick tip: if the verb is a movement verb like 「行く、来る、帰る」, either へ or に works; for "doing something at a place", use で. Times can't take へ: specific points like 7時 or 月曜日 take に, while words like 明日 and 来週 take no particle at all.
What to learn next
Pair it with から (from) and まで (to) and you can state both the starting point and the destination. Then learn "で (means of transport)" and you can say 電車で会社へ行きます (I go to work by train).
n5-27:
The idea in one line
This 「と」 works like English "and": you list things one by one. It also carries a nuance: what I listed is everything, nothing else. If you tell a friend 「パンと牛乳を買いました」, you bought only those two things.
・パンと牛乳を買いました。(I bought bread and milk.)
How to attach it
Noun + と + noun. Both sides must be nouns. After you finish the list, add whatever particle the sentence needs (を, が, は…) at the very end.
鍵＋財布 → 鍵と財布を持ってきました (I brought my keys and wallet.)
For three or more items, put と between each one:
・月曜日と水曜日と金曜日に授業があります。(I have class on Monday, Wednesday and Friday.)
・父と母は台北に住んでいます。(My father and mother live in Taipei.)
It's also very common when ordering food:
・コーヒーとケーキをお願いします。(Coffee and cake, please.)
Easy mistakes
・The particle goes only after the last noun. Say 鍵と財布を持ってきました, not 「鍵を財布を持ってきました」 or 「鍵をと財布を持ってきました」.
・と can only connect nouns. English "and" is very flexible: "cheap and tasty" or "eating and watching TV" all work. But in Japanese you can't use と to join adjectives or actions. For those you'll use the て-form, which you'll learn later.
・と means "just these." If there are other things you haven't mentioned, use や instead.
Telling look-alikes apart
と vs やBoth describe what you brought in your bag:
鍵と財布を持ってきました。 (I brought my keys and wallet: just those two.)
鍵や財布を持ってきました。 (I brought things like my keys and wallet: there's more.)
"and" vs "with"と has another use: "doing something together with someone."
Listing と: ties A and B into one group, and then a particle such as は, が or を follows, so the group acts as one part of the sentence.
友達と私は映画を見ました。 (My friend and I watched a movie: 「友達と私」 is one group, followed by は.)
"With" と: "person + と" says who you did the following action with. Even if a noun comes after it, that noun is a separate element and isn't bundled with the person before と.
友達と映画を見ました。 (I watched a movie with my friend: 「友達と」 says who you watched with, and 「映画を」 is the thing watched. It does not mean "friend and movie.")
When you want to stress "together," you'll often hear 友達と一緒に映画を見ました.
Quick test: take the noun before と and put it in the sentence on its own. 鍵を持ってきました and 財布を持ってきました both make sense, so it's "A and B." But if you change 「友達と映画を見ました」 to 「友達を見ました」, the meaning goes wrong, so that と means "together with someone."
n5-28:
The idea in one line
「や」 is like English "things like A, B, and so on". There are many items, you pick just a few as examples, and you let the listener know that there are others and the list isn't complete.
How to attach it
Noun + や + noun, and often 「など」 (etc.) at the end. Any particle the sentence needs (を, が, に…) still goes at the very end.
牛乳＋卵 → 牛乳や卵
牛乳や卵 → 牛乳や卵など (Adding など makes the "and more" feeling even clearer.)
・冷蔵庫に牛乳や卵があります。(There's milk, eggs and the like in the fridge.)
・週末は掃除や洗濯をします。(On weekends I do things like cleaning and laundry.)
・日本で寿司やラーメンなどを食べました。(In Japan I ate sushi, ramen and so on.)
You can also give three examples, with や between each one:
・机の上にペンやノートや辞書などがあります。(On the desk there are pens, notebooks, dictionaries and so on.)
Telling look-alikes apart
「と」 also connects nouns, but the meaning is quite different. Both describe what's in a bag:
と = that's everything: かばんに財布と鍵があります。 (There's a wallet and keys in the bag, just those two.)
や = examples, there's more: かばんに財布や鍵があります。 (There's a wallet, keys and the like in the bag, plus other things.)
Quick test: if you can say "just these," use と. If you're only giving a few examples and there's an "…and stuff" in your mind, use や.
Easy mistakes
・や can only connect nouns. To give examples of actions you can't say 「食べるや飲む」. Use 「〜たり〜たりします」: 食べたり飲んだりします (I eat and drink, among other things).
・Don't put や after the last noun. You can't end with 「ペンやノートや」. To express "etc.", add など: ペンやノートなど.
・English "and" can also mean "together with someone" ("I'm going with a friend"), but や can't. "I'm going with a friend" is 友達と行きます; you can't say 友達や行きます.
・You don't need a long list to use や. Even two examples are perfectly fine. What matters is the feeling that "the list isn't complete."
What to learn next
The version for actions is 「〜たり〜たりします」: 休みの日は映画を見たり、買い物をしたりします。 (On days off I do things like watch movies and go shopping.)
n5-23:
The idea in one sentence
「を」 is a little tag you attach after a noun. It means "this is the thing the action is done to." In English, word order tells you what's being eaten in "eat bread." Japanese puts the verb at the very end of the sentence, so 「を」 has to mark what you eat, what you watch.
How to connect it
Noun + を + verb. Japanese order is "the thing first, the action last":
パン → パンを食べます (eat bread)
・水を飲みます。 (I drink water.)
・映画を見ます。 (I watch a movie.)
・毎日日本語を勉強します。 (I study Japanese every day.)
When to use it
Object of an actionThis is the main, most common use: what you eat, drink, buy, do. As a beginner, get comfortable with this one first.
・コンビニで傘を買いました。 (I bought an umbrella at the convenience store.)
Place you pass throughUsed with movement verbs like "walk, stroll, cross (a bridge, a road)." It means moving along or through that place.
・公園を散歩します。 (I take a walk in the park.)
・橋を渡ります。 (I cross the bridge.)
Place you leaveUsed with verbs like "leave, get off (a vehicle)." It means departing from there.
・8時に家を出ます。 (I leave home at 8.)
・次の駅で電車を降ります。 (I get off the train at the next station.)
Easy mistakes
