・「を」 is pronounced o, just like 「お」. Don't say "wo." But when typing on a computer or phone, you do need to type wo to get it.
・Even though they sound the same, you still have to write 「を」 and can't write 「お」 instead.
・"Like, understand, want" don't take を. The standard textbook phrasing is 猫が好きです and 英語がわかります, not 猫を好きです.
・In English you "meet friends" and "take a train" with no little word in between, but Japanese needs に: 友達に会います, 電車に乗ります. Getting off is 電車を降ります, though. Getting on uses に and getting off uses を, so memorize them as a pair.
・Don't put two を on the same verb. 日本語を勉強をします sounds unnatural (勉強します can only have one を). Say 日本語を勉強します or 日本語の勉強をします. Different verbs can each take their own を without a problem, for example 本を読んで、ご飯を食べます。 (I read a book, then eat.)
・Friends chatting often drop を: ご飯、食べた？ (Did you eat?). That's casual speech. When you write your own sentences, put the を in first.
Telling similar ones apart
を vs が: Both appear in Japanese sentences, but actions take を, while feelings and abilities take が.
日本語を勉強します。 (I study Japanese: an action)
日本語が好きです。 (I like Japanese: a feeling)
日本語がわかります。 (I understand Japanese: an ability)
を vs で: Take the same bridge. "Crossing the bridge" uses を, while "doing something else on the bridge" uses で.
橋を渡ります。 (I cross the bridge: walking across it)
橋で写真を撮ります。 (I take a photo on the bridge: the bridge is just where it happens, and the thing being shot, 「写真」, is what takes を)
Quick trick: ask yourself, "Is the action done directly to this thing?" If yes, use を. "Like, understand, want" use が. If you're just saying "where something happens," use で.
What to learn next
Some verbs come in pairs, one taking を and the other taking が: ドアを開けます (I open the door), ドアが開きます (the door opens). These are "intransitive and transitive verbs," and they'll come easily once you've got を down.
n5-24:
The idea in one sentence
「で」 is the "at/in (a place), doing (something)" of Japanese. Think of the place as a stage. 「で」 tells the listener that this action is being performed on that stage.
カフェで仕事をします。 (I work at a café.)
How to connect it
Add 「で」 right after the place, then the action you do there.
図書館 → 図書館で勉強します (study at the library)
家 → 家で晩ご飯を食べます (eat dinner at home)
The place can be big or small: a country, a city, a shop, a room, even "here."
When to use it
Doing something somewhereEating, drinking, buying, watching, studying, working, playing, waiting for someone… for any action you "do," put で after the place.
・駅で友達を待ちます。 (I wait for my friend at the station.)
・デパートで靴を買いました。 (I bought shoes at the department store.)
・ここで写真を撮ってもいいですか。 (May I take a photo here?)
Asking whereUse 「どこで」 to ask where something is done.
・そのかばん、どこで買いましたか。 (Where did you buy that bag?)
・どこで昼ご飯を食べますか。 (Where will you eat lunch?)
Telling similar ones apart
「で」 vs 「に」: same place, look at the verb
English says "at the library" either way, but Japanese cares whether you're "staying there" or "doing something there."
図書館にいます。 (I'm at the library: you're simply there, so に)
図書館で勉強します。 (I study at the library: you're doing something there, so で)
If the verb is いる or ある (to be, to exist), use に. If it's an action, use で.
「で」 vs 「へ」: going there, or already there
図書館へ行きます。 (I go to the library: moving toward it, so へ)
図書館で本を読みます。 (I read a book at the library: you've arrived and do something there, so で)
The other 「で」: vehicles and tools
「で」 has another job, where what comes before it is a thing, not a place.
バスで行きます。 (I go by bus: a vehicle)
公園で遊びます。 (I play at the park: a place)
Just check whether the word before it is a "place" or a "tool."
Quick trick: a person or thing "is" there → に; "going" there → へ; "doing" something there → で.
Easy mistakes
・English "at/in" can't always become で. "I'm at home" is 家にいます, not 家でいます.
・"Live in Tokyo" takes に: 東京に住んでいます, not 東京で住んでいます. Living somewhere means being based there, not doing a single action there. This is one of the most common mistakes among learners.
・"Work" with で is fine: 銀行で働いています (I work at a bank). Don't switch 働く to に just because 住む uses に.
・With movement verbs like 行く, 来る, 帰る, the destination doesn't take で. Say 日本へ行きます, not 日本で行きます.
What to learn next
Put 「で」 and 「を」 together and you can say a complete sentence: place + で + thing + を + action.
コンビニでお茶を買いました。 (I bought tea at the convenience store.)
Next, look at 「に」 (location of existence) and compare the two together, and you won't mix up に and で anymore.
n5-32:
The idea in one line
In English you say "I like dogs" or "I understand Korean." Dogs and Korean are the things being liked or understood, so your instinct says to use を. But in Japanese, the thing in front of like, dislike, good at, bad at, understand, can do, and want takes が. Just memorize these as fixed pairings.
Which words take が
Like・dislike好き (like), 嫌い (dislike)
・チョコレートが好きです。 (I like chocolate.)
・私は野菜が嫌いです。 (I dislike vegetables.)
Good at・bad at上手 (good at, skilled), 下手 (bad at, not skilled)
・田中さんは歌が上手です。 (Mr. Tanaka is good at singing.)
Understand・can doわかります (understand), できます (can do)
・韓国語がわかります。 (I understand Korean.)
・テニスができます。 (I can play tennis.)
Wantほしい (want)
・新しいかばんがほしいです。 (I want a new bag.)
How to build it
Thing (noun) + が + one of the words above.
To say who likes it, put "person + は" at the very front: 私は犬が好きです。 (I like dogs.)
In this sentence, は says "we're talking about me," and が says "the thing liked is dogs." Each one does its own job.
To ask what someone likes, just swap the thing for 何: 何が好きですか。 (What do you like?)
Common mistakes
・Don't follow your English instinct and use を. Say 韓国語がわかります, not 韓国語をわかります. It's the same for liking: just memorize 犬が好きです.
・好き, 嫌い, 上手, and 下手 are not verbs. They are followed by です, and you can't add ます.
・When saying "don't like," Japanese speakers very often swap が for は: 魚は好きじゃありません。 (As for fish, I don't like it.) It carries a feeling of "other things are okay, but not this one," and sounds perfectly natural.
・上手 is used to compliment other people. Saying "I'm good at..." about yourself sounds like bragging, so Japanese speakers usually don't use it that way.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
The easiest one to confuse it with is を (the object marker). Look at the same thing placed before different words:
日本語を勉強します。 (I study Japanese.): studying is an action you do, so use を.
日本語がわかります。 (I understand Japanese.): understanding is your own ability, so use が.
料理を作ります。 (I cook.): an action, so use を.
料理が上手です。 (I'm good at cooking.): a skill, so use が.
Quick rule of thumb: if it's an action you "go and do" (eat, read, make, buy), use を. If it's a feeling inside you or an ability you have (like, dislike, good at, understand, can do, want), use が.
What to learn next
For the ほしい pattern, move on to "〜が欲しいです・〜たいです" to learn how to say "I want ~" and "I want to do ~."
n5-33:
The idea in one line
This 「に」 works like the English "in / at": it tells the listener where a person or thing is. In English you say "there's milk in the fridge." In Japanese, you put に after "the fridge" and finish with あります or います.
How to build it
Pattern: place + に + person/thing + が + あります／います
・冷蔵庫に牛乳があります。 (There's milk in the fridge.)
・教室に先生がいます。 (There's a teacher in the classroom.)
あります or います? Ask whether the thing can move on its own: people and animals take います; objects and plants take あります.
How to say positions
In English you say "on the desk," "in the box," "in front of the station." In Japanese, you attach the position word with 「の」 and then add に:
机の上に (on the desk), 箱の中に (in the box), 駅の前に (in front of the station), 机の下に (under the desk)
・駅の前にコンビニがあります。 (There's a convenience store in front of the station.)
The two patterns you'll hear most
What's therePut the place first, and mark the thing you're describing with が.
・公園に子供がいます。 (There are children in the park.)
Where it isTo say where a particular thing is, put that thing first with は. に still follows the place.
・猫は机の下にいます。 (The cat is under the desk.)
・トイレはどこにありますか。 (Where is the restroom?)
Common mistakes
・Here あります／います mean that a person or thing "exists" in that place. When あります means an event or activity "takes place" (e.g. パーティーがあります), the place takes で: 明日、学校で試験があります。 (There's an exam at school tomorrow.)
・English uses "in" both for "there are kids in the park" and "play in the park," but Japanese separates them. Playing is an action, so use で: 公園で遊びます, not 公園に遊びます.
・You can't use あります for people and animals: it's 先生がいます, not 先生があります.
・The place where someone lives also takes に: 姉は大阪に住んでいます。 (My older sister lives in Osaka.)
Telling it apart from look-alikes
The one most easily confused with it is で (place of action). Even with the same park, look at what the sentence is saying:
公園に子供がいます。 (There are children in the park: it only says they are there.)
公園で子供が遊んでいます。 (Children are playing in the park: an action happening there.)
公園でお祭りがあります。 (There's a festival in the park: an event held there.)
Quick rule of thumb: check the end of the sentence. あります／います meaning a person or thing "is there" (and also 住んでいます) takes に. Actions like eating, playing, buying, and working, or an あります meaning an event is "held" (e.g. ホテルでパーティーがあります), take で.
What to learn next
The "existence expressions" lesson teaches how to say "there's nothing" and "there's nobody": 部屋に誰もいません。 (There's nobody in the room.)
n5-35:
The idea in one line
Put 「が」 at the end of a clause and it works like English “…, but …”. You say one thing, then add something that goes against what you'd expect. For “This restaurant is expensive, but it's delicious,” Japanese says この店は高いですが、おいしいです。
How to attach it
The first clause must be a complete sentence. At N5 that usually ends in 「です」 or 「ます」. Add が, put a comma, then continue with the second clause.
高いです → 高いですが、
雨です → 雨ですが、
行きたいです → 行きたいですが、
勉強しました → 勉強しましたが、
If the first half uses 「です・ます」, the second half should too, so the whole sentence stays at the same politeness level.
When to use it
ContrastThe two parts point in opposite directions, or the result isn't what you'd expect.
・日本語は難しいですが、おもしろいです。(Japanese is hard, but it's fun.)
・昨日は雨でしたが、出かけました。(It rained yesterday, but I went out anyway.)
・薬を飲みましたが、まだ頭が痛いです。(I took medicine, but my head still hurts.)
Polite openerBefore asking someone for help or asking a question, you can cushion it with 「すみませんが」 or 「失礼ですが」. Here が doesn't mean “but.” It just softens the tone, much like English “Excuse me, could I ask…”.
・すみませんが、駅はどこですか。(Excuse me, where is the station?)
・失礼ですが、お名前は？(Excuse me, may I ask your name?)
Common mistakes
・English “although” goes at the very start of the sentence, but Japanese が goes at the end of the first half. Don't look for a word at the start of the sentence to match “although.”
・You may see two が in one sentence: 雨が降っていますが、行きます。 (Although it's raining, I'm going anyway.) The first が follows the noun 「雨」 and marks the subject. The second follows the complete clause 「降っています」, and that one means “but.” The test is simple: is the word before が a single noun, or a clause that's already complete?
・Once you use が, you don't need to add でも. 高いですが、おいしいです。 is enough.
・When chatting with friends, saying 「高いが、おいしい」 (が attached directly without です・ます) sounds stiff, like written text. Among friends, けど is more natural.
Telling similar words apart
There are three common ways to say “It's expensive, but it's delicious”:
が: 高いですが、おいしいです。 This is fairly formal, good for customers, people older than you, or letters.
けど: 高いけど、おいしい。 This is the spoken version you'll hear most in everyday chat. You can also add です: 高いですけど、おいしいです。
でも: 高いです。でも、おいしいです。 The first sentence ends with a period, and でも starts the next one.
Quick rule: attached to the end of a clause and you want to sound a bit formal, use が. Chatting with friends, use けど. If the previous sentence is already finished and you're starting a new one with “but,” use でも.
What to learn next
Next, look at 「けど」. It means the same as が but is more casual, and you'll use it almost every time you talk with friends.
n5-36:
The idea in one line
「けど」 is roughly English “…, but…” or “…, though.” It has two uses. One is contrast, as in “It's small, but it's easy to use.” The other is setting the scene: you bring up the topic first, like English “Excuse me, I wanted to ask…”. Japanese people use it constantly in everyday speech.
When to use it
ContrastYou say one thing, then follow with something that contradicts it or is unexpected.
・小さいけど、使いやすいです。(It's small, but it's easy to use.)
・この店は安いけど、おいしいです。(This restaurant is cheap, but it's delicious.)
Setting the sceneYou give a little background first, then ask a question, make an invitation, or make a request. Here けど doesn't mean “but”. It's closer to “So, here's the thing…”. The second part is often left unsaid so the other person can respond.
・明日映画を見に行くけど、一緒に行かない？(I'm going to see a movie tomorrow. Want to come along?)
・すみません、駅に行きたいんですけど…(Excuse me, I'd like to get to the station…)
・もしもし、田中ですけど…(Hello, this is Tanaka…)
How to attach it
けど attaches to the end of the previous clause, and what comes before it must be a complete sentence.
With friends (no です・ます):
Verbs and い-adjectives take it directly: 行く → 行くけど高い → 高いけど
Nouns and な-adjectives need 「だ」 first: 学生 → 学生だけどきれい → きれいだけど
Polite style: use です・ます before it, then add けど.
行きます → 行きますけど高いです → 高いですけど学生です → 学生ですけど
Memorize 「〜たいんですけど…」 as a set phrase. It's useful for asking directions, making requests, and speaking up at a counter.
Common mistakes
・Forgetting だ with nouns and な-adjectives: 学生けど× should be 学生だけど, and 静かけど× should be 静かだけど. Conversely, い-adjectives don't take だ: 高いだけど× should simply be 高いけど.
・English “but” can start the second sentence, but Japanese けど sticks to the end of the first sentence. To start the second sentence with “But…”, use でも (compared below).
・A sentence that stops at 「〜けど…」 isn't unfinished. It's a polite, softer way of not spelling everything out. When translating into English, don't force a “but” into it.
・けど is spoken language. It's natural in chat and when talking to shop staff, but for reports and formal situations 「が」 is safer.
・けれど and けれども mean the same thing. The longer the form, the more formal it is.
Telling similar words apart
Same situation: the clothes are expensive, but you bought them anyway.
けど = everyday speech: 高いけど、買いました。
が = more formal, for writing or formal situations: 高いですが、買いました。
でも = finish the first sentence, then start the second with “but”: 高いです。でも、買いました。
The scene-setting use works the same way. With a boss or someone older, swap けど for が to be more polite: ちょっと聞きたいんですが… (I'd like to ask you something…)
Quick rule: use けど in everyday speech; use が in formal speech and writing; use でも when you split into two sentences and start the second with “but.”
n5-37:
The idea in one line
This 「に」 explains why you go / come / return. In English you say "go to buy something" or "come to hang out." In Japanese, you put the thing you're going to do first, then add 「に行きます」 or 「に来ます」: 買いに行きます (go to buy), 遊びに来ます (come to hang out).
How to form it
VerbsFirst put the verb in its ます form, drop 「ます」, then add 「に」.
買います → drop ます → 買いに行きます
食べます → 食べに行きます見ます → 見に行きます会います → 会いに行きます
・お土産を買いに行きます。(I'm going to buy souvenirs.)
・週末、友達に会いに行きます。(I'm going to see a friend this weekend.)
・昼ごはんを食べに家へ帰ります。(I'm going home to eat lunch.)
・書類を届けに来ました。(I came to deliver some documents.)
NounsNouns that already mean "an action," such as 買い物, 散歩, 旅行 and 食事, can take 「に」 directly.
・デパートへ買い物に行きます。(I'm going shopping at the department store.)
・公園へ散歩に行きませんか。(Shall we go for a walk in the park?)
When a place and a purpose are in the same sentence
The usual order is: place + へ　→　purpose + に　→　行きます.
図書館へ本を借りに行きます。(I'm going to the library to borrow a book.)
Using 「へ」 after the place keeps you from stacking two に in a row with the purpose 「に」, so it sounds clearer.
Common mistakes
・Before に, use the ます form minus ます, not the dictionary form: it's 買いに行きます, not 「買うに行きます」.
・After it, you can only use a verb of movement, most commonly 行きます, 来ます and 帰ります. For sentences that have nothing to do with movement, like "I read books in order to learn Japanese," you can't use this に.
・English says "go + buy," but Japanese says 「買い＋に行く」, so the order is reversed from English. Don't say 「行きに買います」.
・The 「を」 that normally goes with the verb stays: お土産を買いに行きます.
・遊びに来てください。 (Come hang out!) is a very common invitation in Japan, so it's worth memorizing as a whole sentence.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Even with the same 「に行きます」, what comes before に decides the meaning:
Place + に = go where: デパートに行きます。 (I'm going to the department store.)
Action + に = go to do what: 買い物に行きます。 (I'm going shopping.)
Put them together: デパートへ買い物に行きます。 (I'm going shopping at the department store.)
Quick test: if what comes before に is a place, it means where you're going. If it's a verb with ます dropped, or an action noun like 買い物 or 散歩, it means what you're going to do.
n5-39:
The idea in one line
「ね」 is like English "…, right?" or "…, isn't it?": you're talking about something the other person also knows or feels, so you share the feeling or check with them.
「よ」 is like "…, you know!" or "…!" as a heads-up: you're talking about something the other person doesn't know yet, and you're telling or reminding them.
When to use them
ね: sharing a feelingYou both see, taste or feel the same thing, and you say it to connect.
・いい天気ですね。(Nice weather, isn't it?)
・このケーキ、おいしいですね。(This cake is delicious, isn't it?)
ね: checkingYou mostly know, but want to confirm you've got it right. Staff confirming your order use it the same way.
・明日は休みですね。(Tomorrow's a day off, right?)
・コーヒー二つですね。(Two coffees, correct?)
よ: tellingSomething you know and the other person doesn't, like a recommendation or a piece of news.
・この店、安いですよ。(This shop is cheap, you know.)
・この番組、面白いですよ。(This show is fun, you know.)
よ: remindingSomething the other person hasn't noticed, so you point it out.
・もう始まりますよ。(It's about to start!)
・電車が来ましたよ。(The train's here!)
How to attach them
Very simple: finish the sentence and put it right at the end.
Polite form: おいしいです → おいしいですね始まります → 始まりますよ
Casual speech works the same way, just add it directly: いい → いいね行く → 行くよ雨だ → 雨だね
Common mistakes
・Don't add ね to things the other person can't possibly know. If you introduce yourself with 「私は台湾人ですね」, it sounds like you're asking them, "I'm Taiwanese, right?", which is odd. Just say 私は台湾人です。.
・よ is stronger. If you add よ when correcting a teacher or boss, as in 「それは違いますよ」, it can sound like you're lecturing them. With people above you, it's safer to use よ sparingly.
・Intonation of ね: rising checks ("right?"); flat or falling expresses a feeling ("it really is…").
・Learners often want to add a particle to every sentence, the way English speakers sprinkle in "you know" or "right?", but Japanese doesn't need it every time. When you're simply describing something, adding nothing is perfectly natural, and ね or よ on every sentence gets noisy.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Take "it's raining outside". Choose by whether the other person knows:
ね = they see it too, and you share the moment: 雨ですね。 (It's raining, isn't it?)
よ = they're indoors and haven't noticed, so you tell them: 雨ですよ。 (It's raining out there!)
か = you have no idea yourself and you're asking: 雨ですか。 (Is it raining?)
「ね」 and 「か」 can both make a question. The difference is whether you already have an answer in mind:
明日は休みですか。 (Is tomorrow a day off? You don't know and are asking.)
明日は休みですね。 (Tomorrow's a day off, right? You pretty much know and are confirming.)
Quick test: the other person knows too → ね; they don't know and you're telling them → よ; you don't know yourself → か.
What to learn next
The two can be combined into 「よね」. The order is fixed, with よ first, so you can't say 「ねよ」. It means "I remember it being this way, right?": テストは明日ですよね。 (The test is tomorrow, right?)
n5-40:
The idea in one line
Japanese particles work a lot like English prepositions such as "in," "on," and "at": one word often has several meanings. You've already learned the basic uses of を, に, で, は, and か. This lesson gathers their other common uses in one place. When you see a particle, don't memorize just one meaning. Look at the words around it to decide which one it is.
を: leaving and passing through
Place you leaveWhen you come out of a place, get off a vehicle, or graduate, the place takes を. It often appears with 出る, 降りる, and 卒業する.
・7時に家を出ます。(I leave the house at 7.)
・次の駅で電車を降ります。(I get off the train at the next station.)
Place you pass throughWith movement verbs like walking, running, strolling, or crossing a bridge, the route or area you move through takes を.
・毎朝、公園を散歩します。(I take a walk in the park every morning.)
・この橋を渡ってください。(Please cross this bridge.)
に: frequency, where something lands, becoming
FrequencyTime period + に + number of times = how many times per period.
・1日に3回、薬を飲みます。(I take medicine three times a day.)
・週に1回、プールへ行きます。(I go to the pool once a week.)
Where something landsWhen you write on something, sit on something, or put something into something, the spot where the thing ends up "touching or staying" takes に.
・ここに名前を書いてください。(Please write your name here.)
・椅子に座ります。(I sit on the chair.)
BecomingNoun + になる = become ~.
・将来、先生になりたいです。(I want to become a teacher in the future.)
で: range and total
RangeFor "the most ~ out of/in ~," the range takes で.
・兄はクラスでいちばん背が高いです。(My older brother is the tallest in the class.)
TotalQuantity + で = added up, in total. Very common when shopping.
・全部でいくらですか。(How much is it in total?)
・りんごは3つで500円です。(The apples are 500 yen for three.)
は: contrast
ContrastWhen you set two things side by side and give each its own は, it means "A is like this, but B isn't."
・寿司は好きですが、刺身は苦手です。(I like sushi, but sashimi isn't really my thing.)
Even when you mention only one side, it can carry a hint of "other things are a different story":
・お酒は飲みません。(Alcohol, I don't drink.)
か: choosing one of two
ChoiceAかB = A or B, pick one of them.
・月曜日か火曜日に来てください。(Please come on Monday or Tuesday.)
Common mistakes
・Use に for getting on and を for getting off: 電車に乗ります, 電車を降ります. Many learners use the same particle for both.
・The "passing through" を needs a movement verb. For things you do while staying in one place, like playing in a park or eating a boxed lunch, use で: 公園で遊びます.
・It's tempting to think of "write here" as doing something at a place and reach for で. But when you write on paper or sit on a chair, the thing "lands" there, so use に: ここに書いてください.
・The contrast は is still pronounced wa, not ha.
Telling look-alikes apart
か, と, and や can all link two things, but the meanings are quite different. Take buying drinks:
コーヒーと紅茶を買いました。(I bought coffee and tea: both.)
コーヒーや紅茶を買いました。(I bought things like coffee and tea: there was more.)
コーヒーか紅茶を買います。(I'll buy coffee or tea: just one.)
Quick rule: use と for everything on the list, や for a few examples, and か when you pick only one.
What to learn next
The range で lets you ask "which is the most ~?": 果物の中で何がいちばん好きですか。(What do you like best among fruits?)
n5-41:
The idea in one line
The 「ます form」 is a verb wearing its polite coat. The dictionary lists 飲む, but to a teacher, a shop clerk, or someone you've just met, you say 飲みます. This lesson drills one thing: take any verb and turn it into its 〜ます form.
How to convert: first check the verb group
Step 1Pick out Group 3 (する・来る) first. There are only two, so just memorize them:
する → します来る → 来ます(きます)
「Noun + する」 verbs belong here too: 勉強する → 勉強します
Step 2For the rest, decide whether it's Group 1 or Group 2:
・If the last kana is not る (like 書く, 飲む, 会う, 待つ): it's always Group 1.
・If it ends in る and the sound before る ends in a, u, or o (like か in 分かる, く in 作る, の in 乗る): it's always Group 1. (する and 来る were already removed in Step 1, so they don't count here.)
・If it ends in る and the sound before る ends in i or e (like み in 見る, べ in 食べる, き in 起きる): it's mostly Group 2. A few exceptions are actually Group 1, so memorize them: 帰る, 入る, 走る, 知る, 切る.
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the 「い」-row sound of the same consonant row, then add ます.
On the gojūon chart, move from the う-column one step over to the い-column (one step up in a vertical chart, one step left in a horizontal chart): う→い, く→き, ぐ→ぎ, す→し, つ→ち, ぬ→に, ぶ→び, む→み, る→り.
書く → change く to き → 書きます
飲む → 飲みます会う → 会います待つ → 待ちます話す → 話します泳ぐ → 泳ぎます遊ぶ → 遊びます帰る → 帰ります
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop the final 「る」 and add ます.
食べる → 食べます見る → 見ます起きる → 起きます着る → 着ます
How you'll hear it most
Daily habits and things you'll do tomorrow both use the same ます form.
・毎朝パンを食べます。(I eat bread every morning.)
・毎日、日本語を勉強します。(I study Japanese every day.)
・明日、友達が家に来ます。(A friend is coming to my house tomorrow.)
Common mistakes
・You can't just stick ます onto the dictionary form: 飲むます and 行くます are both wrong. Change the last sound first.
・帰る, 入る, 走る, 知る, and 切る look like Group 2 but are really Group 1: it's 帰ります, not 帰ます.
・来ます is read きます, not くます, and not 来ります. Likewise, する does not become すります.
・The 「す」 in 「ます」 is often barely voiced, so it sounds like "mas." That's normal pronunciation, not your ears playing tricks.
What to learn next
The part left after you remove ます (飲み, 食べ, し) comes up constantly. Swap in a different ending and you get a new pattern:
飲みます → 飲みました(drank)
飲みます → 飲みましょう(let's drink)
飲みます → 飲みたいです(I want to drink)
n5-42:
The idea in one line
The te-form is the verb's "connector", like the stud on a LEGO brick that lets you snap something else on. In English you'd say "get up and wash your face." Japanese turns 「起きる」 into its te-form and attaches the next action after it. Many important patterns, such as "please do ~" and "be doing ~", only work once the verb is in te-form. That's why it's called the most important conjugation.
When to use it
Chaining actionsLink several actions together in order.
・朝起きて、顔を洗います。（I get up in the morning, then wash my face）
Attaching to patternsAdd other words after it to make a new meaning.
・ここに名前を書いてください。（Please write your name here）
・今、ご飯を食べています。（I'm eating right now）
Casual requestsWith friends, the te-form alone is a casual request: "do ~ for me."
・ちょっと待って。（Wait a moment）
How to form it: first, which group is the verb?
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): the easiest. Drop 「る」 and add 「て」.
食べる → 食べて見る → 見て起きる → 起きて
Group 3 (only two, just memorize them): する → して来る → 来て（きて）
"Noun + する" verbs like 勉強する work the same way: 勉強する → 勉強して
Group 1 (godan verbs): look at the last kana. There are five groups.
う・つ・る → って
買う → 買って待つ → 待って帰る → 帰って
む・ぶ・ぬ → んで (note the で with the two small dots)
飲む → 飲んで遊ぶ → 遊んで死ぬ → 死んで
く → いて
書く → 書いて聞く → 聞いて
ぐ → いで
急ぐ → 急いで泳ぐ → 泳いで
す → して
話す → 話して貸す → 貸して
The one exception: by the rule, 行く should become 「行いて」, but it's actually 行く → 行って.
A little chant, just repeat it until it sticks: うつる って、むぶぬ んで、く いて、ぐ いで、す して、行く は 行って.
Easy mistakes
・帰る, 入る, 走る and 知る look like Group 2 but are actually Group 1. It's 帰って, not 帰て.
・行って is an exception, but other verbs ending in く, like 書いて and 聞いて, still follow the rule. Don't change them all to って.
・ぐ becomes いで and む・ぶ・ぬ become んで. People often write 泳いて or 飲んて, so don't forget the dots (dakuten).
・The small 「っ」 holds for one beat: 来て (きて, come) and 切って (きって, cut) differ only by that beat, but mean completely different things.
・来て is read きて, not こて or くて.
・The te-form itself has no past or present tense. The last verb decides: シャワーを浴びて、寝ました。（I took a shower, then went to bed）
What to learn next
Once the te-form feels natural, the た-form (the plain past tense) comes almost free. The rules are exactly the same, you just swap て for た and で for だ.
書いて → 書いた飲んで → 飲んだ
After that, you can learn 「～てください」 (please ~), 「～ています」 (be ~ing) and 「～てから」 (after ~). They all rely on the conjugation on this card.
n5-43:
The idea in one line
The dictionary form is the casual version of 「〜ます」, and it's also the form you find in a dictionary. The ない-form is the casual version of 「〜ません」. With a teacher you say 行きます／行きません, and with friends you say 行く／行かない. The meaning is the same, just more relaxed.
When to use it
Chatting with friends and familyJust like ます, it covers present habits and things that haven't happened yet. To ask a question, just raise your intonation at the end.
・明日、何時に起きる？（What time are you getting up tomorrow?）
・7時に起きる。（I get up at 7）
・今日は学校に行かない。（I'm not going to school today）
・私はお酒を飲まない。（I don't drink alcohol）
How to form it: first, which group is the verb?
First, ます-form → dictionary form
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the sound before ます to the same row's 「う」-column sound.
飲みます → み becomes む → 飲む書きます → 書く歌います → 歌う帰ります → 帰る
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): replace ます with る.
食べます → 食べる起きます → 起きる見ます → 見る
Group 3 (only two, just memorize them): します → する来ます → 来る（くる）
Then, dictionary form → ない-form
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the same row's 「あ」-column sound, then add ない.
書く → く becomes か → 書かない飲む → 飲まない待つ → 待たない帰る → 帰らない
If the verb ends in 「う」, change it to 「わ」, not 「あ」:
買う → う becomes わ → 買わない歌う → 歌わない会う → 会わない
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop る and add ない.
食べる → 食べない起きる → 起きない見る → 見ない
Group 3 (just memorize): する → しない来る → 来ない（こない）
"Noun + する" verbs work the same way: 電話する → 電話しない
Easy mistakes
・Verbs ending in 「う」 can't become 「あない」. It's 買わない, not 買あない.
・帰る, 入る, 走る and 知る look like Group 2 but are actually Group 1. It's 帰らない, not 帰ない.
・Keep the three readings of 来る apart: 来る is read くる, 来ます is read きます, and 来ない is read こない.
・The negative of ある (to exist, to be) is ない, not あらない: お金がない。（I have no money）
・The ない-form means "don't (do)", not "can't". 食べない means "I don't eat," not "I can't eat."
Telling similar forms apart
Take the same sentence, "I'm not coming tomorrow." Which form you use depends on who you're talking to:
To a teacher or boss: 明日は来ません。
To a friend or family: 明日は来ない。
The meaning is exactly the same, only the politeness differs. Using 来ない with a senior can sound disrespectful, while sticking to 来ません with a close friend can sound distant.
Quick tip: ます pairs with the dictionary form, and ません pairs with the ない-form. Think about who you're talking to first, then pick the set.
What to learn next
Many more grammar patterns attach to the dictionary form and ない-form, for example asking someone not to do something: ここで写真を撮らないでください。（Please don't take photos here）. Next, you can learn the past forms: 行った／行かなかった.
n5-46:
The idea in one line
In English, an adjective just sits in front of the noun: "tall mountain", "pretty flower". Japanese splits into two patterns: い-adjectives attach directly before the noun, while な-adjectives need a 「な」 in between. Think of that 「な」 as a small connector that only な-adjectives need.
How to connect
い-adjectives (the ones ending in い): change nothing, just put them before the noun.
高い＋山 → 高い山 (a tall mountain)
新しい＋靴 → 新しい靴 (new shoes)
な-adjectives: add 「な」 first, then the noun.
きれい＋な＋花 → きれいな花 (a pretty flower)
静か＋な＋部屋 → 静かな部屋 (a quiet room)
How you'll hear it most often
・新しい靴を買いました。 (I bought new shoes.)
・これはおいしいケーキですね。 (This is a tasty cake, isn't it?)
・静かな部屋がいいです。 (I'd like a quiet room.)
・好きな食べ物は何ですか。 (What's your favorite food?)
Easy mistakes
・きれい and きらい end in い, but they are actually な-adjectives. Say きれいな花 and きらいな食べ物, not きれい花.
・Some learners are tempted to squeeze a 「の」 in between: 「高いの山」 and 「静かの部屋」 are both wrong. い-adjectives take nothing extra; な-adjectives take 「な」.
・"Many people" can't be said as 「多い人」. Say たくさんの人.
・You may also see 大きな家 and 小さな店. These aren't typos: 大きい and 小さい have an extra form that can only go before a noun. 大きい家 and 大きな家 are both correct.
Telling look-alikes apart
End of sentence vs before a nounThe 「な」 of a な-adjective only appears when a noun follows. At the end of a sentence, it goes straight into です.
この部屋は静かです。 (This room is quiet.)
静かな部屋です。 (It's a quiet room.)
You can't say 「この部屋は静かなです」.
Noun + のIf what comes before is a noun, the connector is 「の」, not 「な」.
日本の車 (a Japanese car: noun + の)
新しい車 (a new car: い-adjective, attached directly)
きれいな車 (a pretty car: な-adjective + な)
Quick trick: ask yourself what the word in front is. い-adjective: attach directly. な-adjective: add な. Noun: add の.
What to learn next
Adjectives can also modify verbs, as in 早く起きます (get up early). This is the adverb use of adjectives.
n5-47:
The idea in one line
In English, you describe how an action is done with an adverb: "get up early", "clean thoroughly", "dance well". Japanese does this too: you just change the ending of the adjective, and it can go in front of the verb to say how the action is done.
How to change it: first check which type of adjective it is
い-adjectives (adjectives ending in 「い」): replace the final 「い」 with 「く」.
早い → change い to く → 早く
大きい → 大きく楽しい → 楽しく
・明日は早く起きます。 (I'll get up early tomorrow.)
・名前を大きく書いてください。 (Please write your name big.)
な-adjectives (adjectives that take 「な」 before a noun): just add 「に」.
静か → add に → 静かに
きれい → きれいに上手 → 上手に
・部屋をきれいに掃除しました。 (I cleaned the room until it was spotless.)
・図書館では静かに話してください。 (Please speak quietly in the library.)
An exception to memorize: いい → よく, not いく. Words ending in いい work the same way, for example かっこいい → かっこよく.
・昨日はよく寝ました。 (I slept well yesterday.)
・かっこよく踊りたいです。 (I want to dance in a cool way.)
Word order: say the "how" first
In English the adverb often comes after the verb: "dances well", "writes beautifully". Japanese puts it the other way around: say how first, then the action.
・田中さんは上手に踊ります。 (Mr. Tanaka dances well.)
・字をきれいに書きます。 (I write characters beautifully.)
Easy mistakes
・きれい and 有名 look like they end in い, but they are actually な-adjectives: say きれいに, not きれく.
・You can't put the plain form of an adjective directly before a verb: not 早い起きます but 早く起きます; not 静かな話します but 静かに話します.
・Besides "well, properly", よく is also very often used to mean "often": よく行きます means "I often go." Use the context to tell which one it is.
・早く and 速く are both read はやく, but 「早く」 means early in time and 「速く」 means fast in speed: 早く起きます (get up early), 速く走ります (run fast).
Telling look-alikes apart
It's easy to mix this lesson up with the previous one, adjectives modifying nouns. The only difference is what comes after:
Before a noun (a person or thing): い-adjectives stay the same, な-adjectives add 「な」.
Before a verb (an action): い-adjectives change to 「く」, な-adjectives add 「に」.
・静かな人です。 (He/She is a quiet person.)
・静かに話します。 (I speak quietly.)
・早い電車に乗ります。 (I'll take an earlier train.)
・早く来てください。 (Please come early.)
Quick trick: before a "thing", use 「〜い／〜な」. Before an "action", use 「〜く／〜に」.
What to learn next
The same く／に followed by なります means "become ~", and followed by します means "make it ~": 寒くなりました。 (It got cold.), 静かにしてください。 (Please be quiet.)
n5-44:
The idea in one line
The た-form is the casual version of 「〜ました」, and the なかった-form is the casual version of 「〜ませんでした」. To your teacher you say 「昨日、映画を見ました」, and to a friend 「昨日、映画を見た」. Both mean “I watched a movie yesterday”; the second is just more relaxed.
When to use it
Talking about the past with people you knowFriends and family, when you talk about something that already happened.
・昨日、渋谷で友達に会った。(I met a friend in Shibuya yesterday.)
・今朝は何も食べなかった。(I didn't eat anything this morning.)
Talking to yourself, writing a diaryWhen there's no one you need to be polite to.
・あ、傘を忘れた。(Oh, I forgot my umbrella.)
Connecting to other grammarMany later grammar points need the verb in た-form first, so you really do need this one.
How to make the た-form: first, check which type the verb is
If you already know the て-form, this is the easy way: just change the 「て」 of the て-form to 「た」 and 「で」 to 「だ」.
書いて → 書いた飲んで → 飲んだ食べて → 食べた
Group 1 (godan verbs): look at the last sound and change it like this.
Ending in う・つ・る → った：会う → 会った待つ → 待った帰る → 帰った
Ending in ぬ・む・ぶ → んだ：死ぬ → 死んだ飲む → 飲んだ遊ぶ → 遊んだ
Ending in く → いた：書く → 書いた
Ending in ぐ → いだ：泳ぐ → 泳いだ
Ending in す → した：話す → 話した
The one exception: 行く → 行った (it ends in く, but it is not 行いた)
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop the final 「る」 and add 「た」.
食べる → 食べた見る → 見た起きる → 起きた
Group 3 (only two verbs, just memorize them): する → した来る → 来た（きた）
How to make the なかった-form
First make the ない-form, then change 「ない」 to 「なかった」. The same trick works for all three groups.
飲む → 飲まない → 飲まなかった
会う → 会わない → 会わなかった
食べる → 食べない → 食べなかった
する → しない → しなかった
来る → 来ない（こない） → 来なかった（こなかった）
・昨日はどこにも行かなかった。(I didn't go anywhere yesterday.)
Easy mistakes
・The た-form of 行く is 行った, not 行いた.
・帰る, 走る, 入る and 知る look like Group 2 but are actually Group 1: they become 帰った and 走った, not 帰た or 走た.
・来た is read きた, but 来なかった is read こなかった. The same kanji is read differently.
・The negative of ある is simply ない (there is no 「あらない」), so the past is なかった: 時間がなかった。(I didn't have time.)
・English “I haven't eaten yet” is not 食べなかった. なかった means “didn't do it back then”, about something that's over. For “still haven't done it as of now”, say まだ食べていない.
・The た-form and なかった-form are for talking with friends. When you talk about the past to someone older or senior, always end the sentence with 「〜ました」 or 「〜ませんでした」.
Telling similar forms apart
た-form vs ました: exactly the same meaning; the difference is who you're talking to.
昨日、映画を見ました。(To your teacher: I watched a movie yesterday.)
昨日、映画を見た。(To a friend: I watched a movie yesterday.)
The negative works the same way: 行きませんでした and 行かなかった both mean “didn't go”. The first is polite, the second more casual.
た vs て: only one sound apart, but completely different jobs. 「た」 ends the sentence and says it was done. 「て」 means the sentence isn't finished and something follows, or it's used for making requests.
ご飯を食べた。(I ate.)
ご飯を食べて、すぐ寝た。(I ate and went straight to bed.)
Quick rule of thumb: the sentence ends here and it already happened → た; more is coming after → て; talking to someone older or a customer → go back to ました or ませんでした.
What to learn next
Add 「り」 after the た-form to get 「〜たり〜たりします」 (do things like this and that): 週末は映画を見たり、買い物をしたりします。(On weekends I do things like watch movies and go shopping.)
た-form + 「あとで」 = after doing ~: ご飯を食べたあとで、散歩します。(After eating, I'll go for a walk.)
n5-45:
The idea in one line
The plain form is the casual way of speaking, made by dropping 「です・ます」, and it's also the basic form that many sentence patterns attach to. Every word has four shapes, just like English “go / don't go / went / didn't go”: present affirmative, present negative, past affirmative, past negative.
When to use it
Talking with people you knowAmong family and friends you don't use ます; you just use the plain form.
・昨日、映画を見た。(I watched a movie yesterday.)
Connecting to patternsEven in a very polite sentence, you often need to switch to the plain form in the middle before attaching the next pattern.
・明日は雨が降ると思います。(I think it will rain tomorrow.)
How to form it: first, check which type the verb is
Group 1 (godan verbs)
Negative: change the last sound to the あ-row sound of the same row, then add ない. 行く → change く to か → 行かない
Past: formed the same way as the て-form, but with た instead of て. 行って → 行った飲んで → 飲んだ
Past negative: change the 「い」 of ない to 「かった」. 行かない → 行かなかった
The whole set at a glance: 買う／買わない／買った／買わなかった
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): the easiest. Drop 「る」 and add ない, た, or なかった.
食べる／食べない／食べた／食べなかった
見る／見ない／見た／見なかった
Group 3 (only two verbs, just memorize them)
する／しない／した／しなかった
来る／来ない／来た／来なかった（くる／こない／きた／こなかった）
“Noun + する” verbs like 勉強する change just like する: 勉強しない, 勉強した, 勉強しなかった.
How adjectives and nouns change
い-adjectives: for the negative, change the final い to くない; for the past, change い to かった.
高い／高くない／高かった／高くなかった
な-adjectives: add だ, じゃない, だった, or じゃなかった.
静かだ／静かじゃない／静かだった／静かじゃなかった
Nouns: they change exactly like な-adjectives.
学生だ／学生じゃない／学生だった／学生じゃなかった
A handy pattern: whether it's a verb, adjective or noun, the negative always ends in 「ない」, and it always becomes past the same way: ない → なかった. Remember this and you barely need to memorize the fourth form (past negative) separately.
Compare with ます・です
行きます → 行く行きません → 行かない
行きました → 行った行きませんでした → 行かなかった
い-adjectives are the easiest: just drop です. 高かったです → 高かった
For な-adjectives and nouns, replace です with だ. 学生です → 学生だ
Easy mistakes
・For Group 1 verbs ending in う, the negative uses 「わ」: 買わない, not 買あない.
・The negative of ある is ない, not あらない.
・The past of 行く is 行った, not 行いた.
・As soon as いい conjugates, it switches to a よ- stem: よくない, よかった, よくなかった.
・きれい and 有名 look like い-adjectives but are actually な-adjectives: say きれいじゃない, not きれくない.
・You can't add だ after an い-adjective: just say 高い, not 高いだ.
・Ending a noun or な-adjective with 「だ」 sounds a bit blunt. In chat with friends, people often drop だ or add よ, for example 学生だよ.
・When you ask a friend a question in the plain form, you usually don't add か; just raise your intonation at the end: 明日、来る？(Are you coming tomorrow?)
What to learn next
When the plain form attaches to a pattern, pay special attention to the 「だ」 of nouns and な-adjectives: sometimes it stays, sometimes it's dropped, and sometimes it becomes な.
静かだと思う。(I think it's quiet: だ stays)
静かでしょう。(It's probably quiet: だ is dropped)
学生なの？(You're a student?: だ becomes な)
We'll go through these one by one in the lessons on 「～でしょう」 and the nominalizer 「の」.
n5-50:
The idea in one line
English says "there is" for everything: there's a book on the desk, there's a cat in the room. Japanese adds one step: use あります for things and plants, and います for people and animals. Ask yourself whether it's alive and can move on its own, and you'll know which one to use.
How to build it
Place + に + thing or person + が + あります / います
に marks the location, like "in" or "at"; が marks what is there.
・引き出しにハサミがあります。(There are scissors in the drawer.)
・教室に生徒がいます。(There are students in the classroom.)
あります or います?
あります Things, plants, buildings. A tree is alive, but it doesn't move around, so it takes あります.
・机の上に本があります。(There's a book on the desk.)
・庭に大きい木があります。(There's a big tree in the yard.)
います People and animals. Fish and insects count too.
・部屋に猫がいます。(There's a cat in the room.)
・川に魚がいます。(There are fish in the river.)
Patterns you'll hear most
Where something is To say where something is, put it first with は. The location still takes に.
・ハサミは引き出しにあります。(The scissors are in the drawer.)
・トイレはどこにありますか。(Where is the restroom?)
Not there Change ます to ません: あります → ありませんいます → いません
・教室に誰もいません。(There's no one in the classroom.)
I have ~ For "having" family or time, Japanese also uses these same two words.
・姉が一人います。(I have one older sister.)
・明日、時間がありますか。(Are you free tomorrow?)
Easy mistakes
・People always take います: "There's a teacher" is 先生がいます; saying 「先生があります」 is wrong. Family works the same way: 妹がいます.
・Plants take あります; fish and insects, however tiny, take います because they're alive.
・For things, people and animals "being somewhere", the location takes に: it's 部屋に猫がいます, not 部屋で猫がいます.
・Exception: when what "exists" is an activity or event (テスト, パーティー, 会議…), it means "is held there", and the location takes で: あした学校でテストがあります。(There's a test at school tomorrow.)
・何も ("nothing") and 誰も ("no one") must always be followed by a negative: ありません / いません.
Don't mix it up with similar patterns
Same park, but look at what comes after:
Existing takes に: 公園に犬がいます。(There's a dog in the park.)
Doing an action takes で: 公園で犬と遊びます。(I play with the dog in the park.)
An event being held takes で: 公園でお祭りがあります。(There's a festival at the park.)
Quick test: if it ends in あります / います and a thing, person or animal simply exists there, use に. If it ends in an action verb, or what "exists" is an activity or event, use で.
What to learn next
Add a count: 猫が二匹います。(There are two cats.)
Also, the います inside ～ています ("is ~ing") is the very same word you learned today.
n5-52:
The idea in one line
「〜ています」 covers roughly "is ~ing," "is in the state of ~," "has already ~ed (and still is that way)," and "has been ~ing lately." The key point is that it doesn't describe a single moment but an ongoing state: an action in progress, a result that remains, or something you've been doing these days.
How to build it
Change the verb to its て-form, then add います. If you need a refresher on forming the て-form, go back to the "て-form" lesson.
食べる → 食べて → 食べています
読む → 読んで → 読んでいます
する → して → しています
来る → 来て → 来ています（きています）
Three meanings
In progress The action is happening right now, often together with "今".
・今、洗濯しています。(I'm doing laundry right now.)
・弟はテレビを見ています。(My younger brother is watching TV.)
Result remains Some actions are over in an instant, such as getting married, a door or window opening (開く), or moving to live somewhere. With these verbs, ています doesn't mean "in the middle of"; it means "it happened, and it's still in that state." To describe how something is now, use an intransitive verb like 開く: say 窓が開いています, not 窓を開けています (which sounds more like "someone is opening the window").
・窓が開いています。(The window is open.)
・京都に住んでいます。(I live in Kyoto.)
・姉は結婚しています。(My older sister is married.)
Lately / these days Something you've kept doing recently or for the current period, like a job, your current situation, or a recently formed habit.
・毎朝走っています。(I've been running every morning.)
・父は銀行で働いています。(My father works at a bank.)
Easy mistakes
・結婚しています means "is married," not "is having a wedding right now." Likewise, 住んでいます means "live in"; use it whenever you say where you live now. 京都に住みます would instead mean "I'm going to live in Kyoto (in the future)."
・"I know" is 知っています, but "I don't know" is 知りません, not 知っていません.
・If someone asks もう食べましたか, the "not yet" answer is まだ食べていません, not まだ食べませんでした.
・The 来 in 来ています is read き.
・Among friends, the い is often dropped: 食べています becomes 食べてる. Don't be thrown when you hear it.
Don't mix it up with similar patterns
ます and ています are the pair people confuse most. Compare the same action:
本を読みます。(I read books: a regular habit, or I'm about to read.)
本を読んでいます。(I'm reading a book.)

来月結婚します。(I'm getting married next month.)
もう結婚しています。(I'm already married.)

Both can express habits, but the feel is different:
毎日コーヒーを飲みます。(I drink coffee every day: a general habit or fact.)
最近、毎朝走っています。(I've been running every morning lately: something ongoing these days.)
Quick test: for something happening right now, a state that remains ("already ~ed" / "is in the state of ~"), or "I've been doing this lately," use ています. For a general habit or something you're about to do, use ます.
What to learn next
When you study intransitive and transitive verbs, you'll often see forms like ドアが閉まっています (the door is closed), the "result remains" use. It will make more sense when you compare it with what you learned here.
n5-48:
The idea in one line
In English we say “the book I borrowed last week” or “the school my younger brother goes to”. The describing clause comes after the noun, joined by “that” or “which”. Japanese puts the whole clause before the noun, and there is no “that” or “which” to add. Just put the clause straight in front of the noun.
先週借りた本 (the book I borrowed last week)
How to connect it
The clause that describes the noun uses the plain form, the way you'd talk with friends, without ます or です. Then you attach it directly to the noun.
本を借りました → 借りた → 先週借りた本
VerbsThe form you pick changes the meaning:
見る映画 (a movie I'm going to watch)
見ない映画 (a movie I don't watch)
見た映画 (a movie I watched)
見なかった映画 (a movie I didn't watch)
見ている映画 (a movie I'm watching)
い-adjective endingsAttach directly.
髪が長い人 (a person with long hair)
な-adjective endingsIn the present affirmative, change だ to な.
交通が便利だ → 交通が便利な町 (a town with convenient transport)
It is not 「便利だ町」.
Noun endingsIn the present affirmative, change だ to の, not な.
母が日本人だ → 母が日本人の友達 (a friend whose mother is Japanese)
It is not 「日本人だ友達」, and it is not 「日本人な友達」 either.
In the past or negative, nothing changes. Just attach directly:
静かじゃない部屋 (a room that isn't quiet)
昔、先生だった人 (a person who used to be a teacher)
How you'll hear it most
The whole “noun + clause” chunk works as one big noun inside a sentence. To be polite, only the end of the sentence needs です・ます. The clause before the noun stays in plain form.
・これは母が作ったケーキです。 (This is a cake my mother made.)
・昨日見た映画はおもしろかったです。 (The movie I watched yesterday was interesting.)
・日本で行きたい所はどこですか。 (Where is the place you want to go in Japan?)
・駅の近くにある店で会いましょう。 (Let's meet at the shop near the station.)
Where people slip up
・English needs “that” or “of” in the middle, so it's tempting to add の. 「借りたの本」 is wrong. Say 借りた本.
・Don't use ます inside the clause. 「買いました本」 is wrong. Say 買った本. Leave the politeness to the です・ます at the end of the sentence.
・The person doing the action inside the clause takes が, not は. 「私は作った料理」 is wrong. Say 私が作った料理 (the food I made). You may also see 私の作った料理, where が is swapped for の. The meaning is the same.
・な-adjectives change to な (静かな部屋) and nouns change to の (医者の父, a father who is a doctor). Don't mix them up.
・見た映画 means “a movie I watched”, while 見る映画 means “a movie I'm going to watch or usually watch”. Pick the right tense.
Telling look-alikes apart
Even when you're talking about the same book, the word before it decides whether you need の:
私の本 (my book): a noun comes before, so add の
私が買った本 (the book I bought): a verb comes before, so attach directly
新しい本 (a new book): an い-adjective comes before, so attach directly
Quick test: look at the word right in front of the noun. If it's a noun, add の. If it's a verb or an い-adjective, attach directly. Don't worry about the “that” or “of” you'd say in English.
What to learn next
「〜とき」 (when ~) uses exactly the same connections: 日本へ行くとき (when I go to Japan), 子どものとき (when I was a child).
n5-49:
The idea in one line
「の」 can wrap an action up into “a thing”, much like the English “-ing” in “taking photos”. English lets you say “I like swimming”, because “swimming” already works as a noun. In Japanese, a bare verb can't do that. You first add 「の」 after the verb, which turns it into “swimming / the act of swimming”. Only then can は, が or を follow.
How to connect it
Use the verb in its plain form (the dictionary form, like 泳ぐ and 撮る, not the ます-stem 泳ぎ and 撮り), then add 「の」 directly.
泳ぐ → 泳ぐの (swimming)
写真を撮る → 写真を撮るの (taking photos)
To say “not doing something”, use the ない form plus の: 食べない → 食べないの (not eating)
How you'll hear it most
のが好き・上手Talk about whether you like or are good at doing something. When what follows is 好き, 嫌い, 上手 or 下手, use 「が」.
・小説を読むのが好きです。 (I like reading novels.)
・母は料理を作るのが上手です。 (My mother is good at cooking.)
・私は歌うのが下手です。 (I'm bad at singing.)
のは＋impressionName an activity first, then say what you think of it.
・写真を撮るのは楽しいです。 (Taking photos is fun.)
・日本語を話すのは難しいです。 (Speaking Japanese is difficult.)
・朝ご飯を食べないのは体によくないです。 (Not eating breakfast is bad for your health.)
のを＋actionMake “that thing” the object of an action.
・宿題を出すのを忘れました。 (I forgot to hand in my homework.)
・田中さんが来るのを待っています。 (I'm waiting for Tanaka to come.)
Where people slip up
・Dropping the verb in as-is, the way English does with “-ing”: 泳ぐが好きです is wrong. Say 泳ぐのが好きです.
・You can't use the ます form before の. 「泳ぎますのが好きです」 is wrong. Keep the politeness in です at the end of the sentence.
・If the word is already a noun, don't add の: 音楽が好きです (I like music). Don't say 「音楽のが好きです」.
・Before 好き and 上手, use 「が」. Don't switch to 「を」 just because “swimming” feels like the object of “like”.
・This 「の」 is different from the one in 私の本 (my book). There, a noun comes before it and it means “'s / of”. Here, a verb comes before it and it means “the act of”.
Telling look-alikes apart
「こと」 can also turn an action into “a thing”, and in many cases either one works:
本を読むのが好きです。／本を読むことが好きです。 (Both mean “I like reading books”; こと sounds a bit more formal.)

But some places allow only one of them:
For scenes you see or hear, only の works: 田中さんが走っているのを見ました。 (I saw Tanaka running.)
For a sentence ending like “A is ~”, use こと: 私の趣味は写真を撮ることです。 (My hobby is taking photos.) You can't say 「撮るのです」 here.
Quick test: use の for things you see or hear with your own eyes and ears. Use こと when “is doing ~” sits at the end of the sentence. For likes and for “fun or not”, both work, and の sounds the most natural in everyday speech.
What to learn next
Once you're comfortable with 「こと」, the next step is 〜ことができる = can do ~ / be able to do ~: 私は泳ぐことができます。 (I can swim.)
n5-57:
The idea in one line
English uses "want" for two different things: wanting a thing (I want a new phone) and wanting to do something (I want to go to Japan). Japanese keeps these apart. Use 「欲しい」 for things and 「〜たい」 for actions.
How to form it
Wanting a thingNoun + が欲しいです
・新しいスマホが欲しいです。(I want a new phone.)
・誕生日に時計が欲しいです。(For my birthday, I want a watch.)
Wanting to do somethingFirst put the verb in ます form, drop 「ます」, then add 「たいです」.
行きます → drop ます → 行きたい
飲みます → 飲みたい食べます → 食べたい見ます → 見たい
します → したい来ます → 来たい（きたい）
・日本へ行きたいです。(I want to go to Japan.)
・温泉に入りたいです。(I want to soak in a hot spring.)
Watch the particles
Before 欲しい, use が.
With 〜たい, wherever the verb would normally take 「を」, you can keep 「を」 or switch to 「が」. Both are correct:
水を飲みたいです。／水が飲みたいです。(I want to drink water.)
Other particles can't be swapped; they stay as they were: 友達に会いたいです。(I want to see my friend.) Here 「に」 can't be changed to が.
Negative and past: they conjugate like い-adjectives
欲しい and 〜たい both end in 「い」, so they change exactly like い-adjectives:
欲しいです → 欲しくないです (don't want) 欲しかったです (wanted, back then)
行きたいです → 行きたくないです (don't want to go) 行きたかったです (wanted to go, back then)
・今日は何もしたくないです。(I don't want to do anything today.)
Common mistakes
・たい attaches to the ます stem, not the dictionary form. 「行くたい」 is wrong; say 行きたい.
・たい is already an adjective, so you can't add ます after it. Say 行きたいです, not 「行きたいます」. For the negative, say 行きたくないです, not 「行きたいません」.
・来たい is read きたい.
・Both of these express your own feelings. Saying 「田中さんは車が欲しいです」 directly sounds odd to Japanese ears, because you can't feel what someone else feels. When talking about other people, say 田中さんは車が欲しいと言っていました。(Tanaka said he wants a car.) Asking the other person in a question is fine: 何が欲しいですか。(What do you want?)
・Asking a teacher, boss, or customer 「〜たいですか」 directly sounds like you're prying into what they want to do, which is not very polite. To offer someone a drink, コーヒーはいかがですか。 or コーヒーを飲みませんか。 is more appropriate.
Telling similar-looking ones apart
Take one cup of coffee:
コーヒーが欲しいです。 (I want coffee: what you want is the thing, coffee.)
コーヒーが飲みたいです。 (I want to drink coffee: what you want to do is the action, drinking.)
English speakers most often get stuck on "I want to go to Japan." The word "want" is right there, but what you really want to do is the action "go", so say 日本へ行きたいです。 You can't use 欲しい.
Quick test: take out "want" and look at what follows. If it's a noun (a phone, coffee), use 欲しい. If it's "to" + a verb (to go, to eat, to see), use たい.
What to learn next
It combines with 「に (purpose)」: 映画を見に行きたいです。(I want to go see a movie.) Later you'll also learn how to say what someone else wants: 欲しがっている and 〜たがっている.
n5-59:
The idea in one line
「〜とき」 means "when ~" / "at the time of ~". The difference from English is that Japanese puts 「とき」 at the very end, and everything before it describes that "time", for example 暇なとき (when I'm free) and 子どものとき (when I was a child).
How to form it
「とき」 is itself a noun, so what comes before it attaches exactly the way you've learned for describing a noun.
Verbs: attach directly
行く → 行くとき行かない → 行かないとき行った → 行ったとき
い-adjectives: attach directly
忙しい → 忙しいとき寒い → 寒いとき
な-adjectives: add 「な」
暇 → 暇なとき元気 → 元気なとき
Nouns: add 「の」
子ども → 子どものとき休み → 休みのとき
・暇なとき、何をしますか。(What do you do when you're free?)
・子どものとき、よくこの公園で遊びました。(When I was a child, I often played in this park.)
・わからないとき、先生に聞きます。(When I don't understand, I ask my teacher.)
・時間がないとき、コンビニでご飯を買います。(When I don't have time, I buy a meal at a convenience store.)
The most important point: 行くとき vs 行ったとき
Whether the verb before 「とき」 is in dictionary form or た form doesn't depend on whether the whole sentence is present or past. It depends on whether the action is finished at that point in time.
Dictionary form + ときThe action isn't finished yet: you're about to do it, or you're in the middle of it.
た form + ときThe action is already finished.
・出かけるとき、「いってきます」と言います。(When you leave the house, you say 「いってきます」.)
・家に帰ったとき、「ただいま」と言います。(When you get back home, you say 「ただいま」.)
Here's another pair. Both end in the past tense, but the meanings differ a lot:
・日本に行くとき、辞書を買いました。(When I was going to Japan, I bought a dictionary: before leaving or on the way.)
・日本に行ったとき、辞書を買いました。(When I went to Japan, I bought a dictionary: after arriving in Japan.)
The first sentence is clearly about the past, yet it still uses 行く, because at the moment of buying the dictionary, you hadn't arrived in Japan yet.
Common mistakes
・Nouns need の: 子どものとき, not 子どもとき.
・な-adjectives need な, and you can't use だ: 暇なとき, not 暇とき, and not 暇だとき. Only in the past can you say 暇だったとき.
・Do not add の after verbs and い-adjectives. Many learners, thinking of the noun pattern, say 「行くのとき」, which is wrong.
・Don't use ます or です before 「とき」: 行くとき、〜ます is already polite. Don't say 「行きますとき」. Politeness is decided at the end of the sentence.
・When talking about habits or conditions, は is often added to make 「ときは」, as in 寒いときは、温かいお茶を飲みます。(When it's cold, I drink hot tea.) It sounds very natural.
Telling similar-looking ones apart
The 〜まえに and 〜たあとで you've learned also involve time, and they're easy to mix up with 「とき」.
とき = at that very time, during that process: 家に帰るとき、パンを買いました。(I bought bread on my way home.)
まえに = just "before that", no matter how long before: 家に帰るまえに、パンを買いました。(I bought bread before going home.)
たとき = the point when something is finished: 家に帰ったとき、母はいませんでした。(When I got home, my mother wasn't there.)
たあとで = after finishing, then doing the next thing: 家に帰ったあとで、宿題をしました。(After I got home, I did my homework.)
Quick test: to say "at that moment", use とき. To talk about order, use まえに or あとで.
What to learn next
When the action before 「とき」 means "when it's already done", you use the た form, so make sure you're comfortable with た形 conjugation. Later, at N4, you'll learn 〜たら (if ~, after ~), which you'll often compare with 「とき」.
n5-53:
The idea in one line
In English, listing a series of actions is easy: “I get up, brush my teeth, and leave,” with just commas and “and.” Japanese can't chain verbs like that. Every verb before the last one has to change to て形, which works like “...and then...”. Only the last verb decides whether the sentence is present or past, and whether it is polite or casual.
How to form it
Verbs: just use the て form (see the 「て形」 lesson for how to form it).
起きる → 起きて行く → 行って飲む → 飲んで
い-adjectives: replace the final 「い」 with 「くて」.
安い → replace い with くて → 安くていい → よくて (memorize this exception)
な-adjectives and nouns: just add 「で」.
静か → 静かで学生 → 学生で
When to use it
In sequenceYou finish one thing, then do the next, and you list them in the order they happen.
・朝起きて、歯を磨いて、出かけます。 (I get up in the morning, brush my teeth, then head out.)
・昨日は家に帰って、すぐ寝ました。 (Yesterday I got home and went straight to bed.)
Listing several featuresWhen describing a person or thing, you give two features at once, like “both ... and ...” in English.
・この店は安くて、おいしいです。 (This restaurant is both cheap and tasty.)
・私は台湾人で、大学生です。 (I'm Taiwanese, and I'm a university student.)
Manner or meansThe first action is the “way” or “state” in which the second action happens.
・歩いて駅へ行きます。 (I go to the station on foot.)
・傘を持って出かけます。 (I go out with an umbrella.)
ReasonThe first part is the cause, and the second part is usually a feeling, a state, or “can't do ~”.
・ニュースを聞いて、びっくりしました。 (I heard the news and was shocked.)
・頭が痛くて、何もできませんでした。 (My head hurt, so I couldn't do anything.)
Common mistakes
・Tense and politeness are decided only by the last verb: 昨日、デパートへ行って、靴を買いました。 (Yesterday I went to the department store and bought shoes.) The earlier 行って doesn't change to past; the past tense is left to the final 買いました.
・The い-adjective form is 安くて, not 「安いて」; and いい becomes よくて. The な-adjective form is 静かで, not 「静かくて」.
・When you list two features, they should ideally point the same way (both good or both bad). For one good and one bad, like “cheap but not tasty,” use が instead: この店は安いですが、おいしくないです。 (This restaurant is cheap, but the food isn't good.)
・When て expresses a reason, what follows can't be “let's ~,” “please ~,” or “I want to ~.” To say “It's raining, so let's take a taxi,” switch to から: 雨が降っているから、タクシーで行きましょう。
Don't confuse it with these
All three talk about what you did on the weekend:
映画を見て、ご飯を食べました。 (I watched a movie, then ate: simply telling things in order)
映画を見てから、ご飯を食べました。 (I ate only after the movie ended: the order is emphasized)
映画を見たり、ご飯を食べたりしました。 (I watched a movie, ate, and so on: just examples, order doesn't matter, and I may have done other things too)
Quick tip: use 「て」 to tell things one by one in order, 「てから」 to stress “only after finishing A, do B,” and 「たり～たり」 to give a few examples at random.
What to learn next
Many other common patterns attach to the て form, for example “please ~”: ちょっと待ってください。 (Please wait a moment.) and “be ~ing”: 今、ご飯を食べています。 (I'm eating right now.)
n5-55:
The idea in one line
「〜てください」 is the Japanese way to say “please do ~,” and 「〜ないでください」 means “please don't ~.” When a friend says “Wait a moment, please,” that's ちょっと待ってください, and when a sign says “No photos, please,” that's 写真を撮らないでください. Both use these two patterns.
When to use it
Asking someone for a favorYou ask the other person to do something for you.
・もう一度言ってください。 (Please say it once more.)
InstructionsYou'll hear this a lot from teachers in class, from doctors giving advice, and when steps are being explained.
・ここに名前を書いてください。 (Please write your name here.)
・この薬を毎日飲んでください。 (Please take this medicine every day.)
Asking someone not to do somethingIt works for reminders, prohibitions, and reassurance.
・心配しないでください。 (Please don't worry.)
・教室で食べないでください。 (Please don't eat in the classroom.)
How to form it: please do ~
First change the verb to its て form (the form from the 「て形」 lesson), then add ください directly.
Group 1 (godan verbs): the last kana decides how it changes.
・Verbs ending in う, つ, る → って: 待つ → 待って → 待ってください
・Verbs ending in む, ぶ, ぬ → んで: 読む → 読んでください
・Verbs ending in く → いて: 書く → 書いてください
・Verbs ending in ぐ → いで: 急ぐ → 急いでください
・Verbs ending in す → して: 話す → 話してください
・Exception: 行く → 行ってください (not 行いて)
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop 「る」 and add 「て」.
食べる → 食べてください見る → 見てください
Group 3 (する・来る): する → してください来る → 来てください (きてください)
How to form it: please don't do ~
First change the verb to its ない form, then add でください.
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the matching あ-row sound and add ない.
撮る → change る to ら → 撮らない → 撮らないでください
書く → 書かないでください
Verbs ending in う change to 「わ」: 吸う → 吸わないでください
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop 「る」 and add ない.
忘れる → 忘れない → 忘れないでください
Group 3 (する・来る): する → しないでください来る → 来ないでください (こないでください)
Common mistakes
・“Please don't” is ない followed by で: 見ないでください, not 「見ないてください」, and there is no such form as 「見ませんでください」.
・Verbs ending in う change to 「わ」 in the ない form: 吸わない, 買わない, not 「吸あない」.
・来る is read two different ways: 来てください is read きて, while 来ないでください is read こないで.
・Although it's translated as “please,” it is really telling the other person to do something. When asking a teacher or a boss for a favor, 〜てくださいませんか (could you please ~?) sounds more polite.
・Among friends, ください is often dropped: ちょっと待って。 (Wait a sec.) 見ないで。 (Don't look.)
・Shop staff often say 少々お待ちください (please wait a moment) to customers. That's a more polite form of a different kind, not the て form from this lesson, so just learn to recognize it when you hear it.
Don't confuse it with these
When ください comes after a thing, it means “please give me”; when it comes after a verb in て form, it means “please do.”
・水をください。 (Please give me some water.)
・水を飲んでください。 (Please drink some water.)
Quick tip: “noun + をください” asks someone for an item, while “て form + ください” asks someone to do an action.
n5-65:
The idea in one sentence
In English we say "a sheet of paper" or "a piece of cake", with a little word between the number and the thing. Japanese does this too, and these words are called counters. The choice is based on shape, much like in English: flat, thin things take 枚, and long, thin things take 本. To say "about," add くらい after the amount.
Learn these counters first
つWorks for most things. It's the all-purpose choice when you don't know which counter to use, and it's very common when ordering food. Learn 1 to 10 separately: ひとつ、ふたつ、みっつ、よっつ、いつつ、むっつ、ななつ、やっつ、ここのつ、とお. Past 10, you don't use つ anymore.
・りんごを3つ買いました。(I bought 3 apples.)
人For counting people. 1 and 2 people are special: ひとり、ふたり. From 3 on it's さんにん, and 4 people is よにん.
・家族は4人です。(There are 4 people in my family.)
本Long, thin things: pens, bottles, umbrellas, bananas.
・鉛筆を1本貸してください。(Please lend me a pencil.)
枚Thin, flat things: paper, stamps, shirts, plates.
・切手を5枚ください。(Five stamps, please.)
匹Small animals like cats, dogs and fish.
・うちに猫が2匹います。(I have 2 cats at home.)
Other common ones: 冊 for books, 台 for machines like cars and TVs, and 杯 for cups or glasses of drinks.
How to put them in a sentence
The most natural order is: thing + を (or が) + amount + verb. The amount goes right before the verb, and you don't add another particle after it.
In English you say "buy three apples," but in Japanese it's りんごを3つ買います: the thing comes first, then the amount.
To ask "how many," replace the number with 何: 何人 (なんにん), 何本 (なんぼん), 何枚 (なんまい). For things counted with つ, ask いくつ.
・兄弟は何人いますか。(How many siblings do you have?)
Telling time
時 means "o'clock," and 時間 means "hours (duration)": 2時 is two o'clock, and 2時間 is two hours.
The reading of 分 (minutes) changes, so memorize it: いっぷん、にふん、さんぷん、よんぷん、ごふん、ろっぷん、ななふん、はっぷん、きゅうふん、じゅっぷん.
・毎日7時間寝ます。(I sleep 7 hours every day.)
・駅まで歩いて10分くらいです。(It's about a 10-minute walk to the station.)
・1時間くらいかかります。(It takes about an hour.)
くらい and ぐらい mean the same thing, so you can use either one.
Common mistakes
・The position of "about" is the opposite of English: in English "about an hour" puts "about" first, but in Japanese it's 1時間くらい, with くらい after the amount.
・Don't add another を after the amount: it's りんごを3つ買いました, not 「りんごを3つを買いました」.
・The readings of 本 and 匹 change: 1本いっぽん, 3本さんぼん, 6本ろっぽん; 1匹いっぴき, 3匹さんびき.
・1 and 2 people are ひとり and ふたり, not 「いちにん」 or 「ににん」.
・4 o'clock is 4時 (よじ) and 9 o'clock is 9時 (くじ). Don't read them as よんじ or きゅうじ.
・Always use 人 to count people, never つ.
Telling similar words apart
English uses "about" for everything, but Japanese depends on what comes before it:
くらい follows how long or how much: 3時間くらい待ちました。 (I waited about 3 hours.)
ごろ follows a point in time, like a time of day or a date: 3時ごろ着きます。 (I'll arrive around 3 o'clock.)
In casual speech you'll also hear 「3時くらい」, but the reverse, 「3時間ごろ」, is wrong.
Quick rule: use くらい for "about how long / how much," and ごろ for "around what time."
What to learn next
Add だけ after an amount to mean "only this much": 1つだけください。 (Just one, please.)
n5-66:
The idea in one sentence
Adverbs are little words placed before a verb or adjective to add "how much," "how many," or "how often". The "very" in "very tasty," the "often" in "I often go," and the "not much" in "I don't drink much" are all adverbs in Japanese too. This card covers three groups: degree, quantity, and frequency.
When to use them
Degree: veryとても = very, extremely. It goes before an adjective.
・とても楽しかったです。(It was really fun.)
・このラーメンはとてもおいしいです。(This ramen is very tasty.)
Quantity: a lotたくさん = a lot, many. It's about "amount." Put it before a verb, or use 「たくさんの＋noun」.
・昨日はたくさん食べました。(I ate a lot yesterday.)
・駅にたくさんの人がいます。(There are a lot of people at the station.)
Frequency: how oftenFrom most often to never, they line up like this:
いつも＞よく＞ときどき＞たまに＞あまり～ない＞全然～ない
・いつも7時に起きます。(I always get up at 7.)
・よくこの店に来ます。(I often come to this shop.)
・ときどき料理をします。(I sometimes cook.)
・たまに映画を見ます。(I occasionally watch movies.)
・テレビはあまり見ません。(I don't watch TV much.)
・お酒は全然飲みません。(I don't drink alcohol at all.)
The other meaning of よくBesides "often," よく can also mean "well, thoroughly." The verb after it tells you which meaning it is.
・昨日はよく寝ました。(I slept well yesterday.)
・すみません、よく分かりません。(Sorry, I don't quite understand.)
Common mistakes
・あまり and 全然 must be followed by a negative: 「あまり好きです」 is wrong. Say あまり好きじゃないです (I don't like it much).
・To say "not very tasty," don't just put a negative after 「とても」. Use あまりおいしくないです.
・English "very" and "a lot" are close, but Japanese keeps them apart: use とても for "very tasty" and たくさん for "a lot of people." Saying 「とても人がいます」 is wrong. Say 人がたくさんいます.
・You may hear young Japanese people say 「全然大丈夫」 (totally fine). That's casual speech. For textbooks and exams, stick to 「全然＋negative」.
・An adverb usually goes right before the verb or adjective it modifies: よく行きます. Don't put よく at the end of the sentence.
Telling similar words apart
あまり～ない = not very much, but a little still happens: お酒はあまり飲みません。 (I don't drink much; I have a little now and then.)
全然～ない = not at all, none whatsoever: お酒は全然飲みません。 (I never drink alcohol.)
If someone asks よく行きますか。 (Do you go often?), answer いいえ、あまり行きません。 if you go once in a while, and いいえ、全然行きません。 only if you never go.
Quick rule: use あまり for "not much" and 全然 for "not at all." Both need a negative after them.
What to learn next
Adjectives can also become adverbs, for example 早い → 早く: 早く起きます。 (I get up early.) Check out the lesson on using adjectives as adverbs next.
n5-60:
The idea in one line
「〜でしょう」works like English “probably…” or a tag question like “…, right?” With falling intonation, you're making a guess: “It'll probably rain tomorrow.” With rising intonation, you're checking with the listener: “It's delicious, isn't it?” It's the same phrase, but intonation decides which of the two meanings you get.
When to use it
Guess (falling ↓)You're not 100% sure, just inferring. It's often paired with たぶん (probably), and weather forecasts love it.
・明日はたぶん雨でしょう。(It'll probably rain tomorrow.)
・田中さんはもう帰ったでしょう。(Mr. Tanaka has probably already gone home.)
Confirmation (rising ↑)You think the other person probably feels the same way, so you check and wait for a nod.
・このケーキ、おいしいでしょう？(This cake is delicious, isn't it?)
・ほら、言ったでしょう？(See? Didn't I tell you?)
How to form it
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach it directly. Negative and past forms attach directly too.
降る → 降るでしょう降らない → 降らないでしょう降った → 降ったでしょう
寒い → 寒いでしょう寒くない → 寒くないでしょう
な-adjectives and nouns: drop 「だ」 first, then attach.
静かだ → drop だ → 静かでしょう
学生だ → 学生でしょう雨だ → 雨でしょう
The past 「だった」 stays: 雨だった → 雨だったでしょう
Common mistakes
・After a noun or な-adjective, you can't keep 「だ」: 学生でしょう is correct, and 「学生だでしょう」 is wrong.
・Don't put です before it: 寒いでしょう is enough, and 「寒いですでしょう」 is wrong. でしょう is already the “guessing version” of です, so it's polite as it is.
・Don't use it for your own plans. 「私は明日行くでしょう」 sounds odd. For your own plans, just say 明日行きます.
・The confirming 「でしょう？」 carries a “you surely know this, right?” feel, so it can sound a bit blunt toward a teacher or boss. To ask politely, use 〜でしょうか (“could you tell me…?”), for example 駅はどこでしょうか。 (Where is the station, please?)
・Among friends it's often shortened to でしょ？. Don't be thrown when you hear it; the meaning is the same.
Telling look-alikes apart
ましょう and でしょう both end in 「しょう」, but they mean completely different things:
・一緒に行きましょう。 (Let's go together: an invitation)
・田中さんも行くでしょう。 (Mr. Tanaka will probably go too: a guess)
They attach differently too: ましょう goes after the ます stem (行き＋ましょう), while でしょう goes after plain forms such as the dictionary form (行く＋でしょう).
でしょう？ and ね can both be rendered as “…, right?”, and the difference is whether the other person is feeling it with you:
・Two people walking outside together: 寒いですね。 (It's cold, isn't it?: you both feel it right now, and you're just chiming in)
・A friend has just come in from outside and you're indoors: 外、寒いでしょう？ (It's cold outside, isn't it?: you weren't out there, you're guessing they felt cold and want them to agree)
Quick test: “Let's do ~ together” is ましょう. “Probably ~” or “~, right?” is でしょう. When you both feel it right now and are just agreeing, use ね.
What to learn next
To express even less certainty, “might ~”, use 〜かもしれません: 明日は雨かもしれません。 (It might rain tomorrow.)
n5-61:
The idea in one line
「〜からです」means “because…”. When someone asks どうして (why), just state the reason and add 「からです」 to answer.
When to use it
Answering “why”The other person asks “why” first, and you give only the reason. There's no need to repeat what happened before.
・どうして休んだんですか。(Why did you take the day off?)
・熱があったからです。(Because I had a fever.)
・どうして日本語を勉強しているんですか。(Why are you studying Japanese?)
・日本のアニメが好きだからです。(Because I like Japanese anime.)
Adding the reason yourselfState one thing first, then add the reason in the next sentence.
・今日はパーティーに行きません。忙しいからです。(I'm not going to the party today. It's because I'm busy.)
How to form it
Before 「から」, use the form without ます or です (the plain form you'd use with friends), and let 「です」 at the end handle the politeness.
Verbs: attach directly.
行く → 行くからです行った → 行ったからです行かない → 行かないからです
い-adjectives: attach directly.
高い → 高いからです
な-adjectives and nouns: add 「だ」 in between.
好き → 好きだからです雨 → 雨だからです
Common mistakes
・Forgetting 「だ」 after な-adjectives and nouns: 好きからです and 雨からです are both wrong. Say 好きだからです and 雨だからです.
・The other way around, you can't add 「だ」 to い-adjectives: say 高いからです, not 高いだからです.
・Don't put ます before 「から」: 熱がありましたからです is wrong. Say 熱があったからです.
・English puts “because” at the start, before the reason, but Japanese 「から」 goes after the reason. Don't say から熱があった.
・With friends, just drop です: 熱があったから。 (Because I had a fever.)
Telling look-alikes apart
You've already learned the particle 「から」 (cause/reason). It means the same as 「からです」, and the difference is how the sentence is arranged. For the same event:
〜から、〜The reason comes first and the result second, all in one sentence.
・熱があったから、休みました。(I had a fever, so I took the day off.)
〜からですYou state the result first and add the reason as a separate sentence, or you answer only the reason when asked “why.”
・休みました。熱があったからです。(I took the day off. It's because I had a fever.)
Quick test: if the reason is followed by “so, …”, use 「〜から、」. If the reason itself ends the sentence, use 「〜からです」.
What to learn next
Put the result first and add 「のは」 to make the reason even clearer: 昨日休んだのは、熱があったからです。 (The reason I took yesterday off is that I had a fever.)
n5-67:
The idea in one line
This card covers three kinds of small words that make Japanese sound more like a real person talking:
Connectives = words like "and then, also, but, so." They go at the start of the second sentence and link two sentences together.
Response words = the little sounds you make when answering or starting to speak: "yes, no, um…, uh…"
Onomatopoeia and mimetic words = words that imitate a sound or a look, like "woof woof, splish-splash, beaming." Japanese uses these far more than English does.
Connectives: linking two sentences
It's simple: finish the first sentence, put a connective at the start of the second, and usually add a comma「、」after it.
そしてAnd, and then. Adds something in the same direction.
・この店は安いです。そして、おいしいです。(This shop is cheap, and the food is good too.)
それからAnd then, and also. Used for what happens next, or to add "and also…".
・パンを買いました。それから、牛乳も買いました。(I bought bread. Then I bought milk too.)
でもBut. What follows goes against what came before.
・日本語は難しいです。でも、おもしろいです。(Japanese is hard, but it's fun.)
だからSo. The first sentence is the reason, the second is the result.
・雨が降りました。だから、行きませんでした。(It rained, so I didn't go.)
Response words: answering and starting to speak
はい・いいえYes / no.
・「学生ですか。」「はい、そうです。」("Are you a student?" "Yes, I am.")
あのうUsed to get someone's attention or to start asking something, with a feel of "sorry to bother you."
・あのう、すみません。駅はどこですか。(Um… excuse me, where is the station?)
ええとUsed while you think as you speak, like English "um…" or "let's see…"
・ええと、三つください。(Um… three, please.)
Onomatopoeia and mimetic words: imitating sounds and appearances
Onomatopoeia imitates real sounds. Mimetic words use sound to describe a look or a feeling. They are usually two syllables repeated once.
・雨がザーザー降っています。(The rain is pouring down: onomatopoeia)
・犬がワンワン鳴いています。(The dog is barking woof woof: onomatopoeia)
・お腹がぺこぺこです。(I'm starving: mimetic)
Words like ゆっくり (slowly) and はっきり (clearly) are adverbs describing how an action is done. They don't imitate sounds, but they're just as common:
・ゆっくり話してください。(Please speak slowly.)
Common mistakes
・A connective goes at the start of the second sentence. You can't stick it in the middle: 高いです。でも、買います。 is fine, but you can't say 「高いでも買います」.
・Starting with だから and then 「言ったでしょう」, as in 「だから、言ったでしょう」, sounds like an impatient "I told you so!" Don't use it with people senior to you.
・When you just mean "so," in formal situations or with seniors, you can swap だから for the more polite ですから.
・The response word あのう (also written あの or あのー) shares its origin with the demonstrative あの (that + noun), but they're used differently. To get someone's attention, 「あの、すみません」 or a slightly drawn-out 「あのう…」 both work. The drawn-out version adds a bit more hesitation and a "sorry to bother you" feel.
・はい isn't only "yes." When your name is called, answering はい means "here" or "present."
Telling look-alikes apart
The same situation, "It's expensive, but I'll buy it," can be said two ways:
高いです。でも、買います。 (two sentences, with でも opening the second)
高いですが、買います。 / 高いけど、買う。 (one sentence, with が・けど attached to the end of the first half)

"It rained, so I didn't go" works the same way:
雨が降りました。だから、行きませんでした。 (two sentences, with だから)
雨が降ったから、行きませんでした。 (one sentence, with から attached after the reason)
Quick test: でも・だから stand at the start of a new sentence; が・けど・から attach to the end of the previous clause. Check whether there's a period before it and you'll know which one to use.
n4-17:
The short version
「〜ために」 means "in order to ～" or "for the sake of ～". Before it, put the goal you want to reach; after it, put what you deliberately do to reach it. For example, "I'm saving money in order to buy a car" is: 車を買うために、お金をためています。
How to form it
Verbs: use the dictionary form (the base form you find in a dictionary) + ために.
買う → 買うために勉強する → 勉強するために
Nouns: add の in between.
家族 → 家族のために健康 → 健康のために
When to use it
In order to do somethingAfter a verb, it states the goal you want to accomplish.
・日本語を勉強するために、日本へ来ました。（I came to Japan to study Japanese.）
・資格試験に合格するために、毎日図書館へ通っています。（To pass the certification exam, I go to the library every day.）
For someone's or something's benefitAfter a noun, it means "for the sake of it."
・家族のために、頑張って働いています。（I work hard for my family.）
・健康のために、毎朝走っています。（I run every morning for my health.）
Easy mistakes
・A noun must be followed by の: 家族ために is wrong; say 家族のために.
・Before ために, the verb is always in dictionary form, even when the whole sentence is about the past: 切符を買うために、早く家を出ました。（I left home early to buy a ticket.）You would never say 買ったために.
・The subject before and after is usually the same person: I do something myself for my own goal. For something like "so that my kids can go to college," where someone else is the one who achieves it, use ように instead: 子どもが大学に行けるように、働いています。（I work so that my kids can go to college.）
・Don't put a "can ～" expression (potential form) before it: 日本語が話せるために sounds unnatural; say 日本語が話せるように.
Telling similar forms apart
ために vs ように (purpose)
Both can be translated as "in order to," and the difference is the word before them.
・日本語の新聞を読むために、漢字を勉強しています。（I'm studying kanji in order to read Japanese newspapers.）
・日本語の新聞が読めるように、漢字を勉強しています。（I'm studying kanji so that I can read Japanese newspapers.）
Before ために comes "doing something" (読む); before ように comes "being able to ～" or "becoming a certain state" (読める).
ために (purpose) vs ために (cause)
The form is exactly the same, but it can also mean "because of."
・健康のために、野菜を食べています。（I eat vegetables for my health.）
・雨のために、試合が中止になりました。（Because of the rain, the game was canceled.）
