If what follows is something you choose to do, it means "in order to." If it's a result that already happened and wasn't a choice, it means "because of." The cause usage is rather formal; in everyday speech, "because" is usually expressed with から or ので.
Quick rule of thumb: if what comes before is "doing ～," use ために; if it's "being able to ～," use ように. If what follows is something you do on purpose, ために means "in order to"; if it's a result that happened, ために means "because of."
What to learn next
Change ために to 「ための＋noun」 to mean "a … for ～": 留学のためのお金をためています。（I'm saving money for studying abroad.）
n4-18:
The idea in one line
「〜ために」 goes after a cause and means "because of ~" or "due to ~". It's more formal and objective, like a subway announcement: "Due to a signal failure, trains will be delayed." You'll see it a lot in news, notices, and when explaining a situation to customers or your boss.
When to use it
News & noticesReporting what happened and what resulted.
・大雪のために、新幹線が止まりました。(Due to heavy snow, the Shinkansen stopped running.)
Formal explanationExplaining to a teacher, boss, or customer why something went wrong. It sounds objective, not like an excuse.
・電車が遅れたために、授業に間に合いませんでした。(Because the train was delayed, I didn't make it to class.)
The result that follows is usually something that has already happened and is out of your control, and often something bad, like a suspension, delay, or cancellation.
How to connect it
Put the "cause" before ために; almost any kind of word can go there. Just remember: nouns need an extra 「の」, and な-adjectives need an extra 「な」.
Verb た-form: 起きた → 起きたために
Verb ない-form: 足りない → 足りないために
In progress (ている): 工事をしている → 工事をしているために
State verbs (ある、いる、できる): 用事がある → 用事があるために
い-adjectives attach directly: 狭い → 狭いために
な-adjectives add な: 不便 → 不便なために
Nouns add の: 大雪 → 大雪のために
・道が狭いために、大きい車は通れません。(Because the road is narrow, large vehicles can't get through.)
・用事があるために、会議に出られません。(Because I have something to attend to, I can't take part in the meeting.)
The form you'll hear most
のためNotices and announcements often drop 「に」, giving 「〜のため」 or 「〜ため」. The meaning is the same, but it sounds even more formal.
・工事中のため、この道は通れません。(Road under construction; this road is closed.)
・台風のため、明日の授業は休みです。(Because of the typhoon, tomorrow's class is cancelled.)
Easy mistakes
・A noun must be followed by 「の」: say 大雪のために, not 大雪ために. A な-adjective needs 「な」: 不便なために.
・The second half can't be a request or an invitation such as 「～てください」 or 「～ましょう」.
×雨のために、傘を持っていってください。
○雨なので、傘を持っていってください。(Since it's raining, please take an umbrella.)
・The tone is stiff. If you tell a friend 雨のために行かない, it sounds like you're reading a press release. Between friends, just use 「から」.
Telling look-alikes apart
ために (purpose) vs ために (cause): It's the same word, so you tell them apart by what comes before it.
・日本へ行くために、お金をためています。(I'm saving money in order to go to Japan: purpose)
・雪が降ったために、電車が遅れました。(Because it snowed, the train was delayed: cause)
「Noun + のために」 can mean either. It depends on whether the noun is a goal you're aiming for or an event that has already happened:
・健康のために、毎朝走っています。(I run every morning for my health.)
・病気のために、学校を休みました。(Because of illness, I stayed home from school.)
Quick test: look at what comes before ために. If it's an action you control and are trying to achieve (e.g., the dictionary form of 合格する or 買う), it means "in order to". If it's a た-form, なかった, or ている, a state verb or adjective such as ある, いる, できる, or a noun for an event or state such as 台風, 病気, 事故, it means "because".
Be careful with the ない-form. After an action you control, it often means "in order not to ~", as in 遅れないために、早く家を出ます (I leave home early so as not to be late). It only means "because" after a state you can't control, such as 足りない or わからない.
ために vs から／ので: Take "It's raining, so the match is cancelled." You choose the wording by situation.
・雨だから、試合は中止だって。(It's raining, so I hear the match is cancelled: chatting with a friend)
・雨なので、試合は中止です。(Because it's raining, the match is cancelled: polite explanation)
・大雨のため、試合は中止になりました。(Due to heavy rain, the match has been cancelled: notice or news)
Quick test: use 「から」 with friends, 「ので」 for polite explanations, and 「ため（に）」 only in news, notices, and formal documents. When the second half asks the listener to do something, use ので or から, not ために.
n4-19:
The idea in one line
「〜ように」 means "so that I can ~" or "so that ~ doesn't happen". The key is that the result you want is not fully up to you, so all you can do is prepare. Think of "I set two alarms so I won't oversleep": you can't control whether you oversleep, but you can set the alarms.
How to connect it
The first half states the "state you hope for", and the second half states "what you do for it".
Hoping you'll be able to ~: potential form + ように. The potential form is the "can ~" form, for example 話す → 話せる (can speak).
話せる → 話せるように (so that I can speak)
Hoping something won't happen: ない-form + ように
忘れない → 忘れないように (so that I don't forget)
Verbs that aren't under your control by nature (わかる, 治る, 聞こえる, 〜になる): use the dictionary form + ように directly
治る → 治るように (so that it gets better)
When to use it
So that you can do itYou want to build a certain ability.
・日本語が話せるように、毎日練習しています。(I practice every day so that I can speak Japanese.)
So that it doesn't happenYou prepare ahead to avoid something unwanted.
・忘れないように、メモしておきます。(I'll write it down so I don't forget.)
・風邪をひかないように、暖かくして寝てください。(Please keep warm when you sleep so you don't catch a cold.)
So that someone else can ~The two halves can have different subjects: the first half is about someone else, and the second half is what you do.
・子供が食べられるように、小さく切ります。(I cut it small so the kids can eat it.)
・後ろの人にも聞こえるように、大きい声で話します。(I speak loudly so the people in the back can hear too.)
Easy mistakes
・To say "so that I can speak", you need the potential form 話せる. With plain 話す, the "can" meaning is gone.
・Before ように you always use the dictionary form or the ない-form, even when the whole sentence is about the past: 忘れないように、メモしました。 (I wrote it down so I wouldn't forget.) You never say 「忘れなかったように」.
・English uses "in order to" for everything, but Japanese doesn't use ように every time. For actions you can simply do whenever you choose, like buying, going, or studying, use ために (see below).
・ように itself has no politeness level. Politeness is decided by the sentence ending: メモします is polite, and メモする is the casual version.
Telling look-alikes apart
Both of these talk about "why I study Japanese":
日本で働くために、日本語を勉強しています。 (I study Japanese in order to work in Japan.)
日本人と話せるように、日本語を勉強しています。 (I study Japanese so that I can talk with Japanese people.)
"Going to Japan to work" is an action you can carry out once you decide to, so use ために. "Being able to talk with Japanese people" is an ability that only develops gradually after you study, and you can't just do it on command, so use ように. Saying 「話せるために」 would sound very unnatural.
One more point: when the two halves have different subjects, as in 子供が食べられるように、小さく切ります (the kids eat, I cut), ように is the right choice. ために usually has the same subject in both halves.
Quick test: if what comes before is "can ~" or "not ~", or something you can't control, use ように. If it's an action you can simply go and do when you want, use ために.
What to learn next
When ように is followed directly by する, the meaning becomes "try to ~": 毎日野菜を食べるようにしています。 (I try to eat vegetables every day.)
When ように on its own is followed by another action, it means "so that ~", while ようにする means "make an effort to ~". Don't mix the two up.
n4-20:
The short version
These two look alike. The difference is whether the ending is なる or する.
ようになる = “come to ~”. It describes a result: you couldn't before, and now you can.
ようにする = “I try to ~”. It describes your own ongoing effort: you're still working at it, and there's no guarantee you'll succeed every time.
English “become / come to” and “try to” line up neatly with なる and する.
ようになる: you couldn't before, now you can
Change in abilityThis is the most common use. It follows the potential form (the form meaning “can ~ / be able to ~”, like 話せる or 食べられる), or できる or わかる.
・練習して、日本語が少し話せるようになりました。(After practicing, I've become able to speak a little Japanese.)
・辛い物が食べられるようになった。(I can eat spicy food now.)
Change in habitThis follows the plain dictionary form, and it means “I've come to do this regularly”.
・日本に来てから、毎朝コーヒーを飲むようになった。(Since coming to Japan, I've started drinking coffee every morning.)
The change may come from deliberate practice, or it may happen without you noticing. Either way, the focus is on the result as it stands now.
ようにする: I try to do this
Things you want to do: dictionary form + ようにする　食べる → 食べるようにする
Things you want to avoid: ない form + ようにする　飲まない → 飲まないようにする
ようにしているA habit you've been keeping up lately. This is the most common form.
・毎日野菜を食べるようにしています。(I try to eat vegetables every day.)
・夜はコーヒーを飲まないようにしている。(I try not to drink coffee at night.)
ようにします“From now on I'll be careful.” It's often used in apologies and promises.
・これからは遅れないようにします。(From now on, I'll make sure not to be late.)
ようにしてくださいYou're asking the other person to make an effort. Doctors and teachers say this a lot.
・薬は毎日飲むようにしてください。(Please make sure to take your medicine every day.)
Common mistakes
・To say you've become able to do something, use the potential form before it. 日本語が話せるようになった means “I've become able to speak Japanese.” If you write 日本語を話すようになった, it means “I've started speaking Japanese,” which is about a habit, not an ability.
・When you use the potential form, the 「を」 before it usually changes to 「が」: 日本語が話せる.
・To say you've stopped doing something, Japanese people usually say 〜なくなる directly: 最近、テレビを見なくなった。 (I've stopped watching TV lately.) “見ないようになった” is less common.
・Adjectives and nouns can't take ようになる. “Get bigger” is 大きくなる, “become quiet” is 静かになる, and “become a teacher” is 先生になる. ようになる only attaches to verbs.
Telling similar patterns apart
Here are three ways to talk about getting up early:
ようになった = a result: 早く起きられるようになった。 (I've become able to get up early.)
ようにしている = ongoing effort: 早く起きるようにしている。 (I try to get up early.)
ことにした = a decision: 明日から早く起きることにした。 (I've decided to get up early starting tomorrow.)
One more: ことになった means “it has been decided / arranged that ~”. You didn't change by yourself, and it isn't your own effort: 来月から大阪で働くことになった。 (It's been decided that I'll work in Osaka starting next month.)
Quick rule: “have come to ~” takes ようになる, “try to ~” takes ようにする, “decide to ~” takes ことにする, and “it's been arranged that ~” takes ことになる.
What to learn next
If you drop なる or する, a standalone「ように」can mean “so that ~”: 忘れないように、メモします。 (I'll write it down so I don't forget.)
n4-8:
The short version
「のに」 is like English “even though ~, …” or “and yet …”. The first part is something certain, but the result doesn't match what you'd expect, so you feel “how can that be?” That feeling might be annoyance, surprise, or disappointment.
・薬を飲んだのに、熱が下がらない。(Even though I took medicine, my fever won't go down.)
When to use it
The first part is an established fact. It can be something that already happened, a current state, or something that is sure to happen. The second part is a result that “shouldn't really be that way”.
・約束したのに、彼は来なかった。(Even though we'd agreed, he didn't come.)
・この店は安いのに、おいしい。(This place is cheap, and yet it's delicious.)
・明日テストなのに、全然勉強していない。(Even though there's a test tomorrow, I haven't studied at all.)
The cheap-but-delicious example is a pleasant surprise, so のに isn't always a complaint. The key is “contrary to expectation”.
How to attach it
Use the plain form before it (the form without ます).
Verbs: 行った → 行ったのに来ない → 来ないのに
い-adjectives: 高い → 高いのに
な-adjectives and nouns: add 「な」 first.
静か → 静かなのに日曜日 → 日曜日なのに
For the past tense, use だった: 雨 → 雨だったのに
How you'll hear it most
Trailing offThe result is left unsaid, which leaves a “sigh” feeling. It's very common for complaints and regret.
・せっかく作ったのに…。(And I went to the trouble of making it…)
Common mistakes
・な-adjectives and nouns must have な: say 静かなのに, never 「静かのに」 or 「静かだのに」.
・After のに, you can't put your own intention, an invitation, a command, or a request. Things like “let's ~”, “I'll ~”, and “please ~” don't work.
　× 高いのに、買おう。
　○ 高いけど、買おう。 (It's expensive, but let's buy it.)
・のに carries emotion. If you say 「～のに」 directly to a superior or a customer, it can sound like you're complaining or blaming them, so watch the situation.
・There's another 「のに」 that looks identical and means “for / in order to do ~ (use, take)”: 駅へ行くのに30分かかる。 (It takes 30 minutes to get to the station.) It has no “even though” meaning. You can tell it apart if what follows is about time taken, something needed, or something used.
Telling similar patterns apart
のに = even though ~, … (emotional): 薬を飲んだのに、熱が下がらない。 (Even though I took medicine, my fever won't go down. How can that be?)
けど = although ~, but … (a plain contrast, calmer): 薬を飲んだけど、熱が下がらない。 (I took medicine, but my fever hasn't gone down.)
ても = even if ~, …, and it can talk about hypotheticals that haven't happened yet: 明日雨が降っても、行きます。 (Even if it rains tomorrow, I'll go.)
You can't swap のに into this last sentence, because it's not certain yet whether it will rain tomorrow, and what follows is something you intend to do.
ので goes in exactly the opposite direction: “because ~, so …”, following the result naturally:
雨なので、出かけなかった。 (Because it was raining, I didn't go out.)
雨なのに、彼は出かけた。 (Even though it was raining, he went out.)
Quick rule: if the first part is an established fact (not a hypothetical) and you're thinking “how can that be?”, use のに. For a plain contrast, use けど. For “even if ~”, use ても. When the result follows naturally, use ので.
n4-22:
The idea in one line
「〜ても」 means “even if ～” or “even though ～, still …”. The first half steps back and grants a situation. The second half says the result stays the same anyway. For “Even if it rains, I’m going,” Japanese says 雨が降っても、行きます。
How to form it
Verbs: change to the て form, then add 「も」.
書く → 書いて → 書いても
読む → 読んで → 読んでも (if the て form ends in 「で」, it becomes 「でも」)
食べる → 食べてもする → しても来る → 来ても（きても）
い-adjectives: change the final 「い」 to 「く」, then add 「ても」.
高い → 高くても悪い → 悪くても
な-adjectives and nouns: just add 「でも」.
静か → 静かでも雨 → 雨でも
Even if not ～: change the 「ない」 of the ない form to 「なくても」.
行かない → 行かなくても
When to use it
Even if it happensSuppose a situation, then say your decision won’t change.
・体調が悪くても、試合に出ます。(Even if I don’t feel well, I’ll play in the match.)
・高くても、買います。(Even if it’s expensive, I’ll buy it.)
Tried it, still no luckYou really did it, and the result still fell short of what you expected.
・何度読んでも、意味がわかりません。(Even after reading it many times, I still can’t understand it.)
・電話しても、出ません。(Even when I call him, he doesn’t pick up.)
No matter whatPut a word like いくら, どんなに, 何を or 誰が in front, and it means “no matter how much ～, …”.
・いくら食べても、太りません。(No matter how much I eat, I don’t gain weight.)
・どんなに忙しくても、朝ごはんは食べます。(No matter how busy I am, I eat breakfast.)
・誰が来ても、ドアを開けないでください。(No matter who comes, please don’t open the door.)
Easy mistakes
・Verbs like 読む, 飲む and 遊ぶ have a て form ending in 「で」, so say 読んでも, not 読んても.
・Nouns and な-adjectives take 「でも」: 雨でも, 元気でも. いい becomes よくても, not いくても.
・The second half should say that the result doesn’t change, or goes against expectation. For a natural, expected result, use たら (or ば) for the condition. Use から or ので only when the situation is already a fact and you’re giving a reason.
　雨が降ったら、行きません。(If it rains, I won’t go.)
　雨が降っても、行きます。(Even if it rains, I’ll go.)
・The “even” of “even if” is already built into ても, so you don’t need to add 「も」 in the second half. If you say 雨が降っても、私も行きます, it means “I’m going too (like everyone else).”
・Don’t confuse it with 「〜てもいいです」. Adding いいです changes the meaning to “it’s okay to ～.” 食べてもいいです。(You may eat it.) / 食べても、太りません。(Even if I eat it, I won’t gain weight.)
Telling it apart from similar patterns
のに also has a “but still / even though” feel, but it’s used differently. Same rainy situation:
雨でも、行きます。(Even if it rains, I’ll go: you state your own decision, and whether it rains right now doesn’t matter.)
雨なのに、彼は行きました。(Even though it was raining, he went: it already happened, with a note of surprise or disapproval.)
The point of ても is “nothing in the first half can change the second half.” It can be hypothetical, or something you’ve already tried.
のに always follows something that is already true, and the tone is “even though ～, (surprisingly) …”, often with complaint or surprise. Also, after のに you can’t use phrases like “I will ～” or “please ～”.
Quick test: to say “even if ～, I will / please do ～,” use ても. To complain “even though ～, how come …,” use のに.
What to learn next
Add たとえ in front for a stronger tone: たとえ反対されても、留学します。(Even if people object, I’ll study abroad.)
n4-24:
The idea in one line
「〜てしまう」 covers English ideas like “finish ～ off,” “end up ～ing,” and “accidentally ～.”
It has two meanings. One is doing something completely, finishing it off, like “I ate up the whole cake.” The other is doing something by accident and feeling bad about it, like “Oh no, I forgot my wallet.” What the two share is this: the thing is done, and you can’t undo it.
When to use it
Done completelyIt stresses that the whole thing is thoroughly finished, often with a feel of “in one go” or “let’s get it out of the way.”
・宿題はもう全部やってしまいました。(I’ve already finished all my homework.)
・ご飯の前に、宿題をやってしまおう。(Let’s get the homework done before dinner.)
By accident / regretYou did something you didn’t mean to, or something turned out badly, and you feel “oh no” or “what a shame.” This is the meaning you’ll hear most in daily life.
・財布を忘れてしまいました。(I accidentally forgot my wallet.)
・大事なお皿を割ってしまった。(I broke an important plate.)
・今朝、寝坊してしまいました。(I accidentally overslept this morning.)
Sometimes both meanings show up at once, so let the context decide: ケーキを全部食べてしまった。 can simply mean “I ate up the whole cake,” or “I ended up eating the whole thing (oops).”
How to form it
Change the verb to the て form, then add しまう.
忘れる → 忘れて → 忘れてしまう
割る → 割って → 割ってしまう
飲む → 飲んで → 飲んでしまう
しまう itself conjugates as a group 1 (godan) verb: polite is しまいます, past is しまいました, and among friends it’s しまった. Since you’re mostly talking about things that already happened, the past form is the one you’ll hear most.
How you’ll hear it most
Spoken contractionIn speech, 「てしまう」 often shrinks to ちゃう, and 「でしまう」 to じゃう.
食べてしまった → 食べちゃった
行ってしまう → 行っちゃう
飲んでしまった → 飲んじゃった
・あ、ケーキ全部食べちゃった。(Ah, I ate the whole cake.)
As a standalone phraseThe しまった！ you blurt out when you realize a mistake means “Oh no!” or “Damn!”
Easy mistakes
・Verbs whose て form ends in 「んで」 (飲む, 読む, 遊ぶ, 死ぬ) take でしまう, which contracts to じゃう: 飲んじゃった, not 飲んちゃった.
・ちゃう and じゃう are casual. They sound natural with friends, but with a boss, a customer, or in a letter, 〜てしまいました is safer.
・The verb しまう on its own means “to put away”: 本をかばんにしまう。(I put the book away in my bag.) With no て form in front, it’s not this grammar point.
・In English, “I forgot” is enough by itself, so many learners skip しまう. 忘れた is grammatically fine, but it sounds like a plain statement of fact. Saying 忘れてしまった is what brings out the “oh no, I feel bad” mood.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
For the same event, the plain past 「た」 and 「てしまった」 feel different:
た = simply says what happened: 財布を忘れた。(I forgot my wallet.)
てしまった = adds the feeling of “oh no, what a shame”: 財布を忘れてしまった。(Oh no, I forgot my wallet.)

た = ate: ケーキを食べた。(I ate the cake.)
てしまった = ate it all up, or ended up eating it by accident: ケーキを食べてしまった。(I ate up the cake.)
Quick test: when in English you’d want to say “ended up ～ing,” “went and ～ed,” “～ed it all up,” or “oh no, I ～ed,” use てしまう in Japanese. If you’re just stating what happened, plain た is enough.
What to learn next
Another “て form + a verb” pattern is 〜ておく (doing something in advance as preparation), and it’s worth comparing the two. Spoken contractions like ちゃう and じゃう will be covered all together in the lesson on contracted forms.
n4-28:
The idea in one line
「ところ」originally means "place," but here it becomes a point in time. It lines up neatly with English "about to…", "in the middle of…" and "just…": change the form of the verb before it, and you show how far along the action is.
One situation, three answers
A friend calls and asks 「今、大丈夫？」(Is now a good time?). You can answer like this:
・ごめん、今から出かけるところ。(Sorry, I'm about to head out.)
・今、ご飯を食べているところ。(I'm in the middle of eating right now.)
・ちょうど今、家に着いたところ。(I just got home.)
This is where 「ところ」shows up most: telling someone what you're doing right now. With friends you can just say 「ところ」; to be more polite, add 「です」.
How to form it
About to doDictionary form (the base form you find in the dictionary) + ところ. The action hasn't started yet but is about to.
食べる → 食べるところです (about to eat)
・これから晩ご飯を作るところです。(I'm about to start making dinner.)
In the middle of doingている + ところ. The action is halfway through and not finished.
食べている → 食べているところです (in the middle of eating)
・今、宿題をしているところです。(I'm doing my homework right now.)
Just finishedた-form (the past-tense form) + ところ. The action has only just ended.
食べた → 食べたところです (just finished eating)
・今、起きたところです。(I just woke up.)
Words that often appear with it: これから, 今から (with "about to"), 今 (with "in the middle of"), ちょうど, 今 (with "just finished").
You can use it in the past too
Change 「です」to 「でした」and you can say what stage you were at at a certain moment in the past.
・電話が来たとき、お風呂に入っているところでした。(When the phone rang, I was in the middle of taking a bath.)
・友達が来たとき、ちょうど出かけるところでした。(When my friend came, I was just about to head out.)
Easy mistakes
・These are three different points in time, and if you pick the wrong form the meaning changes: dictionary form = not started yet, ている = in progress, た-form = just ended. 「食べるところです」means "about to eat," not "eating right now."
・Before ところ, use the plain form, not ます: it's 行くところです, not 行きますところです.
・「ているところ」describes an action in progress at a specific point in time (now, or a certain moment in the past). Daily habits can only use plain ている: 毎日日本語を勉強しています。(I study Japanese every day.) You wouldn't say 「毎日勉強しているところです」.
・States that simply continue, like 「住んでいる」or 「結婚している」, can't take ところ either.
・「たところ」means really just now, usually within a few minutes, or a few hours at most. If you've already been in Japan for three months, don't say 「来たところです」.
Don't mix it up with its look-alike
たところ and たばかり (n4-29) both translate as "just…".
At the moment you've just walked into the station, both work: 今、駅に着いたところです。/ 今、駅に着いたばかりです。 (I just arrived at the station.)
But if some time has passed and it only feels recent to you, you can only use たばかり: 日本に来たばかりです。 (I've only just come to Japan, e.g. three months ago.)
Also, たばかり can go directly before a noun: 買ったばかりの靴 (shoes I just bought). たところ can't be used that way.
Quick rule of thumb: if it really happened just now and the timing is precise, use たところ; if a while has passed but it still feels new, use たばかり.
What to learn next
Put 「もう少しで」before 「dictionary form + ところでした」and it becomes "almost…": もう少しで電車に遅れるところでした。 (I almost missed the train.)
n4-31:
The idea in one line
「〜そう」means "looks…" or "seems about to…". You use it when you see how something looks and a feeling pops up right away. For example, you see a cake and say "That looks delicious," or you see a dark sky and say "It looks like it's going to rain."
When to use it
Verbs: about to happenYou see a sign and feel that something is about to happen.
・空が暗いですね。雨が降りそうです。(The sky is so dark. It looks like it's going to rain.)
・あ、ボタンが取れそう。(Oh, that button is about to come off.)
Adjectives: looks…An impression you get from the outward appearance.
・このケーキ、おいしそう！(This cake looks delicious!)
・田中さんは今日も元気そうですね。(Mr. Tanaka looks full of energy today too.)
How to form it
Verbs: change to the ます-form, drop ます, and add そう.
降る → 降ります → 降りそう
泣く → 泣きそうできる → できそう
い-adjectives: drop the final 「い」and add そう.
おいしい → おいしそう熱い → 熱そう
な-adjectives: add そう directly, with no だ.
元気 → 元気そう暇 → 暇そう
Two exceptions to memorize: いい → よさそうない → なさそう
To say "looks not…", attach to the negative form of the adjective: おいしくない → おいしくなさそう
To say a verb "doesn't look like it will happen," use 降りそうにない or 降りそうもない (it doesn't look like it will rain).
The forms you'll hear most
そう behaves like a な-adjective: before a noun it becomes そうな, and before a verb it becomes そうに.
・おいしそうなパンですね。(That's some delicious-looking bread.)
・子どもたちが楽しそうに遊んでいる。(The children are playing and seem to be having fun.)
Easy mistakes
・The 「looks…」form of いい is よさそう; you can't say いさそう. And いいそう would mean "I hear it's good."
・かわいそう means "poor thing," not "looks cute."
・Don't use そう for things that are obvious at a glance. If a flower is beautiful, just say きれいですね, not きれいそう ("looks beautiful").
・You can't add this そう directly after a noun. You can't say 学生そう for "looks like a student."
・Verb + そう often means "about to…," not just "seems to": 泣きそう means "about to cry."
Don't mix it up with its look-alike
The 「〜そうです (hearsay)」in the next lesson means "I hear that…". It looks almost identical; only the form before it differs. Compare using the same words:
Verb: 雨が降りそうです。 (It looks like it's going to rain.)
　　　雨が降るそうです。 (I hear it's going to rain.)
い-adjective: おいしそうです。 (It looks delicious.)
　　　　おいしいそうです。 (I hear it's delicious.)
な-adjective: 元気そうです。 (He looks full of energy.)
　　　　元気だそうです。 (I hear he's full of energy.)
Quick rule of thumb: if what comes before そう is the dictionary or plain form (降る, おいしい, 元気だ) = hearsay. If the verb has ます dropped, the い-adjective has い dropped, or the な-adjective is attached directly with no だ (降り, おいし, 元気) = appearance.
What to learn next
Next, learn 「〜そうです (hearsay)」and practice the two side by side. After that comes 「〜ようです・〜みたいです」, which is "it seems that…" based on clues you've picked up.
n4-32:
The idea in one line
This 「〜そうです」 means "I heard that..." or "they say that...", and in Japanese it goes at the very end of the sentence. When you pick something up from the news, a weather forecast, or a friend and want to pass it on, you add 「そうです」 after that sentence. It tells the listener, "This isn't my own claim. I heard it from someone else."
・新しい社長は厳しいそうです。(I heard the new president is strict.)
・田中さんはもう帰ったそうです。(I heard Tanaka has already gone home.)
How to form it
Put the plain form before it, meaning the casual form without ます or です. Think of it this way: say the whole sentence you heard in casual speech, then stick そうです on the end.
Verbs: 降る → 降るそうです来ない → 来ないそうです結婚した → 結婚したそうです
い-adjectives: attach directly. 高い → 高いそうです
な-adjectives and nouns: you must add だ first. 静か → 静かだそうです雨 → 雨だそうです
How you'll usually hear it
Name the source firstIt often follows 「〜によると」 (according to ~) or 「〜の話では」 (from what ~ says), so you say where you heard it before giving the information.
・天気予報によると、明日は雨だそうです。(According to the weather forecast, it will rain tomorrow.)
・林さんの話では、あの店はおいしいそうです。(According to Mr. Lin, that restaurant is good.)
With friendsSwap です for だ to get the casual version: 明日は休みだそうだ。 In casual chat, though, 「〜んだって」 and 「〜って」 are even more common: 明日、休みなんだって。 (I heard tomorrow's a day off.)
Common mistakes
・The most common slip is forgetting だ after nouns and な-adjectives. Say 雨だそうです and 元気だそうです. Without だ, the meaning shifts or the sentence doesn't work at all (see below).
・You can't put the ます form before it: it's 行くそうです, not 「行きますそうです」.
・For "I heard it was..." or "I heard it isn't...", put the past or negative in the clause before it. そうです itself never changes: 雨だったそうです (I heard it rained). You can't say 「雨だそうでした」.
・In English, "I heard that..." can open the sentence, but in Japanese そうです always comes at the end.
Telling it apart from its look-alike
The 様態そうです from the previous lesson ("looks like...") is spelled exactly the same. The difference is what comes before it:
このかばんは高いそうです。 (I heard this bag is expensive: someone told me.)
このかばんは高そうです。 (This bag looks expensive: I'm judging with my own eyes.)

雨が降るそうです。 (I heard it's going to rain: I saw the forecast.)
雨が降りそうです。 (It looks like it's about to rain: the sky is dark.)

先生は元気だそうです。 (I heard the teacher is doing well.)
先生は元気そうです。 (The teacher looks energetic.)

「いい」 is a special case: "I heard it's good" is いいそうです, while "it looks good" is よさそうです.
Quick test: if what comes before そうです is a complete sentence (高い, 降る, 元気だ), it means "I heard". If the word looks chopped short (高, 降り, 元気), it means "looks like".
What to study next
Compare this lesson with 「〜らしいです」, which can also mean "I hear / it seems", and with 「〜と言っていました」, which quotes someone's exact words.
n4-33:
The idea in one line
「〜ようです」 and 「〜みたいです」 mean "it seems..." or "it looks like...". You've seen, heard, or sensed some clues, and you reach a conclusion on your own. Both mean the same thing, but ようです is more formal and みたいです is more casual. In everyday conversation, みたい sounds the most natural.
When to use it
Guessing from cluesThis is the most common use. You aren't 100% sure, but you have some evidence.
・電気が消えていますね。田中さんはもう帰ったようです。(The lights are off. It seems Mr. Tanaka has already gone home.)
・外がうるさいですね。何かあったみたいです。(It's noisy outside. It seems something happened.)
・風邪をひいたみたいです。(I think I've caught a cold.)
The last sentence is based on how your own body feels, such as a sore throat or chills. That counts as a clue too, so this is very common.
Comparison: "like..."You know it isn't the real thing, you're just saying it's very similar. It often appears with まるで (just like).
・まるで夢のようです。(It's just like a dream.)
・田中さんは日本語が上手で、日本人みたいです。(Mr. Tanaka's Japanese is so good that he's like a native Japanese person.)
How to form it
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly. Both patterns work the same way.
帰った → 帰ったようです／帰ったみたいです
忙しい → 忙しいようです／忙しいみたいです
な-adjectives and nouns are different (in the present tense):
ようです: な-adjectives take 「な」, and nouns take 「の」.
静か → 静かなようです学生 → 学生のようです
みたいです: add nothing, attach directly.
静か → 静かみたいです学生 → 学生みたいです
In the past tense, both take 「だった」: 学生だったようです／学生だったみたいです.
How you'll usually hear it
Among friendsDrop です and say 「〜みたい」 or 「〜みたいだね」. ようだ is more like written language and is rarely used in chat.
・あの店、休みみたい。(That shop looks closed.)
Before a nounIt becomes 「ような／みたいな」 + noun, meaning "a ... like ~".
・田中さんみたいな人になりたいです。(I want to become a person like Mr. Tanaka.)
Before an actionIt becomes 「ように／みたいに」, meaning "(doing something) like ~".
・子どもみたいに喜んでいます。(He's delighted like a little kid.)
Common mistakes
・Nouns and な-adjectives are the easiest to get wrong. It's 学生みたい and 学生のようです, not 「学生のみたい」. It's 静かみたい, not 「静かなみたい」.
・Don't use it for things you've already confirmed with your own eyes. If you're standing in the rain, just say 雨が降っています. Say 雨が降っているようです only when you hear the rain or see someone outside holding an umbrella.
・学生みたい can mean "he seems to be a student" (a guess) or "he's like a student" (but isn't). Context tells you which.
・In reports and formal situations, use ようです. みたい is too casual.
Telling it apart from its look-alikes
Take rain as the example:
そうです (appearance) = judging by looks, it's about to happen: 雨が降りそうです。 (It looks like it's about to rain: the sky is full of dark clouds, but it hasn't started yet.)
ようです／みたいです = guessing from clues that it's already happening: 雨が降っているみたいです。 (It seems to be raining: you can hear the rain.)
らしいです = closer to something you heard from others: 東京は雨が降っているらしいです。 (I hear it's raining in Tokyo: from the news or a friend.)
Adjectives work the same way: おいしそう means "looks delicious", judged by appearance alone. おいしいみたい means "it seems to be delicious", for example when you see a long line there every day.
Quick test: "judging by looks alone, about to..." uses そう. "I have clues and I'm guessing it seems..." uses よう／みたい. "I heard that..." uses らしい.
What to study next
Next, study 〜らしいです side by side with the two kinds of 〜そうです (appearance and hearsay). That will complete your toolkit for expressing guesses.
n4-34:
The idea in one line
「らしい」 has two meanings. The first is "I hear that ~ / it seems that ~", like telling a friend, "Hey, I heard Nakamura is changing jobs." The news came from somewhere else, and you aren't 100% sure yourself. The second is "typical of ~ / truly ~-like", as in English "very spring-like" or "so manly."
When to use it
I hear / it seemsYou heard or saw some information, and based on it you think "it must be like this."
・中村さんは会社をやめるらしいです。（I hear Nakamura is quitting the company.）
・あの店のラーメンはおいしいらしいよ。（I hear the ramen at that place is really good.）
・田中さんは昨日休んだらしいです。（It seems Tanaka took the day off yesterday.）
Typical of ~After a noun, it means "just what you'd expect of this role or season." It usually carries a note of praise.
・今日は春らしい天気ですね。（It's such a spring-like day today, isn't it?）
・彼は本当に男らしい人です。（He's really a manly guy.）
This 「らしい」 behaves like an i-adjective (an adjective ending in い, like 高い), so the negative is らしくない:
・今日はなんだか田中さんらしくないですね。（Tanaka seems a bit unlike himself today.）
How to form it
Verbs and i-adjectives: use the plain form (without ます) and attach it directly.
行く → 行くらしい行かない → 行かないらしい高い → 高いらしい
Na-adjectives and nouns: drop 「だ」 first, then attach.
静かだ → drop だ → 静からしい雨だ → 雨らしい
In the past 「だった」, keep it and don't drop anything:雨だった → 雨だったらしい
With superiors or in formal situations, add 「です」 to make it polite. With friends, 「らしい」 alone is fine.
Common mistakes
・Don't leave 「だ」 after na-adjectives and nouns: say 静からしい, not 静かだらしい.
・The ます form can't connect directly to らしい: say 行くらしいです, not 行きますらしい.
・The same word can have two meanings: あの人は学生らしい。 can mean "That person seems to be a student." 本当に学生らしい服ですね。 means "Those are really student-like clothes." Judge by context. If a degree word like 「本当に」 or 「とても」 comes before it, it's most likely the second meaning.
・The second meaning is positive: "fits what it should be." Calling a child 子供らしい praises their innocence. To say an adult is childish, Japanese uses 子供っぽい, not 子供らしい.
・The first meaning is for things you heard and haven't confirmed yourself. If you saw it with your own eyes and are sure, just say it directly without らしい.
Telling similar forms apart
Talking about tomorrow's weather:
そうです (hearsay): 天気予報によると、明日は雨だそうです。（According to the weather forecast, it will rain tomorrow.）There's a clear source, and you're just passing it along as is.
らしいです: 明日は雨らしいです。（It seems it'll rain tomorrow.）It's still something you heard, but the source is vaguer, like "everyone seems to be saying so," and it adds a bit of your own judgment, so it sounds less certain.
ようです・みたいです: (looking out the window) 雨が降っているみたいです。（It looks like it's raining outside.）This is a judgment you make after seeing or feeling something yourself.
Here's another example people often mix up. There's a piece of cake on the table:
おいしそう！（It looks so good!）This is an impression from what your eyes see, using 「そうです (appearance)」.
このケーキ、おいしいらしいよ。（I hear this cake is really good.）This is something you heard from someone else.
Quick tip: if the information is "what someone else said," use らしい or そうです (hearsay). Use そうです to relay it exactly as heard, and らしい when the source is vaguer and you add a bit of your own guess. If it's "what you saw or felt yourself," use ようです, みたいです, or ～そう (appearance).
What to study next
Review n4-32 「～そうです (hearsay)」 and n4-33 「～ようです・～みたいです」 together. Once you can separate "heard from others" from "seen yourself," you'll rarely get these conjecture sentences wrong.
n4-35:
The idea in one line
「〜はずです」 means "it should be ~ / it must be ~ (as far as logic goes)". You have grounds for it, such as having seen the timetable, having heard it from the person, or knowing he's a doctor. From those grounds you draw a conclusion you feel confident about, and that's when you use はず. It's the "should" in "He gets off work at six, so he should be home by now."
When to use it
Inference with groundsFirst there's a "because ~," then you conclude "so it should be ~."
・田中さんは6時に会社を出たから、もう家に着いたはずです。（Mr. Tanaka left the company at six, so he should be home by now.）
・木村さんは医者だから、薬に詳しいはずです。（Mr. Kimura is a doctor, so he should know a lot about medicine.）
No wonderWhen you see the cause and suddenly understand, 「〜はずだ」 is often used.
・窓が開いている。寒いはずだ。（The window is open. No wonder it's so cold.）
How to form it
It attaches the same way as when a noun follows:
Verbs: attach directly to the plain form (the form without ます).
行く → 行くはず行かない → 行かないはず行った → 行ったはず
I-adjectives: attach directly. 高い → 高いはず
Na-adjectives: add 「な」. 静か → 静かなはず
Nouns: add 「の」. 休み → 休みのはず
For the past, na-adjectives and nouns use 「だった」: 学生だったはず.
With friends say 「はずだ」; with teachers and customers say 「はずです」.
Forms you'll hear most
はずがない"There's no way ~." A strong negation.
・あの人がうそをつくはずがありません。（There's no way that person would lie.）
はずだった"It was supposed to ~," but it didn't happen.
・電車は10時に着くはずだったのに、30分も遅れた。（The train was supposed to arrive at ten, but it was thirty minutes late.）
はずなのに"It should be ~, so how come…?"
・鍵はかばんに入れたはずなのに、ない。（I'm sure I put the key in my bag, but it's not there.）
Common mistakes
・English "should" has two meanings: "He should be there by now" is a guess, and "You should go to bed early" is advice. はず covers only the guess. To give advice, use 早く寝たほうがいいですよ. If you say 早く寝るはずです, it means "by all logic, you'll go to bed early."
・Nouns need の and na-adjectives need な: say 休みのはず and 静かなはず, not 「休みはず」 or 「学生だはず」.
・Don't use はず for things you've decided to do yourself. In English you might say "I should go tomorrow," but in Japanese say 明日は行くつもりです or 行くと思います. 行くはずです sounds like "according to the schedule, I'm going to go."
・来ないはずです means "he shouldn't be coming," a guess. 来るはずがありません means "there's no way he'd come," which is much stronger.
Telling similar forms apart
Waiting for Mr. Tanaka:
田中さんは来るはずです。（He said he'd come, so he should come: you have grounds and are confident.）
田中さんは来るでしょう。（He'll probably come: an ordinary guess.）
田中さんは来るかもしれません。（He might come, or he might not: about fifty-fifty.）
Quick tip: if you can state your grounds ("because ~, so…") and feel confident, use はず. If you're just guessing offhand, use でしょう. If you're not very sure, use かもしれません.
What to study next
At N3 you'll learn 「べき」 (should do ~), which is exactly the other meaning of English "should." Memorize はず and べき separately and you'll stop mixing them up.
n4-54:
The idea in one sentence
The ば form means “if ~, then ~”, with the sense of “as long as ~”. 安ければ買います = As long as it's cheap, I'll buy it. The emphasis is on the condition in the first half: once it's met, the result follows.
When to use it
As long as ~Once a certain condition is met, a certain result follows.
・安ければ買います。(If it's cheap, I'll buy it.)
・急げば間に合いますよ。(If you hurry, you'll make it.)
Universal truthsNature and common sense, things that happen “every time.”
・春になれば、桜が咲きます。(When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.)
If not ~The negative version, often used as a warning: “if you don't do it, you're in trouble.”
・急がなければ、間に合いません。(If you don't hurry, you won't make it.)
How to form it: check the verb group first
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the 「え」-row sound of the same row, then add 「ば」.
行く → change く to け → 行けば
飲む → 飲めば買う → 買えば待つ → 待てば帰る → 帰れば
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop the final 「る」 and add 「れば」.
食べる → 食べれば起きる → 起きれば見る → 見れば
Group 3 (only two, just memorize them): する → すれば来る → 来れば(くれば)
“If not ~”: first make the ない form, then drop the 「い」 of 「ない」 and add 「ければ」.
行かない → 行かなければ食べない → 食べなければ
い-adjectives: drop the final 「い」 and add 「ければ」.
安い → 安ければ寒い → 寒ければ
な-adjectives and nouns: no ば here, just add 「なら」.
静か → 静かなら学生 → 学生なら
Easy mistakes
・来れば is read くれば, not きれば or これば.
・いい becomes よければ; there is no 「いければ」. Example: よければ、どうぞ。 (If you don't mind, please go ahead.)
・Group 1 doesn't just add れば: it's 行けば, not 行くれば.
・When the first half is an action (go, arrive, eat…) and the second half is a request like “please ~” or a suggestion like “let's ~”, ば sounds odd. Switch to たら:
×駅に着けば、電話してください。
○駅に着いたら、電話してください。 (Call me once you get to the station.)
If the first half is a state (ある, いる, できる, adjectives), it's fine: 時間があれば、来てください。 (If you have time, please come.)
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Japanese has four kinds of “if.” Let's compare them in one situation, going to the station:
ば = as long as ~: 駅まで歩けば、10分で着きます。 (If you walk to the station, you'll be there in 10 minutes.)
たら = after ~; the second half can be a request or an invitation: 駅に着いたら、電話してください。 (Call me once you get to the station.)
と = whenever ~, it always happens; think giving directions or a machine's reaction: この道をまっすぐ行くと、駅があります。 (If you go straight down this road, you'll find the station.)
なら = picks up what the other person said and gives advice; the event hasn't happened yet: 駅に行くなら、この道が近いですよ。 (If you're going to the station, this road is shorter.)
Quick rule of thumb: use ば for “as long as ~”; use たら for “after ~” or when the second half is a request or invitation; use と for “whenever ~, it always happens”; use なら for “if you say you're going to ~.” When in doubt, start with たら. It's the least likely to be wrong.
What to learn next
Add 「いい」 afterward to mean “it'd be good if ~.” It's very common for asking someone's advice: どうすればいいですか。 (What should I do?)
Add 「なりません」 after 「なければ」 and you get “must ~”: 明日は早く起きなければなりません。 (I have to get up early tomorrow.)
n4-55:
The idea in one sentence
「〜たら」 means “if ~” or “when ~ / once ~”. You use it for “if I have money, I want to travel” and “I'll call you when I get home.” It's the most common everyday way to express a condition. It also has one special use: “I did ~ and found that ~.”
How to form it: if you know the た form, you know たら
Make the た form first, then just add 「ら」. The verb た form is made just like the て form, except that て becomes た and で becomes だ.
行く → 行った → 行ったら
飲む → 飲んだ → 飲んだら
食べる → 食べた → 食べたら
する → したら来る → 来たら(きたら)
Adjectives and nouns work too. Same idea: put them in the past form, then add ら:
高い → 高かったら暇 → 暇だったら雨 → 雨だったら
Negatives are the same: 行かない → 行かなかったら (if I don't go)
When to use it
If ~It may or may not happen; it's just a hypothesis.
・お金があったら、旅行したい。(If I had money, I'd want to travel.)
・明日雨だったら、行きません。(If it rains tomorrow, I won't go.)
Once ~, thenSomething that will definitely happen; you're saying what you'll do “when the time comes.”
・家に帰ったら、電話します。(I'll call you when I get home.)
・駅に着いたら、連絡してください。(Please contact me when you get to the station.)
Found that ~After doing something, you discover something unexpected. Here the second half must be in the past tense.
・窓を開けたら、猫がいた。(When I opened the window, there was a cat.)
・家に帰ったら、母が来ていました。(When I got home, my mom had come over.)
Easy mistakes
・With たら, the first half always happens first and the second half after it. 日本へ行ったら、ガイドブックを買います。 means “I'll buy a guidebook once I'm in Japan.” If you mean “I'll buy one before I leave,” you need なら (see below).
・来たら is read きたら, not こたら.
・Don't use たら to tell a series of things you did in the past. “I went home and ate” is 家に帰って、ご飯を食べました。 「たら + past tense」 is specifically for “and then I ran into / discovered something,” so putting a deliberate action of your own in the second half sounds strange.
・To make the “if” clearer, you can put もし in front: もし雨だったら. But you can't add もし to the “once ~” kind of thing that will surely happen: もし家に帰ったら sounds like you're not sure you'll make it home.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
At N4 you learn four conditionals: たら, ば, と, なら. Let's look at them in the same situation:
たら = the all-purpose one; the second half can be a request, a wish, or a plan: 春になったら、日本へ行きたい。 (When spring comes, I want to go to Japan.)
と = it always happens this way, like a natural phenomenon: 春になると、桜が咲きます。 (When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.)
ば = stresses “as long as this condition is met, ~”: 春になれば、暖かくなります。 (Once spring comes, it gets warm.)
なら = follows what the other person said and gives advice, and you can talk about the later event first: 日本へ行くなら、春がいいですよ。 (If you're going to Japan, spring is a good time.)
The difference is clearest when you ask someone to do something: 駅に着いたら、電話してください。 sounds natural. If you switch to と or ば, as in 「駅に着くと」 or 「駅に着けば」, and then add 「電話してください」, Japanese speakers will find it wrong.
Quick rule of thumb: when you can't decide, use たら. It works in most cases. The exceptions: for “it's like that every time,” と is more common; for “I heard the other person is going to do something, so here's some advice,” use なら.
What to learn next
Add 「いいです」 afterward and it becomes advice: 先生に聞いたらいいですよ。 (You should just ask your teacher.)
n4-56:
The idea in one line
「なら」 is like English “if it's about X…” or “in that case…”. Say a friend tells you, “I want to go to a hot spring.” You pick up on that and reply, “If it's hot springs you want, Hakone is nice.” You first take up what the other person brought up, then give your suggestion or thought. That's the most common use of なら.
When to use it
Replying with adviceThe other person mentions something, and you give an opinion about it.
・A：週末、温泉に行きたいな。 (I really want to go to a hot spring this weekend.)
・B：温泉なら、箱根がいいよ。 (If it's hot springs, Hakone is nice.)
Assume first, then state your plan“If that's the case, then I'll…”.
・あなたが行くなら、私も行きます。 (If you're going, I'll go too.)
・家賃が予算内なら、契約したいです。 (If the rent is within my budget, I'd like to sign the contract.)
How to attach it
Verbs: attach directly to the plain form (the form without ます).
行く → 行くなら行かない → 行かないなら
い-adjectives: attach directly. 高い → 高いなら
な-adjectives: drop 「だ」 first, then attach. 静かだ → 静かなら
Nouns: attach directly. 日本語 → 日本語なら
How you'll hear it most
Noun + ならIt means “if we're talking about X,” narrowing the topic down to that one thing.
・コーヒーなら、駅前の店がおいしいですよ。 (If it's coffee, the shop in front of the station is really good.)
それならIt goes at the start of a sentence and means “in that case.” In casual speech people often say just 「なら」.
・A：明日は忙しいです。 (I'm busy tomorrow.)
・B：それなら、あさってにしましょう。 (In that case, let's make it the day after tomorrow.)
Easy mistakes
・With nouns and な-adjectives, don't add だ: say 学生なら, not 学生だなら.
・The thing after なら can happen before the thing in front of it: 京都へ行くなら、ホテルを早く予約したほうがいいですよ。 (If you're going to Kyoto, you'd better book a hotel early.) Booking the hotel happens before the trip. This is exactly the opposite of たら.
・What follows なら is mostly advice, a request, your own plan or a judgment. For things that always happen, like “when spring comes, flowers bloom,” don't use なら; use と: 春になると、桜が咲きます。 (When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.)
Telling it apart from look-alikes
なら and たら can both be translated as “if,” so they're the easiest to mix up. The difference is when the second action happens. Take the same trip to Japan:
なら = you do it before going:
・日本へ行くなら、日本語を勉強しておいたほうがいいよ。 (If you're going to Japan, you'd better study some Japanese first.)
たら = you do it after arriving:
・日本へ行ったら、ラーメンを食べたい。 (When I get to Japan, I want to eat ramen.)
If you changed the first sentence to 「行ったら」, it would mean “start studying Japanese once you've arrived in Japan,” which isn't what you meant. Conversely, “call me when you get to the station” can only happen after you arrive, so use たら: 駅に着いたら、電話してください。 (Please call me when you get to the station.)
Quick rule of thumb: use なら for “not done yet, here's advice,” and たら for “it happens after you've done it or arrived.” When the other person has just mentioned something and you reply with an opinion, it's almost always なら.
What to study next
Japanese has four main ways to say “if”: と, ば, たら and なら. Once you've learned なら, try comparing it with 〜ば (n4-54) and 〜と (n4-57) to see when each one fits.
n4-59:
The idea in one line
The passive form (受身形) is like English “be + past participle”: 先生に褒められた means “I was praised by the teacher.” But Japanese uses the passive much more than English does, and it often carries a feeling of “this happened to me and it was a nuisance or bad luck”, like English “I got rained on” or “I had my cake eaten.”
How to form it: first check the verb group
Group 1 (五段 verbs): change the last sound to the same row's 「あ」-column sound, then add 「れる」.
書く → change く to か → 書かれる
踏む → 踏まれる叱る → 叱られる
Watch out for verbs ending in 「う」: the う doesn't become あ, it becomes わ:
言う → change う to わ → 言われる誘う → 誘われる
You can also think from the ます form: change the 「き」 of 書きます to 「か」, then add 「れます」 → 書かれます.
Group 2 (一段 verbs): drop the final 「る」 and add 「られる」.
食べる → 食べられる見る → 見られる
Group 3 (only two, just memorize them): する → される来る → 来られる (こられる)
Once you've formed 「〜れる／〜られる」, keep conjugating it like a Group 2 verb: 叱られます, 叱られた, 叱られて.
The three most common passives
In every type, the person who does the action takes 「に」.
Something was done to me(私は) person に + passive. This is the closest to the English passive, and it works for both good and bad things.
先生が私を褒めた。 (The teacher praised me.) → turned into the passive:
・私は先生に褒められた。 (I was praised by the teacher.)
・母に叱られました。 (I was scolded by my mother.)
Something of mine was affected(私は) person に + thing を + passive. Japanese likes to make the affected person the subject, and the thing takes 「を」.
・電車で足を踏まれた。 (I had my foot stepped on on the train.)
・弟にケーキを食べられた。 (My little brother ate my cake on me.)
Being put out by somethingWhat someone else did wasn't really about you, but you ended up suffering from it. Even actions like “rain” and “cry” can become passive. English wouldn't normally use a passive for these.
・雨に降られて、びしょびしょになった。 (I got rained on and ended up soaked.)
・夜中に子供に泣かれて、寝られなかった。 (The child cried in the middle of the night, and I couldn't sleep.)
Easy mistakes
・The passive of 言う is 言われる, not 「言あれる」 or 「言られる」. 買う and 使う work the same way, with わ.
・The person doing the action takes 「に」: it's 先生に褒められた, not 「先生が褒められた」, which would mean “the teacher was praised.”
・In English you can say “my foot got stepped on,” but don't translate it word for word as 私の足が踏まれた; the natural way is 足を踏まれた.
・English “got + past participle” often suggests something bad, but the Japanese passive works for good things too: 褒められた (was praised) and 誘われた (was invited) are both very common.
・When you see a passive sentence, ask yourself, “Is the subject the one who is affected, or even put out?” That will help you catch the nuance.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Passive (受身形) vs potential (可能形): for Group 2 verbs and 来る, the two forms look exactly the same.
犬にパンを食べられた。 (The dog ate my bread: passive)
このパンはまだ食べられる。 (This bread is still edible: potential)
If there's a 「person に」 and the sentence is about who had something done to them, it's the passive. If it's about “can or can't,” it's the potential.
〜られる vs 〜てもらう: both can describe someone coming to see you.
友達に来られて困った。 (A friend showed up, and it put me in a bind.)
友達に来てもらって助かった。 (A friend came to help, and it was a real lifesaver.)
The passive often carries a feeling of “I was bothered.” 〜てもらう means “I received the other person's help” and carries gratitude.
Quick rule of thumb: when you're thinking “this happened to me, what bad luck,” use 〜れる／〜られる. When you're thinking “someone helped me, how nice,” use 〜てもらう.
What to study next
Next is the causative form (making someone do something): 書かせる. Beyond that is the causative-passive (being made to do something): 母に野菜を食べさせられた。 (I was made to eat vegetables by my mother.) Also, the same 〜れる／〜られる can be used to show respect to someone of higher status, as in 先生が書かれた本 (the book the teacher wrote). You'll meet that again when you learn honorific forms.
n4-62:
The idea in one line
Honorific language (尊敬語) is what you use when talking about what the other person, or someone senior to you, is doing. You swap the action for a more respectful expression. It's like turning “Are you coming?” into “Will you be joining us?”, or “What do you want?” into “What would you like?”. The action is the same; only the wording gets more respectful.
When to use it
Use it when the person doing the action is someone you should respect, such as a teacher, boss, customer, or elder. You can use it when speaking to them directly, or when mentioning them in front of other people.
・先生はもうお帰りになりました。(The teacher has already gone home.)
・週末は何をなさいますか。(What will you be doing this weekend?)
How to form it: think in two steps
Step 1: Check whether the verb has its own special honorific form
Very common verbs have their own honorific forms. If one exists, you usually use it first:
いる・行く・来る → いらっしゃる
言う → おっしゃる
食べる・飲む → 召し上がる
見る → ご覧になる
する → なさる
くれる → くださる
知っている → ご存じだ
・社長は明日大阪へいらっしゃいます。(The president will go to Osaka tomorrow.)
・この本、もうご覧になりましたか。(Have you already looked at this book?)
Step 2: If there's no special form, use “お + ます-stem + になる”
Change the verb to its ます form, drop ます, then add お in front and になる at the end.
待つ → 待ちます → drop ます → お待ちになる
帰る → お帰りになる書く → お書きになる
For “Chinese-character noun + する” verbs, ご is usually used: 利用する → ご利用になる
・部長は何時にお戻りになりますか。(What time will the manager be back?)
Verbs like 見る・言う・する・いる・来る must use their special forms; don't force the formula on them. A few verbs, such as 飲む, accept both: 何を召し上がりますか。 and 何をお飲みになりますか。 (What would you like to drink?) both sound natural.
There is also a lighter honorific form with 「れる・られる」 (for example 社長が帰られました), which is covered separately in n4-74.
How you'll hear it most
In shopsいらっしゃいませ。 (Welcome!) This actually comes from いらっしゃる.
Please ~お + ます-stem + ください: 少々お待ちください。 (Please wait a moment.)
Asking if they know somethingこのお店、ご存じですか。 (Do you know this shop?)
Easy mistakes
・Honorific language must never be used about yourself. To say “I'm going tomorrow,” you can't say 私がいらっしゃいます. Use plain polite speech or humble language: 私が参ります.
・Don't force the formula on these verbs: you can't say お見になる、お言いになる、おしになる. Say ご覧になる、おっしゃる、なさる.
・The ます forms are easy to get wrong: they are いらっしゃいます、おっしゃいます、なさいます、くださいます, not いらっしゃります or おっしゃります.
・When you talk to outside customers about your own boss at your company, don't use honorifics; lower your own company's people. For example, if a customer calls asking for the manager, reply 田中は今おりません。 and don't say “部長はいらっしゃいません”.
Don't confuse it with similar forms
Humble language (n4-63) is also keigo, but it goes the opposite way: honorific language raises the other person, while humble language lowers yourself. Look at the same conversation:
A：この資料、ご覧になりましたか。 (Have you looked at this document? The other person looks, so honorific.)
B：はい、拝見しました。 (Yes, I've looked at it. I look, so humble.)
A：何を召し上がりますか。 (What would you like to eat?)
B：じゃ、ケーキをいただきます。 (Then I'll have the cake.)
Quick test: first ask who is doing the action. If it's the other person or a senior, use honorific language. If it's you (or someone on your side), use humble language.
What to learn next
Next, learn humble language (n4-63). Memorizing the two together is the best way to avoid mixing them up. Then look at the honorific use of 「れる・られる」 (n4-74).
n4-63:
The idea in one line
Humble language (謙譲語) means talking about your own actions in a lowered way, so the other person naturally comes across as higher. English does this a little too: “Allow me to carry that for you,” “I'd be happy to assist.” Japanese humble language is the same idea, but it's used far more often and far more systematically.
When to use it
Use it with customers, teachers, bosses, and others you should respect when talking about what you yourself are going to do. In part-time jobs, at work, or when writing to a teacher, you'll run into it almost every day.
Method 1: お + verb + します
Drop ます from the ます form, add 「お」 in front and 「します」 at the end.
持ちます → drop ます → お持ちします
待ちます → お待ちします
送ります → お送りします
For Chinese-character nouns like 「案内」 and 「連絡」, you usually add 「ご」 in front:
案内します → ご案内します
連絡します → ご連絡します
・荷物、お持ちします。(Let me carry your luggage.)
・駅までお送りします。(I'll see you to the station.)
・あとでご連絡します。(I'll contact you later.)
This pattern only works for actions done for the other person, or involving them. Eating or sleeping by yourself has nothing to do with them, so you can't apply it there.
Method 2: Swap in a special verb
Some common verbs have their own humble versions. You replace the verb entirely and don't use お～します. For N4, memorize these:
行く・来る → 参ります
いる → おります
言う → 申します
する → いたします
食べる・飲む・もらう → いただきます
見る → 拝見します
to ask, to visit the other person's place → 伺います
知っている → 存じております
会う → お目にかかります
The 「いただきます」 you say before a meal is actually this humble いただく.
・はじめまして、林と申します。(Nice to meet you, my name is Lin.)
・資料、拝見しました。(I've looked at the materials.)
・では、お先に失礼いたします。(Well then, if you'll excuse me, I'll leave first.)
When talking to outsiders about the actions of your own family, you also use humble language, because family counts as “your side.”
・父は今、出かけております。(My father is out right now.)
Easy mistakes
・Humble language is only for yourself (and your own side). Saying いただいてください to invite your teacher to eat is wrong; say 召し上がってください. And to ask whether your teacher is going, you can't say 先生も参りますか; say 先生もいらっしゃいますか.
・If a verb has its own special version, use that: don't say お見します, say 拝見します; don't say お行きします, say 参ります or 伺います.
・お待ちします means “I'll wait for you,” while お待ちください means “please wait.” The subject is different. When a shop clerk says 少々お待ちください, they're asking you to wait; when they say お待ちしております, they're the ones waiting for you.
・参ります just makes “go, come” polite; 伺います means “go to the other person's place.” 来週、大阪へ参ります。 (I'm going to Osaka next week.) / 明日、先生のお宅に伺います。 (Tomorrow I'll visit the teacher's home.)
Don't confuse it with similar forms
The form most easily confused with this is honorific language. For the same event, if the other person is the subject, use honorific language (raising them); if you are the subject, use humble language (lowering yourself).
・先生も召し上がりますか。(Will you have some too, teacher? The other person eats, so honorific.)
・はい、私もいただきます。(Yes, I'll have some too. I eat, so humble.)
・先生、傘をお持ちになりましたか。(Teacher, did you bring an umbrella? The other person brings it.)
・傘、お持ちします。(Let me carry your umbrella. I carry it.)
Quick test: first ask “Who is doing this action?” If the other person: honorific (お～になる、いらっしゃる、召し上がる). If you: humble (お～します、参ります、いただきます).
What to learn next
Next, learn 「〜させていただきます」, a very humble way of saying “I'm going to do ~” (literally “I receive your permission to do ~”), for example 本日は休ませていただきます。 (Please allow me to take today off.) You'll hear it every day at part-time jobs and at work.
n4-60:
The idea in one line
The causative form is how Japanese says “make someone do…” or “let someone do…”. Think “Mom makes her kid eat vegetables” or “The manager lets the part-timer leave early.” In both cases Japanese turns the verb into 「〜せる／〜さ せる」. It can mean forcing someone to do it, or letting someone do what they want to do (permission). Context tells you which.
When to use it
ForceYou tell someone to do it, whether they want to or not.
・母は子供に野菜を食べさせます。(Mom makes her kid eat vegetables.)
PermissionThey want to do it, and you let them.
・子供が遊びたがっていたので、公園で遊ばせました。(My kid really wanted to play, so I let him play at the park.)
Causing a feelingMaking someone worry or making someone happy also uses the causative.
・親を心配させたくない。(I don’t want to make my parents worry.)
How to form it: check the verb group first
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to its 「あ」-row equivalent, then add 「せる」.
書く → く becomes か → 書かせる
飲む → 飲ませる帰る → 帰らせる待つ → 待たせる
Verbs ending in 「う」 change to わ: 買う → 買わせる
Tip: it uses the same sound as the ない form. Take 書かない, drop ない, add せる, and you get 書かせる.
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop the final 「る」 and add 「させる」.
食べる → 食べさせる見る → 見させる起きる → 起きさせる
Group 3 (only two verbs, just memorize them): する → させる来る → 来させる (こさせる)
Verbs like 勉強する and 残業する work the same way: 勉強する → 勉強させる
Once formed, it is just an ordinary Group 2 verb and conjugates as usual: 書かせます, 書かせた, 書かせない.
The person being told: に or を?
The pattern looks like this: the person giving the orderは　the person doing itに／を　〜させる
How to choose: first check whether the sentence already has another 「を」 (what is eaten, what is written).
There is another をThe person doing the action can only take に. Japanese doesn’t like two 「を」 in one sentence.
・先生は生徒に作文を書かせます。(The teacher makes the students write an essay.)
・子供に日本語を勉強させています。(I’m having my child study Japanese.)
No other をEither を or に works. With を, the sense of force is stronger.
・先生は学生を立たせました。(The teacher made the student stand up.)
・部長は毎日私を残業させます。(My department head makes me work overtime every day.)
・部長は毎日私に残業させます。(My department head makes me work overtime every day.)
Forms you’ll hear most
させてください“Please let me…”: you want to do it and you’re asking for permission.
・少し休ませてください。(Please let me rest for a bit.)
・私にやらせてください。(Let me do it.)
待たせる“Make someone wait”: extremely common in apologies.
・お待たせしました。(Sorry to keep you waiting.)
・待たせてごめんね。(Sorry to keep you waiting.)
Easy mistakes
・Verbs ending in 「う」 change to わ: it’s 買わせる and 言わせる, not 「買あせる」.
・帰る, 入る, and 走る are Group 1: it’s 帰らせる, not 「帰させる」.
・来させる is read こさせる, not きさせる.
・The causative is a top-down form, so don’t use it to direct someone senior to you. Saying 先生に説明させる for “I asked the teacher to explain” sounds very rude. Say 先生に説明してもらう instead (or, more politely, 説明していただく).
Telling look-alikes apart
させる vs てもらう: in English, “have a friend take my photo” could mean either, but Japanese treats them very differently.
友達に写真を撮らせた。 (I made my friend take a photo: it sounds like you’re ordering them around.)
友達に写真を撮ってもらった。 (I asked my friend to take a photo for me: they did you a favor, and it carries thanks.)
させる vs される (passive): one syllable apart, completely opposite directions.
友達を1時間待たせた。 (I kept my friend waiting for an hour: it’s my doing.)
友達に1時間待たされた。 (My friend kept me waiting for an hour: I’m the one who lost out.)
Quick trick: 「せ」 means I make someone else do something; 「れ」 means something is done to me by someone else; and to ask someone for a favor, use 「てもらう」.
What to learn next
Causative + passive = being forced to do something (the causative-passive): 母に野菜を食べさせられた。 (I was made to eat vegetables by my mom.)
Also, 〜させていただきます, which you hear all the time in customer service, comes from the causative too.
n4-61:
The idea in one line
The causative-passive means “be made to do…” or “be sent off to do…”. The key point: you are the one doing the action, but you don’t want to, because someone else is forcing you. Think “As a kid, I was made to eat green peppers by my mom”: you’re the one eating, Mom is the one forcing, and there’s a hint of complaint in the tone.
Where it comes from
The name is long, but it is really two things stacked together: the causative (make someone do something) + the passive (be ~ed).
First, from Mom’s point of view:
・母は私にピーマンを食べさせた。(Mom made me eat green peppers.)
Tell it from “my” point of view and it becomes the causative-passive:
・私は母にピーマンを食べさせられた。(I was made to eat green peppers by my mom.)
The person being forced (me) takes は or が, and the person forcing you takes に.
How to form it: check the verb group first
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop 「る」 and add 「させられる」.
食べる → 食べさせられる見る → 見させられる
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to its 「あ」-row equivalent, then add 「される」. This is the version Japanese people use most.
行く → く becomes か → 行かされる
飲む → 飲まされる待つ → 待たされる買う → う becomes わ → 買わされる
Adding 「せられる」 is also correct (行かせられる), just longer and less common.
Group 3 (only two verbs, just memorize them): する → させられる来る → 来させられる (こさせられる)
For the polite form, replace the final る with ます: 待たされる → 待たされます
Forms you’ll hear most
・駅で30分も待たされた。(I was kept waiting at the station for a whole 30 minutes.)
・部長にお酒を飲まされました。(My department head made me drink alcohol.)
・子供の頃、毎日ピアノを練習させられた。(As a kid, I was made to practice piano every day.)
Easy mistakes
・Group 1 verbs ending in 「す」 can’t use される: 話す becomes 話させられる, not 話さされる.
・Verbs ending in 「う」 change to 「わ」, not 「あ」: it’s 買わされる, not 買あされる.
・The causative-passive of 来る is read こさせられる, not きさせられる.
・食べさせる means “make someone else eat,” while 食べさせられる means “be made to eat.” Without 「られる」 the meaning flips completely.
・It carries a feeling of reluctance, so don’t use it for happy things. To say a senior colleague treated you to a meal, say 先輩におごってもらった. If you said 先輩におごらされた, it would mean “I was forced to pay for my senior.”
Telling look-alikes apart
Passive = the action is done by the other person, and you’re on the receiving end: 先生に叱られた。 (I was scolded by the teacher: the teacher does the scolding.)
Causative-passive = the action is done by you, but you’re forced into it: 先生に立たされた。 (I was made to stand by the teacher: I’m the one standing.)
てもらう = the other person does something for you, and you’re grateful: 先生に作文を直してもらった。 (The teacher corrected my essay for me.)
Quick trick: ask yourself, “Who is doing this action?” If the other person does it to you, it’s the passive. If you do it unwillingly, it’s the causative-passive. If the other person helps you and you’re grateful, use てもらう.
What to learn next
To say “please allow me to…” politely, use the te-form of the causative plus いただきます (〜させていただきます): 発表する → 発表させる → 発表させていただきます。 (Allow me to give the presentation.)
n4-7:
The gist in one line
「ので」 means “because ~, so ~”. Like 「から」, it gives a reason. The difference is that 「ので」 sounds more polite, as if you're explaining the situation. English “because” is closer to から, while “since” or “as” is closer to ので. When you give a reason to a teacher, a boss, or a customer, ので is the safest choice.
When to use it
Giving a reason politelyMost common at work, in class, and when talking with people you don't know well.
・用事があるので、お先に失礼します。(I have something to do, so I'll head out first.)
・道が混んでいたので、遅れました。(The roads were crowded, so I was late.)
Making a requestGive the reason first, then ask for help. It sounds very polite.
・寒いので、窓を閉めてください。(It's cold, so please close the window.)
Declining indirectlyJapanese speakers often give only the reason and leave the sentence unfinished. The other person gets the message.
・明日はちょっと用事があるので…。(I have something on tomorrow, so…)
How to attach it
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly.
行く → 行くので行った → 行ったので痛い → 痛いので
な-adjectives and nouns: add 「な」 in between.
静か → 静かなので雨 → 雨なので
For something in the past, use 「だった」: 雨 → 雨だったので
For a more formal tone, you can also attach it after ます or です. You hear this a lot in shops and workplaces:
雨が降っていますので、お気をつけください。(It's raining, so please be careful.)
Easy mistakes
・Nouns and な-adjectives can't take だ directly: 雨だので is wrong. Say 雨なので.
・い-adjectives are the opposite: no な. It's 痛いので, not 痛いなので.
・When you answer 「Why?」, you can end the sentence with 電車が遅れたからです, but you can't say 遅れたのでです.
・ので doesn't suit harsh commands. 「うるさいので、黙れ」 sounds odd. Use から for that.
Don't confuse it with look-alikes
から vs ので: the same situation, taking a day off with a fever.
熱があるから、休む。(I have a fever, so I'm taking a day off. Said to a friend, more direct.)
熱があるので、休ませてください。(Because I have a fever, please let me rest. Said to a boss, more polite.)
For scolding or warning, only から works: 危ないから、触るな！(It's dangerous, don't touch it!)
ので vs のに: only one syllable apart, but the meaning is very different.
薬を飲んだので、治った。(I took medicine, so I got better.)
薬を飲んだのに、治らない。(Even though I took medicine, I'm not getting better.)
Quick tip: to give a reason politely, use ので. To stress your point, sound forceful, or give an order, use から. For “even though ~”, it's のに.
What to learn next
When you have more than one reason, you can list them one by one with 「し」: 雨も降っているし、寒いし、今日は出かけない。(It's raining, and it's cold too, so I'm not going out today.)
n4-5:
The gist in one line
「〜やすい」 means “easy to ~”, and 「〜にくい」 means “hard to ~”. Japanese uses them for things like “this pen is easy to write with” or “this name is hard to remember.”
How to attach it
First turn the verb into the ます form, drop 「ます」, then add やすい or にくい.
書く → 書きます → drop ます → 書きやすい
食べる → 食べます → 食べにくい
話す → 話しやすい覚える → 覚えにくいする → しやすい来る → 来やすい（きやすい）
Once attached, the whole word works as an い-adjective and conjugates just like 「おいしい」:
書きやすい → 書きやすかった (it was easy to write)
わかりやすい → わかりやすくて (easy to understand, and…)
You can also put it right before a noun: 使いやすいアプリ (an easy-to-use app)
When to use it
Easy / hard to doHow smoothly things go when a person does the action.
・この靴は軽くて歩きやすいです。(These shoes are light and easy to walk in.)
・先生の説明はわかりやすいです。(The teacher's explanations are easy to understand.)
・この魚は骨が多くて食べにくいです。(This fish has a lot of bones, so it's a hassle to eat.)
Likely / unlikely to happenThis isn't about a person doing something on purpose. It's about things or people that tend to end up that way.
・白い服は汚れやすいです。(White clothes get dirty easily.)
・冬は風邪をひきやすいです。(You catch colds easily in winter.)
・このコップは割れにくいです。(This cup doesn't break easily.)
Easy mistakes
・Attach it to the ます form minus ます, not the dictionary form. It's 書きやすい, not 書くやすい.
・食べやすい does not mean “tasty”! It means “easy to eat, convenient to eat.” For “delicious,” use おいしい. In the same way, 食べにくい means “awkward to eat, a hassle to eat,” not “tastes bad” (that's まずい).
・To say “hard to write,” Japanese speakers usually just say 書きにくい. It's more natural than 書きやすくない.
・割れやすい means “breaks easily.” It describes the nature of the thing, not “easy to break on purpose.”
Don't confuse it with look-alikes
「〜そうです」 (looks like it will ~) also attaches to the ます form minus ます, so it's easy to mix up with やすい:
割れそう = judging by its appearance, you guess in the moment that it will break: このお皿、薄くて割れそう。(This plate is so thin, it looks like it's going to break.)
割れやすい = you know it's fragile by nature, as a characteristic: このお皿は割れやすいから、気をつけて。(This plate breaks easily, so be careful.)
Quick tip: for “looks like it's about to ~,” use そう. For “inherently prone to ~” or “easy to do,” use やすい.
What to learn next
Other patterns also take the ます form minus ます and add something, like 食べすぎる (eat too much) and 書き方 (way of writing). Learn the pattern once and you get all of these together.
n4-10:
The idea in one line
「〜たことがあります」 means “have (ever) done ~”. It says whether you have had this experience at some point in your life. “I've been to Japan” is 日本へ行ったことがあります。 and “I've never eaten cilantro” is パクチーを食べたことがありません。
How to form it
First turn the verb into its た-form (the plain past tense, the form behind “ate” and “went”), then add ことがあります.
The た-form is made just like the て-form, except て becomes た and で becomes だ:
Group 1 (godan verbs): 行く → 行った書く → 書いた飲む → 飲んだ乗る → 乗った
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop 「る」 and add た. 食べる → 食べた見る → 見た
Group 3 (only two, just memorize them): する → した来る → 来た（きた）
Then attach the whole phrase: 食べた → 食べたことがあります
How you'll hear it most
Have doneTalking about your own experience. You can add a number of times in front.
・着物を着たことがあります。(I've worn a kimono.)
・大阪には二回行ったことがあります。(I've been to Osaka twice.)
Never doneChange あります to ありません. Add 「一度も」 to mean “not even once.”
・一度も雪を見たことがありません。(I've never seen snow, not even once.)
Asking someoneAdd か at the end. You don't need to repeat the whole sentence in your answer. あります／ありません is enough.
・馬に乗ったことがありますか。(Have you ever ridden a horse?)
・はい、あります。／いいえ、ありません。(Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.)
Casual versionWith friends, use ことがある／ことがない. In speech, が is often dropped.
・富士山、登ったことある？(Have you climbed Mt. Fuji?)
Common mistakes
・It's about whether you've had the experience at any point in your life, so don't use it for recent things like just now or yesterday. さっき食べたことがある is wrong. Just say さっき食べた. A long-ago, broad time frame like “as a kid” is fine: 子どものころ、日本に住んだことがあります。 (I lived in Japan when I was a kid.)
・Don't use it for things everyone has obviously done. If you say ご飯を食べたことがあります for “I've eaten rice,” it sounds very odd to Japanese people, as if eating a meal were some rare experience.
・“Have never done” is 食べたことがありません, not 食べなかったことがあります. The latter means “there was a time when I didn't eat.”
・The verb before it must be in the た-form. With the dictionary form the meaning changes completely. See below.
・In 来たことがあります, 来 is read き, not く or こ.
Don't mix it up with look-alikes
た-form + ことがあります = have done ~ (experience)
納豆を食べたことがあります。(I've eaten natto.)
Dictionary form + ことがあります = sometimes does ~ (happens occasionally)
納豆を食べることがあります。(I sometimes eat natto.)
Also, English “have you eaten?” can mean “have you eaten yet?” In that case Japanese does not use ことがある:
もう食べましたか。(Have you eaten yet?)
食べたことがありますか。(Have you ever eaten it? = Do you have that experience?)
Quick test: if you can say “Have you ever ~?”, use たことがある. If it means “Have you ~ yet?”, use もう〜ました. If the verb before it is in the dictionary form, it means “sometimes.”
What to learn next
Pair it with 「〜てみたい」 (want to try ~). It's great for self-introductions and small talk:
温泉に入ったことがないので、一度入ってみたいです。(I've never been in a hot spring, so I'd like to try one once.)
n4-45:
The idea in one line
「〜んです」 is like saying “the thing is…”, “it's just that…”, or “is something wrong?” in English. The meaning of the sentence doesn't change, but it adds a layer of feeling: I'm giving you the background, or I've noticed a situation and want to know what's going on. Japanese people use it all the time. In speech it's almost always 「んです」, while 「のです」 is the version for writing and speeches.
When to use it
Explaining a reasonWhen someone asks you why, or when you feel you should explain the reason.
・どうして昨日休んだんですか。(Why were you off yesterday?)
・熱があったんです。(I had a fever.)
Asking about something you seeYou see a situation in front of you and want to know what's behind it.
・どうしたんですか。(What happened?)
・雨が降っているんですか。(Is it raining outside? Said when you see the other person come in with a wet umbrella.)
Setting the scene before you askUse 「〜んですが」 or 「〜んですけど」 to lay out the situation first, then make your request or ask your question. It's a very natural way to open.
・すみません、駅に行きたいんですが…。(Excuse me, I'd like to get to the station…)
Sharing news or feelingsTelling someone something on your own initiative, or stressing how you feel.
・実は来月結婚するんです。(Actually, I'm getting married next month.)
・本当に困っているんです。(I'm really in trouble.)
How to form it
Verbs and い-adjectives: take the plain form (the form without ます or です) and add んです directly.
行く → 行くんです行かない → 行かないんです行った → 行ったんです高い → 高いんです
な-adjectives and nouns: in the present affirmative, you need to add な in between.
好き → 好きなんです学生 → 学生なんです
For past or negative, just attach the plain form with no な: 学生だった → 学生だったんです好きじゃない → 好きじゃないんです
When talking with friends, use 「〜んだ」 or 「〜の」 to explain, and 「〜の？」 to ask: どうしたの？ (What's wrong?)
Common mistakes
・Forgetting な with な-adjectives and nouns: it's not 学生んです or 学生だんです, it's 学生なんです.
・It can't follow ます or です: not 行きますんです or 高いですんです, but 行くんです and 高いんです.
・Don't put it in every sentence. To state a plain fact, ます is enough. If every sentence ends in んです, you sound like you're constantly explaining yourself or making excuses.
・When you ask about someone's actions with 「〜んですか」, the wrong tone or situation can sound like you're pressing or interrogating them. For example, 何をしているんですか in a harsh voice becomes “What do you think you're doing!”, and どうして遅れたんですか can also sound like you're demanding an explanation. When asking someone older or senior, soften your tone, and you can start with あのう.
Don't mix it up with look-alikes
Same situation: a coworker's plans for tomorrow.
〜ますか = a plain question, with no clues to go on:
明日、どこかへ行きますか。(Are you going anywhere tomorrow?)
〜んですか = you see your coworker dragging a suitcase and want to know what's going on:
どこかへ行くんですか。(Are you going somewhere?)
The answer works the same way. To give the reason, use んです: 大阪に出張なんです。(I'm going to Osaka on a business trip.)
Quick test: if you've noticed something and want to know the reason behind it, use んですか. If you're just asking about something plainly, use ますか.
What to learn next
Follow 「〜んですが」 with a request, and you get a very polite way of asking: 日本語がよくわからないんですが、ゆっくり話していただけませんか。(I don't understand Japanese very well. Could you please speak more slowly?)
n4-47:
The idea in one line
Both are about "deciding," but the difference is who made the call.
ことにする = "I've decided to ~," so you make the decision yourself.
ことになる = "It's turned out that ~," so it may have been arranged by your company or school, or things may simply have worked out that way. It's like the difference between "I decided to move" and "I've been transferred to Osaka."
How to form it
Something you will do: dictionary form + ことにする／ことになる
行く → 行くことにする
Something you won't do: ない form + ことにする／ことになる
行かない → 行かないことにする
A decision is usually already made by the time you talk about it, so the past tense is the most common: ことにした, ことになった.
The four forms you'll hear most
ことにしたA decision you've just made yourself.
・来年、日本に留学することにしました。(I've decided to study abroad in Japan next year.)
・今日はどこにも行かないことにした。(I've decided not to go anywhere today.)
ことになったSomeone else decided, or things simply worked out that way.
・来月から大阪に転勤することになりました。(I'm being transferred to Osaka from next month.)
・6月に結婚することになりました。(I'm getting married in June.)
Getting married is clearly your own decision, so why use なる? Because なる sounds like "things have come to this point," which is more low-key and polite. Japanese people often say it this way when telling coworkers or their boss.
ことにしているA rule you set for yourself and keep following.
・寝る前はスマホを見ないことにしている。(I make it a rule not to look at my phone before bed.)
ことになっているA rule or custom set by a group, not by you.
・この寮では、10時までに帰ることになっている。(In this dorm, you're supposed to be back by 10.)
Easy mistakes
・After a noun, attach にする directly with no こと: when ordering, say コーヒーにします (I'll have coffee). Only a verb needs こと before にする: コーヒーをやめることにします (I've decided to give up coffee).
・The particle is に, not を: 行くことにした, not 「行くことをした」.
・When telling someone you're leaving your job, 辞めることにしました sounds like "I decided this myself," so your stance is very clear. 辞めることになりました is softer and less direct.
・ことにしている means "a rule I set myself," while ことになっている means "that's just the rule." Don't describe a dorm rule with ことにしている.
Don't mix it up with similar patterns
Take the same idea, "walking every day":
ことにする = the moment you make the decision: 毎日歩くことにした。 (I've decided to walk every day.)
ようにする = making an effort to do it: 毎日歩くようにしている。 (I try to walk every day.)
つもり = a plan in your head that isn't settled yet: 毎日歩くつもりだ。 (I plan to walk every day.)
Also, ことになる and ようになる are often confused:
日本で働くことになった。 (I'm going to work in Japan: it's been arranged, the matter is settled.)
日本語が話せるようになった。 (I've become able to speak Japanese: an ability or habit has gradually changed.)
Quick tip: use ことにする for "I decided," ことになる for "it's been settled," ようにする for "I try to," and つもり for "I plan to."
n4-48:
The idea in one line
「〜まま」means "just leaving it as it is" or "with ~ still on/open/going": a state doesn't change, and you go straight on to the next action. Think of leaving the house with the AC still on, or walking into a room with your shoes still on. It often carries the feeling of "you should have changed that first, but didn't."
How to form it
Verb た form + まま: the most common. You did an action, it left a state behind, and that state never changed.
開けた → 開けたまま (left open)
つけた → つけたまま (left the light or TV on)
Verb ない form + まま: the state of continuing not to do something.
言わない → 言わないまま (without ever saying it)
Noun + の + まま: 昔 → 昔のまま (the same as before)
この・その・あの + まま: このまま (like this), そのまま (like that)
Adjectives work too: い-adjectives attach directly, as in 若いまま (staying young); な-adjectives need な, as in きれいなまま (staying clean).
How you'll hear it most
Ended up that way by accidentUsed with 「〜てしまう」 to show regret or "oops."
・眼鏡をかけたままシャワーを浴びてしまった。(I took a shower with my glasses still on.)
・テレビをつけたまま寝てしまった。(I fell asleep with the TV still on.)
Rules and remindersTelling someone not to do something while in a certain state.
