・靴を履いたまま部屋に入らないでください。(Please don't enter the room with your shoes on.)
Never did itWith the ない form, for something that was never done from start to finish.
・何も言わないまま帰ってしまった。(He went home without saying anything.)
このまま・そのままYou'll hear these constantly in daily life, especially from shop staff and customer service.
・そのままお待ちください。(Please wait just as you are.)
・袋はいりません。このままで大丈夫です。(I don't need a bag. I'm fine carrying it as it is.)
At the end of a sentenceUse 「〜のままだ／のままです」 to say "it's still the same."
・この町は昔のままだ。(This town is exactly the same as it used to be.)
Easy mistakes
・The た here is not "past tense"; it means "it has already become that state." You use the た form even when talking about the present or future: 靴を履いたまま入ってもいいですよ。 (It's fine to come in with your shoes on.)
・To say "staying in a state," don't use the dictionary form: ×眼鏡をかけるまま, but ○眼鏡をかけたまま.
・A noun must always take の: ×昔まま, but ○昔のまま.
・English "while ~ing" or "with ~ on" isn't always まま. If you're just doing two things at the same time (eating while watching something), Japanese uses ながら; see below.
Don't mix it up with similar patterns
〜ながら = two actions happening at the same time, and you're actively doing both:
テレビを見ながら勉強した。 (I studied while watching TV.)
〜たまま = a state left untouched while you go on to the next action:
テレビをつけたまま勉強した。 (I studied with the TV left on.)
In the first sentence you're really watching TV; in the second the TV is just on, and you may not be watching at all.
〜て = a plain "doing something with ~," with no sense of "should have changed it":
帽子をかぶって出かけた。 (I put on a hat and went out.)
〜たまま = the listener feels "shouldn't you have changed that first?":
帽子をかぶったまま教室に入った。 (He walked into the classroom with his hat still on, as if he should have taken it off first.)
Quick tip: two things done together is ながら; leaving a state alone and going on to the next action is たまま.
What to learn next
Add 「にしておく」 to get deliberately keeping it that way: 窓を開けたままにしておいてください。 (Please leave the window open; don't close it.)
n4-15:
The idea in one line
「〜なくてもいいです」means "you don't have to ~" or "it's fine not to ~". Think of a shop assistant telling you "You don't need to take your shoes off." It means you can skip it, and it's also fine if you do it.
When to use it
Telling someone they needn't do somethingUse it to put the other person at ease or save them effort.
・明日は来なくてもいいです。(You don't have to come tomorrow.)
・全部食べなくてもいいですよ。(You don't have to eat it all.)
Asking whether something is necessaryAdd 「か」 at the end and it becomes "Is it okay not to ~?"
・靴を脱がなくてもいいですか。(Do I not need to take my shoes off?)
・はい、脱がなくてもいいですよ。(Right, you don't need to.)
How to form it
First turn the verb into its ない form (the "not ~" form). Then replace the final 「い」 with 「くて」 and add 「もいい」.
行かない → replace い with くて → 行かなくて → add もいい → 行かなくてもいい
To make it polite, add 「です」 at the end.
Conjugation: first, which type of verb is it?
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the matching 「あ」-row sound, add ない, then change it to なくてもいい.
書く → change く to か → 書かなくてもいい
待つ → 待たなくてもいい帰る → 帰らなくてもいい
Verbs ending in 「う」 change to わ: 買う → 買わなくてもいい
Exception: the ない form of ある is just 「ない」, so it becomes なくてもいい, not あらなくてもいい.
・予約がなくてもいいですか。(Is it okay without a reservation?)
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop 「る」 and add なくてもいい.
食べる → 食べなくてもいい慌てる → 慌てなくてもいい
Group 3 (just two verbs, so memorize them): する → しなくてもいい来る → 来なくてもいい(こなくても)
・今日は残業しなくてもいいです。(You don't have to work overtime today.)
How you'll hear it most
Between friendsSwap 「です」 for 「よ」, and the 「も」 often gets dropped too.
・無理しなくていいよ。(No need to push yourself.)
Another way to say itReplace 「いい」 with 「大丈夫」; the meaning is the same.
・返事しなくても大丈夫です。(You don't need to reply.)
More politeAt work, in shops and in formal notices you'll hear 「なくてもかまいません」.
・印鑑は持ってこなくてもかまいません。(You don't need to bring your seal.)
Easy mistakes
・You can't attach ても straight onto ない: 「行かないてもいい」 is wrong. Change い to くて to get 行かなくてもいい.
・The ない form of 買う is 買わない, not 買あない; the ない form of ある is ない, not あらない.
・In English, "you don't have to come" and "you must not come" can sound close, but they are very different. 来なくてもいい means "you can skip it, but you're welcome to come." It does not mean "please don't come."
・When someone asks 「〜なくてもいいですか」 and the answer is "you must do it," answer with いいえ、〜なければなりません. Don't just say いいえ and stop there.
Telling look-alikes apart
Here are four ways to talk about "going to the office tomorrow":
てもいい = you may do it: 明日、会社に行ってもいいです。(You may go to the office tomorrow.)
なくてもいい = you don't have to: 明日、会社に行かなくてもいいです。(You don't have to go to the office tomorrow.)
てはいけない = you must not: 明日、会社に行ってはいけません。(You must not go to the office tomorrow.)
なければならない = you must: 明日、会社に行かなければなりません。(You must go to the office tomorrow.)
Another one that's often confused with it is 「ないでください」:
来ないでください。(Please don't come: you're telling them not to.)
来なくてもいいです。(You don't have to come: either way is fine.)
Quick rule of thumb: to say "no need, skip it," use なくてもいい. To say "don't do it, not allowed," use ないでください or てはいけない.
What to learn next
Adjectives and nouns can express the same idea: 高くなくてもいいです。(It doesn't have to be expensive.), 上手じゃなくてもいいです。(You don't have to be good at it.) Next, learn 「〜なければなりません」, and you'll be able to say both "you don't have to" and "you must" clearly.
n4-16:
The idea in one line
「〜なければなりません」means "must ~" or "have to ~". The Japanese logic is interesting: it literally says "if you don't do it, it won't do." If not doing it is unacceptable, then you have to do it.
When to use it
Rules and obligationsUse it for rules and duties: things your school or company requires, or things the situation forces you to do.
・明日までにレポートを出さなければなりません。(You must hand in the report by tomorrow.)
・学校では制服を着なければなりません。(At school, you have to wear a uniform.)
Feeling you have to do it yourselfNobody has set a rule; you just feel "I really should do this now."
・もう11時だ。帰らなければならない。(It's already 11 o'clock. I have to go home.)
・薬を毎日飲まなければなりません。(I have to take my medicine every day.)
How to form it
Three steps: turn the verb into its ない form (the "not ~" form), drop the final 「ない」, then add なければなりません.
行く → 行かない → drop ない → 行か → 行かなければなりません
Group 1 (godan verbs):
書く → 書かなければなりません
待つ → 待たなければなりません
買う → 買わなければなりません (verbs ending in う become わ, not あ)
Group 2 (ichidan verbs):
食べる → 食べなければなりません
起きる → 起きなければなりません
Group 3 (just two verbs, so memorize them):
する → しなければなりません
来る → 来なければなりません(こなければ)
How you'll hear it most
なければなりませんThe polite form, for teachers, bosses and customers.
なければならないThe plain form, for talking to yourself and for writing.
なきゃ／ないとCasual speech between friends: 「なければ」 shrinks to 「なきゃ」, or you just stop at 「ないと」.
・あ、もう行かなきゃ。(Oh, I've got to go now.)
・明日早いから、早く寝ないと。(I have an early start tomorrow, so I'd better get to bed.)
To say "had to ~" in the past, change the ending to なりませんでした:
・昨日は遅くまで働かなければなりませんでした。(Yesterday I had to work until late.)
You'll also hear 「〜なければいけません」. It means almost the same thing and is very common in everyday conversation.
Easy mistakes
・It attaches to the ない form, not the dictionary form (the base form you'd find in a dictionary): it's not 行くなければ but 行かなければ.
・It's long and easy to misread. Break it into 「な・け・れ・ば」 + 「なりません」 to remember it; it's not なくれば or なけば.
・Don't see the 「ません」 at the end and think it means "don't do it." The whole phrase means you must do it.
・来る is read こなければ, not きなければ.
・「なきゃ」 and 「ないと」 are for friends. With a boss or teacher, use the full なければなりません.
・When asking someone to do something, saying "you must ~" outright sounds harsh. 「〜てください」 is the usual, politer choice.
Telling look-alikes apart
These four often show up together on tests. Here they are with the same situation, "going to school tomorrow":
明日、学校に行かなければなりません。(You have to go to school tomorrow.)
明日、学校に行かなくてもいいです。(You don't have to go to school tomorrow.)
明日、学校に行ってもいいです。(You may go to school tomorrow.)
明日、学校に行ってはいけません。(You must not go to school tomorrow.)
Watch out: if someone asks 「〜なければなりませんか」 ("Do I have to ~?") and you want to answer "no need," say なくてもいいです. It isn't a negative of なければなりません.
・名前を書かなければなりませんか。(Do I have to write my name?)
・いいえ、書かなくてもいいです。(No, you don't have to. It's fine not to write it.)
Another frequent mix-up is ほうがいい, which is only a "suggestion" and not mandatory:
薬を飲んだほうがいいです。(You'd better take some medicine.)
薬を飲まなければなりません。(You have to take your medicine.)
Quick rule of thumb: "must" is なければなりません, "don't have to" is なくてもいい, and "had better" is ほうがいい.
n4-13:
The gist in one line
「〜てもいいです」means “you may ~” or “it's okay to ~”. Add「か」at the end and it becomes “May I ~?” or “Is it okay to ~?”, the most common way to ask permission in Japan. In a shop, when you want to take a photo, sit in an empty seat or try something on, this is how you start the question.
How to attach it
Change the verb to its te-form, then add「もいいです」。
使う → 使って → 使ってもいいです
How to conjugate: first check the verb group
Group 1 (godan verbs): look at the last kana.
う、つ、る → って：座る → 座って待つ → 待って
む、ぶ、ぬ → んで：休む → 休んで呼ぶ → 呼んで
く → いて：書く → 書いて(the only exception is 行く → 行って)
ぐ → いで：泳ぐ → 泳いで
す → して：話す → 話して
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop「る」and add て.
食べる → 食べて見る → 見て
Group 3 (only two verbs, just memorize them)：する → して来る → 来て（きて）
How you'll hear it most
Asking permissionAdd「か」at the end.
・この椅子を使ってもいいですか。(May I use this chair?)
・ここに座ってもいいですか。(May I sit here?)
How to answerYes: はい、どうぞ。(Yes, go ahead), いいですよ。(Sure)
No: すみません、ちょっと…。(Sorry, that's a bit difficult…)
Telling someone it's okayIt's common to add「よ」at the end, which sounds friendlier.
・明日は休んでもいいですよ。(You can take tomorrow off)
・鉛筆で書いてもいいです。(You may write in pencil)
Between friendsDrop です, and in casual speech even「も」is often dropped.
・これ、食べていい？(Can I eat this?)
To ask more politely of a boss or a customer, swap いい for よろしい: 写真を撮ってもよろしいですか。(Would it be all right to take a photo?)
Easy mistakes
・When the te-form ends in「で」, what follows is「でもいい」: 休んでもいい. Don't write 休んてもいい.
・When someone asks「〜てもいいですか」and you want to say no, textbooks teach いいえ、いけません, but in real conversation it sounds harsh, like scolding. In daily life people mostly say すみません、ちょっと….
・「〜てもいいですよ」grants permission, and it sounds a bit like talking down to someone. Saying 帰ってもいいですよ to a teacher or boss would be very rude.
・English “can” also covers ability, as in “I can speak Japanese”. That is really “I'm able to speak it”, so Japanese says 日本語が話せます. If you say 日本語を話してもいいです, it means “you're allowed to speak Japanese”.
Telling apart the look-alikes
The four patterns “may, must not, don't have to, have to” look alike. Here they are with one and the same situation:
Do it, OK明日は来てもいいです。(You may come tomorrow)
Do it, NG明日は来てはいけません。(You must not come tomorrow)
Don't do it, OK明日は来なくてもいいです。(You don't have to come tomorrow)
Don't do it, NG明日は来なくてはいけません。(You have to come tomorrow)
The last one is also often said as 来なければなりません, with the same meaning.
Quick trick: first check whether the front part is「て」or「なくて」, then whether the ending is「いい」or「いけない」.
Also don't mix it up with ことができます:
ここで泳いでもいいですか。(May I swim here?: asking if it's allowed)
泳ぐことができますか。(Can you swim?: asking if you're able)
Quick trick: for “is it allowed?” use てもいい; for “can you / are you able to?” use ことができる.
What to learn next
Learn the other three cells of the table above: 「〜てはいけません」(prohibition), 「〜なくてもいいです」(not necessary), and 「〜なければなりません」(obligation).
n4-14:
The gist in one line
「〜てはいけません」means “must not ~” or “not allowed to ~”. You'll hear it when a teacher announces rules, when someone explains the rules of a place, or when parents tell a child “don't lie”. (Real signs mostly say「撮影禁止」or「〜ないでください」instead of writing out the whole sentence.)
When to use it
Explaining rulesRules of a school, company or place, spoken aloud to someone.
・ここで写真を撮ってはいけません。(You must not take photos here)
・授業中に寝てはいけません。(You must not sleep during class)
Teaching kids, stating general rulesWhen adults speak to children, or talk about things everyone should follow, the plain form「〜てはいけない」(without ます) is common.
・うそをついてはいけないよ。(You mustn't lie, okay?)
How to attach it
First change the verb to its te-form (the same form that goes before「〜てください」), then add「はいけません」directly.
撮る → 撮って → 撮ってはいけません
食べる → 食べて → 食べてはいけません
する → して → してはいけません
Some Group 1 (godan) verbs have a te-form ending in「で」, so it becomes「ではいけません」:
飲む → 飲んで → 飲んではいけません
遊ぶ → 遊んで → 遊んではいけません
How you'll hear it most
〜てはいけませんThe polite form, used when explaining rules.
〜てはいけないThe plain form, for family, friends and children.
〜ちゃいけないThe shortened spoken form: 「ては」becomes「ちゃ」and「では」becomes「じゃ」.
・危ないから、ここで遊んじゃいけないよ。(It's dangerous, so you mustn't play here, okay?)
〜ちゃだめSwap「いけない」for「だめ」and it gets even more casual. Parents scolding kids use it all the time.
・まだ食べちゃだめ。(You can't eat yet)
Easy mistakes
・The「は」in「ては」is pronounced wa, not ha.
・After「飲んで」「遊んで」you need では. Don't write 飲んてはいけません. When shortened it also becomes「じゃ」: 飲んじゃだめ.
・This phrase is very strong, like laying down a rule. Don't use it directly with bosses, customers or elders. Say 〜ないでください (please don't ~) instead, or the phrase shops often use, 〜はご遠慮ください.
・Textbooks often teach「〜てもいいですか」→「いいえ、〜てはいけません」, but in real life that reply comes across as harsh. Japanese people usually say すみません、ここはちょっと…, using「ちょっと」to decline gently.
Telling apart the look-alikes
“May / must not / don't have to / have to” are easy to tangle. Here they are in one situation (a doctor's instructions about medicine):
てもいい = may do: この薬は飲んでもいいです。(You may take this medicine)
てはいけない = must not do: この薬は飲んではいけません。(You must not take this medicine)
なくてもいい = don't have to do: この薬は飲まなくてもいいです。(You don't have to take this medicine)
なければならない = have to do: この薬は飲まなければなりません。(You have to take this medicine)
The one to be most careful with is「なくてはいけません」. It also contains「いけません」, but it means must, the same as「なければなりません」:
飲んではいけません (must not take it)
飲まなくてはいけません (have to take it)
Only a few syllables differ, yet the meaning is completely opposite.
Quick trick: look at what comes before「はいけません」. A regular te-form (飲んで) → must not; 「なくて」(飲まなくて) → have to.
n4-21:
The idea in one line
「し」works like English "and what's more…" or "not only X, but also Y". When you explain why, you stack up reasons one by one and then lead to your conclusion. For example, "This place is cheap, and it's tasty, so I come here often." In Japanese, し links "cheap" and "tasty".
・この店は安いし、おいしいし、よく来ます。(This place is cheap and tasty, so I come often.)
How to form it
Put the plain form (the form without ます or です) in front, then add し directly.
Verbs: 降る → 降るしない → ないし疲れた → 疲れたし
い-adjectives: 安い → 安いし遠くない → 遠くないし
な-adjectives: add 「だ」 first, then し. 静か → 静かだし
Nouns: add 「だ」 here too. 雨 → 雨だし
When speaking to superiors or customers, you can use the polite form too: 便利ですし, あまり時間もありませんし.
When to use it
Stacking reasons to reach a conclusionThis is the most common use. 「も」 often goes after each reason, giving a "this too, and that too…" feel.
・お金もないし、時間もないし、旅行は無理です。(I have no money and no time either, so a trip is out of the question.)
・雨も降っているし、疲れているし、タクシーで帰りましょう。(It's raining, and we're tired, so let's take a taxi home.)
Describing the good or bad points of a person or thingUse it to list the features of a person or a place.
・田中さんは優しいし、おもしろいし、みんなに人気がある。(Tanaka is kind and funny, and popular with everyone.)
Giving just one reasonYou can also give only one. It sounds like "(there are other reasons too, but) this alone is enough…", and the tone is softer.
・もう遅いし、そろそろ帰ります。(It's already late, so I'll head home soon.)
You can even leave the conclusion unsaid and let the other person figure it out. This is very handy for turning someone down:
今日はちょっと疲れてるし…(I'm a bit tired today, so…)
Common mistakes
・な-adjectives and nouns must take だ: it's 静かだし and 雨だし, never 「静かし」 or 「雨し」.
・Stacked reasons should point in the same direction, all supporting the same conclusion. To say "I like this place," stack "cheap" and "tasty"; don't mix a good point with a bad one.
・し carries a sense of "and that's not all." If you have just one clear reason and want to state it plainly and firmly, 「から」 or 「ので」 is more direct.
Telling similar patterns apart
し = stacks several reasons, with the tone "X, and Y, so…":
この店は安いし、おいしいし、よく来ます。(It's cheap and tasty, so I come often.)
から・ので = states plainly "it's because of this":
この店は安いから、よく来ます。(Because it's cheap, I come often.)
たり also lists several things, but it gives examples of actions you do, not reasons:
週末は映画を見たり、買い物をしたりします。(On weekends I do things like watch movies and go shopping.)
週末は暇だし、天気もいいし、出かけよう。(I'm free this weekend and the weather's nice, so let's go out.)
Quick rule of thumb: explaining "why" with several stacked reasons → し; one clear reason → から・ので; listing "what you do" → たり.
What to learn next
If you want to add one more reason after you've finished, use 「それに」 (besides, on top of that) to start the next sentence: この部屋は広いし、駅にも近い。それに家賃も安い。(This room is spacious and close to the station. On top of that, the rent is cheap.)
n4-36:
The idea in one line
「〜でしょう」 is like English "probably…" or "I guess…". With a falling ending, you're guessing; with a rising ending, it becomes "…, right?" and you're checking with the other person. 「だろう」 is the plain form. The meaning is the same, but it isn't polite.
When to use it
Guessing (falling intonation)You aren't sure, but you feel it's most likely so. Weather forecasts love it.
・明日は雨が降るでしょう。(It will probably rain tomorrow.)
・田中さんはもう家に帰ったでしょう。(Mr. Tanaka has probably already gone home.)
It often appears with 「たぶん」 (probably): たぶん大丈夫でしょう。(It's probably fine.)
Checking (rising intonation)You think the other person knows too and will agree, so you ask to get a nod. In speech it's often shortened to 「でしょ？」.
・これ、おいしいでしょう？(This is tasty, right?)
・ほら、言ったでしょ？(See? Didn't I tell you?)
How to form it
Put the plain form (without です or ます) in front, then add でしょう or だろう.
Verbs: 行く → 行くでしょう行かない → 行かないでしょう行った → 行ったでしょう
い-adjectives: add it directly. 高い → 高いでしょう
Nouns and な-adjectives: drop だ first, then add it. 学生だ → 学生でしょう元気だ → 元気でしょう
In the past tense, keep 「だった」: 学生だった → 学生だったでしょう
Choosing between でしょう and だろう
でしょう: polite. Use it with people you don't know well, in formal settings, and in news and weather reports.
だろう: plain. It shows up most in thoughts, talking to yourself, and writing.
・明日は晴れるだろう。(It'll probably clear up tomorrow: thinking to yourself)
Saying 「だろう」 or 「だろ？」 directly to someone sounds masculine and a bit pushy. When chatting with friends, many people (especially women) say 「でしょ？」.
Common mistakes
・Don't keep だ after nouns and な-adjectives: say 学生でしょう, not 「学生だでしょう」.
・English "will" is not always でしょう. "I'll go tomorrow" is your own decision, so just say 明日行きます. Saying 「行くでしょう」 sounds like you're guessing whether you yourself will go, which is odd.
・The confirming 「でしょう？」 carries a feel of "you must know this, right?", so it can sound a bit rude to a teacher or boss. Switching to 「〜ですよね」 is safer.
・でしょう is pronounced with a long vowel (でしょー); the short 「でしょ」 is the shortened spoken version.
Telling similar patterns apart
Same question: will Mr. Tanaka come today?
・田中さんは来るでしょう。(Mr. Tanaka will probably come.) → I think he most likely will.
・田中さんは来るかもしれません。(Mr. Tanaka might come.) → Fifty-fifty; it wouldn't be a surprise if he didn't.
・田中さんは来るはずです。(Mr. Tanaka should come.) → There's a basis for it, e.g. he said himself yesterday that he'd come.
Quick rule of thumb: 「might」 → かもしれない, 「probably」 → でしょう, 「should, as expected」 → はずだ.
What to learn next
Adding 「と思います」 afterward makes it softer, and both men and women use it a lot: 明日は寒くなるだろうと思います。(I think it'll probably get cold tomorrow.)
Turning でしょう into the question 「でしょうか」 is more polite than 「ですか」: すみません、駅はどこでしょうか。(Excuse me, where is the station?)
n4-11:
The idea in one line
「〜ほうがいい」 means “you'd better ～” or “you'd better not ～”. If your friend has a fever and you say “You should go see a doctor,” that's 病院に行ったほうがいい. It's advice, with a hint of “if you don't, things might not go so well.”
How to form it
Better to do ～verb た-form + ほうがいい
休む → 休んだほうがいい行く → 行ったほうがいい
食べる → 食べたほうがいいする → したほうがいい
If the た-form still feels shaky, work from the て-form: just swap 「て」 for 「た」 and 「で」 for 「だ」.休んで → 休んだ
Better not to ～verb ない-form + ほうがいい
行く → 行かないほうがいい食べる → 食べないほうがいい
来る → 来ないほうがいい（こない）
The ending depends on who you're talking to: with friends, say 「〜ほうがいいよ」; to be more polite, say 「〜ほうがいいです」.
・雨が降りそうだから、傘を持っていったほうがいいよ。（It looks like rain, so you'd better take an umbrella.）
・寝る前にコーヒーを飲まないほうがいいです。（You'd better not drink coffee before bed.）
Where people slip up
・It uses the た-form, but it's not past tense. 行ったほうがいい tells you to go now or later, not that you “have gone.”
・Your instinct may be to use the dictionary form: 「行くほうがいい」. When giving someone specific advice, Japanese speakers normally say 行ったほうがいい, so memorize it that way to be safe.
・For the negative, use just the ない-form, with no further change to the た-form: it's 行かないほうがいい, not 「行かなかったほうがいい」.
・The tone is actually not that light. Saying 「〜たほうがいいですよ」 straight to your boss or teacher can sound like you're telling them what to do. To soften it, add 「と思います」: 少し休んだほうがいいと思います。（I think you'd better rest a little.）
・In kanji, 「ほう」 is written 「方」, and here it's read ほう, not the かた of 「〜方」 (“way of doing ~”).
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Same situation, a sore throat:
たほうがいい = advice. You could skip it, it's just not ideal: のどが痛いなら、薬を飲んだほうがいいですよ。（If your throat hurts, you'd better take some medicine.）
なければなりません = a rule. You must do it: この薬は一日三回飲まなければなりません。（You must take this medicine three times a day.）
たらいい = suggesting one way to do it, in a lighter tone: のどが痛いときは、温かいお茶を飲んだらいいですよ。（When your throat hurts, it's good to drink some hot tea.）
Quick rule of thumb: “you'd better ～ (or it won't be good)” takes ほうがいい; “you must ～” takes なければなりません; “just do ～ and you'll be fine” takes たらいい.
What to learn next
Change いい to よかった and you get regret, “I should have ～”: 傘を持ってきたほうがよかった。（I should have brought an umbrella.）
n4-12:
The idea in one line
「〜すぎる」 means “too ～” or “～ too much”. Eating too much, drinking too much, too expensive, too hard: whenever something goes past the right amount, add 「すぎる」 after it. For a polite tone, say 「すぎます」.
・昨日、ゲームをやりすぎました。（I played too many video games yesterday.）
・このかばんは高すぎます。（This bag is too expensive.）
How to form it
VerbsChange to the ます-form, drop 「ます」, and add すぎる. All three verb groups work the same way.
飲む → 飲みます → 飲みすぎる
食べる → 食べます → 食べすぎる
する → します → しすぎる（e.g. 心配しすぎる = to worry too much）
い-adjectivesDrop the final 「い」 and add すぎる.
高い → 高すぎる難しい → 難しすぎる
な-adjectivesAttach it directly, without adding な.
静か → 静かすぎる派手 → 派手すぎる
すぎる itself conjugates too
すぎる conjugates like a Group 2 (ichidan) verb: drop 「る」 and add the ending.
すぎる → すぎますすぎる → すぎたすぎる → すぎて
The most common form is 「すぎて」, which gives the reason for the result that follows:
・食べすぎて、お腹が痛いです。（I ate too much, and my stomach hurts.）
・この部屋は静かすぎて、ちょっとこわいです。（This room is too quiet, and it's a little scary.）
Forms you'll hear a lot
Becomes a nounVerb ます-stem + すぎ, without the る, becomes a noun meaning “too much ～” or “overdoing ～.”
・飲みすぎに気をつけてください。（Please be careful not to drink too much.）
ApologyYou hear this a lot after an argument.
・さっきは言いすぎました。ごめんなさい。（I went too far with what I said earlier. I'm sorry.）
Where people slip up
・You must drop the 「い」 of い-adjectives: it's 高すぎる, not 高いすぎる.
・Don't add な to な-adjectives: it's 静かすぎる, not 静かなすぎる.
・「いい」 has to become 「よ」: よすぎる (too good). If you write いいすぎる, Japanese people will hear it as 言いすぎる (to say too much, to go too far).
・「ない」 (not having) becomes なさすぎる: 時間がなさすぎる (there's far too little time). But 少ない follows the normal rule: 少なすぎる.
・すぎる usually carries a feeling of “past the limit, not great.” Young people do use かわいすぎる to praise someone, but for ordinary “really tasty” or “really pretty,” とても is the safer choice.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
English has the same split between “very” and “too,” and Japanese keeps them apart too. Same situation:
このかばんはとても高いです。（This bag is very expensive.）: it just describes the price as high.
このかばんは高すぎます。（This bag is too expensive.）: it's beyond what you can accept, and the implication is “I won't buy it.”
Quick rule of thumb: if you can follow it with “so it's no good / so there's a problem,” use すぎる. If you're just saying the degree is high, use とても.
What to learn next
Combine it with 「〜ないようにする」 and you get a favorite line of doctors: 飲みすぎないようにしてください。（Please try not to drink too much.）
n4-6:
The idea in one line
「〜方」 works like English "how to ~" or "the way of ~ing": how to write, how to read, how to use, how to eat. It turns an action into "the way to do it." You'll use it all the time when you ask "How do I use this?" or "How do I get there?"
How to form it
Put the verb in ます form, drop ます, then add 方（かた）.
Group 1 (godan verbs) and Group 2 (ichidan verbs) work the same way:
書きます → drop ます → 書き方 (how to write)
読みます → 読み方 (how to read)使います → 使い方 (how to use)
食べます → 食べ方 (how to eat)見ます → 見方 (how to look at something, a point of view)
Group 3 (する・来る) needs to be memorized separately:
・する becomes 仕方（しかた）.
・For 「noun ＋ する」 verbs, say noun ＋ の ＋ 仕方: 勉強する → 勉強の仕方掃除する → 掃除の仕方
・来る becomes 来方（きかた）, but you'll hear 行き方 much more often.
How you'll hear it most
Asking for a methodYou don't know how to do something, so you ask someone to teach you.
・この漢字の読み方を教えてください。 (Please tell me how to read this kanji.)
・駅への行き方がわかりません。 (I don't know how to get to the station.)
・日本語の勉強の仕方を教えてください。 (Please teach me how to study Japanese.)
Describing how someone does somethingIt isn't always a "method." It can also mean the manner or habit someone has when doing it.
・彼は話し方がやさしいです。 (He has a gentle way of speaking.)
・箸の持ち方がきれいですね。 (You hold your chopsticks so properly, don't you!)
Easy mistakes
・Change を to の. 「〜方」 is already a noun, so を can't come before it: 本を読む → 本の読み方, not 「本を読み方」.
・「に／へ」 usually becomes 「への」: 駅に行く → 駅への行き方.
・Since it's a noun, it takes particles like が and を after it: 使い方がわかりません, 書き方を教えてください.
・Here 方 is read かた, and it doesn't turn into がた: 書き方 is read かきかた.
・For verbs like 勉強する and 掃除する, don't follow the formula and make 「勉強し方」. Say 勉強の仕方.
Don't confuse it with a look-alike
The same kanji 「方」 is read ほう in 〜ほうがいいです, and the meaning is completely different.
書き方を教えてください。 (Please teach me how to write it: method)
名前を書いたほうがいいです。 (You should write your name: advice)
Quick test: if what comes before is 「ます form minus ます」 (書き, 読み), it's read かた = "how to ~." If it's the た form, ない form, or dictionary form (書いた, 書かない), it's read ほう = comparison or advice.
What to learn next
「〜やすい・〜にくい」 also attach to the ます form minus ます, so it's handy to learn them together: このペンは書きやすいです。 (This pen is easy to write with.)
n4-9:
The idea in one line
「〜ことができます」 means "can ~", "be able to ~", or "know how to ~". It's simple: add 「こと」 to an action to turn it into "the act of doing it," then say it "can be done (できます)."
When to use it
AbilityYou've studied or practiced, so you can do it.
・私は日本語を話すことができます。 (I can speak Japanese.)
・ピアノを弾くことができます。 (I can play the piano.)
Circumstances allow itIt's not about whether you have the skill. The place or the rules let you do it.
・この図書館ではWi-Fiを使うことができます。 (You can use Wi-Fi at this library.)
・このカードはコンビニでも使うことができます。 (This card can be used at convenience stores too.)
How to form it
Use the dictionary form of the verb (the form you find in a dictionary) and add 「ことができます」. All three verb groups work the same way, with no extra changes.
If you only remember the ます form, change it back to the dictionary form first: 書きます → 書く → 書くことができます
食べる → 食べることができますする → することができます来る → 来ることができます（くる）
For "can't," change ます to ません. For "was able to (at that time)," change it to ました:
漢字を書くことができません。 (I can't write kanji.)
昨日はゆっくり休むことができました。 (Yesterday I was able to get a good rest.)
Nouns for skills, sports, and languages can also take 「ができます」 directly: 日本語ができます。 (I can do Japanese / I speak Japanese.), テニスができます。 (I can play tennis.)
Ordinary nouns can't be used this way. For example, you don't say 「電車ができます」. You say 電車に乗ることができます.
Easy mistakes
・What comes before must be the dictionary form, never the ます form. You don't say 「行きますことができます」. It's 行くことができます.
・The original 「を」 stays: ピアノを弾くことができます. You don't need to change it to が.
・English "will" (future) can't be expressed with ことができます. "It will rain tomorrow" is 明日は雨が降るでしょう or 雨が降るかもしれません.
・わかる already means "to understand," so don't add ことができます. Just say 日本語がわかります.
・To ask permission on the spot ("May I ~?"), 〜てもいいですか sounds more natural.
Don't confuse it with look-alikes
The potential form (話せる, 書ける) means almost the same as ことができます:
日本語を話すことができます。 (I can speak Japanese: more formal, stiffer)
日本語が話せます。 (I can speak Japanese: more common in everyday speech)
You'll often see ことができます on notices, in manuals, and in formal self-introductions. With friends, people mostly use the potential form. If you haven't learned the potential form yet, ことができます is always safe.
〜てもいいです means "I allow you to do it":
ここで写真を撮ることができます。 (You can take photos here: explaining the rules or the situation)
ここで写真を撮ってもいいですよ。 (You may take photos here: the speaker is giving permission)
Quick test: to talk about ability or possibility ("can or can't"), use ことができます or the potential form. To talk about permission ("allowed or not"), use てもいいです.
What to learn next
A more casual way to say the same thing is the potential form, for example 話す → 話せる.
n4-1:
The idea in one line
「〜までに」means "by…" or "no later than…" (it has to be done before then). In other words, it sets a deadline. Think of a bill that says "Please pay by May 10". That "by" is までに. The key point: you finish one thing before that point in time.
When to use it
Giving a deadlineA teacher, boss, or shop tells you "this has to be done by such-and-such a time".
・レポートは金曜日までに出してください。(Please hand in the report by Friday.)
・明日までにお願いします。(Could you get it to me by tomorrow, please?)
Your own goalsSetting a deadline for yourself.
・5時までに駅に着きたい。(I want to get to the station by 5:00.)
・夏までに5キロやせたい。(I want to lose 5 kg by summer.)
How to attach it
Times, days, and events take までに directly:
3時 → 3時までに試験 → 試験までに
Verbs use the plain dictionary form (辭書形) plus までに, meaning "before ~ happens":
帰る → 帰るまでに
・母が帰るまでに部屋を片付けます。(I'll tidy my room before my mom gets back.)
Telling it apart from its look-alike
It differs by just one 「に」, but the meaning changes a lot.
まで = an action keeps going until that time, then stops.
までに = you get something done before that time, and then it's finished.
・5時まで待ちます。(I'll wait until 5:00. I wait continuously from now until 5:00.)
・5時までに来てください。(Please come by 5:00. Coming at 4:00 or 4:30 is fine.)
・10時まで勉強します。(I'll study until 10:00.)
・10時までにお風呂に入ります。(I'll take a bath before 10:00.)
Quick test: if you'd say "until" in English, use まで. If you'd say "by" or "no later than", use までに.
Common mistakes
・When you mean "keep doing something up to that time" (waiting until 5:00, studying until 10:00), use まで, not までに. For example, 5時までに待ちます is wrong. Say 5時まで待ちます. But if you mean "get something done before a certain time", までに works, as in 試験までに勉強しておきます (I'll get my studying done before the exam). Japanese people say this all the time.
・金曜日までに normally includes Friday itself. Handing it in on Friday still counts as on time, so it doesn't have to be Thursday.
・A verb before it must be in dictionary form: you say 日本に来るまでに, never 「来たまでに」.
What to learn next
Add 「は」 to get までには, which adds the nuance "at the very least, before ~": 夜までには帰ります。 (I'll definitely be back by evening at the latest.)
n4-23:
The idea in one line
「〜てみる」means "try ...ing" or "give it a try": try eating it, try it on, try asking. You don't know the result yet, so you do it once to see what happens. Add「みる」after the verb's て-form. For the polite form, say「みます」.
When to use it
Trying somethingIt's your first time and you don't know how it'll turn out, so you give it a go.
・納豆を食べてみた。(I tried natto.)
・わからないから、駅員さんに聞いてみます。(I don't know, so I'll try asking the station staff.)
Trying on / trying outVery common in shops. Follow it with「〜てもいいですか」to ask permission.
・この服、着てみてもいいですか。(May I try this on?)
Asking someone to try「〜てみてください」= please try ...ing.
・この靴、はいてみてください。(Please try these shoes on.)
Wanting to try「〜てみたい」= I'd like to try ...ing. Use it for things you've never done and are curious about.
・一度、富士山に登ってみたい。(I'd like to try climbing Mt. Fuji once.)
How to form it
Change the verb to its て-form, then add「みる」。
行く → 行って → 行ってみる
食べる → 食べて → 食べてみる
する → して → してみる
「みる」itself is a Group 2 (ichidan) verb, so it follows the Group 2 rules afterward: drop the る and attach the ending.
やってみる → やってみますやってみたやってみたいやってみて
Easy mistakes
・This「みる」is normally written in hiragana, not as 見る. It no longer means "look with your eyes." So 聞いてみる means "try asking," and has nothing to do with eyes.
・If you really do mean "try looking," that's 見てみる. The first 見る is "look" and the second みる is "try." It isn't a typo or a repeat.
・Use it only for things you decide to do yourself. You can't add てみる to things outside your control, like rain or illness. You can't say「雨が降ってみる」.
・試してみる sounds redundant, since both parts mean "try," but Japanese people really do say it and it sounds natural.
・In a shop, ちょっと考えてみます (I'll think about it) is often a polite "no for now." Don't expect the person to come back and buy.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
てみた = the focus is on having tried. You're usually talking about that one occasion and then giving your impression:
納豆を食べてみた。けっこうおいしかった。 (I tried natto, and it was actually pretty good.)
たことがある = the focus is on whether you have the experience:
納豆を食べたことがある。 (I've eaten natto.)
たい = simply "want to do": 沖縄に行きたい。 (I want to go to Okinawa.)
てみたい = you've never done it, you're curious, and you want to "try it once": 沖縄に行ってみたい。 (I'd like to go and see Okinawa.)
Quick test: if you can say "try ...ing" or "give it a try" in English, use てみる. If you mean "have done ...", use たことがある. If it's just "want to ...", use たい. If you're curious and want to experience it once, use てみたい.
What to learn next
These are also "て-form + a verb" patterns. Next, try 〜てしまう (to do something by accident / to finish doing) and 〜ておく (to do something in advance). They're formed the same way, only the meanings differ.
n4-25:
The idea in one line
「〜ておきます」means "do ... in advance" or "get ... ready beforehand". Buy your tickets before a trip, chill the beer before friends come over. Japanese uses「〜ておく」for these actions you do now for the sake of what comes later. It can also mean "leave it as it is, don't touch it."
When to use it
Preparing aheadYou do something now for the sake of something later. This is the most common use.
・出張の前に切符を買っておきます。(I'll buy the ticket before the business trip.)
・会議の前に資料を読んでおきます。(I'll read through the materials before the meeting.)
・ホテルはもう予約しておきました。(I've already booked the hotel.)
Leaving as isYou deliberately keep something in its current state and don't touch it.
・窓を開けておいてください。(Please leave the window open.)
・そのままにしておいてください。(Please leave it just as it is.)
How to form it
Change the verb to its て-form, then add「おく」(polite: 「おきます」).
買う → 買って → 買っておく
読む → 読んで → 読んでおく
食べる → 食べて → 食べておく
する → して → しておく
The「おく」at the end conjugates too, just like the Group 1 (godan) verb 置く:
Past: 買っておきました (I bought it in advance.)
Making a request: 買っておいてください (Please buy it ahead of time for me.)
What you'll hear most
Casual contractionWhen talking with friends,「ておく」is often shortened to「とく」, and「でおく」to「どく」:
買っておく → 買っとく
置いておく → 置いとく
読んでおく → 読んどく
When asking a friend for something,「ておいて」also shortens to「といて」:
言っておいて → 言っといて
・ビール、冷やしとくね。(I'll get the beer chilled ahead of time, okay?)
Easy mistakes
・置いておいてください isn't a typo with a repeated word. The first 置いて is the action "put," and the later おいて is ておく meaning "for now." Together it means "please just leave it there."
・The て-form after「ん」is「で」, so it's 読んでおく, not 読んておく.
・切符を買います on its own is just "I buy a ticket." It has no sense of getting it done in advance. Add ておく to get that feeling.
・The contracted 買っとく (buy in advance) looks like 買っちゃう (end up buying / buy it, oops), but the meanings are completely different. Don't mix them up when listening.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
The "leaving as is" ておく and「〜まま」can both be translated as "left open," but they feel different. Take a window that's open:
ておく = you leave it open on purpose, with a reason: 暑いから、窓を開けておきました。 (It was hot, so I left the window open.)
まま = the state didn't change, and you went on to do something else, often because you forgot or shouldn't have: 窓を開けたまま出かけてしまった。 (I went out and left the window open.)
Quick test: if there's a purpose and you chose to keep it that way, use ておく. If the state simply stayed unchanged and things carried on (often without you noticing), use まま.
What to learn next
There are more "て-form + a verb" patterns, such as 〜てみる (try ...ing) and 〜てしまう (finish doing / oops). Learn them together and you'll quickly get used to this way of attaching verbs.
n4-29:
The idea in one line
「〜たばかりです」means “have just ~” or “only just ~”. The key is that the speaker feels “not much time has passed.” Say you tell a coworker “I just joined the company.” It may have been three months, but it still feels new to you, so you can say it this way.
How to form it
Take the た-form of the verb and add「ばかりです」.
The た-form is made the same way as the て-form: change 「て」to「た」and「で」to「だ」.
入って → 入った → 入ったばかりです
飲んで → 飲んだ → 飲んだばかりです
食べて → 食べた → 食べたばかりです
来て → 来た（きた）→ 来たばかりです
With friends, drop「です」or swap it for「だ」: 来たばかりだよ。
When to use it
Really just happenedSomething from a few minutes or a few hours ago.
・さっきご飯を食べたばかりです。(I just ate a little while ago.)
Still feels newIt has actually been months or even a year, but to you it hasn’t been long.
・去年大学を卒業したばかりです。(I only graduated from university last year.)
Forms you’ll hear most
ばかりの＋noun“A thing that was just ~ed.”
・買ったばかりの傘をなくしました。(I lost the umbrella I had just bought.)
ばかりで“Because I’ve only just ~, so…” Often used to explain that you’re still not used to things.
・日本に来たばかりで、まだよくわかりません。(I’ve only just come to Japan, so I don’t really understand yet.)
ばかりなのに“Even though it was only just ~,” with a note of frustration or complaint.
・昨日洗ったばかりなのに、もう汚れた。(I only washed it yesterday, and it’s already dirty.)
Easy mistakes
・Before a noun, add の: it’s 買ったばかりの靴, not「買ったばかり靴」.
・You must use the た-form. 食べたばかり means “just finished eating,” while 食べてばかり means “eating all the time, doing nothing but eating.” The meanings are very different.
・You can only use it for things that have already happened. It doesn’t work for “about to go” or “will do in a bit.”
・Among friends it’s often shortened to ばっか: 来たばっかだよ。(I only just got here.) Don’t say it this way to someone senior to you.
Telling it apart from a similar pattern
たところです (n4-28) also means “just ~,” but it talks about the objective moment right now, usually within the last few minutes. たばかりです is about how you feel, and the time span can be short or long.
For very recent events, both work:
・今、家に着いたところです。(I’ve just got home.)
・今、家に着いたばかりです。(I’ve only just got home.)
When the time span is longer, only ばかり works:
・先月、日本に来たばかりです。(I only came to Japan last month.) ○
・「先月、日本に来たところです」×
Quick tip: if there’s a longer time word like「先月」or「去年」, use ばかり. If you’ve literally just finished something this moment, ところ works too.
What to learn next
The same「ばかり」with a different meaning, “nothing but ~, always ~” (n4-49): 弟はゲームばかりしている。(My younger brother does nothing but play video games.)
n4-37:
The idea in one line
「BよりAのほうが～」means “A is more ~ than B.” You put two things side by side and pick the one that is “more ~.”
・バスより電車のほうが速いです。(Trains are faster than buses.)
How to form it
Nounnoun＋より、noun＋のほうが
・夏より冬のほうが好きです。(I like winter better than summer.)
Verbdictionary form＋より、dictionary form＋ほうが (no の in between)
・外で食べるより、家で作るほうが安いです。(Cooking at home is cheaper than eating out.)
After ほうが you can use an adjective, or a feeling expression like 好きです or 落ち着きます.
You can also swap the two parts without changing the meaning. The focus is still on the ほうが side: 電車のほうがバスより速いです。
Forms you’ll hear most
Answering “which one?”When someone asks「AとBと、どちらが～ですか」(Which is more ~, A or B?), you answer「Aのほうが～です」. Both things have just been mentioned, so より is usually left out.
・電車とバスと、どちらが速いですか。(Which is faster, the train or the bus?)
・電車のほうが速いです。(The train is faster.)
・コーヒーと紅茶と、どちらがいいですか。(Coffee or tea, which would you like?)
・紅茶のほうがいいです。(Tea is better.)
Easy mistakes
・より goes after the “baseline”, the side that is less ~. ほうが goes after the side that is more ~. Don’t think of it as “who wins or loses”: 兄より弟のほうが下手です。(The younger brother is worse at it than the older brother.) In this sentence the older brother, right before より, is actually the better one.
・In English “than” comes before the thing you compare to (“faster than the bus”). In Japanese, より goes after バス: バスより.
・Attach ほうが directly to a verb, with no の: ×歩くのほうが　○歩くほうが. Only nouns take の: 電車のほうが.
・The kanji for ほう is 方, read ほう here, meaning “that side.” It’s different from the 方 in 読み方 (かた, “way of doing”).
Telling it apart from similar patterns
AはBより～: simply describes A.
電車はバスより速いです。(Trains are faster than buses.)
BよりAのほうが～: puts the two side by side and stresses “it’s the A side.”
バスより電車のほうが速いです。(Trains are faster than buses.)
The two sentences mean almost the same, but when you’re answering「どちら？」, use ほうが.
verb た-form＋ほうがいい: gives advice, “you’d better ~.”
疲れているなら、休んだほうがいいですよ。(If you’re tired, you’d better take a rest.)
タクシーより歩いたほうがいいですよ。(Walking is better than taking a taxi.) ← It has より, but with the た-form it’s still advice.
AよりBのほうがいい: a comparison, stating a preference.
コーヒーより紅茶のほうがいいです。(Tea is better than coffee.)
Quick tip: look at the verb form. 「verb た-form＋ほうがいい」(休んだほうがいい) is advice. 「dictionary form＋ほうが＋adjective」(歩くほうが早い) and「noun のほうが～」are comparisons. Note that「AよりBのほうがいいです」is also a comparison (B is better).
What to learn next
To say it the other way, “B is not as ~ as A,” use「ほど…ない」: バスは電車ほど速くないです。(Buses are not as fast as trains.)
To compare three or more things and say “the most ~,” use「でいちばん」: クラスで田中さんがいちばん背が高いです。(Tanaka is the tallest in the class.)
n4-26:
The idea in one line
「〜てくる」 and 「〜ていく」 work a lot like the English direction words "come" and "go" added to a verb. "Come running" is 走ってくる, and "take it along" is 持っていく. They work for time too: "it's getting cold" uses てくる, and "keep doing it from now on" uses ていく.
Remember this: くる = toward me, building up to now; いく = away from me, from now onward.
How to form it
Put the verb in te-form, then add くる or いく.
降る → 降って → 降ってきた
持つ → 持って → 持っていきます
The くる at the end conjugates like the normal verb「来る」: てきます, てきました, てこない. In this pattern it's usually written in hiragana.
When to use it
Toward / away from hereUse てくる when the action moves toward the speaker, and ていく when it moves away from the speaker.
・弟が走ってきた。(My little brother came running.)
・雨が降りそうだから、傘を持っていきます。(It looks like rain, so I'll take an umbrella.)
Go and come backてくる can also mean "go do something, then return here."
・ちょっと飲み物を買ってきます。(I'll go buy a drink and be right back.)
Changing up to nowFor a gradual change from the past up to now, you usually use the past form てきました.
・最近、日本語が面白くなってきました。(Lately, Japanese has been getting more and more interesting.)
From now onSomething that continues from now on, or keeps getting more and more ～.
・これからも日本語を勉強していきます。(I'll keep studying Japanese from now on, too.)
Something appears, and you notice itA change starts and you become aware of it, like rain, hunger, or sleepiness.
・あ、雨が降ってきた。(Oh, it's started raining.)
・お腹がすいてきた。(I'm starting to get hungry.)
Common mistakes
・The phrase you say when leaving home, 行ってきます, means "I'll go and come back," so it means "I'm heading out," not literally "I go and come."
・Whether you use come or go depends on where the speaker is. If you're taking something to someone's home, English often says "I'll bring it over to you," but Japanese usually says 持っていきます, because the thing is leaving your side.
・雨が降ってきた means "it has started to rain," not "the rain is drifting toward me."
・The 「きた」 in てきた is read きた, and the negative てこない is read こない.
・In casual speech, ていく is often shortened to てく, for example 持ってく. This is spoken style.
Telling similar patterns apart
Three ways to say it's getting cold:
・寒くなった。(It got cold: states only the result.)
・寒くなってきた。(It's gradually getting cold: you feel the change building up.)
・これから寒くなっていく。(It's going to keep getting colder: looks ahead.)

Two ways to say it started raining:
・雨が降り始めた。(It began to rain: simply states the start.)
・雨が降ってきた。(It's started raining: carries a sense of "I just noticed." This is the most natural thing to say when you look up and see rain.)
Quick rule of thumb: use 「なった」 to state only the result; use 「てきた」 when you feel the change coming up to now; use 「ていく」 when your eyes are on what comes next.
What to learn next
Combined with 「ようになる」, it can express an ability that develops gradually: 日本語が少し話せるようになってきた。(I've gradually become able to speak a little Japanese.)
n4-27:
The idea in one line
These three are like the English "start ~ing," "keep ~ing," and "finish ~ing." They split one action into three stages: just starting, in progress, and done.
読みはじめる = start reading
読み続ける = keep reading, continue reading
読み終わる = finish reading
How to form it
First put the verb in ます form, drop ます, and attach はじめる, 続ける, or 終わる directly to what's left.
読む → 読みます → drop ます → 読み → 読みはじめる
食べる → 食べます → drop ます → 食べ → 食べ続ける
勉強する → 勉強します → drop ます → 勉強し → 勉強し終わる
Once attached, the last word conjugates by its own rules:
はじめる and 続ける are Group 2 (ichidan) verbs: 読みはじめる → 読みはじめました
終わる is a Group 1 (godan) verb: 読み終わる → 読み終わりました
「はじめる」 can also be written with kanji as 始める, but after a verb it's often written in hiragana.
When to use it
はじめる: startAn action begins at this moment. It works for things people do and for natural changes like weather.
・去年から日本語を勉強しはじめました。(I started studying Japanese last year.)
・あ、雨が降りはじめた。(Oh, it's started to rain.)
続ける: keep going, continueThe action doesn't stop and keeps going. It often appears with 「ずっと」 or a length of time.
・彼は1時間も話し続けた。(He talked for a whole hour straight.)
・これからも日本語を勉強し続けたいです。(I want to keep studying Japanese from now on, too.)
終わる: finishSomething with an endpoint gets done, like finishing a book or a meal.
・この本、やっと読み終わった。(I finally finished this book.)
・食べ終わったら、お皿を洗ってね。(When you're done eating, wash the dishes, okay?)
Common mistakes
・Always attach it to the ます form with ます dropped. 読むはじめる and 読んではじめる are both wrong; say 読みはじめる.
・Even when the subject is a natural phenomenon like rain or wind, you still use はじめる: 雨が降りはじめた. You wouldn't say 「降りはじまった」.
・終わる is for actions that have a "finished" endpoint, like reading, eating, writing, or watching. You don't say 「降り終わった」 when rain stops; use 雨がやんだ.
・終わる is Group 1, so its ます form is 終わります; はじめる and 続ける are Group 2, giving はじめます and 続けます. Don't mix up how they conjugate.
Telling similar patterns apart
〜ている vs 〜続けている
子どもが泣いている。(The child is crying.): simply describes the crying happening now.
子どもがずっと泣き続けている。(The child keeps crying and crying.): stresses that it's gone on a long time and hasn't stopped.
〜終わる vs 〜てしまう
Both might come out as "finished eating" in English, but the focus is different.
ケーキを食べ終わった。(I finished the cake.): just says the eating action is over, in a neutral tone.
弟のケーキを食べてしまった。(I ate my little brother's cake.): carries a feeling of "ate it all up" or "oops, I didn't mean to."
Quick rule of thumb: use ている to say something is in progress; use 続ける to stress it hasn't stopped; use 終わる to simply say it's done; use てしまう when you feel "ate it all up" or "oops."
What to learn next
If you want to pinpoint timing more finely, like "about to start," "in the middle of," or "just finished," learn 〜ところです next: 今から食べるところです。(I'm just about to start eating.)
n4-42:
The idea in one line
「〜ようと思います」means "I'm thinking of ~ing" or "I plan to ~". Use it to tell someone about a plan you already have in mind, like "I'm thinking of cleaning my room this weekend."
・週末は部屋を掃除しようと思います。（I'm thinking of cleaning my room this weekend）
How to form it
First turn the verb into the volitional form (the 「〜よう」「〜こう」 form, the "let's ~" form), then add と思います. See n4-51 for how to make the volitional form. Here's a quick review:
Group 1 (godan verbs)：行く → change く to こ, add う → 行こうと思います
Group 2 (ichidan verbs)：寝る → drop る, add よう → 寝ようと思います
Group 3 (する・来る)：する → しようと思います来る → 来ようと思います（こよう）
Forms you'll hear most
ようと思いますStates your plan right now. It's often a thought you've only just had.
・今日は早く寝ようと思います。（I'm thinking of going to bed early today）
ようと思っていますThis plan has been in your mind for a while. It's very common for longer-term plans.
・来年、日本へ留学しようと思っています。（I'm planning to study in Japan next year）
ようかと思っていますWith an extra 「か」 in the middle, it means "I'm wondering whether to ~". You're still undecided.
・仕事を辞めようかと思っています。（I'm wondering whether to quit my job）
Common mistakes
・行くと思います and 行こうと思います differ by only one sound, but the meanings are far apart. The first is "I think (he) will go," a guess. Only the second means "I'm planning to go."
・"I'm not planning to go" can't be said as 行かないと思います. That means "I think (he) won't go." To say you don't plan to, use 行かないつもりです.
・〜ようと思います only works for your own plans. To talk about someone else's plan, switch to 〜ようと思っています: 兄は車を買おうと思っています。（My older brother is thinking of buying a car）
・When asking what the other person plans to do, 思っています sounds more natural: 夏休みは何をしようと思っていますか。（What are you planning to do over summer break?）
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Even for the same "going to Japan," these three patterns feel different:
たい = simply "want to," a wish in your heart, with no plan necessarily: 日本へ行きたいです。（I want to go to Japan）
ようと思う = "thinking of / planning to." The idea is already there, but it's softer and leaves some flexibility: 日本へ行こうと思います。（I'm thinking of going to Japan）
つもり = the plan is firmer, almost settled: 日本へ行くつもりです。（I intend to go to Japan）
Quick test: if it's just "I'd love to ~," use たい. If it's "I'm thinking of ~," use ようと思う. If it's "I've already planned to ~," use つもり. When you say "I want to go" in English, stop and ask yourself: is it a wish or a plan?
What to learn next
Once the plan is really settled, you can use 「〜ことにします」: 来年、日本へ行くことにしました。（I've decided to go to Japan next year）
n4-43:
The idea in one line
「〜か（どうか）」tucks a question inside a sentence. In English you say "I don't know whether he'll come." The part in the middle is really a question, just not asked on its own. In Japanese you add 「か」 or 「かどうか」 after that part to signal: this is a question.
・彼が来るかどうか、分かりません。（I don't know whether he'll come）
Two types: with or without a word like "who, where, what"
No question wordWhen the answer to the question is just yes or no, use かどうか. It's the same as English "whether ~ or not" or "if ~." Just 「か」 also works, and it's common in speech.
・鍵をかけたかどうか、覚えていない。（I don't remember whether I locked the door）
・週末に時間があるか、確認してください。（Please check whether you're free this weekend）
With a question wordIf the sentence already has a word like 誰, どこ, 何 or いつ, add only 「か」, not どうか.
・会議が何時に始まるか、知っていますか。（Do you know what time the meeting starts?）
・トイレがどこか、教えてください。（Please tell me where the restroom is）
Verbs that most often follow: 分からない, 知っている, 決まる, 確認する, 聞く, 考える, 覚えている. They all mean things like knowing, checking or deciding.
How to form it
Always use the plain form before it (the form without ます or です).
Verbs: 行きます → 行くかどうか行きました → 行ったかどうか
い-adjectives: おいしいです → おいしいかどうか
Nouns and な-adjectives: drop だ and attach か directly. 本当です → 本当かどうか静かです → 静かかどうか
You can also say 「来るか来ないか」, which means the same as 来るかどうか.
Common mistakes
・In English, "whether" or "if" is a separate word you can't skip, and Japanese works the same way: か is required. 彼が来る分かりません is wrong.
・Even when the whole sentence is polite, the part in the middle stays in plain form. Put the politeness at the end: say 行くかどうか分かりません, not 「行きますかどうか」.
・Don't add だ after nouns or な-adjectives: say 学生かどうか, not 「学生だかどうか」.
・Don't add どうか when there's a question word: say どこがいいか, not 「どこがいいかどうか」.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Both have 「か」 and both carry some uncertainty, so beginners often mix this up with かもしれない.
彼は来るかどうか分からない。（I don't know whether he'll come: you have no idea, you're just saying "I'm not sure about this"）
彼は来るかもしれない。（He might come: you're guessing, and you think it's possible he'll come）
Quick test: if a verb like 「分からない、確認する、教えて」 follows, it's かどうか. If the sentence ends right there and means "maybe ~," it's かもしれない.
What to learn next
It pairs nicely with 「〜てみます」: 行けるかどうか、先生に聞いてみます。（I'll ask my teacher whether I can go）
n4-40:
The idea in one line
「〜と言います」 means "so-and-so says ~". 言う is "to say," and the と before it is a marker telling the listener "the quoted content ends here." It works much like quotation marks in English.
Two ways to say it: quote directly or report in your own words
Direct quotePut exactly what the person said inside 「」, then add と言いました. If the original has ます, keep the ます.
・先生は「明日テストをします」と言いました。（The teacher said, "We'll have a test tomorrow."）
Reporting in your own wordsDrop the 「」, change the content to the plain form (the casual form with no ます or です), then add と.
テストをします → テストをする
行きません → 行かない
・先生は明日テストをすると言いました。（The teacher said there will be a test tomorrow.）
・彼は行かないと言いました。（He said he's not going.）
How to connect it
When reporting, verbs and い-adjectives take the plain form and connect directly to と. Nouns and な-adjectives need an extra 「だ」.
寒い → 寒いと言いました
好きです → 好きだと言いました
学生です → 学生だと言いました
The forms you'll hear most
と言っていましたThe most natural way to pass on a message for someone. It means "he did say ~, you know."
・田中さんは今日は来ないと言っていました。（Mr. Tanaka said he won't be coming today.）
Introducing yourselfSaying your name.
・はじめまして、林と言います。（Nice to meet you, my name is Lin.）
Asking how to say somethingYou'll definitely use this when learning Japanese.
・これは日本語で何と言いますか。（How do you say this in Japanese?）
Common mistakes
・When quoting the content of what someone said (a sentence or a longer passage), use と, not を: × 明日テストをするを言いました → ○ 明日テストをすると言いました. But when the object is a plain noun, as in 名前を言う (say a name) or お礼を言う (say thanks), use を. Keep these two cases apart.
・言う is spelled いう, but it's actually pronounced ゆう.
・Forgetting だ after a noun or な-adjective when reporting is the most common mistake. Say 雨だと言っていました.
・When reporting, "I" has to change to the right person. If he originally said 「私は行きません」, your report becomes "He said he isn't going." In Japanese just say 彼は行かないと言いました, with no 私 needed.
・When reporting what a teacher or boss said in a formal setting, you'll switch to the more respectful おっしゃいました. You'll meet it when you study honorific language.
Don't mix it up with look-alikes
Here are two ways to report "Mr. Tanaka isn't coming":
田中さんは来ないと言っていました。（Mr. Tanaka said himself that he isn't coming.）
田中さんは来ないそうです。（I hear Mr. Tanaka isn't coming.）
「と言う」 makes clear who said it. 「そうです」 just means "I hear that." The news may have come from Tanaka himself or from someone else, and the source isn't the point.
Quick rule: to say "so-and-so said ~," use と言う. To say just "I hear ~," use そうです.
What to learn next
Swap 言います for 思います and you get "I think ~": 明日は雨だと思います。（I think it will rain tomorrow.） The connection rules are exactly the same, including adding だ.
Among friends, と言っていた is often shortened to って: 田中さん、来ないって。（Tanaka says he's not coming.）
n4-41:
The idea in one line
「〜と思います」 means "I think ~" or "I feel ~". Use it to give your opinion or to guess how something will turn out. Japanese people use it a lot. Even when they're quite sure, they often add と思います so the sentence doesn't sound too blunt.
When to use it
Giving an opinionYour impression or judgment of something.
・このラーメンはおいしいと思います。（I think this ramen is delicious.）
GuessingYou're not 100% sure, but you think it's probably so.
・明日は雨が降ると思います。（I think it will rain tomorrow.）
・田中さんはもう帰ったと思います。（I think Mr. Tanaka has probably already gone home.）
Asking for someone's opinionUse 「どう思いますか」. You don't need to memorize a separate pattern.
・この服、どう思いますか。（What do you think of this outfit?）
How to connect it
Put the plain form before it, meaning the form without です or ます (the dictionary form, ない, た, and so on).
Verbs and い-adjectives connect directly:
行く → 行くと思います行かない → 行かないと思います高い → 高いと思います
Nouns and な-adjectives need だ first:
学生 → 学生だと思います静か → 静かだと思います
With friends, change 思います to 思う: おいしいと思う。
Common mistakes
・Forgetting だ after a noun or な-adjective: say 学生だと思います, not 「学生と思います」.
・Don't put です or ます before と: say おいしいと思います, not 「おいしいですと思います」. The final 「思います」 already makes it polite enough.
・To say "I don't think he'll come," Japanese normally puts the negative inside the quote: 彼は来ないと思います。 (literally "I think he won't come"). If you say 来るとは思いません, it means "I really don't think he'll come," which is much stronger and sounds like pushing back.
・「と思います」 is only for what you think. To say what someone else thinks, use 「と思っています」: 母は私がまだ子どもだと思っています。（My mother thinks I'm still a child.）
Don't mix it up with look-alikes
行くと思います vs 行こうと思います: only one syllable apart, but the meaning is very different.
・明日のパーティー、田中さんは行くと思います。（About tomorrow's party, I think Mr. Tanaka will go.）
・明日のパーティー、私も行こうと思います。（About tomorrow's party, I'm thinking of going too.）
Plain form before it = you're guessing what will happen. Volitional form before it (行こう, 食べよう) = you plan to do it.
と思います vs かもしれません: they differ in how sure you are.
・明日は雨が降ると思います。（I think it will rain tomorrow: fairly sure.）
・明日は雨が降るかもしれません。（It might rain tomorrow: fifty-fifty.）
Quick rule: for "I think / I guess," use plain form + と思います. For "I'm planning to," use volitional form + と思います. For just "maybe," use かもしれません.
What to learn next
Put the volitional form before it and you get "I'm thinking of ~": 来年、日本へ行こうと思います。（I'm thinking of going to Japan next year.）
n4-49:
The idea in one line
「〜ばかり」means "all the time," "nothing but," "keeps on ~ing". When a mom scolds her kid with "All you do is play video games," Japanese uses ばかり. The key point: the speaker feels there's too much of it, and that it's not good, so it often carries a complaining or scolding tone.
How to form it
Too much of the action itselfVerb て-form + ばかりいる: stresses "keeps doing this and nothing else."
遊ぶ → 遊んで → 遊んでばかりいる (does nothing but play)
寝る → 寝て → 寝てばかりいる (does nothing but sleep)
・うちの犬は一日中寝てばかりいる。 (Our dog does nothing but sleep all day.)
Always the same objectNoun + ばかり + verb: stresses "this is all that gets done."
・弟はゲームばかりしている。 (My little brother does nothing but play video games.)
・彼はいつも文句ばかり言っている。 (He's always complaining.)
You can also add 「です／だ」 straight after the noun to describe "everywhere you look, it's ~":
・最近、雨ばかりですね。 (It's been nothing but rain lately, hasn't it?)
How you'll hear it most
Scolding「〜てばかりいないで」 = "stop ~ing all the time." It's often followed by 〜なさい, a classic line from parents and teachers.
・遊んでばかりいないで、勉強しなさい。 (Stop playing all the time and study.)
・泣いてばかりいないで、話してよ。 (Stop just crying and talk to me.)
Self-deprecatingYou can say it about yourself too, with a feel of "ugh, why am I always like this?"
・最近、食べてばかりいる。 (Lately all I do is eat.)
Common pitfalls
・When ばかり follows a noun, the original 「を」 is usually dropped: say 漫画ばかり読む, not 「漫画をばかり読む」.
・It describes a state that keeps repeating over a period of time; it can't be used for something that happened only once.
・The tone is critical, so using it about your teacher, boss, or a customer is rude. Be careful.
・In casual conversation people often say ばっかり, e.g. 遊んでばっかり. Same meaning, just more colloquial.
Telling similar forms apart
たばかり (n4-29) = just finished doing something, nothing to do with frequency:
ご飯を食べたばかりです。 (I just finished eating.)
てばかりいる = keeps doing something:
お菓子を食べてばかりいる。 (Keeps eating sweets all the time.)
だけ = only this, simply stating a fact with no dissatisfaction:
朝はコーヒーだけ飲みました。 (I only had coffee in the morning.)
ばかり = all the time, too much, with a complaint:
コーヒーばかり飲んでいる。 (Does nothing but drink coffee.)
Quick tip: if it comes after 「た」, it means "just did"; if it comes after 「て」, it means "keeps doing." To simply say "only this," use だけ; to grumble "why is it always this?", use ばかり.
n4-50:
The idea in one line
「〜場合」means "in the case that ~" or "if ~ happens". The "In case of fire, please ~" or "If you have any problems, please ~" you see in train stations, hotel rooms, and manuals is said in Japanese with 「場合」. It's more formal than 「〜たら」 and often appears in rules, notices, and explanations from staff or customer service.
When to use it
Rules and noticesYou set up a situation that "might or might not happen" and tell the other person what to do if it does. It's often followed by 「〜てください」 or a rule.
・地震の場合は、机の下に隠れてください。 (In the event of an earthquake, please hide under a desk.)
・雨の場合は、試合は中止です。 (If it rains, the match is cancelled.)
・分からない場合は、先生に聞いてください。 (If you don't understand, please ask the teacher.)
「場合」is almost always followed by 「は」, making 「〜場合は」. Just memorize it as a set.
How to form it
Verbs: attach directly to the dictionary form, ない form, or た form.
遅れる → 遅れる場合行けない → 行けない場合忘れた → 忘れた場合
い-adjectives: attach directly. 熱が高い → 熱が高い場合
な-adjectives: keep 「な」. 無理 → 無理な場合
Nouns: add 「の」 in between. 雨 → 雨の場合火事 → 火事の場合
Dictionary form vs. た formWhether you use the dictionary form or the た form changes the meaning slightly:
・遅れる場合は、電話してください。 (If you're going to be late, please call: you contact them before you're late.)
・カードをなくした場合は、すぐ連絡してください。 (If you happen to lose your card, please contact us right away: after the thing has happened.)
Common pitfalls
・「場合」is read ばあい, not ばしょ.
・Nouns and な-adjectives can't take 「だ」 directly: not 「雨だ場合」 but 雨の場合; not 「無理だ場合」 but 無理な場合.
・な-adjectives take な; don't confuse them with nouns and write 「の」.
・「場合」can only be used for things that may or may not happen. For something certain to arrive, like "when it hits 10 o'clock," you can't say 「10時になった場合」; use 10時になったら.
・You also can't use it for things that already happened: you can't say 「昨日雨が降った場合」 for "when it rained yesterday."
・The tone is fairly formal. When chatting with friends and saying "if it rains, we won't go," 雨だったら sounds more natural.
Telling similar forms apart
Both mean "if it rains":
場合: 雨の場合は、イベントは中止です。 (In case of rain, the event is cancelled.) → Sounds like a rule written on a notice.
たら: 雨が降ったら、家で映画を見よう。 (If it rains, let's watch a movie at home.) → Casual talk between friends.
Also, 「たら」 can be used for things that will definitely happen (駅に着いたら、電話して。 Call me when you get to the station), but 「場合」 can't.
Quick tip: if you can translate it as "in the event of ~" or "should ~ occur," and you're talking about rules or instructions, use 「場合」. For everyday chat, or things that will definitely happen, use 「たら」.
What to learn next
Other ways of saying "if" are worth comparing together: 〜ば (conditional form), 〜なら, and 〜と. Each has a slightly different feel.
n4-44:
The idea in one line
Feelings like “want,” “scared,” and “cold” are known only to the person feeling them. So when Japanese talks about someone else's feelings, it doesn't flatly say “he wants it.” It says “he shows signs of wanting it.” That's 「〜がる」. It's a bit like English “he keeps asking for…” or “he acts scared.”
When to use it
What someone else wantsA younger brother, a friend, a child, even a pet: you can see they really want something or really want to do something.
・弟が新しいゲーム機を欲しがっています。(My little brother keeps wanting a new game console.)
・彼女はずっと日本へ行きたがっています。(She has really wanted to go to Japan for a long time.)
Someone else's feelingsFear, cold, pain, dislike: you can tell from their expression and behavior.
・子どもが注射を怖がっています。(The child is scared of shots.)
・娘は野菜を嫌がって、食べません。(My daughter hates vegetables and won't eat them.)
How to form it
Only adjectives that express emotions or sensations can take 「がる」 (欲しい, 怖い, 痛い, 寒い, 嫌だ…).
い-adjectives: drop the final 「い」 and add 「がる」.
欲しい → 欲しがる怖い → 怖がる痛い → 痛がる
Wanting to do something: first change the verb to 「〜たい」, then drop the 「い」 and add 「がる」.
行く → 行きたい → 行きたがる働く → 働きたい → 働きたがる
な-adjectives: drop 「だ」 and add 「がる」, for example 嫌だ → 嫌がる残念だ → 残念がる. Not many な-adjectives work this way. The common ones are 嫌がる, 残念がる, 不思議がる, and 面倒がる.
Note: 大きい isn't a feeling, so you can't say ×大きがる. And although 好き is an emotion, you don't say ×好きがる either.
Once it becomes 「がる」, it conjugates like 帰る, as a Group 1 (godan) verb: がります, がりません, がっています, がった.
The form you'll hear most
がっていますTo say “right now he really wants it / is really scared,” you'll almost always use this form. Just saying 欲しがります sounds more like a habit or tendency: “he's the type who does this.”
・犬が散歩に行きたがっている。(The dog wants to go for a walk.)
Common mistakes
・Don't use がる for yourself: for your own feelings, just say 私は新しいスマホが欲しいです, not 「私は欲しがっています」. The reverse also holds. In English “he wants it” is perfectly natural, but saying 弟は欲しいです directly in Japanese sounds odd. You need 欲しがっています.
・The particle changes: 水が欲しい takes 「を」 once it becomes がる: 弟は水を欲しがっている.
・Don't use がる when asking the person you're talking to: with a friend, just ask 何が食べたい？ (What do you want to eat?).
・Don't use it for superiors or elders: 「〜がる」 describes how someone appears from the outside, so using it about a teacher or boss sounds like you're commenting on their feelings, which isn't polite enough. Don't say 先生が帰りたがっています. A better way is 先生は帰りたいとおっしゃっていました。 (The teacher said he wanted to go home.)
Telling similar forms apart
For “my little brother wants a new phone,” there are three ways to say it, and they differ in whose feeling it is and how you know:
欲しい = your own feeling: 私は新しいスマホが欲しいです。 (I want a new phone.)
欲しがっている = he has said it or shown it: 弟は新しいスマホを欲しがっています。 (My little brother keeps asking for a new phone.)
欲しそう = he hasn't said anything; you're guessing from how he looks: 弟は新しいスマホが欲しそうです。 (My little brother looks like he wants a new phone.)
Quick rule of thumb: use 「たい・欲しい」 for your own feelings, 「がっている」 for what someone else has shown, and 「そう」 when you're only guessing from their face.
What to learn next
When you'd rather not comment on someone's feelings, you can report what they said instead: 姉は留学したいと言っています。 (My older sister says she wants to study abroad.)
n4-46:
The idea in one line
「〜なさい」 is like a parent saying “Go to bed, now!” or “Wash your hands properly!” It carries an adult's authority, but it isn't scolding. It's a command from a higher position to a lower one, most often from parents to children and teachers to students.
When to use it
Parent to childTelling a child to do what they should be doing. Moms in Japanese dramas and anime say this every day.
・早く寝なさい。(Go to bed, now.)
・宿題を先にやりなさい。(Do your homework first.)
Teacher to studentInstructions in class.
・よく聞きなさい。(Listen carefully.)
Exam questionsThe JLPT and Japanese school tests often word questions this way. When you see it, read it as a “please do…” instruction.
・正しいものを選びなさい。(Choose the correct answer.)
How to form it
Put the verb in its ます form, drop ます, and add なさい. It's the same for all three verb groups, so there's no extra rule to memorize.
行きます → drop ます → 行きなさい
洗います → 洗いなさい食べます → 食べなさい寝ます → 寝なさい
勉強します → 勉強しなさい来ます → 来なさい (きなさい)
Common mistakes
・It doesn't sound harsh, but it is not polite. Saying 「座りなさい」 to a teacher, boss, or customer would be very rude. To ask someone to do something politely, use 「座ってください」.
・来なさい is read きなさい, not こなさい.
・To tell someone “don't…,” なさい has no negative form, so you can't just attach ない. Use 「〜ないで」 or 「〜てはいけません」 instead, for example 走らないで (don't run).
・おやすみなさい, おかえりなさい, and ごめんなさい do contain なさい, but they're fixed greetings and have no command meaning. Still, ごめんなさい is rather casual. To apologize to a boss or customer, use 「すみません」 or 「申し訳ありません」.
Telling similar forms apart
Even for the same “go to bed early,” changing the form changes the tone and the relationship between speaker and listener:
〜なさい = from above, with a tone of discipline (mom to child):
・もう11時だよ。早く寝なさい。(It's already 11. Go to bed.)
Command form = direct and forceful, mostly used by men, or in arguments and emergencies:
・早く寝ろ。(Go to bed, already!)
〜てください = a polite request, used by doctors to patients, shop staff to customers, and so on:
・今日は早く寝てくださいね。(Please get some rest early today.)
〜てね = a light reminder between friends or family:
・今日は早く寝てね。(Go to bed early today, okay?)
Quick rule of thumb: use なさい when an adult is “disciplining” a child; use てください to politely ask for help; use てね for a casual reminder to a friend; ろ is the harshest, so beginners should avoid it.
What to learn next
Next, learn the “command form and prohibitive form” (寝ろ, 寝るな). You'll understand the more direct commands in Japanese dramas, and see more clearly why なさい counts as “mild.”
n4-51:
The idea in one line
The volitional form is the casual version of 「〜ましょう」. With a coworker you say 一緒に行きましょう, and with a friend you say 一緒に行こう. The meaning is the same, "let's…", but the tone is more relaxed.
When to use it
Inviting someoneAsk the other person to do something together with you.
・一緒に行こう。(Let's go together.)
・ちょっと休もう。(Let's take a short break.)
Psyching yourself upUse it to make a decision in your head or talk to yourself. No one else needs to be around.
・よし、明日から早く起きよう。(Okay, starting tomorrow I'll get up early.)
Offering to helpAdd 「か」 at the end and it becomes "Shall I… for you?"
・荷物、持とうか。(Shall I carry your bags?)
How to form it: first check the verb group
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the 「お」-row sound of the same row, then add 「う」.
行く → change く to こ → 行こう
飲む → 飲もう待つ → 待とう話す → 話そう帰る → 帰ろう会う → 会おう
You can also think of it from the ます-form: change the 「き」 of 行きます to 「こ」, then add 「う」.
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop the final 「る」 and add 「よう」.
食べる → 食べよう起きる → 起きよう見る → 見よう
Group 3 (just two verbs, memorize them): する → しよう来る → 来よう（こよう）
Easy mistakes
・The こう in 「行こう」 is a long vowel, so it sounds like 「いこー」. Saying it short, 「いこ」, is a very cutesy, casual way of talking, with a different tone.
・会う becomes 会おう. Don't mix it up with the ない-form 会わない and write 「会わう」.
・帰る and 入る look like Group 2 but are actually Group 1: it's 帰ろう, not 帰よう.
・The volitional form of 来る is read こよう, not きよう.
・It can only express what you yourself will do, or inviting the other person to do it with you. You can't use it to tell someone else to go do something. To say "let's invite our friend too", change it to 友達も呼ぼう (let's call our friend too).
・This is how friends talk to each other. With a teacher or a customer, go back to 「〜ましょう」.
Telling it apart from similar forms
There are three ways to invite a friend to a movie:
映画を見に行こう。 (Let's go see a movie.): a direct invitation, with a feel of "it's settled, then!"
映画を見に行かない？ (Want to go see a movie?): you ask whether they want to go first, which leaves them more room.
映画を見に行きましょう。 (Let's go see a movie.): the polite version of 「行こう」, for people you don't know well or for elders.
Rule of thumb: if the person is a friend and you expect them to say yes, use 「行こう」. If you want to check first, use 「行かない？」. If the person calls for politeness, use 「行きましょう」.
What to learn next
Add 「と思います」 after it and it means "I'm thinking of…" or "I plan to…": 来年、日本へ行こうと思います。 (I'm thinking of going to Japan next year.)
n4-52:
The idea in one line
The potential form is the English "can…" / "be able to…", built right into the verb. 書く means "to write", and 書ける means "can write, be able to write". When Japanese people talk about whether they can or can't do something, this is the form they use most.
When to use it
Can (a learned skill)You studied or practiced it, so you can do it.
・韓国語が書けます。(I can write Korean.)
・ピアノが弾けますか。(Can you play the piano?)
Can / may (circumstances allow)This isn't about skill, but about whether time, place, or rules allow it.
・ここで写真が撮れますか。(Can I take photos here?)
・明日は来られますか。(Can you come tomorrow?)
Can eat, can stomachWith food, it often means "can you stomach it?"
・納豆が食べられますか。(Can you eat natto?)
How to form it: first check the verb group
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the 「え」-row sound of the same row, then add 「る」.
書く → change く to け → 書ける
話す → 話せる飲む → 飲める買う → 買える待つ → 待てる帰る → 帰れる
You can also think of it from the ます-form: change the 「き」 of 書きます to 「け」 → 書けます.
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop the final 「る」 and add 「られる」.
食べる → 食べられる見る → 見られる起きる → 起きられる
Group 3 (just two verbs, memorize them): する → できる来る → 来られる（こられる）
Verbs of the 「noun + する」 type work the same way: replace する with できる: 説明する → 説明できる
Once formed, keep conjugating
After you form the potential, it is itself a Group 2 verb. To say "can't" or "was able to", just keep conjugating it by the Group 2 rules:
書ける → 書けます書ける → 書けない書ける → 書けた
・朝、なかなか起きられない。(I just can't get up in the morning.)
Particles: を often becomes が
After a verb becomes potential, the original 「を」 usually changes to 「が」:
日本語を話す → 日本語が話せる
You'll also hear を used in everyday conversation, but textbooks and exams mainly use が, so remembering が is the safest.
Easy mistakes
・帰る, 入る, and 走る look like Group 2 but are actually Group 1: it's 帰れる, not 帰られる.
・The potential form of 来る is read こられる, not きられる.
・The potential of する is the whole replacement できる. You can't force it through the rules yourself.
・In casual speech you often hear 食べれる, 見れる, and 来れる (without the 「ら」). Japanese people really do say this all the time, but in textbooks, exams, and formal situations you should still use 食べられる, 見られる, and 来られる.
・When something is visible or audible naturally, without any effort, Japanese uses 見える and 聞こえる: ここから富士山が見える。 (You can see Mt. Fuji from here.) 見られる and 聞ける mean having the chance or means to go watch or listen: このアプリで映画が見られる。 (You can watch movies with this app.)
Telling it apart from similar forms
〜ことができる, which you learned earlier, means the same as the potential form:
・日本語が話せます。 (I can speak Japanese.)
・日本語を話すことができます。 (I am able to speak Japanese.)
The difference is length and feel. The potential form is shorter and the most common in everyday chat. ことができる is longer and more formal, and you often see it in manuals, notices, and speeches. One more point: the verb before ことができる doesn't change form, and the particle stays 「を」.
Rule of thumb: use the potential form in everyday speech. When you want to sound more formal and clear, use ことができる. They mean the same thing, so neither is wrong.
What to learn next
Add 「ようになる」 after it and it means "have become able to…": 日本語が少し話せるようになりました。 (I've become able to speak a little Japanese.)
n4-53:
The idea in one line
The imperative is the bare shout of "Do it!", and the prohibitive is "Don't!". Think of English "Run!" or "Don't come in!", with no politeness at all. Said to a real person in daily life, both sound harsh. You'll hear them most in anime, sports, and emergencies.
When to use it
Emergencies, dangerThere's no time to be polite.
・危ない！逃げろ！(Watch out! Run!)
Cheering someone onShouted from the sidelines. This doesn't sound harsh, and both men and women do it.
・頑張れ！負けるな！(Go for it! Don't lose!)
Reporting what someone told youAdd 「と言われた」 to say "someone told me to ~". This is the case you'll use most yourself.
・医者にお酒を飲むなと言われた。(The doctor told me not to drink alcohol.)
・父に早く寝ろと言われた。(My dad told me to go to bed early.)
Signs, superior to subordinateThe 「止まれ」 (Stop) written on roads is an imperative. You'll also hear it in arguments, or when a coach yells at players.
How to form it: first check the verb group
Imperative
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the 「え」-row sound of the same row.
行く → change く to け → 行け
走る → 走れ飲む → 飲め待つ → 待て急ぐ → 急げ
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop the final 「る」 and add 「ろ」.
食べる → 食べろ起きる → 起きろ見る → 見ろ
Group 3 (only two, just memorize them): する → しろ来る → 来い（こい）
The prohibitive is much simpler. It doesn't depend on the group: just add 「な」 to the dictionary form.
行く → 行くな食べる → 食べるなする → するな来る → 来るな（くるな）
Common mistakes
・Using the imperative with a teacher, boss, or customer is very rude. Don't take 「待て！」 and 「見ろ！」 from anime and use them on real people.
・帰る, 入る, and 走る are Group 1, so they become 帰れ and 入れ, not 帰ろ or 入ろ.
・来い is read こい, but 来るな is read くるな. The two readings differ.
・The imperative looks a lot like the potential form: 読め means "read it!", while 読める means "can read it". The difference is whether there's a final 「る」.
・「な」 must follow the dictionary form: 行くな means "don't go". If you drop ます and add な instead, as in 行きな, it's a colloquial "go on, go", which means the exact opposite.
Telling similar forms apart
Here are three ways to tell a kid to go to bed:
早く寝ろ！ (Get to bed, now!): the harshest, a straight-up shout.
早く寝なさい。 (Go to bed.): the tone parents and teachers use with children. It has a top-down feel but isn't rude.
早く寝てね。 (Go to bed early, okay?): an ordinary, gentle request.
Here are three ways to say not to enter a room:
入るな！ (Don't come in!): the harshest.
入ってはいけません。 (You must not go in.): states a rule or explains a ban, in a more formal tone.
入らないでください。 (Please don't go in.): a polite request.
Quick rule of thumb: shouting uses the imperative or prohibitive; an adult managing a child uses なさい; stating rules uses てはいけません; asking someone a favor uses てください or ないでください.
What to learn next
The imperative of くれる is くれ, not くれろ. Men often say ちょっと待ってくれ。 (Wait a sec for me), which is a bit softer than just 「待て」.
n4-57:
The idea in one line
This 「と」 means "whenever ~ / as soon as ~, then ~". Whenever A happens, B follows every time, with no exceptions, like "press the switch and the light comes on". That's why it's used most for natural patterns, how machines work, giving directions, and fixed habits.
When to use it
Natural patternsThings that just happen that way, and no one can change them.
・春になると、桜が咲きます。(When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.)
・夜になると、街の灯りがつきます。(When night falls, the street lights come on.)
Operating machinesYou do this action, and the machine responds.
・このボタンを押すと、ドアが開きます。(When you press this button, the door opens.)
・この鍵を回すと、金庫が開きます。(When you turn this key, the safe opens.)
Giving directionsYou'll hear this pattern a lot when asking the way in Japan.
・まっすぐ行くと、右に駅があります。(Go straight and the station is on your right.)
Fixed habitsEvery time you do A, you always go on to do B.
・父は家に帰ると、すぐテレビをつけます。(As soon as my dad gets home, he turns on the TV.)
How to attach it
Put the plain form, with no ます and no past tense, before 「と」. Verbs most often use the dictionary form, and the ない form for "not ~".
Verb dictionary form: 押す → 押すと
Verb ない form: 急がない → 急がないと
い-adjectives attach directly: 寒い → 寒いと
な-adjectives and nouns need だ first: 雨 → 雨だと
・急がないと、遅れるよ。(If you don't hurry, you'll be late.)
・寒いと、手が冷たくなります。(When it's cold, my hands get icy.)
Common mistakes
・After 「と」 you can't use requests, commands, invitations, or your own intentions like "I'll ~". 「と」 describes a result that happens naturally, not something you want to do.
　×駅に着くと、電話してください。
　○駅に着いたら、電話してください。(When you get to the station, please call me.)
・Before 「と」 you always use the non-past form (dictionary form or ない form), even when talking about the past. The past tense goes only at the end of the sentence: 子どものころ、冬になると、よく雪が降りました。 (When I was a kid, it often snowed when winter came.) You can't say 「押したと」.
・「と」 also means "with" (友達と) and marks a quote (と言います). It's only this "whenever ~, then ~" pattern when one action or clause is followed by another event.
Telling similar forms apart
と = A, then B, every time. Only things that will happen go after it: 春になると、桜が咲きます。 (When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.)
たら = after A happens, do B. Requests, invitations, and your own plans can follow: 春になったら、花見に行こう。 (When spring comes, let's go see the blossoms.)
