ば = stresses "as long as condition A is met": このボタンを押せば、ドアが開きます。 (If you just press this button, the door opens.)
なら = picks up what the other person said and gives advice: 京都へ行くなら、春がいいですよ。 (If you're going to Kyoto, spring is nice.)
Quick rule of thumb: if what follows is "please ~", "let's ~", or "I'll ~", use たら. If it's a result that "always happens", use と.
What to learn next
「と」 can also go before 「いい」 to express a hope: 明日、晴れるといいですね。 (I hope it clears up tomorrow.) This usage is covered in n4-58.
n4-67:
The idea in one line
Take a question word like 「何、誰、どこ、いつ」 and add 「でも」, and it becomes English "anything" / "anyone" / "anywhere" / "anytime". It means everything is fine, with no exceptions.
What you'll hear most
何でも＝anything
誰でも＝anyone
どこでも＝anywhere
いつでも＝anytime, whenever
どれでも＝any one (choosing from three or more)
どちらでも＝either one (choosing from two)
どんな＋noun＋でも＝any kind of ~, no matter what kind of ~
・私は何でも食べます。(I eat anything.)
・この問題は誰でもできます。(Anyone can do this problem.)
・いつでも連絡してください。(Contact me anytime.)
・どんな仕事でも頑張ります。(I'll work hard at any job.)
Answering "anything is fine"Add 「いいです」 after it and you get the super common "any is fine" reply.
・A：いつがいいですか。　B：いつでもいいですよ。(A: When works for you?　B: Anytime is fine!)
・赤と青、どちらでもいいです。(Red or blue, either one is fine.)
What happens to the original particle?
が, を: they simply disappear. Don't keep them.
何を食べますか → 何でも食べます (you never say 何をでも)
に, と, へ and the like: keep them, and put them before でも.
・彼は誰にでも優しいです。(He's kind to everyone.)
・妹は誰とでもすぐ友だちになれます。(My younger sister can become friends with anyone right away.)
Where people slip up
・何でも is read なんでも, not なにでも.
・To say "not ~ anything" you can't use でも. Use 「も」 plus a negative: 何も食べません (I don't eat anything). 何でも食べません does not mean "I don't eat anything", so don't say it that way.
・If a friend sincerely asks "What do you want to eat?" and you just flatly answer 何でもいいです, it can sound a bit like "whatever." Try 何でも好きです (I like everything), or just suggest something.
・When there's no question word before it, でも means something else: 子どもでもわかります means "Even a child can understand."
Telling look-alikes apart
With the same 「何」, the word that follows changes the meaning a lot:
何でも食べます。(I eat anything: everything is OK)
何も食べません。(I eat nothing: not a single thing)
何か食べます。(I'll eat something: some item, not decided yet)

「誰」 works the same way:
誰でも知っています。(Anyone knows.)
誰も知りません。(Nobody knows.)
誰か知っていますか。(Does anyone know?)
Quick rule of thumb: "everything is OK" takes でも; "not a single one" takes も with a negative; "some one, but I'm not sure which" takes か.
What to learn next
A question word followed by a verb in 「ても」 form means "no matter what you do ~": 何を言っても、彼は聞きません。(No matter what you say, he won't listen.)
n4-68:
The idea in one line
「とか」 is like English casual "~ or something," "like ~ and stuff," "things like ~". You toss out a few examples, meaning "not just these, there's more." It's more casual than 「や」, and you'll hear it all the time among friends.
When to use it
Casual examplesGive two or three examples to show there are others too.
・コンビニでパンとかおにぎりとか買った。(I bought bread, rice balls, and stuff at the convenience store.)
Just one, to soften your toneWhen inviting someone or giving advice, even one example is fine. It sounds less pushy, like English "Want to grab dinner or something?"
・今度、ご飯とか行かない？(Want to go grab a meal or something sometime?)
・疲れたら、少し寝るとかしたほうがいいよ。(If you're tired, you should maybe take a little nap or something.)
Reporting something you heard「～とか言ってた」＝"I think (he/she) said ~." It shows you remember roughly, but you're not totally sure.
・田中さん、来週休むとか言ってたよ。(I think Tanaka said he's taking next week off.)
How to attach it
Nouns: just add とか. パン → パンとかおにぎりとか
Verbs: use the plain form without ます (dictionary form), then add とか. 寝ます → 寝るとか
After the last とか you can add 「を」「に」「が」, but in casual talk 「を」 is often just dropped: お茶とかお菓子とか買ってきた。(I bought tea, snacks, and stuff and came back.)
Where people slip up
・とか is very casual. In reports, or when talking to your boss or customers, use 「や」 for nouns and 「〜たり〜たりする」 for actions to be safe.
・The most common pattern puts とか after every item (AとかBとか). You'll also hear it only after the first one, but as soon as 「とか」 appears, it means there's more, not that this is everything.
・「とか」 and 「と」 differ by just one syllable, but the meaning is very different: と means "just these," while とか means "a few examples."
・Some people stick とか into every sentence, which can sound vague and noncommittal. Don't overuse it in formal situations.
Telling look-alikes apart
All describing what's in the fridge:
と＝lists everything, just these: 冷蔵庫に牛乳と卵があります。(There's milk and eggs in the fridge.)
や＝examples, and there's more, standard register: 冷蔵庫に牛乳や卵があります。(There's milk, eggs, and so on in the fridge.)
とか＝examples, and there's more, casual tone: 冷蔵庫に牛乳とか卵とかあるよ。(There's milk and eggs and stuff in the fridge.)
Also, 「や」 can only attach to nouns. To list actions, the standard way is 「〜たり〜たりする」; in casual talk you can use とか too, but it's more colloquial.
週末は本を読んだり、音楽を聞いたりします。(On weekends I read books, listen to music, and so on: standard.)
週末は本を読むとか、音楽を聞くとかしてる。(On weekends I read or listen to music or something: casual.)
Quick rule of thumb: for "just these," use 「と」. For example nouns, use 「や」 in a more formal tone and 「とか」 in casual talk. For example actions, use 「たり」 normally, and 「とか」 is fine in casual talk.
What to learn next
Another way to list things one by one: the particle し lists reasons: 安いし、おいしいし、よくこの店に来る。(It's cheap and tasty, so I come to this place often.)
n4-58:
The idea in one line
This pattern is the Japanese way of saying "you could just ~" or "I hope ~". It has two uses: giving advice ("Just ask your teacher") and making a wish ("I hope it clears up tomorrow"). Before it you can use any of the three conditional forms, たら, ば or と, and いい follows.
When to use it
Giving adviceYou're telling the other person, "Do this and it'll be solved." The tone is light, and it often comes with 「よ」.
・医者に相談したらいいですよ。(You could just talk to a doctor.)
・分からなかったら、先生に聞けばいいよ。(If you don't understand, just ask the teacher.)
・疲れたときは、少し休むといいですよ。(When you're tired, it's a good idea to rest a little.)
Asking what to doTurn it into a question and it means "What should I do?" Here it's almost always たら or ば, and it's very common.
・駅までどう行けばいいですか。(How should I get to the station?)
・何を持っていったらいいですか。(What should I bring?)
Making a wishYou hope something will happen, usually something you can't control. It often comes with 「ね」 (talking to someone) or 「なあ」 (talking to yourself). 「といい」 is especially common for this use.
・明日、晴れるといいですね。(I hope it clears up tomorrow.)
・雨が降らないといいね。(I hope it doesn't rain.)
・試験に合格できたらいいなあ。(It would be great if I could pass the exam.)
How to form it
たら: Make the た-form first, then add ら.
行く → 行った → 行ったら食べる → 食べた → 食べたら
ば: Make the ば-form.
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the え-row sound of the same row, then add ば.行く → change く to け → 行けば
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop る and add れば.食べる → 食べれば
Group 3 (する・来る): する → すれば来る → 来れば（くれば）
と: Use the non-past plain form, meaning the dictionary form or the ない form. な-adjectives and nouns need だ.
晴れる → 晴れるといい降らない → 降らないといい元気 → 元気だといい
Adding のに: a pity it isn't so
When the sentence ends in 「ばいいのに」 or 「たらいいのに」, it means "if only ~, but it's not that way," with a sense of regret or dissatisfaction.
・早く春が来ればいいのに。(I wish spring would hurry up and come. It hasn't yet.)
・早く言えばいいのに。(You could have just said so sooner!)
Easy mistakes
・You can't put the た-form before 「と」: 飲むといい and 降らないといい are correct, but 飲んだといい is wrong.
・「～たらいいですよ」 has a "let me tell you what to do" feel, so it can come across as a bit blunt to a teacher or boss. 〜たらいかがですか is more polite.
・「～ばいいのに」 aimed at another person often carries a complaint. 早く言えばいいのに is basically scolding the listener, so don't use it with people above you.
・Don't translate "I hope it's sunny tomorrow" word for word as 「希望します」. In everyday Japanese people just say 明日晴れるといいですね.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
All three end in 「いい」, but the meanings differ:
薬を飲んだほうがいいですよ。(You'd better take medicine.) → ほうがいい is a recommendation that implies "it's bad if you don't," so it's stronger.
薬を飲んだらいいですよ。(You could just take some medicine.) → たらいい casually offers a way to solve it.
薬を飲んでもいいですよ。(You may take medicine.) → てもいい gives permission, not advice.
Quick test: "you'd better ~" is ほうがいい, "you could just ~" is たらいい, and "you may ~" is てもいい.
What to learn next
The past form 〜ばよかった means "I should have ~" and expresses regret: もっと勉強すればよかった。(I wish I had studied more.)
n4-64:
The idea in one line
「〜させていただきます」 is like English "Allow me to ~" or "I'll go ahead and ~". It talks about something you are going to do, but the tone is very humble, as if you're doing it only because the other person kindly allows it. You'll hear it often in meetings, on stage, and when speaking to superiors or customers.
When to use it
On stage, formal occasionsSay it first when you're about to explain something, introduce yourself, or give a presentation.
・では、説明させていただきます。(Well then, allow me to explain.)
・自己紹介させていただきます。(Allow me to introduce myself.)
Things that affect the other personFor things that affect others, like taking a day off, leaving early, or using someone's belongings, this makes you sound more polite.
・明日は休ませていただきます。(I'll be taking tomorrow off, if I may.)
Shop noticesYou'll also see it often on signs posted at shop entrances.
・本日は休ませていただきます。(We are closed today.)
How to form it
First turn the verb into the causative form ("let/make someone do"), then into the て-form 「〜させて／〜せて」, and add いただきます.
How to conjugate: first check the verb group
Group 1 (godan verbs): Change the last sound to the あ-row sound of the same row, add 「せて」, then add いただきます.
休む → change む to ま → 休ませていただきます
帰る → 帰らせていただきます
Watch out for verbs ending in 「う」: the 「う」 becomes 「わ」: 使う → 使わせていただきます
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): Drop the final 「る」, add 「させて」, then add いただきます.
考える → 考えさせていただきます
Group 3 (only two verbs, just memorize them):
する → させていただきます (説明する becomes 説明させていただきます)
来る → 来させていただきます（こさせて）, which is used less often.
To sum up: only Group 2 and Group 3 (する → させて, 来る → 来させて) have 「さ」. Group 1 is simply the あ-row sound + せて.
Easy mistakes
・Don't add an extra 「さ」 to Group 1: it's 休ませていただきます, not 休まさせていただきます, and 読ませていただきます, not 読まさせて. Even native speakers often make this mistake, but it counts as wrong on exams.
・使う becomes 使わせて, not 使あせて.
・It always talks about something you will do. You can't use it for other people.
・It isn't really "asking"; it's closer to politely announcing "I'm going to do this." If you actually want permission, use 「〜させていただけませんか」 below.
・Don't use it for everything. For things that don't involve the other person and need nobody's approval, saying 「させていただきます」 over and over sounds roundabout. Plain 「〜ます」 is enough.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Say you want to leave work early today. There are three ways to put it to your boss:
させていただきます = a polite announcement, as if it's already decided:
今日は早く帰らせていただきます。(I'll be leaving early today, if I may.)
させてください = asking the other person to let you, more direct:
今日は早く帰らせてください。(Please let me leave early today.)
させていただけませんか = a real question that the other person can refuse, the most polite:
今日は早く帰らせていただけませんか。(Could I possibly leave early today?)
Quick test: an ending in 「ます」 announces, 「ください」 requests, and only 「ませんか」 truly asks. Until you've got approval, 「〜させていただけませんか」 is the safest choice.
What to learn next
Next, look at humble language (謙讓語). Special humble forms that lower yourself, like 参ります and 申します, often appear together with 「させていただきます」.
n4-65:
The idea in one line
In English you soften “What’s your name?” into “May I ask your name?” Japanese does something similar: put お or ご before a noun and it sounds more polite and refined.
「ございます」 is the shop-staff / hotel version of あります. It means the same thing, “there is / I have,” just more politely.
When to use お・ご
The other person’s thingsWhen you talk about the other person’s name, family or address, adding お・ご shows respect.
・お名前をお願いします。（May I have your name, please?）
・ご家族はお元気ですか。（Is your family doing well?）
Just sounding niceSome words take お・ご simply to sound more refined. You can use these for your own things too, and they’re very common in daily life.
・お茶を飲みませんか。（Would you like some tea?）
・もうご飯を食べました。（I’ve already eaten.）
Which one: お or ご?
Native Japanese words (kanji with Japanese readings, or words that are already in hiragana) mostly take お:
お名前、お店、お水、お手紙
Words borrowed from Chinese (kanji read with the Chinese-derived on’yomi readings, often two-kanji compounds) mostly take ご:
ご住所、ご家族、ご予約、ご連絡
But there are quite a few exceptions. お電話、お時間、お食事 are all kanji compounds, yet they always take お. Just memorize them one by one when you meet them; don’t force the rule.
Katakana loanwords usually don’t take it: just say コーヒー.
ございます: the polite form of あります
あります → ございますありません → ございませんありました → ございました
You actually already know it: it’s the part inside ありがとうございます and おはようございます.
・お手洗いはあちらにございます。（The restroom is over there.）
・赤いのもございますよ。（We have red ones too.）
・申し訳ございません。（I’m very sorry.）
Also, でございます is the polite version of です, and staff use it a lot when introducing things:
・こちらがメニューでございます。（This is the menu.）
Easy mistakes
・Respectful お・ご can’t be applied to yourself: when introducing yourself, say 私の名前は, not 「私のお名前は」. Only “make it sound nice” words like お茶 and ご飯 can be used for yourself too.
・ございます is only for things and matters, never for people. To say whether a person is there, use おります or いらっしゃいます below.
・「でございます」 can’t be used to talk about the other person: to ask “Are you Mr. Tanaka?” say 田中様でいらっしゃいますか, not 「田中様でございますか」.
・More お・ご isn’t better. Adding them to words that don’t usually take them sounds odd. Learn the ones in your textbook and the ones staff say all the time, and that’s enough.
Telling look-alikes apart
In the same shop, here are the ways to say “there is / is here”:
あります (generally polite): トイレはあちらにあります。（The toilet is over there.）
ございます (more polite, for things): お手洗いはあちらにございます。（The restroom is over there.）
おります (for people on your own side; humbles yourself): 店長は事務所におります。（The manager is in the office.）
いらっしゃいます (for the other person or customers; raises them up): 田中様はいらっしゃいますか。（Is Mr. Tanaka in?）
Quick rule of thumb: for things use ございます; for people, use おります for your own side and いらっしゃいます for the other person.
What to learn next
お・ご can also attach to verbs to make honorific or humble expressions, for example 少々お待ちください。（Please wait a moment.） Next, take a look at honorific language (尊敬語) and humble language (謙譲語).
n4-66:
The idea in one line
Contractions are Japanese words that get squashed together in fast speech. Just like English “going to” becomes “gonna,” Japanese people turn 見ている into 見てる when they chat. The meaning is exactly the same; it’s just more spoken and casual.
When to use them
Everyday chatWhen talking with friends and family. You’ll hear this almost everywhere in dramas, anime and manga.
AvoidIn formal situations such as writing reports, emailing your boss, or interviews, use the full forms.
The four you’ll hear most
1. ている → てる: drop the い in the middle.
見ている → drop い → 見てる
If it was 「でいる」, it becomes 「でる」: 読んでいる → 読んでる
・何してるの？（What are you doing?）
2. ておく → とく: 「て」 and 「お」 merge into a single 「と」.
買っておく → 買っとく
If it was 「でおく」, it becomes 「どく」: 読んでおく → 読んどく
・飲み物、買っとくね。（I’ll buy the drinks ahead of time, okay?）
3. てしまう → ちゃう: 「てしま」 shrinks to 「ちゃ」.
食べてしまう → 食べちゃう
If it was 「でしまう」, it becomes 「じゃう」: 飲んでしまう → 飲んじゃう
・ケーキ、全部食べちゃった。（I ate the whole cake.）
4. では → じゃ: 学生ではない → 学生じゃない
They still conjugate after contracting
The contracted forms change into past, negative and て-form as usual:
見てる → 見てた／見てない
買っとく → 買っといた／買っといて
食べちゃう → 食べちゃった
・宿題、まだ終わってない。（I haven’t finished my homework yet.）
・明日までに読んどいて。（Read it before tomorrow, okay?）
Easy mistakes
・If the original was 「で」, the contraction becomes voiced too: it’s 飲んじゃう, not 飲んちゃう, and 読んどく, not 読んとく.
・見てる (watching right now) and 見とく (watch in advance) sound similar but mean completely different things, so listen carefully.
・A “contraction + ます” like 見てます is very common in shops and among coworkers, but in documents and letters you should still write 見ています.
・Contraction only makes the speech more relaxed; the meaning doesn’t change. ちゃう can still mean “finish doing,” or “accidentally / oops.”
Telling look-alikes apart
ては also contracts to ちゃ. It differs from ちゃう by only a hair, but the meaning is very different:
食べちゃった。（I ate it up.）＝食べてしまった
食べちゃだめ。（You mustn’t eat it.）＝食べてはだめ
Quick rule of thumb: if 「う」 or 「った」 follows, it’s てしまう; if 「だめ」 or 「いけない」 follows, it’s ては.
What to learn next
In casual speech, 「なければ」 contracts to 「なきゃ」: もう帰らなきゃ。（I’ve got to go home now.）
n4-71:
The idea in one line
In English you say "I smell something nice" or "I hear a strange noise." Japanese doesn't use 「ある」 here. It uses 「noun + がする」. The idea is that a sound, taste, or smell shows up on its own and you perceive it. The polite form is 「がします」.
How to form it
The thing you perceive (noun) + が + します (する among friends).
You usually put an adjective in front to describe what kind of sound or smell it is:
匂い → いい匂いがします (there's a nice smell)
音 → 変な音がします (there's a strange sound)
Common patterns
Sound音 (sounds of things), 声 (voices of people or animals)
・外で変な音がします。 (There's a strange noise outside.)
・隣の部屋から子どもの声がする。 (I can hear a child's voice from the next room.)
Smell匂い, 香り (a fragrance, a more refined word)
・台所からいい匂いがする。 (A nice smell is coming from the kitchen.)
TasteThe 味 you notice when eating
・このお茶、レモンの味がする。 (This tea tastes like lemon.)
Feeling感じがする means "it gives off a ~ feeling," and 気がする means "I have a feeling that ~." You can put a whole sentence directly before 気がする (use the plain form of the verb, the one without ます).
・あの人は優しい感じがします。 (That person comes across as kind.)
・前に会った気がします。 (I feel like we've met before.)
Common mistakes
・The particle is が, not を: say 音がする, never 「音をする」.
・Use がする for what you smell or hear right now. You wouldn't normally say 「いい匂いがあります」.
・In English the subject is "I" ("I smell something nice"), but in Japanese the subject is the smell itself. Don't say 「私はいい匂いがします」. To say where a smell is, say この部屋は変な匂いがします (This room smells strange).
・Things you see don't take がする: colors and shapes don't work this way, so you can't say 「きれいな色がします」.
・A noun must come before it. You can't say 「甘いがします」. Say 甘い匂いがします or 甘い味がします.
Telling similar patterns apart
音がする vs 聞こえる
外で音がする。 (There's a sound outside.): the focus is that a sound is occurring.
外の音が聞こえる。 (I can hear the sounds outside.): the focus is whether you can hear it, so it's often used in cases like よく聞こえない (I can't hear well).
気がする vs と思う
彼は来ないと思います。 (I think he won't come.): a clearer opinion or judgment.
彼は来ない気がします。 (I have a feeling he won't come.): hard to put into words, more of a hunch, and less certain.
Quick tip: use がする for "there's a sound/smell," and 聞こえる for "can/can't hear." Use と思う for a confident opinion, and 気がする for a mere hunch.
n4-72:
The idea in one line
「〜さ」turns an adjective into a noun, much like English turns "high" into "height" or "important" into "importance." 高い means "high," and 高さ means "height." Use it to talk about how ~ something is, or the feeling of being ~.
How to form it
い-adjectives: drop the final 「い」 and add 「さ」.
高い → drop い → 高さ (height)
深い → 深さ (depth) 重い → 重さ (weight) 寒い → 寒さ (the cold) 大きい → 大きさ (size)
な-adjectives: just add 「さ」 directly, with no な in between.
便利 → 便利さ (convenience) 親切 → 親切さ (kindness) 大切 → 大切さ (importance)
Ones to memorize:
いい → よさ (good point, merit. Since いい comes from よい, you don't say いいさ)
静か → 静けさ (quietness, stillness. 静かさ isn't normally used)
When to use it
Numbers and measurementsFor things you can measure, like height, length, and weight, it's often followed by a number or 「どのくらい」.
・富士山の高さは3776メートルです。 (Mt. Fuji's height is 3,776 meters.)
・この部屋の広さはどのくらいですか。 (About how big is this room?)
Feelings and qualitiesFor how strongly something comes across, or its good points and characteristics.
・北海道の冬の寒さにびっくりしました。 (I was shocked by how cold winter in Hokkaido is.)
・病気になって、健康の大切さが分かりました。 (After getting sick, I realized how important health is.)
・この店のよさは安いところです。 (This shop's good point is that it's cheap.)
・夜の静けさが好きです。 (I like the quietness of the night.)
Common mistakes
・Drop the い: it's 高さ, not 高いさ.
・な-adjectives don't take な: it's 便利さ, not 便利なさ.
・Once you add さ it's a noun, so connect it with 「の」 before it and use は・が・を・に after it: 冬の寒さ, not 冬は寒さ.
・「高さ」「重さ」「大きさ」 are neutral measures, just like "height" and "weight" in English. Even for a very short mountain, you still ask about its 高さ, never 低さ.
Telling similar words apart
You've already learned 楽しみ. It and 楽しさ both come from 楽しい, but the meanings differ.
楽しさ = how fun something is, that sense of enjoyment: 日本語の楽しさが分かりました。 (I understood the joy of learning Japanese.)
楽しみ = anticipation, looking forward: 旅行を楽しみにしています。 (I'm looking forward to the trip.)
Quick tip: use さ for degree, like "how fun, how cold, how important." Use 楽しみ for "looking forward to it."
What to learn next
A handy pattern for asking about size: 〜の長さはどのくらいですか。 (About how long is ~?) Swap 長さ for 重さ, 大きさ, or 深さ to ask about all kinds of things.
n4-69:
The idea in one line
「〜ずに」 is the formal version of 「〜ないで」. It means "without doing ~" or "not doing ~, but ...". In English you might say "he left without telling anyone" in conversation, but "he departed without notice" in writing. The meaning is the same, and 「〜ずに」 is just more bookish and refined.
When to use it
Did B without doing AYou skipped something you would normally do and went straight to the next thing.
・朝ご飯を食べずに出かけた。(I left without eating breakfast.)
・誰にも言わずに会社を辞めた。(I quit my job without telling anyone.)
Instead of A, BYou drop one way of doing something and choose another.
・バスに乗らずに、歩いて帰った。(I didn't take the bus; I walked home.)
How to form it: first check the verb group
First put the verb in its ない form, then remove 「ない」 and replace it with 「ず」 or 「ずに」.
Group 1 (godan verbs):
行く → 行かない → 行かず
言う → 言わず
持つ → 持たず
Group 2 (ichidan verbs):
食べる → 食べない → 食べず
見る → 見ず
Group 3 (only two verbs, just memorize them):
する → せず (not しず)
来る → 来ず（こず）
Forms you'll hear most
The form is bookish overall, but a few expressions are common in everyday speech too. Memorize these as whole sentences:
・遠慮せずに食べてください。(Please don't hold back, go ahead and eat.)
・気にせずに休んでね。(Don't worry about it, just get some rest.)
・思わず笑ってしまった。(I couldn't help laughing.)
Common mistakes
・する becomes せず, not しず: 勉強せずに.
・For Group 1 verbs ending in 「う」, the ない form uses 「わ」: 言わず, 買わず, not 言あず.
・来ず is read こず, not きず.
・You can't use it to ask someone to do something. "Please don't ~" can only be 食べないでください; there is no such thing as 「食べずにください」.
・When chatting with friends, ordinary verbs mostly take 「ないで」. Using 「ずに」 everywhere sounds a bit like reading from a script. The fixed expressions above are the exception.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
ないで = the casual version: 傘を持たないで出かけた。(I went out without an umbrella.)
ずに = the formal, written version, with exactly the same meaning: 傘を持たずに出かけた。(I went out without an umbrella.)
In writing you'll also often see 「ず」 followed directly by a comma. This often means "because ~ didn't happen", much like 「なくて」: バスが来ず、遅刻してしまった。(The bus didn't come, so I ended up late.)
Quick tip: when you see 「ずに」, swap it for 「ないで」 in your head and you'll understand it. When you're unsure what to say out loud, 「ないで」 is the safest choice.
n4-70:
The idea in one line
「こと」 works like "the act of ~" or "~ing". In English you can simply say "Reading is fun", but in Japanese a verb can't be the subject on its own. You first add 「こと」 after it, which packages "read" into "the act of reading". Only then can it be the subject or the answer in a sentence.
When to use it
As the subjectPut it before 「は」 or 「が」, then say what it is like.
・毎日運動することは大切です。(Exercising every day is important.)
・遅刻しないことが大切です。(Not being late is important.)
As the answerFor "My hobby is ~" or "My dream is ~", when the "~" is an action, use 「～ことです」.
・私の趣味は写真を撮ることです。(My hobby is taking photos.)
・夢は日本で働くことです。(My dream is to work in Japan.)
How to attach it
Verbs connect directly, with no change in form: 読む → 読むこと
For "not doing", use the ない form: 読まない → 読まないこと
For "having done", use the た form: 読んだ → 読んだこと
Adjectives can take it too. Then it feels more like "a ~ thing": 楽しい → 楽しいこと (fun things). Remember to add な after な-adjectives: 好き → 好きなこと (things you like)
You've actually met it already. The 「こと」 inside ことができます, たことがあります and ことにします is this same "the act of ~".
Common mistakes
・Following English instinct, where "reading" can be a subject, and using the bare verb as the subject: 本を読むが好きです is wrong. You always need こと or の in between: 本を読むことが好きです.
・Forgetting the な after a な-adjective: say 好きなこと, not 好きこと or 好きだこと.
・「Noun＋のこと」 is a different meaning, "about ~": 彼のことが好きです means "I like him (as a person)". It is not the same as turning an action into a noun here, so don't mix them up.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
「の」 can also turn an action into "the act of ~". In many cases either one works, but some positions allow only one of them. It isn't simply that 「こと」 is more formal.
Either worksWhen it is followed by an evaluation like 「好き」, 「大切」 or 「難しい」.
・本を読むのが好きです。(I like reading: more common in conversation)
・本を読むことが好きです。(I like reading: slightly more formal)
Only ことAt the end of a sentence in 「～は～ことです」, and in fixed patterns like ことができます.
・趣味は本を読むことです。(My hobby is reading.)
Switching to 「のです」 is wrong. The 「の」 would be heard as the explanatory 「のです」, which sounds very unnatural, so the sentence ending must be 「ことです」. In the same way, 日本語を話すことができます can't be changed to use の.
Only のWhen you see or hear an action actually happening in front of you.
・犬が走るのを見ました。(I saw a dog running.)
・隣の部屋で誰かが歌っているのが聞こえます。(I can hear someone singing in the next room.)
Here, 走ることを見ました and 歌っていることが聞こえます are both wrong.
Quick tip: before 「～です」 at the end of a sentence, and in fixed patterns like ことができる, use こと. For actions you see or hear happening right in front of you, use の. With 「好き」 or 「大切」 either works, but の sounds smoother in conversation.
n4-73:
The idea in one line
「〜ことがあります」means "sometimes ~" or "there are times when ~". It says something doesn't happen every time, but does happen now and then. It's like the "delays may occur" notices you see in train announcements or on online shopping pages. They warn you that this situation is possible.
How to form it
Sometimes you do it: dictionary form + ことがあります
遅れる → 遅れることがあります (sometimes I'm late / it's sometimes delayed)
Sometimes you don't do it: ない form + ことがあります
食べない → 食べないことがあります (sometimes I don't eat)
With friends, use the plain form ことがある. The meaning is the same.
When to use it
Describing your own habitsIt's not an everyday thing, but it happens occasionally. It often appears with ときどき (sometimes) and たまに (once in a while).
・忙しいとき、朝ご飯を食べないことがあります。 (When I'm busy, I sometimes skip breakfast.)
・たまに電車で寝てしまうことがある。 (I occasionally fall asleep on the train.)
Warnings and announcementsShops, stations and product descriptions love this pattern. It tells you up front, "this can happen, so be aware."
・雨の日は、バスが遅れることがあります。 (On rainy days, the bus is sometimes delayed.)
・商品の色が写真と違うことがあります。 (The color of the product may sometimes differ from the photo.)
Common mistakes
・You can't use it for things that happen every day, always, or without fail. 毎日コーヒーを飲むことがあります is wrong. If you drink it every day, just say 毎日コーヒーを飲みます.
・English words like "will" and "can" cover many meanings, and not all of them map to ことがあります. "I can speak Japanese" is 日本語が話せます, and "It will rain tomorrow" is 明日は雨が降るでしょう. Use ことがあります only for "sometimes".
・The verb before it must be in dictionary form or ない form. If you use the た form, the meaning changes completely (see below).
・You'll often hear 遅れることもあります. Swapping が for も changes the tone to "it may also happen that ~", which is softer and very common in announcements.
Telling similar patterns apart
Dictionary form + ことがある = sometimes does (a present tendency)
この電車は遅れることがあります。 (This train is sometimes delayed.)
た form + ことがある = has done ~ before (a past experience)
この電車は遅れたことがあります。 (This train has been delayed before.)
It's only one word's difference. The first means "this happens now and then in general," and the second means "this has happened at least once in the past."
かもしれません = a guess about whether it will happen this one time
明日は電車が遅れるかもしれません。 (The train might be delayed tomorrow.)
ことがあります = describes the usual situation, where you run into it once in a while
雪の日は電車が遅れることがあります。 (On snowy days, trains are sometimes delayed.)
Quick test: "have done ~ before" takes た form + ことがある. "Sometimes does ~ in general" takes dictionary form + ことがある. "Might ~ this time" takes かもしれません.
What to learn next
It also works with nouns. Add の after the noun: この時間は満席のことがあります。 (This time slot is sometimes fully booked.)
n4-74:
The idea in one line
In English, you soften your language with seniors: "Would you like some tea?" instead of "Want some tea?" Japanese has a similar trick: put the actions of seniors, superiors and customers into the「れる・られる」form, and it sounds respectful.
For example, "the company president went home" is normally 帰りました, and the more respectful version is 帰られました. It's the easiest entry point into honorific language, and it's a fairly light level of politeness.
When to use it
Talking about a senior's actionsWhen you tell someone what a teacher or boss did.
・部長はもう帰られました。 (The department head has already gone home.)
・社長は来週、大阪に出張されます。 (The president will go on a business trip to Osaka next week.)
Asking them directlyWhen you ask a teacher or customer what they're going to do.
・先生はいつ日本へ行かれますか。 (When will you go to Japan, teacher?)
・何を飲まれますか。 (What would you like to drink?)
How to form it: first check the verb group
Good news: it looks exactly like the passive form, so if you know the passive, you already know this.
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the「あ」-row sound of the same row, then add「れる」.
行く → change く to か → 行かれる
読む → 読まれる話す → 話される帰る → 帰られる
Verbs ending in「う」change to わ, not あ: 会う → 会われる
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop the final「る」and add「られる」.
出かける → 出かけられる始める → 始められる
Group 3 (only two verbs, just memorize them): する → される (出発する → 出発される), 来る → 来られる (こられる)
In actual speech, you usually follow it with ます: 行かれる → 行かれます, and the past is 行かれました.
Common mistakes
・Use it only for other people. Using the honorific form for your own actions sounds odd. 私は明日行かれます is wrong. Say 私は明日行きます.
・Don't use it for your own family when talking to outsiders either. You can't say 父は帰られました. Just say 父は帰りました.
・会う becomes 会われる, not「あれる」.
・For Group 2 verbs and 来る, the honorific form happens to look identical to the potential form ("can ~"). 来られます could mean "you will come" or "you can come." To avoid confusion, Japanese speakers often switch to dedicated honorific verbs, such as いらっしゃる for 来る, 召し上がる for 食べる, and ご覧になる for 見る.
・Don't stack two honorific forms together. お帰りになられる is often heard, but it's considered over-polite and incorrect. Pick just one.
Telling similar forms apart
Honorific form = the senior person does the action themselves, and nobody is being acted upon:
部長が帰られました。 (The department head went home.)
Passive form = someone is having something done to them, and the person doing it is often marked with「に」:
部長に怒られました。 (I was scolded by the department head.)
Potential form = asks "can they or can't they?":
先生は刺身が食べられますか。 (Can you eat sashimi, teacher?)
They all use the same「られます」, so you have to rely on context to tell which one it is.
Quick test: if the subject is a senior person doing the action themselves, with no sense of "being done to" and no "can or can't," it's the honorific form.
What to learn next
A more polite pattern is「お + ます-stem + になる」: 社長はお帰りになりました。 (The president went home.) It's more courteous than 帰られました. Check out the lesson on 尊敬語 (honorific language) next.
n3-42:
The idea in one line
「〜わけがない」means "there's no way ~" or "how could ~?". Here 「わけ」 means "reason" or "logic", so 「わけがない」 literally says "there's no logic to it." You're saying with total confidence that this is simply impossible.
When to use it
Declaring something impossibleBased on common sense, or on what you know about someone, you're sure this could never happen.
・そんなに簡単に成功するわけがない。(There's no way you'd succeed that easily.)
・こんな値段で本物が手に入るわけがない。(There's no way you can get the real thing at this price.)
・あんなに練習したんだから、負けるわけがない。(After practicing that hard, there's no way we'll lose.)
Pushing back on someoneIn casual chat, it's like saying "no way, come on." In speech, 「が」 is often dropped, giving 「わけない」.
・宝くじなんて、当たるわけないよ。(A lottery? No way you'd win.)
・そんなわけないでしょ。(No way, right?)
How to form it
Verbs: attach directly. Negative and past forms work too.
負ける → 負けるわけがない知らない → 知らないわけがない
い-adjectives: attach directly.
高い → 高いわけがない
な-adjectives: replace 「だ」 with 「な」.
好きだ → 好きなわけがない
Nouns: replace 「だ」 with 「の」. In more formal speech you can use 「である」.
本物だ → 本物のわけがない
To be polite, say 「わけがありません」.
Common mistakes
・With な-adjectives and nouns, you can't keep 「だ」 before it: 好きだわけがない and 本物だわけがない are both wrong.
・「〜ないわけがない」 stacks two negatives, so it actually means "definitely will": 彼が期限を守らないわけがない。 (There's no way he wouldn't keep the deadline = he'll definitely keep it.)
・English "can't" covers two different ideas, and Japanese separates them. "I can't go out and play, I have an exam tomorrow" means you aren't in a position to / shouldn't, so you need わけにはいかない: 明日は試験だから、遊びに行くわけにはいかない。 (I have an exam tomorrow, so I can't go out and play.) If you wrote 遊びに行くわけがない, it would become "there's no way I'd go out and play."
・The tone is very strong, with a "what nonsense are you saying?" feel. Answering a boss or an elder with そんなわけないです sounds harsh. Try それはないと思います instead.
Telling similar patterns apart
Situation: you offer Tanaka some cake and he says no thanks. Someone nearby asks you, "Does Tanaka hate cake?"
わけがない = strong denial, in a "no way, come on!" tone:
・田中さんがケーキが嫌いなわけがないよ。毎日食べてるもん。(There's no way Tanaka hates cake. He eats it every day!)
はずがない = reasoned conclusion that it shouldn't be so, in a calmer tone:
・田中さんは甘いものが大好きだから、ケーキが嫌いなはずがない。(Tanaka loves sweets, so he can't possibly hate cake.)
The two are often interchangeable. The difference is that はずがない leans toward "going by the clues I have, it shouldn't be so," while わけがない leans toward "it just makes no sense," and in speech it carries stronger emotion.
わけではない = "it's not that ~". It only corrects a misunderstanding and has no sense of "impossible" at all. If Tanaka explained himself, he'd say:
・甘いものが嫌いなわけではない。今はおなかがいっぱいなだけだ。(It's not that I dislike sweets. I'm just full right now.)
Quick tip: for "no way," use わけがない. For "by all logic it shouldn't be," use はずがない. For "it's not that ~," use わけではない.
What to learn next
The 「わけ」 family also includes わけではない (it's not that ~) and わけにはいかない (can't ~). Add the closest in meaning, はずがない, and studying them together is the best way to avoid mixing them up.
n3-43:
The idea in one line
「〜わけではない」means "it's not that ~" or "that doesn't mean ~". The other person may assume something, and you step in to clarify: "It's not what you think." It's like English "It's not that I dislike it, it's just…", and the real reason usually follows.
When to use it
Clearing up a misunderstandingThe other person seems to have misread you, so you set things straight.
・反対しているわけではありません。ちょっと心配なだけです。(It's not that I'm against it. I'm just a little worried.)
・別に怒っているわけじゃないよ。(It's not like I'm angry.)
Not everything is like thatUsed with 「みんな」, 「いつも」 or 「全部」, it means "not necessarily always so."
・日本人がみんな納豆が好きなわけではない。(Not every Japanese person likes natto.)
・高い服がいつもいいわけではない。(Expensive clothes aren't always better.)
Softly decliningYou don't want to shut things down outright, so you first deny a possible misunderstanding, then give your reason.
・料理が嫌いなわけじゃないけど、毎日はちょっと…。(It's not that I hate cooking, but every day is a bit much...)
How to form it
Put the plain form before it, meaning the form without ます (dictionary, ない and た forms all work).
Verbs: 行く → 行くわけではない行った → 行ったわけではない
い-adjectives: 忙しい → 忙しいわけではない
な-adjectives: add な　嫌い → 嫌いなわけではない
Nouns: add な, or use 「という」　学生 → 学生というわけではない
In speech it often becomes わけじゃない. For a more polite tone, use わけではありません or わけじゃありません.
Common mistakes
・After な-adjectives and nouns you can't use だ: say 嫌いなわけではない, not 「嫌いだわけではない」.
・The 「わけ」 here doesn't mean "reason," so don't translate it as "there's no reason."
・It's softer than a plain denial: 嫌いじゃない means "I don't dislike it," while 嫌いなわけじゃない means "it's not that I dislike it (there's another reason)," so an explanation usually follows.
・With a negative before it, it's a double negative: 行きたくないわけじゃない。 (It's not that I don't want to go.) This means you actually kind of want to go.
Telling similar patterns apart
All talking about whether a shop is expensive:
わけではない = it's not that: この店、高いわけではないけど、ちょっと遠い。 (It's not that this shop is expensive, it's just a bit far.)
わけがない = no way: 100円ショップだから、高いわけがない。 (It's a 100-yen shop, so there's no way it's expensive.)
わけだ = no wonder: 有名なシェフの店か。高いわけだ。 (Oh, it's a famous chef's restaurant. No wonder it's expensive.)
Quick tip: use わけではない for "it's not that ~," わけがない for "no way ~," and わけだ for "no wonder ~."
What to learn next
「〜ないことはない」 (it's not that I can't ~) is close in meaning to 「〜ないわけではない」, and both carry a "well, I guess it's possible" tone: 辛い料理も食べられないことはない。 (It's not that I can't eat spicy food either.)
n3-8:
The idea in one line
「〜にとって」means "for ~" or "to ~" in the sense of "from ~'s point of view." First you say whose perspective you're taking, then you say how important, difficult, or good something is for that person. The same thing can feel completely different depending on who you ask, and にとって marks "whose feeling this is."
・私にとって、家族が一番大切です。(To me, family is the most important thing.)
How to attach it
Just add にとって directly to a noun. It's most often a person, but animals, companies, and countries work too.
私 → 私にとって外国人 → 外国人にとって
・外国人にとって、敬語は難しい。(For foreigners, honorific language is difficult.)
・猫にとって、この部屋は暑すぎるかもしれない。(For a cat, this room might be too hot.)
Forms you'll hear most
にとってcan go at the start of a sentence or in the middle. It means "from this person's standpoint, this is how things are." A comma after it is optional.
・この経験は私にとって大きな財産だ。(This experience is a great asset to me.)
にとってはadds は, which brings in a sense of contrast: "for this person it's so, but maybe not for others."
・大人にとっては短い時間でも、子供にとっては長い。(Even a time that's short for adults is long for children.)
にとっての＋nounpacks "the ... for ~" into a single noun phrase, so you need to add の in between.
・子供にとっての幸せを考えてみましょう。(Let's think about what happiness means for children.)
Common mistakes
・What follows にとって is an evaluation: 大切, 難しい, 便利, 貴重, 意味がある, and so on. It can't be followed by an attitude or action directed at a person. To say "The teacher is kind to the students," use 先生は学生に対して親切だ. Saying 先生は学生にとって親切だ is wrong.
・English "for" and "to" cover a lot of ground, but Japanese splits those meanings into different patterns. Don't write にとって every time you'd say "for" or "to."
・The matter of の: 私にとって、幸せは家族と過ごす時間です。 is completely correct, because にとって modifies the whole sentence. You only need にとっての when you turn "the ... for ~" into a single noun block, for example when it comes before を as an object.
Telling similar patterns apart
All of these involve "students," but each grammar point changes the meaning:
にとって = an evaluation from the students' point of view: 学生にとって、この先生は怖い存在だ。 (To the students, this teacher is a scary presence.)
に対して = an attitude or action directed toward the students: この先生は学生に対して厳しい。 (This teacher is strict with the students.)
について = the topic of speech or thought: 先生は学生について話した。 (The teacher talked about the students.)
Another one that's easy to mix up is として, which means "in the capacity of ~" or "as ~":
親として、子供を守りたい。 (As a parent, I want to protect my child.)
親にとって、子供は宝物だ。 (To a parent, a child is a treasure.)
Quick rule of thumb: if what follows is a feeling or evaluation like "important, difficult, precious," use にとって. If it's an attitude toward a person like "strict, kind, opposed," use に対して. If it's "talk, investigate, discuss," use について. If you want to say "as a ~," use として.
n3-28:
The idea in one line
「〜に関して」means "regarding ~" or "concerning ~". It means about the same as 「〜について」, but it sounds more formal and stiffer. In casual chat you'd say "about that," while a company notice or a news report would say "regarding this matter." You'll see it a lot in news, company notices, school announcements, and customer service replies.
How to attach it
It always follows a noun. What comes next decides which form you use:
Followed by a clauseNoun + に関して, followed by a full sentence (what someone does, how things are).
・事故の原因に関して、今調べています。(Regarding the cause of the accident, we are investigating now.)
・この件に関して、何か質問はありますか。(Regarding this matter, do you have any questions?)
Followed by a nounNoun + に関する + noun modifies the noun that follows, giving "a ○○ related to ~."
・環境問題に関する本を探しています。(I'm looking for a book about environmental issues.)
・日本の文化に関するレポートを書きました。(I wrote a report on Japanese culture.)
Before a noun you can also say に関しての, as in 環境問題に関しての本. The meaning is the same.
Forms you'll hear most
に関してはAdding は gives the feel of "as for the ○○ part," and it's often used when explaining something or answering a question.
・料金に関しては、こちらをご覧ください。(As for the fees, please see here.)
に関しましてA more polite version. You'll hear it often in business calls and formal explanations.
・この件に関しまして、後ほどご連絡いたします。(Regarding this matter, we will contact you later.)
Common mistakes
・Before a noun, you need に関する or に関しての. 環境問題に関して本 is wrong; say 環境問題に関する本.
・It's very formal, so using it with friends sounds odd, as if you were in a meeting. When friends talk about something like yesterday's movie, について is enough.
・English "to" or "toward" doesn't always map onto に関して. In "be polite to customers," the attitude is directed at someone, so you need に対して, not に関して.
Telling similar patterns apart
について = "about ~." It works in both everyday and formal settings, so it has the widest range. に関して means the same thing, just more formal.
昨日の試合について話そうよ。 (Let's talk about yesterday's game: chatting with a friend.)
昨日の試合に関して、監督がコメントを発表した。 (Regarding yesterday's game, the coach released a statement: news.)
One more thing to remember: before a noun, について becomes についての, as in 日本についての本.
に対して = "toward ~," about whom an attitude or action is directed.
お客様に対して、丁寧な言葉を使います。 (We use polite language toward customers.)
You can't swap in に関して here, because you're not talking about the topic of customers but speaking directly to them.
にとって = "for ~ / to ~," evaluating something from someone's standpoint.
私にとって、家族が一番大切です。 (To me, family is the most important thing.)
Quick rule of thumb: if you can say "regarding ~" or "related to ~" in English, use に関して (formal) or について (everyday). Use に対して for "toward someone," and にとって for "for someone / from someone's point of view."
n3-3:
The idea in one line
〜について is the Japanese way of saying “about ~” or “regarding ~”. You put out a topic first, then follow it with a verb like “talk, ask, look up, think.” That tells the listener what the content of your conversation or research is.
・この映画についてどう思う？(What do you think about this movie?)
How to connect it
Followed by a verb: noun + について
日本の文化 → 日本の文化について調べる (look into Japanese culture)
Followed by a noun: noun + についての + noun
日本の文化 → 日本の文化についての本 (a book about Japanese culture)
After a whole sentence: add 「こと」 or 「か」 first to turn it into a topic.
留学する → 留学することについて (about studying abroad)
どうする → どうするかについて話し合う (discuss what to do)
Memory aid: について comes from 「に＋就いて」, which carries the feeling of “centering on this matter,” so it points to a subject you're discussing.
The forms you'll hear most
について＋verbThe basic pattern. The verb is usually something like “talk, write, ask, look up, think.”
・将来について考えたことある？(Have you ever thought about your future?)
・旅行の予定について話しましょう。(Let's talk about our travel plans.)
についての＋nounModifies the noun that follows, like English “a ~ about …”.
・日本の歴史についての本を読んでいます。(I'm reading a book about Japanese history.)
についてはPulls the topic out to talk about it on its own, with the feel of “as for ~” or “as far as ~ goes.”
・料金については、受付で聞いてください。(As for the fees, please ask at the reception desk.)
につきましてThe very polite version. You'll hear it a lot from customer service and in company announcements.
・この件につきましては、後ほどご連絡いたします。(Regarding this matter, we will contact you later.)
Common mistakes
・When a noun follows, you must add 「の」: 日本の文化について本 is wrong; say 日本の文化についての本.
・When a verb comes before it, add こと first: 日本で働くについて is wrong; say 日本で働くことについて.
・English “about” is very flexible, but について needs an action tied to the “content” (talk, ask, look up, think, discuss). Watch out: 先生について行く is a different expression meaning “follow the teacher,” not “go about the teacher.”
・私について (about me) and 私にとって (for me / to me) look almost the same, but the meanings are completely different.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Even when you're talking about “children,” changing the phrase changes the meaning a lot:
について = the topic being discussed: 子どもの教育について話す。 (talk about children's education)
に対して = an attitude or action aimed at someone: 子どもに対して優しい。 (kind to children)
にとって = an evaluation from someone's standpoint: 子どもにとって大切なことだ。 (It's something important for children.)
There's also に関して, which means almost the same thing and can be swapped in most of the time. It's just more formal and stiffer, and common in announcements, news and reports:
新しいルールについて説明します。 (I'll explain the new rules. Everyday speech)
新しいルールに関して説明します。 (Regarding the new rules, I will give an explanation. More formal)
When modifying a noun, the counterpart of についての is に関する.
Quick rule of thumb: for “what we're talking about or looking up,” use について; for “how someone is toward someone,” use に対して; for “from someone's point of view,” use にとって; and in formal writing where you want “regarding,” you can switch to に関して.
n3-2:
The idea in one line
「〜に対して」 has two meanings:
The first is “toward ~” or “directed at ~”. It works like an arrow, showing who or what an attitude, action or reaction is aimed at.
The second is “in contrast to ~”, which sets two sides next to each other: A is like this, but B is like that.
When to use it
Target of an attitudeBeing strict, gentle or polite toward someone.
・先生は学生に対して厳しい。(The teacher is strict with the students.)
・彼女は誰に対しても優しい。(She's kind to everyone.)
Target of a responseAnswering or reacting to a question, opinion or proposal.
・質問に対して、丁寧に答えた。(In response to the question, I answered carefully.)
・新しいルールに対して、反対の意見が多い。(Many people oppose the new rules.)
ContrastUse it when two sides are clearly different.
・兄が静かなのに対して、弟はにぎやかだ。(My older brother is quiet, whereas my younger brother is lively.)
・東京は雨だったのに対して、大阪は晴れていた。(It was raining in Tokyo, whereas it was sunny in Osaka.)
How to connect it
The “toward ~” use: attach に対して directly to a noun.
お客様 → お客様に対して
When a noun follows, change it to に対する:
先生に対して → 先生に対する態度 (attitude toward the teacher)
The “in contrast to ~” use: put a whole sentence before it, then add のに対して.
Verbs and い-adjectives connect directly: よく食べる → よく食べるのに対して
な-adjectives and nouns need 「な」 first: 静か → 静かなのに対して学生 → 学生なのに対して
For past events, use the past form: 雨だった → 雨だったのに対して
Common mistakes
・The particle before it is に, not を: 「先生を対して」 is wrong.
・Before a noun, use に対する: 「先生に対して態度」 is wrong; say 先生に対する態度.
・The contrast use always needs 「の」 before it: 「静かに対して」 is wrong; say 静かなのに対して.
・English “to,” “for” and “toward” are very broad, and not every one of them can become に対して. “Good for your health” is 体にいい; “interested in Japanese culture” is 日本文化に興味がある; “for me / to me” is 私にとって.
・に対して sounds fairly formal. In casual chat, “nice to my friends” is perfectly natural as 友達に優しい.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Even when the subject is the same “new rules,” a different phrase changes the meaning:
について = what the topic is (about ~): 新しいルールについて説明した。 (I explained the new rules.)
に対して = who or what an attitude or reaction is aimed at (toward ~): 新しいルールに対して、文句を言う人が多い。 (Many people are complaining about the new rules.)
にとって = an evaluation from someone's standpoint (for ~ / to ~): 学生にとって、新しいルールは厳しすぎる。 (For students, the new rules are too strict.)
This pair is the easiest to mix up:
先生は学生に対して厳しい。 (The teacher is strict with the students: the teacher is the one being strict.)
この試験は学生にとって難しい。 (This exam is hard for students: the students are the ones who find it hard.)
Also, に関して means the same as について, just more formal.
Quick rule of thumb: for “what topic,” use について; for “how someone acts toward someone, or reacts to something,” use に対して; for “how it is from someone's standpoint,” use にとって.
What to learn next
Next, study 〜にとって and 〜に関して so you can sort out all of these “toward / about” expressions at once.
n4-75:
The idea in one line
In English, you say “drink, don’t drink, can drink, be drunk, make him drink” by adding words around “drink” (or switching to a different form). Japanese changes the tail end of the verb, and how it changes depends on which group the verb belongs to. So whichever form you’re learning, step one is always to sort the verb into its group. Get that right and the rest is just applying rules.
Step 1: Work out which group the verb is in
Look at the dictionary form (the unconjugated form you find in a dictionary, e.g. 飲む, 食べる) and ask yourself three questions in order:
1. Is it する or 来る? If so, it’s Group 3 (する・来る). “Noun + する” verbs like 勉強する and 掃除する belong here too.
2. Does it end in something other than る? Verbs like 飲む, 書く, 買う, 話す are always Group 1 (godan verbs).
3. If it ends in る, listen to the sound just before る:
If it’s an “i” or “e” sound, it’s usually Group 2 (ichidan verbs): 食べる (べ is be), 起きる (き is ki), 見る (み is mi).
If it’s an “a, u, o” sound, it’s Group 1: わかる, 作る, 乗る.
Step 3 has a few exceptions. 帰る, 入る, 走る, 知る, 切る, 要る look like Group 2 but are actually Group 1. Just memorize them.
One verb, six of the most common forms
Group 1: using 飲む as the example. You swap the final “む” for another sound in the same row:
む becomes み, add ます: 飲む → 飲みます (drink, polite)
む becomes ま, add ない: 飲む → 飲まない (don’t drink)
む becomes め, add る: 飲む → 飲める (can drink, potential form)
む becomes ま, add れる: 飲む → 飲まれる (be drunk, passive form)
む becomes ま, add せる: 飲む → 飲ませる (make someone drink, causative form)
The Group 1 て-form follows its own set of rules, decided by the last kana:
う・つ・る → って: 買う → 買って待つ → 待って帰る → 帰って
む・ぶ・ぬ → んで: 飲む → 飲んで遊ぶ → 遊んで
く → いて: 書く → 書いて　ぐ → いで: 泳ぐ → 泳いで
す → して: 話す → 話して
Group 2: using 食べる as the example. This is the easiest group. Always drop the る, then add the ending:
食べます, 食べない, 食べて, 食べられる (can eat), 食べられる (be eaten), 食べさせる (make someone eat)
For Group 2, the potential and passive forms look exactly the same, so you can only tell them apart from context.
Group 3: only two verbs, so just memorize them
する: します, しない, して, できる (can do), される (be done), させる (make someone do)
来る: 来ます, 来ない, 来て, 来られる (can come; the passive looks the same), 来させる (make someone come)
The kanji in 来る never changes, but its reading does:
dictionary form and ば-form use く (くる, くれば);
ます-form, て-form and た-form use き (きます, きて, きた);
ない-form, potential, passive and causative use こ (こない, こられる, こさせる).
The forms don’t change one after another
Every one of the forms above is made directly from the dictionary form. You don’t need to turn a verb into the ます-form before making the て-form, or into the potential before making the passive.
One handy pattern: the potential, passive and causative all end in “〜る”, so once you’ve made them, each one is a new Group 2 verb and can be conjugated further with the Group 2 rules:
飲める → 飲めます飲める → 飲めない
・日本語の新聞が読めます。 (I can read Japanese newspapers.)
・漢字はまだあまり書けない。 (I still can’t write kanji very well.)
Easy mistakes
・Exceptions like 帰る are Group 1, so you say 帰ります, 帰らない, 帰って, not 帰ます, 帰ない, 帰て.
・For verbs ending in う, the う changes to わ, not あ, in the ない-form, passive and causative: 買わない, 買われる, 買わせる.
・The て-form of 行く is 行って. It doesn’t follow the “く → いて” rule, so you can’t say 行いて.
・For “noun + する” verbs, the potential form replaces する with できる: 勉強できる (can study). 勉強される is the passive and means something different.
・In casual speech you’ll often hear 食べれる and 見れる (with the ら dropped). It’s very common in conversation, but on exams and in formal writing use 食べられる and 見られる.
Telling similar-looking forms apart
With the same verb 飲む, the potential, passive and causative differ by only a sound or two, yet the meanings are completely different:
Can: potential form
・少しならお酒が飲める。 (I can drink alcohol if it’s just a little.)
Be done to: passive form
・弟に私のジュースを飲まれた。 (My little brother drank my juice.)
Make/let someone: causative form
・子どもに薬を飲ませる。 (I make my child take medicine.)
Quick check: for Group 1, look at the ending. “e-row sound + る” means can, “a-row sound + れる” means passive, and “a-row sound + せる” means causative. For Group 2, “られる” can be either potential or passive, so rely on context. “させる” is always causative.
What to learn next
Once the groups feel familiar, study the forms one at a time: the volitional form (飲もう), the potential form, the ば-form (飲めば), the passive form and the causative form. Last, learn the causative-passive form, which stacks the causative and the passive (飲ませられる／飲まされる, to be forced to drink).
n3-41:
The idea in one line
「〜わけだ」 is the Japanese for “no wonder…” or “so that’s why…”, and it can also mean “in other words…”. You already know a fact, then you learn the reason behind it (or you do the math on the information). When the two click together and you think “ahh, that makes sense,” you use わけだ.
(わけ is written 「訳」 in kanji, and it means reason or logic.)
When to use it
No wonderSomething has seemed odd for a while, and now you know why, so it all makes sense. It often appears with 道理で (no wonder) and 〜のか (oh, so it’s…).
・道理で寒いわけだ。雪が降っている。 (No wonder it’s so cold. It’s snowing.)
・3年も住んでいたのか。日本語が上手なわけだ。 (You lived there for three years? No wonder your Japanese is so good.)
In other wordsYou restate the earlier information in a different way, or work out a result, as if saying “so the conclusion is…”.
・8時に出て9時に着いたから、1時間かかったわけだ。 (I left at 8 and arrived at 9, so in other words it took an hour.)
・「明日は会社が休みです。」「じゃあ、ゆっくり寝られるわけですね。」 (“The office is closed tomorrow.” “Then that means you can get a good sleep.”)
How to form it
Verbs: attach directly to the plain form (the form without ます; past and negative both work)
眠れない → 眠れないわけだかかった → かかったわけだ
い-adjectives: attach directly
寒い → 寒いわけだ
な-adjectives: keep the 「な」
上手 → 上手なわけだ
Nouns: add 「な」 (more formal writing uses 「である」)
休み → 休みなわけだ
To be polite to someone, switch to わけです. In conversation it’s often shortened to わけか or わけね.
Easy mistakes
・After な-adjectives and nouns, you can’t attach わけ directly. Say 上手なわけだ, not 「上手わけだ」.
・わけだ isn’t a casual guess. There has to be a fact or reason you already know, and you’re just connecting it to the result.
・When it’s used about someone else’s shortcomings, as in だから失敗したわけだ (no wonder it failed), it can sound a bit like “well, of course,” so be careful with seniors and customers.
・Don’t mix it up with わけがない, わけではない or わけにはいかない. They differ by only a few characters but mean completely different things.
Telling similar-looking forms apart
はずだ also means judging based on a reason. The key difference is when the result isn’t confirmed yet: if you’re only inferring what should be true, you can only use はずだ, not わけだ. Take the same situation: Mr. Tanaka lived in the US for ten years.
わけだYou’ve already heard him speak English and found it fluent, and now you know why:
10年もアメリカにいたのか。英語がうまいわけだ。 (He was in the US for ten years? No wonder his English is so good.)
はずだYou haven’t heard him speak English yet and are only inferring (わけだ doesn’t work here):
10年もアメリカにいたから、英語がうまいはずだ。 (He was in the US for ten years, so his English should be good.)
Another one: 彼は来ると言っていたから、来るはずだ。 (He said he’d come, so he should come.) The person hasn’t shown up and the outcome isn’t confirmed yet, so it’s はずだ.
That said, for the “no wonder” use, はずだ also works. 道理で寒いはずだ。 and 10年もアメリカにいたのか。英語がうまいはずだ。 are both perfectly natural and mean about the same as わけだ.
If you don’t even have a reason and are just guessing “probably,” that’s だろう／でしょう, not はずだ or わけだ.
Quick check: when the result isn’t confirmed and you’re only inferring, use はずだ only. When the result is already in front of you and you’re saying “no wonder / I see,” both わけだ and はずだ work.
What to learn next
Next, learn the rest of the わけ family: わけがない (there’s no way), わけではない (it’s not that…), わけにはいかない (can’t, for reasons of principle or circumstance). Also, when you finish explaining a reason and want to wrap up, you often say というわけで (so, that’s why…): というわけで、明日は休みます。 (So that’s why I’m taking tomorrow off.)
n3-44:
The idea in one line
「〜わけにはいかない」 means “I can't (just) ~”. The point isn't that you're unable to do it. It's that, given what's reasonable, what people expect, or your position, it wouldn't be right to do it. Your boss is still working overtime and you think, “I can't just leave before him.” That's the feeling.
How to form it
Can't doDictionary form + わけにはいかない
帰る → 帰るわけにはいかない (I can't just go home)
Can't not doない form + わけにはいかない means you have to do it.
行かない → 行かないわけにはいかない (I can't not go = I have to go)
The ない form is the “don't ~” form of a verb, for example 行く → 行かない食べる → 食べない.
With seniors or guests, be more polite by changing いかない to いきません: 休むわけにはいきません (I can't take the day off)
When to use it
Can't just doYou shouldn't do it, because of the reasons or your position.
・車で来たから、お酒を飲むわけにはいかない。 (I came by car, so I can't drink.)
・明日は大事な会議だから、休むわけにはいかない。 (I have an important meeting tomorrow, so I can't take the day off.)
Can't not doYou don't really want to, but social obligation and responsibility are there, so you do it anyway.
・先輩に頼まれたから、手伝わないわけにはいかない。 (My senior asked me, so I can't not help.)
・約束したから、行かないわけにはいかない。 (I promised, so I can't not go.)
Forms you'll hear most
わけにもいかないChange は to も and it becomes “I can't ~ either.” It's often used when you're torn between two things.
・早く帰りたいけど、先に帰るわけにもいかない。 (I'd love to go home early, but it wouldn't feel right to leave before everyone else.)
In fast speech, は is sometimes dropped, giving わけにいかない. The meaning is the same.
Common mistakes
・Don't use it for things you can't do because of skill or ability. “I can't swim” is 泳げない, not 泳ぐわけにはいかない.
・It ends in いかない, not いけない. 「わけにはいけない」 is wrong.
・Whether the verb before it is affirmative or negative flips the meaning: 飲むわけにはいかない = I can't drink; 飲まないわけにはいかない = I can't not drink.
・Don't use it for simply “not wanting to.” That's 行きたくない. Behind わけにはいかない there is always a “by rights” reason.
・It's mostly used for your own situation: the speaker feels “I can't very well ~.”
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Let's take the same topic, a company get-together, and see the difference:
Negative potential form = you can't, because of circumstances: 熱があって、飲み会に行けない。 (I have a fever, so I can't go.)
わけにはいかない = you can't very well, because of obligation or position: 部長も来るから、行かないわけにはいかない。 (The department head is coming too, so I can't not go.)
わけがない = I judge it impossible: 田中さんは忙しいから、来るわけがない。 (Tanaka is so busy, there's no way he'll come.)
わけではない = it's not that…: 飲み会が嫌いなわけではない。 (It's not that I dislike get-togethers.)
Quick tip: “can't do it” takes the potential form, “I can't very well ~” is わけにはいかない, “no way” is わけがない, and “it's not that…” is わけではない.
What to learn next
The N2 pattern 「〜ざるを得ない」 also means “have no choice but to ~,” but it sounds stiffer and more formal, like written language: 行かざるを得ない。 (I have no choice but to go.)
n3-61:
The idea in one line
「〜べきだ」 means “should ~” or “ought to ~”. It isn't a guess about what will happen. It's about right and wrong: you feel this is the right thing to do. Just like we say “you should pay back money you borrow,” in Japanese that's 借りたお金は返すべきだ。
How to form it
Verb dictionary form + べきだ
守る → 守るべきだ (should follow/keep)
謝る → 謝るべきだ (should apologize)
Saying “shouldn't”: Still use the dictionary form, and change 「だ」 to 「ではない」.
言う → 言うべきではない (shouldn't say)
する is special: both するべき and すべき are correct. You'll see すべき more in writing and the news, and you'll hear both in speech.
確認する → 確認すべきだ
Nouns and な-adjectives: add 「であるべきだ」.
公平 → 公平であるべきだ
・先生は公平であるべきだ。 (Teachers should be fair.)
Forms you'll hear most
べきだ／べきですSay what you feel someone ought to do.
・約束は守るべきだ。 (You should keep your promises.)
・若いうちに、いろいろな経験をするべきです。 (You should try all kinds of experiences while you're young.)
べきではないThings you feel one shouldn't do.
・人の悪口を言うべきではない。 (You shouldn't badmouth other people.)
べきだったLooking back with regret: you should have done it, but you didn't. Conversely, べきではなかった means “shouldn't have done it.”
・あのとき、ちゃんと謝るべきだった。 (I should have apologized properly back then.)
・あんなこと、言うべきではなかった。 (I really shouldn't have said that.)
べき＋名詞“The … that one should ~,” placed directly before a noun.
・今やるべきことは何だろう。 (I wonder what I should be doing now.)
Common mistakes
・Don't say 「言わないべき」 for the negative. Say 言うべきではない. Before べき, always use the dictionary form.
・する doesn't become 「しべき」. It's only するべき or すべき.
・The tone is strong, with a preachy “this is the right way” feel. Saying 「〜べきです」 straight to a boss or an elder can easily sound like you're lecturing them. To give advice, use 〜たほうがいいと思います instead. Even when you do use べき, at least add と思います to soften it.
・べき is what the speaker personally feels one should do, not a rule. For things you absolutely must do, like laws and school rules, use 〜なければならない: 日本では、車は左側を走らなければならない。 (In Japan, cars must drive on the left.) Swapping in べき here would sound like a personal opinion, which is odd.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
べき vs はず: English “should” has two meanings, and Japanese splits them into two expressions.
べき = ought to (a judgment of right and wrong)
はず = should be / is expected to (an inference)
・田中さんは約束を守るべきだ。 (Tanaka should keep his promises: I think he ought to.)
・田中さんは約束を守るはずだ。 (Tanaka should keep his promise: I expect he will.)
べきではない vs ものではない: Both can be translated as “shouldn't.” ものではない is about social common sense, something everyone knows, much like an elder telling a child “people just don't do that.” べきではない is more the speaker's own judgment and opinion.
・約束を破るものではない。 (You just don't break promises: common sense.)
・約束を破るべきではない。 (You shouldn't break promises: I think it's wrong.)
Quick tip: use べき for “ought to / ought not to,” and はず for “should be / is expected to.” When you want the “people just don't do that” tone of common sense, use ものではない.
n3-13:
The idea in one line
The most common meaning of 「〜うちに」 is "while ~", as in "strike while the iron is hot." The current state will change later, so you do it quickly while there's still time. It has a second meaning too: "as you keep doing ~, before you know it…". Both are very common.
When to use it
While ~ lastsThe current state (hot, young, still a student) won't last forever, so you take the chance.
・熱いうちに召し上がってください。(Please eat it while it's hot.)
・学生のうちに、たくさん本を読んでおきたい。(I want to read lots of books while I'm still a student.)
・両親が元気なうちに、一緒に旅行したい。(I want to travel with my parents while they're still healthy.)
Before ~ happensWith the ない form + うちに, it means "before something happens," with a bit of a sense of hurry.
・暗くならないうちに帰ろう。(Let's go home before it gets dark.)
・忘れないうちに、メモしておこう。(Let me jot it down before I forget.)
Before you know it…You keep doing something, and as you do, a change shows up.
・話しているうちに、仲良くなった。(We got close as we talked.)
・何度も聞いているうちに、歌詞を覚えた。(After listening to it many times, I ended up memorizing the lyrics.)
・知らないうちに寝てしまった。(I fell asleep without realizing it.)
How to form it
Verb ている form: 話している → 話しているうちに
Verb ない form: 忘れない → 忘れないうちに
い-adjectives: attach directly　熱い → 熱いうちに
な-adjectives: add な　元気 → 元気なうちに
Nouns: add の　学生 → 学生のうちに
The dictionary form works too, but it's mostly with verbs that describe a "state," like 日本にいるうちに (while you're still in Japan).
Easy mistakes
・You can't attach the た form: ×話したうちに. Say 話しているうちに.
・Don't mix up な-adjectives and nouns: 元気なうちに, not 元気のうちに; 学生のうちに, not 学生なうちに. い-adjectives take no の: 若いうちに, not 若いのうちに.
・Don't be thrown by the negative in 「ないうちに」. It means "before it happens," not "while not doing ~."
・The "while ~" use is usually followed by something you want or plan to do: 〜ておこう, 〜たい, 〜てください.
・The "before you know it" use is followed by a change that happens naturally, often 〜なった or 〜てしまった, not something you do on purpose.
Telling similar patterns apart
間に simply means "during that period," with no special feeling: 日本にいる間に、富士山に登りたい。 (I want to climb Mt. Fuji during my time in Japan.)
うちに carries the feeling of "while you still can, because the chance will be gone later": 日本にいるうちに、富士山に登りたい。 (I want to climb Mt. Fuji while I'm still in Japan.)
If the time span has a clear start and end, like "between 3 and 5 o'clock," you can only use 3時から5時の間に, not うちに.
前に and ないうちに look alike too:
雨が降る前に帰ろう。 (Let's go home before it rains: simply the order of events.)
雨が降らないうちに帰ろう。 (Let's get home before it starts raining: more of a sense of hurry.)
Quick test: if you mean "hurry up while there's still time," use うちに; if you're just giving the time period, use 間に; if you're only stating the order of events, use 前に.
What to learn next
Next, look at 「〜間に」 and 「〜最中に」 (in the middle of ~ing). Compare all three together and you won't mix up the ways of talking about time.
n3-20:
The idea in one line
「〜ば〜ほど」 means "the more ~, the more ~." Think "the more you practice, the better you get" or "the more I think about it, the more annoyed I am." The more you do the first thing, or the higher its degree, the more obvious the result becomes.
Japanese does this by saying the same word twice: the first time in the ば form (the "if ~" form), the second time in its plain form, and then adding ほど.
・練習すればするほど上手になる。(The more you practice, the better you get.)
How to form it
VerbsFirst change the verb to the ば form, then add the dictionary form of the same verb, then ほど.
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the え-row sound of the same row, then add ば.
読む → む becomes め → 読めば読むほど
行く → 行けば行くほど
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop る and add れば.
食べる → 食べれば食べるほど
Group 3: する → すればするほど来る → 来れば来るほど（くればくるほど）
For "noun + する" verbs like 勉強する, the second part usually keeps just する: 勉強すればするほど.
い-adjectivesDrop い and add ければ, then follow with the original い-adjective + ほど.
安い → 安ければ安いほど
な-adjectivesUse なら the first time, then な + ほど the second time.
静か → 静かなら静かなほど
How you'll hear it most
・日本語は勉強すればするほど面白くなる。(The more you study Japanese, the more interesting it gets.)
・この本は読めば読むほど好きになる。(The more I read this book, the more I like it.)
・返事は早ければ早いほどいいです。(The sooner you reply, the better.)
・部屋は静かなら静かなほどいい。(The quieter the room, the better.)
「早ければ早いほどいい」 and 「多ければ多いほどいい」 are almost set phrases. Memorize them whole and they'll come in handy.
Easy mistakes
・Both parts must be the same word. English says "the more A, the more B," but Japanese says A twice and puts B in the clause that follows.
・The second one uses the plain form, with no second ば: it's 考えれば考えるほど, not 考えれば考えればほど.
・The ば form of いい is よければ, not いければ: よければよいほど.
・来れば is read くれば, not きれば.
・With な-adjectives, the first part is なら and the second is な. They're different, so don't write 静かなら静かならほど.
Telling similar patterns apart
〜ば〜ほど: 練習すればするほど上手になる。 (The more you practice, the better you get.)
〜ほど (dropping the first ば): 練習するほど上手になる。 (Same meaning.)
The version without ば is shorter; the version with ば makes the "the more… the more…" feeling clearer and stronger.
〜とともに: 年をとるとともに、体力が落ちる。 (As we get older, our stamina declines.)
Compare: 年をとればとるほど、体力が落ちる。 (The older you get, the more your stamina drops.)
とともに means "along with / as ~" and is more formal and bookish; ば〜ほど means "the more ~, the more ~" and is common in both speech and writing.
Quick test: if you want to say "the more ~, the more ~," use ば〜ほど; use とともに only when you want the more formal "as ~" or "along with ~."
What to learn next
On its own, 「〜ほど」 also means "to the extent of ~," for example 泣きたいほど痛い (it hurts so much I want to cry). Check out the 「〜ほど」 card next.
n3-33:
The idea in one line
「〜っぽい」is a lot like English "-ish" or "-y", or "kind of like ~". Think of calling someone "childish" or saying a shirt looks "cheap". After certain verbs, it means "tends to ~ / is prone to ~", as in "forgetful" or "quick to get angry". It's very casual and you'll hear it all the time in everyday conversation.
When to use it
Seems like ~Noun + っぽい: it isn't actually that thing, but it gives that impression.
・彼はもう30歳なのに、子供っぽい。(He's already 30, but he's so childish.)
・今日はちょっと風邪っぽい。(I feel a bit like I'm coming down with a cold today.)
~-ish in color, with a hint of ~い-adjective + っぽい: often used for colors or textures.
・白っぽいシャツを買った。(I bought a whitish shirt.)
Tends to ~Verb + っぽい: describes a person's character.
・父は年を取って、怒りっぽくなった。(My dad has gotten older and become easily irritated.)
・私は飽きっぽいから、何をしても続かない。(I get bored easily, so I can't stick with anything.)
How to form it
Nouns: just add っぽい.
子供 → 子供っぽい
風邪 → 風邪っぽい(seems like a slight cold)
い-adjectives: drop the final い, then add っぽい.
安い → drop い → 安っぽい
白い → 白っぽい
Verbs: change to the ます form, drop ます, then add っぽい.
忘れます → drop ます → 忘れっぽい
怒ります → 怒りっぽい
Once attached, 「〜っぽい」becomes a whole い-adjective and conjugates just like 高い:
忘れっぽい → 忘れっぽくなった(became forgetful)
子供っぽい → 子供っぽくない(not childish)
Common mistakes
・You can't attach it to just any verb. The common ones are few: 忘れっぽい, 怒りっぽい, 飽きっぽい. Don't invent words like 食べっぽい.
・安っぽい doesn't mean "inexpensive." It means "looks cheap, tacky," and it's negative: このバッグは安っぽい。(This bag looks cheap.) To say something is low-priced, use 安い.
・It often carries a slightly critical tone. Calling an adult 子供っぽい isn't a compliment; on the other hand, calling a child or young person 大人っぽい (mature) is usually praise.
・It's very casual, so avoid it in reports and formal writing.
・Young people also attach っぽい to a whole sentence to mean "it seems like ~": あの店、もう閉まったっぽい。(That shop seems to have closed already.) This is very casual. It's fine with friends, but don't use it with your seniors.
Don't confuse it with similar forms
らしい: 子供らしい is how a child naturally should be, usually praise for an actual child; 子供っぽい means not a child, yet acting like one, usually said about adults.
・元気で子供らしい子だ。(He's a lively, genuinely childlike kid.)
・彼は考え方が子供っぽい。(His way of thinking is childish.)
がち: 忘れっぽい describes a person's character; 忘れがち describes something that often happens, and you can say clearly what gets forgotten.
・彼は忘れっぽい。(He's forgetful.)
・私はメールの返事を忘れがちだ。(I often forget to reply to emails.)
気味: 風邪っぽい and 風邪気味 both mean "a bit of a cold." っぽい is more casual and fine with friends; when asking your company for time off or explaining to a doctor, 風邪気味 is safer.
Quick rule of thumb: use らしい for "truly is that way, as it should be"; use っぽい for "isn't, but resembles" or "tends to ~ by personality"; use がち for "something often happens."
What to learn next
Two other patterns also describe tendencies: 〜がち and 〜気味. Studying all three together makes them easier to tell apart.
n3-34:
The idea in one line
「〜がち」means "tends to ~", "is prone to ~", "often ends up ~ing". It describes a tendency that happens often and is usually undesirable, such as catching colds easily, running late, or forgetting things.
・冬は風邪を引きがちだ。(In winter, people tend to catch colds.)
How to form it
VerbsChange to the ます form, drop ます, then add がち.
休みます → 休みがち (often absent)
遅れます → 遅れがち (often late, often behind)
します → しがち (tends to do)
NounsAttach directly, but only a fixed few common ones work. Not every noun can take it.
病気がち (often sick), 留守がち (often not at home), 曇りがち (often cloudy)
How you'll hear it most
〜がちだAt the end of a sentence, saying a person or thing often does this.
・忙しいと、食事を抜きがちだ。(When I'm busy, I tend to skip meals.)
・彼は最近、学校を休みがちだ。(He's been missing school a lot lately.)
〜がちな + nounBefore a noun, it works like 「静かな部屋」.
・これは初心者にありがちなミスです。(This is a mistake beginners often make.)
Common mistakes
・It can't attach to the dictionary form: it's 休みがち, not 「休むがち」.
・It carries an undesirable nuance, so it's generally not used for good things. To say "I study often," just say よく勉強する. Saying 「勉強しがち」 would sound odd, as if studying were a bad habit.
・You can't use it for something that happened only once. がち means "often, prone to," not "this time."
・Don't attach it to nouns freely. For now, just remember common ones like 病気がち and 留守がち.
・The ガチ that young people say ("serious, for real, super") is slang and has nothing to do with 「〜がち」here.
Don't confuse it with similar forms
がち = a tendency that happens often: 子どものころは病気がちだった。(I was often sick as a child.)
気味 = you feel a bit that way right now: 今日はちょっと風邪気味だ。(I feel a bit like I have a cold today.)
がち = something that easily happens: 人の名前は忘れがちだ。(I often forget people's names.)
っぽい = the person has that quality overall: 祖父は最近忘れっぽい。(My grandfather has become forgetful lately.)
Quick rule of thumb: use がち for "often tends to ~," 気味 for "a bit ~ right now," and っぽい for "the person is generally ~-ish."
What to learn next
Next, look at 〜気味 and 〜っぽい. Remembering these three together is the best way to avoid mixing them up.
n3-30:
The idea in one line
「〜にしては」 means “for a ~…” or “considering that it's ~, it's surprisingly…”. You have an expectation about someone's status or about a fact, and reality turns out different from that expectation. That's when you use it.
For example, you see a child's very neat handwriting and say “Nice handwriting for a kid.” That's 子どもにしては、字がきれいだ。
When to use it
Better than expectedYou didn't expect much, but the result is good, and there's a hint of praise.
・初めて作ったにしては、おいしいね。(Pretty tasty for a first try!)
・新人にしては、よくやっている。(He's doing well for a newcomer.)
Worse than expectedYou expected a lot, but the result is a letdown, and there's a hint of complaint.
・有名な店にしては、あまりおいしくなかった。(For a famous restaurant, it wasn't that good.)
Weather, timeIt doesn't match what you'd expect for the season or the time.
・4月にしては寒いですね。(It's cold for April, isn't it?)
How to form it
Nouns: attach directly, with no の and no だ in between.
プロ → プロにしては4月 → 4月にしては
Verbs: use the plain form (dictionary form, た-form, and other forms without ます).
初めて作った → 初めて作ったにしては3年も住んでいる → 3年も住んでいるにしては
Common mistakes
・After a noun, attach にしては directly, without の: say 子どもにしては, not 子どものにしては. (The one with の is 子どものわりに, so don't mix them up.)
・What comes before it should be a concrete status, number, or fact, like 「新人」「60歳」「千円」「初めて」. Words that just name a range or category, like “age,” “price,” or “height,” can't attach directly: 値段にしては sounds unnatural, so switch to 値段のわりに.
・い-adjectives generally don't attach directly to にしては. 「安いにしては」 sounds odd, so use 安いわりに instead.
・The second half is your evaluation or impression. It doesn't take commands or decisions like “please ~” or “I'll ~.”
・You can use it about yourself too: 私にしては、よく頑張ったと思う。(For me, I think I worked pretty hard.)
Telling similar patterns apart
わりに (n3-29) also means “different from what you'd expect,” and English often translates both as “for a ~.” The difference is what comes before it.
Same situation, an older man who looks very young:
あの人は60歳にしては若く見える。(He looks young for 60.) → a concrete 「60歳」 comes before it
あの人は年のわりに若く見える。(He looks young for his age.) → a range word like “age” comes before it
Same cheap, tasty restaurant:
千円にしてはおいしい。(Tasty for a thousand yen.)
値段のわりにおいしい。／安いわりにおいしい。(Tasty for the price / Cheap, yet tasty.)
Also, にしては carries more of an in-the-moment “wait, this is supposed to be ~!” surprise, and the evaluation it carries is stronger.
として (n3-5) is also often translated as “as a ~,” but it means speaking from the standpoint of that role. It has no “different from expectation” meaning.
先生として、生徒を守りたい。(As a teacher, I want to protect my students.)
先生にしては、字が汚いね。(Pretty messy handwriting for a teacher, huh.)
Quick rule of thumb: if a concrete status, number, or fact comes first and the result surprises you, use にしては. If a range word like “age” or “price,” or an adjective, comes first, use わりに. If you're just saying “in the role of ~” with no surprise, use として.
n3-5:
The idea in one line
「〜として」 means “as a ~,” “in the capacity of ~,” or “as (a) ~”. Put a noun before it to say what role, status, or purpose something is done in.
When to use it
Status・positionDoing something in a certain capacity. This is the most common use.
・留学生として日本に来ました。(I came to Japan as an international student.)
・彼は医者として、また父として尊敬されている。(He is respected both as a doctor and as a father.)
As・for the purpose ofTreating something as having a certain use.
・これはお土産として買いました。(I bought this as a souvenir.)
As a categorySaying that something is known or regarded “as a ~.”
・京都は観光地として有名です。(Kyoto is famous as a tourist destination.)
How to form it
It's simple: noun + として.
先生 → 先生として趣味 → 趣味として
Forms you'll hear most
としての＋nounWhen a noun follows, add 「の」 in between.
・親としての責任がある。(I have a responsibility as a parent.)
私としては“From my standpoint.” A polite way to give your own opinion, very common in meetings and at work.
・私としては、この案に賛成です。(Personally, I'm in favor of this proposal.)
Common mistakes
・When a noun follows, use としての: say 医者としての仕事, not 「医者として仕事」 to mean “a doctor's job.”
・The “for” in “For students, studying is important” is not として. Say 学生にとって、勉強は大切だ。 Writing 「学生として、勉強は大切だ」 sounds very odd.
・As a rule, put a noun before として. Don't attach a verb or adjective directly.
Telling similar patterns apart
として = the noun before it is the subject's own status or role:
父として、子どもを守りたい。(As a father, I want to protect my child. The speaker is the father.)
にとって = the noun before it is whose point of view the feeling or judgment comes from:
父にとって、子どもは一番大切だ。(To a father, his child is the most important thing. It's seen from the father's perspective.)
One more pair: 京都は観光地として有名だ。(Kyoto is a tourist destination, and is famous in that capacity.) / 私にとって、京都は特別な場所だ。(From my point of view, Kyoto is a special place.)
Quick rule of thumb: if the noun before it is the subject's own status, role, or category (he is a doctor, Kyoto is a tourist destination), use として. If it's “whose point of view the feeling or judgment comes from” (to a parent, to me), use にとって.
What to learn next
Review 〜にとって from the same lesson alongside this one. You can also see として in 〜をはじめ（として） (“starting with ~”).
n3-21:
The idea in one line
「〜ないことはない」 is the Japanese version of "I guess I could" or "It's not that I can't". Two negatives stack up, so the meaning is really "possible", but it's a discounted yes. You can barely manage it, or it's technically possible, but you don't really want to or aren't keen. Say a friend invites you on a 4 a.m. hike and you answer "Well, I guess I could go…". Everyone can tell you'd rather not.
How to form it
Change the verb to its ない form, then add ことはない or こともない.
行ける → 行けない → 行けないことはない (I could go, I suppose)
食べられる → 食べられない → 食べられないこともない (I could eat it, I suppose)
It's most often used with "can / can't" expressions like 行ける, できる and 食べられる, because this pattern is mostly about whether you're able to do something.
If the ない form still feels shaky, here's a quick review:
