Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last kana to its あ-column counterpart, then add ない. 行く → く becomes か → 行かない. Verbs ending in う change to わ: 会う → 会わない
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop 「る」 and add ない. 食べる → 食べない
Group 3 (する・来る): する → しない来る → 来ない（こない）
When to use it
Barely doableIt's a bit of a stretch, but you could do it if you had to.
・この量なら、一人で食べられないことはない。(If it's this much, I could finish it by myself, I suppose.)
Followed by a "but"The most common shape adds 「けど／が」 and then states the real concern.
・駅まで歩けないことはないけど、ちょっと遠いね。(I could walk to the station, I guess, but it's a bit far.)
・行けないこともないが、あまり気が進まない。(I could go, I suppose, but I'm not really into the idea.)
Noncommittal answerUse it when someone asks you something and you don't want to say yes outright, but you don't want to flatly refuse either.
・明日までにできる？(Can you get it done by tomorrow?)
・できないことはないですけど…。(Well, it's not impossible, but…)
What's the difference between ことはない and こともない? The meaning is almost the same and you can swap them. こともない has an extra 「も」, which makes it softer and vaguer, like saying "well… I guess it's kind of okay."
Common mistakes
・This sentence is affirmative. 行けないことはない means "I can go" (just reluctantly). Don't see two negatives and assume it means "I can't go."
・It is not an enthusiastic "yes". If a friend invites you and you reply 行けないことはない, they'll sense you don't really want to come. If you truly want to go, say 行けるよ or いいね、行こう. Answering your boss or a client this way can also come across as uncooperative.
・The verb before it must be in the ない form. Without the ない, 行くことはない becomes "there's no need to go", which is a completely different meaning.
Telling similar patterns apart
Take karaoke as the topic. The only thing that changes is what comes before, and the meaning changes completely:
ない form + ことはない = "it's not that I don't…": カラオケは行かないことはないけど、年に一回くらいかな。 (It's not that I never go to karaoke, but maybe once a year.)
Dictionary form + ことはない = "no need to…": 嫌なら、無理して行くことはないよ。 (If you don't like it, there's no need to force yourself to go.)
た form + ことはない = "have never…": カラオケには一度も行ったことはない。 (I've never once been to karaoke.)
ないわけではない = "it's not that…": カラオケが好きじゃないわけではない。 (It's not that I don't like karaoke.)
The last one is close to ないことはない. The difference is that わけではない focuses on correcting the other person's misunderstanding: "it's not what you think." ないことはない focuses on "it's possible, or barely okay."
Quick test: ない + ことはない = "it's not that I can't…"; dictionary form + ことはない = "no need to…"; た form + ことはない = "have never…", yet another meaning. To correct someone's misunderstanding, use わけではない.
n3-29:
The idea in one line
「〜わりに」 is the Japanese version of "for a …, it's quite …" or "you'd expect X, but actually …". From the first part you imagine how things "should" turn out, and when reality differs from that expectation, you use わりに. It's like telling a friend "For the price, this place gives you a lot of food." That's the feel of わりに.
When to use it
Pleasant surpriseThe result is better than you'd expect.
・この店は、値段のわりに量が多い。(For the price, this place serves a lot of food.)
・彼はよく食べるわりに、太らない。(He eats so much, yet he doesn't gain weight.)
Unpleasant surpriseThe result is worse than you'd expect, with a slightly disappointed tone.
・よく勉強したわりに、点数が悪かった。(Considering how much I studied, my score was bad.)
・彼は体が大きいわりには、気が小さい。(For someone so big, he's pretty timid.)
For extra emphasis you can say わりには. The meaning is the same.
How to form it
Verbs: attach directly; use the た form for past events.
よく食べる → よく食べるわりに
勉強した → 勉強したわりに
い-adjectives: attach directly.
近い → 近いわりに
な-adjectives: change だ to な.
丈夫だ → 丈夫なわりに
Nouns: add の.
年齢 → 年齢のわりに
・この部屋は駅から近いわりに、家賃が安い。(This room is close to the station, yet the rent is cheap.)
・このかばんは丈夫なわりに軽い。(This bag is sturdy, yet light.)
・父は年齢のわりに元気だ。(My dad is full of energy for his age.)
Common mistakes
・Use 「な」 after な-adjectives and add 「の」 after nouns: it's 丈夫なわりに and 年齢のわりに, not 丈夫だわりに or 年齢わりに.
・It only works when the result is "different from what you'd expect." It's natural that expensive things taste good, so 値段が高いわりにおいしい sounds odd. The right version is 値段が高いわりにおいしくない (so expensive, yet not tasty).
・What comes before it should ideally be something with a scale, like high/low or more/less: age, price, height, amount of study.
・What follows should describe or evaluate something. You can't follow it with requests or invitations like 「Please ～」 or 「Let's ～」.
・わりに placed alone before an adjective (often also わりと) is a different usage, meaning "more … than expected": 今日のテストはわりに簡単だった。 (Today's test was easier than I expected.)
Telling similar patterns apart
にしては also means "for a …, unexpectedly", and both translate into English almost the same way. The difference is what goes before it.
わりに: what comes before can be a general degree like "age" or "price", and it can also follow adjectives and verbs.
にしては: what comes before is a specific number, status or fact, like 「60歳」「1000円」「初めて」. It mainly follows nouns and verbs, and rarely adjectives.
・父は年齢のわりに若く見える。(My dad looks young for his age.)
・父は60歳にしては若く見える。(My dad looks young for a 60-year-old.)
・この料理は値段のわりにおいしい。(This dish is tasty for the price.)
・この料理は1000円にしてはおいしい。(This dish is tasty for 1000 yen.)
Conversely, 「年齢にしては」 and 「値段にしては」 sound unnatural, because "age" and "price" are not specific figures.
Quick test: if what comes before is a general degree like "age" or "price", or an adjective, use わりに. If it's a specific number or status like "60 years old", "1000 yen" or "the first time", use にしては.
n3-17:
The idea in one line
「〜さえ〜ば」means "as long as ~, then ~" or "all you need is ~". You don't need anything else: this one condition is enough. When you'd say "As long as I have internet, I can work anywhere," Japanese uses this pattern.
・時間さえあれば、もっと旅行したい。（As long as I have time, I want to travel more.）
How to form it
First, a quick review of how the ば-form (the "if ~" form) is made, word by word:
書く → change く to け → 書けば
ある → あれば
いい → よければ
名詞＋さえ＋〜ばThe most common pattern. Put さえ right after the thing you want to emphasize, then use the ば-form of a verb or adjective.
・天気さえよければ、明日は富士山が見える。（As long as the weather is good, you'll be able to see Mt. Fuji tomorrow.）
動詞＋さえすればEmphasizes "as long as you just do this action." Put the verb in ます-form, drop ます, then add さえすれば.
飲みます → drop ます → 飲みさえすれば
・この薬を飲みさえすれば、すぐ治りますよ。（As long as you take this medicine, you'll get better soon.）
・ボタンを押しさえすれば、あとは機械がやってくれる。（All you have to do is press the button, and the machine does the rest.）
て形＋さえいればEmphasizes "as long as you just stay in this state."
待って → 待ってさえいれば
・ここで待ってさえいれば、大丈夫です。（As long as you wait here, you'll be fine.）
形容詞＋さえあればFor い-adjectives, change い to く. For な-adjectives, add で. Then attach さえあれば.
安い → 安くさえあれば静か → 静かでさえあれば
・静かでさえあれば、狭い部屋でもかまわない。（As long as it's quiet, I don't mind even a small room.）
In speech, it often becomes たら or なら
If you swap ば for 「たら」 or 「なら」, the meaning is still "as long as ~". You'll hear this a lot in conversation.
・時間さえあったら、手伝うよ。（As long as I have time, I'll help.）
・あなたさえいいなら、私はそれでいい。（As long as you're happy with it, I'm fine with it too.）
Common mistakes
・With verbs, use the ます-form minus ます: it's 飲みさえすれば, not 「飲むさえすれば」.
・さえ replaces 「が」 and 「を」 after a noun: it's お金さえあれば, not 「お金がさえあれば」.
・It means "as long as", not "only if". 練習さえすれば means "just practice and that's enough." The point is that the condition is easy, not that "nothing else will do."
・さえ must be followed by a conditional form (ば, たら, なら) to mean "as long as". Without one, さえ means "even ~".
Don't confuse it with look-alikes
It's the same さえ, but what follows decides the meaning:
さえ〜ば／たら／なら = as long as ~: ひらがなさえ読めれば、このゲームはできる。（As long as you can read hiragana, you can play this game.）
さえ on its own = even ~: ひらがなさえ読めない。（I can't even read hiragana.）
Quick tip: check whether さえ is followed by a conditional form (〜ば, 〜たら, 〜なら). If it is, it means "as long as". If not, it means "even ~".
What to learn next
The stand-alone 〜さえ ("even ~") is worth studying alongside the similar 〜すら and 〜まで.
n3-24:
The idea in one line
「〜代わりに」means "B in place of A". It can be swapping things, people or methods. It can also be a trade like "you help me, I'll treat you," or a gain and a loss like "the pay is high, but in return it's exhausting." The core is always the same: one side for the other, evenly balanced.
When to use it
Swapping things or methodsYou would normally use or do A, but you use or do B instead.
・砂糖の代わりに、はちみつを使った。（I used honey instead of sugar.）
・今日は外食する代わりに、家で作ろう。（Instead of eating out today, let's cook at home.）
Swapping peopleA was supposed to do it, but B does it instead.
・社長の代わりに、部長が会議に出た。（The department head attended the meeting in place of the president.）
・私の代わりに電話に出てくれる？（Can you answer the phone for me?）
Trading favorsI do A, and you do B.
・英語を教える代わりに、日本語を教えてもらっている。（I teach them English, and in exchange they teach me Japanese.）
・宿題を手伝ってもらった代わりに、昼ご飯をおごった。（They helped me with my homework, so in return I treated them to lunch.）
Good and badOne good point comes with a matching bad point, or the other way around.
・給料が高い代わりに、仕事がきつい。（The pay is high, but in return the work is tough.）
・この部屋は駅から遠い代わりに、家賃が安い。（This room is far from the station, but in return the rent is cheap.）
How to form it
Nouns: add 「の」 in between. 砂糖 → 砂糖の代わりに
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly to the plain form. Affirmative, negative and past all work.
行く → 行く代わりに行かない → 行かない代わりに手伝ってもらった → 手伝ってもらった代わりに
高い → 高い代わりに効かない → 効かない代わりに
な-adjectives: keep the 「な」. 便利 → 便利な代わりに
When you mean "instead of doing A, do B," the verb is usually in dictionary form, e.g. 行く代わりに.
・この薬はあまり効かない代わりに、副作用もない。（This medicine isn't very effective, but in return it has no side effects either.）
The form you'll hear most
その代わりPlaced alone at the start of a sentence, it means "but in return ~". It's very common when you're setting terms with a friend.
・車、貸してあげる。その代わり、ガソリン入れてきてね。（I'll lend you my car. In return, fill up the tank for me, okay?）
Common mistakes
・The word order is the reverse of English: English says "honey instead of sugar," with the new thing first. Japanese is 砂糖の代わりにはちみつ, with the thing being replaced before 「代わりに」. If you follow the English order and write はちみつの代わりに砂糖, the meaning is completely flipped.
・Don't drop the 「の」 after a noun or the 「な」 after a な-adjective.
・For the "good and bad" use, the two sides must offset each other. For a plain "but," use 「けど」: 日本語は難しいけど、毎日勉強している。 You can't replace it with 代わりに here.
Don't confuse it with look-alikes
代わりに = one good, one bad, evenly balanced:
この店は高い代わりに、すごくおいしい。（This place is expensive, but in return it's really delicious.）
わりに = considering A, the result is not what you'd expect:
この店は高いわりに、あまりおいしくない。（For how expensive this place is, it's not that good.）
Also, 反面 can express a good and a bad side too (給料が高い反面、仕事がきつい。). The meaning is very close to 代わりに, but it's more formal and leans toward describing two sides of the same thing.
Quick tip: if it feels like "one for the other, it evens out," use 代わりに. If it feels like "considering ~, how come it's like this?", use わりに.
n3-7:
The idea in one line
「〜せいで」means "it's because of ~" or "~ is to blame". When something turns out badly and you want to say what caused it, this is the phrase.
Switch to 「〜せいか」 and the tone steps back: it becomes "maybe because of ~", meaning you're not quite sure of the cause yourself.
When to use it
せいでThe result is bad, and you're sure who or what caused it. There's a hint of blame or complaint.
・雨のせいで、試合が中止になった。(Because of the rain, the match was cancelled.)
・私が寝坊したせいで、みんなを待たせてしまった。(It's my fault for oversleeping; I made everyone wait.)
せいかYou're only guessing at the cause, and it may not really be so. In English it's often "maybe it's because of ~" or "perhaps due to ~".
・年のせいか、最近疲れやすい。(Maybe it's my age, but I get tired easily these days.)
・寝不足のせいか、頭がぼんやりする。(Maybe it's from lack of sleep, but my head feels foggy.)
At the end of a sentencePut the cause last, and it becomes "~ is because of ~" or "~ is to blame".
・失敗したのは準備不足のせいだ。(The failure was due to a lack of preparation.)
・私のせいです。すみません。(It's my fault. I'm sorry.)
How to attach it
「せい」is itself a noun, so what comes before it works just like before a noun.
Noun: add 「の」風邪 → 風邪のせいで
な-adjective: add 「な」下手 → 下手なせいで
い-adjective: attach directly狭い → 狭いせいで
Verb: use the plain form (the form without ます); the past tense is fine too食べすぎた → 食べすぎたせいで
せいか attaches in exactly the same way; just swap で for か.
Easy mistakes
・Nouns must take 「の」: it's 雪のせいで, not 「雪せいで」.
・な-adjectives take 「な」, not 「だ」: it's 暇なせいか, not 「暇だせいか」.
・Don't use せいで for good results. For "Thanks to my teacher, I passed," use おかげで. With せいで it would sound like you're blaming the teacher for your passing, which is odd.
・Saying あなたのせいで to someone's face is a direct accusation. It's harsh, so be careful.
・The very common 気のせいだよ is a set phrase meaning "you're just imagining it."
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Even with the same cause, "because of the rain," a different result means a different word:
せいで = bad result, you blame it: 雨のせいで、花火大会が中止になった。(Because of the rain, the fireworks festival was cancelled.)
おかげで = good result, you're thankful for it: 雨のおかげで、涼しくなった。(Thanks to the rain, it got cooler.)
Conversely, using おかげで for a bad result is sarcasm: 君のおかげで、また怒られたよ。(Thanks to you, I got scolded again.)
Quick rule: to say "it's ~'s fault," use せいで; to say "thanks to ~," use おかげで; if the cause is uncertain and you're just guessing, use せいか.
n3-9:
The idea in one line
「とともに」can be written with kanji as 「と共に」, and it's close to English "together with ~" or "along with ~ / as ~". It's a fairly formal, written expression, common in news, speeches, essays and greetings. It feels like saying "together with my family" or "as times change"; people don't use it much in casual chat.
When to use it
TogetherDoing something with someone. It's the formal version of 「と一緒に」.
・家族とともに新居で新年を迎えた。(I welcomed the new year in our new home together with my family.)
・チームの仲間とともに優勝を喜んだ。(I celebrated the championship together with my teammates.)
Along with / asWhen the first thing changes, the second changes with it. This is the usage most tested at N3.
・年齢とともに体力が落ちてきた。(As I've gotten older, my stamina has declined.)
・人口が減るとともに、町の店も少なくなった。(As the population shrank, the shops in town became fewer too.)
At the same timeThe moment A happens, B happens too.
・ベルが鳴るとともに、子どもたちは教室を飛び出した。(The moment the bell rang, the children dashed out of the classroom.)
How to attach it
Noun + とともに
家族 → 家族とともに技術の発展 → 技術の発展とともに
Verb dictionary form (the base form you'd look up in a dictionary) + とともに
増える → 増えるとともに鳴る → 鳴るとともに
A step further: Noun + であるとともに = "is ~, and at the same time is also ~."
・彼は医者であるとともに、作家でもある。(He is a doctor and also a writer.)
Easy mistakes
・It's very formal. Saying 友達とともにラーメンを食べた to a friend sounds like reading out an official document. In speech, use 友達と一緒に.
・In the "along with" usage, the second half must describe what changes, not just a fixed habit: ×年をとるとともに、毎日運動している　○年をとるとともに、運動する時間が増えた.
・Verbs always take the dictionary form, even for past events; the past tense goes at the end of the sentence: ×増えたとともに　○人口が増えるとともに、町がにぎやかになった.
・The particle before it is 「と」, not 「に」: 家族とともに, not 家族にともに.
・In books it's often written with kanji as と共に. Both spellings are correct.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
と一緒に = everyday, spoken "together": 家族と一緒に旅行した。(I traveled with my family.)
とともに = formal "together": 家族とともに旅行した。(Same meaning, but it reads like an essay or the news.)
Also, と一緒に can't mean "along with a change," so you can't say ×年齢と一緒に体力が落ちた.
につれて = only means "as (something changes)": 年をとるにつれて、体力が落ちてきた。(As I've gotten older, my stamina has declined.)
とともに = can also mean "as," in a more formal tone: 年をとるとともに、体力が落ちてきた。
The difference: につれて can't be used for "together" or "at the same time," while とともに covers all three.
Quick rule: for everyday "together," use と一緒に. For "as (something changes)," both につれて and とともに work, and the more formal it is, the more it leans toward とともに. For "together" or "at the same time" in a formal register, choose とともに.
n3-47:
The idea in one line
「〜ものだ」is like saying "that's just how it is" or "that's what you're supposed to do". It states a truth or common sense that everyone accepts, not your personal opinion. Its opposite, 「〜ものではない」, is the voice of an elder saying "you shouldn't ~" or "that's no way to behave", with a bit of a lecture in it.
When to use it
That's just how it isDescribes the nature of people or things, or how the world works. It often carries a sigh of "well, that's life."
・人は誰でも間違えるものだ。（Everyone makes mistakes. That's just human.）
・時間が経つのは早いものだ。（Time sure flies.）
That's what you should doSays what one "should do" according to social common sense.
・お年寄りには親切にするものだ。（You should be kind to the elderly.）
・人の話は最後まで聞くものだ。（You should listen to people until they finish.）
You shouldn'tUse 「〜ものではない」 to advise or scold someone.
・食べ物を粗末にするものではない。（You shouldn't waste food.）
Nostalgia for the pastWith 「た form + ものだ」 you talk about things you used to do often, with a feeling of "ah, those days...". It often appears with 「よく」.
・子供の頃は、よくこの川で遊んだものだ。（As a kid, I used to play by this river a lot.）
How to form it
Verb dictionary form: 間違える → 間違えるものだ
Verb ない form: 変わらない → 変わらないものだ
い-adjectives attach directly: 早い → 早いものだ
な-adjectives need な: 元気 → 元気なものだ
Nostalgia uses the た form: 遊んだ → 遊んだものだ
"Shouldn't" uses the dictionary form: 言う → 言うものではない
In casual speech it is often shortened to もんだ and もんじゃない: そんなこと言うもんじゃないよ。（You shouldn't say things like that, you know.）
Common mistakes
・ものだ states a widely accepted truth. You can't use it for your own plan on one particular occasion. For "I'm going to school tomorrow," just say 明日学校へ行きます, with no ものだ.
・「ないものだ」 and 「ものではない」 mean different things: 人は簡単には変わらないものだ means "people just don't change easily" (human nature), while 人の悪口を言うものではない means "you shouldn't speak ill of others" (advice).
・The nostalgic use is for things you did often in the past. It doesn't work for a one-time event: if you had ramen yesterday, say 昨日ラーメンを食べた, with no ものだ.
・ものではない is a scolding tone, so it sounds rude toward a boss or teacher. It's normally used by elders to younger people, or parents to children.
Telling it apart from similar forms
All of these mean "should," so look at whose viewpoint it is:
ものだ = social common sense says it should be this way, a general principle: 約束は守るものだ。（You're supposed to keep promises.）
べきだ = the speaker's own judgment that it should be done. It's more direct and stronger: あなたはこの約束を守るべきだ。（You should keep this promise.）
ことだ = giving advice to the person in front of you, "you'd better ~": 約束を守りたいなら、メモしておくことだ。（If you want to keep your promise, you'd better write it down.）
Quick test: for "people are supposed to..." use ものだ; for "I think you should..." use べきだ; for advice like "you'd better..." use ことだ. Also, ものだから gives a reason ("because..."), and it is a different thing from the ものだ here.
What to learn next
Two more patterns also state principles and advise people: 「〜べきだ・〜べきではない」 and 「〜ことだ」. Look at them next. Comparing all three side by side will make it clearer which one to use when.
n3-1:
The idea in one line
「〜において」is the formal "at / in ~". English does the same thing: in everyday speech you say "we had a meeting in Taipei," but in an official document it becomes "the meeting was held in Taipei." Japanese works alike: in daily speech you say 「台北で」, but in formal writing, news, or speeches it becomes 「台北において」. The meaning is still "at/in ~", just much more formal.
When to use it
WhereWhere an event or ceremony takes place. This is most common in news.
・開会式は台北において行われた。（The opening ceremony was held in Taipei.）
On what occasionA "setting" such as a meeting, interview, or match.
・面接において、一番大切なのは第一印象だ。（In an interview, the most important thing is the first impression.）
In which fieldA particular field or area.
・医療の分野において、AIの活用が進んでいる。（In the medical field, the use of AI is advancing.）
How to form it
It always follows a noun. What matters is what comes after:
An action or a full sentence follows → use において
京都で開催された → 京都において開催された（held in Kyoto）
A noun follows directly → use における. It works like "in" or "of" before a noun, the role 「での」 plays in casual speech.
日本での問題 → 日本における問題（problems in Japan）
・日本における外国人労働者の数は年々増えている。（The number of foreign workers in Japan is increasing every year.）
You can also add 「は」 or 「も」 after it for emphasis:
・この点においては、私も同じ意見です。（On this point, I share the same opinion.）
Common mistakes
・Don't use it for small everyday things: コンビニにおいてパンを買った sounds like an official document and feels odd. For your own daily life, just say コンビニでパンを買った.
・Switch to における when a noun follows: you can't say 「日本において経済」. Say 日本における経済.
・It only replaces the で meaning "where / on what occasion". The で of means or tools can't be swapped: はしで食べる (eat with chopsticks) can't become 「はしにおいて」.
・For "something exists somewhere" you use に, not で, so it can't become において either. Say 公園に子どもがいる.
Telling it apart from similar forms
で = works in speech and everyday situations: 会議で決まりました。（It was decided at the meeting.）
において = the formal way to say the same thing: 会議において決定されました。（It was decided at the meeting.）
について looks similar but means something completely different: "about ~", giving the content or topic. Look at this sentence, where both appear together:
・会議において、環境問題について話し合った。（At the meeting, we discussed environmental issues.）
「会議」 is where the discussion happened, and 「環境問題」 is what was discussed.
Quick test: if you'd say "at / in ~" in English, it's において. If you'd say "about / regarding ~", it's について.
What to learn next
The pattern of 「〜て」 before an action and 「〜る」 before a noun shows up in many grammar points, such as 〜に関して／〜に関する and 〜によって／〜による. Once you've got this one, those will be easy.
n3-12:
The idea in one line
「〜最中に」means "right in the middle of ~, when suddenly …". You're partway through something, busy with it, and then something else interrupts you or an accident happens. Think "in the middle of a presentation, the power went out" or "in the middle of an interview, my phone rang." What follows is usually something sudden that catches you off guard.
When to use it
Interrupted midwayThis is the most typical use.
・会議の最中に、電話が鳴った。(In the middle of the meeting, a phone rang.)
・シャワーを浴びている最中に、お湯が出なくなった。(Right in the middle of my shower, the hot water suddenly stopped.)
最中だAt the end of a sentence, it means "I'm in the middle of ~ right now." It's very common for answering the phone or politely turning someone down.
・今、食事の最中なので、あとでかけ直します。(I'm in the middle of a meal right now, so I'll call you back later.)
How to form it
Verbs: first change to the 「〜ている」 form, then add 最中に.
食べる → 食べている → 食べている最中に
話す → 話している最中に
Nouns: noun + の + 最中に. The noun has to be an activity that is in progress, like 会議, 試合, 授業 or 面接.
試合 → 試合の最中に
Common mistakes
・With verbs you must use the 「ている」 form: say 食べている最中に, not 食べる最中に.
・Don't drop the 「の」 after a noun: 授業の最中に, not 授業最中に.
・Here 「最中」 is read さいちゅう.
・It needs an action that is ongoing over a stretch of time. Actions that finish in an instant, like 着く and 始まる, can't take 最中に. Verbs that just describe a state, like いる and ある, don't work either.
・What follows is usually something sudden that interrupts. If you just want to say "during that time I did something," 最中に sounds odd.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
最中に = while you're in the middle of doing something, you're suddenly interrupted or something unexpected happens: 寝ている最中に、地震が起きた。 (While I was sleeping, an earthquake hit.)
間に = taking advantage of that period to get something done (it can be deliberate): 子どもが寝ている間に、部屋を片付けた。 (While the kids were asleep, I tidied up the room.)
If you changed the second sentence to 「寝ている最中に、部屋を片付けた」, it would sound off, because tidying a room isn't something that "suddenly pops up."
〜中 (for example 会議中) simply says "in progress" in a neutral way, and you often see it on door signs and notices. 〜の最中 is stronger and stresses "right in the thick of it, at the busiest point."
Quick test: for "in the middle of ~, suddenly …" use 最中に. For "taking advantage of the time while ~, I did …" use 間に.
What to learn next
To make it even stronger, you can say 「真っ最中」: 今、テストの真っ最中だ。 (I'm right in the middle of a test at this very moment.)
n3-14:
The idea in one line
「～間に」means "while ~ (something happened)" or "while ~ (I got something done)". Picture a period of time as a line. 「間に」 plants a flag on that line: at some moment within that period, something happened, or you finished something.
When to use it
Happened while you weren't lookingSomething happened while you were away or not paying attention.
・留守の間に宅配便が届いた。(A package was delivered while I was out.)
・知らない間に、もう夜の12時になっていた。(Before I knew it, it was already midnight.)
Getting something done in that timeYou use a stretch of time to finish something.
・子どもが寝ている間に、部屋を掃除した。(I cleaned the room while the kids were asleep.)
・日本にいる間に、富士山に登りたい。(I want to climb Mt. Fuji while I'm in Japan.)
How to form it
What comes before it must be a period of time or a continuing state.
Verbs: for actions like "sleep, eat, watch," you usually use the ている form (～ている), which turns them into a "be in the middle of ~" stretch of time. いる and ある are already states, so you can use them as they are. The ない form (～ない) also works.
寝る → 寝ている間に日本にいる → 日本にいる間に知らない → 知らない間に
Nouns: put 「の」 in between.
留守 → 留守の間に夏休み → 夏休みの間に
Common mistakes
・You must add 「の」 after a noun: say 留守の間に, not 「留守間に」.
・Here 「間」 is read あいだ. The 「かん」 in 一週間 is a different reading, so don't mix them up.
・English just says "while ~" for both, but in Japanese it depends on what comes next. If the second part keeps going the whole time, you don't add に. So don't follow 「間に」 with 「ずっと～」: 寝ている間に、ずっと雨が降っていた is wrong, and you need to drop the に.
・Even when the whole sentence is about the past, the first part is usually still 「ている間に」. Put the past 「た」 only at the end: 寝ている間に地震があった。 (There was an earthquake while I was sleeping.)
Telling it apart from similar patterns
All of these are about summer vacation:
・夏休みの間、ずっとアルバイトをしていた。(I worked part-time the whole summer vacation.)
・夏休みの間に、運転免許を取った。(Sometime during summer vacation, I got my driver's license.)
・夏休みのうちに、宿題を終わらせたい。(I want to finish my homework before summer vacation ends.)
間 (without に) = you do something continuously through that whole period, often with 「ずっと」 after it.
間に = at some moment within that period, something happened or got done.
うちに = adds a feeling of "while there's still time", implying that once the period is over, it won't be so easy.
There's also 最中に = you're right in the middle of something and of all times you get interrupted: シャワーを浴びている最中に、電話が鳴った。 (I was in the middle of my shower when, of all times, the phone rang.)
Quick test: if what follows is "keeps doing ~ the whole time," use 間. If it's "something happened / got done," use 間に. If you mean "hurry up while you still can," use うちに.
n3-4:
The idea in one line
「によって」 works a lot like English “by”, “through” or “depending on”. Put a noun in front of it to say that something was done by it, caused by it, or depends on it. In English you'll translate it as “through”, “because of”, “depending on” or “by”, depending on context. It's especially common in news, explanatory writing and formal situations.
How to connect it
It always attaches directly to a noun, with no 「の」. What comes after decides which form you use:
A verb or a full clause follows → によって: 台風によって電車が止まった。 (The trains stopped because of the typhoon.)
A noun follows directly → による: 台風による停電 (a power outage caused by the typhoon)
In writing you'll also see 「により」. It means the same as によって, just more formal.
The patterns you'll hear most
Varies by ～“It depends on ～; it's different for each ～.” It's almost always followed by words meaning “different”, such as 違う, 異なる or 変わる.
・地域によって食文化が異なる。 (Food culture differs by region.)
・人によって考え方が違う。 (Everyone thinks differently.)
Cause“Because of ～; caused by ～.” The tone is objective, like a news report.
・台風による停電が続いている。 (The power outage caused by the typhoon is still continuing.)
・事故によって電車が遅れています。 (The trains are delayed because of an accident.)
Means / method“Through ～.” This is the more formal way to say it.
・この問題は話し合いによって解決した。 (This problem was resolved through discussion.)
The “by whom” in passive sentencesUsed to say who made a work, an invention or a building.
・この小説は有名な作家によって書かれた。 (This novel was written by a famous author.)
・電話はベルによって発明された。 (The telephone was invented by Bell.)
によってはAdd 「は」 and the meaning becomes “some ～ will…”. You're picking out just some of them.
・店によって値段が違う。 (Prices differ from shop to shop.)
・店によっては、カードが使えない。 (Some shops don't accept cards.)
Common mistakes
・Passives don't always use によって. In everyday “scolded by someone” or “told by someone”, use 「に」: 母に叱られた。 (I was scolded by my mom.) Saying 「母によって叱られた」 sounds odd. によって is reserved for “who made something”.
・For everyday means, just use 「で」: バスで行く. You don't say 「バスによって行く」. The “through” of によって is formal and fits bigger things like methods and systems.
・による must be followed by a noun. If a clause follows, go back to によって. Don't write 「台風による電車が止まった」.
・“Varies by ～” and “some ～ will…” differ only by 「は」, but the meaning changes. Check whether it's there.
Telling it apart from similar forms
All of these can mean “because of the typhoon”, but the tone is very different:
によって = states the cause objectively, with no emotion: 台風によって電車が止まった。 (The trains stopped because of the typhoon.)
せいで = blames it, with a complaining tone: 台風のせいで旅行に行けなかった。 (It's the typhoon's fault that I couldn't go on the trip.)
おかげで = thanks to it, with a tone of relief or gratitude: 台風のおかげで学校が休みになった。 (Thanks to the typhoon, school was cancelled.)
With a noun, せいで and おかげで need 「の」 before them (雨のせいで), while によって attaches directly with no 「の」 (雨によって).
Quick tip: use によって to state a cause flatly, like a news report; use せいで to complain; use おかげで when you feel grateful or relieved.
n3-6:
The idea in one line
「〜おかげで」 means “thanks to ～” or “luckily there was ～”. Put the cause that brought a good result in front, then state that good result. There's a touch of gratitude in the tone.
When to use it
Thanking someoneThings went well because someone helped.
・先生のおかげで、合格できました。 (Thanks to my teacher, I passed.)
・友達が手伝ってくれたおかげで、早く終わった。 (Thanks to my friend's help, it was finished quickly.)
A good causeIt doesn't have to be a person. Weather, surroundings or things all work, as long as they brought a good result.
・この薬を飲んだおかげで、熱が下がった。 (Thanks to taking this medicine, my fever went down.)
・駅が近いおかげで、通勤が楽です。 (Luckily the station is close, so commuting is easy.)
How to connect it
Nouns: add 「の」 in between.
先輩 → 先輩のおかげで
Verbs: attach directly to the plain form (the dictionary form, the た-form and so on, without ます). The good result has usually already happened, so the た-form is the most common.
頑張った → 頑張ったおかげで
い-adjectives: attach directly.
近い → 近いおかげで
よかった → よかったおかげで
な-adjectives: use 「な」 in the present and 「だった」 in the past.
静か → 静かなおかげで
元気だった → 元気だったおかげで
The patterns you'll hear most
おかげさまでWhen someone asks how you are, you politely answer “thanks to you”. You can say it even if the other person didn't actually do anything for you.
・お元気ですか。——おかげさまで、元気です。 (How are you? — Thanks to you, I'm well.)
〜のおかげですPlaced at the end of a sentence to give someone the credit.
・合格できたのは、先生のおかげです。 (I passed all thanks to my teacher.)
SarcasmJust like English “thanks a lot”, you can use it sarcastically to needle someone when the result was actually bad.
・君のおかげで、全部やり直しだよ。 (Thanks a lot to you, we have to redo everything.)
Common mistakes
・A noun must be followed by 「の」: it's 先生のおかげで, not 先生おかげで.
・A な-adjective in the present can't take 「だ」: it's 静かなおかげで, not 静かだおかげで.
・What follows must be a result that has already happened or is certain to happen. It can't be an invitation or a request, like “let's ～” or “please ～”.
・English “because” is very broad, but not every “because” can become おかげで. To simply explain a cause (for example, the match was cancelled because it rained), use から or ので. Using おかげで would sound as if you were happy the match was cancelled.
Telling it apart from similar forms
おかげで = thanks to ～, and the result is good, with gratitude:
雨が降ったおかげで、涼しくなった。 (Thanks to the rain, it got cooler.)
せいで = it's ～'s fault, and the result is bad, with complaint or blame:
雨が降ったせいで、試合が中止になった。 (Because of the rain, the match was cancelled.)
The two connect in exactly the same way. The only difference is whether you feel grateful or want to complain about the result.
Quick tip: use おかげで for “thanks to / luckily there was”; use せいで for “it's ～'s fault”; use から or ので when you're just stating a cause with no good or bad feeling.
n3-10:
The idea in one line
ところ originally means "place", but here it means "a point in time". Think of an action as having three stages: not started yet, halfway through, just finished. ところだ tells the listener which stage you're in right now, much like English "about to…", "in the middle of…" and "just finished…".
How to attach it: the form before it picks the stage
About to doDictionary form (the base form you find in a dictionary) + ところだ. The action has not started yet, but it's about to.
・今から出かけるところです。(I'm just about to head out.)
・A：もうご飯食べた？　B：ううん、これから食べるところ。(A: Have you eaten yet? B: Not yet, I'm just about to.)
In the middle ofて form + いる + ところだ. The action is halfway through and not finished yet.
・今シャワーを浴びているところだから、あとでかけ直すね。(I'm in the shower right now, so I'll call you back later.)
・今調べているところなので、少々お待ちください。(I'm looking into it right now, so please wait a moment.)
Just finishedた form (past tense) + ところだ. The action ended just a moment ago.
・たった今、家に帰ってきたところです。(I just got home this very second.)
・会議がちょうど終わったところです。(The meeting has just ended.)
It's clearest to see all three with the same verb:
食べる → 食べるところ (about to eat)
食べる → 食べているところ (in the middle of eating)
食べる → 食べたところ (just finished eating)
With seniors and customers, say ところです; with friends you can just say ところ. In casual speech, ているところ often shrinks to てるところ.
When to use it
It shows up most when someone asks "what are you doing right now?", on phone calls, and when replying to messages, to explain your situation at this moment. It often appears with これから and 今から (about to), 今 (in the middle of), and たった今 and ちょうど (just). When you see these words, you know which stage is meant.
Easy mistakes
・Dictionary form + ところ means not started yet. 今食べるところ means "I'm about to eat", not "I'm eating". For "I'm eating", say 食べているところ.
・ているところ only works with actions that are really in motion. Verbs that describe a state, like 住んでいる and 知っている, can't be used this way: you can't say 「住んでいるところだ」.
・たところ means really just a moment ago. You can't say 「先月日本に来たところだ」, because last month doesn't count as "just now". Use たばかり instead (see below).
・Only ところだ at the end of a sentence has this meaning. 「〜たところ、…」 with a comma, continuing the sentence, is a different grammar point ("I did ~, and then found that…"). Don't mix them up.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
たところだ and たばかりだ both translate as "just did ~". The difference is how recent "just" really is.
たところだ: the moment is right now, a few minutes ago at most.
今、駅に着いたところです。 (I just arrived at the station.)
たばかりだ: the speaker feels it hasn't been long, which could be days or even months.
先月日本に来たばかりです。 (I only came to Japan last month.)
Also, たばかり often carries a feeling of "I only just ~, so / and yet…": 買ったばかりなのに、もう壊れた。 (I only just bought it and it's already broken.)
Quick test: if you can swap in "right this very moment", use たところ. If you mean "not long ago, still feels fresh", use たばかり. When unsure, if it was before today, use たばかり.
What to learn next
Dictionary form + ところだった = almost did ~ (luckily it didn't happen): もう少しで電車に乗り遅れるところだった。 (I almost missed the train.)
n3-11:
The idea in one line
「〜たばかり」 means "only just ~" or "it hasn't been long since ~". The key is that you feel the time has been short, so it often carries a mood like "I'm not used to it yet" or "again already?".
・日本に来たばかりで、まだ慣れない。(I've only just come to Japan, so I'm not used to it yet.)
How to attach it
Always attach it to the verb's た form (past tense, like 食べた and 行った), then add ばかり.
食べる → 食べた → 食べたばかり
買う → 買った → 買ったばかり
来る → 来た → 来たばかり
The forms you'll hear most
At sentence end〜たばかりだ / 〜たばかりです
・先月結婚したばかりです。(I only got married last month.)
More to say〜たばかりで gives a reason: "since I only just ~, …"
・起きたばかりで、頭がぼんやりしている。(I only just woke up, so my head is still foggy.)
Modifying a noun〜たばかりの + noun
・これは買ったばかりの靴です。(These are shoes I just bought.)
Complaint, surprise〜たばかりなのに means "I only just ~, and yet already…"
・さっき食べたばかりなのに、もうお腹がすいた。(I only just ate, and I'm already hungry again.)
Easy mistakes
・The form before it must be the た form. Writing 来るばかり or 食べるばかり gives a different meaning (explained below).
・To modify a noun, you need の: it's 買ったばかりの靴, not 買ったばかり靴.
・How long "just" lasts depends on your feeling: 去年入社したばかりです (I only joined the company last year) is perfectly fine, even though it was a year ago.
・Among friends it's often shortened to たばっか: 今起きたばっか。 (I just woke up.)
Telling it apart from similar patterns
〜たところだ (n3-10 ところだ) also means "just ~", but it points to the exact moment the action ended, really seconds or minutes ago.
・今、駅に着いたところです。 (I've just arrived at the station.)
・今、駅に着いたばかりです。 (I only just arrived at the station.)
Both work for this kind of "just now" situation. But once the time stretches out, only たばかり works:
・先月引っ越したばかりです。 (I only moved last month.) ○
・先月引っ越したところです。 ×
If the form before ばかり changes, the meaning changes:
Dictionary form + ばかり mostly means "keeps changing in one direction (more and more ~)", for example 物価は上がるばかりだ。 (Prices just keep going up.) It can also mean "does nothing but ~", for example 彼女は泣くばかりで何も言わない。 (She just keeps crying and says nothing.)
て form + ばかりいる = always doing only one thing: 弟はゲームをしてばかりいる。 (My little brother does nothing but play video games.)
Quick test: look at what comes before ばかり. The た form means "only just ~", the dictionary form means "keeps ~ (more and more ~ / nothing but ~)", and the て form means "always ~". If the sentence mentions a longer time, like "last month" or "last year", use たばかり for "just ~", not たところ.
n3-18:
The idea in one line
「〜としたら」means "if it really were the case that…". You take something uncertain, or even unlikely, and suppose it's true, then say "what would happen" or "what I'd want to do." It's like a friend saying, "Okay, hypothetically, say you won the lottery…"
When to use it
Pure hypothesisUse it for things that are unlikely or haven't happened. It often appears with もし or 仮に ("suppose").
・もし宝くじが当たったとしたら、何に使う？(If you won the lottery, what would you spend it on?)
・一週間休めるとしたら、どこに行きたい？(If you could take a week off, where would you want to go?)
Reasoning from what you heardYou take what someone said, or news you heard, as true for now, and draw a conclusion from it.
・彼の話が本当だとすれば、大変なことだ。(If what he says is true, this is serious.)
At the start of a sentenceAdd だ in front to get だとしたら or だとすると. It means "in that case," and you continue from what the other person just said.
・A：明日は台風が来るらしいよ。(I hear a typhoon is coming tomorrow.)
・B：だとすると、旅行は無理だね。(In that case, the trip is probably off.)
How to connect it
Verbs and い-adjectives attach directly:
行く → 行くとしたら当たった → 当たったとしたら高い → 高いとしたら
Nouns and な-adjectives need だ first:
雨 → 雨だとしたら暇 → 暇だとしたら
All three forms, としたら, とすれば and とすると, connect the same way.
Choosing among the three
としたら: the most conversational and the easiest to use. It's the most natural choice when what follows is your own wish or plan, like "I want to…" or "I'll…".
とすれば・とすると: these have more of a "reasoning" feel, and are often followed by a judgment like 〜だろう, 〜はずだ or 〜必要がある.
・明日雨だとすれば、運動会は延期だろう。(If it rains tomorrow, the sports day will probably be postponed.)
Common mistakes
・Don't forget だ after nouns and な-adjectives: say 雨だとしたら, not 「雨としたら」.
・If you attach としたら directly to a noun without だ, it takes a different meaning, "from the standpoint of…": 親としたら、心配だろう。 (From a parent's standpoint, they'd probably be worried.)
・Don't use it for things that will definitely happen. "Call me when you get home" is 家に着いたら電話して. If you said 「着いたとしたら」, it would sound like you doubt the person will make it home.
・とすると doesn't combine well with "I want to…" or "please…". In those cases, switch to としたら.
Telling it apart from similar forms
たら = the ordinary "if / after…", where the thing may really happen:
宝くじが当たったら、車を買う。 (If I win the lottery, I'll buy a car.)
としたら = specifically stresses "this is only a hypothesis":
宝くじが当たったとしたら、車を買う。 (Suppose I really did win, I'd buy a car.)
For things that are sure to happen, only たら works: 家に着いたら連絡するね。 (I'll get in touch once I'm home.)
Quick test: if you could say "suppose that…" or "in the event that…" in English, use としたら. If it's just "once/after…, then…", use たら.
n3-19:
The idea in one line
「〜たところ」means "I did X, and as a result I found out…". You first do something (call and ask, look something up, try something out), and only then learn a result. For example: "I called the shop to ask, and it turned out they were sold out."
The ところ here has nothing to do with "place." Just think of it as a switch that introduces the result.
How to connect it
Verb た-form + ところ.
聞く → 聞いた → 聞いたところ
調べる → 調べた → 調べたところ
電話する → 電話した → 電話したところ
The sentence has two halves: the first is what you did, and the second is what you found out or what happened after doing it.
When to use it
Found out by askingInformation you get after asking someone or calling to check.
・店に電話したところ、もう売り切れだった。(I called the shop, and it turned out they were already sold out.)
・先生に相談したところ、いいアドバイスをもらえた。(I talked it over with my teacher and got some good advice.)
Found out by tryingThe result after looking into something or trying it out.
・詳しく調べたところ、原因がわかった。(I looked into it carefully and found the cause.)
・この薬を飲んだところ、熱が下がった。(I took this medicine, and my fever went down.)
The tone is fairly formal. You'll see it a lot in reports, business emails and news. When chatting with friends, people mostly just use 「〜たら」.
Common mistakes
・The second half is something that has already happened or become known, so it's mostly in the past tense. It can't be followed by what you're about to do, or by a request or command:
×調べたところ、先生に聞きます。
○調べてから、先生に聞きます。 (I'll look it up first, then ask my teacher.)
・The first half is usually something you did on purpose. Things that happen naturally, like rain, don't work well there:
×雨が降ったところ、涼しくなった。
○雨が降ったら、涼しくなった。 (After it rained, it got cooler.)
・The point is "the result you discovered after doing something," so the pattern itself doesn't mean "because X, Y." Sometimes the two halves happen to be cause and effect (medicine → fever down), and sometimes they aren't (calling the shop didn't cause the sell-out; it just let you find out). Both are fine.
Telling it apart from similar forms
たところ = you did something, and a result follows in the same sentence:
駅員に聞いたところ、電車は遅れているそうだ。 (I asked a station attendant, and he said the train is delayed.)
たところだ = you just now finished doing it, and the sentence ends there:
今、駅員に聞いたところだ。 (I just asked a station attendant.)
たら = can also mean "I did X and found that…", but it's more casual and has a wider range of uses:
駅員に聞いたら、電車が遅れてるって。 (I asked a station attendant, and he said the train is delayed.)
Quick test: if 「ところ」 is followed by a comma and another clause giving a result, it's たところ. If the sentence stops at 「ところだ」, it means "just finished." Use たところ for results in formal situations, and たら when chatting with friends.
What to study next
Go back and compare the three time points of 〜ところだ (about to do, in the middle of doing, just did). That way you won't mix it up with たところ.
n3-15:
The idea in one line
「〜ついでに」 means "while I'm at it" or "on the way". A is something you were going to do anyway, and since you're already doing it, you take the chance to do B too. For example, "I'm going downstairs to take out the trash, so I'll grab the mail while I'm at it": taking out the trash is A, and getting the mail is B.
How to form it
There are three patterns. What comes before ついでに is always the thing you were going to do anyway:
Noun + の + ついでに　買い物 → 買い物のついでに
Verb dictionary form + ついでに　行く → 行くついでに
Verb た-form + ついでに　来た → 来たついでに
The noun has to stand for an activity, such as 買い物, 散歩, 出張 or 旅行.
Dictionary form or た-form?
Dictionary formA hasn't happened yet, and you're about to head out to do it. You do B on the side. It's often used to ask someone a favor.
・コンビニに行くついでに、お茶を買ってきてくれる？(When you go to the convenience store, could you pick up some tea for me too?)
・出かけるついでに、ゴミを出してくるね。(I'll take out the trash on my way out, okay?)
た-formYou're already there, or A has already happened, and you use the chance to do B.
・京都に来たついでに、奈良にも行ってみた。(Since I was already in Kyoto, I went over to Nara too.)
・本屋に寄ったついでに、ノートも買った。(While I was at the bookstore, I bought a notebook too.)
Noun のThe simplest pattern, and very handy in daily life.
・買い物のついでに、銀行に寄った。(I went shopping and stopped by the bank while I was out.)
・出張のついでに、大阪の友達に会った。(While I was on a business trip, I met up with a friend in Osaka.)
What you'll hear most often
ついでに can also stand alone at the start of a sentence, simply meaning "while you're at it." A is already clear from context, so you don't need to repeat it.
・あ、ついでに牛乳も買ってきて。(Oh, and grab some milk while you're at it.)
Common mistakes
・The main task goes first and the side task goes second. If you swap them, the meaning changes: the other task becomes the real purpose.
・What comes before it must be an action, not a bare place. You can't say 「駅のついでに」; say 駅に行くついでに.
・Both A and B must be things you choose to do yourself. Things that happen naturally, like rain, don't fit. You can't say 「雨が降ったついでに」.
・English "by the way" adds extra information. For that, Japanese usually uses ちなみに, not ついでに.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
"While I'm at it" and "while doing…" can blur together in English, but Japanese keeps them clearly apart. Take the same train station scene:
ついでに = you use the chance of doing A to do one more thing. The two things don't have to happen at the same time: 駅に行くついでに、手紙を出した。(I mailed a letter on my way to the station.)
ながら = two things happen at the same time: 音楽を聞きながら、駅まで歩いた。(I walked to the station while listening to music.)
Quick test: if you're "doing one more thing while you're at it," use ついでに. If you're doing two things at once, use ながら.
n3-16:
The idea in one line
「〜てからでないと」 means "only after ~ can you ~" or "unless you ~ first, you can't ~". Think "you need a ticket before you can enter" or "wash your hands before you eat." The point is that the order can't be reversed, and the first thing must be finished first.
Break it down and it makes sense
It's really three pieces put together:
て-form (having done ~) + から (after) + でないと (if it's not the case)
Together it means "if it's not after having done ~," in other words, "without doing ~ first."
How to form it
Put the verb in the て-form, then add 「からでないと」 directly.
食べる → 食べて → 食べてからでないと
する → して → してからでないと
聞く → 聞いて → 聞いてからでないと
What comes after it
The second half is almost always a negative: "not allowed," "can't," "no way". Typical endings are できない, わからない, だめだ, 無理だ, and the negative potential form of a verb.
・手を洗ってからでないと、おやつはだめだよ。(No snacks unless you wash your hands first.)
・実際に見てからでないと、買うかどうか決められない。(I can't decide whether to buy it until I've seen it in person.)
・お金を払ってからでないと、商品はお渡しできません。(We can't hand over the product until payment has been made.)
What you'll hear most often
からでないとThe standard form, fine in both speech and writing.
からでなければMore formal and stiff. You often see it in notices and instructions.
からじゃないとThe casual spoken version between friends.
・宿題やってからじゃないと、ゲームはできないよ。(You can't play video games until you've done your homework.)
Common mistakes
・The second half can't be a positive "you can" sentence. 予約してからでないと、入れます is wrong. To say "make a reservation, then go in," just use the plain 予約してから入ります.
・Don't drop the 「で」 in the middle. 「てからないと」 is wrong.
・Get the て-form right: 行く becomes 行って and 書く becomes 書いて. One mistake here breaks the whole sentence.
・It carries a sense of "rule" or "condition." When speaking to customers, use polite endings such as できません and お渡しできません.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
One situation: you need to read the contract before signing.
てから = simply states the order, A then B: 内容を確認してから、サインします。(I'll check the contents, then sign.)
てからでないと = stresses that you must do A first, or B is impossible: 内容を確認してからでないと、サインできません。(I can't sign until I've checked the contents.)
た上で = you finish A and then do B based on it. More formal and careful: 内容を確認した上で、サインします。(I'll sign after confirming the contents.)
Quick test: if what follows is "can do / will do," use てから or た上で. If what follows is "not allowed / can't," and you want to stress "you have to ~ first," use てからでないと.
What to learn next
Move on to 「〜上で」 (n3-23). It's very common in formal settings for saying "first ~, then ~": よく考えた上で、決めてください。(Please decide after thinking it over carefully.)
n3-22:
The idea in one line
「〜以上（は）」means "since…, then…" or "now that…, then…". You first state something that is already settled, then follow with "so I definitely have to…" or "so I should…". It's like saying, "You already said yes, so you have to follow through." It carries a sense of "given this, I'm taking responsibility."
How to form it
Verbs: attach directly to the plain form (the form without ます).
約束した → 約束した以上 (now that we've promised)
やる → やる以上 (since I'm going to do it)
来ない → 来ない以上 (since they're not coming)
Nouns and な-adjectives: you need to add 「である」 in between. You can't attach directly.
学生 → 学生である以上 (since you're a student)
プロ → プロである以上 (since you're a professional)
The following 「は」 is optional. Adding it makes the tone a bit stronger, but the meaning is the same.
What comes after it
The key is the second half: it must express the speaker's resolve, obligation, or judgment, not simply describe something that happened.
I will… (resolve)
・引き受けた以上は、最後までやります。 (Since I've taken this on, I'll see it through to the end.)
・やる以上は、一番を目指したい。 (If I'm going to do it, I want to aim for first place.)
Should… / must… (obligation)
・日本に住んでいる以上、日本の法律を守らなければならない。 (As long as you live in Japan, you must obey Japanese law.)
・プロである以上、言い訳はできない。 (Since you're a professional, you can't make excuses.)
Then all we can do is… (judgment)
・本人が来ない以上、この話は進められない。 (If the person themselves isn't coming, we can't move this discussion forward.)
With the た form, it means "it has already happened, so…". With the dictionary form, it means "since I'm going to do this / since this is my role, so…".
Common mistakes
・Nouns need である: it's 学生である以上, not 「学生な以上」. Writing 学生以上 directly would be read as a different meaning (student level or above).
・The second half can't be just a plain fact. You can't say 「雨が降った以上、試合が中止になった」, because "the game was cancelled" is just something that happened, not a resolve or a judgment.
・Don't mix it up with the other meanings of 以上: 三人以上 means "three people or more", and 以上です said at the end of a report means "That's all."
・The tone is fairly serious and resolute. It's often used for topics like responsibility, promises, and roles. Using it for small matters sounds a bit exaggerated.
How it differs from similar patterns
The one most easily confused with it is から, which simply gives a reason.
約束したから、行きます。 (Because we made a promise, I'll go.): just explains the reason.
約束した以上、行かなければならない。 (Now that we've promised, I have to go.): stresses "this is settled, and I have a responsibility."
Also, 雨が降ったから、試合が中止になった。 (Because it rained, the game was cancelled.) works with から, but not with 以上, because what follows is just an event.
Quick test: if what follows is a resolve or judgment like "I must / I should / all we can do is…", use 以上. If you're just stating a cause and its result, use から.
What to learn next
It often appears together with べきだ: 約束した以上、守るべきだ。 (Since we promised, we should keep it.) Later you'll also meet からには and 上は, which mean almost the same thing. 上は is more formal and more written in style.
n3-23:
The idea in one line
「〜上で」has two meanings, and the form before it tells you which one:
After the た form: "do ～ properly first, and then…", as in "decide after talking it over."
After the dictionary form (the base form you find in a dictionary): "in the process of doing ～", as in "when living in Japan, keigo is important."
How to form it
① Do it first, then…た form + 上で / noun + の + 上で
相談する → 相談した上で確認 → 確認の上で
・よく考えた上で、返事します。 (I'll give you my answer after thinking it over carefully.)
・家族とよく相談した上で、転職を決めた。 (I decided to change jobs after talking it over thoroughly with my family.)
The point is that the first action is a necessary preparation, and only once it's done do you move on to the second. The second part often uses actions like 決める, 申し込む, and 返事する, which involve making decisions or handling procedures.
② In the matter of ～dictionary form + 上で / noun + の + 上で
生活する → 生活する上で仕事 → 仕事の上で
・日本で生活する上で、敬語は大切だ。 (When living in Japan, keigo is important.)
・この本は日本語を勉強する上で役に立つ。 (This book is useful when studying Japanese.)
・仕事の上での付き合いは大切です。 (Relationships in the workplace are important.)
What follows is mostly an evaluation: 大切だ, 必要だ, 欠かせない, 役に立つ, 注意が必要だ. When a noun follows, change the で to での, as in 仕事の上での付き合い above.
How you'll most often see it
On notices, forms, and store instructions you'll often see 「ご + noun + の上」, with the で frequently dropped. It's a very polite, written-style expression.
・内容をご確認の上、サインしてください。 (Please sign after confirming the contents.)
Common mistakes
・Use the wrong form and the meaning changes: 相談した上で means "after talking it over", while 相談する上で means "in the matter of talking it over" (e.g. 相談する上で大切なこと = what's important when consulting someone). To say "after doing ～, then…", always use the た form.
・① isn't a casual "and then". ご飯を食べた上で、テレビを見た sounds odd. For everyday sequences, 〜てから is enough.
・Here 「上」 is read うえ. There's also 仕事上, attached directly to a noun and read しごとじょう. It means about the same as 仕事の上で, but the spelling and reading differ, so don't mix them up.
・Don't write it as 「上に」. 〜上に means "not only ～ but also ～", which is a different grammar point.
How it differs from similar patterns
た上で vs てから
家族と相談してから決めます。 (I'll talk with my family first, then decide: simply states the order.)
家族と相談した上で決めます。 (I'll talk it over properly with my family and decide based on that: stresses that you've seriously done this step.)
てから works in any situation. た上で is more formal and used for important decisions.
る上で vs ために
日本で働くために、日本語を勉強しています。 (I'm studying Japanese in order to work in Japan.)
日本で働く上で、日本語は欠かせません。 (When working in Japan, Japanese is indispensable.)
Both can come out as "to…" in English ("To work in Japan, you need Japanese"), but ために is followed by what you do for that purpose, while る上で is followed by what's needed or important for that activity.
Quick test: to say "do ～ properly first, then…", use た上で. To say "when doing ～, what matters is…", use る上で. If what follows is "I do something (for that goal)", use ために.
n3-27:
The idea in one line
「〜をはじめ」means "starting with ~" or "~ and others, all of which…". You name the most representative, best-known item first, then bring in the rest of the same group. It's like introducing Taiwanese street food: you start with "bubble tea," then add "beef noodle soup, fried chicken cutlet, and so on."
How to connect it
Only a noun can come before it. をはじめ and をはじめとして mean the same thing; adding として makes it more formal and complete.
東京 → 東京をはじめ社長 → 社長をはじめとして
If you want to attach a noun directly afterward, use をはじめとする＋noun: 寿司をはじめとする日本料理 (Japanese food, with sushi as the leading example).
How you'll usually hear it
Giving a representativeName the most famous one first, then say there are many more.
・日本には、東京をはじめ、大きな都市がたくさんある。 (Japan has many big cities, starting with Tokyo.)
The top-ranking person leadsIt goes from the person at the very top to everyone else. You hear it a lot at companies and ceremonies.
・社長をはじめ、社員全員が会議に出た。 (Everyone attended the meeting, from the company president to all the employees.)
をはじめとするUsed as a modifier, with a noun right after it.
・寿司をはじめとする日本料理は、海外でも人気だ。 (Japanese food, sushi first among it, is popular overseas too.)
Common mistakes
・Put the item that is most representative, most famous, or highest in rank first. 社員をはじめ、社長も参加した sounds odd because the order is backwards. Say 社長をはじめ、社員も参加した.
・You must follow it with "and others." It often pairs with や, など, 多くの, 全員, and も. If you're only talking about one thing, you can't use it.
・The はじめ here does not mean "beginning" in time. "Starting in September" is 9月から, not 9月をはじめ.
・The tone is fairly formal, common in news, guided tours, and speeches. When chatting with friends, 京都とか奈良とか sounds more natural.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
を中心に also puts one thing first, but the meaning is different. Look at the same rain:
東京をはじめ、関東の各地で雨が降った。 (It rained across the Kanto area, Tokyo included.)
→ Everywhere got rain; Tokyo is just named first.
東京を中心に雨が降った。 (It rained centered on Tokyo.)
→ The rain was concentrated around Tokyo, which is the core, and it thins out the farther you go.
Quick rule: to say "~ and all these others…," use をはじめ; to say "the focus or core is ~," use を中心に.
n3-31:
The idea in one line
「〜ほど」means "to the extent that…" or "so much that…". Instead of just saying "very," you throw out a picture and let the listener feel how extreme it is. It's like English "tired to death" or "laughed until I cried"; in Japanese that's 死ぬほど疲れた and 涙が出るほど笑った.
First, get the sentence order
In English we often say "I was exhausted" first, then "to death." Japanese tends to go the other way around: first the picture, then what it describes.
【picture】＋ほど＋【what it's like】
・涙が出るほど感動した。 (I was moved to tears.)
・眠れないほど楽しみにしていた。 (I was looking forward to it so much I couldn't sleep.)
How to connect it
Verbs: dictionary form or ない form, then just add ほど.
涙が出る → 涙が出るほど眠れない → 眠れないほど
い-adjectives: just add ほど.
痛い → 痛いほど
な-adjectives: add な first, then ほど.
不思議 → 不思議なほど
Nouns: just add ほど.
山 → 山ほど
How you'll usually hear it
死ぬほどVery common in speech. It means "like crazy," not that someone is actually dying.
・このラーメン、死ぬほどおいしい。 (This ramen is insanely good.)
山ほどSo many it piles up like a mountain, meaning "a ton."
・宿題が山ほどある。 (I have a mountain of homework.)
痛いほどわかるYou understand so well it hurts, meaning "I totally get it."
・その気持ち、痛いほどわかるよ。 (I totally understand how you feel.)
ほどだYou can also put it at the end of a sentence: state the situation first, then add the exaggerated degree last.
・寒くて、手が動かないほどだった。 (It was so cold that my hands wouldn't move.)
Common mistakes
・Don't follow English word order: say 涙が出るほど感動した, not "感動したほど涙が出る."
・Don't forget the な with な-adjectives: it's 不思議なほど, not 不思議ほど.
・When ほど follows a quantity, the meaning changes: 3時間ほど待った means "I waited about 3 hours." Here it means "about," not exaggeration.
・With a negative, it's a different usage too: 今年の夏は去年ほど暑くない means "This summer isn't as hot as last year." It's a comparison, not "hot to the point of…"
Telling it apart from similar patterns
ほど vs. くらい: for "extreme degree," they're mostly interchangeable.
涙が出るほど笑った。／涙が出るくらい笑った。 (Both mean "I laughed until I cried.")
くらい is more casual, and ほど is a little more formal.
But for a low degree, "just a small thing," only くらい works:
名前くらい自分で書いて。 (At least write your own name.)
You can't swap in ほど here, because ほど pushes toward "extreme."
ほど vs. ば〜ほど: 練習すればするほど上手になる means "the more you practice, the better you get." It describes two things changing together, which is different from the "to the extent that" meaning here.
Quick rule: to say "so extreme that…," both ほど and くらい work; to say "a small thing like this, at least…," only くらい works; when you see 「～ば～ほど」, it means "the more ~, the more ~."
n3-25:
The gist in one line
The 限 in に限り and に限って means “limit,” so the idea is narrowing the scope down to just this one thing. It has two very different uses. One is the notice-board “limited to ～”. The other is the everyday complaint “of all ～, it had to be ～”, like saying in English, “Of course the light turns red just when I'm in a hurry.”
How to attach it
It goes after a noun.
A noun attaches directly: 本日 → 本日に限り
To say “at times when ～” or “on days when ～,” first finish the phrase with a verb plus とき or 日, then attach it:
急いでいる → add とき → 急いでいるときに限って
傘を持っていない → add 日 → 傘を持っていない日に限って
When to use it
Limited to ～You'll often see this on store promotions, tickets, and rules. It sounds formal and is mostly written as に限り. It means “only within this range.”
・先着100名様に限り、特典をプレゼントします。(A special gift for the first 100 customers only.)
・このチケットは当日に限り有効です。(This ticket is valid on the day only.)
Of all ～, it had to be ～Things are usually fine, but trouble strikes at exactly the worst moment. This use takes に限って. What follows is usually something unlucky or unwelcome, and the tone carries a bit of a complaint.
・傘を持っていない日に限って、急に雨が降る。(It suddenly rains on the very day I don't have an umbrella.)
・急いでいるときに限って、信号に引っかかる。(I always get stuck at a red light just when I'm in a hurry.)
・休みの日に限って、朝早く目が覚める。(I wake up early on exactly the days I'm off.)
Not them, of all peoplePut a person you trust before it, and follow with “it can't be that ～.” It means “others might, but they absolutely wouldn't.”
・うちの子に限って、うそをつくはずがない。(My child, of all people, would never lie.)
・あの真面目な田中さんに限って、約束を忘れるなんてありえない。(Someone as serious as Mr. Tanaka could never forget a promise.)
Common mix-ups
・The “limited to” meaning is very formal, the voice of notices and ads. When chatting with a friend and saying “just today,” 今日だけ is enough. 今日に限り would sound like you're reading out a public notice.
・The “of all times” に限って is followed by something bad almost every time. Don't use it for good things.
・The “not them, of all people” use must be followed by a negative, such as はずがない or ありえない. Even if you stop at うちの子に限って, a Japanese listener will understand you're about to say “impossible.”
・Don't confuse it with に限る. That one means “～ is the best / nothing beats ～”: 暑い日は冷たいビールに限る。 (On a hot day, nothing beats a cold beer.) The spelling differs only slightly, but the meaning is completely different.
Telling look-alikes apart
All of these are about “today,” but the usage changes the meaning a lot:
本日に限り、入場無料です。(Free admission today only.) → a notice, “limited to”
今日に限って、財布を忘れた。(Of all days, I forgot my wallet today.) → a complaint, “of all times”
あの人に限って、そんなことはしない。(They, of all people, wouldn't do such a thing.) → trust, “not them”
A quick test: if you see it on a notice or in the rules, it's “limited to.” If you're talking about your own bad luck, it's “of all times.” If a person comes before it and “impossible” comes after, it's “not them, of all people.”
What to learn next
Make it negative as に限らず and it means “not only ～”: この店は週末に限らず、いつも混んでいる。 (This shop is crowded not only on weekends but all the time.)
n3-32:
The idea in one line
「〜くらい」 works like English "so ~ that ~" or "to the point of ~". In English you say "laughed so hard my stomach hurt" or "so tired I didn't want to move." You paint a concrete picture to show how extreme something was. Japanese does this with くらい: お腹が痛くなるくらい笑った。 (I laughed so hard my stomach hurt.) くらい and ぐらい mean exactly the same thing, so you can use either.
When to use it
Exaggerated descriptionPut a vivid picture before くらい. What follows is the state you actually want to describe.
・手が震えるくらい緊張した。 (I was so nervous my hands were shaking.)
・泣きたいくらい悔しかった。 (I was so frustrated I wanted to cry.)
・朝の電車は動けないくらい混んでいる。 (The morning train is so crowded you can't even move.)
Just a little thingThe opposite direction: you play the degree down, with a "no big deal" feel.
・これくらい、自分でできるよ。 (I can do something like this myself.)
At least ~Used for "the bare minimum you should do," often with a hint of complaint.
・忙しくても、電話くらいしてよ。 (Even if you're busy, you could at least call.)
No one/nothing is more ~ than「Noun＋くらい～はない」 is for strong praise or emphasis.
・田中さんくらい優しい人はいない。 (There's no one as kind as Mr. Tanaka.)
How to attach it
Verbs: attach directly to the dictionary form or ない form. For things you want to do, you can also use 「たい」.
震える → 震えるくらい動けない → 動けないくらい泣きたい → 泣きたいくらい
い-adjectives: attach directly. 痛い → 痛いくらい
な-adjectives: add 「な」 first. 不思議 → 不思議なくらい
Nouns: attach directly, with no 「の」 in between. これ → これくらい田中さん → 田中さんくらい
Easy mistakes
・Number (quantity) ＋くらい means "about," as in 三時間くらい (about three hours). With verbs, adjectives, or non-quantity nouns like これ and 田中さん, くらい means "to the extent of ~."
・Don't flip the order. What comes before くらい is the picture you're using as a comparison, and what comes after is the real state: 手が震えるくらい緊張した, not 「緊張したくらい手が震えた」.
・The verb before くらい is usually just the dictionary form or ない form. For past events, only the end of the sentence changes to past tense: 声が出ないくらい驚いた。 (I was so shocked I couldn't speak.)
・Don't forget 「な」 with な-adjectives, and don't add an extra 「の」 after nouns: say これくらい, not 「これのくらい」.
・The "just a little thing" use sounds dismissive. Saying これくらいできるでしょう (surely you can do this much) to someone senior to you sounds very rude.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
ほど also means "to the extent of ~." For exaggerated descriptions you can use either one, but くらい is more conversational, while ほど is more formal and written:
手が震えるくらい緊張した。 (chatting with a friend)
手が震えるほど緊張した。 (writing an essay, giving a speech)
But for the "just a little thing" and "at least" meanings, only くらい works. これほど instead means "this much ~," meaning you feel the degree is large:
これくらい簡単だよ。 (It's easy, just this much.)
これほど難しいとは思わなかった。 (I never thought it would be this difficult.)
Also, comparisons like "not as ~ as ~" need ほど: 今年は去年ほど寒くない。 (This year isn't as cold as last year.)
Quick rule of thumb: for "just a little thing" or "at least ~," use くらい. For "not as ~ as ~" or formal writing, use ほど. For simply exaggerating a degree, either works, though you hear くらい more in speech.
n3-35:
The idea in one line
「〜気味」 means "a bit ~" or "a slight touch of ~". Say your throat feels off and you tell someone, "I think I'm coming down with a bit of a cold." In Japanese that's 風邪気味です. It's mostly used when your body or situation shows a small, not-so-good sign that isn't serious yet.
When to use it
Physical conditionThe most common use: a bit of a cold, a bit tired, a bit overweight, a bit short on sleep.
・風邪気味なので、今日は早く寝ます。 (I'm coming down with a cold, so I'll go to bed early today.)
・最近、ちょっと太り気味なんだ。 (I've been putting on a little weight lately.)
・寝不足気味で、授業中に眠くなった。 (I'm a bit sleep-deprived, so I got sleepy during class.)
Feelings, progress of thingsYou can also use it for being a bit nervous or things running a bit behind.
・初めての発表なので、少し緊張気味です。 (It's my first presentation, so I'm a little nervous.)
・工事が予定より遅れ気味だ。 (The construction is running a bit behind schedule.)
How to attach it
Verbs: take the ます form, drop ます, and attach 気味 directly.
疲れます → 疲れ気味太ります → 太り気味遅れます → 遅れ気味
Nouns: attach directly.
風邪 → 風邪気味緊張 → 緊張気味運動不足 → 運動不足気味
「〜気味」 itself behaves like a noun. Add だ／です at the end of a sentence, use の before a noun, and use で or なので to connect to the next clause.
・風邪気味の人は、マスクをしてください。 (If you're coming down with a cold, please wear a mask.)
Easy mistakes
・When attached to another word, it's read ぎみ, not きみ: 風邪気味 is read かぜぎみ.
・Verbs must be in the ます-stem form (ます removed), not the dictionary form: say 太り気味, not 太る気味.
・Adjectives don't attach directly to 気味. For "a bit hot," you don't say 暑い気味. You say ちょっと暑い.
・It's used almost only for unfavorable situations. You wouldn't use 気味 for "a bit happy" or "a bit energetic."
・Before a noun, use の: 風邪気味の人, not 風邪気味な人.
・Even though 気味 already means "a bit," Japanese speakers very often add 少し or ちょっと before it. It sounds natural, not redundant.
・気味が悪い (read きみがわるい) means "creepy, unsettling." It has nothing to do with this grammar point, so don't mix them up.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
〜がち = tends to be that way, is prone to it (frequency, habit).
〜気味 = there's a sign of being that way right now (current state).
・今日はちょっと風邪気味です。 (I'm a bit under the weather today, like a cold coming on.)
・冬は風邪をひきがちです。 (I tend to catch colds in winter.)
〜っぽい can also be used as 風邪っぽい (seems like a cold). The meaning is very close to 風邪気味, but it's more casual, suited to chatting with friends. With your boss or a doctor, 風邪気味です is more appropriate. っぽい also has a much wider range: 子どもっぽい (childish) and 白っぽい (whitish) both use っぽい, and these can't be replaced with 気味.
Quick rule of thumb: for "lately I often ~," use がち. For "right now I'm a bit ~," use 気味. For a casual "seems like ~" with friends, you can use っぽい.
n3-36:
The idea in one line
「〜っぱなし」 means "left that way, never dealt with", as in "left on and never turned off." Think of a parent nagging: "You left the light on again!" "Your clothes are just dumped on the floor!" In Japanese that's つけっぱなし, 出しっぱなし, 脱ぎっぱなし. It usually carries a tone of complaint or annoyance.
How to form it
Take the ます form, drop ます, and add 「っぱなし」 directly. It works the same for all three verb groups, so there's no need to split them up.
つけます → drop ます → つけっぱなし (left on)
出します → 出しっぱなし (taken out and not put away)
脱ぎます → 脱ぎっぱなし (taken off and left lying around)
開けます → 開けっぱなし (opened and left open)
When to use it
Should have been undone, but wasn'tYou did something, and afterwards you were supposed to turn it off, put it away, or tidy up, but you just left it. This is by far the most common use.
・テレビをつけっぱなしで寝てしまった。 (I fell asleep with the TV still on.)
・水が出しっぱなしだよ。 (The water's still running!)
・服を脱ぎっぱなしにしないで。 (Don't just leave your clothes lying where you took them off.)
Staying in the same state nonstopOne thing goes on and on without a break, usually with a feeling of "for too long, I'm exhausted."
・今日は一日中立ちっぱなしで、足が痛い。 (I've been on my feet all day, and my legs hurt.)
・朝から働きっぱなしで疲れた。 (I've been working nonstop since morning and I'm tired.)
Common patterns
・〜っぱなしだ: 窓が開けっぱなしだ。 (The window has been left open.)
・〜っぱなしで、〜: what follows is the result, like "fell asleep with the TV on" above.
・〜っぱなしにする: to leave something as it is. To tell someone not to, say 〜っぱなしにしないで.
・〜っぱなしの＋noun: 出しっぱなしの本 (a book that was taken out and never put back)
Easy mistakes
・It attaches to the ます form minus ます, not the dictionary form. Say つけっぱなし, not つけるっぱなし.
・There's a small っ in the middle. Pause for a beat: 「つけ・っ・ぱなし」, not つけぱなし.
・It often carries a complaint about something that should have been dealt with and wasn't (especially the "should have undone it" use). If you're just stating that something was done in a certain state, with no complaint, 「〜たまま」 is more natural. But the "on my feet all day / working nonstop" use can't be swapped for たまま: 立ったまま only means "standing (while doing something)"; it doesn't mean "standing for a long time."
・The point of っぱなし is "leaving it in that state," and it isn't always an accident. You can also use it for something kept that way on purpose, like 換気のために窓を開けっぱなしにしている。 (I'm keeping the window open all the time for ventilation.) If you want to stress "set it up in advance for a purpose," use 〜ておく.
Telling similar forms apart
Take "went out with the window open":
〜たまま = simply states the condition, with no particular emotion: 窓を開けたまま出かけた。 (I went out with the window open.)
〜っぱなし = carries the annoyance of "should have closed it, didn't": 窓を開けっぱなしで出かけた。 (I went out leaving the window wide open.)
〜ておく = keeping it that way on purpose, with a goal: 暑いから、窓を開けておいた。 (It was hot, so I left the window open.)
The attachment differs too: たまま takes the た form, ておく takes the て form, and っぱなし takes the ます form minus ます.
Quick rule of thumb: to complain "why isn't this ever put away," use っぱなし. To just say "in that state," use たまま. For "deliberately set it up beforehand," use ておく.
n3-37:
The idea in one line
Both express "a good fit for a certain kind of person." The difference is whether it was made specifically for them.
向き（むき） = "well suited to ~." It looks at the nature of the thing itself, regardless of who it was originally made for.
向け（むけ） = "designed specifically for ~." It was aimed at that group from the start, like "kids' edition" or "for beginners" in English.
How to form it
Both attach directly to a noun, to show "for whom" or "for what situation."
At the end of a sentence: 子供 → 子供向きだ子供 → 子供向けだ
Before a noun: you can add 「の」 (初心者向けの講座), or join them directly into one compound (初心者向け講座, 子供向け番組). Both are correct. The joined style is especially common in titles, ads, and product descriptions. When making your own sentences, the version with 「の」 is the safest.
Before a verb: 向けに + verbs like 作る or 書く means "made for ~."
When to use it
向きThe thing's own qualities happen to suit someone. It's often used to comment on houses, jobs, personalities, and clothes.
・この部屋は一人暮らし向きだ。 (This room is well suited to living alone.)
・彼は営業向きの性格だ。 (He has a personality well suited to sales.)
For "not suited," say 不向き:
・この靴は長く歩くのには不向きだ。 (These shoes aren't suited to walking long distances.)
向けA product, program, or service was aimed at a certain group when it was designed.
・外国人向けのパンフレットをください。 (Could I have a brochure for foreign visitors, please?)
・このアプリは高齢者向けに作られている。 (This app is designed for older people.)
Easy mistakes
・Pronunciation: 向き is むき and 向け is むけ. They differ only in the last sound, so listen carefully.
・For "made for ~," use 向けに作る. You can't say 向きに作る, because 向き isn't about the purpose of making something.
・"Not suited" exists only as 不向き. There's no 「不向け」.
・南向きの部屋 means "a south-facing room." Here 向き means direction, a different meaning from "suited to," so don't mix them up.
Telling similar forms apart
Take the same book and its relation to children:
これは子供向けの本だ。 (This is a children's book, written for kids from the start.)
大人向けに書かれた本だが、やさしいので子供向きでもある。 (This book was written for adults, but it's easy, so it also suits children.)
The second sentence shows the difference clearly: who it was made for is 向け, and who it turns out to suit is 向き. One book can be both.
Quick rule of thumb: if you can swap in "made specifically for ~," use 向け. If you just feel "it suits ~ well," use 向き.
What to learn next
向き comes from the verb 向く (to be suited), so you can also say この仕事は私に向いている。 (This job suits me.) and 私は細かい作業に向いていない。 (I'm not suited to detailed work.).
n3-40:
The idea in one line
「〜ようになる」means "come to ~" or "get to the point where I can ~ / start ~ing." The key is it wasn't like this before, but now it is, like "I can finally travel to Japan on my own now" or "my kid has started putting on shoes by himself lately." For a change that has already happened, you usually use the past form 「ようになった」.
How to connect it
Ability changedYou couldn't before, but now you can: put the potential form (the form that means "can ~") in front.
読む → 読める → 読めるようになった
起きる → 起きられる → 起きられるようになった
Exception: verbs like わかる, 見える, 聞こえる and できる already carry the meaning of "can," so you use the dictionary form directly: わかるようになった.
・息子がひらがなを読めるようになった。(My son can read hiragana now.)
・練習して、泳げるようになった。(After practicing, I learned how to swim.)
Habit changedYou weren't doing it before, but now you've started: dictionary form + ようになる.
・結婚してから、毎日料理するようになった。(Since getting married, I've started cooking every day.)
・何度も通ううちに、店員と雑談するようになった。(After going there so many times, I gradually started chatting with the staff.)
Quick review of the potential form
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the 「え」-row sound of the same row, then add る.
読む → change む to め → 読める話す → 話せる
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop る and add られる.
食べる → 食べられる
Group 3 (just memorize them): する → できる来る → 来られる（こられる）
Forms you'll hear most often
ようになりたいYou want to become able to do something.
・日本語がペラペラ話せるようになりたい。(I want to get to where I can speak fluent Japanese.)
ようになるThe present form says "you'll come to ~ later."
・毎日練習すれば、すぐ泳げるようになりますよ。(If you practice every day, you'll be able to swim in no time.)
ようになってきたThe change is happening little by little.
・日本語が少しわかるようになってきた。(I'm gradually starting to understand a bit of Japanese.)
Common mistakes
・To say you "learned to do" something, use the potential form: 泳げるようになった means "I learned to swim," while 泳ぐようになった means "I've started swimming" (it became a habit). They're different. But with わかる, 見える, 聞こえる and できる, use the dictionary form directly; you can't say わかれる or 見えられる.
・To say "no longer ~," 「なくなる」 is more common in everyday speech: 辛いものが食べられなくなった (I can't eat spicy food anymore), タバコを吸わなくなった (I don't smoke anymore).
・When you want to say "become some state," adjectives and nouns can't connect directly to ようになる: "became busy" is 忙しくなった, "became pretty" is きれいになった, and "became a teacher" is 先生になった. Extra note: noun + のようになる means "become like ~," for example 先生のようになりたい (I want to become like a teacher). It does not mean "become a teacher," so they're different.
・You can also use it for results you worked hard to achieve, not only for things that happen "naturally." What matters is that the result has changed.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Take "getting up early" as an example:
ようにする = deliberately making an effort: 毎朝6時に起きるようにしている。 (I try to get up at 6 every morning.)
ようになる = the result has changed: 朝6時に起きられるようになった。 (I can get up at 6 now.)
ことになる = it was decided or arranged: 来月から、6時に出勤することになった。 (It's been decided that I'll start work at 6 from next month.)
Quick tip: "try to ~" is ようにする, "can ~ now" is ようになる, and "it's been decided that ~" is ことになる.
n3-45:
The idea in one line
「〜はずだ」means "should be ~" or "is supposed to be ~" (based on reasoning). You have grounds (something you saw, something you know, something arranged in advance), and from them you draw a conclusion you're quite confident about. For example, if you see the lights on at a friend's house, you think "he should be home," which in Japanese is 家にいるはずだ.
How to connect it
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly to the plain form (the form without ます or です).
来る → 来るはずだ来た → 来たはずだ高い → 高いはずだ
な-adjectives: replace だ with な.
便利だ → 便利なはずだ
Nouns: replace だ with の.
休みだ → 休みのはずだ
To be more polite, change だ to です: 来るはずです.
When to use it
Reasoned conclusionYou draw a conclusion from known facts.
・彼は医者だから、詳しいはずだ。(He's a doctor, so he should know a lot about it.)
・電気がついているから、家にいるはずだ。(The lights are on, so he should be home.)
According to plan or scheduleWhat should happen based on a timetable or something you agreed on.
・田中さんは3時に来るはずです。(Mr. Tanaka should arrive at three.)
・荷物は明日届くはずです。(The package should arrive tomorrow.)
I was sure ~, but…Use 「はずなのに」 when you're certain, yet things turned out differently, with a "that's strange" feeling.
・ここに置いたはずなのに、ない。(I'm sure I put it here, but it's gone.)
No wonderYou first notice the result, then discover the reason and it clicks.
・寒いはずだ。雪が降っている。(No wonder it's so cold. It's snowing.)
Common mistakes
・English "should" has two meanings: "it's probably the case" and "you ought to." はず has only the first one. "You should go to bed earlier" is advice, so you can't use はず.
・Nouns need の: it's 医者のはずだ, not 「医者だはずだ」; with な-adjectives, say 便利なはずだ.
・Don't use はず when you have no grounds and are just guessing. はず sounds very confident, so a wrong guess comes across as presumptuous.
・Don't use はず for things you yourself want to do. "I plan to go tomorrow" is 明日行くつもりだ. はず is about what should happen by logic or by plan, not about your intention.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
はずだ = it should be so (reasoned conclusion): 会議は3時に始まるはずだ。 (According to the schedule, the meeting should start at three.)
