べきだ = you ought to do it (obligation, opinion): 会議は時間どおりに始めるべきだ。 (Meetings should start on time.)
ないはずだ = it shouldn't be so (calm conclusion): 彼は今日来ないはずだ。 (He shouldn't be coming today.)
はずがない = there's no way (strong denial): 彼が来るはずがない。 (There's no way he'd come.)
Quick tip: use はず for "it should be so," べき for "you ought to do ~"; use ないはず for "probably not" and はずがない for "impossible."
What to learn next
The past form 「はずだった」 = it was supposed to ~, but didn't: 3時に着くはずだったのに、電車が遅れた。 (I was supposed to arrive at three, but the train was delayed.)
Next, you can learn 〜はずがない, which expresses "impossible."
n3-46:
The idea in one line
「〜はずがない」means "there's no way ～" / "it can't possibly be ～". You have a reason in mind: she's careful, the door was locked, he practiced for so long. Following that reasoning through, you conclude "this can't possibly be true."
When to use it
Reasoning it outYou have grounds for it, so you say "impossible" with confidence.
・彼女があんなミスをするはずがない。(There's no way she'd make a mistake like that.)
・あんなに練習したんだから、負けるはずがない。(He practiced that much, so there's no way he'll lose.)
Not believing what's in front of youWhen something unexpected happens, you blurt out "No way..."
・え、財布がない？そんなはずない。さっきまであったのに。(Huh, my wallet's gone? That can't be. It was right here a moment ago.)
How to form it
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly.
負ける → 負けるはずがない暑い → 暑いはずがない
な-adjectives: add 「な」 in between.
下手 → 下手なはずがない
Nouns: add 「の」 in between.
犯人 → 犯人のはずがない
To say "there's no way they did it" or "there's no way they don't ～", put the past or negative form before はず:
行った → 行ったはずがない (there's no way they've been there)
知らない → 知らないはずがない (there's no way they don't know)
・まだ4月だから、そんなに暑いはずがない。(It's only April, so it can't be that hot.)
・10年も日本に住んでいるんだから、日本語が下手なはずがない。(He's lived in Japan for 10 years, so there's no way his Japanese is bad.)
・あんなに優しい人が犯人のはずがない。(Someone that kind can't possibly be the culprit.)
How you'll most often hear it
「が」often becomes 「は」 for stronger emphasis, and in casual speech the particle is often dropped altogether. The version you'll hear most is そんなはずはない or そんなはずない ("That can't be," "How could that be?"). Memorize the whole phrase.
Common mistakes
・Nouns and な-adjectives can't attach directly: say 犯人のはずがない, not 「犯人だはずがない」.
・English "can't" covers several meanings, but Japanese keeps them apart. はずがない only means "impossible / can't be true." You can't use it for "not allowed" or "not able to (ability)." "You can't smoke here" is ここでたばこを吸ってはいけません, and "I can't swim" is 泳げません.
・知らないはずがない means "there's no way he doesn't know," which amounts to "he must know." Don't translate it as "there's no way he knows."
・The tone is strong. Saying あなたにできるはずがない ("There's no way you can do it") to someone's face is hurtful, so be careful.
Telling it apart from similar forms
Take the same question, "Will he come?", and note how the tone changes:
はずだ = he should come (confident): 彼は来るはずだ。 (He should be coming.)
ないはずだ = he shouldn't come (leaning negative, but not final): 彼は来ないはずだ。 (He shouldn't be coming.)
はずがない = absolutely impossible (final): 彼が来るはずがない。 (There's no way he's coming.)
わけがない = nearly the same meaning as はずがない, and interchangeable in most cases. You hear it more in everyday chat, and it sounds blunter and more emotional: 彼が来るわけがない。 (How could he possibly come?)
Quick rule of thumb: use ないはずだ for "probably not" and はずがない for "absolutely impossible." When talking with friends or when you're more worked up, people often switch to わけがない.
n3-48:
The idea in one line
「〜ことだ」is what an elder or senior says when giving you advice: "Take my word for it, just ～" / "What you need to do is ～." For example, a senior tells you, "Want to pass N3? Just memorize vocabulary every day." In Japanese that's 毎日単語を覚えることだ。
How to form it
Telling someone to do something: dictionary form + ことだ
休む → 休むことだ (just get some rest)
Telling someone not to do something: ない form + ことだ
無理をしない → 無理をしないことだ (don't push yourself)
When to use it
Giving adviceYou often first say "if you want to ～" or "in order to ～," then give the answer with ことだ.
・風邪のときは、ゆっくり休むことだ。(When you have a cold, just rest up properly.)
・やせたいなら、甘いものを減らすことだ。(If you want to lose weight, cut down on sweets.)
Advising against somethingWith the ない form, the tone is like "just don't ～."
・試験の前の日は、夜遅くまで勉強しないことだ。(The day before the exam, don't stay up late studying.)
Besides face-to-face advice, you'll also see this pattern often in self-help books, newspaper columns, and seniors' words of experience.
Common mistakes
・This is a top-down tone, with a bit of an "I know better than you" feel. Don't use it with teachers, bosses, or customers. Even changing it to 〜ことです is still impolite. With someone senior, use 〜たほうがいいと思います instead.
・Only the dictionary form or ない form can come before it, not the た form: 休んだことだ does not mean "you should rest."
・If an adjective comes before it, as in うらやましいことだ or 残念なことだ, it expresses a feeling (how enviable, how regrettable), so it's not advice. Don't mix them up.
Telling it apart from similar forms
Say a friend has a cold but insists on going to work:
ことだ = advice aimed at you: 今日は休むことだ。 (Take the day off today.)
べきだ = reasoning about what one should or shouldn't do: 病気のときは休むべきだ。 (When you're sick, you should rest.) べきだ can also look back critically: 昨日休むべきだった。 (You should have taken yesterday off.) ことだ has no such use.
ものだ = common sense in society: 体調が悪いときは無理をしないものだ。 (When you're feeling unwell, you shouldn't push yourself.)
ことはない = "there's no need to ～," used to reassure someone: そんなに心配することはない。 (There's no need to worry that much.) This differs from 心配しないことだ。 (Just don't worry.): the former says "no need," while the latter urges you "not to."
Quick rule of thumb: use ことだ for "just do ～" to the person in front of you; べきだ for reasoning about what one should or shouldn't do; ものだ for common sense everyone knows; and ことはない for "no need to ～."
What to learn next
Next, look at 〜ことはない (no need to ～) and 〜べきだ (should ～). Memorize the three together and you'll be least likely to mix them up.
n3-38:
The idea in one line
「〜一方だ」 means “just keeps getting more and more ~,” “only gets worse,” “goes from bad to worse”. Something keeps changing in the same direction, with no sign of stopping or turning back, and it's usually a change for the worse.
・物価は上がる一方だ。(Prices only go up, never down.)
How to form it
Dictionary form of the verb (the base form you find in a dictionary) + 一方だ.
増える → 増える一方だ (keeps increasing)
悪化する → 悪化する一方だ (keeps getting worse)
The verb in front has to be a “change” verb, like 増える, 減る, 上がる, 下がる, 広がる, 進む.
形容詞Adjectives can't attach directly. First turn them into 「〜くなる」 or 「〜になる」 (become ~), then add 一方だ.
寒い → change い to く and add なる → 寒くなる一方だ
不便 → add になる → 不便になる一方だ
How you'll hear it most
Complaining that things are getting worseVery common in the news and when you talk with people about how things are going.
・最近、仕事が増える一方だ。(Lately my workload just keeps growing.)
・父の病気は悪くなる一方だ。(My father's illness keeps getting worse.)
・この町は人が減って、寂しくなる一方だ。(This town keeps losing people and getting lonelier and lonelier.)
Neutral trendsIt doesn't have to be bad news. You can also use it for something that's simply shooting upward.
・このアプリの利用者は増える一方だ。(This app's users just keep increasing.)
For past events, use 一方だった: その後、二人の関係は悪くなる一方だった。(After that, the two of them kept growing further apart.)
Where people slip up
・English “keeps ~ing” can tempt you to use this for “keeps doing an action.” That's wrong. 一方だ is only for change:
　×弟は毎日ゲームをする一方だ。
　○弟は毎日ゲームばかりしている。(My brother plays video games every day.)
・What comes before must be the dictionary form. Don't attach ている or ます: ×増えている一方だ, ×増えます一方だ. To be more polite, just change the ending: 増える一方です.
・Don't attach i-adjectives directly: ×寒い一方だ. Say 寒くなる一方だ.
・The tone carries a helpless feeling of “no improvement in sight,” so it's rarely used for good news.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
〜一方だ (at the end of a sentence) = keeps changing in one direction: 家賃は高くなる一方だ。(Rent just keeps getting more expensive.)
〜ばかりだ (after the dictionary form) = almost the same meaning, more colloquial, and used almost only for bad things: 家賃は高くなるばかりだ。(Rent just keeps getting more expensive.)
〜一方で (in the middle of a sentence) = “on the other hand,” used to contrast two things, unrelated to change: この町は便利な一方で、家賃が高い。(This town is convenient, but on the other hand the rent is high.)
Quick tip: 一方だ at the end of a sentence means “only keeps getting more and more ~”; 一方で in the middle of a sentence means “on the other hand.” When you see 一方, check where it is first.
What to learn next
To talk about the process of “gradually becoming ~,” learn 「〜てくる・〜ていく」 next: だんだん寒くなってきた。(It's gradually gotten colder.)
n3-39:
The idea in one line
「〜ようにする」 means “I try to ~” or “I make an effort to ~”. It's like saying “I've been trying to drink fewer sodas lately.” The point is that you're making a deliberate effort, with no guarantee you'll manage it every time.
How to form it
Things you do: dictionary form (the base form you find in a dictionary) + ようにする
早く寝る → 早く寝るようにする (try to go to bed early)
Things you avoid: ない form + ようにする
忘れない → 忘れないようにする (try not to forget)
To make it polite, just change the very end: ようにする → ようにします
The three forms you'll hear most
ようにしているA habit you've been keeping up lately. The most common one in daily life.
・毎晩10時までに寝るようにしている。(I try to be in bed by 10 every night.)
・エレベーターより階段を使うようにしている。(I try to take the stairs instead of the elevator.)
ようにするYou'll start paying attention from now on.
・これからは遅刻しないようにします。(From now on, I'll make sure not to be late.)
ようにしてくださいAsking the other person to try to do something. Doctors and teachers use it a lot.
・水をたくさん飲むようにしてください。(Please try to drink plenty of water.)
Where people slip up
・Only the dictionary form or ない form can come before it, not the ます form or た form. You can't say 寝ますようにする or 寝たようにする. For politeness, change the ending: 寝るようにします.
・For “I usually try to ~,” use ようにしている. With ようにする／ようにします, it sounds like “from now on I'll pay attention,” as if you haven't started yet.
・It only works for things you can control yourself. For something like “I hope it doesn't rain,” you can't use ようにする, because whether it rains isn't up to you.
・ようにしてください sounds like a reminder or instruction. It's natural from a doctor to a patient or a teacher to a student, but with a boss or a customer it can sound like you're telling them how to do things, so be careful.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
All three are about “speaking Japanese,” but change the ending and the meaning changes:
ようになる = gradually come to be that way (a result): 日本語が話せるようになった。(I've become able to speak Japanese.)
ようにする = deliberately make an effort yourself: 毎日日本語を話すようにしている。(I try to speak Japanese every day.)
ことにする = make a decision: 毎日日本語を話すことにした。(I decided to speak Japanese every day.)
Quick tip: “have come to ~” is ようになる, “try to ~” is ようにする, and “decide to ~” is ことにする.
What to learn next
「〜ようになる」 (come to ~) often shows up alongside this lesson, so learn it next. There's also another 「〜ように」 meaning “so that ~” or “in order to ~,” for example: 忘れないように、メモしておく。(I'll write it down so I don't forget.) It looks a lot like ようにする, so compare the two once you get to it.
n3-49:
The idea in one line
「〜ことはない」 means “there's no need to ~” or “no reason to ~”. When someone is worried, apologizing, or rushing, you use it to say “you don't have to.” It usually sounds a bit reassuring, as if you're telling them to relax.
How to form it
Take the dictionary form of the verb (the base form you'd look up) and add ことはない.
心配する → 心配することはない (no need to worry)
謝る → 謝ることはない (no need to apologize)
急ぐ → 急ぐことはない (no need to rush)
For a more polite version: ことはありません. With friends, people often drop 「は」 to get ことない, then add よ at the end.
How you'll hear it most
ReassuringWhen the other person is worrying or blaming themselves.
・大したことじゃないから、気にすることないよ。 (It's no big deal, so don't worry about it.)
Telling someone not to go to the troubleOften appears together with 「わざわざ」 (going out of one's way).
・わざわざ来ることはないよ。電話でいいから。 (You don't need to come all the way here. A phone call is fine.)
Why bother ~Put 「何も」 in front and it becomes a slightly exasperated “why on earth would you ~?”
・何もそんなに怒ることはないでしょう。 (There's no need to get that angry.)
Common mistakes
・What comes before it is always the dictionary form. Switch to the た-form and the meaning changes completely to “have never ~” (compared below).
・It means “there's no need,” not “you must not.” 行くことはない means “you don't have to go,” so you're still free to go if you want. To say “you're not allowed to go,” use 行ってはいけない.
・This phrase carries the tone of “I've judged it for you: it's not necessary,” which is natural with friends and juniors. With a boss or a customer, saying 「〜ことはありません」 directly can sound a bit like you're instructing them. 大丈夫です or ご心配なく is safer.
・Sometimes it means “won't happen”: もう二度と会うことはないだろう。 (We probably won't ever meet again.) When you're comforting or advising someone it means “no need,” and when you're talking about possibility it means “won't.” Let the context tell you which.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Take “going to Japan.” Change the verb form in front and the meaning shifts a lot:
Dictionary form + ことはない = no need to: 日本へ行くことはない。 (There's no need to go to Japan.)
た-form + ことはない = have never done: 日本へ行ったことはない。 (I've never been to Japan.)
ない-form + ことはない = it's not that I never: 日本へ行かないことはない。 (It's not that I never go to Japan. I do go once in a while.)
Quick trick: look at the word right before 「こと」. Dictionary form means “no need,” た means “have never,” and ない means “it's not that I don't.”
What to learn next
Its opposite is 「〜ことだ」, meaning “you'd better do it”: 心配なら、医者に相談することだ。 (If you're worried, you should talk to a doctor.) One urges you to do something, the other says you don't have to.
A very close phrase is 心配する必要はない (there's no need to worry). It sounds more objective and stiffer, and you'll often see it in written text.
n3-50:
The idea in one line
Both express a “decision.” The difference is who made the call.
ことにする = I decided it myself: “I've decided to quit smoking.”
ことになる = it wasn't my call. The company arranged it, a group discussed it, or things simply turned out that way: “The company is transferring me.”
English “I've decided to ~” matches ことにする, while “it's been decided that I'll ~” or “I'm being made to ~” matches ことになる.
How to form it
Things you will do: dictionary form + ことにする／ことになる　やめる → やめることにした
Things you won't do: ない-form + ことにする／ことになる　帰らない → 帰らないことにした
How you'll hear it most
ことにしたI made the decision myself.
・タバコをやめることにした。 (I've decided to quit smoking.)
・今年の夏は実家に帰らないことにした。 (I've decided not to go back to my parents' home this summer.)
ことになったThe company, school, or someone else decided, and I'm just accepting the result.
・来月から大阪に転勤することになった。 (I'm being transferred to Osaka starting next month.)
Announcing your own newsEven when it was your own decision, Japanese speakers often use ことになりました when announcing things like a marriage or leaving a job. It sounds humbler, like “things have come to this point,” and doesn't stress “this is what I wanted.”
・実は、結婚することになりました。 (Actually, I'm getting married.)
ことにしているA rule you set for yourself and keep following.
・寝る前はスマホを見ないことにしている。 (I make it a rule not to look at my phone before bed.)
ことになっているA rule, a custom, or something already scheduled.
・この部屋では靴を脱ぐことになっています。 (In this room, you're supposed to take off your shoes.)
・明日、田中さんと会うことになっている。 (I'm meeting Mr. Tanaka tomorrow. It's already arranged.)
Common mistakes
・In English you might say “I've decided” or “I'm going to.” Japanese normally uses the past tense ことにした to show the decision has already been made.
・Nouns like 旅行 or 勉強 that can take する must become verbs first: 旅行することにした, not 旅行ことにした. (Ordinary nouns attach directly to にする, as in コーヒーにする, which means “I'll go with ~.” That's a different usage from this one.)
・ことになる doesn't always involve someone making a decision. It can also mean “if things go on like this, you'll end up ~”: 今やめたら、後で後悔することになるよ。 (If you quit now, you'll regret it later.)
・ことにしている is a rule you set yourself, while ことになっている is a rule set from outside. Don't mix them up.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Take “getting up early”:
ことにする = deciding it yourself: 明日から6時に起きることにした。 (I've decided to get up at six starting tomorrow.)
ことになる = being arranged or circumstances turning out that way: 仕事の関係で、毎朝6時に起きることになった。 (Because of work, I end up having to get up at six every morning.)
ようにする = trying to do it: 毎朝6時に起きるようにしている。 (I try to get up at six every morning.)
ようになる = gradually becoming able to: 6時に起きられるようになった。 (I've become able to get up at six.)
Quick trick: if it feels like a “decision,” use こと. If it's “try to” or “become,” use よう. Then ask who decided: if you made the call, use する. If someone else arranged it or it just turned out that way, use なる.
What to learn next
When ことにする follows a past-tense verb, it can also mean “I'll treat it as if ~”: 今の話は聞かなかったことにする。 (I'll pretend I didn't hear what was just said.)
n3-53:
The idea in one line
「ために」has two meanings. The most common is “in order to ~”, which states a purpose. The other, more formal one is “because of ~”, which states a reason. English uses different words for these, but Japanese uses the same ために for both, so you tell them apart from context.
Usage 1: in order to ~ (purpose)
In order to do somethingUse the dictionary form of the verb + ために. With a noun, add 「の」 first: noun + のために.
・日本に留学するために、アルバイトでお金をためている。(I'm saving money from my part-time job in order to study abroad in Japan.)
・健康のために、毎朝歩いている。(I walk every morning for my health.)
For someone's sakePut a person before it and it means “for someone.”
・家族のために、毎日がんばって働いている。(I work hard every day for my family.)
Usage 2: because of ~ (reason)
Formal “because”It can follow the た form or dictionary form of a verb, an い-adjective, a な-adjective + な, or a noun + の. It's very common in news, station announcements, and notices, and the に is often dropped, leaving just 「ため」. What follows is usually a result that has already happened and is somewhat negative, but not always.
・大雪のために、電車が止まった。(The trains stopped because of the heavy snow.)
・事故があったために、道が混んでいる。(The roads are congested because there was an accident.)
・台風のため、今日の授業は休みです。(Because of the typhoon, today's class is cancelled.)
How to tell which one it is
If the first part is something you want to achieve that hasn't happened yet, and the second part is the effort you make for it, it means “in order to.”
If the first part is something that already happened, or a state, and the second part is the result it caused, it means “because of.”
If you see a た form (あった, 降った), it is definitely a reason. Noun + のために can be either, so look at what follows: 試験のために勉強する (study for the exam), 雪のために遅れた (was late because of the snow).
Common mistakes
・A noun must be followed by の: you can't say 健康ために; say 健康のために.
・It can't follow the ます form: you can't say 合格しますために; say 合格するために.
・With the “in order to” ために, the subject before and after is usually the same person, and the first part must be an action you can decide to do yourself. For abilities or states like “can speak,” “can hear,” or “can understand,” use ように instead (compared below).
・The “because of” ために is formal, and what follows can't be a request, invitation, or command. You can't say 雨のために傘を持っていこう; say 雨だから、傘を持っていこう。 (It's raining, so let's take an umbrella.) In everyday conversation, から or ので is enough for giving a reason.
Telling it apart from a look-alike
The “in order to” ために and ように can both be translated as “in order to,” but what goes before them is different.
Some things can be said either way; it just depends on how you look at it:
・N2に合格するために、毎日勉強している。 (I study every day in order to pass N2.): 合格する is something you set out to achieve.
・N2に合格できるように、毎日勉強している。 (I study every day so that I can pass N2.): 合格できる is a state you hope to reach.
The following can only use ように:
・みんなに聞こえるように、大きな声で話した。 (I spoke loudly so that everyone could hear.)
・子どもにも読めるように、ひらがなで書いた。 (I wrote it in hiragana so that children could read it too.)
聞こえる and 読める are abilities or states, and in the second sentence the subjects differ (I write, the children read), so ために can't be used.
Quick rule: if the first part is “an action you actively do yourself,” use ために. If it's an ability or state like「できる、わかる、聞こえる、見える」, or the subjects differ, use ように.
What to learn next
For the purpose meaning, look at 「〜ように」 next (n3-54). For the reason meaning, compare 「〜おかげで」 (thanks to ~, a good result) and 「〜せいで」 (because of ~, a bad result); they also express the speaker's gratitude or complaint.
n3-54:
The idea in one line
「〜ように」means “so that ~” or “so as not to ~.” The first half states the result you hope for, and the second half says what you did to bring it about: 後ろの人にも聞こえるように、マイクを使った。 (I used a microphone so that the people in the back could hear too.)
How to form it
When you hope you “can ~ / will be able to ~”: dictionary form + ように
聞こえる → 聞こえるように
話す → first change it to “can speak” 話せる → 話せるように
When you hope “not to ~”: ない form + ように
忘れる → 忘れない → 忘れないように
What usually goes before it
The key point: what comes before ように is a result you can't directly decide; you can only work toward making it happen. Common types:
Can ~The first part is a “can ~ / be able to ~” expression (potential form).
・字幕なしでドラマが見られるように、毎日日本語を聞いています。(I listen to Japanese every day so that I can watch dramas without subtitles.)
・日本語で話せるように、毎日練習している。(I practice every day so that I can talk in Japanese.)
Things that happen on their ownThese are not actions you can do just by wanting to, such as 聞こえる (can be heard), 間に合う (make it in time), and 治る (get better, recover).
・風邪が早く治るように、薬を飲んで寝た。(I took medicine and went to bed so that my cold would get better quickly.)
・最終便に間に合うように、早めに空港へ向かった。(I headed to the airport early so that I'd make the last flight.)
Not to ~ない form + ように = “so as not to ~.” Here it can be used even with actions you can control yourself.
・忘れないように、メモしておこう。(Let me write it down so I don't forget.)
・遅れないように、早めに家を出た。(I left home early so as not to be late.)
Extra: the two subjects can differ
This isn't a separate usage, just a feature of ように: the person in the first half can be different from the one in the second half. In the sentence below, the one who “understands” is the child, and the one who “explains” is me.
・子どもにも分かるように、簡単な言葉で説明した。(I explained it in simple words so that even a child could understand.)
Common mistakes
・For an action you decide to do yourself, the affirmative form can't be followed directly by ように:
× 日本語を勉強するように、日本へ来た。
○ 日本語を勉強するために、日本へ来た。 (I came to Japan in order to study Japanese.)
・Noun + 「のように」means “like ~,” which has nothing to do with the “so that” meaning here: 子どものように笑う (laugh like a child).
・ように is followed by a new action, while ようにする means “I'll try to ~.” Don't mix them up: 忘れないように、メモする (write it down so as not to forget) vs 忘れないようにする (I'll try not to forget).
Telling it apart from a look-alike
Take saving money to study abroad:
留学するために、お金をためている。 (I'm saving money in order to study abroad.)
留学できるように、お金をためている。 (I'm saving money so that I can study abroad.)
Before ために comes something you decide to do yourself, and “studying abroad” is the goal itself. Before ように comes whether you can or will be able to; “being able to study abroad” depends on whether you have enough money.
Also, with ために the subject before and after must be the same person, while ように allows different people. And ために can follow a noun directly (健康のために), but ように can't.
Quick rule: if you have full say over the first action, use ために. If the first part is “can ~” or “not to ~,” or depends on luck or other people, use ように.
What to learn next
「〜ようにと」introduces the content of a prayer, wish, or instruction, for example 合格できるようにと祈った (I prayed that I would pass). You can also go back and compare 「〜ようにする」 and 「〜ようになる」.
n3-55:
The idea in one line
「〜ようにと」 is used to report what someone told you to do, like English “The teacher told us to be on time” or “The doctor told me to cut down on salt.” You're not repeating their exact words. You're passing on the gist of what they want done. The と works like closing quotation marks: it marks everything before it as the content of the instruction.
How to form it
Something the person should do: dictionary form + ようにと　守る → 守るようにと
Something the person should not do: ない form + ようにと　遅れない → 遅れないようにと
It's followed by verbs of passing on a message: 言う, 伝える, 注意する, 頼む, and also the verbs of wishing and praying, 祈る and 願う.
In speech, the 「と」 is often dropped, giving 「〜ように言われた」 with the same meaning. When 「と」 is there, it puts more weight on “this is what they told me.”
The forms you'll hear most
Being told「〜ようにと言われた」: someone told me to do something. This is the most common one in daily life.
・母に早く帰るようにと言われた。（My mom told me to come home early）
・医者にお酒を飲まないようにと言われた。（The doctor told me not to drink alcohol）
Passing on a message「〜ようにと伝えてください」: you're asking someone to relay a message to a third person.
・田中さんに、明日は8時に来るようにと伝えてください。（Please tell Mr. Tanaka to come at 8 tomorrow）
Praying or wishing「〜ようにと祈る」: you hope that something will come true.
・試験に合格できるようにと祈った。（I prayed that I'd pass the exam）
Common pitfalls
・The action before ように is done by the person who was told, not by the person giving the instruction. In 母に早く帰るように言われた, the one who should come home early is me, not my mom.
・Use the dictionary form or the ない form for the instruction, never the た form: say 帰るように言われた, not 「帰ったように言われた」. With verbs like 「言う」 and 「注意する」, don't put the ます form before ように either.
・「ように言う」 has a flavor of giving instructions, so it suits talking down to someone or to a peer. If you're asking a teacher or boss to do something, 「ように言った」 sounds like you ordered them around. Say 「〜てくださいとお願いした」 instead, which is more polite.
Don't mix it up with look-alikes
「」と言った = a direct quote of the exact words: 先生は「時間を守りなさい」と言った。（The teacher said, “Be on time.”）
ようにと言った = a report of the gist: 先生は時間を守るようにと言った。（The teacher told us to be on time）
The 「〜なさい」 or 「〜てください」 of the original words becomes 「〜ように」 when you report them.
ように (so that) = you do something yourself for a purpose: 忘れないようにメモした。（I wrote a note so I wouldn't forget）
ようにと (instruction) = someone told me to do something: 忘れないようにと言われた。（I was told not to forget）
Quick test: if ように is followed by a message verb like 言う, 伝える, 注意する or 頼む, it's an instruction. If it's followed by an action you do yourself, it means “so that.”
What to learn next
When something you were told to do becomes your own habit, you get 「〜ようにしている」: 医者に言われてから、塩分を控えるようにしている。（Ever since the doctor told me to, I try to cut down on salt）
n3-56:
The idea in one line
「〜ことから」 means “from the fact that ~, ...”. Think of a tour guide saying, “This mountain is called Pot Mountain because it looks like a pot,” or a detective reasoning, “Judging from the broken window, someone broke in.” First you put a visible fact, then you give the name or conclusion that comes from that fact.
When to use it
Origin of a nameIt explains why something has a certain name or why it's called that. It's often followed by 「〜と呼ばれる」 or 「〜という名前がついた」.
・山の形が鍋に似ていることから、「鍋山」という名前がついた。（Because the mountain's shape resembles a pot, it was named “Nabeyama”）
・いつも笑顔でいることから、彼は「太陽」と呼ばれている。（Because he's always smiling, he's called “the Sun”）
Basis for a judgmentYou draw a conclusion from a clue. It's often followed by 「〜と分かる」 or 「〜と考えられる」.
・窓が割れていることから、泥棒に入られたと分かった。（From the broken window, we could tell a burglar had broken in）
・道がぬれていることから、夜の間に雨が降ったと考えられる。（Judging from the wet road, it probably rained during the night）
Giving backgroundIn introductory or explanatory writing, it tells how something came about.
・この地域は温泉が湧いていることから、観光地として知られている。（Because hot springs well up in this area, it's known as a tourist destination）
How to form it
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach the plain form directly (the form without ます or です). Present, past and negative all work.
似ている → 似ていることから割れた → 割れたことから安い → 安いことから
な-adjectives: keep 「な」, or change it to 「である」.
静か → 静かなことから静か → 静かであることから
Nouns: add 「である」.
港町 → 港町であることから
Common pitfalls
・After a noun, use である: it's 港町であることから, not 「港町だことから」 and not 「港町のことから」.
・This is written, formal language, common in news, travel guides and explanatory texts. Using 「〜ことから」 when chatting with a friend sounds stiff. In everyday speech, 「から」 or 「ので」 is enough.
・What follows can only be a fact, a name or a judgment. It can't be an invitation, request or command such as “Let's ~,” “Please ~” or “Give me ~.”
・The reason in front should be a fact everyone can see and verify. It's not the place for your own feelings or excuses. To say “I'm tired, so I'm heading home,” use 「から」 or 「ので」.
Don't mix it up with look-alikes
Take the same fact, “the road is wet”:
から・ので = the everyday “because.” What follows can be anything: a warning, an invitation, a request.
・道がぬれているから、気をつけてね。（The road is wet, so be careful）
ことから = “drawing a conclusion from this fact.” What follows can only be a judgment or a name.
・道がぬれていることから、雨が降ったと分かる。（From the fact that the road is wet, we can tell it rained）
Saying 「道がぬれていることから、気をつけてね」 is wrong, because what follows has turned into a warning to the listener.
Quick test: if you can replace it in English with “judging from the fact that ~ (you can tell / that's why it's called ~),” use ことから. If it's just a plain “because,” use から or ので.
What to learn next
When explaining where a name comes from, the passive 「〜と呼ばれている」 (is called ~) almost always follows, so it's a good chance to review 「～（ら）れる（受身）」.
n3-51:
The idea in one line
「〜ようだ」「〜みたいだ」 mean "it seems like ~" or "it looks like ~". You use them when you've seen, heard, or sensed some clues and reached your own judgment, but you're not 100% sure. The two mean the same thing: みたい is the casual, spoken version, while ようだ is more formal and can be used in writing too.
When to use it
Guessing from cluesThe clues are things you yourself saw, heard, or sensed.
・隣の部屋、電気が消えている。留守のようだ。(The lights are off next door. It seems nobody's home.)
・あれ、鍵がない。どこかで落としたみたい。(Huh, my keys are gone. I must have dropped them somewhere.)
It's also very common for describing how you feel physically. It means "that's how it feels to me, but I can't say for sure."
・ちょっと熱があるみたい。(I think I have a bit of a fever.)
Like ~It isn't actually that thing, but it's very similar. It often appears with まるで (just like, as if).
・まるで夢みたい。(It's just like a dream.)
・今日は春のように暖かい。(It's warm today, like spring.)
How to form it
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly to the plain form (the form without ます or です). Both patterns work the same way.
降っている → 降っているようだ／降っているみたいだ
寒い → 寒いようだ／寒いみたいだ
Nouns and な-adjectives: here the two differ, so make a note of it.
Noun + ようだ needs 「の」 first: 留守 → 留守のようだ
Noun + みたいだ attaches directly: 留守 → 留守みたいだ
な-adjective + ようだ needs 「な」 first: 静か → 静かなようだ
な-adjective + みたいだ attaches directly: 静か → 静かみたいだ
For past events, nouns and な-adjectives become 「だった」 first, and then the two patterns are identical: 留守だった → 留守だったようだ／留守だったみたいだ
To be polite, swap だ for です: ようです, みたいです.
The forms you'll hear most
Before a noun it becomes ような／みたいな; before an action or adjective it becomes ように／みたいに.
・お寿司みたいな日本料理が好きです。(I like Japanese food such as sushi.)
・日本人みたいに日本語を話したい。(I want to speak Japanese like a Japanese person.)
Common mistakes
・After a noun: ようだ needs の, みたいだ doesn't. 学生のようだ and 学生みたいだ are both correct; 「学生のみたい」 and 「学生ようだ」 are both wrong.
・Many people think the plain form should keep 「だ」 and write 「留守だみたい」. That's wrong. For a present-tense noun, attach directly: 留守みたい.
・みたい sounds the same as 「見たい」 (want to see), so check the context: 子供みたい means "like a child," while 映画が見たい means "I want to see a movie."
・みたい is colloquial. For reports, essays, and formal letters, use ようです. みたいです is fine when chatting with someone older, but ようです is more appropriate in formal situations.
Telling similar forms apart
Take the same "it's raining." What matters is where your information comes from:
ようだ／みたいだ = you inferred it from clues you saw yourself: みんな傘をさしている。雨が降っているみたいだ。(Everyone has an umbrella up. It seems to be raining.)
らしい = you heard it from someone else and haven't confirmed it: 田中さんの話では、外は雨が降っているらしい。(According to Tanaka, it's apparently raining outside.)
そうだ (appearance) = it looks like it's about to happen, but it hasn't yet: 空が暗い。雨が降りそうだ。(The sky is dark. It looks like it's going to rain.) This one attaches differently: drop ます from the ます-form and add そうだ: 降ります → 降りそうだ
Quick rule: if you're guessing from what you saw or felt yourself, use ようだ／みたい. If you heard it from someone, use らしい. If it looks like it's "about to ~," use そうだ.
n3-52:
The idea in one line
「らしい」 has two meanings, almost like two different English phrases:
①"I hear that ~" / "apparently ~": a guess based on information you heard or read, or on objective clues, not something you can confirm yourself.
②"typical of ~" / "very ~-like": like saying "it feels really springlike" or "that's just like him."
When to use it
① Hearsay / apparentlyYou pass along something you heard or saw, while also signaling "that's just what I heard, no guarantees."
・来週から気温が下がるらしい。(I hear temperatures will drop starting next week.)
・田中さん、会社を辞めるらしいよ。(I heard Tanaka is quitting the company.)
・あの店のラーメン、すごくおいしいらしい。(Apparently the ramen at that place is really good.)
・地面が濡れている。雨が降ったらしい。(The ground is wet. It seems it rained.)
② Typical of ~Put a noun before it to say "it has exactly the feel that thing should have." It's usually a compliment.
・今日は春らしい天気ですね。(It's really springlike weather today, isn't it?)
・彼の発言はいかにも彼らしい。(That comment is so typical of him.)
・遅刻するなんて、彼らしくない。(Being late? That's not like him.)
How to form it
Meaning ①
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly. Past and negative forms are fine too.
行く → 行くらしい行かない → 行かないらしい高い → 高いらしい
な-adjectives and nouns: drop だ, then attach.
静かだ → drop だ → 静からしい雨だ → 雨らしい
For the past, keep だった: 雨だった → 雨だったらしい
Meaning ②
Noun + らしい: 春らしい, 学生らしい, 彼らしい
It's often strengthened with いかにも or 本当に, for example いかにも先生らしい話し方 (a way of speaking that's very much like a teacher).
「らしい」 itself conjugates like an い-adjective: らしくない, らしかった, らしいです.
Common mistakes
・Don't add an extra だ after な-adjectives or nouns: it's 静からしい, not 静かだらしい.
・When attached directly to a noun, either meaning is possible, so check the context. For example, 先生らしい人が来た is usually ①, "someone who seems to be a teacher came," not "a person with a teacherly manner."
・Put the negative in the right place: "I hear he's not coming" is 来ないらしい (①, the verb before it is negated). 彼らしくない is ②, "not like him."
・① means "I heard this from somewhere," so you can't use it for things you experience firsthand. If you yourself are going tomorrow, say 明日行きます. Saying 「明日行くらしい」 sounds like you're talking about someone else.
Telling similar forms apart
らしい (①) = hearsay: 午後から雨が降るらしい。(I hear it's going to rain from the afternoon.)
そうだ (hearsay) = you clearly pass along a specific source: 天気予報によると、午後から雨が降るそうだ。(According to the weather forecast, it's going to rain from the afternoon.)
ようだ・みたいだ = you saw or sensed it yourself: 傘を持った人が入ってきた。雨が降っているみたい。(Someone came in carrying an umbrella. It seems to be raining.)
Also, when you see a sign right in front of you and feel something is about to happen, use 雨が降りそうだ (it looks like it's going to rain).
Quick rule: to simply relay what you heard as-is, use そうだ. For a "probably so" guess based on what you heard or on objective clues, use らしい. For a judgment based on your own feelings or experience, use ようだ・みたいだ.
らしい (②) vs. っぽい are also often confused:
子どもらしい笑顔 (a smile with a child's innocence): the person really is a child and fits what a child should be like, so it leans toward praise.
大人なのに子どもっぽい。 (They're an adult but act childish.): not a child, yet resembling one, which often carries a negative tone.
Quick rule: use らしい for "it really is that, and has that quality"; use っぽい for "it actually isn't, but it's a bit like it."
n3-59:
The idea in one line
「〜を通じて」and「〜を通して」have two meanings. The first is "through ~" or "via ~". Something happens by going through a person or a channel, as in "met through a friend" or "got in touch through the internet." The second is "throughout ~". You put a period of time before it to say that something holds from start to finish, like "all year round" in English.
How to attach it
It's simple. Attach it directly after a noun:
友達 → 友達を通じて一年 → 一年を通して
To use it before a noun and modify that noun, add 「の」in between: ボランティアを通しての出会い (a connection made through volunteering)
When to use it
Through a person or channelSomeone acts as the go-between, or you use a channel such as the internet, the phone, or the media.
・友達を通じて、今の彼女と知り合った。 (I met my current girlfriend through a friend.)
・インターネットを通じて、世界中の人と話せる。 (Through the internet, you can talk with people all over the world.)
Through an experienceYou went through some experience and learned or felt something from it.
・アルバイトを通して、敬語の使い方を覚えた。 (Through my part-time job, I learned how to use honorific language.)
Throughout a periodPut a span of time like 「一年」or 「一生」before it to say that something holds for that whole period.
・この島は一年を通して暖かい。 (This island is warm all year round.)
・祖父は一生を通じて、同じ会社で働いた。 (My grandfather worked at the same company his whole life.)
を通じて vs を通して: what's the difference?
In most cases the two are interchangeable and mean about the same thing, so don't stress. If you have to split hairs:
を通じて is used more for "channels" like the internet, the phone, or personal connections.
を通して has more of a feeling of "doing it yourself, on purpose, firsthand," so it's common when talking about experience, practice, or experiments.
When you're not sure, either choice won't be badly wrong.
Common mistakes
・Don't use it for vehicles or ordinary tools. "Go by bus" is バスで行く, and "cut with scissors" is はさみで切る. You can't say バスを通して行く. を通じて is about "the person or channel something passes through," not the tool in your hand.
・"Pass an exam" is not this grammar. Say 試験に合格する. The English "through" in "get through an exam" doesn't map onto を通して either.
・The particle before it is を. Don't write に.
・For the "throughout a period" use, put a span of time before it, such as 一年, 一生, or 四季. It means "during that whole period," not "after that time has passed."
・The tone is fairly formal and very common in news, essays, and self-introductions. When chatting with friends and saying "introduced by a friend," people often say 友達の紹介で.
Don't confuse it with look-alikes
Take "passing a message to the teacher":
メールで先生に伝えた。 (I told the teacher by email.): で = the tool or method, the most ordinary everyday choice.
先輩を通じて先生に伝えた。 (I told the teacher through a senior student.): を通じて = a person or channel in the middle carried it for you.

Another easy one to mix up is によって, which says "by what means something is achieved" or "what caused something":
この研究によって、病気の原因が分かった。 (Thanks to this research, the cause of the disease was found.)
If you met someone through a friend's introduction, say 友達を通じて知り合った, not 友達によって知り合った.
Quick test: if a "person, channel, or experience" sits in the middle as a go-between, use を通じて / を通して. For a plain tool or a vehicle, use で. For a method or a cause, use によって.
What to learn next
Other patterns in the "noun + を + ~" shape are worth looking at next: 〜を中心に (centered on ~) and 〜をはじめ (starting with ~). These often show up together in the same article.
n3-60:
The idea in one line
「〜に基づいて」means "based on ~" or "in accordance with ~". It tells you what you rely on as your basis when you do something. A film's opening credits often say "This film is based on a true story," and in Japanese that's この映画は実話に基づいている。
What goes before it is the basis for "what you're going on," such as facts, data, rules, or experience.
How to attach it
Followed by an actionnoun + に基づいて + verb
・規則に基づいて判断します。 (I'll judge according to the rules.)
・データに基づいて計画を立てた。 (I made a plan based on the data.)
Followed by a nounnoun + に基づく / に基づいた + noun. Both forms are common.
・調査結果に基づく報告書 (a report based on the survey results)
・経験に基づいたアドバイス (advice based on experience)
At the end of a sentenceUse 〜に基づいている to mean "is based on ~."
・この話は事実に基づいています。 (This story is based on fact.)
In news and official documents you'll also see に基づき. It means the same as に基づいて, just more bookish.
Common mistakes
・What goes before it must be a basis, not a person directly. For "what the teacher said," say 先生の話に基づいて, not 「先生に基づいて」.
・Before a noun, use 基づく / 基づいた. Don't write 「データに基づいて計画」.
・It's read もとづいて. The kana is 「づ」, not 「ず」, so when typing, enter motodu.
・The tone is fairly formal and it often appears in reports, the news, and work settings. It's less common in casual chat with friends.
Don't confuse it with look-alikes
Even with the same topic, "data," these three phrases mean different things:
データについて説明します。 (I'll explain the data itself.)
データに基づいて説明します。 (I'll explain using the data as my basis, for example explaining a plan or a conclusion.)
データによると、売り上げが増えています。 (According to the data, sales are increasing.)
「によると」names the source of information, and what follows is "what the data says." It can't be followed by an action you take yourself.
Quick test: for "about ~" use について. For "according to ~" (it shows, I hear) use によると. For "doing or judging something on the basis of ~" use に基づいて.
n3-62:
The idea in one line
「〜ものだから」and「〜もので」work like English "It's just that…, you see, so…". Say you're late and tell your boss, "Sorry, the train was delayed, you see…" That slightly defensive, please-understand-me tone is exactly what these carry.
When to use it
Explaining when apologizingWhen you've made a mistake or caused trouble, add your reason to show "I didn't mean to."
・すみません、電車が止まっていたものですから。(Sorry, the train had stopped, you see…)
・寝坊したもので、遅れてしまいました。(I overslept, so I ended up being late.)
The first sentence「電車が止まっていたものですから。」stops right at「ものですから。」. It gives only the reason and leaves the rest unsaid. You'll hear this all the time in apologies.
Explaining your situationA soft way to explain why you can't do something, or why you did something.
・子どもがまだ小さいもので、夜はあまり出かけられないんです。(My child is still little, so I can't go out much at night.)
So ~ that I couldn't help itExplaining that you ended up doing something because you couldn't resist.
・あまりにおいしかったものだから、全部食べちゃった。(It was so delicious that I ate it all.)
How to form it
Verbs: plain form, attached directly　寝坊した → 寝坊したものだから
い-adjectives: attached directly　忙しい → 忙しいものだから
な-adjectives: add「な」　静か → 静かなものだから
Nouns: also add「な」　初めて → 初めてなもので
In speech it's often shortened to もんだから or もんで. With superiors and customers, use ものですから. もので is already a bit polite, so it's common in formal situations too.
Common mistakes
・After a な-adjective or noun it's「な」, not「だ」: say 静かなものだから, not「静かだものだから」.
・The second half can't be a command, request, invitation, or your own intention. 雨が降っているものだから、傘を持っていってください。 is wrong. Change it to 雨が降っているから、傘を持っていってください。 (It's raining, so please take an umbrella.)
・It's for your own situation and personal reasons. For objective explanations of causes, as in news or reports, don't use it; use ので or ため.
・If you use it constantly when you're clearly at fault, it sounds like you're making excuses. When you really are in the wrong, a sincere apology matters more.
Telling it apart from similar forms
から／ので = simply states the reason: 電車が遅れたので、遅刻しました。 (The train was delayed, so I was late.)
ものだから = states the reason and adds "it wasn't my fault, please understand": 電車が遅れたものですから、遅刻してしまいました。 (The train was delayed, you see, so I ended up late…)
If the second half tells people to do something, you can only use から／ので: 電車が遅れているから、タクシーで行こう。 (The train is delayed, so let's take a taxi.)
ものだ (at the end of a sentence) = an exclamation, "that's just how it is." It isn't giving a reason: 時間が経つのは早いものだ。 (Time really flies.)
ものだから has「から」or「で」after it, so it is always giving a reason.
Quick test: if you want the listener's understanding and you're explaining your own situation, use ものだから／もので. If the second half tells someone to do something or invites them, switch to から／ので. If the sentence ends at「ものだ。」, it's an exclamation, not a reason.
What to learn next
In everyday conversation there's an even shorter, more childlike version that ends the sentence with もん: だって、知らなかったんだもん。 (But I just didn't know!) Use it only with people you're very close to.
n3-63:
The idea in one line
「さえ」means "even ~". It deliberately picks the most basic, most obvious example, meaning "if even this is the case, then the rest goes without saying." For "I'm so busy I don't even have time to eat," Japanese says: 忙しくて、ご飯を食べる時間さえない。
How to form it
After nounsAdd さえ directly after the noun. Drop the original「が」or「を」; さえ replaces it.
時間がない → 時間さえない (don't even have time)
自分の名前を書けない → 自分の名前さえ書けない (can't even write my own name)
Keep other particlesDon't drop「に」「で」「と」; just put さえ after them.
家族に話していない → 家族にさえ話していない (haven't even told my family)
Saying "even a certain person"To stress "even this person…", you'll often hear「でさえ」: 子供でさえ知っている。 (Even children know.)
After verbsTo say "don't even ~", drop ます from the verb and add さえしない.
見ます → drop ます → 見さえしない (doesn't even look)
・彼は私の顔を見さえしなかった。(He didn't even look at my face.)
When to use it
Followed by a negativeThis is the most common use: you don't even have, or can't even do, the most basic thing.
・忙しくて、水を飲む時間さえなかった。(I was so busy I didn't even have time to drink water.)
・足が痛くて、歩くことさえできない。(My leg hurts so much I can't even walk.)
Followed by a positiveEven the least likely person knows it or can do it, which implies "everyone else surely should too."
・そんなことは、子供でさえ知っている。(Even a child knows that.)
・この問題は、先生でさえ間違えた。(Even the teacher got this question wrong.)
Common mistakes
・You must drop「が」and「を」: 「時間がさえない」is wrong; say 時間さえない. But keep「に」「で」「と」, so it's 家族にさえ, not 家族さえ.
・さえ is fairly strong and formal. When chatting with friends, many people just use「も」: 時間もない. The meaning is similar, just without the heavy "even this" feel.
・On its own, さえ means "even ~", not "if only". Many learners see さえ and translate it as "if only," but for that meaning it must be followed by a conditional form (see the next section).
Telling it apart from similar forms
Both talk about "time," but what follows changes the meaning a lot:
さえ = even ~: 最近は寝る時間さえない。 (Lately I don't even have time to sleep.)
さえ〜ば = as long as ~: 時間さえあれば、旅行に行きたい。 (As long as I have time, I want to go traveling.)
さえ〜たら／なら also means "as long as ~": 時間さえあったら、行けるのに。 (If only I had time, I could go.)
Quick test: if さえ is followed by an "if" conditional, it means "as long as ~." That includes「〜ば」and also「〜たら」「〜なら」, such as あれば, あったら, あるなら. If there's no such conditional, it means "even ~."
What to learn next
Next, learn「〜さえ〜ば」(as long as ~): この薬さえ飲めば、すぐ治りますよ。 (As long as you take this medicine, you'll get better soon.)
n3-64:
The idea in one sentence
「〜こそ」 works like a highlighter run over the word before it. It means 「this is the one」, 「this is what's really ～」, or 「this time for sure」. 今年頑張る just means "I'll do my best this year," but 今年こそ頑張る becomes "This year I'm giving it everything, no matter what." It's much stronger.
When to use it
This time, for sureYou failed before, and now you've made up your mind. It often appears with 今年, 明日 and 次.
・今年こそ合格するぞ。(I'm passing this year, for sure!)
・次こそ負けないよ。(I definitely won't lose next time.)
I'm the one who ～When someone thanks you, apologizes, or asks for your kind regard, you reply "No, it's me who should say that." こちらこそ works as a complete reply on its own, and it's very handy.
・A：いつもありがとう。　B：こちらこそ。(A: Thanks for everything. B: No, thank you.)
・A：遅れてすみません。　B：いえ、こちらこそすみません。(A: Sorry I'm late. B: Not at all, I'm the one who's sorry.)
This is the oneIt stresses "not anything else, exactly this."
・今こそ挑戦するときだ。(Now is exactly the time to take on the challenge.)
・これこそ私が探していた本だ。(This is exactly the book I've been looking for.)
How to form it
Basically it's noun + こそ. If the original sentence has は or が, just replace it with こそ:
今年は頑張る → 今年こそ頑張る
これが大切だ → これこそ大切だ
を is usually dropped too, with こそ attached directly.
With particles like に and で, keep them and put こそ after them:
・あなたにこそ見てほしい。(You're the one I most want to see it.)
Common mistakes
・は and が can't go before こそ. Forms like 今年はこそ and 私がこそ are wrong, so remove them first. The same goes for を, which is normally dropped. Placing them after こそ is fine, though: 今年こそは and これこそが are both common.
・こちらこそ is very polite, but あなたこそ and お前こそ are often used to snap back in an argument: お前こそ何してるんだよ。 (What are YOU doing, then?). Don't use these with people senior to you.
・こそ is strong. It's there to highlight a key point. If you add it to every word, it's like highlighting the whole page, so nothing stands out.
Don't confuse it with similar forms
Both talk about this year's exam:
今年は合格したい。 (I want to pass this year.): A neutral statement with no special emotion.
今年こそ合格したい。 (I want to pass this year, for sure.): You didn't pass before, and this time you're determined.
こそ is often studied together with さえ, but they point in opposite directions. さえ means "even ～": it gives an extreme example to imply that everything else goes without saying. It works in both affirmative and negative sentences, for example 簡単な問題さえできなかった。 (I couldn't even do the easy questions.) and 子供でさえ知っている。 (Even children know it.) こそ, on the other hand, makes that word the star.
Quick test: to say "this is the one," "this time for sure," or "I'm the one who...," use こそ. To say "even ～," use さえ. For a plain, ordinary statement, just use は.
What to learn next
からこそ means "precisely because ～," and it stresses the reason: 好きだからこそ、厳しく言うんだ。 (I'm only this strict with you because I care.) You'll also hear だからこそ a lot, meaning "precisely because of that."
n3-65:
The idea in one sentence
「〜そうだ」 means "looks like ～" or "seems ～". You haven't tasted the cake yet, but just looking at it you think "that looks delicious," and in Japanese that's おいしそう. The key point is that you see how something looks right now and make an intuitive guess. You haven't actually confirmed it.
When to use it
Guessing from appearanceAdjective + そう means "looks ～."
・このケーキ、おいしそう。(This cake looks so good.)
・田中さん、今日は元気そうですね。(Mr. Tanaka looks energetic today.)
About to happenVerb + そう mostly means "looks like it's about to ～."
・空が暗くなってきた。雨が降りそうだ。(The sky's getting dark. It looks like it's going to rain.)
・シャツのボタンが取れそう。(The button on my shirt looks like it's about to come off.)
How to form it
い-adjectives: drop the final 「い」 and add そう.
おいしい → drop い → おいしそう高い → 高そう
な-adjectives: just add そう.
元気 → 元気そう暇 → 暇そう
Verbs: change to the ます form, drop ます, and add そう.
降ります → drop ます → 降りそう落ちます → 落ちそう
Two exceptions to memorize: いい → よさそうない → なさそう
Before a noun use そうな, and before a verb use そうに:
・高そうな時計ですね。(That's an expensive-looking watch.)
・子どもたちが楽しそうに遊んでいる。(The children are playing and look like they're having fun.)
Saying "doesn't look ～"
Adjectives: おいしくなさそう (doesn't look tasty), 暇じゃなさそう (doesn't look free)
Verbs: use 「そうにない」 or 「そうもない」.
・この仕事は今日中に終わりそうにない。(It doesn't look like this work will be finished today.)
Common mistakes
・You can't say 「いそう」 for いい. Say よさそう: 天気がよさそうだ (The weather looks nice).
・You can't add this そう directly to a noun: ×学生そうだ. To say "looks like a student," use 学生みたいだ.
・Don't use そう for things that are obvious at a glance and need no guessing. A red flower is simply 赤い, not 「赤そう」.
・かわいそう means "poor thing," not "looks cute." To say something is cute, use かわいい.
・With verbs, そう often means "about to ～": 泣きそう means "about to cry," not "seems to be crying."
Don't confuse it with similar forms
The hearsay そうだ (the next grammar point) looks almost identical, but the meaning is completely different. Compare them on the same topic:
雨が降りそうだ。 (Looking at the sky, it looks like rain is coming.)
雨が降るそうだ。 (I heard from the weather forecast that it will rain.)
おいしそうだ。 (It looks tasty.)
おいしいそうだ。 (I heard it's tasty.)
元気そうだ。 (He looks energetic.)
元気だそうだ。 (I heard he's energetic.)
Nouns only have the hearsay version: 学生だそうだ。 (I heard he's a student.)
Quick tests:
・Verbs and い-adjectives: if the part before そう is shortened (降り, おいし), it means "looks like." If the full form comes before it (降る, おいしい), it means "I heard."
・な-adjectives and nouns: check whether there's a 「だ」. 元気そうだ = looks like; 元気だそうだ = I heard; 学生だそうだ = I heard he's a student.
Also, ようだ・みたいだ mean "seems like" too, but they're more of a judgment you make after putting several clues together. そう is a first impression from a single glance. You see a cake and say おいしそう. You say おいしいみたい only after seeing everyone enjoying it.
n3-66:
The idea in one line
「〜そうだ」means “I hear that…” or “they say…”. When you pick something up from the news, a friend, or the weather forecast and want to pass it on, you add そうだ at the end of the sentence. The key point: you didn't see this yourself and you're not guessing. Someone else said it.
When to use it
Passing on what you heardRelay what someone else said as it is.
・田中さんは来月結婚するそうです。(I hear Mr. Tanaka is getting married next month.)
・部長は今日、会社に来ないそうです。(I hear the department head isn't coming to the office today.)
Naming the sourceYou'll often see「〜によると」or「〜の話では」in front, making clear where you heard it.
・天気予報によると、明日は雨だそうだ。(According to the weather forecast, it will rain tomorrow.)
・先生の話では、来週テストがあるそうです。(The teacher says there's a test next week.)
How to form it
First put the content you're relaying into the plain form (the form without ます or です), then add そうだ. Tense and affirmative/negative are all handled inside the part before そうだ.
Verbs: 降る → 降るそうだ降った → 降ったそうだ降らない → 降らないそうだ
i-adjectives: 寒い → 寒いそうだ寒かった → 寒かったそうだ
na-adjectives: you need to add だ　静か → 静かだそうだ
Nouns: add だ here too　雨 → 雨だそうだ雨だった → 雨だったそうだ
When talking to a teacher or a customer, change the ending to そうです.
How you'll hear it most
Among friendsIn casual speech people more often use「〜って」or「〜んだって」. The meaning is the same: “I hear that…”.
・田中さん、来月結婚するんだって。(I heard Tanaka's getting married next month!)
・明日、雨だって。(Apparently it's going to rain tomorrow.)
Easy mistakes
・After a noun or na-adjective, you can't drop だ. Writing 静かそうだ turns it into “looks quiet,” which is a completely different meaning. “I hear it's quiet” is 静かだそうだ.
・そうだ itself can't be made negative or past. You can't say ×来るそうではない or ×来るそうだった. Change the part before it instead: 来ないそうだ (I hear he's not coming), 来たそうだ (I hear he came).
・In English, “I hear that…” sits at the start of the sentence, but Japanese そうだ always goes at the very end.
・For hearsay with いい, it's いいそうだ (I hear it's good). よさそうだ means “looks good,” which is the other そうだ.
Don't confuse it with look-alikes
Appearance そうだ (n3-65): something you see or sense yourself, “looks like… / is about to…”. For verbs, take ます off the ます-form; for adjectives, drop い; then add そうだ.
Hearsay そうだ (this lesson): something someone told you, “I hear that…”, attached to the full plain form.
Both about the weather:
・雨が降りそうだ。(It looks like it's about to rain: you judge from looking at the sky.)
・雨が降るそうだ。(I hear it's going to rain: you got it from the forecast.)
Both about a cake:
・このケーキはおいしそうだ。(This cake looks delicious.)
・このケーキはおいしいそうだ。(I hear this cake is delicious.)
らしい (n3-52) can also be translated as “I hear,” but with そうだ someone clearly said it and you're relaying it. らしい is more like “it seems that…”: the source is vaguer, or you're inferring from things you heard or saw.
・田中さんは来月結婚するそうだ。(I hear Mr. Tanaka is getting married next month: someone told me so.)
・田中さんは来月結婚するらしい。(It seems Mr. Tanaka is getting married next month: I've picked up some rumors.)
Quick test: if what comes before is the full form like「降る、おいしい、雨だ」, it means “I hear.” If it's the clipped form like「降り、おいし」, it means “looks like.”
n3-67:
The idea in one line
Think of「くる」and「いく」as arrows: くる = moving toward “me, now”, いく = moving away from “me, now”. てくる often matches English “come / start to / has been getting…”, and ていく often matches “go / keep on…ing from here.”
How to form it
Put the verb in the te-form, then add くる or いく.
増える → 増えて → 増えてくる
なる → なって → なっていく
The くる or いく at the end conjugates as usual: てきます, てきた, ていきます, ていった.
When to use it
Direction in spaceUse てくる when something or someone comes toward you, and ていく when it leaves your side. What matters is where you are when you speak.
・雨が降りそうだから、傘を持っていこう。(It looks like rain, so let's take an umbrella with us.)
・友達がケーキを持ってきてくれた。(A friend brought me a cake.)
Go do something and come backてくる can also mean “go do something and then come back.” The 行ってきます you say when leaving the house means “I'll go and be back.”
・ちょっとコンビニで飲み物を買ってくる。(I'll go grab a drink at the convenience store and be right back.)
Change: up to nowてきた = it has been changing from the past up to now, and you can feel it now.
・最近、日本語が少し分かってきた。(Lately I've started to understand a bit of Japanese.)
・ここ数年、オンライン会議が増えてきた。(Online meetings have become more and more common over the past few years.)
Change: from now onていく = starting now, it will keep changing or keep going.
・これからどんどん寒くなっていく。(It's going to get colder and colder from now on.)
・これからも日本語の勉強を続けていきたい。(I want to keep studying Japanese from now on, too.)
Starting to happenてきた is also often used to say a state has “started to appear,” like English “it's starting to…”.
・あ、雨が降ってきた。(Oh, it's started to rain.)
・お腹がすいてきた。(I'm getting hungry.)
Easy mistakes
・Direction depends on where you are when you speak, not where the listener is. If you promise your teacher in person at school, you're already at the place the thing will be delivered to, so はい、明日持ってきます。 is perfectly natural.
・English “I'll go buy it” doesn't say whether you come back. If you'll return after buying, Japanese speakers often say 買ってくる. 買っていく means “buy it and take it somewhere else,” for example お土産を買っていく (buy a souvenir to take along).
・When talking about time, don't mix up “up to now” and “from now on”: if これから comes before it, you need ていく. You can't say 「これから寒くなってきた」.
・くる and いく here are usually written in hiragana. The past form is てきた, not 「てくた」; the past of ていく is ていった.
・In casual speech ていく often becomes 「てく」, as in 寒くなってく. Don't mistake it for a different grammar point when you hear it.
Don't confuse it with look-alikes
Three ways to say “the weather is getting colder”:
寒くなってきた。(It's already been getting colder and colder, and you can feel it now.)
寒くなっていく。(It's going to get colder and colder from now on.)
寒くなる一方だ。(It just keeps getting colder with no end in sight, often with a hint of helplessness.)
The first two differ in time direction, while 一方だ stresses “it only keeps developing in this one direction.”
Quick test: looking from the past up to now, use てきた. Looking from now onward, use ていく. For “it just keeps getting worse and won't stop,” use 一方だ.
What to learn next
Add ている after てきた to get てきている, meaning “this change is still going on now”: 外国人観光客が増えてきている。(The number of foreign tourists keeps growing, and it's still rising.)
n3-57:
The idea in one line
「〜たびに」 means "every time ~, ~". Whenever the first thing happens, the second thing follows, with almost no exceptions. Think "every time I hear this song, I want to cry" or "I buy souvenirs on every business trip." That's this pattern.
When to use it
A feeling or reaction that comes every timeWhenever something happens, the same feeling rises up in you.
・この写真を見るたびに、学生時代を思い出す。（Every time I look at this photo, I remember my school days.）
・この歌を聞くたびに、泣いてしまう。（Every time I hear this song, I end up crying.）
Something you do every timeWhenever something happens, you always do a certain action.
・出張のたびにお土産を買って帰る。（I buy a souvenir and bring it home every time I go on a business trip.）
A change you notice every timeEach time you meet, you find that something is different.
・彼に会うたびに、背が伸びている。（Every time I see him, he's grown taller.）
How to form it
Verbs: dictionary form (the base form you'd look up in a dictionary) + たびに.
会う → 会うたびに見る → 見るたびに来る → 来るたびに
Nouns: add 「の」 in between.
旅行 → 旅行のたびに試験 → 試験のたびに
The noun should be something that happens repeatedly, like 出張, 旅行, 試験, 引っ越し. Both 雨のたびに and 雨が降るたびに are fine.
Common mistakes
・Even when you're talking about the past, the verb before it stays in dictionary form. Put the past 「た」 at the end of the sentence only: 子供のころ、祖母の家に行くたびに、お菓子をもらった。（When I was a kid, every time I went to my grandmother's house, I got sweets.）Don't say 「行ったたびに」.
・What comes before it must be something that can happen many times. Things that happen once in a lifetime (being born, graduating from university) can't be used.
・A noun before it must stand for "an event." Nouns that aren't events, like 本 or 先生, don't work. Switch to a verb: 本を読むたびに（every time I read a book）.
・For everyday routines that happen as a matter of course, like brushing your teeth or eating breakfast, Japanese people usually just say 毎朝 or いつも. Using たびに makes it sound like you're stressing something special, which feels odd.
・たびに is also often written with kanji as 度に. It's read the same way, so don't mistake it for a different grammar point.
Don't mix it up with similar patterns
Take the same situation, "going to Japan":
日本へ行くたびに、ラーメンを食べる。（Every time I go to Japan, I eat ramen.）
　→ Stresses "every single time, without missing once."
日本へ行くときは、いつもラーメンを食べる。（When I go to Japan, I always eat ramen.）
　→ Almost the same meaning, but the tone is plainer and more everyday.
二年ごとに日本へ行く。（I go to Japan every two years.）
　→ ごとに can follow a number, to say "every so often" or "every so many." たびに can't do that, so you can't say 「二年のたびに」.
Quick rule: if what comes before is a number or a time interval, use ごとに. If it's an event and you want to say "every time ~, ~," use たびに, or the lighter 「ときはいつも」 if you want it to sound more relaxed.
n3-58:
The idea in one line
「〜を中心に」 means "centered on ~," "with ~ as the core," "mainly ~". You treat something as the core and things unfold around it, or you say where the focus or main range of something lies.
When to use it
PlacesSpreading out or distributed around a certain place.
・駅を中心に店が並んでいる。（Shops line the streets centered on the station.）
・九州を中心に大雨が降った。（Heavy rain fell mainly around Kyushu.）
PeopleWith a certain person as the core, everyone moves around them.
・田中さんを中心に、新しいチームができた。（A new team was formed with Mr. Tanaka at its core.）
Main range and focus"Mainly ~," but it doesn't mean only that.
・このアニメは子どもを中心に人気がある。（This anime is popular mainly among children.）
・今日は文法を中心に復習しよう。（Let's review mainly grammar today.）
How to form it
What comes before it is always a noun, and an action or state follows:
駅 → 駅を中心に　You can also say 駅を中心にして or 駅を中心として, with the same meaning.
When it needs to modify a noun directly, change it to を中心とした (or を中心とする):
・野菜を中心とした食事（a diet centered on vegetables）
・東京を中心とした関東地方（the Kanto region, centered on Tokyo）
Common mistakes
・The particle is を: 駅を中心に, not 「駅に中心に」 or 「駅が中心に」.
・You can't put a verb directly before it; use a noun. To say "focusing on studying," use 勉強を中心に.
・「を中心に」 is different from 「の中心に」. 公園の中心に噴水がある。 means "There's a fountain right in the middle of the park." It only describes a position, not something "unfolding around ~."
・"Mainly ~" doesn't mean "only": 若者を中心に人気だ means most fans are young people, but people of other ages like it too.
・When modifying a noun after it, don't write 「野菜を中心にの食事」. Use 野菜を中心とした食事.
Don't mix it up with similar patterns
をはじめ（として） = "starting with A, and also B, C…" It picks one representative example, and the point is that there are others besides it.
を中心に = "mainly A," and the point is that A is the core and carries the most weight.
Compare them in the same situation:
・このお菓子は東京を中心に人気がある。（This sweet is popular mainly in Tokyo.）
・このお菓子は東京をはじめ、大阪や福岡でも人気がある。（This sweet is popular in Tokyo, and also in Osaka, Fukuoka, and elsewhere.）
Quick rule: to say "mainly in A, centered on A," use を中心に. To say "A is just one example, and B and C are the same," use をはじめ.
n3-68:
The idea in one line
All three are 「te-form + a little tail」. The difference is what you want to say:
ている = how things are now (in the middle of doing something, or staying in a state)
てある = someone set something up and it's still that way (you can tell it was done on purpose)
ておく = do it ahead of time, for later (like English "go ahead and ~" or "~ in advance")
Picture walking into a meeting room and seeing the window open. Just describing "the window is open" uses ている. Saying "someone has already opened the window" uses てある. Before the meeting, when you say "I'll open the window first," you use ておく.
How to form it
All of them attach after the verb's te-form:
開ける → 開けて → 開けている／開けてある／開けておく
ている: how things are now
In progressThe action is happening right now.
・今、ご飯を食べている。(I'm eating right now.)
State remainsSomething happened, and the result has stayed that way.
・エアコンがついている。(The air conditioner is on.)
・姉は結婚している。(My older sister is married.)
てある: someone set it up, and it stays
Result + done by someoneThe focus is "it's like this now, and someone did it on purpose." Who did it usually goes unsaid. The thing in front is mostly marked with が.
・ドアに名前が書いてある。(A name is written on the door.)
・ビールが冷やしてある。(The beer has been chilled.)
ておく: do it in advance
Preparing aheadYou get something done first, for later.
・旅行の前に、ホテルを予約しておく。(Before the trip, I'll book the hotel ahead of time.)
Leave as isYou deliberately keep it that way and don't touch it.
・窓は開けておいてください。(Please leave the window open. No need to close it.)
In speech it's often shortened to とく:買っておく → 買っとく読んでおく → 読んどく
・ジュース、買っとくね。(I'll go ahead and buy the juice, okay?)
Easy mistakes
・First, separate two kinds of verbs: verbs where things change by themselves (開く, つく, 閉まる; the thing takes が), and verbs where someone acts on it (開ける, つける, 閉める; the thing takes を).
・てある goes with the "someone acts on it" type: 窓が開けてある is correct, while 窓が開いてある is not said.
・窓が開けている is wrong; it would come out like "the window is opening something." Say either 窓が開いている or 窓が開けてある.
・結婚している means "is married," not "is getting married right now"; 知っている means "know." Don't turn every ている into "is ~ing."
・The casual 「てる」 is a contraction of ている, while 「とく」 is the one that means ておく. Don't mix them up.
Telling look-alikes apart
One window, four ways to say it:
・窓が開いている。(The window is open: just describing what you see.)
・窓が開けてある。(The window has been opened: you sense someone opened it on purpose for some reason.)
・窓を開けておく。(I'll open the window in advance: because it'll be needed soon.)
・田中さんが窓を開けている。(Mr. Tanaka is opening the window: the focus is on the person's action.)
Also, once you've done something with ておいた, the resulting state becomes てある: 昨日資料を準備しておいたから、もう準備してある。(I prepared the materials yesterday, so they're already ready.)
Quick rule of thumb: to describe only how something looks, use 「が＋ている」. To stress "someone set it up and it's still that way," use 「が＋てある」. To say "do it first, for later," use 「を＋ておく」.
What to learn next
「〜っぱなし」 also leaves something as it is, but it's mostly about forgetting to put it away or just leaving it, with a negative feel: 窓を開けっぱなしにした。(I left the window open and never closed it.) That's the exact opposite of the deliberate 開けておく.
n3-69:
The idea in one line
In English, "do it for me" or "help" covers everything: he did it for me, I did it for him, I asked him to do it for me. Japanese adds くれる、あげる、もらう after the verb to show which direction the favor travels.
くれる: someone else → me (someone does it for me)
あげる: me → someone else (I do it for someone)
もらう: I receive the favor from someone (I get someone to do it for me)
How to form it
Change the verb to its te-form, then attach directly.
手伝う → 手伝って → 手伝ってくれる
教える → 教えて → 教えてもらう
Looking at the three separately: it's all about particles
てくれるThe star is the other person, and the doer takes が. "Me" usually goes unsaid. My family counts as "my side" too, so you can use it for them.
・友達が引っ越しを手伝ってくれた。(My friend helped me move.)
・母がお弁当を作ってくれた。(My mom made me a lunch box.)
てもらうThe star is me, and the doer takes に.
・駅員さんに道を教えてもらった。(I had the station attendant tell me the way.)
・先生にほめてもらった。(I got praised by my teacher.)
てあげるThe star is me, and the particle after the other person depends on the original verb.
・妹に本を読んであげた。(I read a book to my little sister.)
・友達を駅まで送ってあげた。(I saw my friend off to the station.)
The form you'll hear most: asking a favor
Turn it into a question and it means "could you ~ for me?" The further down the list, the more polite.
・ちょっと手伝ってくれる？(Can you give me a hand? To a friend.)
・この書類、確認してもらえますか。(Could you check this document for me?)
・もう少しゆっくり話してもらえませんか。(Could you speak a little more slowly?)
Easy mistakes
・Wrong direction: くれる can only point toward "my side." For "I taught my friend," you can't say 友達に教えてくれた; say 友達に教えてあげた.
・Wrong particle: くれる goes with が, もらう goes with に. 友達に手伝ってくれた is wrong.
・Translating too plainly sounds cold: for "He bought it for me," saying 彼が買った is grammatical, but it sounds like you aren't grateful. When someone does something for you, Japanese people almost always add くれた.
・てあげる is rude toward superiors: it feels like "I'm doing you a favor." Saying 荷物を持ってあげます to a teacher won't do; say お持ちします (let me carry that for you). Even with friends, saying 「～てあげる」 to their face can sound condescending, so people often say 手伝おうか？ (want me to help?) instead.
・もらう doesn't always mean "ask": in ほめてもらった, you didn't ask the teacher for anything; you just received the benefit.
Telling look-alikes apart
てくれる and てもらう often describe the same event; the difference is who the star is.
田中さんが傘を貸してくれた。(Mr. Tanaka lent me his umbrella: the star is Tanaka, and the focus is his kindness.)
田中さんに傘を貸してもらった。(I got to borrow an umbrella from Mr. Tanaka: the star is me, and it often feels like "I was the one who asked.")
Quick rule of thumb: if the doer takes が, use くれる; if it takes に, use もらう. To stress the other person's kindness, use くれる; to say "I asked and got help," use もらう.
What to learn next
With teachers and superiors, switch to the honorific versions: くれる → くださる, もらう → いただく.
・先生が教えてくださいました。(The teacher taught me.)
・先生に教えていただきました。(I had the teacher teach me.)
n3-70:
The idea in one line
「〜させる」 means "make someone do ~" or "let someone do ~". A mother makes her child eat vegetables, a boss lets employees leave early: both use it. It can mean forcing someone or allowing them, and the context tells you which.
When to use it
Making someone doYou tell someone to do something, usually from a higher position to a lower one, such as parents to a child or a manager to a subordinate.
・母は子供に野菜を食べさせた。(Mom made her child eat vegetables.)
Letting someone doThe other person already wants to do it, and you allow it or step back and let them.
・父は私を一人で旅行に行かせてくれた。(My dad let me go on a trip by myself.)
Causing a feelingMaking someone cry, making someone happy, making someone worry.
・彼女を泣かせてしまった。(I made my girlfriend cry.)
・親を心配させたくない。(I don't want to make my parents worry.)
How to form it: check the verb group first
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the 「あ」-row sound of the same row, then add 「せる」.
書く → change く to か → 書かせる
飲む → 飲ませる待つ → 待たせる帰る → 帰らせる
Watch out for verbs ending in 「う」: the 「う」 changes to わ: 買う → change う to わ → 買わせる
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop the final 「る」 and add 「させる」.
食べる → 食べさせる見る → 見させる調べる → 調べさせる
Group 3 (only two verbs, just memorize them): する → させる来る → 来させる（こさせる）
Once formed, 「〜させる」 is itself a Group 2 verb, so it conjugates like one: 書かせます, 書かせた, 書かせて, 書かせない.
Who makes, who does: particle placement
Basic pattern: the person who makes + は／が, the person who does it + に or を, and 〜させる at the end. Whether the doer takes に or を depends on whether the action already has its own 「を」:
Actions that already have a 「を」 object (read a book, eat a meal, do homework): the doer takes に, because を is already used by the object.
・先生は学生に教科書を読ませた。(The teacher had the students read the textbook.)
Actions with no 「を」 object (go, play, cry, wait): the doer usually takes を.
・子供を公園で遊ばせる。(I let my child play in the park.)
The second case can also use に, as in 子供に自由に遊ばせる, which sounds more like "respecting the other person and letting them do whatever they like." When you're just starting, the basic rule above is enough.
Forms you'll hear most
〜させてください"Please let me ~." A polite way to ask permission when you want to do something.
・少し考えさせてください。(Please let me think about it for a moment.)
・ここで働かせてください。(Please let me work here.)
待たせる"Make someone wait." Very common in apologies.
・待たせてごめん。(Sorry to keep you waiting.)
・お待たせしました。(Thank you for waiting. / Sorry to keep you waiting.)
Easy mistakes
・Verbs ending in 「う」 change to わ: 買わせる, 会わせる, 使わせる, not 買あせる.
・来させる is read こさせる, not きさせる.
・Don't add an extra 「さ」 to Group 1 verbs: it's 読ませる, not 読まさせる. Japanese people often say it that way too, but it's generally considered incorrect.
・Don't use させる toward teachers, bosses, or customers, because it sounds like you're giving them orders. To ask someone above you to do something, use 「〜てもらう」 or 「〜ていただく」: 先生に説明していただきました。(The teacher kindly explained it to me.)
・English happily says "This movie moved me," but in Japanese it's more natural to say この映画に感動した ("I was moved by this movie"). A literal translation like この映画は私を感動させた sounds like translationese.
Telling look-alikes apart
Take the same event, cleaning a room, and look at who orders and who does it:
させる: 母は私に部屋を掃除させた。(Mom made me clean my room: Mom orders, I do it.)
させられる: 私は母に部屋を掃除させられた。(I was made to clean my room by Mom: I'm still the one cleaning, but it's told from my side, with a feeling of reluctance.)
てもらう: 私は母に部屋を掃除してもらった。(I had Mom clean my room for me: I asked, Mom did it.)
Quick test: if the subject makes someone else do it, it's させる. If the subject is the one being forced, it's させられる. If the subject asks someone to do it for them, it's てもらう.
What to learn next
Add the passive to させる and you get 「being forced to do ~」: 〜させられる (causative-passive): 子供のころ、毎日ピアノを練習させられた。(When I was a kid, I was made to practice piano every day.)
n3-71:
The idea in one line
「〜（ら）れる」 is the Japanese passive, like English "was/got ~ed". It puts the focus on the person who receives the action: not "the teacher scolded me" but "I was scolded by the teacher." Japanese also has a special use: when something happens that causes you trouble, you can use it to complain, like "I had such bad luck."
How to form it: check the verb group first
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the 「あ」-row sound of the same row, then add 「れる」.
呼ぶ → change ぶ to ば → 呼ばれる
踏む → 踏まれる叱る → 叱られる
Watch out for verbs ending in う: う doesn't become あ, it becomes わ.
言う → 言われる買う → 買われる
The easiest way to think of it: make the ない form, remove ない, and add れる. 言わない → 言われる
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop the final 「る」 and add 「られる」.
褒める → 褒められる見る → 見られる
Group 3 (only two verbs, just memorize them): する → される来る → 来られる（こられる）
Once formed, it is itself a Group 2 verb and keeps conjugating by the Group 2 rules:
褒められる → 褒められた褒められます褒められない
How to use it
Basic pattern: (me) は + the person who does the action + に + passive form. The doer takes 「に」.
・私は先生に叱られた。(I was scolded by the teacher.)
・上司にアイデアを褒められた。(My idea was praised by my boss.)
It isn't always bad news: you can also use it for being praised or being chosen.
Forms you'll hear most
Body or belongings affectedYour foot gets stepped on, your wallet gets stolen. Japanese usually says "I + thing + を + passive," so the main character is still "I."
・電車で足を踏まれた。(I had my foot stepped on on the train.)
・駅で財布を盗まれた。(I had my wallet stolen at the station.)
Bad luck, troubleSomething someone else did (or even the weather) inconveniences you. English has no neat equivalent for this (you can't say "I was cried by the baby"), which makes it a very distinctive feature of Japanese.
・帰りに雨に降られた。(I got caught in the rain on the way home.)
・夜中に赤ちゃんに泣かれて、全然寝られなかった。(The baby kept crying in the middle of the night, and I couldn't sleep at all.)
Objective descriptionCommon in news and introductions. It carries no emotion and doesn't say who did it.
・このお寺は500年前に建てられた。(This temple was built 500 years ago.)
Easy mistakes
・Verbs ending in う change it to わ: it's 買われる, not 買あれる.
・The doer takes 「に」: 先生に叱られた means "I was scolded by the teacher"; written as 先生が叱られた it becomes "The teacher was scolded."
・English says "my foot got stepped on," but Japanese doesn't say 私の足が踏まれた. Say 足を踏まれた.
・The passive of a Group 2 verb looks exactly like its potential form: 食べられる can mean "be eaten" or "can eat," so check the context.
・来られる is read こられる, not きられる.
Telling look-alikes apart
られる (passive) = someone else's action lands on me, and I'm the one who "takes" it:
弟にケーキを食べられた。(My little brother ate my cake.)
させる (causative) = I make or let someone else do it:
弟にケーキを食べさせた。(I let my little brother eat the cake.)
てもらう = someone does it for me, and I'm grateful:
先生に作文を褒めてもらった。(The teacher praised my essay, and I'm happy about it.)
Saying the same thing with 褒められた just states the fact that you were praised, without any particular note of gratitude.
Quick test: "was ~ed" uses れる・られる, "make someone ~" uses せる・させる, and "someone did ~ for me (thankfully)" uses てもらう.
What to learn next
Combine the causative and the passive and you get "being forced to do ~": 母に野菜を食べさせられた。(I was made to eat vegetables by my mom.)
n3-76:
The idea in one line
All three of these, 「～てたまらない」「～てしかたがない」「～てならない」, mean "I can't stand it" or "it's killing me." Use them when a feeling gets so strong you can't hold it down: so hot you can't stand it, homesick to the point of aching, worried sick. The three mean nearly the same thing. They differ in tone and setting.
When to use it
Physical sensationsHot, cold, pain, sleepiness, hunger, itching.
・お腹が空いてたまらない。(I'm starving, I can't stand it.)
・足が痛くてしかたがない。(My foot hurts like crazy.)
EmotionsHappy, sad, lonely, worried, bothered.
・試験の結果が心配でならない。(I'm incredibly worried about the exam results.)
Wanting to do something badlyPut 「〜たい」 in front and you get "I want to ~ so badly I can't stand it."
・家族に会いたくてたまらない。(I miss my family so much, I can't bear it.)
How to attach it
The key is that the word in front must first be in its 「て」 form, and each type of word changes differently:
Verbs: use the て-form as is　気になる → 気になってしかたがない
い-adjectives: replace the final 「い」 with 「くて」　暑い → 暑くてたまらない
な-adjectives: just add 「で」　心配 → 心配でならない
「〜たい」 changes just like an い-adjective: 会いたい → 会いたくて
Telling similar forms apart
Here are three ways to say "I'm dying of sleepiness":
・眠くてたまらない。(The most direct and vivid. Common in speech.)
・眠くてしかたがない。(Sleepy non-stop, and you can't shake it. In speech it's often said as 眠くてしょうがない.)
・眠くてならない。(Same meaning, but more formal and bookish. Rare in everyday chat.)
ならない has one especially common pattern: "I just can't shake the feeling that ~." Here ならない is the usual choice, and たまらない is rarely used this way.
・何か忘れているような気がしてならない。(I keep feeling like I've forgotten something.)
・彼の話は嘘のように思えてならない。(However I look at it, his story sounds like a lie.)
Quick rule of thumb: when you're talking to a friend about "~ like crazy," use たまらない or しょうがない. In writing, or for "I can't help feeling that ~," use ならない.
Common mistakes
・Don't attach て directly to an い-adjective: it's 暑くてたまらない, not 暑いてたまらない. For な-adjectives it's 心配で, not 心配て.
・This describes your own feelings. For other people, add ようだ or らしい: 弟は寂しくてたまらないようだ。(My little brother seems to be terribly lonely.)
・It only works with sensations and emotions, not plain descriptions. You can't say 広くてたまらない for "this room is huge." Use something like すごく広い instead.
・てならない is not the same as てはならない! Add one 「は」 and it means "must not ~": ここに入ってはならない。(You must not enter here.)
・しかたがない on its own means "it can't be helped": 雨だから、しかたがない。(It's raining, so it can't be helped.) It only means "~ unbearably" after a て-form.
What to learn next
