On its own, たまらない often means "so good I can't stand it": 仕事の後のビール、たまらない！(A beer after work, nothing beats it!)
n3-77:
The idea in one line
「〜どおりに／〜とおりに」 means "as ~", "just like ~", "according to ~". Use it for cooking by the recipe, following the plan, or writing what the teacher said. The kanji is 「通り」. Picture a model that has already drawn the route, and you simply follow it.
When to use it
Following a modelYou have something to follow, such as a recipe, a manual, a plan, or what someone said, and you do it that way.
・説明書どおりに組み立てた。(I assembled it following the instructions.)
・先生が言ったとおりに書いてください。(Please write it the way the teacher said.)
Just as expectedThe result matches what you thought or predicted, a bit like "just as I expected."
・予想どおり、試験は難しかった。(Just as expected, the exam was hard.)
・思ったとおり、彼は来なかった。(Just as I thought, he didn't come.)
How to attach it
What matters is whether a noun or a verb comes before it, because the reading changes:
Noun directly attached: read どおり (with the voiced mark)
計画 → 計画どおり予定 → 予定どおり
Noun with 「の」 in between: read とおり
説明書 → 説明書のとおり
Verb: dictionary form or た-form, read とおり
言う → 言うとおり教わった → 教わったとおり
Also, そのとおりです ("That's right," "You're exactly right") is a very common way to agree when the other person has it right.
What follows depends on what you want to say:
Before an action, use 「に」, which is often dropped in speech: 計画どおり進んでいる。(Things are going according to plan.)
Before a noun, use 「の」: 予想どおりの結果だった。(It was the result we expected.)
At the end of a sentence, use 「だ／です」: 結果は期待どおりだった。(The result was just what we hoped for.)
Dictionary form or た-form?
た-formThe model has already happened: something already taught, said, or seen. This is the most common.
・見たとおりに話してください。(Please tell it the way you saw it.)
Dictionary formThe model is happening right now, or you mean "do what someone says" in general.
・私が言うとおりに書いてください。(Please write down what I'm saying, as I say it.)
・親の言うとおりにする。(I do as my parents say.)
Common mistakes
・Only a noun attached directly is read どおり. With の in between it becomes とおり: 説明書のとおり is right, not 説明書のどおり; 計画どおり is right, not 計画とおり.
・After a verb, read it とおり. Don't write the voiced どおり.
・In English you "follow the plan," but in Japanese you don't add を before it: 計画をどおりに is wrong.
・Before a noun you must have の: 予想どおりの結果. You can't say 予想どおり結果.
・In Japan you'll see street names like 銀座通り. That 「通り」 means "street" and has nothing to do with this grammar.
Telling similar forms apart
どおりに = you do it exactly like the model: マニュアルどおりに対応した。(I handled it exactly by the manual.)
に基づいて = you use it as a basis or foundation: マニュアルに基づいて対応した。(I handled it based on the manual.)
Also, "the result was just as expected" only works with どおり, as in 予想どおり. You can't swap in に基づいて.
Quick rule of thumb: for following something exactly, or "just as I expected," use どおり／とおり. If you're only using something as a basis or foundation, use に基づいて.
n3-72:
The idea in one sentence
「〜させられる」 means "be made to do ~" or "be forced to do ~". You're the one doing it, but you don't want to; someone else is making you. It usually carries a note of resentment or complaint.
Where it comes from
It's two grammar points stacked together: 「させる」 = make someone do something, and 「られる」 = passive.
Mom told me to clean. Said from Mom's point of view:
・母は私に部屋を掃除させた。(Mom made me clean my room)
Now switch to my point of view, and it becomes "I was made to clean by Mom":
・私は母に部屋を掃除させられた。(I was made to clean my room by Mom)
The subject becomes "I", and the person making you do it is marked with に.
How to form it: check the verb group first
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the 「あ」-row sound in the same row, then add 「される」.
書く → く becomes か → 書かされる
飲む → 飲まされる待つ → 待たされる買う → 買わされる
Note that verbs ending in 「う」 change to 「わ」, not 「あ」.
This is the short form commonly used in speech. The full form is 書かせられる. Both are correct, but you'll hear the short form more in everyday talk.
An exception within Group 1: verbs ending in 「す」 can't use the short form; they take 「させられる」.
話す → 話させられる出す → 出させられる
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop the final 「る」 and add 「させられる」.
食べる → 食べさせられるやめる → やめさせられる
Group 3 (just two verbs, memorize them): する → させられる来る → 来させられる (こさせられる)
"Noun + する" verbs like 残業する and スピーチする work the same way: 残業する → 残業させられる
What you'll hear most
Forced to doThe basic use: complaining about something you didn't want to do.
・子どものころ、毎日ピアノを練習させられた。(As a kid, I was made to practice piano every day)
・飲み会でお酒をたくさん飲まされた。(I got made to drink a lot at the drinking party)
Kept waiting待たされる is very common. It means "I was kept waiting for ages."
・病院で一時間も待たされた。(I was kept waiting at the hospital for a whole hour)
Can't help butUsed with verbs like 「think」 or 「be moved」, it means "something makes you can't-help-but ~." There's no complaint in it.
・この映画にはいろいろ考えさせられた。(This movie really made me think about a lot of things)
Common mistakes
・話す becomes 話させられる; you can't say 「話さされる」. All verbs ending in 「す」 work this way.
・Mark the person making you do it with に: 先生に作文を書かされた。(I was made to write an essay by the teacher)
・It carries a feeling of "I didn't want to." If someone kindly lets you do something and you're grateful, using this form turns it into a complaint and sounds rude.
・Don't mix up 書かされる with the ordinary passive 書かれる: with the extra 「さ」, the meaning goes from "be written" to "be forced to write."
Tell it apart from look-alikes
られる = someone does something to me, and the other person is the doer: 母に叱られた。(I was scolded by Mom; Mom did the scolding)
させられる = someone makes me do something, I'm the doer, and I don't want to: 母に掃除させられた。(I was made to clean by Mom; I did the cleaning)
Now compare 「させてもらう」. It's also someone letting you do something, but the feeling is completely the opposite:
させてもらう = I want to do it, the other person allows me, and I'm grateful: 店長に頼んで、休ませてもらった。(I asked the manager, and he let me take the day off)
させられる = I don't want to, the other person forces me: 熱があって、店長に無理やり休まされた。(I had a fever, and the manager forced me to go home and rest)
A quick test: ask "who does the action?" If the other person does it, it's られる. If I do it reluctantly, it's させられる. If I do it and I wanted to, it's させてもらう.
What to learn next
If 「させる」 and 「られる」 still feel shaky, go back and review 〜させる (causative) and 〜られる (passive). This grammar point is just those two stacked together.
n3-73:
The idea in one sentence
「〜ても」 means "even if ~, ... anyway" or "no matter ~, ...". Whatever happens in the first part, the result in the second part is unaffected and stays the same. It's like saying "Even if it rains, I'm going": the rain can't change the fact that you're going.
・雨が降っても、行きます。(Even if it rains, I'll go)
・高くても、買いたい。(Even if it's expensive, I want to buy it)
How to attach it
Verbs: change to the て-form first, then add も.
書く → 書いて → 書いても食べる → 食べて → 食べてもする → しても来る → 来ても (きても)
For verbs whose て-form ends in 「で」, adding も gives 「でも」: 読む → 読んで → 読んでも
い-adjectives: replace the final 「い」 with 「くても」.
高い → 高くても忙しい → 忙しくても
な-adjectives and nouns: just add 「でも」.
下手 → 下手でも日曜日 → 日曜日でも
・料理が下手でも、大丈夫です。(Even if you're not good at cooking, it's fine)
・日曜日でも、仕事がある。(Even on Sunday, I have work)
Negative "even if not ~": change ない to なくても. 行かない → 行かなくても
What you'll hear most
Question word + てもPut "what, who, where, when" in front and it becomes "no matter ~, ...".
・何を食べても、おいしい。(No matter what I eat, it's delicious)
・いつ行っても、混んでいる。(No matter when I go, it's crowded)
・何度確認しても、ミスが見つからない。(No matter how many times I check, I can't find the mistake)
どんなに／いくら〜ても"No matter how much ~, ..." It stresses that even a high degree makes no difference.
・どんなに忙しくても、朝ご飯は必ず食べる。(No matter how busy I am, I always eat breakfast)
・いくら練習しても、上手にならない。(No matter how much I practice, I don't get any better)
たとえ〜ても"Even if ~ really happens, ..." The tone is firmer and often expresses determination.
・たとえ反対されても、留学したい。(Even if people object, I still want to study abroad)
Common mistakes
・Nouns and な-adjectives take でも directly: 下手でも, not 「下手くても」.
・いい must become よくても, not 「いくても」.
・Verbs must go to the て-form first: 読んでも, not 「読むでも」.
・Use ても only when the result goes against what you'd normally expect. A fever going down after taking medicine is the expected result, so you can't say 「薬を飲んでも、熱が下がった」. Say 薬を飲んだら、熱が下がった。 (After I took medicine, my fever went down). With ても it would be 薬を飲んでも、熱が下がらない。 (Even if I take medicine, my fever doesn't go down)
Tell it apart from look-alikes
Take the same rainy-day outing. Change the grammar and the meaning changes:
たら = if ~, then ... (the condition holds and the result follows): 雨が降ったら、行かない。 (If it rains, I won't go)
ても = even if ~, ... (the condition doesn't change the result): 雨が降っても、行く。 (Even if it rains, I'll go)
のに = even though ~, ... (something that has already happened, with a sense of surprise or dissatisfaction, like "how come?"): 雨が降っているのに、傘を持たないで出かけた。 (Even though it's raining, he went out without an umbrella)
ても can talk about hypotheticals that haven't happened yet, and can be followed by "let's" or "please": 雨が降っても、行きましょう。 (Even if it rains, let's go). のに talks about something that has already happened, so it can't be followed by "let's" or "please." That's why you can't say 「雨が降っているのに、行きましょう」.
A quick test: for "if ~, then ..." use たら; for "even if / no matter ~, ..." use ても; for "even though ~, ..." use のに.
n3-74:
The idea in one line
「〜たことがある」means "have done ~ before" / "have the experience of ~". What matters isn't which day you did something, but whether you have this experience in your life. When a friend asks "Have you ever tried stinky tofu?", that's exactly the question being asked.
・富士山に登ったことがある。(I've climbed Mt. Fuji.)
・日本の温泉に入ったことがありますか。(Have you ever been in a Japanese hot spring?)
How to form it
Verb た-form (the "〜た" past form) + ことがある.
For a politer tone, say ことがあります. If you don't have the experience, swap ある for ない:
食べたことがある → 食べたことがない (have never eaten)
How it changes: first, identify the verb group
The た-form is just the て-form with 「て」 swapped for 「た」, so if you know the て-form, you know the た-form.
Group 1 (godan verbs): look at the last sound.
会う → 会った飲む → 飲んだ書く → 書いた泳ぐ → 泳いだ話す → 話した
Watch out: 行く → 行った, not 行いた.
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop 「る」 and add 「た」.
食べる → 食べた見る → 見た
Group 3 (only two, just memorize them): する → した来る → 来た（きた）
How you'll hear it most
Asking about experienceGreat for starting a conversation. When you answer, you don't need to repeat the whole sentence; 「あります／ありません」 is enough.
・沖縄に行ったことがありますか。(Have you ever been to Okinawa?)
・はい、あります。(Yes, I have.)
・いいえ、一度もありません。(No, never, not even once.)
Adding frequencyOften appears with 一度, 何度も, and 一度も〜ない.
・あの店には何度も行ったことがある。(I've been to that shop many times.)
・納豆は一度も食べたことがない。(I've never eaten natto, not even once.)
A past stateUse 〜ていたことがある to mean "there was a period in the past when I ~".
・子どものころ、大阪に住んでいたことがある。(I lived in Osaka when I was a kid.)
Common mistakes
・Not every English "I've done ~" or "I went" is this pattern. "I went to the supermarket yesterday" just reports something you did yesterday. In Japanese, 昨日スーパーに行きました is all you need. You can't say 昨日スーパーに行ったことがあります.
・Don't use it for things that just happened or are very recent: specific, near time points like さっき, 昨日, and 先週 don't fit with "life experience". A long stretch of time like 子どものころ is fine.
・Everyday, taken-for-granted things sound odd too: if you say "I've eaten rice" or "I've ridden the subway", a Japanese person will think, "Why mention that?" Use it for experiences that are somewhat special, ones not everyone has.
・What comes before it must be the た-form. If you write 行くことがある, the meaning changes completely (see below).
Telling look-alikes apart
Both use 「ことがある」, but the form before it changes the meaning completely:
た-form + ことがある = have done it before (past experience)
Dictionary form + ことがある = sometimes does it (something that happens occasionally)
・一人で映画を見に行ったことがある。(I've been to see a movie alone before.)
・一人で映画を見に行くことがある。(I sometimes go to see a movie alone.)
The first sentence only says it has happened at least once, and it may not be something you still do. The second says that you occasionally do it now.
Quick trick: if you see 「た」 before it, think "have done ~ before". If you see the dictionary form, think "sometimes ~".
What to learn next
Another pattern that starts with the「た-form」is 〜たばかり (just did ~). It talks about something that happened very recently, which is the opposite of "experience", so it helps to learn them together.
n3-75:
The idea in one line
「〜ことができる」means "can ~" / "be able to ~". The meaning is close to the potential form (like 話せる and 行ける), but it sounds fuller and more formal. You'll see it often in announcements, explanations, interviews, and formal situations.
When to use it
Having a skill (ability)You've learned it and have the ability to do it.
・彼はピアノを弾くことができる。(He can play the piano.)
Permission, being possibleThe rules allow it, or the conditions make it possible.
・ここで写真を撮ることができます。(You can take photos here.)
・この展示は予約なしで入場することができます。(You can enter this exhibition without a reservation.)
How to form it
Use the verb's dictionary form (the original form you'd look up in a dictionary) and add 「ことができる」 right after it. The good news is that you don't need to worry about the verb group; you attach it the same way every time.
話す → 話すことができる食べる → 食べることができる
する → することができる来る → 来ることができる（くる）
To say "can't" or "was able to", change only the final 「できる」:
できる → できない(can't)できる → できた(was able to)
Nouns have a pattern too: nouns that stand for an "activity", such as a language, a sport, or a skill, can take 「ができる」 directly: 日本語ができる (can speak Japanese), テニスができる (can play tennis).
Ordinary object nouns don't work this way. For example, "can drive" is 車の運転ができる or 車を運転することができる; you can't say 車ができる. 本ができる means "the book is finished", not "can read books".
How you'll hear it most
ことができますShops and notices tell you what you can do.
・カードで払うことができます。(You can pay by card.)
ことはできませんThe rules say no. In the negative, 「が」 often becomes 「は」, which sounds more like "this particular thing can't be done".
・ここでたばこを吸うことはできません。(You can't smoke here.)
ことができましたYou finally managed it after some effort.
・やっと切符を買うことができました。(I was finally able to buy a ticket.)
ことができるようになったYou couldn't before, but now you can.
・オンラインで申請することができるようになった。(You can now apply online.)
Common mistakes
・Always use the dictionary form before it, never the ます-form: say 行くことができる, not 行きますことができる.
・The 「を」 before the verb stays as it is: 日本語を話すことができる. It's when you switch to the potential form that 「を」 often becomes 「が」: 日本語が話せる.
・When chatting with friends, the potential form sounds more natural. Asking a friend 明日来ることができる？ sounds stiff; people usually say 明日来られる？ (Can you come tomorrow?).
・English "will" doesn't always map to ことができる. "It will rain tomorrow" is a prediction and has nothing to do with ability, so you say 明日は雨が降るでしょう.
Telling look-alikes apart
「ことができる」and「ことがある」differ by only one word, but the meanings are very different. Compare them using the same action:
ことができる = can, be able to: 納豆を食べることができる。(I can eat natto.)
Potential form = same meaning, more casual: 納豆が食べられる。(I can eat natto.)
た-form + ことがある = have done it before: 納豆を食べたことがある。(I've eaten natto before.)
Dictionary form + ことがある = sometimes does it: 納豆を食べることがある。(I sometimes eat natto.)
Quick trick: look at whether it ends in「できる」or「ある」. できる = can or can't; ある = have or haven't (done it before, or sometimes do it).
What to learn next
Adding 「ようになる」 afterward means "come to be able to ~": 日本語で電話することができるようになった。(I've become able to talk on the phone in Japanese.)
n3-78:
The idea in one line
「〜っけ」is what you use when you used to know something and can't recall it right now. It's like saying in English, "Wait, what time is tomorrow's meeting again? I forgot," or "His birthday is next week, right?" You're thinking out loud as you ask.
When to use it
Can't rememberAsk someone, or mutter to yourself.
・明日のミーティングは何時からだっけ？(What time does tomorrow's meeting start again? I forgot.)
・あれ、鍵どこに置いたっけ？(Huh, where did I put my keys?)
Checking your memoryYou have an answer in mind and want to make sure you've got it right.
・彼の誕生日は来週だっけ？(His birthday is next week, right?)
ReminiscingTalking to yourself about the past. The ending doesn't rise, and it has a "back then..." feel.
・子どものころ、よくこの公園で遊んだっけ。(I used to play in this park a lot as a kid, didn't I.)
How to form it
Nouns and な-adjectives: add「だ」or「だった」first, then っけ.
明日 → 明日だっけ静か → 静かだったっけ
Verbs: to ask about something in the past, use the た form + っけ.
言う → 言った → 言ったっけ
For something that hasn't happened yet,「〜んだっけ」usually sounds more natural.
来る → 来るんだっけ (He's coming, right?)
い-adjectives: change い to かった, then add っけ.
高い → 高かったっけ (Was that place expensive? I forget.)
To be more polite: say「でしたっけ」or「ましたっけ」.
・すみません、お名前は何でしたっけ？(Excuse me, your name was... I can't recall it right now.)
・前に言いましたっけ？(Did I mention that to you before?)
Common mistakes
・You can't attach っけ directly to a noun: 明日っけ is wrong; say 明日だっけ.
・っけ only works if you knew it before. If you're asking a stranger for directions for the first time, you can't say 駅はどこだっけ？; say 駅はどこですか。
・You can use the past form even for something tomorrow: 明日の会議、何時からだったっけ？ The「た」here doesn't mean the meeting is already over. It points to "that thing I heard earlier."
・「だっけ」is the casual, friends version. With a boss or customers, switch to「でしたっけ」「ましたっけ」, which you hear a lot at work. Still, skip it in job interviews and formal letters.
・Hold the small「っ」for a beat: だっけ is pronounced dakke. Without that beat it becomes だけ, which means "only."
Telling similar forms apart
Here are three ways to ask a friend what time tomorrow's meeting is:
明日の会議、何時から？: a plain question; you genuinely don't know.
明日の会議、何時からだっけ？: you heard it, but you forgot.
明日の会議、何時からかな。: you're wondering to yourself, and you don't need an answer.
Quick rule of thumb: use っけ for "I used to know it but forgot"; use a normal question for "I never knew it."
n3-79:
The idea in one line
「〜反面」is the English "on the other hand" or "the flip side". You describe one side of something, then the opposite side of that same thing. For example, "This job pays well, but I'm really busy": one thing, two opposite sides. That's when you use 反面.
When to use it
One good, one badThe most common use: the same person or thing has both strengths and weaknesses.
・この仕事は給料がいい反面、休みが少ない。(This job pays well, but there's little time off.)
・一人暮らしは自由な反面、寂しいこともある。(Living alone gives you freedom, but it can also get lonely.)
Mixed feelingsYou feel two opposite things at once. This is also very common.
・卒業はうれしい反面、少し寂しい。(I'm happy to graduate, but I'm also a little sad.)
Sentence-initialAfter finishing one sentence, start the next with「その反面」, meaning "on the other hand."
・スマホは便利だ。その反面、使いすぎると目が疲れる。(Smartphones are convenient. On the other hand, using them too much tires your eyes.)
How to form it
Verbs: attach directly; the past form works too.
便利になった → 便利になった反面
い-adjectives: attach directly.
速い → 速い反面
な-adjectives: add「な」, or use the more formal「である」.
便利 → 便利な反面／便利である反面
Nouns: add「である」.
有名人 → 有名人である反面
・彼女は有名人である反面、自由な時間が少ない。(She's a celebrity, but in exchange she has little free time.)
Common mistakes
・な-adjectives can't attach directly: say 便利な反面, not「便利反面」or「便利だ反面」.
・Nouns take である; don't say「学生な反面」.
・反面 describes two sides of the same thing. Using it to compare two different people, like "my older brother is tall, my younger brother is short," sounds odd.
・反面 is written and formal, common in essays, news and reports. In casual conversation with friends, plain けど is fine: 給料はいいけど、忙しい。 (The pay is good, but I'm busy.)
・It's read はんめん.
Telling similar forms apart
反面 = two sides of one thing: 兄は優しい反面、気が弱い。 (My older brother is gentle, but on the flip side he's timid.)
一方で = can describe two sides of one thing, or contrast two different things: 兄はスポーツが好きな一方で、弟は本が好きだ。 (My older brother likes sports, while my younger brother likes books.)
に対して = used specifically to contrast two different things: 兄は背が高いのに対して、弟は低い。 (My older brother is tall, whereas my younger brother is short.)
Quick rule of thumb: one subject, with its good and bad sides, use 反面. Two subjects compared against each other, use 一方で or に対して.
Also, 一方だ at the end of a sentence means "more and more..." It's a different thing from the 「一方で」 here, so don't mix them up.
n2-37:
The idea in one line
「〜かねる」 is like what customer service says: “I'm afraid we're unable to help with that.” It's also like the official-letter phrase “We regret that we cannot comply.” Literally it means “I'd like to, but it's awkward to,” and in practice it's a very polite refusal, or a way of saying you're in a tough spot.
When to use it
Polite refusalStaff, customer service and companies use this most when speaking to the public. It softens a flat “no.”
・返品はお受けいたしかねます。(We're unable to accept returns.)
・その件についてはお答えしかねます。(I'm afraid I can't answer that.)
・申し訳ございませんが、私ではわかりかねます。(I'm sorry, but I'm not able to say on this one.)
Can't accept it inwardlyYour position or feelings won't let you nod along.
・その意見には賛成しかねます。(I can't bring myself to agree with that opinion.)
Can't make up your mind決めかねる is a very common set phrase meaning “to hesitate, to be unable to decide.”
・どちらにするか決めかねている。(I still can't decide which one to pick.)
How to form it
Put the verb in its ます form, drop 「ます」, then add 「かねる」.
答えます → 答えかねるわかります → わかりかねるします → しかねる
For extra politeness, swap する for the humble いたす: いたします → いたしかねます
In real life you'll hear the polite form 「〜かねます」 most.
Easy mistakes
・Don't use it for physical inability. “Too heavy to lift” is 重くて持てない, not 重くて持ちかねる. かねる is about rules, position or feelings: “it's awkward” or “I'm unwilling.”
・わかりかねます has no negative in it, but it means “I don't know.” Don't hear it as “I understand.”
・かねます and かねません mean opposite things. お答えしかねます means “I can't answer,” while 起こりかねません means “it could very well happen.” Only one ん separates them, so don't mix them up.
・It's very formal, so it sounds odd with friends. Between friends, ちょっと無理 is enough.
・Learn these two fixed expressions separately: 見るに見かねて手伝った (I couldn't just watch, so I helped) and お待ちかねの新商品 (the new product everyone's been waiting for). Neither one is a refusal.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Say a customer asks for a return:
できない = a direct “can't,” fairly blunt: 返品はできません。 (Returns aren't possible.)
かねる = a polite, indirect refusal: 返品はお受けいたしかねます。 (We're unable to accept returns.)
がたい isn't for refusing people. It describes something as “hard to ~”: 信じがたい話だ。 (That's a hard-to-believe story.)
かねない = worry that something bad might happen: このままでは事故になりかねない。 (If this goes on, it could well end in an accident.)
Quick test: politely turning down someone's request → かねる. Describing something as hard to believe or accept → がたい. Worrying “this might happen” → かねない.
What to learn next
The next lesson is 「〜かねない」. It looks almost identical but means the opposite, so it's a good one to learn together.
n2-54:
The idea in one line
「〜につれて」 means “as ~, gradually ~.” The first thing changes slowly, and the second thing changes slowly along with it. It's like “As the weather gets colder, more and more people order hot drinks”: two things changing together.
How to form it
VerbAdd につれて directly to the dictionary form (the base form you'd look up).
時間が経つ → 時間が経つにつれて (as time passes)
慣れる → 慣れるにつれて (as you get used to it)
NounAdd につれて directly, but the noun itself must carry a sense of “change,” like 成長, 進化, 変化 or 高齢化.
成長 → 成長につれて (as someone grows)
In writing you'll often see the shorter 「につれ」. The meaning is the same.
When to use it
Use it when both things change little by little. The second half often pairs with 「〜てきた」, 「〜ていく」 or 「〜くなる」 to bring out the “gradually” feeling.
・日本の生活に慣れるにつれて、毎日が楽しくなってきた。(As I got used to life in Japan, every day became more enjoyable.)
・年を取るにつれて、体力が落ちてきた。(As I've gotten older, my stamina has declined.)
・子どもの成長につれて、家が狭く感じるようになった。(As the kids grew, the house started to feel small.)
Easy mistakes
・Don't use it for things that happen all at once. “Graduating,” “moving” and “getting married” are one-time events, so you can't say 卒業するにつれて. The first part must be a change that unfolds gradually.
・The second half can't be “I will ~” or “Please ~.” It has to describe a change that follows naturally, not your own plans or a request. A sentence like “As your Japanese improves, let's chat more” can't use につれて.
・You can't put just any noun in front. 雨につれて is wrong because “rain” itself isn't a change. Say 雨が強くなるにつれて (as the rain gets heavier).
・English “as” and “along with” cover a lot of ground, but につれて only handles “both sides change gradually in step.” Don't use it every time you'd say “as.”
Telling it apart from look-alikes
に伴って: very close in meaning, but more formal and common in news and announcements. The first part can also be a one-time event.
・人口が増えるにつれて、ゴミの問題が深刻になった。(As the population grew, the garbage problem became serious.)
・人口が増えるに伴って、ゴミの問題が深刻になった。(Same meaning, more formal.)
Both work. But with a one-time event like moving:
・引っ越しに伴って、住所が変わります。(Your address will change due to the move.)
につれて can't be used here.
に応じて: “depending on ~.” The focus is a correspondence, not change over time.
・年齢に応じて、料金が違います。(The fee differs depending on age.)
Here, people of different ages pay different prices. It's not one person growing older and the price shifting along with them, so につれて doesn't fit.
Quick test: if you can say “as ~, gradually ~,” use につれて. If it's more formal, or the first part is a one-time event, use に伴って. If it means “depending on ~,” use に応じて.
n2-2:
The idea in one line
Dictionary form + ばかりだ means “nothing but more and more ~,” “only getting worse,” “going steadily downhill.” Things keep moving in one direction with no sign of improvement or turning back, and the speaker usually sounds resigned or worried.
When to use it
Getting worse and worseThe most common use. You'll hear it all the time when people complain about prices, the economy, health or workload.
・物価は上がるばかりだ。(Prices only go up, never down.)
・父の病気は悪くなるばかりだった。(My father's illness just got worse day by day.)
Mid-sentenceChange it to ばかりで, then add another thing that makes the situation even more frustrating.
・仕事は増えるばかりで、給料は全然上がらない。(The work only keeps piling up, and my pay doesn't go up at all.)
Occasionally for good thingsIt's possible, but less common, and mostly describes an objective trend.
・この店の人気は高まるばかりだ。(This shop just keeps getting more popular.)
How to form it
Verb dictionary form (the base form you'd look up in a dictionary) + ばかりだ. The verb in front must be a verb of change, like 増える, 減る, 上がる, 広がる or 悪化する.
増える → 増えるばかりだ
Adjectives first take なる to mean “become ~”, and then you add ばかりだ:
悪い → 悪くなる → 悪くなるばかりだ
不便 → 不便になる → 不便になるばかりだ
For things in the past, use ばかりだった.
Easy mistakes
・If the verb in front isn't a verb of change, the meaning shifts to “does nothing but ~”: 彼女はただ泣くばかりだった。(She did nothing but cry.) This is not “more and more.”
・「あとは～ばかりだ」means “all that's left is ~”: 準備はできた。あとは出発するばかりだ。(Everything's ready. All that's left is to leave.)
・Noun + ばかり means “nothing but ~”: 甘い物ばかり食べている。(I eat nothing but sweets.) That's a different thing from the “more and more” meaning here.
・It's not usually used for your own progress. To say “my Japanese is getting better and better,” 日本語がどんどん上手になっている sounds more natural.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
The same ばかり means completely different things depending on the form before it:
・日本に来たばかりだ。(I just arrived in Japan: た-form + ばかり = “just did ~”)
・毎日ゲームをしてばかりいる。(He does nothing but play video games every day: て-form + ばかりいる = “keeps doing ~ all the time”)
・帰国してから、日本語は忘れるばかりだ。(Since going back home, I just keep forgetting more and more Japanese: dictionary form + ばかりだ = “more and more ~”)
Compared with 「～つつある」: Both describe change, but the tone differs.
・景気は回復しつつある。(The economy is gradually recovering.)
・景気は悪くなるばかりだ。(The economy can only get worse and worse.)
つつある simply states, calmly, that “a change is in progress.” It's more formal and works for good or bad. ばかりだ stresses “it can't be stopped, it only goes one way,” with a sense of resignation.
There's also ～一方だ, which means almost the same as ばかりだ and can often replace it: 人口は減る一方だ。(The population only keeps shrinking.)
Quick rule: look at what comes before ばかり. た-form means “just did ~,” て-form means “keeps doing ~,” and dictionary form with a verb of change means “more and more ~.”
n2-5:
The idea in one line
〜たとたん（に）means “the moment I ~, suddenly ~.” Think of a cat bolting out the instant you open the door, or getting dizzy the second you stand up. The first action has only just finished, and then something unexpected pops up.
How to form it
Put the verb in the た-form (the same form as the past tense 「～た」) and add とたん. You can add or drop に, with no change in meaning.
開ける → 開けたとたん出る → 出たとたん飲む → 飲んだとたんに
The action in front is usually something that finishes in an instant, like opening a door, going out, standing up or seeing something.
When to use it
Something suddenly happens outsideOther people, animals or the weather suddenly do something.
・家を出たとたん、雨が降り出した。(The moment I left the house, it started to rain.)
・窓を開けたとたん、虫が入ってきた。(The moment I opened the window, a bug flew in.)
Body and feelings out of your controlIt also works for reactions in your own body, as long as you didn't do them on purpose.
・立ち上がったとたん、めまいがした。(The moment I stood up, I felt dizzy.)
・母の声を聞いたとたん、涙が出てきた。(The moment I heard my mother's voice, tears came to my eyes.)
Easy mistakes
・The form in front must be the た-form: say 開けたとたん, never 「開けるとたん」.
・What follows is something that has already happened and was unexpected, so the sentence usually ends in the past tense.
・You can't follow it with will, invitations or commands, such as “I'll ~,” “let's ~” or “please ~.” 「家に着いたとたん、電話してください」is wrong.
・You also can't follow it with an action you do on purpose. 「家に帰ったとたん、シャワーを浴びた」sounds unnatural, because taking a shower is something you decided to do. In that case use 家に帰ってすぐ、シャワーを浴びた。(As soon as I got home, I took a shower right away.)
Telling it apart from look-alikes
〜次第 is also often translated as “as soon as ~,” but it works the opposite way. Take the same situation:
駅に着いたとたん、電車が行ってしまった。(The moment I got to the station, the train left.)
→ It already happened and was unexpected, so use とたん.
駅に着き次第、連絡します。(I'll contact you as soon as I get to the station.)
→ It hasn't happened yet and it's something I intend to do, so use 次第.
次第 attaches to the ます-form with ます removed (着きます → 着き次第), and it's often used in work and formal situations.
Quick rule: if what follows is something that pops up suddenly and you can't control it, use とたん. If it's something you'll go and do next, use 次第.
What to learn next
とたん can also start a sentence in the form 「その途端」, meaning “at that very moment”:
ドアを開けた。その途端、猫が飛び出した。(I opened the door. At that very moment, the cat dashed out.)
n2-8:
The idea in one line
「〜からには」means "since you've already ~, then you must ~" or "now that ~, you'd better ~". First you state something that's already decided, already happened, or can't be undone. Then you say "so I'm definitely going to…". In English you'd say "If you're going to do it, do it right." In Japanese that's: やるからには、一番を目指す。 (Since I'm doing it, I'm aiming to be number one.)
How to attach it
It's most often used with verbs. What matters is whether you use the た-form or the dictionary form, because the meaning changes:
Something already done: た-form + からには　引き受けた → 引き受けたからには (since I've already taken it on)
Something you've decided to do but haven't done yet: dictionary form + からには　留学する → 留学するからには (since I'm going to study abroad)
Nouns and な-adjectives: add 「である」 in between　プロ → プロであるからには (since you're a professional)
What comes after it
After からには, the sentence is always about "so this is the attitude I should have." It's never just a statement that something happened. The four most common patterns are:
DeterminationI will definitely follow through.
・約束したからには、必ず守る。 (Since I made a promise, I'll definitely keep it.)
ObligationOften paired with 「なければならない」 or 「べきだ」.
・試合に出るからには、毎日練習しなければならない。 (If you're going to compete, you have to practice every day.)
Asking the other personOften paired with 「てください」.
・日本に住むからには、ゴミの出し方はちゃんと覚えてください。 (If you're going to live in Japan, please learn properly how to take out the trash.)
A natural expectationOften paired with 「はずだ」.
・彼がやると言ったからには、ちゃんとやるはずだ。 (Since he said he'd do it, he should do it properly.)
How you'll hear it most
These lines are almost set phrases, so memorize them whole:
・やるからには、本気でやろう。 (If we're doing it, let's do it seriously.)
・こうなったからには、もうやるしかない。 (Now that it's come to this, we have no choice but to do it.)
・自分で決めたからには、最後までがんばる。 (Since I decided this myself, I'll keep at it to the end.)
Easy mistakes
・What follows can't be just a fact about something that already happened.
×日本に来たからには、寿司を食べた。
○日本に来たからには、本場の寿司を食べたい。 (Since I've come to Japan, I want to eat authentic sushi.)
・Nouns can't attach directly: not プロからには, but プロであるからには.
・Don't mix up the た-form and the dictionary form: 結婚したからには means "now that we're married", while 結婚するからには means "since we've decided to marry".
・It carries a sense of "I'm taking this on," so the tone is strong. If you're just giving a plain reason, like "it rained, so I took an umbrella," use 「から」 instead of からには.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
からこそ (n2-9) = "precisely because ~". It stresses that this is the reason.
からには = "since ~, then ~". It focuses on what you should do next.
Both about a job you love:
・好きな仕事を選んだからには、簡単にはやめない。 (Since I chose a job I love, I won't quit easily.)
・好きな仕事だからこそ、毎日がんばれる。 (It's precisely because it's a job I love that I can give it my best every day.)
上は (n2-32) = almost the same meaning as からには, but stiffer and more formal, mostly used in writing or formal settings. The commonly heard 「以上（は）」 is also very close in meaning.
・引き受けたからには、最後までやります。 (Since I've taken it on, I'll see it through to the end: fine in everyday speech.)
・引き受けた上は、最後までやり遂げる所存です。 (Having taken it on, I intend to carry it through to the end: formal settings.)
Quick tip: use からには for "since ~, then ~"; use からこそ for "precisely because ~"; and for the same "since" in a more formal register, switch to 上は.
n2-25:
The idea in one line
「〜どころか」means "far from ~, it's actually…" or "never mind ~, not even…". First you mention an A that everyone assumes, then you say the real situation is very far from A, often the complete opposite. For example, you expect a day off to be restful, but it turns out to be "not restful at all, more tiring than work."
How to attach it
Verbs: dictionary form + どころか　やせる → やせるどころか
い-adjectives: attach directly　安い → 安いどころか
な-adjectives and nouns: attach directly, don't add だ　簡単 → 簡単どころか旅行 → 旅行どころか
How you'll hear it most
The opposite insteadNot only did A not happen, things went the other way. Often followed by 逆に, かえって, or もっと.
・ダイエットしているのに、やせるどころか太ってしまった。 (I'm on a diet, but far from losing weight, I actually gained weight.)
・薬を飲んだのに、よくなるどころか、もっと悪くなった。 (I took medicine, but instead of getting better, I got worse.)
Not even B, let alone AA is the harder thing and B is the more basic thing. If you can't even do B, A is out of the question. Often followed by 「も」 or 「さえ」 + a negative.
・忙しくて、旅行どころか、週末に休むこともできない。 (I'm so busy that, never mind traveling, I can't even rest on weekends.)
・彼は漢字どころか、ひらがなも読めない。 (He can't even read hiragana, let alone kanji.)
Far more than AThe reality is much more extreme than A, in the same direction but going far beyond it.
・1万円どころか、5万円もかかった。 (Far from 10,000 yen, it cost a whole 50,000.)
それどころかPlaced at the start of a sentence to respond to the other person: "Not at all, in fact…". Very common in conversation.
・「迷惑だった？」「それどころか、すごく助かったよ。」 ("Was I a bother?" "Not at all, you were a huge help.")
Easy mistakes
・Don't add だ after nouns or な-adjectives: say 簡単どころか, not 簡単だどころか.
・Don't flip the order in "not even B, let alone A": put the harder thing as A and the more basic thing as B. 「漢字どころか、ひらがなも読めない」 works, but reversing it as 「ひらがなどころか、漢字も読めない」 makes the meaning odd.
・When A and B are both good things and you just want to "add one more," you can't use どころか. To say "this restaurant is tasty and also cheap," you can't say 美味しいどころか安い; use ばかりか or だけでなく instead.
・どころか carries a feeling of surprise or being taken aback, so it suits unexpected results. Don't force it onto plain, matter-of-fact statements.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
All about a rainy day:
ばかりか = A holds true, and B is added on top: 雨ばかりか、雷まで鳴りだした。 (Not only rain, but thunder started rumbling too.)
どころか = A is overturned and the reality is the opposite: 雨がやむどころか、どんどん強くなっている。 (Far from stopping, the rain is getting heavier and heavier.)
どころじゃない = right now you have no room at all for A: 雨がひどくて、花見どころじゃない。 (The rain is so bad that flower viewing is out of the question.)
Quick tip: "not only A, but also B" is ばかりか; "far from A, it's the opposite" is どころか; "no time or mood for A right now" is どころじゃない.
n2-26:
The idea in one line
「〜ばかりか」 and 「〜ばかりでなく」 mean "not only ~, but also ~" or "not just ~, even ~". You state one thing, then add a bigger one on top. In everyday speech people usually say 「〜だけじゃなくて」. ばかりか and ばかりでなく sound more formal and show up often in writing, news and speeches.
When to use it
Piling on good thingsOne advantage after another.
・この店は安いばかりでなく、味もいい。(This shop is not only cheap, the food is good too.)
・その歌は子どもばかりか、大人にも人気がある。(That song is popular not only with children but with adults too.)
Piling on bad thingsThings were already bad, and then something even worse happened. ばかりか is especially common in this "and on top of that..." situation, with a hint of surprise or annoyance.
・遅刻したばかりか、資料も忘れてきた。(He was not only late, he even forgot the documents.)
・彼は謝らないばかりか、文句まで言ってきた。(He not only didn't apologize, he even complained to me.)
The second half often pairs with 「も」「まで」「さえ」, meaning "even ~". That makes the "on top of that" feeling clearer.
How to connect it
Verbs: attach directly　遅刻した → 遅刻したばかりか
い-adjectives: attach directly　安い → 安いばかりか
な-adjectives: add 「な」　便利 → 便利なばかりか
Nouns: attach directly, no だ　子ども → 子どもばかりか
(In more formal writing, な-adjectives and nouns can also connect with 「である」, for example 学生であるばかりでなく.)
ばかりでなく connects in exactly the same way.
・この町は交通が便利なばかりか、家賃も安い。(This town is not only convenient for transport, the rent is cheap too.)
Easy mistakes
・Don't put だ after a noun: say 日本語ばかりか, not 「日本語だばかりか」. Remember to add な after な-adjectives: きれいなばかりか.
・Don't follow ばかりか with a request, command or decision, like "please do ~", "you must ~" or "I will ~". In those cases use ばかりでなく (or だけでなく): 肉ばかりでなく、野菜も食べなさい。 (Don't eat only meat, eat vegetables too.) Saying 「肉ばかりか、野菜も食べなさい」 sounds unnatural.
・Don't confuse it with plain 「ばかり」: 日本語ばかり勉強している means "I study only Japanese", while 日本語ばかりか英語も勉強している means "I study not only Japanese, but English too." One extra か changes the meaning a lot.
Telling similar patterns apart
どころか is also often translated as "not only ~", but it works differently. The key is whether the first thing is actually true.
ばかりか: the first part is true, and the second part adds more.
彼は英語ばかりか、フランス語も話せる。 (He speaks not only English but French too. He does speak English.)
どころか: the first part is out of the question, and reality is even further off.
彼はフランス語どころか、英語も話せない。 (Never mind French, he can't even speak English. He can't speak French.)
やせるどころか、太ってしまった。 (Far from losing weight, I actually gained weight.)
のみならず means about the same as ばかりか and ばかりでなく, but it is more bookish and stiff, and mostly appears in writing or formal settings.
Quick test: if the first thing is true and you're adding another, use ばかりか or ばかりでなく. If the first thing is not true at all, or the result is the complete opposite, use どころか. If the second half asks someone to do something, choose ばかりでなく.
What to learn next
These all belong to the same "not only ~" family. Look at 〜のみならず, 〜はもちろん, 〜上に and 〜に限らず, and compare how each one feels.
n2-35:
The idea in one line
「〜ざるを得ない」 means "have no choice but to ~" or "can't help but ~". You don't really want to, but given the situation there is no other option, so you have to do it. It's like saying in English, "I had no choice, so I just gritted my teeth and went."
It's easier to remember if you break it apart: ざる is the classical Japanese "not", and 得ない means "can't". Together that's "can't not do it", which equals "have no choice but to". 得ない is read えない.
When to use it
Forced by circumstancesFor some reason, you're forced to do something you'd rather not do.
・台風が来るので、旅行を中止せざるを得ない。(A typhoon is coming, so we have no choice but to cancel the trip.)
・人が足りないので、休みの日も出勤せざるを得なかった。(We were short-staffed, so I had no choice but to go to work on my day off.)
Have to admit / have to sayOften used with 認める and 言う, meaning "I don't like it, but that's the fact."
・彼の実力は認めざるを得ない。(I have to admit his ability.)
・残念ながら、この計画は失敗だったと言わざるを得ない。(Unfortunately, I have to say this plan was a failure.)
How to form it: first check the verb group
Change the verb to its ない-form, drop the ない, then add ざるを得ない.
Group 1 (godan verbs):
行く → 行かない → drop ない → 行かざるを得ない
言う → 言わない → 言わざるを得ない
従う → 従わない → 従わざるを得ない
Group 2 (ichidan verbs):
認める → 認めない → 認めざるを得ない
諦める → 諦めざるを得ない
Group 3 (both are exceptions, just memorize them):
する → せざるを得ない (not しざる)
来る → 来ざるを得ない (こざるをえない)
The past tense is 得なかった, and the polite form is 得ません.
Easy mistakes
・する becomes せざる. 「しざるを得ない」 is wrong. "Noun + する" verbs like 中止する and 出勤する work the same way: 中止せざるを得ない.
・For verbs ending in う, like 言う and 従う, the ない-form uses わ: 言わない. So it's 言わざる, not 「言あざる」.
・得ない is read えない. Don't read it as とくない or うない.
・This is a fairly formal, written-style expression, common in news, reports and formal situations. When chatting with friends, a phrase like 行くしかない sounds more natural for "have no choice but to".
・It carries the flavor of "I don't actually want to", so don't use it for things you really want to do.
Telling similar patterns apart
なければならない = should/must do because of rules or reason, not necessarily with any emotion:
明日は会議だから、早く行かなければならない。 (There's a meeting tomorrow, so I have to go early.)
ざるを得ない = you didn't want to, but the situation leaves you no choice:
熱があるが、代わりの人がいないので、行かざるを得ない。 (I have a fever, but there's nobody to cover for me, so I have no choice but to go.)
ずにはいられない (it looks similar, with ず/ざる in both) = you can't hold back, can't help it. The emotion just bursts out by itself:
部長の冗談がおもしろくて、笑わずにはいられなかった。 (The manager's joke was so funny I couldn't help laughing.)
部長の冗談はつまらなかったが、笑わざるを得なかった。 (The manager's joke was boring, but I had no choice but to laugh along.)
Quick test: for a plain "should do", use なければならない. For "don't want to, but no choice", use ざるを得ない. For "can't help it", use ずにはいられない.
What to learn next
It often appears with "since ~" clauses: 上司の判断である以上、従わざるを得ない。 (Since it's the boss's decision, we have no choice but to follow.) Next, try 〜上は and 〜からには, which also express "since ~, then ~".
n2-6:
The idea in one line
「〜次第」means "as soon as ~, right away ~". Think of what customer service says: "We'll let you know as soon as your order arrives" or "We'll tell you the moment the results are out." It's the formal, slightly businesslike "as soon as ~".
How to attach it
Verbs: change to the ます form, drop ます, and attach 次第 directly.
届きます → drop ます → 届き次第
終わります → 終わり次第わかります → わかり次第見つけます → 見つけ次第
Action nouns that can take する (like 到着する and 決定する): usually you drop する and attach 次第 straight to the noun.
到着する → 到着次第決定する → 決定次第
(You'll also see 到着し次第. It means the same thing.)
When to use it
I'll do it right awayThe first part is something that hasn't happened yet but you're waiting for. The second part is what the speaker plans to do.
・荷物が届き次第、ご連絡いたします。(We'll contact you as soon as the package arrives.)
・詳しいことがわかり次第、お知らせします。(We'll let you know as soon as the details are confirmed.)
Asking the other person to act right awayThe second part can also be a request or an instruction.
・到着次第、お電話ください。(Please call me as soon as you arrive.)
・準備ができ次第、始めてください。(Please start as soon as you're ready.)
Easy mistakes
・You can't use it for things that already happened: "It started raining as soon as I got to the station" can't use 次第. What follows 次第 is something you're going to do next, never a past-tense event.
・What follows has to be something a person can choose to do (contact, leave, ask someone to do something). It can't be an uncontrollable result like "it started raining" or "I was startled."
・It doesn't attach to the dictionary form: it's 届き次第, not 届く次第.
・The tone is very formal and sounds stiff with friends. Among friends, just say 着いたらすぐ連絡するね (I'll message you as soon as I get there).
Another meaning: depends on ~
Noun + 次第だ／次第で「次第」has another common use meaning "it depends on ~".
・成功するかどうかは、君の努力次第だ。(Whether you succeed depends on your effort.)
・天気次第で、予定が変わるかもしれません。(Depending on the weather, the plans might change.)
This is a different thing from the "as soon as ~" use above. After an ordinary noun (effort, weather, money, etc.), you'll usually see 次第だ／次第で, meaning "depends on." After an action noun that can take する, like 到着 or 決定, followed by what you'll do, it means "as soon as ~."
Telling it apart from a similar-looking pattern
Both can mean "as soon as I get home ~":
次第 = hasn't happened yet, and I'll act right away when it does: 家に着き次第、電話します。 (I'll call you as soon as I get home.)
たとたん = already happened, and something unexpected pops up at that very moment: 家に着いたとたん、雨が降り出した。 (The moment I got home, it suddenly started to rain.)
Quick test: if it hasn't happened yet and you'll act right once it's done, use 次第. If it already happened and something unexpected occurred in that instant, use たとたん.
n2-11:
The idea in one line
「〜ものの」means "I did ~, but..." or "although ~, ...". For example: "I bought the ticket, but in the end I couldn't go." The first part is true and you admit it, but what follows doesn't go the way you'd expect. It often carries a feeling of "ah, it didn't work out."
When to use it
Did it, but nothing came of itThis is the most common use. You did something, but things didn't continue as expected.
・チケットを買ったものの、結局行けなかった。(I bought the ticket, but in the end I couldn't go.)
・ジムに入会したものの、忙しくて一度しか行っていない。(I joined a gym, but I've been too busy and have only gone once.)
・やると言ったものの、正直自信がない。(I said I'd do it, but honestly I'm not confident.)
A gap between the two partsThe first part makes you expect a certain result, but the second part isn't that. The second part doesn't have to be something bad.
・このアパートは駅から遠いものの、家賃が安い。(This apartment is far from the station, but the rent is cheap.)
How to attach it
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly.
買った → 買ったものの遠い → 遠いものの
な-adjectives: change 「だ」 to 「な」, or to 「である」.
簡単だ → 簡単なものの簡単だ → 簡単であるものの
Nouns: change 「だ」 to 「である」.
学生だ → 学生であるものの
The form you'll hear most
とはいうものの"That said, but..." It can come at the end of a clause, or stand alone at the start of a sentence.
・日本に十年住んでいるとはいうものの、敬語はまだ苦手だ。(Even though I've lived in Japan for ten years, I'm still not good at honorific speech.)
・ダイエット中だ。とはいうものの、甘いものはやめられない。(I'm on a diet. That said, I can't give up sweets.)
Easy mistakes
・Nouns and な-adjectives can't take 「だ」 directly: it's not 静かだものの but 静かなものの, and nouns use 学生であるものの.
・The second half can't contain your own intention, a command, or a request. You can't say 高いものの、買おう or 高いものの、買ってください. Use 「けど」 there: 高いけど、買おう.
・The first half has to be something that's already a fact. You can't use it for things that haven't happened or are just hypothetical.
・The tone is fairly formal and shows up in writing, news, and formal settings. When chatting with friends, 買ったけど、行けなかった sounds more natural.
Telling it apart from similar-looking patterns
ものの = "I did ~, but..." The focus is acknowledging the first part, but the result falls short, often with a note of regret:
チケットを買ったものの、行けなかった。 (I bought the ticket, but couldn't go.)
にもかかわらず = "despite ~, ..." The focus is a sharp contrast between the two parts, often with surprise or dissatisfaction, and it's often used about other people:
チケットを買ったにもかかわらず、彼は来なかった。 (Even though he'd bought a ticket, he didn't come.)
ものなら only looks similar and means something totally different: "if it were possible to ~":
行けるものなら、行きたかった。 (If I could have gone, I would have wanted to.)
Quick test: for "I did ~, but..." use ものの. For "despite ~" use にもかかわらず. If you see "if it were possible to ~," that's ものなら, not a contrast.
What to learn next
Other patterns with a similar "although" meaning are とはいえ, つつも, and ながらも. It helps to compare them side by side.
n2-15:
The idea in one line
「〜にしても」is the English "even if ~, still ~" or "even granting that ~". You give way first and accept the other person's reason (fine, you're busy), but your conclusion doesn't change (you could at least have been in touch). It often carries a complaining or critical tone: "that still doesn't excuse it."
How to form it
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly to the plain form.
忙しい → 忙しいにしても知らなかった → 知らなかったにしても
Nouns and な-adjectives: in the present tense, don't add だ; attach directly. In the past tense, use だった.
冗談 → 冗談にしても大変 → 大変にしても冗談だった → 冗談だったにしても
Patterns you'll hear most
Even if ~You concede a point, then give your own opinion or complaint. It's often preceded by 「いくら」(no matter how much).
・いくら忙しいにしても、返事ぐらいはしてほしい。(No matter how busy you are, I'd like at least a reply.)
・冗談にしても、言っていいことと悪いことがある。(Even if it's a joke, there are things you can say and things you can't.)
No matter ~Put a question word like 「何、どこ、誰」in front.
・何をするにしても、健康が一番だ。(Whatever you do, health comes first.)
AにしてもBにしても"Whether A or B," the result is the same. A and B are usually things of the same kind, or two opposite choices.
・行くにしても行かないにしても、早めに連絡してください。(Whether you go or not, please let me know early.)
・電車にしてもバスにしても、朝は混む。(Whether it's the train or the bus, it's crowded in the morning.)
それにしてもThis has become a fixed phrase meaning "even so" or "still, though." It's super common in conversation.
・「バスが遅れたんだって。」「それにしても遅すぎるよ。」("I heard the bus was late." "Even so, that's way too late.")
Common mistakes
・Don't add だ after a noun: say 冗談にしても, not 「冗談だにしても」.
・The second half is usually your own view: criticism, dissatisfaction, advice or a judgment. It pairs often with 「はずだ」「べきだ」「〜てほしい」「〜ない」.
・English "even if" can be quite neutral, but 「にしても」often has a flavor of "I can understand that, but it's still not OK." Said straight to a superior, it can sound like you're blaming them.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
にしては = "for ~, surprisingly ~." The result differs from what you'd expect:
初めてにしては上手だね。(For a first time, that's really good!)
にしても = "even if it's ~, still ~." The reason can't be used as an excuse:
初めてにしても、これはひどすぎる。(Even if it's your first time, this is way too bad.)
にしろ・にせよ: nearly identical in meaning and usage to にしても, just more formal. にしても is the most colloquial; にせよ leans toward writing and formal settings.
いずれにしても、明日また連絡します。／いずれにせよ、明日また連絡します。(In any case, I'll contact you again tomorrow.)
Quick tip: to say "even if ~," use にしても; to say "for ~, surprisingly," use にしては. One syllable apart, very different meanings.
What to learn next
More formal synonyms: 〜にしろ・〜にせよ.
n2-18:
The idea in one line
「〜ものなら」has two meanings, and you can tell them apart by the form of the verb in front:
・After the potential form (行ける, 戻れる): "if only I could ~" (but it's hard). It's like sighing, "If only I could do it over."
・After the volitional form (〜よう, 〜おう): "if you should ~, you're in trouble." It's like warning someone, "Don't you dare be even a minute late."
How to form it
Usage ①: potential form + ものなら (the potential form is the "can do ~" form)
戻る → 戻れるものなら食べる → 食べられるものならする → できるものなら
Usage ②: volitional form + ものなら (the volitional form is the 〜よう／〜おう form, so you often see 「〜ようものなら」)
言う → 言おうものなら遅れる → 遅れようものなら失敗する → 失敗しようものなら
In speech, ものなら often becomes もんなら: 戻れるもんなら戻りたいよ。(If I could go back, I would, believe me.)
When to use it
A wistful wishUsage ①. You know it's hard, almost impossible, but you can't help saying "if only it were possible..." It's usually followed by a wish like 「〜たい」「〜てあげたい」.
・戻れるものなら、高校時代に戻りたい。(If I could, I'd go back to my high school days.)
・代われるものなら、代わってあげたい。(If only I could, I'd take your place.)
・休めるものなら、一週間ぐらい休みたい。(If I could take time off, I'd love a week.)
A challengeAlso usage ①, but followed by the imperative 「〜てみろ」. It means "go ahead and try, if you can," assuming the other person can't, and deliberately provoking them.
・やれるものなら、やってみろ。(If you think you can, go ahead and try.)
A warningUsage ②. It means "if you do ~, you'll be in big trouble." It's often used with 「少しでも」「一度でも」「一分でも」, exaggerating how terrible the consequences would be.
・うちの父は、門限を一分でも過ぎようものなら、すごく怒る。(My dad gets furious if I'm even one minute past curfew.)
・部長の前でそんなことを言おうものなら、大変なことになるよ。(If you said something like that in front of the department head, it would turn into a huge mess.)
Common mistakes
・Usage ① must use the potential form: say 行けるものなら, not 行くものなら.
・Usage ② uses the volitional form: 言おうものなら, 遅れようものなら. Don't mix the two patterns.
・Usage ① carries a sense of "hard to do." If something is actually easy, it sounds odd, and a plain 「〜たら」 is enough.
・Usage ① is usually followed by a wish (〜たい) or a command (〜てみろ), rarely by a plain statement.
・「やれるものならやってみろ」 is a provocation. Say it to a senior or a boss and you're guaranteed a fight.
・Both usages can be translated as "if ~" in English, but the meanings are very different: the potential form is "I'd love to, but I can't," and the volitional form is "don't you dare."
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Even for the same "I want to go," 〜たら and 〜ものなら show different levels of confidence on your part:
〜たら = a simple hypothetical that could really happen: 時間があったら、行きたい。(If I have time, I'd like to go.)
〜ものなら = you feel it's nearly impossible and are just saying it: 行けるものなら、行きたい。(If only I could go... but I probably can't.)
Quick tip: if you feel there's a chance, use たら. If you feel there's little hope and you're just saying it, use potential form + ものなら. To warn someone "if you dare, you're done," use 〜ようものなら.
n2-19:
The idea in one line
「〜ないことには」 means “unless you ~ first, there's no way to ~”. The first thing is a threshold: if you don't cross it, the rest is off the table. Think of “How would you know if it's good if you've never tried it?” or “Without the boss's approval, nothing can happen.”
When to use it
You can't know until you tryThe most common use. The first part is almost always 「〜てみない」 (“don't try”).
・食べてみないことには、おいしいかどうかわからない。(Unless you try it, you can't tell if it's good.)
・やってみないことには、何とも言えません。(Until I actually try it, I really can't say.)
PrerequisiteIf one thing isn't done first, the next step can't go ahead.
・部長がOKしないことには、この企画は進められない。(Unless the department head signs off, we can't move this project forward.)
How to form it
Take the verb's ない form and add 「ことには」 directly. First, a quick review of how to make the ない form:
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the matching 「あ」-row sound, then add ない.行く → change く to か → 行かない会う → 会わない (う becomes わ)
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop 「る」 and add ない.見る → 見ない
Group 3: する → しない来る → 来ない (こない)
Put together: 確認しない → 確認しないことには
These are the endings that most often follow in the second half. Learn them as set phrases: わからない, 何とも言えない, 始まらない, 決められない, 話にならない.
Common mistakes
・The second half must be a result like “can't / don't know / doesn't work out”. It can't be a positive outcome: 勉強しないことには、合格できる is wrong.
・The second half also can't be a command, request, or invitation: 確認しないことには、電話してください sounds unnatural.
・Don't mix it up with 「〜ないことはない」, which means “it's not that I don't ~”: 行けないことはない (it's not that I can't go). One small difference in wording, a completely different meaning.
・The tone is fairly formal and common at work and in writing. With friends, people more often say 「やってみないとわからない」.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
ないことには = the thing hasn't happened yet, and you stress “nothing works until you do it first.” The second half is always negative:
住んでみないことには、その町のよさはわからない。 (Unless you actually live there, you won't know how good the town is.)
てはじめて = the thing has already been done, and “only after doing it did I realize for the first time.” The second half is what you found out or understood (good or bad):
住んでみてはじめて、その町のよさがわかった。 (Only after living there did I understand how good the town is.)
ないと／なければ = the most general “if you don't ~.” The second half is less restricted and can be a warning, a result, a judgment, and so on (but after 「〜ないと」 you can't use sentences of will or request, like 「～ましょう」 or 「～てください」):
予約しないと、入れないよ。 (If you don't book, you won't get in.)
You can also say 「予約しないことには、入れない」, but it sounds harder, as if stressing that “booking is an absolute requirement.”
Quick rule of thumb: to say “nothing can happen before you do it,” use ないことには. For “you only know once you've done it,” use てはじめて. For an ordinary “if you don't ~,” ないと／なければ is enough.
n2-29:
The idea in one line
「〜にすぎない」 means “it's merely ~” or “it's nothing more than ~”. The speaker deliberately plays something down, as if to say “that's all it is, no big deal.”
How to form it
Nouns: attach directly, with no だ in between.
噂 → 噂にすぎない (it's just a rumor)
Verbs: attach to the plain form (dictionary form or た form).
従った → 従ったにすぎない (he was merely following orders)
For the past tense, use にすぎなかった; for a polite style, use にすぎません.
When to use it
Downplaying somethingStresses “that's all it is, don't read too much into it.”
・それはただの噂にすぎない。(That's nothing more than a rumor.)
・彼は命令に従ったにすぎない。(He was merely following orders.)
Small numbersOften appears with 「わずか」 (“a mere”) to emphasize how small the number is.
・参加者はわずか5人にすぎなかった。(There were only five participants, a mere five.)
Modesty when praisedSaid about yourself, it becomes “I didn't do anything special.”
・私は当たり前のことをしたにすぎません。(I only did what anyone should do.)
How you'll usually hear it
It's often preceded by ただの, 単なる (“mere”), ほんの (“just a little”), or わずか, which strengthen the “only” feeling.
When the sentence isn't finished and continues, it becomes にすぎず:
・これは一つの例にすぎず、問題はほかにもたくさんある。(This is only one example, and there are plenty of other problems.)
Common mistakes
・Don't add だ after a noun: write 噂にすぎない, not 「噂だにすぎない」.
・It's a different thing from 「〜すぎる」 (“too ~”). 高すぎない means “not too expensive,” while にすぎない always has 「に」 in front and means “nothing more than.”
・The tone is fairly formal and very common in news, reports, and speeches. With friends, ただの噂だよ or 〜だけだよ sounds more natural.
・It carries a judgment of “not worth mentioning.” Said about someone else, as in 彼はまだ新入社員にすぎない, it can sound a bit dismissive. Said about yourself, it comes across as modest.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
にすぎない = plays something down: “it's merely ~”:
今回の成功は偶然にすぎない。 (This success is nothing more than luck.)
にほかならない = states something flatly: “it is precisely ~, nothing else”:
今回の成功はみんなの努力の結果にほかならない。 (This success is nothing other than the result of everyone's hard work.)
Both look like 「〜にＸない」, and both can end up translated with something like “nothing but ~” in English, so they're easy to mix up. But the tone is actually the opposite: the first belittles, the second affirms strongly.
Quick rule of thumb: to say “it's nothing special,” use にすぎない. To say “it's exactly that and nothing else,” use にほかならない.
n2-41:
The idea in one line
「〜に違いない」 means "must be ~" or "has to be ~". You see a clue and draw a confident conclusion, like a detective: "The light is on, so someone must be inside." It expresses your inference, not a confirmed fact.
When to use it
Concluding from a clueThere is evidence or a situation in front of you that makes you very sure.
・電気がついている。誰かいるに違いない。 (The light is on. Someone must be there.)
・顔がそっくりだ。あの二人は兄弟に違いない。 (Their faces look exactly alike. Those two must be brothers.)
Inferring about the pastPut the verb in the past form to guess "it must have been ~."
・彼女はもう知っていたに違いない。 (She must have known already.)
It often appears together with きっと, which makes the tone even more certain: きっと疲れているに違いない。 (He must be exhausted.)
How to form it
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly. Present, past and negative all work.
来る → 来るに違いない来た → 来たに違いない来ない → 来ないに違いない
高い → 高いに違いない
な-adjectives and nouns: drop 「だ」 first, then attach.
大変だ → 大変に違いない犯人だ → 犯人に違いない
In more formal writing you will also see 犯人であるに違いない.
Common mistakes
・Don't keep 「だ」 after a な-adjective or noun: 大変だに違いない is wrong.
・English "must" can also express obligation ("You must come!"), but 「に違いない」 only means "I'm confident this is the case." You can't use it to tell someone to do something.
・Don't use it for things you know for certain yourself. Saying 私は学生に違いない about your own status or feelings sounds like you're guessing about yourself, which is strange.
・It has a slightly written, novel-like feel. When chatting with friends, Japanese people more often say きっと〜だよ or 〜に決まってる.
・The polite form is 〜に違いありません.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
はず = based on known facts or arrangements, "it should be ~":
昨日送ったから、今日届くはずだ。 (I sent it yesterday, so it should arrive today.)
に違いない = you see a clue and reason your way to a conclusion:
窓が割れている。泥棒が入ったに違いない。 (The window is broken. A burglar must have broken in.)
Swapping in はず here would sound unnatural, because you aren't calculating from a known arrangement. You're making a judgment from what you see in front of you. Also, はず can be followed by "but it turned out otherwise": 来るはずなのに来ない。 (He's supposed to come, but he hasn't.) に違いない has no such use.
に決まっている = "of course it is ~!" It's more subjective and colloquial, and often carries emotion:
そんな話、嘘に決まってるよ。 (A story like that? Of course it's a lie!)
に相違ない = same meaning as に違いない, but stiffer and more formal, mostly found in writing.
Quick rule of thumb: use 「はず」 when you reason from logic or arrangements; use 「に違いない」 when you reach a conclusion from a clue; use 「に決まってる」 for an emotional "of course it is!" in conversation.
What to learn next
Next, look at 〜に決まっている and 〜に相違ない, which also express confidence, and sort out the differences in tone and situation.
n2-43:
The idea in one line
「〜に相違ない」 is the formal-suit version of 「〜に違いない」. It means "must be ~" or "surely is ~." You feel very sure, but it is still an inference. The tone is like "undoubtedly" or "it must be the case that…" in a report or newspaper commentary. You wouldn't say it in everyday chat.
First, the word itself: 相違 is read そうい and means "difference, discrepancy." So 相違ない literally means "there is no discrepancy," that is, "it can't be otherwise."
How to form it
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly to the plain form (the form without ます or です).
知っている → 知っているに相違ない (must know)
高かった → 高かったに相違ない (must have been expensive)
Nouns and な-adjectives: don't add だ, just attach directly.
彼 → 彼に相違ない (must be him)
有名 → 有名に相違ない (must be famous)
For the past, use だった: 彼だったに相違ない (it must have been him)
When to use it
Written inferenceIn reports, papers, newspaper commentary and detective novels, to draw a conclusion from clues.
・犯人はこの近くに住んでいるに相違ない。 (The culprit must live near here.)
・この結果は全員の努力の賜物に相違ない。 (This result must be the fruit of everyone's effort.)
Polite versionChange it to 〜に相違ありません to state your inference in a formal setting.
・犯人はあの男に相違ありません。 (The culprit must be that man.)
Confirming facts: testimony and documentsThis type is not an inference. When giving testimony, answering the police or filling out documents, 相違ありません is a set phrase meaning "that is correct, there is no mistake," about something you already know yourself.
・これは私の財布に相違ありません。 (This is indeed my wallet.)
・上記のとおり相違ありません。 (The above is true and correct.)
The second sentence is often printed at the bottom of application forms and written affirmations. There is no に before 相違 because it means "there is no discrepancy with what is written above."
Common mistakes
・After nouns and な-adjectives, don't add だ: it's 彼に相違ない, not 彼だに相違ない.
・The 「相」 in 相違 is read そう, and the whole word is read そうい.
・Saying あの店、おいしいに相違ない to a friend would sound odd, like you're acting in a detective drama. In casual speech, use おいしいに違いない or きっとおいしいよ.
・When used as an inference, the core is a confident guess. You wouldn't use 「〜に相違ない」 to guess at something you confirmed with your own eyes or already knew. The exception is 相違ありません as a set phrase for confirming or certifying (the testimony and documents type above).
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Same situation: he succeeded. Why?
に違いない = the general "it must be ~," usable in both speech and writing:
彼が成功したのは、努力したからに違いない。 (The reason he succeeded must be that he worked hard.)
に相違ない = same meaning, but stiffer and more formal, found almost only in writing:
彼が成功したのは、努力したからに相違ない。 (The reason he succeeded is undoubtedly that he worked hard.)
に決まっている = colloquial and subjective, "of course that's why," often with a tone that brooks no argument:
努力したからに決まってるよ。 (Of course it's because he worked hard!)
にほかならない = not an inference but a firm assertion by the speaker, "nothing other than ~," used to explain a cause or essence:
彼の成功は、努力の結果にほかならない。 (His success is nothing other than the result of hard work.)
Quick rule of thumb: use に違いない for a general inference; use に相違ない for the same inference when writing a report or essay; use に決まっている for "of course!" with friends; use にほかならない to stress "it's precisely this, nothing else."
n2-50:
The idea in one line
「〜に伴って」 is the formal “along with ~” / “as ~ (changes)” you see in news reports and official notices. One thing happens or changes, and something else happens or changes with it. A notice like “Due to the office relocation, our phone number will change” is exactly where Japanese reaches for it.
When to use it
Changing togetherWhen the first thing changes, the second changes with it. It is often used for gradual changes such as population, the economy, or temperature.
・年を取るに伴って、体力が落ちてきた。(As I've gotten older, my stamina has declined.)
・気温の上昇に伴い、電気の使用量が増えている。(As temperatures rise, electricity use keeps increasing.)
Bringing another event with itThe first part is a one-time event, and something else happens as a result or side effect. This is extremely common in notices and news.
・地震に伴い、津波が発生した。(The earthquake was accompanied by a tsunami.)
・事務所の移転に伴い、電話番号が変わります。(Due to the office relocation, our phone number will change.)
・工事に伴って、この道は来週から通れなくなります。(Because of construction, this road will be closed from next week.)
How to form it
Noun + に伴って: The most common pattern. The noun is usually one that expresses change or an event, like “increase, development, spread, relocation”.
人口の増加 → 人口の増加に伴って
Verb dictionary form + に伴って, or with の added: のに伴って. You'll see both.
人口が増える → 人口が増えるに伴って
年を取る → 年を取るのに伴って
に伴って and に伴い mean the same thing, but に伴い is more formal and is the favorite in news headlines and notices.
To connect directly to a noun, change it to に伴う + noun: 台風に伴う大雨 (heavy rain accompanying a typhoon)
Common mistakes
・The kanji 伴 is read とも here, as in ともなって. Don't read it as ばん.
・It's very formal, the language of news, reports and notices. If you tell a friend “it got cold, so everyone started wearing coats”, using it would sound like reading a press release. In casual speech, 〜につれて or even 〜と sounds more natural.
・With nouns, the noun before it usually takes の: it's 経済の発展に伴って, not 経済が発展に伴って.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
につれて also means “as ~”, but it only covers “one side changes little by little, and the other side changes little by little along with it”.
Both work with the same topic, just with a different tone:
人口が増えるにつれて、町がにぎやかになった。(As the population grew, the town became livelier. Explanation or conversation both work.)
人口の増加に伴って、住宅不足が深刻化した。(With the population increase, the housing shortage became serious. News or report tone.)
But if the first part is a one-time event, only に伴って works:
○地震に伴い、津波が発生した。
×地震につれて、津波が発生した。(An earthquake isn't a “gradual change”, so につれて can't be used.)
Quick rule of thumb: for things that happen once, like an earthquake, a move or construction, use only に伴って. When both sides are changing gradually, either works. Casual talk leans toward につれて; news and notices lean toward に伴って.
What to learn next
Another pattern about things linking together is 〜に応じて (adjusting according to ~), as in 人数に応じて、部屋を選べます。 (You can choose a room according to the number of people.) Its focus is “responding to different situations”, not “changing along with something”, so it's a good one to memorize as a contrast with に伴って.
n2-57:
The idea in one line
Think of 「〜まい」 as the negative counterpart of the volitional form 「〜よう」, and a stiff, written-style one at that. 行こう means “I'll go”, so 行くまい means “I will never go (again)”. It has a second meaning, “probably won't ~”, much like the literary English “I shall never…” and “surely it won't…”.
When to use it
Resolving not toYou make up your mind: “I will never ~ again”. It often appears with 二度と (never again), and is often followed by と思う, と心に誓う or と決める.
・あの店には二度と行くまい。(I will never go to that shop again.)
・二度とあのようなミスは犯すまいと心に誓った。(I vowed to myself never to make a mistake like that again.)
Guessing it won'tIt means the same as ないだろう, used to guess that someone or something “probably won't ~”.
・彼は今さら戻ってくるまい。(At this point, he probably won't come back.)
・そんなことはあるまい。(Surely nothing like that could happen.)
How to tell which one it is: if the subject is “I” and it's about resolve, it's the first type. If the subject is someone else or something else, it's the second.
How to form it
Group 1 (godan verbs): Add まい directly to the dictionary form.
行く → 行くまい乗る → 乗るまいある → あるまい
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): Drop 「る」 and add まい, or keep it and add まい to the dictionary form. Both are correct.
食べる → 食べまい／食べるまい
Group 3 (する・来る): There are several forms, and you should recognize them all.
する → するまい／すまい (some people also say しまい)
来る → 来るまい／来まい
「来まい」 is traditionally read こまい, but きまい is also common today. You'll see both readings.
Common mistakes
・With Group 1 verbs, まい attaches to the dictionary form, not to something that looks like the ない form: it's 行くまい, not 「行かまい」, and certainly not 「行かないまい」.
・まい is itself negative, and there is no affirmative version. To say “I'll do it”, use the volitional form 行こう.
・It can't be used to tell someone else not to do something. あなたは行くまい isn't “don't go”; it sounds like “you probably won't go”. To tell someone not to go, say 行かないで.
・When 「〜まい」 ends a sentence to express resolve, the person resolving is the speaker.
・It's very written and stiff. Saying もう行くまい to a friend would sound like novel narration. In speech, もう二度と行かない is enough.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Same situation: guessing whether he'll come tomorrow.
ないだろう: The general form, fine in both speech and writing.
・彼は明日来ないだろう。(He probably won't come tomorrow.)
まい: The same meaning, but written and stiff, and the tone stays reserved: “probably”.
・彼は明日来るまい。(He surely won't come tomorrow.)
っこない: Colloquial and very firm: “no way”.
・あんなに怒っていたんだから、来っこないよ。(He was that angry, so there's no way he'll come.)
Quick rule of thumb: in everyday speech use ないだろう; for a reserved “probably not” in writing use まい; for a flat “no way” in casual talk use っこない.
What to learn next
まい often shows up in two set phrases:
「〜うが〜まいが」 means “whether or not you do ~”: 行こうが行くまいが、私の自由だ。 (Whether I go or not is my choice.)
「〜ではあるまいし」 means “it's not like ~”: 子どもじゃあるまいし、一人で行けるよ。 (It's not like I'm a child; I can go by myself.)
n2-62:
The idea in one line
「〜に越したことはない」 means "it's best if you can ~" or "nothing beats ~". It states something everyone agrees with, like saying "well, obviously." The tone is mild, not a command.
Literally, 越す means "to exceed," so the whole phrase says "there's nothing better than this." That's how it comes to mean "this is best."
How to form it
Verbs: dictionary form or ない form + に越したことはない
確認する → 確認するに越したことはない (it's best to double-check)
使わない → 使わないに越したことはない (it's best not to use it if you can)
い-adjectives: attach directly
安い → 安いに越したことはない
な-adjectives and nouns: attach directly, or add である (more formal)
安全 → 安全に越したことはない／安全であるに越したことはない
How you'll hear it most
Stating common senseUsed on its own, it means "you can't go wrong doing this."
・準備は早いに越したことはない。 (Of course, the earlier you prepare, the better.)
・薬は飲まないに越したことはない。 (It's best not to take medicine if you can avoid it.)
Followed by けど・がThis is the most common use: first you admit "it's best if you can," then you say "but in reality…".
・経験はあるに越したことはないが、なくても大丈夫です。 (Experience is ideal, but it's fine if you don't have any.)
・値段は安いに越したことはないけど、品質も大事だよ。 (Cheaper is always better, but quality matters too, you know.)
Job ads often use the first kind of phrasing. It means "not required, but a plus if you have it."
Easy mistakes
・Write 越した, not 越す: 越すことはない is wrong.
・Use the dictionary form before it, not the た form: 早く行ったに越したことはない is wrong. Say 早く行くに越したことはない.
・Don't see only the 「ことはない」 at the end and assume it means "no need." The meaning is quite different (see the comparison below).
・It means "great if you can," not "you must." You wouldn't use it to firmly demand something from someone.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Same situation: "Is there a hurry?"
ことはない = no need to: そんなに急ぐことはない。 (There's no need to rush that much.)
に越したことはない = it's best if you can: 急ぐに越したことはない。 (Of course, the faster the better.)
Same situation: "Leaving early."
ほうがいい = gives the other person direct advice: 早く出たほうがいいよ。 (You'd better leave early.)
に越したことはない = states a general truth, softer and leaves room: 早く出るに越したことはない。 (Leaving early is always best.)
Another one with a similar feel: に限る = "~ is the best, go for it," which is your own strong recommendation: 暑い日は冷たいビールに限る。 (On a hot day, nothing beats a cold beer.) に越したことはない is common sense everyone agrees with, and the tone is calmer.
Quick tip: when you see 「に越した」, think "it doesn't get better than this." Only 「ことはない」 on its own means "no need." To advise someone directly, use 「ほうがいい」.
n2-1:
The idea in one line
「〜つつある」 means "is gradually ~ing" or "is increasingly ~". It describes a change that is happening and hasn't finished yet, like the news saying "temperatures keep rising" or "the economy is gradually recovering." The tone is fairly formal, and you'll mostly see it in news, reports, and articles.
When to use it
Change in progressSomething is slowly shifting in one direction, and it's still shifting now.
・景気は少しずつ回復しつつある。 (The economy is slowly recovering.)
・この町の人口は減りつつある。 (This town's population is gradually shrinking.)
・日本でもキャッシュレス決済が広がりつつある。 (In Japan too, cashless payment is becoming more widespread.)
Heading step by step toward a resultWith verbs like "disappear" or "approach," which describe changes that complete in a moment, it means "is moving step by step toward that result, but hasn't reached it yet."
・台風が日本に近づきつつある。 (The typhoon is gradually approaching Japan.)
・伝統的な祭りが消えつつある。 (Traditional festivals are gradually disappearing.)
Past tenseChange it to 「つつあった」 to say something was in the middle of changing at that time.
・当時、この町は大きく変わりつつあった。 (At that time, this town was undergoing big changes.)
How to form it
Put the verb in ます form, then drop ます and add 「つつある」.
増えます → 増えつつある進みます → 進みつつある
回復します → 回復しつつある失われます → 失われつつある
To be more polite, say 「つつあります」: 景気は回復しつつあります。
Easy mistakes
・It attaches to the ます stem, not the dictionary form: say 増えつつある, not 「増えるつつある」; say 回復しつつある, not 「回復するつつある」.
・The ending is ある, not いる.
・It only works with verbs that describe change, such as 増える, 減る, 変わる, 広がる, 進む, and 「〜化する」. Ordinary actions can't use it: "I'm eating" is ご飯を食べている, not 「ご飯を食べつつある」.
・It's very bookish. If you tell a friend "it's been getting colder lately," the natural way is 最近、だんだん寒くなってきたね。 Saying 「寒くなりつつある」 would sound like a news broadcast.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
〜ている: with verbs like "disappear," it means the change is already complete.
・その技術はもう失われている。 (That technology has already been lost.)
〜つつある: means still changing, not finished yet.
・その技術は失われつつある。 (That technology is gradually being lost.)
With verbs like "increase" and "decrease," 人口が減っている can also mean "is decreasing," and the meaning is very close. The difference is that つつある puts more emphasis on the ongoing process of change, and it's more formal.
〜ばかりだ (after the dictionary form): things only move in one direction, almost always getting worse, with a tone of worry or complaint.
・景気は悪くなるばかりだ。 (The economy just keeps getting worse.)
〜つつある: simply describes a change, either for the better or for the worse.
・景気は回復しつつある。 (The economy is gradually recovering.)
〜つつ（も）: with no ある after it, the meaning is completely different: "while ~ing" or "even though ~."
・体に悪いと知りつつ、タバコがやめられない。 (Even though I know it's bad for my health, I can't quit smoking.)
Quick tip: when you see 「つつ＋ある」, think "is gradually ~ing." For "has already become ~," use ている. For "only getting worse and worse," use ばかりだ. If there's only 「つつ」 with no ある, it means "while ~ing / even though ~."
What to learn next
Since this is also about change, a good next step is 「〜につれて」 (as ~), for example 年をとるにつれて、体力が落ちてきた。 (As I've gotten older, my stamina has declined.)
n2-3:
The idea in one line
「AからBにかけて」 means "from A through B, roughly" or "across this area / this stretch of time". The key word is "roughly": neither the start nor the end is a precise line. It's a fuzzy range. A weather forecast says "rain tonight into tomorrow." It doesn't say what minute it starts or stops, and Japanese uses にかけて for exactly that.
When to use it
Time rangeSomething happens within a rough period of time. It might continue the whole time, or it might come and go.
・今夜から明日の朝にかけて、強い雨が降るでしょう。 (Heavy rain is expected from tonight into tomorrow morning.)
・この辺りは、年末から正月にかけてとても混む。 (This area gets very crowded from the end of the year through New Year's.)
Place rangeA whole area stretching from one place to another. Very common in weather reports and news.
・九州から四国にかけて、大雨に注意してください。 (From Kyushu to Shikoku, please watch out for heavy rain.)
Body partYou'll also hear this in daily life, and it's especially handy at the doctor's when describing where it hurts.
・首から肩にかけてが痛いんです。 (It hurts from my neck down to my shoulders.)
How to form it
Basic pattern: noun + から + noun + にかけて
3月から4月 → 3月から4月にかけて

You can sometimes drop the 「から」 part and just say "toward ~ / around ~":
・週末にかけて、天気が崩れるでしょう。 (The weather will turn bad toward the weekend.)
When it comes before a noun, it becomes にかけての:
・春から夏にかけての季節が一番好きだ。 (My favorite time of year is from spring into summer.)
Common mistakes
・English "from A to B" covers everything, but Japanese splits it up. When the time is precise, like working hours or business hours, use から～まで.
　×9時から6時にかけて働きます。
　○9時から6時まで働きます。
・Only a noun can go before it, and it has to be something you can draw a range around: time, place, body part. Verbs don't work, and neither do people: for "from Mr. A to Mr. B" you don't use にかけて.
・Don't forget 「の」 before a following noun: it's 夏にかけての旅行, not 夏にかけて旅行.
・The tone is written and formal, most common in news, weather reports and explanatory writing. You'll hear it in everyday talk too, but for times, spoken Japanese more often just uses から～まで.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
から～まで = the start and end are clear and exact: 会議は1時から3時までです。 (The meeting is from one to three.)
にかけて = roughly within this range: 午後から夕方にかけて雨が降る。 (It will rain from the afternoon into the evening.)
にわたって = stresses that the whole span is covered, on a large scale. It often follows words of length or size like 「3日間」「10年」「全国」: 雨が3日間にわたって降り続いた。 (The rain kept falling for three full days.)
