One more: にかけては has an extra 「は」 and means something completely different: "when it comes to ~". 料理の腕にかけては、彼に勝てる人はいない。 (When it comes to cooking skill, nobody can beat him.) If you see the 「は」 and the sentence goes on to praise someone's ability, that's this one.
Quick rule of thumb: exact times use まで, rough ranges use にかけて, and "the whole long stretch" uses にわたって. If there's an extra 「は」 and the sentence is about ability, it's にかけては.
n2-4:
The idea in one line
「〜末（に）」 means "after going through a lot of ~, in the end…". Before it comes a process that took time and effort (long discussions, long agonizing, long hard work), and after it comes the result you finally arrived at. It's like saying, "We argued all night and in the end decided to go to Japan."
How to form it
Nounnoun + の + 末（に）
議論 → 議論の末に (after discussion)
苦労 → 苦労の末に (after a lot of hardship)
Verbverb た-form + 末（に）
悩む → 悩んだ → 悩んだ末に (after agonizing for a long time)
考える → 考えた → 考えた末に (after thinking it over for a long time)
You can drop 「に」 with no change in meaning. Before a noun, use 「末の」: 悩んだ末の決断 (a decision made after long agonizing).
How you'll hear it most
It's often followed by 「ようやく」「やっと」「ついに」, stressing "finally."
・長い話し合いの末、やっと契約が決まった。 (After long negotiations, the contract was finally settled.)
・何度も迷った末に、この部屋に決めた。 (After going back and forth many times, I finally chose this room.)
The result doesn't have to be good. Bad outcomes work too, since 「末」 just states objectively how things ended up.
・長い闘病の末に亡くなった。 (After a long battle with illness, he passed away.)
・悩んだ末、進学を諦めた。 (After agonizing for a long time, I gave up on further study.)
Common mistakes
・Verbs must be in the た-form: it's 悩んだ末, not 「悩む末」.
・Here 末 is read すえ, not まつ.
・What comes before it has to be "a process," something that takes time like discussing, striving, agonizing or negotiating. A bare length of time doesn't work: 「3時間の末」 sounds unnatural, so say 3時間の議論の末.
・「time noun + の末」 is a different meaning, "the end of ~": 来月の末に引っ越す means "I'm moving at the end of next month," not "after going through next month."
・What follows is a result that has already come out, usually in the past tense (決めた、決まった、出た). You can't follow it with "let's ~" or "please ~".
・The tone is fairly formal and common in news, reports and formal explanations. With friends, people more often say 「結局」.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
The same-level 「〜あげく（に）」 attaches the same way (た-form / noun + の) and also means "after going through a lot of ~, in the end…". The difference is the speaker's feeling.
末 = objectively states the final result. Good, bad or neutral all work:
さんざん迷った末、何も買わなかった。 (After a lot of hesitating, I ended up buying nothing.)
あげく = carries dissatisfaction or resignation, with the feeling of "after all that, you won't believe what happened…":
さんざん迷ったあげく、何も買わなかった。 (After all that hesitating, I ended up buying nothing!)
So when the result is good, as in 努力の末に合格した (after hard work, I passed), you normally wouldn't swap in あげく.
Quick rule of thumb: to simply report the result, use 末. If you're complaining or feeling resigned, as in "after all that, it came to this," use あげく.
What to learn next
Next, try 〜あげく（に）. Practicing the two together makes the difference in tone easier to catch.
n2-7:
The idea in one line
「〜て以来」 means "ever since ~, and it has stayed that way". Put a past event in front as the starting point, and the second half describes the state that has continued from then until now. Think of sentences like "Ever since I moved, I've been running every morning."
How to form it
Verb て-form + 以来 (read いらい). You already know the て-form, so just attach it:
来る → 来て以来会う → 会って以来卒業する → 卒業して以来
The passive works too: 導入される → 導入されて以来
When to use it
A state that continues up to nowIt often pairs with 「ている」 and 「ずっと」.
・日本に来て以来、ずっとこのアパートに住んでいる。 (Ever since I came to Japan, I've lived in this apartment the whole time.)
・子どもが生まれて以来、ゆっくり映画を見る時間がない。 (Ever since our child was born, I haven't had time to watch a movie in peace.)
Not once since then…It often pairs with 「一度も」 and 「〜ていない」.
・彼とけんかして以来、一度も話していない。 (Ever since I had a fight with him, we haven't spoken even once.)
Became something since thenWith 「〜ようになった」, it means a change happened and has lasted until now.
・留学して以来、字幕なしでドラマが見られるようになった。 (Ever since I studied abroad, I've become able to watch dramas without subtitles.)
Common mistakes
・It attaches to the て-form, not the た-form: say 卒業して以来, not 「卒業した以来」.
・The second half can't be a one-time event. "Since coming to Japan, I went to Kyoto once" can't use 以来: ×日本に来て以来、一度京都へ行った。 For a simple "after that, I did something," use 日本に来てから、京都へ行った。
・The first half must be something that has already happened. You can't use it for future plans.
・The starting point is usually some time ago. "Ever since I just finished lunch" sounds odd in English, and it's just as odd in Japanese.
・It sounds fairly formal and bookish. In casual conversation, many people say 〜てから、ずっと instead.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Take the same event, moving house:
てから = just the order of events, "did A, then B":
引っ越してから、ジョギングを始めた。 (After I moved, I started jogging.)
て以来 = it has been this way from then until now:
引っ越して以来、毎朝ジョギングしている。 (Ever since I moved, I've been jogging every morning.)
をきっかけに = stresses that the event was the trigger that got things started:
引っ越しをきっかけに、ジョギングを始めた。 (Moving house was the trigger; I started jogging.)
Quick test: if you can add "and it's still like that today" to the second half, use て以来. If it's just "and then," use てから. If you mean "that event is why I started," use をきっかけに.
What to learn next
以来 can also follow a time noun directly, or you can use それ以来 (since then) to pick up the previous sentence:
・去年の春以来、彼から連絡がない。 (I haven't heard from him since last spring.)
・一度飲みすぎて倒れた。それ以来、お酒は飲んでいない。 (I once drank too much and collapsed. I haven't had a drop since then.)
n2-9:
The idea in one line
「〜からこそ」 means "precisely because ~, (that's why) ~". The ordinary 「から」 just states a reason. Add 「こそ」 and it's like highlighting the reason with a marker: this is the reason, and nothing else. It's often used when going against the usual way of thinking: most people would feel A makes you not want to do something, but you do it precisely because of A.
How to form it
The "plain form" is the form without です・ます.
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly.
思う → 思うからこそ頑張った → 頑張ったからこそ忙しい → 忙しいからこそ
Nouns and な-adjectives: add 「だ」 in between.
家族 → 家族だからこそ大切 → 大切だからこそ
When to use it
Stressing the real reasonYou're telling the listener: this is exactly why I act this way.
・あなたのことを思うからこそ、厳しく言うんです。 (It's precisely because I care about you that I'm being so harsh.)
・毎日練習したからこそ、本番で落ち着いていられた。 (It's precisely because I practiced every day that I could stay calm on the day.)
Against the usual expectationNormally you'd expect the opposite reaction, but you say "it's exactly because of this that I ~."
・忙しいからこそ、休みの日を大切にしている。 (It's precisely because I'm busy that I treasure my days off.)
・失敗したからこそ、わかったこともある。 (There are things I only understood because I failed.)
だからこそPlaced at the start of a sentence, it picks up what the previous sentence said and means "and that's exactly why." This usage is very common.
・この仕事は大変です。だからこそ、やりがいがあります。 (This job is tough. And that's exactly why it's rewarding.)
The second half often ends in 「のだ」 or 「んです」. This adds an explanatory tone, as in "the fact is…", which goes well with からこそ.
Common mistakes
・Don't forget 「だ」 after nouns and な-adjectives: it's 家族だからこそ, not 「家族からこそ」.
・Only 「から」 works here, not 「ので」: there's no 「ので＋こそ」 pattern.
・Don't use it for ordinary, negative, trivial reasons. For "I overslept, so I was late," just say 寝坊したから遅刻した. Saying 「寝坊したからこそ遅刻した」 would sound very odd, as if oversleeping were some grand reason.
・In English you'd say "It's precisely because … that …", but the second half of the Japanese sentence needs no separate word for that "that." こそ already carries the emphasis.
・This phrase is emotionally heavy, so it shows up more in sincere talk, speeches and essays. Using it constantly for small everyday matters sounds dramatic.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
から = simply giving a reason.
・心配だから、電話した。 (I was worried, so I called.)
からこそ = stresses "this is the reason," often used when the other person has misunderstood, or when you want to make a strong point.
・心配だからこそ、何度も電話したんです。 (It's precisely because I was worried that I called you again and again.)
からには = "now that ~, then ~," followed by a resolution or something you should do.
・留学するからには、しっかり勉強したい。 (Now that I'm going to study abroad, I want to study seriously.)
からこそ = "precisely because ~," followed by a result or action that came from it.
・留学したからこそ、台湾の良さに気づいた。 (It's precisely because I studied abroad that I realized how good Taiwan is.)
Quick test: if "now that ~, I'll ~" fits, use からには. If "precisely because ~, ~" fits, use からこそ. If it's just an ordinary "because ~, so ~," plain から is enough.
n2-10:
The idea in one line
「〜にもかかわらず」means "in spite of ~" / "even though ~, still ~". You state a fact first, then follow it with a result that is the opposite of what you'd expect. It's very close to 「のに」, but it's more formal and objective. You'll see it a lot in news, reports, speeches and business settings, and rarely in casual chat with friends.
When to use it
Unexpected resultThings should have gone one way, but they didn't.
・何度も確認したにもかかわらず、同じミスをしてしまった。 (Even though I checked several times, I still made the same mistake.)
・雨にもかかわらず、たくさんの人が集まった。 (Despite the rain, a lot of people gathered.)
Describing the present situationThe second half doesn't have to be past tense. It can describe something that's still going on.
・反対が多いにもかかわらず、政府は計画を進めている。 (Despite strong opposition, the government is pushing ahead with the plan.)
・彼はお金持ちであるにもかかわらず、質素な生活をしている。 (Although he's wealthy, he lives a simple life.)
Thanks in formal settingsA set phrase you'll hear all the time in speeches and business emails.
・本日はお忙しいにもかかわらず、お集まりいただきありがとうございます。 (Thank you all for coming today despite your busy schedules.)
How to connect it
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly to the plain form (the dictionary form, or the た-form or ない-form).
努力した → 努力したにもかかわらず寒い → 寒いにもかかわらず
Nouns and な-adjectives: don't add 「だ」. Either attach directly, or add 「である」.
雨 → 雨にもかかわらず学生 → 学生であるにもかかわらず
不便 → 不便にもかかわらず (you can also say 不便であるにもかかわらず)
For the past, 「だった」 works fine: 学生だったにもかかわらず.
Easy mistakes
・Don't add だ after a noun: say 雨にもかかわらず, not 「雨だにもかかわらず」.
・The second half states a fact (something that has happened or is still going on). You can't follow it with will, invitations, commands or requests, like "let's ~", "please ~" or "I'll ~". To say "Even if it rains, let's go out," use ても: 雨でも出かけよう。
・The first half must also be a fact. English "even if" is often hypothetical (it hasn't happened yet). For that, use 「ても」, not にもかかわらず.
・It's very formal. If you're complaining to a friend, "I told you already and you still won't listen," のに sounds much more natural. にもかかわらず would sound like you're reading out a press release.
Telling similar patterns apart
のに = carries your own feelings (dissatisfaction, regret, surprise). It's very common in speech, and you can even leave it hanging at the end of a sentence.
にもかかわらず = a more calm, objective statement. It's formal and leans toward written language.
・何度も説明したのに、全然わかってくれない！ (I've explained it so many times, and you still don't get it!)
・何度も説明したにもかかわらず、理解してもらえなかった。 (Despite explaining it several times, I couldn't get them to understand.)
Trailing off mid-sentence, as in せっかく作ったのに。 (And I went to the trouble of making it...), only works with のに. You can't do it with にもかかわらず.
Another look-alike that's very easy to misread is にかかわらず, without the 「も」. It means something completely different: "regardless of ~".
・年齢にかかわらず、誰でも参加できます。 (Regardless of age, anyone can take part.)
・天気にかかわらず、試合は行います。 (The match will go ahead regardless of the weather.)
Quick rule of thumb: to complain or show emotion, use のに. To say "even though ~, still ~" in a formal, objective way, use にもかかわらず. When you see 「にかかわらず」, first check for 「も」. With も it means "even though"; without も it means "regardless of".
What to learn next
At the start of a sentence it becomes 「それにもかかわらず」, meaning "despite that" or "even so", and it picks up the previous sentence: 何度も注意された。それにもかかわらず、彼は遅刻を続けた。 (He was warned many times. Even so, he kept showing up late.)
Other N2 patterns meaning "although ~, but ~" are ものの and とはいえ. Try studying them side by side.
n2-12:
The idea in one line
「〜とはいえ」means "even though ~, still …" / "that may be true, but …". You first admit a fact, then add: "But it's not as simple as you might think."
Take "Even though it's spring, the mornings are still cold." You admit it's spring, but the impression that "spring = warm" isn't entirely true.
When to use it
"Even though it's ~"The first half is a fact that gives people a certain impression, and the second half says the reality is different from that impression.
・春とはいえ、朝晩はまだ寒い。 (Even though it's spring, mornings and evenings are still cold.)
・日本に5年住んでいるとはいえ、敬語はまだ苦手だ。 (Even though I've lived in Japan for five years, I'm still not good at keigo.)
・安いとはいえ、毎日買うと結構な金額になる。 (Cheap as it is, buying it every day adds up to quite a lot.)
At the start of a sentenceOn its own at the start of a sentence, it means "having said that" and picks up the previous sentence.
・仕事は大変だ。とはいえ、辞めるつもりはない。 (The work is tough. Having said that, I don't plan to quit.)
How to connect it
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly.
慣れている → 慣れているとはいえ合格した → 合格したとはいえ安い → 安いとはいえ
Nouns and な-adjectives: the 「だ」 is usually dropped, so attach とはいえ directly (adding だ is also possible).
春 → 春とはいえ便利 → 便利とはいえ
・便利とはいえ、スマホばかり見るのはよくない。 (Handy as it is, staring at your phone all the time isn't good.)
Easy mistakes
・The 「は」 is read as わ: とはいえ is pronounced 「とわいえ」.
・The first half must be a fact that already holds. You can't put a hypothetical that hasn't happened yet. "Even if it rains tomorrow" is 明日雨が降っても, not とはいえ.
・The second half must say something that runs against expectations, and it often appears with まだ or やはり. It doesn't mean "so", so you can't follow it with something that simply continues the first half.
・とはいえ feels somewhat written and formal. In casual talk with friends, people more often say とは言っても or って言っても.
Telling similar patterns apart
ものの also means "although ~, but", but its most natural use is "you did something, but the result fell short of expectations":
・チケットを買ったものの、結局行けなかった。 (I did buy the ticket, but in the end I couldn't go.)
If the first half is a noun, ものの has to become 「noun + である + ものの」, which sounds stiff. That's where とはいえ flows nicely:
・プロとはいえ、ミスすることもある。 (Even though they're pros, they sometimes make mistakes.)
にもかかわらず means "in spite of ~, …" and stresses that the result is unexpected, often with a tone of surprise or blame:
・雨にもかかわらず、たくさんの人が来た。 (Despite the rain, a lot of people came.)
とはいえ doesn't carry that strong sense of surprise. It's more like admitting the first fact and then calmly adding "but…".
Quick rule of thumb: for "even though it's ~ (an identity or state), that doesn't mean …", use とはいえ. For "I did ~, but the result wasn't …", use ものの. For "in spite of ~, it even …", use にもかかわらず.
What to learn next
とはいうものの means almost the same thing, and it can also open a sentence as "having said that": とはいうものの、やはり心配だ。 (Having said that, I'm still worried.)
n2-13:
The idea in one line
「〜くせに」 is the English “even though you…” / “and you of all people…”, said with some heat. When someone says 「知ってるくせに」, it doesn't just mean “even though you know.” Behind it is another line: “that's so unfair of you.” It isn't a neutral description. You're scolding or calling someone out.
How to form it
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly (present or past both work)
知っている → 知っているくせに若い → 若いくせに言った → 言ったくせに
な-adjectives: keep the な, then attach　下手 → 下手なくせに
Nouns: add の, then attach　子ども → 子どものくせに
How you'll hear it most
Calling someone outThe first half states the person's situation or ability, and the second half says what they did that's out of line.
・知っているくせに、教えてくれない。(You know, and yet you won't tell me.)
・行くって言ったくせに、来なかった。(You said you'd go, and then you didn't show up.)
・下手なくせに、いつも自慢する。(You're bad at it, yet you're always bragging.)
・子どものくせに、生意気なことを言うな。(You're just a kid, so don't talk back like that.)
Leaving it unfinishedYou skip the second half and stop right at くせに. It often has a playful, teasing or sulky tone.
・本当は好きなくせに。(You actually like it, don't you.)
Common mistakes
・Nouns and な-adjectives can't take だ: it's 子どものくせに and 下手なくせに, not 「子どもだくせに」or 「下手だくせに」.
・Both halves must be about the same person. “He knows, and he still won't say” works. If the subjects differ, you can't use くせに.
・The tone is harsh, basically scolding, so don't use it with your boss, customers or elders, and it doesn't belong in formal writing.
・It's mostly aimed at other people. Aimed at yourself, it becomes self-deprecating: 日本人のくせに、漢字が苦手なんです。(I'm Japanese, yet I'm not great at kanji.)
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Same situation: he knows the answer but won't tell me.
くせに = you're annoyed and blaming him: 彼は知っているくせに、教えてくれない。
のに = you find it surprising or regrettable, with a milder tone: 彼は知っているのに、教えてくれない。
にもかかわらず = formal, written, no emotion: 彼は事情を知っているにもかかわらず、説明しなかった。(Although he understood the situation, he did not explain it.)
のに has a wider range. It works in these two cases where くせに doesn't:
Different subjects in each half: 雨なのに、彼は出かけた。(Even though it was raining, he went out.)
Your own regret, with no one to blame: 一生懸命勉強したのに、落ちた。(I studied so hard, and I still failed.)
Quick rule of thumb: use くせに when you want to call someone out; use のに when you just find it regrettable or surprising; use にもかかわらず for formal situations.
n2-14:
The idea in one line
「〜一方で」 is like the English “while… , on the other hand…”. You set two things side by side: on one side A, on the other side B. It's especially common in news, reports and articles, and the tone is fairly formal.
When to use it
Contrasting two sidesUse it when one thing has both good and bad sides, or when two people or places are in opposite situations. You put them next to each other to compare.
・この仕事は大変な一方で、やりがいもある。(This job is tough, but on the other hand it's also rewarding.)
・都市部の人口が増える一方で、地方の人口は減っている。(While the population of urban areas is growing, that of rural areas is shrinking.)
・兄はスポーツが得意な一方で、弟は本を読むのが好きだ。(My older brother is good at sports, whereas my younger brother likes reading.)
Doing two things at onceOne person does A and also does B. Here there's no sense of “opposite”. It just says they're covering both sides.
・彼は会社で働く一方で、週末は小説を書いている。(He works at a company, and at the same time he writes novels on weekends.)
・田中先生は研究を続ける一方で、学生の指導にも力を入れている。(Professor Tanaka continues his research while also putting real effort into guiding his students.)
How to form it
Put the plain form before it, meaning the form without ます or です. Verbs and い-adjectives attach directly; な-adjectives and nouns need extra care.
Verbs: 増える → 増える一方で, and the past form also works: 伸びた → 伸びた一方で
い-adjectives: 忙しい → 忙しい一方で
な-adjectives: keep 「な」: 便利 → 便利な一方で (便利である一方で is also possible)
Nouns: add 「である」: 学生 → 学生である一方で
You can drop 「で」 and say just 「一方」, which feels more written.
It can also stand alone at the start of a sentence, meaning “on the other hand”: その一方で、一方、.
・給料は上がった。その一方で、残業も増えた。(My salary went up. On the other hand, the overtime increased too.)
Common mistakes
・な-adjectives can't take だ: 「便利だ一方で」 is wrong; say 便利な一方で. Nouns are the same: not 「学生だ一方で」 but 学生である一方で.
・It's formal. Saying 「仕事は大変な一方で…」 to a friend would sound like you're reading a press release. In everyday talk, けど is enough: 仕事は大変だけど、楽しいよ。(Work is hard, but it's fun, you know.)
・When 「一方」 goes at the very end as 「一方だ」, the meaning changes completely. See below.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Same topic, population:
一方で (mid-sentence) = contrasting two sides
・都市の人口は増える一方で、地方は減っている。(City populations are growing, while on the other hand rural areas are shrinking.)
一方だ (at the end of the sentence) = something keeps changing in one direction only
・都市の人口は増える一方だ。(City populations just keep growing.)
Before 一方だ you can only put verbs that express change, like 増える, 減る and 悪くなる, and it's mostly used for changes in a bad direction.
ばかりだ (change) means almost the same as 一方だ, but leans more toward “getting worse and worse”, often with a sense of worry or helplessness.
・父の病気は悪くなるばかりだ。(My father's illness just keeps getting worse.)
Quick rule of thumb: if 「一方」 is followed by more words and you're comparing two things, it's 一方で. If 「一方」 sits at the end and the sentence stops there, meaning “keeps on ~ing”, it's 一方だ.
What to learn next
一方で simply sets two things side by side. If you want to say “although A, B happened”, with a twist of “not what you'd expect”, learn 〜ものの and 〜にもかかわらず next.
n2-16:
The idea in one line
「〜つつも」 means "even though I know ~, I still ~" or "I kept meaning to ~, but ended up ~". Think of "I know staying up late is bad for me, yet I scroll on my phone until 3 a.m." It captures the feeling of knowing it in your head while your actions don't follow. It leans written, so you'll see it more in articles, news, and formal settings.
How to form it
Take the verb's ます form, drop ます, and add つつ（も）.
思う → 思います → 思いつつ
知る → 知ります → 知りつつ
言う → 言います → 言いつつ
食べる → 食べます → 食べつつ
する → します → しつつ
It attaches to verbs only. Adjectives and nouns can't take it directly.
How you'll usually hear it
although ~, yet ~The first half is what's in your mind, and the second half is an action that goes against it. The most common forms are 「〜と知りつつ」, 「〜と思いつつ」, and 「〜と言いつつ」. The second half often uses てしまう or られない, which adds a hint of regret or inability.
・体に悪いと知りつつも、夜更かしがやめられない。（I know it's bad for my health, yet I can't stop staying up late.）
・早く返事をしなきゃと思いつつ、一週間たってしまった。（I kept thinking I had to reply soon, and a week went by.）
・ダイエット中だと言いつつ、ケーキを二つも食べた。（She says she's on a diet, yet she ate two slices of cake.）
while ~ing「つつ」 without 「も」 has another meaning: two things happening at the same time. It's the written-style version of 「ながら」.
・景色を楽しみつつ、山道を歩いた。（We walked the mountain path while enjoying the scenery.）
・皆さんの意見を聞きつつ、計画を進めていきます。（We'll move the plan forward while listening to everyone's opinions.）
Common mistakes
・It attaches to the ます form, not the dictionary form: 知りつつ is correct, and 「知るつつ」 is wrong.
・The same person must be the subject on both sides. "My mother objected, but I went abroad to study anyway" involves two people, so you can't use つつ. Say 母は反対したが、私は留学した。
・With 「も」 it is always "although ~, yet ~". With just 「つつ」, you have to use context to decide whether it means "although" or "while".
・It leans written. When chatting with friends, 「〜けど」 or 「〜のに」 is usually enough. That said, set phrases like 「〜と思いつつ」 and 「〜と知りつつ」 do show up in speech too.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
つつも vs ながらも: The meaning is almost the same, and in one sentence you can often swap them.
悪いと知りつつも、やってしまった。
悪いと知りながらも、やってしまった。（I knew it was wrong, but I did it anyway.）
The difference: つつも attaches to verbs only and sounds more like writing. ながらも can also attach to adjectives and nouns, as in 狭いながらも楽しい我が家 (small, but a happy home), and there you can't swap in つつも.
つつも vs つつある: They differ by one character but mean completely different things. つつある means "is gradually becoming ~" and has no "although" meaning.
景気は回復しつつある。（The economy is gradually recovering.）
Quick tip: for "knowing ~, yet ~", use つつも. If what comes before is an adjective or noun, switch to ながらも. When you see つつある, think "gradually becoming".
n2-17:
The idea in one line
This 「〜ながら（も）」 means "although ~, yet ~" or "even though ~, still ~". You state one situation first, then follow it with a result you wouldn't expect.
You learned 「音楽を聞きながら勉強する」 (study while listening to music) at N4, and that one means doing two things at once. This one looks exactly the same but means something completely different.
How to form it
Verbs: Use the ます form, drop ます, and add ながら. The most common shape is 「〜ている」.
住んでいます → 住んでいながら知ります → 知りながら
い-adjectives: Attach directly, and keep the い as is. 狭い → 狭いながら
な-adjectives: Drop the な and attach. 残念な → 残念ながら
Nouns: Attach directly. 子ども → 子どもながら
Adding 「も」 to make 「ながらも」 means the same thing, with a slightly stronger "although" feel.
・近くに住んでいながら、一度も行ったことがない。（Even though I live nearby, I've never once been there.）
・悪いと知りながら、うそをついてしまった。（I knew it was wrong, yet I told a lie.）
・彼は学生ながら、自分で会社を経営している。（Although he's still a student, he runs his own company.）
・狭いながらも、住み心地のいい部屋だ。（It's small, but it's a very comfortable room to live in.）
How you'll usually hear it
A few of these have become set phrases that you'll hear a lot in daily life and at work. Memorizing them as whole sentences is the fastest way.
残念ながら"Unfortunately." It's often used when announcing bad news.
・残念ながら、明日の試合は中止になりました。（Unfortunately, tomorrow's game has been cancelled.）
勝手ながらCommon on shop notices. It means "we apologize for taking the liberty of ~".
・勝手ながら、本日は休業させていただきます。（We apologize, but we will be closed today.）
陰ながら"Quietly, behind the scenes."
・陰ながら応援しています。（I'm quietly cheering you on.）
我ながら"Even I have to admit."
・我ながらよくできたと思う。（Even I think I did a good job.）
Common mistakes
・Don't add extra pieces when connecting: it's 狭いながら, not 狭くながら; 残念ながら, not 残念なながら; and 子どもながら, not 子どものながら.
・Apart from the set phrases above, this pattern is written and formal, the kind of thing you'd use in articles, news, and interviews. With friends, 「狭いけど、いい部屋だよ」 sounds more natural.
・昔ながらの and 生まれながらの don't mean "although". 昔ながらの町並み means "a street that keeps its old-time look", and 生まれながらの才能 means "an innate talent". Learn them separately.
・Both halves usually talk about the same person or the same thing, as in "although he's a student, (he) runs a company".
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Simultaneous ながら = while ~ing: テレビを見ながらご飯を食べる。（I eat while watching TV.）
Contrastive ながら = although ~, yet ~: 毎日テレビを見ていながら、そのニュースを知らなかった。（Even though I watch TV every day, I didn't know about that news.）
つつ（も）: It means almost the same as contrastive ながら（も）, but it's more written and attaches to verbs only.
悪いと知りつつも、うそをついてしまった。（I knew it was wrong, yet I told a lie.）
You can't use it with adjectives or nouns: say 狭いながらも, not 狭いつつも.
くせに: It also means "even though ~", but it carries blame or dissatisfaction, like a spoken complaint.
知っているくせに、教えてくれない。（You know perfectly well, and you still won't tell me!）
知っていながら、教えてくれなかった。（He knew, yet he didn't tell me. This one sounds more like a calm statement.）
Quick tip: if what comes before is an adjective or noun, or if 「も」 follows, it's "although". If it follows a verb, check whether the second half goes against expectation. If it does, it's "although"; if not, it's "while ~ing". Use くせに to complain to someone, and ながら or つつ when writing.
n2-20:
The idea in one line
「〜に限らず」means “not only ~” or “not limited to ~”. You first name the thing everyone would naturally think of, then say the range is actually wider and other things apply too.
It's like saying “Not just weekends, weekdays are crowded too.” In Japanese: 週末に限らず、平日も混んでいる。
How to attach it
Put a noun in front and add 「に限らず」directly.
学生 → 学生に限らず (not only students)
日本 → 日本に限らず (not only Japan)
「限らず」is read かぎらず and means “not limited to.” The second half often contains words like も, 誰でも, or 何でも, which stretch the range wider.
When to use it
The range is bigger than you'd thinkPeople assume only A is like this, but B and C are too.
・この店は週末に限らず、平日もいつも混んでいる。 (This shop is crowded not only on weekends but always on weekdays too.)
・この公園は子どもに限らず、大人にも人気がある。 (This park is popular not only with children but with adults too.)
・日本に限らず、アジア全体で少子化が進んでいる。 (Not only in Japan: the birth rate is falling across all of Asia.)
No restrictions, open to anyoneVery common in notices and event descriptions.
・学生に限らず、誰でも参加できます。 (Not limited to students. Anyone can join.)
Easy mistakes
・It's the opposite of 「に限り」and 「に限って」: 本日に限り半額 means “half price today only,” while 本日に限らず means “not only today.” That one extra 「ず」flips the meaning completely, so watch for it when reading notices.
・It basically follows a noun. A verb can't go directly before it, so you can't say 「食べるに限らず」. To talk about actions, 「〜ばかりでなく」sounds more natural.
・The tone is formal and written. You'll see it in news, notices, and essays. With friends, just say 〜だけじゃなくて.
・What comes first should be “the thing everyone would already think of,” and what follows is “what's also included.” If you reverse the order, the sentence sounds odd.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
に限らず = what comes before is one specific thing, and the meaning is “not only that”:
学生に限らず、社会人も参加できる。 (Not only students; working adults can join too.)
を問わず = what comes before is a category that splits into several types, and the meaning is “no matter which type”:
このイベントは年齢を問わず、誰でも参加できる。 (This event is open to anyone, regardless of age.)
「年齢」splits into many ages, so you use を問わず. 「学生」is one specific group, so you use に限らず.
Quick test: if you can replace the word with “whatever kind of ○○” (年齢, 性別, 国籍, 経験, 天候), use を問わず. If it's one specific person, place, or thing (学生, 日本, 週末), use に限らず.
とは限らない: it also contains 「限」, but it goes at the end of the sentence and means “not necessarily”: 高い物がいい物とは限らない。 (Expensive things aren't necessarily good.) This is a completely different thing from “not only ~.”
Also, のみならず and ばかりでなく mean “not only ~, but also ~,” and with a noun in front they're often interchangeable with に限らず. The difference is that に限らず only takes nouns, and its focus is “the range isn't limited to this.”
What to learn next
Next, study 〜を問わず (regardless of ~), plus 〜のみならず and 〜ばかりか, which also mean “not only ~.” Then you'll have this whole “range” group covered.
n2-21:
The idea in one line
「〜を問わず」means “regardless of ~” or “no matter ~.” 問う means “to ask, to question,” so 問わず is “without asking,” that is, “regardless.” A job ad that says “all ages welcome, no experience required” would say 年齢を問わず and 経験を問わず in Japanese. It means the result is the same whichever type of that condition applies.
When to use it
Recruiting and noticesYou'll see it most in job ads, event sign-ups, and shop notices, meaning “this condition has no restrictions.”
・年齢を問わず、どなたでもご参加いただけます。 (Anyone can take part, regardless of age.)
・このアルバイトは経験を問わず、誰でも応募できます。 (This part-time job doesn't require experience. Anyone can apply.)
Describing a situationSay that something isn't affected by a condition and holds true in every case.
・この歌は世代を問わず愛されている。 (This song is loved by every generation.)
・昼夜を問わず、工事の音がうるさい。 (Day or night, the construction noise is loud.)
How to attach it
Add を問わず directly to a noun. The noun in front is one of two kinds:
Words that naturally have many types: 年齢, 性別, 国籍, 経験, 天候
A pair of opposites: 男女, 昼夜, 経験の有無 (with or without experience)
You can also attach it to 「〜かどうか」: 経験があるかどうか → 経験があるかどうかを問わず
Forms you'll hear most
は問いませんGoes at the end of a sentence. Very common in job ads.
・年齢は問いません。 (Age doesn't matter.)
Dropping をOn posters and recruitment notices, to keep things short, it's often written as 年齢問わず or 経験問わず.
Easy mistakes
・What comes before must be a word that “has different types.” 学生を問わず doesn't work, because “student” is just one type and there's nothing to be “regardless” about. Say 学生かどうかを問わず or 学生・社会人を問わず instead.
・「問わず」is read とわず. It's the negative form of 問う, so don't write it as 問えず.
・This is a very formal, written expression. With friends, 関係なく sounds more natural: 年とか関係なく、誰でも楽しめるよ。 (Age doesn't matter, anyone can enjoy it!)
・The particle is always 「を」. Don't swap it for に or が.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
に限らず = not only A, but B too ~ (you give one representative example, then widen the range):
このアプリは若者に限らず、お年寄りにも人気だ。 (This app is popular not only with young people but with older people too.)
を問わず = whichever type A is, it's the same (the condition isn't taken into account at all):
このアプリは年齢を問わず人気だ。 (This app is popular regardless of age.)
Also, にかかわらず means almost the same as を問わず: 天候にかかわらず実施します。 (It will be held regardless of the weather.)
If you add 「も」in the middle, it becomes にもかかわらず, which means something completely different: “in spite of ~.” 雨にもかかわらず、たくさんの人が来た。 (Despite the rain, many people came.)
Quick test: “not only A, but B too” uses に限らず; “no matter what A is” uses を問わず; “in spite of A” uses にもかかわらず.
n2-22:
The idea in one line
「〜にわたって」is like the English news phrases "spanning ~", "across ~", "over a period of ~" or "throughout ~". Think "heavy rain for three days straight" or "power outages across the whole country." The point is to stress a long time or a wide area, covered from start to finish, the whole stretch included.
How to connect it
Noun + にわたって. The noun before it needs to be a length or a whole area. The three most common types are:
A long time3日間、10年、長年、長期間
・会議は5時間にわたって続いた。(The meeting went on for a full five hours.)
A wide area全国、広範囲、関東全域、多方面
・台風の影響で、関東全域にわたって大雨が降った。(Because of the typhoon, heavy rain fell across the entire Kanto region.)
Number of times / amount3回、数ページ
・この特集は3回にわたって放送されます。(This special will be broadcast in three parts.)
Forms you'll hear most
にわたり: Same meaning, but more formal and written. Press releases and public notices love it.
・調査は全国にわたり実施された。(The survey was carried out nationwide.)
にわたる＋noun: Use this form when a noun follows directly.
・長年にわたる研究の成果が発表された。(The results of many years of research were announced.)
にわたった＋noun: For something that has already finished.
・2時間にわたった話し合いは、結論が出ないまま終わった。(The two-hour discussion ended without reaching a conclusion.)
Common mistakes
・You can't put a point in time or a single place before it: you can't say 「3時にわたって」or 「月曜日にわたって」. It needs a "stretch" or a "whole area," like 3時間, 1週間 or 全国.
・It carries a feeling of "so long, so wide," so using it for small things sounds odd. 10分にわたってシャワーを浴びた sounds like a news report on your shower.
・The tone is fairly formal and shows up in news, reports and notices. When chatting with friends, 3日間ずっと雨だった (it rained for three days straight) sounds much more natural.
・When a noun follows directly, use にわたる: say 3時間にわたる会議, not 「3時間にわたって会議」.
・This grammar comes from the verb 渡る. You'll occasionally see it written 「に渡って」, but it's mostly written in hiragana.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
The one most easily confused with it is 〜にかけて. Both talk about range, but from different angles.
にかけて: Tells you from where to where. It gives a start and an end point, and the range is rough.
・3月から5月にかけて工事が行われる。(Construction will take place from around March to May.)
にわたって: Tells you how long in total, or how big the whole area is, stressing length and breadth.
・3か月にわたって工事が行われる。(Construction will go on for three months.)
It works the same way with places: 九州から関西にかけて雨が降る (rain will fall from Kyushu to the Kansai area) lays out the range, while 西日本全域にわたって雨が降る (rain will fall across all of western Japan) stresses how large the range is.
Quick test: if the sentence has two endpoints, "A から B," you'll usually use にかけて. If there's only one "total length" or "whole area" before it, like 3か月 or 全国, use にわたって.
n2-23:
The idea in one line
「〜をもとに」is the English "based on ~" or "using ~ as a basis." What comes before it is the material or starting point, and what follows is the new thing you made from it. Think "a movie based on a true story" or "curry made from Grandma's recipe."
How to connect it
A noun always comes before it, followed by をもとに or をもとにして. The meaning is the same, but the version with して is a bit more complete.
データ → データをもとに (based on the data)
When a noun follows directly, change it to をもとにした＋noun:
実話 → 実話をもとにした映画 (a movie based on a true story)
Forms you'll hear most
をもとに＋actionIt's often followed by verbs that produce something, like make, write, think up, decide or predict.
・アンケートの結果をもとに、新しいメニューを考えた。(Based on the survey results, we came up with a new menu.)
・祖母のレシピをもとにして、カレーを作ってみた。(I tried making curry based on my grandmother's recipe.)
をもとに作られたVery common when introducing the source of a work.
・このドラマは人気漫画をもとに作られた。(This drama was made based on a popular manga.)
Common mistakes
・In kanji it's 基に or 元に, read もとに, not 「きに」. Writing it in hiragana is perfectly fine too.
・Only a noun can come before it. If you want to put a whole clause there, first turn it into a noun with 「こと」: 調べたことをもとに、レポートを書いた。 (I wrote the report based on what I found out.)
・When English "according to the weather report, it will rain tomorrow" cites an information source, Japanese doesn't use をもとに. Use によると: 天気予報によると、明日は雨だそうだ。
・What follows needs an action or result like "make / come up with / decide." Plain statements like "is there" or "like" don't fit.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
をもとに = using something as raw material or a starting point, which you can then process, extend or adapt:
このデータをもとに、新しい企画を考えた。 (Using this data as a starting point, I came up with a new plan.)
に基づいて = following some basis without departing from it:
このデータに基づいて、結論を出した。 (I drew a conclusion based on this data.)
When judging according to laws or rules, 法律に基づいて判断する is the more natural and formal choice. をもとに leans toward "take it as material and make something," so it feels weaker with laws and rules. In formal settings, we recommend に基づいて.
Quick test: if the result is "using it as a base to make something new," use をもとに. If the result is "following its rules or evidence," use に基づいて.
What to learn next
Another pattern with the same shape, "noun + を + 〜に," is をきっかけに, meaning "triggered by ~": 留学をきっかけに、料理を始めた。 (Studying abroad was what got me started on cooking.) What comes before it is "the start of events," not "material," so try remembering the two side by side.
n2-24:
The idea in one line
「〜に応じて」means "depending on ~" or "in line with ~". Think of a bento shop owner who "decides how many lunches to order based on the headcount": when the first thing changes, what follows adjusts to match.
How to attach it
It attaches directly to a noun: 収入 → 収入に応じて (depending on income)
The noun is usually something that varies by person or situation, like income, age, ability, level, budget, circumstances, or needs.
It's read おうじて. In writing you'll also often see に応じ, with the 「て」 dropped. The meaning is the same.
・収入に応じて、税金が決まる。 (Taxes are determined according to income.)
・年齢に応じて、料金が変わります。 (The fee changes depending on age.)
How you'll hear it most
必要に応じて means "as needed." You'll see it all the time in company documents and notices.
・必要に応じて、資料を追加してください。 (Please add materials as needed.)
に応じた＋noun This is the form you use most when a noun follows.
・レベルに応じたクラスを選べます。 (You can choose a class that matches your level.)
There is also a に応じての＋noun form (e.g. 能力に応じての配置). It means the same thing but is less common, so as a beginner just remember に応じた.
Common mistakes
・What follows must be something that adjusts or changes accordingly. You can't use it to simply say "according to the news": ニュースによると、明日は雨だ。 (According to the news, it will rain tomorrow.) Use によると here.
・The tone is fairly formal, common in notices, explanations, and the workplace. With friends, に合わせて or によって is more common.
・The verb 応じる on its own often means "to respond to, to accept": インタビューに応じる (to agree to an interview). Don't mix it up with the "adjust according to ~" meaning.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Same topic, income and taxes:
に応じて = adjusting to match what comes before: 収入に応じて、税金が決まる。 (Taxes are set according to income.)
によって = differs depending on what comes before; the focus is on "it's different": 収入によって、税金が違う。 (Taxes differ depending on income.)
につれて = as the first thing keeps changing, the second changes gradually along with it: 収入が増えるにつれて、税金も増える。 (As income rises, taxes rise too.)
When no one is actively "adjusting to match," によって sounds more natural: 国によって、習慣が違う。 (Customs differ from country to country.) Swapping in に応じて here would sound odd.
Quick rule of thumb: use に応じて for "adjust to match it," によって for "differs depending on it," and につれて for "the more ~, the more ~."
What to learn next
Other patterns for "changing along with something" are 〜に伴って (along with ~) and 〜につれて. Try studying them side by side.
n2-27:
The idea in one line
「〜のみならず」is the formal version of "not only ~, but also…". It means the same as the familiar 「だけでなく」, but it's used in reports, news, and speeches, not in chats with friends.
Break it apart and it makes sense: のみ = だけ (only), ならず = "is not," so together: "not just A."
When to use it
Adding more You state A, then add B, and B is usually bigger or broader in scope. The second half often has も, でも, or にも to mean "B too."
・国内のみならず、海外でも高い評価を得ている。 (It is highly regarded not only in Japan but also overseas.)
・この店は学生のみならず、社会人にも人気がある。 (This shop is popular not only with students but also with working adults.)
How to attach it
Nouns: attach directly. 日本 → 日本のみならず
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly to the plain form (the dictionary form, or the た-form or ない-form).
話せる → 話せるのみならず狭い → 狭いのみならず
な-adjectives: add である; you can't use 「だ」. 静かだ → 静かであるのみならず
You can also add である to a noun when you want to stress status or nature: 医者であるのみならず
・彼は英語が話せるのみならず、中国語も読める。 (He can not only speak English but also read Chinese.)
・この部屋は狭いのみならず、駅からも遠い。 (This room is not only small but also far from the station.)
・この町は静かであるのみならず、交通も便利だ。 (This town is not only quiet but also has convenient transportation.)
How you'll hear it most
ただ〜のみならず Adding 「ただ」 in front makes it "not merely ~," with a stronger tone.
・これはただ個人の問題のみならず、社会全体の問題でもある。 (This is not merely an individual problem, but a problem for society as a whole.)
At the start of a sentence Used on its own as a conjunction, it means "not only that."
・彼は仕事が速い。のみならず、ミスもほとんどない。 (He works fast. Not only that, he hardly ever makes mistakes.)
Common mistakes
・With な-adjectives, don't say 静かだのみならず; say 静かであるのみならず.
・It's stiff and very formal. With friends, use だけじゃなく for "not only ~"; のみならず would sound like you're reading an official document.
・It adds on; it doesn't mean "not A but B." The two parts need to match: if A is a place, B should be a place too; if A is a problem, B should be a problem. Remember to add 「も」 in the second half.
・The direction must stay consistent: good with good, bad with bad. You can't use it for contrasting things.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Same situation: both adults and kids love this game.
だけでなく = the most general form, usable in both speech and writing: このゲームは子どもだけでなく、大人にも人気がある。
のみならず = same meaning, in a formal, written tone: このゲームは子どものみならず、大人にも人気がある。
ばかりか = carries a sense of surprise, "who would have thought even ~": このゲームは子どもばかりか、大人まで夢中になっている。 (Not just kids; even adults are hooked.)
に限らず = the focus is "not limited to the range of A," and the second half often pairs with 誰でも or どこでも: このゲームは子どもに限らず、誰でも楽しめる。 (This game isn't limited to kids; anyone can enjoy it.)
Quick rule of thumb: use だけじゃなく when chatting and のみならず when writing; use ばかりか for the surprise of "even ~"; use に限らず for "no limits, anyone can."
n2-28:
The idea in one line
「AはもちろんBも」means "A goes without saying, and even B ~", much like "not to mention B" in English. A is the obvious one everyone would think of. B is the extra, less expected one you add on top.
・この店は味はもちろん、サービスもいい。(The food is great, of course, and the service is good too.)
How to form it
Basically you attach 「はもちろん」directly to a noun. The second half usually picks it up with も or まで:
子供 → 子供はもちろん、大人も
・子供はもちろん、大人も楽しめる映画です。(A movie kids will love, not to mention adults.)
・家具はもちろん、家電までついている部屋だ。(A room that comes with furniture, and even appliances.)
If the noun is followed by a small particle like 「で」or「に」, keep it and add 「はもちろん」after it:
・日本ではもちろん、海外でも人気がある。(It's popular in Japan, of course, and abroad too.)
To talk about an action, first add 「の」after the verb to turn it into a noun:
・話すのはもちろん、書くのも得意だ。(He's good at speaking, of course, and at writing too.)
Common mistakes
・Don't flip the order: put the "naturally expected" item first. At a theme park, people think of kids first, so 子供はもちろん、大人も sounds natural.
・When the sentence ends in a negative, put the "hard" item first: 漢字はもちろん、ひらがなも書けない。(He can't write kanji, of course, and can't even write hiragana.) Not being able to write kanji is normal. The point is that he can't even write easy hiragana.
・Remember to follow up with も or まで. 英語はもちろん、スペイン語が話せる sounds awkward without the も.
・This is different from a standalone 「もちろん」(of course): もちろん行きます means "Of course I'll go," with no "A goes without saying, and even B" meaning.
Telling similar patterns apart
All three can be translated as "not only A, but B too ~". Here they are with the same sentence:
はもちろん = A is obvious to begin with: 彼は英語はもちろん、中国語も話せる。(He speaks English, of course, and Chinese too.)
ばかりか = the focus is on B being a bit surprising: 彼は英語ばかりか、中国語も話せる。(He doesn't just speak English; he even speaks Chinese.)
のみならず = about the same as ばかりか, but very formal, mostly used in writing or speeches: 彼は英語のみならず、中国語も話せる。
One more practical difference: after はもちろん you can use a request or a decision, like "please ~" or "I'll ~". ばかりか isn't really used that way.
・準備はもちろん、片付けも手伝ってください。(Please help with the cleanup as well as the preparation.)
Quick rule of thumb: to say "A goes without saying", use はもちろん. To stress "even B, how surprising!", use ばかりか. Save のみならず for formal writing.
What to learn next
「〜はもちろんのこと」means the same thing, with slightly more emphasis. In writing you'll often see the more formal 〜はもとより: 国内はもとより、海外からも注文が来る。(Orders come in from within the country, of course, and from overseas too.)
n2-30:
The idea in one line
「〜だけのことはある」means "No wonder ~", "As you'd expect from ~", "It really lives up to ~". You see an impressive result, then look back and say: yes, this fits perfectly with who they are, what was spent, or the effort put in. It lives up to its reputation.
The だけ here doesn't mean "only". The feeling of the whole phrase is: "Being ~, of course they have that ability. It figures."
When to use it
Status that lives up to its nameAn expert, a famous restaurant, or a famous person performs as well as their reputation suggests.
・さすがプロだけのことはある。(As you'd expect from a pro.)
・英語がペラペラだ。5年もアメリカに住んでいただけのことはある。(His English is fluent. No wonder, after living in America for five years.)
Money well spentLike the English "you get what you pay for".
・このいす、全然疲れない。高かっただけのことはある。(This chair never gets tiring, no matter how long you sit. It's expensive for a reason.)
No wonder it's popularAfter experiencing it yourself, you feel everyone's praise was justified.
・このパン、本当においしい。行列ができるだけのことはあるね。(This bread is really good. No wonder there's a line.)
How to form it
Verbs: plain form directly　練習した → 練習しただけのことはある
い-adjectives: directly　高い → 高いだけのことはある
な-adjectives: keep the 「な」　有名 → 有名なだけのことはある
Nouns: directly, without だ　プロ → プロだけのことはある
For a politer tone, say だけのことはありますね.
How you'll usually hear it
It's often paired with さすが, which strengthens the "as you'd expect" feel. A very common order is to state the result you saw first, then add だけのことはある as the conclusion.
・景色が最高だ。さすが有名なだけのことはある。(The view is amazing. No wonder it's so famous.)
For something whose result has already come out, you can also use the past 「あった」. It's often used to say effort paid off.
・合格できた。毎日勉強しただけのことはあった。(I passed. Studying every day really paid off.)
Common mistakes
・If you read だけ as "only", the whole sentence becomes completely confusing. Here it means "as you'd expect, living up to the name".
・Don't add だ after a noun: say プロだけのことはある, not プロだだけのことはある.
・Keep 「な」on な-adjectives: say 有名なだけのことはある, not 有名だけのことはある.
・You need an actual result you've seen as evidence. If something hasn't happened yet and you're only guessing, you can't use it.
・As a beginner, remember this is for praise and agreement. Don't use it to complain that something is bad.
Telling similar patterns apart
だけあって: it also means "as you'd expect from", but it goes in the middle of the sentence, followed directly by the result, so everything fits in one sentence.
・さすがプロだけあって、写真がきれいだ。(As you'd expect from a pro, the photos are beautiful.)
だけのことはある: it goes at the end of the sentence as the final conclusion.
・写真がきれいだ。さすがプロだけのことはある。(The photos are beautiful. As you'd expect from a pro.)
ことだから: it's also tied to a person's character or ability, but it's a guess made before the result is out. The form is noun + の + ことだから.
・田中さんのことだから、きっと今回も合格するよ。(Knowing Tanaka, he'll surely pass this time too.)
・一回で合格した。さすが田中さんだけのことはある。(He passed on the first try. That's Tanaka for you.)
Quick rule of thumb: if the result isn't out yet and you're guessing, use ことだから. If the result is out and you're impressed, use だけのことはある. If you want to continue straight into the result within the same sentence, switch to だけあって.
What to learn next
Another pattern that gives a positive evaluation is 〜に値する (worth ~), for example この映画は見るに値する。(This movie is worth watching.)
n2-33:
The idea in one line
「〜上に」means "not only ~, but also ~" or "~, and on top of that ~". You state one point, then pile a second one on top in the same direction: good plus good, or bad plus bad.
・この部屋は駅から近い上に、家賃も安い。(This room is close to the station, and the rent is cheap too.)
・道に迷った上に、雨にも降られた。(I got lost, and on top of that, I got caught in the rain.)
How to form it
Verbs: attach directly, in either present or past.
寝坊した → 寝坊した上に
い-adjectives: attach directly.
安い → 安い上に
な-adjectives: change 「だ」 to 「な」.
親切だ → 親切な上に
Nouns: add 「である」 or 「の」. In writing, 「である」 is more common.
医者 → 医者である上に
・彼女は親切な上に、仕事も早い。(She's kind, and she works fast too.)
・今日は寝坊した上に、財布まで忘れてしまった。(Today I overslept, and I even forgot my wallet.)
・彼は医者である上に、作家としても有名だ。(He's a doctor, and he's also famous as a writer.)
You'll notice the second half often has も or まで, because the meaning is "this too ~" or "even this ~".
Easy mistakes
・Read it as うえに, not じょうに.
・Both halves must point in the same direction. 安い上に、まずい。 is wrong: cheap is a plus and tasting bad is a minus. For one good and one bad, use 安いけど、まずい。 (It's cheap, but it tastes awful.)
・Don't keep 「だ」 on な-adjectives: say 便利な上に, not 便利だ上に.
・A 「上に」 sentence describes or evaluates things, so don't follow it directly with "please do ~" or "let's ~". If you want to persuade someone, state both facts first, then lead into it with から: 寒い上に風も強いから、今日は家にいよう。 (It's cold and windy too, so let's stay home today.)
・The 「上に」 in 机の上に本がある。 means "on top of the desk". That's about position and has nothing to do with this grammar point. Context makes it obvious.
Telling similar patterns apart
All three contain 「上」 but mean completely different things. Let's compare them in a work context:
上に = and also (two facts stacked together): この仕事は給料が安い上に、残業も多い。 (This job has low pay, and there's a lot of overtime too.)
上で = do A first, then B: 条件をよく確認した上で、契約します。 (I'll sign the contract after checking the terms carefully.)
上は = since ~, then I must: 引き受けた上は、最後までやります。 (Since I've taken it on, I'll see it through to the end.)
Quick test: if you can say "and also" in English, it's 上に. If it's "after doing ~, then", it's 上で. If it's "now that ~, then", it's 上は.
What to learn next
その上 at the start of a sentence also means "and what's more": この店は安い。その上、おいしい。 (This restaurant is cheap. And it's delicious, too.)
For a stronger "not only ~, but even ~", go on to 〜ばかりか and 〜のみならず.
n2-34:
The idea in one line
「〜のことだから」means "knowing his personality, he'll surely ~" or "you know what he's like, he'll probably ~". You know well how a certain person usually acts, and you use that knowledge as the basis for guessing what they'll do this time.
When to use it
Guessing from personalityIn the first half, mention a person you know well, ideally with a hint of their personality. In the second half, give your guess.
・時間に厳しい部長のことだから、もう会議室にいるはずだ。(Our department head is so strict about time, so he should already be in the meeting room.)
・優しい彼女のことだから、きっと手伝ってくれるよ。(She's so kind, so she'll definitely help you.)
・弟のことだから、どうせまだ寝ているよ。(You know my little brother, he's probably still asleep anyway.)
Works for companies and shops tooIf everyone knows how it usually operates, you can use it for them as well.
・あの会社のことだから、また値上げするだろう。(Knowing that company, they'll probably raise prices again.)
How to form it
Add 「の」 after the noun, then 「ことだから」:
彼 → 彼のことだから
あの会社 → あの会社のことだから
Often a word describing their personality goes in front, to make the basis clearer:
真面目な彼 → 真面目な彼のことだから
The second half is usually your guess, so it often appears together with だろう, きっと, はずだ, and に違いない.
Easy mistakes
・Don't drop 「の」: it's 彼のことだから, not 彼ことだから.
・The person in the first half must be someone whose habits you know well, and usually the listener knows their personality too. You can't use it for someone you've just met, because you don't really know them.
・The second half is "I guess" or "I judge", not a fact that has already happened. If you're completely certain, you don't need this pattern.
・Translating it as just "because it's him" can make it sound like an ordinary reason. The real point is "based on what I know about him".
Telling similar patterns apart
Same situation, guessing whether a friend will be on time:
Noun + だから = because he's a certain kind of person or has a certain status (the reason is a fact or a category): 彼は日本人だから、時間を守るだろう。 (He's Japanese, so he'll probably be punctual.)
Noun + のことだから = based on what I know about this person: 彼のことだから、時間を守るだろう。 (Knowing him, he'll probably be punctual.)
In the first sentence, the reason is the status of being "Japanese". In the second, you know him personally and know he's always on time.
Quick test: if the reason is "he is ~ (a status or fact)", use だから. If the reason is "I know he's just that kind of person", use のことだから.
What to learn next
The second half is often used for a confident guess, so go on to 〜に違いない (it must be ~) and 〜に決まっている (it's definitely ~): あの人のことだから、また忘れたに決まっている。 (You know what he's like, he's definitely forgotten again.)
n2-31:
The idea in one line
「〜に値する」 means "worth ~ing" or "deserving of ~", in a more formal, written register. A news report says "this discovery deserves attention," and a book review says "this book is worth reading." Japanese uses this pattern for both. It means that the person or thing measures up and has real value, and deserves that kind of assessment.
How to attach it
Noun + に値する: 尊敬 → 尊敬に値する (worthy of respect)
Verb dictionary form (the base form you find in a dictionary) + に値する: 読む → 読むに値する (worth reading)
値する is read あたいする. It is a verb in its own right and conjugates like する: 値しない, 値します.
How you'll hear it most
Positive evaluationThese are the words that most often come before it: 尊敬, 称賛, 信頼, 注目, 一読, 検討, 特筆. For now, just memorize them as fixed combinations.
・彼の努力は称賛に値する。 (His effort deserves praise.)
・この本は一読に値する。 (This book is worth reading.)
・このデータは注目に値する。 (This data deserves attention.)
Negative: not worth itSwitch to 値しない and the tone gets very blunt, basically "not worth bothering with at all."
・そんな噂は信じるに値しない。 (A rumor like that isn't worth believing.)
・その意見は検討に値しない。 (That opinion isn't worth considering.)
Before a nounYou can use it directly to describe a person or thing.
・彼は信頼に値する人物だ。 (He is a person worthy of trust.)
Easy mistakes
・The particle is always に: it's 尊敬に値する, not 尊敬を値する.
・Read it あたいする. The 「値」 in 値段 is read ね, so don't mix them up.
・It can't attach to the ます-form: you can't say 「読みますに値する」. To be polite, change the ending instead: 読むに値します.
・It's stiff and written. If you're chatting with a friend about a bowl of ramen, just say このラーメン、食べる価値あるよ. Saying 食べるに値する would sound like you're writing a food review.
・In English, "totally worth it" often means good value, as in "totally worth it after the discount." Japanese uses お得 for that, not に値する.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
価値がある: It means almost the same as に値する, but it works in both everyday and written contexts, and it's the most common way to say it.
この本は読む価値がある。 (This book is worth reading: fine in casual talk.)
この本は一読に値する。 (This book is worth a read: book reviews, formal settings.)
だけのことはある: This is also praise, but the focus is "no wonder, as expected of ~". It says the result matches the person's background and effort. Take one situation, hearing a piano performance:
彼の演奏は称賛に値する。 (His performance deserves praise: it says the performance earns the praise.)
さすが十年ウィーンで学んだだけのことはある。 (As expected of someone who studied in Vienna for ten years: it says the good result matches his history.)
Quick rule: to say "worth ~ing," use に値する in formal settings and 価値がある in everyday speech. To say "no wonder, as expected of ~," use だけのことはある.
What to learn next
The N1 pattern 「〜に足る」 is very close in meaning, "sufficient to ~, qualified to ~": 信頼に足る人物 (a person sufficiently trustworthy).
n2-32:
The idea in one line
「〜上は」 means "since ~, then (should) ~" or "now that ~, then ~." The first half states something already settled, such as your role, a decision you made, or the point things have reached. The second half says "so I will / should do this." The feel is close to English "since you promised, follow through," only it sounds more formal and stiff, and often carries a sense of resolve.
When to use it
Responsibility that comes with a roleSince you hold this role, you should do what that role requires.
・教師である上は、生徒の手本にならなければならない。 (Since I'm a teacher, I must set an example for my students.)
If you did it, own itSince you agreed or decided, you see it through to the end.
・引き受けた上は、最後まで責任を持ちます。 (Now that I've taken it on, I'll take responsibility to the end.)
・やると決めた上は、もう迷わない。 (Now that I've decided to do it, I won't hesitate anymore.)
Given how things have turned outThings have already come to this, so you have to face it.
・こうなった上は、正直に話すしかない。 (Now that it's come to this, all I can do is tell the truth.)
How to attach it
Verbs: dictionary form or た-form, then add は directly.
試合に出る → 試合に出る上は (since I'm going to play in the match)
約束した → 約束した上は (since I promised)
Nouns: you need to insert 「である」 in between.
社会人 → 社会人である上は (since I'm a working adult)
What can follow
The second half has to express your resolve, an obligation, a suggestion, or a judgment. These are the endings you'll see most:
〜なければならない (must), 〜べきだ (should), 〜しかない (have no choice but to), 〜つもりだ (intend to), 〜たい (want to).
・試合に出る上は、絶対に勝ちたい。 (Since I'm going to play in the match, I definitely want to win.)
Easy mistakes
・Read it うえは, not じょうは.
・A noun can't attach directly: 学生である上は is correct, and 「学生だ上は」 is wrong.
・The first half must be something already settled, not a hypothetical. You can't add 「もし」 to get 「もし約束した上は」.
・The second half can't just state a fact. A sentence like 「日本に来た上は、毎日雨だった」 doesn't work, because "it rained every day" is neither your resolve nor your judgment.
・It's formal and written. Using it with a friend sounds stiff, and in everyday speech people mostly use からには.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
からには: It means almost the same thing, "since ~, then ~."
・引き受けた上は、最後まで頑張ります。 (Since I've taken it on, I'll do my best to the end.)
・引き受けたからには、最後まで頑張ります。 (Same as above.)
The difference is the setting: 上は is stiffer and common in writing, speeches, and solemn declarations. からには also works in formal settings, and you hear it more in everyday conversation.
上に: It differs by just one particle, but the meaning is completely different: "not only ~ but also ~."
・この店は安い上に、おいしい。 (This place is not only cheap, it's also delicious.)
・店長である上は、遅刻はできない。 (Since I'm the store manager, I can't be late.)
Quick rule: if the second half adds one more plus or minus, use 上に. If it says "so I should, I must, I have no choice," use 上は. When talking with friends, think of からには first for "since ~."
n2-36:
The idea in one line
「〜ずにはいられない」 means "can't help ~ing" or "can't help but ~". A feeling or urge wells up inside you, you can't hold it down, and you end up doing it. Literally it's "if I don't do ~, I can't stay put," which is another way of saying "I couldn't help doing it."
When to use it
A feeling wells upYou hear or see something, and a certain feeling rises on its own.
・この歌を聞くと、昔を思い出さずにはいられない。(Every time I hear this song, I can't help remembering the old days.)
・彼の努力には、感心せずにはいられない。(Seeing how hard he works, I can't help but admire him.)
Can't stop yourself from speaking or actingYou could have held back, but you just can't stop yourself.
・困っている人を見ると、声をかけずにはいられない。(When I see someone in trouble, I can't help going up to ask if they're okay.)
・あまりにひどい話で、一言言わずにはいられなかった。(It was such an awful thing that I couldn't help saying something.)
How to form it: first check which verb group
First put the verb into its 「ない」 form, then choose which version to attach:
・ず version: drop 「ない」 and add ずにはいられない
・ないで version: keep 「ない」 and add ではいられない
The meaning is the same. The ず version is more common and more written in tone; the ないで version is a little more conversational.
Group 1 (godan verbs):
泣く → 泣かない → drop ない → 泣か → 泣かずにはいられない
言う → 言わずにはいられない
Group 2 (ichidan verbs):
食べる → 食べずにはいられない食べる → 食べないではいられない
Group 3 (memorize these):
する → せずにはいられない心配する → 心配せずにはいられない
来る → 来ずにはいられない（こずには）
The ないで version just uses the regular ない form: 心配しないではいられない.
Easy mistakes
・The ず form of する is せず, not しず: 心配せずには is correct. But the ないで version is 心配しないでは, so don't mix the two.
・来ずには is read こずには, not きずには.
・The ない form of 言う is 言わない, so it's 言わずには, not 言あずには.
・With all those negatives, it's tempting to translate it as "can't not ~," which sounds like someone is forcing you. In fact it's about not being able to stop yourself, so "couldn't help doing it" is the most accurate way to remember it.
・The subject is usually I. To talk about someone else, add ようだ or らしい: 彼は文句を言わずにはいられないようだ。(He seems unable to stop himself from complaining.)
Telling it apart from look-alikes
ざるを得ない = you don't want to, but circumstances force you, so you have no choice:
部長の冗談は全然おもしろくないけど、笑わざるを得なかった。(The department head's joke wasn't funny at all, but I had no choice but to laugh.)
ずにはいられない = the feeling bubbles up and you can't help yourself:
友だちの冗談がおもしろすぎて、笑わずにはいられなかった。(My friend's joke was so funny that I couldn't help laughing.)
てたまらない = describes a very strong inner feeling, and you might still be holding back:
ケーキが食べたくてたまらない。(I'm dying to eat cake.)
ずにはいられない = describes an action you can't stop, and you've usually already done it:
ケーキを見ると、食べずにはいられない。(The moment I see cake, I can't help eating it.)
Quick rule of thumb: "couldn't help doing it" is ずにはいられない, "didn't want to but had to" is ざるを得ない, and "feeling it so much I can't stand it" is てたまらない.
n2-38:
The idea in one line
「〜かねない」 means "if this keeps up, you might end up ~ing", and what follows is always something bad. It's like saying in English, "Keep pulling all-nighters like that and you'll end up in trouble." It carries a note of reminder or warning.
When to use it
Warning about a bad outcomeYou often state a cause or condition first (〜と, 〜ば, このままでは), then use かねない to say what bad thing might happen.
・無理を続けると、体を壊しかねない。(If you keep pushing yourself, you could end up ruining your health.)
・そんな言い方をしたら、誤解されかねないよ。(If you put it like that, you might get misunderstood, you know.)
That person is capable of itYou say that someone really is the type who would do something like that, with a negative judgment.
・あの人なら、約束を忘れかねない。(Knowing him, he might actually forget the appointment.)
How to attach it
First put the verb into the ます form, drop 「ます」, then add 「かねない」.
壊す → 壊します → 壊しかねない
忘れる → 忘れます → 忘れかねない
誤解する → 誤解します → 誤解しかねない
To make it polite, use かねません:
・このままでは、計画が中止になりかねません。(If things stay as they are, the plan could end up being canceled.)
Easy mistakes
・It ends in 「ない」, but it doesn't mean "won't". It means "might." Don't automatically translate ない as "not."
・Use it only for bad things. For good things, use かもしれない: ×合格しかねない → ○合格するかもしれない (might pass).
・It attaches only to the ます form with ます dropped, not to the dictionary form or the ない form: ×壊すかねない, ×壊さないかねない.
・The tone is fairly formal and is common in news, company reports, and doctors' warnings. In casual chat with friends, people more often say 〜かもしれない or 〜ちゃうかも.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
かねる = "(because of one's position) can't ~, not in a position to ~." It's often a shop clerk or customer service rep politely declining.
かねない = "might end up ~ing (something bad)."
Say someone has been asked a sensitive question:
・その質問にはお答えしかねます。(I'm afraid I can't answer that question.)
・その質問に答えたら、誤解されかねない。(If I answer that question, I might get misunderstood.)
かもしれない = a plain "maybe," usable for good or bad things, with a neutral tone. かねない is only for bad things and adds a "watch out" feeling of warning.
・明日は晴れるかもしれない。(It might clear up tomorrow.)
・このまま遊んでいたら、試験に落ちかねない。(If you keep goofing off like this, you could end up failing the exam.)
Quick rule of thumb: "can't ~, I'm afraid I'm unable to ~" is かねる (it has no ない, yet it means "can't"); "if this goes on, something bad might happen" is かねない; and a "maybe" that doesn't care about good or bad is かもしれない.
What to learn next
〜得る also means "it's possible," but it works for good and bad alike and sounds more objective: これは誰にでも起こり得ることだ。(This is something that could happen to anyone.)
n2-39:
The idea in one line
「〜得る」 means "it's possible that ~", and 「〜得ない」 means "it's impossible that ~". The tone is like "it could happen" or "it can't happen" in English news and reports, so it's fairly formal. The one you've probably heard most is the line from Japanese dramas, ありえない！, meaning "No way!" or "You've got to be kidding!"
How to form it
Change the verb to its ます form, drop ます, and add 「得る」.
起こります → drop ます → 起こり得る (can happen)
あります → あり得る (can exist / is possible)
考えます → 考え得る (conceivable)
します → し得る (can do / is possible to do)
How to read it: only one place where you have a choice
Only the base form 「得る」 (at the end of a sentence or before a noun) can be read either うる or える. あり得る can be ありうる or ありえる, and both are correct. In news and writing, ありうる is more common.
Every other form is always read with 「え」: 得ない (えない), 得ます (えます), 得た (えた).
When to use it
PossibleYou state objectively that something could happen. It works for good things and bad things alike.
・誰にでも起こり得る問題だ。 (This is a problem that could happen to anyone.)
・それは十分あり得る話だ。 (That's entirely possible.)
ImpossibleYou declare that something cannot happen.
・そんなことは現実的にあり得ない。 (Something like that can't happen in reality.)
Conceivable / doableOften appears together with 「限り」 or 「すべて」.
・考え得る方法は全部試した。 (I tried every method I could think of.)
Casualありえない is the exception. Friends use it all the time in conversation to show shock or disbelief.
・え、また遅刻？ありえない！ (What, late again? No way!)
Easy mistakes
・It talks about whether something can happen, not whether a person has a skill. "I can swim" is 泳げる, never 泳ぎ得る.
・The negative is only read えない: it's ありえない, and there is no such reading as 「ありうない」.
・Apart from ありえない and ありえる, forms like 起こり得る lean toward written language. In everyday chat, 起こるかもしれない sounds more natural.
・ざるを得ない also contains 「得ない」, but the meaning is completely different: 行かざるを得ない means "have no choice but to go", not "it's impossible to go".
・When 「得る」 stands alone as a verb, it's read える and means "to obtain", as in 賞を得る (win a prize). That's a different usage from this one.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
得る vs かねない: Both mean "it could happen", but かねない is used only when you're worried something bad will happen.
このままでは事故が起こり得る。 (If this goes on, an accident could happen: calm statement)
このままでは事故が起こりかねない。 (If this goes on, we might end up with an accident: said with worry)
For good things, only 得る works: 努力すれば誰でも成功し得る。 (With effort, anyone can succeed.) Swap in かねない here and it's wrong.
得ない vs っこない: Both mean "impossible", but っこない is a very casual, subjective "as if that could ever happen".
一日で終わることはあり得ない。 (It's impossible to finish in one day: formal, objective)
一日で終わりっこないよ。 (There's no way I can finish that in a day: complaining to a friend)
Quick rule of thumb: for an objective "possible / impossible", use 得る・得ない. For worry about something bad, use かねない. For "as if!" with a friend, use っこない.
n2-40:
The idea in one line
「〜っこない」 means "no way ~" or "as if ~ could ever happen". The speaker has already decided "this will absolutely never happen." The tone is strong and very casual, often carrying a hint of "come on" or "get real."
・そんなこと、できっこないよ。 (There's no way anyone could do that!)
How to form it
Change the verb to its ます form, drop ます, and add 「っこない」.
できます → できっこない
間に合います → 間に合いっこない
分かります → 分かりっこない
勝てます → 勝てっこない
The forms you'll hear most
Can't be doneIt pairs most often with 「できる」, 「分かる」, 「間に合う」, or verbs about whether you can pull something off, like 「勝てる」, 「受かる」, 「取れる」. It means "there's simply no way."
・あんな強いチームに勝てっこない。 (There's no way we can beat a team that strong.)
・今から走っても間に合いっこないよ。 (Even if we run now, there's no way we'll make it.)
・説明したって、あの人には分かりっこない。 (Even if I explain it, there's no way that person will get it.)
Someone wouldn't do thatWhen you talk about someone else's behavior, it means "there's no way they'd do that."
・あの頑固な父が謝りっこない。 (My stubborn dad would never apologize, no way.)
Easy mistakes
・Attach it to the form with ます dropped, not the dictionary form: say 分かりっこない, never 「分かるっこない」.
・「っこない」 is already negative, so don't put ない before it.
・It attaches only to verbs, not directly to adjectives or nouns.
・「っこ」 has a small っ, so pause for a beat before 「こ」. Don't read it as 「こない」, or it will sound like 「来ない」.
・This is how friends talk, and it's blunt. It isn't suitable for your boss or customers, or for written reports.
・Saying 「君にはできっこない」 ("There's no way you can do it") to someone is like looking down on them to their face. It really stings, so use it carefully.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Here are three ways to say the same thing: "With this much work, there's no way it'll be done in a day."
一日で終わりっこない。 (っこない: casual and emotional, like complaining)
一日で終わるわけがない。 (わけがない: "how could it be", works in speech and writing)
一日で終わるはずがない。 (はずがない: "impossible" by logical deduction, calmer)
Note that the attachment differs: わけがない and はずがない attach to the dictionary form (終わる), while っこない attaches to the form with ます dropped (終わり).
Quick rule of thumb: when you're grumbling or venting to a friend, use 「っこない」. When you want to sound more formal, switch to 「わけがない」 or 「はずがない」.
What to learn next
The opposite meaning is 「〜に決まっている」 = "it's bound to ~, no doubt about it": そんなの、失敗するに決まっている。 (Doing it that way is bound to fail.)
n2-42:
The idea in one line
「〜に決まっている」 means "It's definitely ~, obviously". The speaker has already made up their mind and sounds completely sure, with a hint of "Isn't that obvious?"
How to form it
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly. Past and negative forms work too.
行く → 行くに決まっている高い → 高いに決まっている忘れた → 忘れたに決まっている
Nouns and な-adjectives: don't add だ. Attach に directly.
嘘 → 嘘に決まっている無理 → 無理に決まっている
In casual conversation it's often shortened to 〜に決まってる. The politer form is 〜に決まっています.
When to use it
Obviously soYou don't need evidence. You're simply sure it must be this way.
・こんな時間に電話なんて、急用に決まってる。(A call at this hour? It's obviously something urgent.)
・そんなに安いのは偽物に決まってるよ。(Something that cheap? It's a fake, obviously.)
Of courseSomeone asks about something obvious, and you answer "Well, duh."
・「一緒に行く？」「行くに決まってるじゃん！」("Want to go together?" "Of course I'm going!")
・10時間も歩いたんだから、疲れたに決まってるでしょ。(You walked for 10 hours. Of course you're tired.)
Common mistakes
・Don't add だ after nouns or な-adjectives: 嘘だに決まっている is wrong. Say 嘘に決まっている.
・This is the speaker's own subjective conviction, and it sounds strong. Saying 「〜に決まっています」 to a boss or a customer can come across as presumptuous, even confrontational. It's also rarely used in formal writing or reports.
・In English, "it has to be" or "must" can also express obligation ("you must come"), but に決まっている never means that. To say "Be sure to come tomorrow," use 明日は必ず来てください.
・決まっている originally means "has already been decided." So sometimes it's meant literally: 会議は月曜日に決まっている。 (The meeting has been set for Monday.) Check the context to tell which one it is.
Don't confuse it with similar forms
Same situation: your friend still hasn't shown up.
に違いない = an inference based on some grounds. It sounds calm and works in both speech and writing:
道が混んでいるに違いない。 (The roads must be jammed.)
に決まっている = more subjective and more emotional, used almost only in conversation:
道が混んでいるに決まってるよ。 (The roads are jammed, obviously.)
に相違ない = same meaning as に違いない, but stiff, mostly found in writing and novels:
道が混んでいるに相違ない。 (The roads are undoubtedly congested.)
The opposite direction is っこない = "no way that ~," which is also casual and subjective:
あの人が時間通りに来っこないよ。 (There's no way he'll come on time.)
Quick rule: for calm reasoning use に違いない, for writing use に相違ない, and for a "Obviously!" or "Of course!" tone use に決まっている. To say "no way," use っこない.
n2-44:
The idea in one line
「〜ものだ」 means "How ~ it is!" or "Back in the day…". It doesn't report facts. It speaks with a reflective, life-experience feeling, like an older person looking at a photo and saying, "Time really flies, doesn't it?"
How to form it
Verbs in plain form: 変わる → 変わるものだ
い-adjectives: 早い → 早いものだ
な-adjectives keep 「な」: 静か → 静かなものだ
For things in the past, use the た form: 遊んだ → 遊んだものだ
In speech it's often shortened to もんだ, and なあ is often added at the end: 早いもんだなあ。 For a politer tone, use ものです.
How you'll hear it most
Reflecting on lifeA sigh about time, life, or change.
・月日がたつのは早いものだ。(How quickly time passes!)
・この町もずいぶん変わったものだ。(This town has changed so much, hasn't it?)
Nostalgiaた form + ものだ, often together with 「よく」, talks about things you used to do often.
・子供の頃はよくこの川で遊んだものだ。(As a kid, I used to play in this river all the time.)
・学生時代は朝まで友達と話したものだ。(In my student days, I'd often talk with friends until morning.)
Admiration or disbelief「よく～たものだ」 = "how could you possibly ~" or "you actually managed to ~."
・よくそんなことが言えたものだ。(I can't believe you had the nerve to say that.)
Common mistakes
・The nostalgic use only works for things you did repeatedly in the past. It can't be used for something that happened once: 去年京都へ行ったものだ is wrong. Just say 去年京都へ行った.
・「よく」 has two meanings: in よく遊んだものだ, よく means "often"; in よく言えたものだ, よく means "how could you / actually." Check the context.
・For small things right in front of you, like the weather being hot or the food being good, plain 暑いなあ or おいしいね is enough. Forcing ものだ in sounds like you're giving a speech on the meaning of life.
・You can't put 「だ」 between a な-adjective and ものだ: 静かだものだ is wrong.
Don't confuse it with similar forms
ものだ (naturally ~ / should ~): states general truths or rules, with little emotion.
年をとると、物忘れが多くなるものだ。 (As people get older, they naturally get more forgetful.)
人の話は最後まで聞くものだ。 (You should listen to what people say until the end.)
ものだ (exclamation): the same form, but with a feeling of reflection.
子供が大きくなるのは本当に早いものだ。 (Kids really do grow up fast.)
ものがある: something makes you feel a certain quality. It's used to evaluate works, people, and performances.
彼の歌には人の心を打つものがある。 (There's something in his songs that moves people.)
Quick rule: if you can add 「本当に」 or 「なあ」 and it still reads as heartfelt, it's the exclamation. If it calmly states a principle or rule, it's "naturally ~." If you're saying "something has a certain quality," it's ものがある.
What to learn next
Next, look at 〜ものがある, then go back and review the "naturally ~" ものだ. Comparing all three side by side is the best way to avoid mixing them up.
n2-45:
The idea in one line
「〜ぶり」 has two completely different uses:
① After an action = "the way someone does it, how they go about it", like English "his work performance" or "the way she talks."
② After a length of time = "for the first time in ~, after a gap of ~". It's the ぶり in 久しぶり, which you already know.
Use ①: the way someone does something
How to attach itAdd ぶり directly to a noun: 仕事 → 仕事ぶり (work performance)
For verbs, change to the ます form, drop ます, then add ぶり: 話します → drop ます → 話しぶり (way of speaking) 暮らします → 暮らしぶり (way of living)
・彼の仕事ぶりはみんなに認められている。(Everyone recognizes how well he works.)
・彼女の話しぶりから、自信を感じた。(I could sense her confidence from the way she spoke.)
・駅の混雑ぶりに驚いた。(I was shocked at how crowded the station was.)
It's mostly used to describe or evaluate how someone else or a certain situation comes across. A few words are usually pronounced with 「っぷり」, such as 食べっぷり and 飲みっぷり:
・いい食べっぷりだね。(You really dig in, don't you!)
Use ②: again after a gap
How to attach itLength of time + ぶり. It's often followed by 「に + verb」, 「の + noun」, or simply 「だ／です」.
・5年ぶりに母校を訪れた。(I visited my old school for the first time in five years.)
・10年ぶりの再会だった。(It was a reunion after ten years.)
・久しぶりの休みだ。(Finally, a day off after a long time.)
・田中さん、3年ぶりですね。(Mr. Tanaka, it's been three years!)
The key point: during that stretch of time it didn't happen, and now it has happened again.
Common mistakes
・Use ② can't be followed by a negative. To say "I haven't seen them in three years," you can't say 3年ぶりに会わなかった. Say 3年間会っていない.
・Use ② always means "it happened before, and now it's happening again." If you're doing something for the first time, there's no "again," so you can't use ぶり.
・Use ① doesn't attach to just any word. The common ones are few: 仕事ぶり, 話しぶり, 暮らしぶり, 生活ぶり, 活躍ぶり, 混雑ぶり. The most practical approach is to memorize them as whole vocabulary items.
・Verbs attach in the ます-stem form: it's 話しぶり, not 話すぶり.
Telling similar patterns apart
Take the same "after graduation" situation:
て以来 = a state has continued without a break since then: 卒業して以来、彼には一度も会っていない。 (I haven't seen him even once since graduating.)
ぶり = after all that time, it happened again: 卒業以来、5年ぶりに彼に会った。 (I saw him again for the first time in five years since graduating.)
後 = simply "after ~," whether or not it had happened before: 卒業して5年後に結婚した。 (I got married five years after graduating.)
Quick test: to say "ever since then, it's been like this," use て以来. To say "after a long gap, it happened again," use ぶり. To say just "after ~," use 後.
n2-46:
The idea in one line
「〜がたい」 means "hard to ~" or "difficult to bring yourself to ~". The point isn't that your ability falls short, but that you can't get past it emotionally: something is so outrageous that it's really hard to believe, accept, or forgive. The tone is fairly formal, and you see it a lot in news, writing, and formal settings.
How to attach it
Change the verb to the ます form, drop ます, then add がたい.
信じる → 信じます → 信じがたい
許す → 許します → 許しがたい
理解する → 理解します → 理解しがたい
Once attached, the whole word behaves like an い-adjective: you can put it before a noun or change it to the past tense.
信じがたい → 信じがたかった (it was hard to believe)
How you'll hear it most
At the end of a sentenceDirectly says "I really find it hard to ~."
・彼のあの行動は今でも理解しがたい。(I still find that behavior of his hard to understand.)
・この結果は受け入れがたい。(This result is hard to accept.)
Before a nounUsed as an adjective. This is the most common form, and many of these are already set phrases.
・それは信じがたい話だ。(That's a hard-to-believe story.)
・留学は忘れがたい経験になった。(Studying abroad became an unforgettable experience.)
・許しがたい行為だ。(It's an unforgivable act.)
Other common ones: 想像しがたい (hard to imagine), 言いがたい (hard to say), 得がたい (rare and precious), 耐えがたい (unbearable).
Common mistakes
・It attaches to the ます form minus ます, not the dictionary form: say 信じがたい, not 信じるがたい.
・Don't use がたい when the thing itself is hard to use or do. A pen that's hard to write with is このペンは書きにくい, not 書きがたい.
・The tone is stiff and formal. Chatting with friends, 信じられない and 許せない sound more natural; 信じがたい would sound a bit like reading from a script.
・In writing it's often spelled with the kanji 「難い」, which is read がたい here.
Telling similar patterns apart
にくい = the thing itself is hard to ~, physically or technically difficult:
