この説明は分かりにくい。 (This explanation is hard to follow: it's unclear.)
がたい = emotionally hard to accept, believe, or forgive:
彼の考えは理解しがたい。 (I really can't understand his way of thinking: I can't get on board with it.)
かねる = from your own position, you can't comfortably do something. Often used to decline politely:
その件にはお答えしかねます。 (I'm afraid I can't answer that matter.)
Quick test: for something awkward to use or understand, use にくい. For something you can't get past emotionally, use がたい. To politely turn someone down, use かねる.
What to learn next
The ありがたい you say every day actually comes from 「有り難い」. It originally meant "rare, hard to come by," and only later came to mean "worth being thankful for."
n2-47:
The idea in one line
「〜かける」 means 'halfway through ~': halfway through a book, halfway through a meal, halfway through a sentence. The action has started but isn't finished, so it stops midway. After certain verbs it takes on the meaning 'almost ~' or 'about to ~'.
How to form it
Take the verb's ます form, drop 「ます」, and add 「かける」 or 「かけの」.
読みます → 読みかける食べます → 食べかけるします → しかける
「かける」 itself conjugates as a Group 2 (ichidan) verb: かけた, かけて, かけている.
To modify a noun, use かけの + noun: 飲みかけのコーヒー (a half-finished coffee).
To end a sentence, use かけだ: この本はまだ読みかけだ。 (I haven't finished this book yet.)
When to use it
Halfway throughAttach it to actions you do deliberately, like reading, eating, writing, or speaking, to show you stopped partway.
・読みかけの小説が本棚に積まれている。 (Half-read novels are piled up on the bookshelf.)
・何か言いかけて、やめた。 (He started to say something, then stopped.)
・飲みかけのコーヒー、捨ててもいい？ (Is it okay to throw out this half-drunk coffee?)
Almost, about toAttach it to sudden changes like dying, drowning, going out, or forgetting. It means 'just about to happen', or 'it nearly happened, but didn't'.
・子供のころ、海で溺れかけたことがある。 (When I was a kid, I almost drowned in the sea.)
・道で死にかけた猫を見つけた。 (I found a cat on the road that was close to death.)
・忘れかけていた夢を思い出した。 (I remembered a dream I had almost forgotten.)
Common mistakes
・話しかける does not mean 'to stop halfway through speaking'. It means 'to speak to someone, to strike up a conversation'. For 'stop halfway through saying something', use 言いかける. 呼びかける (to appeal to, call out to) and 出かける (to go out) are also fixed words and have nothing to do with 'halfway'.
・To modify a noun, 「かけの」 is the most common form: 食べかけのパン (a half-eaten piece of bread). Don't write 「食べかけパン」.
・Verbs of 'existence or state', like ある and いる, have no start or end, so they can't take かける.
・The same 「かける」 can mean 'halfway' or 'almost'. The verb before it tells you which: 死にかける always means 'nearly die', never 'halfway dead'.
Don't confuse it with similar forms
Compare them in the same situation:
かける = already close to that point, or stopped midway: 火が消えかけている。 (The fire is about to go out, with just a little left.)
つつある = changing little by little, with the focus on the process of change: 火が消えつつある。 (The fire is gradually dying down.)
Also, つつある is mostly used in writing and news reports, while かける and かけの are very common in everyday speech.
Quick tip: to say 'stopped halfway' or 'almost ~', use かける. To say 'gradually changing', use つつある.
What to learn next
Its opposite is 〜きる (to finish, to do all the way through): 一晩で読みきった。 (I read it all in one night.)
n2-48:
The idea in one line
「〜ことなく」 is like the formal, written-style 'without ever ~', 'never ~', 'not even once ~'. It means the same as 「〜ないで」 (without doing ~, ...) but is much more formal, and often appears in news, articles, and speeches.
What comes before it is the thing that did not happen: 休むことなく = without resting, without stopping.
How to form it
Add ことなく directly to the dictionary form of the verb (the base form you find in a dictionary).
休む → 休むことなく (without resting)
迷う → 迷うことなく (without hesitation)
Noun + する verbs work the same way: 遅刻する → 遅刻することなく (without being late)
Passive forms can also be used: 気づかれる → 気づかれることなく (without being noticed)
ことなく itself has no past or present tense. The tense comes from the end of the sentence.
How you'll most often see it
一度も・一日もPut these words before it to stress 'not even once'.
・彼は一日も休むことなく働き続けた。 (He kept working without taking a single day off.)
Long-term persistenceUse it to say something stayed the same or went on uninterrupted for a long time.
・この店は40年間、変わることなく同じ味を守っている。 (For 40 years, this restaurant has kept the same flavor without change.)
Expressing resolveVery popular in speeches and award acceptance remarks.
・これからも初心を忘れることなく、頑張ってまいります。 (From now on, too, I will keep working hard without forgetting my original resolve.)
・彼女は迷うことなく、この道を選んだ。 (She chose this path without hesitation.)
Common mistakes
・It attaches to the affirmative dictionary form, not the ない form: ○休むことなく　×休まないことなく.
・When you see 「休む」, don't think 'did rest'. ことなく negates the whole preceding action.
・You can't drop する from noun + する verbs: ×連絡ことなく　○連絡することなく.
・This expression is stiff. To a friend, just say 食べないで出かけた for 'went out without eating breakfast'. Using ことなく would sound like an official document.
・It's usually used for things that might have happened but didn't (didn't rest even though tired, didn't hesitate even though you might have). So it often carries a sense of 'determined' or 'admirable'.
Don't confuse it with similar forms
Here are three ways to say 'He worked without resting':
休まないで働いた。 (Casual; the most common in conversation.)
休まずに働いた。 (Slightly formal; fine in both speech and writing.)
休むことなく働いた。 (The most literary, with a weight of 'consistently, throughout'.)
The meaning is the same; the difference is the level of formality.
But 「ないで」 has another use: not doing A, doing B instead. In that case, ことなく is usually not used.
・電車に乗らないで、歩いて帰った。 (I didn't take the train; I walked home instead.)
Changing this sentence to 「電車に乗ることなく」 would sound very unnatural.
Quick tip: use ないで for casual talk and ずに for a bit more formality. Use ことなく when you want a news or speech tone, or to stress 'not even once'. For 'not A, but B instead', stick with ないで or ずに.
n2-49:
The idea in one line
「〜ようがない」means "there's simply no way to ~" or "I can't even begin to ~". The 「よう」 here means "method", so 「ようがない」 means there's no method at all. It's not that you don't want to, and it's not that you lack the ability. The situation just leaves you no way in.
When to use it
Missing conditions or meansYou want to do something, but a key thing (information, a tool, a clue) is missing, so you have no way to get started.
・住所も電話番号も知らないので、連絡しようがない。(I don't know the address or the phone number, so there's no way to contact them.)
・この部品はもう売っていないから、直しようがないね。(They don't sell this part anymore, so there's no way to fix it.)
ようもないWith an extra 「も」 in the middle, it's stronger, with the feel of "not even the slightest way."
・道が雪で埋まっていて、進みようもなかった。(The road was buried in snow, so there was no way to move forward at all.)
It's common in both writing and speech. Saying 「直しようがないよ」 to a friend sounds perfectly natural.
How to form it
Take the verb's ます form, drop ます, and add 「ようがない」.
書きます → drop ます → 書きようがない
食べます → 食べようがない連絡します → 連絡しようがない
Noun + のしようがないWith nouns like 「連絡、説明、返事」, you'll often hear 「noun + の + しようがない」 too.
説明しようがない → 説明のしようがない (both are correct)
Before a noun「が」 often becomes 「の」, giving 「ようのない + noun」. 「ようがない + noun」 is also fine.
・言いようのない寂しさを感じた。(I felt a loneliness I couldn't put into words.)
Forms you'll hear most
In speech, these set phrases come up most:
どうしようもない: nothing can be done, whatever you try. You can also use it to call someone hopeless.
しょうがない: can't be helped, oh well. It's really just 「しようがない」 said fast.
言いようがない: (so good or so bad that) it's beyond words.
・雨じゃしょうがないね。(If it's raining, there's nothing we can do.)
Common mistakes
・It attaches to the ます form, not the volitional form: it's 書きようがない, not 「書こうがない」.
・The 「しよう」 in 連絡しようがない looks just like the しよう of "let's do it", but it's actually 「し + よう (method)」. The meaning is completely different.
・It talks about having no method or means, not about ability. "I can't swim" is 泳げない; you can't say 「泳ぎようがない」.
Telling look-alikes apart
Same situation: you're asked a question and can't answer.
Negative potential form = a plain "can't", for any reason at all: その質問には答えられない。 (I can't answer that question.)
ようがない = you have no information or basis, so there's no way to answer: 何も聞いていないので、答えようがない。 (I haven't been told anything, so there's no way I can answer.)
かねる = you actually could answer, but your position makes it awkward. Customer service staff and shop clerks use it to refuse politely: その件についてはお答えしかねます。 (I'm afraid we're unable to answer regarding that matter.)
Quick rule of thumb: use ようがない for "no method, nowhere to start"; use かねる for "my position makes this awkward, so I'm politely declining"; and use the negative potential form for a plain "can't" with any reason.
n2-51:
The idea in one line
「〜際（に）」is the formal version of "when ~". Think of the gap between English "when you leave" and "upon leaving". Japanese station announcements, shop notices and company emails use it a lot. It sounds more polite than 「時」 and more like an official notice.
When to use it
Notices and announcementsSpeaking to customers or the public, reminding them what to watch out for when they do something.
・お降りの際は、足元にご注意ください。(Please watch your step when getting off.)
・ご利用の際は、こちらのカードをお見せください。(Please show this card when you use the service.)
Business and formal situationsWriting letters, or speaking to a superior or a client.
・先日お会いした際に、いろいろ教えていただきました。(When we met the other day, you taught me a great deal.)
How to form it
Nouns: add 「の」 and then 際.
入場 → 入場の際申し込み → 申し込みの際
Verbs: attach 際 directly to the dictionary form or the た form.
来る → 来る際会う → 会った際
The difference between the dictionary form and the た form is the same as with 「時」: the dictionary form is for the time before you do it, when you're about to; the た form is for after it's done, that one occasion.
・日本へ行く際に、パスポートを作りました。(I got a passport when I was going to Japan: before departure.)
・日本へ行った際に、友達に会いました。(I met a friend when I went to Japan: after arriving.)
Following it with 「に」 is the plain "at the time of ~". Switching to 「は」 adds a reminder feel, like "in this situation, please...", which is why notices so often write 「〜の際は」. Both are correct.
Forms you'll hear most
「お／ご + noun + の際」: the お or ご in front shows respect to the customer, so just memorize each phrase as a set.
お帰りの際 (when you head home), お降りの際 (when you get off), ご来店の際 (when you visit the store), ご利用の際 (when you use it)
Common mistakes
・A noun must be followed by 「の」: it's 入場の際, not 入場際.
・際 is read さい.
・Don't use it in casual chat. For "when I ate yesterday", just say 昨日ご飯を食べた時. Saying 「食べた際」 would sound like you're writing a report.
・際 refers to the moment you do a certain action. It isn't used for a period of time or a state: "when I was a kid" is 子どもの時, not 子どもの際. Adjectives don't normally take 際 either; "when I'm busy" is 忙しい時.
Telling look-alikes apart
Same situation: logging in to a website.
時 = the general expression, usable anywhere: ログインする時、パスワードを入れます。 (When you log in, you enter your password.)
際 = the formal expression, common in notices and instructions: ログインの際は、パスワードを入力してください。 (Please enter your password when logging in.)
場合 = "in the case that ~", for something not everyone will run into: パスワードを忘れた場合は、こちらをクリックしてください。 (If you forget your password, please click here.)
Everyone has to enter a password to log in, so it's 際; only some people forget their password, so it's 場合.
Quick rule of thumb: use 「時」 when chatting with friends; use 「際」 for notices and when speaking to customers; use 「場合」 for "in case ~ happens".
What to learn next
「〜に先立って」 is also formal and means "before ~": 開会に先立って、社長が挨拶をしました。 (Before the meeting began, the president gave a greeting.)
n2-52:
The idea in one line
「〜からすると」 means “from the standpoint of ~” or “judging from ~”. Put a person before it and you step into that person’s shoes. Put a clue before it (a facial expression, someone’s appearance, grades) and you’re drawing a conclusion from that clue.
How to connect it
Noun + からすると / からすれば / からしたら
All three mean the same thing. からしたら is more colloquial, and you’ll hear it a lot in casual conversation.
親 → 親からすると彼の表情 → 彼の表情からすれば
When to use it
Taking someone’s standpointPut a person or group before it, for example 親, 子供, 外国人, 会社. It means “this is how it looks from that person’s side,” which may not match how you feel yourself.
・親からすると、子供の将来を心配するのは自然なことだ。(From a parent’s point of view, worrying about their child’s future is only natural.)
・子供からしたら、大人の話はつまらないだろう。(From a child’s point of view, grown-ups’ conversations are probably boring.)
・外国人からすれば、敬語はかなり難しい。(From a foreigner’s point of view, honorific language is quite difficult.)
Judging from a cluePut a visible clue before it, for example 表情, 様子, 話し方, 成績. The sentence often ends with ようだ, らしい, はずだ or だろう, showing “this is my inference.”
・彼の表情からすると、何か隠しているようだ。(Judging from his expression, he seems to be hiding something.)
・この成績からすれば、合格できるはずだ。(Judging from these grades, you should be able to pass.)
・空の様子からすると、午後は雨になりそうだ。(Judging from the look of the sky, it looks like rain this afternoon.)
Easy mistakes
・The 「から」 here is not “because”. 親からすると doesn’t mean “because of the parents”; it means “from the parents’ side.” Also don’t mix it up with からには (since ~, then ~) or からこそ (precisely because ~).
・Only a noun can come before it. If you want to use an action as the clue, turn it into a noun first, as in 彼の話し方からすると. You can’t say 「話すからすると」 directly.
・すれば and したら look like “if ~,” but here they carry no hypothetical meaning. All three simply mean “judging from ~.”
・The second half of the sentence gives a view or judgment. Don’t follow it with a decision or a request, such as “I’m going to ~” or “Please ~.”
Telling it apart from similar forms
にとって = what something is to a person. It is often followed by an evaluative word (大切, ありがたい, 難しい).
・子供にとって、親は一番大切な存在だ。(For a child, parents are the most important people.)
からすると = you step into that person’s position and say how they would see or think about it.
・子供からすると、親の注意はうるさいだけだろう。(From a child’s point of view, a parent’s warnings are probably just nagging.)
Also, the “judging from a clue” use can’t be replaced with にとって. You wouldn’t say 「表情にとって」 (use からすると or から見ると instead).

から見ると = mostly interchangeable with からすると, and it works for both uses: “from someone’s standpoint” and “judging from a clue.”
・あの様子から見ると、何かあったらしい。(Judging from how he looks, something seems to have happened.)
Quick rule of thumb: to say what value or effect something has for a person, use にとって. To say “how it would look to that person” or to infer something from a clue, use からすると; から見ると usually works there too.
n2-53:
The idea in one line
「〜にかけては」 means “when it comes to ~, (someone) is really good.” You name a field first, such as cooking, math, or sales, and then follow with praise like “no one can match them” or “they’re second to none.” The point of the whole sentence is that this person is especially strong in this area.
How to connect it
Noun + にかけては
料理 → 料理にかけては (when it comes to cooking)
If you want to talk about an action, first add 「こと」 to make it a noun:
走る → 走ることにかけては (when it comes to running)
The patterns you’ll hear most
Praising someone elseIt’s most often followed by 「右に出る者はいない」 (no one surpasses them) or 「かなう人はいない」 (no one can match them).
・和食にかけては、彼女の右に出る者はいない。(When it comes to Japanese cooking, no one surpasses her.)
・営業にかけては、彼が社内一だ。(When it comes to sales, he’s number one in the company.)
Talking about yourselfIt’s followed by 「誰にも負けない」 (I won’t lose to anyone) or 「自信がある」 (I’m confident).
・記憶力にかけては、誰にも負けない。(When it comes to memory, I won’t lose to anyone.)
・人の名前を覚えることにかけては、自信がある。(When it comes to remembering people’s names, I’m confident.)
Easy mistakes
・What comes before it must be a skill or a field someone is good at, and what follows must be an evaluation of strong ability. A topic unrelated to ability, like 「日本の天気にかけては」, doesn’t work.
・If you use it with a weakness, as in “when it comes to making excuses, he’s a genius,” it becomes sarcastic or joking, not real praise.
・Don’t drop the 「は」. Without it you get 「にかけて」, which is read as a different grammar point that expresses a range of time or place.
・This expression is on the formal side, like when introducing someone or writing an essay. With friends, it’s more common to say 「料理なら誰にも負けない」 (if it’s cooking, I won’t lose to anyone).
Telling it apart from similar forms
にかけて (without は) = a range from one point to another, with a time or place before it:
・今夜から明日の朝にかけて、雨が降るでしょう。(It will probably rain from tonight through tomorrow morning.)
にかけては = when it comes to a particular skill:
・数学にかけては、クラスで彼に勝てる人はいない。(When it comes to math, no one in the class can beat him.)
に関しては = simply “regarding ~.” It just names the topic, and what follows can be anything:
・料理に関しては、母に聞いてください。(About cooking, please ask my mother.)
にかけては = what follows is always praise of ability in that area:
・料理にかけては、母にかなう人はいない。(When it comes to cooking, no one can match my mother.)
Quick rule of thumb: if a time or place comes before it, use にかけて. If you’re just introducing a topic, use に関しては. Use にかけては only when you want to say “he’s the best in this area.”
n2-58:
The idea in one line
「〜とは限らない」means "not necessarily ~" or "doesn't always ~". Everyone assumes "it's always like this," and you step in with "not always, there are exceptions." In English you'd say "expensive doesn't always mean good." In Japanese that's 高いものがいいとは限らない。
When to use it
Challenging a stereotypeYou hit the brakes on an idea that "everyone takes for granted."
・日本人がみんな寿司が好きだとは限らない。(Not all Japanese people necessarily like sushi.)
・先生の言うことがいつも正しいとは限らない。(What the teacher says isn't always right.)
Warning of a riskThings aren't guaranteed to go as expected, so you prepare ahead.
・天気予報が当たるとは限らないから、傘を持っていこう。(The weather forecast isn't always right, so let's take an umbrella.)
How to form it
Put a complete sentence in plain form (the form without です・ます) before it, then attach とは限らない directly.
Verb: 成功する → 成功するとは限らない
い-adjective: 高い → 高いとは限らない
な-adjective: 便利だ → 便利だとは限らない (だ is often dropped: 便利とは限らない)
Noun: 本物だ → 本物だとは限らない (you can also say 本物とは限らない)
With seniors or in formal situations, use とは限りません.
How you'll usually hear it
必ずしも〜Adding 必ずしも (not necessarily) in front makes the "not necessarily" feel clearer. It's very common in written text.
・有名な大学を出た人が、必ずしも仕事ができるとは限らない。(People who graduated from famous universities aren't necessarily good at their jobs.)
からといって〜It means "you can't say it's definitely ~ just because ~." It's most useful to memorize the whole phrase together.
・安いからといって、お得だとは限らない。(Just because something is cheap doesn't mean it's a good deal.)
みんな・いつも・全てWords meaning "all" or "every time" often appear before it, because とは限らない is made precisely to overturn a claim that "everything is like this."
Common pitfalls
・It means "not necessarily," not "is not." 高いものがいいとは限らない only says that expensive things aren't guaranteed to be good. It doesn't say expensive things are bad.
・必ずしも must be followed by a negative. You can't say 「必ずしもいい」. You have to say 必ずしもいいとは限らない.
・Watch out for 〜ないとも限らない, because the meaning flips: 事故が起きないとも限らない。 means "we can't guarantee an accident won't happen," that is, an accident could still happen. It's used to urge caution.
・限る is read かぎる, so it's かぎらない. Don't read it as げんらない.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
All three talk about "whether a place is crowded on weekends":
に限らず = not only ~ (a wider range): この店は週末に限らず、いつも混んでいる。 (This shop is crowded not only on weekends but all the time.)
とは限らない = not necessarily ~ (there are exceptions): 週末だからといって、混んでいるとは限らない。 (Even if it's the weekend, it's not necessarily crowded.)
に決まっている = definitely ~ (you're very sure): 週末だから、混んでいるに決まっている。 (It's the weekend, so it's bound to be crowded.)
A quick rule of thumb: noun + に限らず = "not only ~"; whole sentence + とは限らない = "not necessarily ~." To say "definitely," use に決まっている. To say "not necessarily," use とは限らない.
n2-59:
The idea in one line
「〜をきっかけに」means "prompted by ~, I started…" or "taking ~ as an opportunity, I…". Before it you put the event that triggered you, and after it comes the new action or change that began as a result. For example: "I started cooking for myself after coming to Japan," or "I started paying attention to my health after getting sick."
・日本に来たのをきっかけに、料理を始めた。(After coming to Japan, I started cooking for myself.)
・入院をきっかけに、健康に気をつけるようになった。(After being hospitalized, I started taking care of my health.)
How to form it
NounAttach it directly: 留学 → 留学をきっかけに
VerbFirst add「の」or「こと」to turn it into a noun-like event, then attach: 子どもが生まれた → 子どもが生まれたのをきっかけに
・子どもが生まれたのをきっかけに、タバコをやめた。(After my child was born, I quit smoking.)
It's often paired with expressions of "starting" or "changing," like 「始めた」「ようになった」「やめた」.
How you'll usually hear it
がきっかけでThis makes the triggering event the subject. It's very common in spoken Japanese.
・友達の一言がきっかけで、転職を考えるようになった。(A single remark from a friend got me thinking about changing jobs.)
きっかけは〜This is a question you'll be asked all the time in interviews and self-introductions.
・日本語を始めたきっかけは何ですか。(What made you start learning Japanese?)
・アニメがきっかけです。(It was anime.)
をきっかけとしてThe meaning is the same but it's more formal, and you see it more often in news and written text.
Common pitfalls
・Before a verb you must add「の」or「こと」: say 日本に来たのをきっかけに, and never just 「日本に来たをきっかけに」.
・「を」goes with「に」and「が」goes with「で」: 留学をきっかけに / 留学がきっかけで. Don't split these pairs and mix them up.
・It describes something that triggers you to start something new, not a plain cause. For a direct result like "the trains stopped because of heavy rain," 大雨で電車が止まった is enough, and using きっかけ would sound odd.
・Both good and bad events can go before it. Illness, a breakup, or being scolded can all be a きっかけ.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
All three are about the same event, "moving house":
をきっかけに = moving triggers you to start something new:
引っ越しをきっかけに、ジョギングを始めた。 (Taking the move as a chance, I started jogging.)
て以来 = ever since then, a state has continued:
引っ越して以来、毎朝ジョギングしている。 (Ever since I moved, I've been jogging every morning.)
に伴って = things that naturally go along with moving, not something you were inspired to do:
引っ越しに伴って、住所変更の手続きをした。 (Along with the move, I did the paperwork for the change of address.)
A quick rule of thumb: "Because of that, I started ~" is をきっかけに. "Ever since then, I've kept ~" is て以来. "When that happens, ~ naturally follows" is に伴って.
What to learn next
More formal versions are 「〜を機に」and「〜を契機に」, which are very common in company announcements and the news: 結婚を機に、仕事を辞めた。 (Taking marriage as an opportunity, I quit my job.)
n2-55:
The idea in one line
「〜にしろ／〜にせよ」means "whether A or B, ..." or "even if it's ..., still ...". You first throw out a few possibilities, then state a conclusion or opinion that doesn't change because of them. The two forms mean the same thing, but にせよ is more formal and shows up more in writing and formal settings.
When to use it
Whether A or BYou put two (or more) options side by side, and the conclusion is the same whichever one it is. This is the most common pattern.
・行くにしろ行かないにしろ、早めに連絡してください。(Whether you go or not, please let me know early.)
・肉にせよ魚にせよ、新鮮なものを選びたい。(Whether it's meat or fish, I want to pick something fresh.)
No matter whatPut a question word like 「何」「どちら」「誰」 in front, and it means "it's the same whichever one it is."
・何をするにしろ、健康が一番大事だ。(Whatever you do, health matters most.)
・いずれにせよ、一度会って話しましょう。(Either way, let's meet and talk once.)
いずれにせよ and どっちにしろ are almost set phrases meaning "anyway" or "in any case." You'll hear them a lot in meetings and in everyday conversation.
Even if ～With just one situation, it means "even if that's really the case, still ..." It often carries a slightly disapproving or cautionary tone.
・冗談にしろ、そんなことを言うべきではない。(Even as a joke, you shouldn't say something like that.)
・忙しいにせよ、電話ぐらいできたはずだ。(Even if you were busy, you could at least have made a phone call.)
How to connect it
Verbs and い-adjectives: use the plain form (the form without ます; affirmative, negative and past are all fine) and attach it directly.
行く → 行くにしろ
行かない → 行かないにしろ
高い → 高いにせよ
Nouns and な-adjectives: attach directly, or add 「である」 first (more formal). You can't put だ in between.
学生 → 学生にしろ
不便 → 不便にせよ
不便 → 不便であるにせよ
Easy mistakes
・After nouns and な-adjectives, don't add だ: 学生だにしろ and 不便だにせよ are both wrong.
・With 「AにしろBにしろ」, A and B should be the same kind of thing, on equal footing: 賛成にしろ反対にしろ, 行くにしろ行かないにしろ.
・The second half is usually your opinion, request or advice, with things like べきだ, てください, ほうがいい.
・しろ and せよ are originally the imperative forms of する, but here they have no commanding meaning at all. 勉強しろ means "Go study!", while 勉強にしろ遊びにしろ means "whether it's studying or playing." The difference is whether 「に」 is there.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
にしても: almost the same meaning as にしろ and にせよ; the difference is the level of formality.
・行くにしても行かないにしても、連絡してね。(Whether you go or not, let me know, okay? — between friends)
・出席されるにせよされないにせよ、ご連絡ください。(Whether you will attend or not, please contact us. — formal notice)
From casual to formal, the order is roughly: にしても → にしろ → にせよ.
を問わず: "regardless of, without distinction." It attaches only to nouns, often to a whole range like 「年齢」 or 「男女」, and is used in rules and job ads.
・年齢を問わず、誰でも参加できます。(Regardless of age, anyone can take part.)
・大人にしろ子どもにしろ、参加費は同じだ。(Whether adult or child, the participation fee is the same.)
Quick rule of thumb: for a condition covering a whole range ("regardless of ..."), use を問わず. To list specific options one by one and then give a conclusion, use にしろ・にせよ. Chatting with friends, にしても sounds most natural; in writing and formal settings, use にせよ.
n2-56:
The idea in one line
「〜にほかならない」means "it is precisely ...", "it is nothing other than ...", or "when you get down to it, it's ...". The speaker concludes with total confidence: this is the answer, and nothing else.
「ほか」means "other," so 「ほかならない」 literally says "it can't be anything other than this," which is how it comes to mean "it is exactly this." The tone is stiff, and it mostly appears in writing, speeches and news commentary.
When to use it
Declaring the essence"A is, at bottom, B": you reveal what something really is.
・この結果は、皆さんの協力の成果にほかならない。(This result is nothing other than the fruit of everyone's cooperation.)
・彼の説明は、言い訳にほかならない。(His explanation is, plainly speaking, just an excuse.)
Declaring the causeUse 「〜のは、〜からにほかならない」, meaning "the reason that ... is nothing other than that ..."
・彼が合格できたのは、毎日努力したからにほかならない。(The reason he passed is simply that he worked hard every day.)
・事故が起きたのは、安全確認を怠ったからにほかならない。(The accident happened for no other reason than that safety checks were neglected.)
How to connect it
Nouns: attach directly. 努力の結果 → 努力の結果にほかならない
Giving a cause: plain form, add 「から」 first, then attach. 努力した → 努力したからにほかならない
Stating the essence of an action: dictionary form of the verb plus 「こと」, which turns it into a noun, then attach. 逃げる → 逃げることにほかならない
・何もしないのは、問題から逃げることにほかならない。(Doing nothing is, in essence, running away from the problem.)
In speeches and formal settings, to be more polite, say にほかなりません.
Easy mistakes
・When you see 「ならない」, don't assume it's a negative or "must not." Here it's a very strong affirmation: "it is exactly this."
・A verb can't attach directly: say 遅れたからにほかならない, not 遅れたにほかならない.
・When the first half uses 「〜のは」 to ask "why did this happen?", the natural ending is 「〜からにほかならない」 or 「〜のおかげにほかならない」. Putting in just a noun easily makes the two halves not match up.
・Using it with friends sounds like you're reading out a thesis. In casual speech, 「〜からだよ」 or 「まさに〜だ」 is enough.
・It's a firm assertion, not a guess. Don't use it for things you're not sure about.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
にすぎない = "it's just ...", with a feeling of looking down on something.
彼の成功は運がよかったからにすぎない。(His success is only because he was lucky.)
彼の成功は努力の結果にほかならない。(His success is nothing other than the result of hard work.)
The two look alike, but one belittles and the other draws a conclusion.
からこそ = stresses "precisely because of this reason, this result came about." It can go mid-sentence, or at the end as 「〜のは〜からこそだ」. It's also common in speech and often carries emotion.
努力したからこそ、合格できた。(Precisely because I worked hard, I passed.)
合格できたのは、努力したからこそだ。(The reason I could pass is precisely that I worked hard.)
合格できたのは、努力したからにほかならない。(The reason I could pass is nothing other than that I worked hard.)
The last two mean nearly the same thing; the difference is in tone. からこそ emphasizes that reason, while にほかならない declares "it's nothing else", which is stiffer and more written, like drawing a conclusion in a report.
Quick rule of thumb: to say "it's just ..." with a bit of disdain, use にすぎない. To stress "precisely because ... , ...", use からこそ. To confidently conclude "it's nothing else, it's ...", use にほかならない.
What to learn next
Since this is also a very confident tone, try comparing 〜に違いない and 〜に相違ない. They express a strong inference, "it must be ...", whereas にほかならない directly asserts "it is ...".
n2-60:
The idea in one line
「〜あげく」 works like English “after all that fuss, in the end…” or “after going through all that, it turned out…”. What comes before is a long, tiring process, and what follows is usually a disappointing result nobody wanted. The speaker often sounds a little annoyed, or like it was all for nothing.
・さんざん待たされたあげく、満席だと言われた。（After being left waiting forever, I was told they were full）
How to form it
Verbs take the た form (the past-tense form), followed by あげく:
迷う → 迷ったあげく悩む → 悩んだあげく
Nouns take 「の」 first:
議論 → 議論のあげくけんか → けんかのあげく
You can add 「に」 after it or leave it off; the meaning is the same. It can also be written with kanji as 挙げ句, so recognize that too.
How you'll most often hear it
All for nothingBefore it you'll often see さんざん (thoroughly, relentlessly) or 何度も (many times), and after it often 結局 (in the end).
・さんざん迷ったあげく、結局何も買わなかった。（After agonizing for ages, I ended up buying nothing）
・長時間の議論のあげく、何も決まらなかった。（After a long discussion, nothing got decided）
A reluctant decisionYou thought about it for a long time and finally had to settle on something.
・悩んだあげく、旅行には行かないことにした。（After agonizing over it, I decided not to go on the trip）
あげくの果てにA fixed phrase meaning “and in the end, he even…”. It's used when things keep getting worse until they reach the most extreme point.
・彼は遅刻を繰り返し、あげくの果てに無断で休んだ。（He kept showing up late, and in the end he even stayed away without telling anyone）
Common mistakes
・Verbs must be in the た form: 迷うあげく is wrong; say 迷ったあげく.
・What comes before must be a process that drags on or repeats. Actions that are over in a moment don't work: ドアを開けたあげく and 一度電話したあげく both sound odd. Something like 何度も電話したあげく、やっと通じたと思ったら留守電だった。 (I called again and again, and just when I thought I'd finally gotten through, it was voicemail) sounds natural.
・What follows is an outcome that has already happened, so the sentence usually ends in the past tense. You can't follow it with things that haven't happened yet, like “let's ~” or “please ~”.
・Don't use it when the result is good: 努力したあげく合格した sounds odd. Switch to 末に, covered below.
Telling it apart from a similar pattern
末に also means “after going through ~, finally…”, and it's formed the same way (た form / noun + の + 末に). The difference is that 末に is more neutral. It works with good or bad results and is very common in news and formal writing. あげく carries a grumbling “after all that, it still ended up like this” feel and almost only takes bad results.
Here's the same long meeting both ways:
何度も話し合った末に、新しい計画が決まった。（After discussing it many times, we finally settled on a new plan: a good result, so only 末に works）
何度も話し合ったあげく、結局何も決まらなかった。（We discussed it many times, and still nothing got decided: a grumbling tone, so あげく fits best）
Quick rule of thumb: if the result is good or you're simply stating facts, use 末に. If you want to grumble “after all that, this is what we got…”, use あげく.
n2-61:
The idea in one line
「〜てはじめて」 works like English “only after ~ did I realize/understand…” or “not until ~ did…”. Think of the saying “you don't know what you've got till it's gone”: the first half is something you experienced firsthand, and the second half is what you only then understood, or felt for the first time. The key point is that before that, you really didn't get it.
How to form it
Take the て form of a verb and add 「はじめて」 directly (it's also often written with kanji as 「初めて」).
なる → なって → なってはじめて
する → して → してはじめて
言われる → 言われて → 言われてはじめて
You usually put a comma after it, then the thing you only realized later.
When to use it
Understanding only after experiencingIt's most often followed by words of understanding or discovery, such as わかる, 気づく, 知る and 実感する.
・親になってはじめて、親の気持ちがわかった。（Only after becoming a parent myself did I understand how my parents felt）
・一人暮らしをしてはじめて、家事の大変さに気づいた。（Only after living on my own did I realize how hard housework is）
・言われてはじめて気づきました。（I only noticed when someone pointed it out）
General truthsUse the present tense to say “you only really ~ once you've ~”.
・病気になってはじめて、健康のありがたさがわかる。（You only learn how precious health is once you fall ill）
Common mistakes
・The second half can't be your own intention, a command, or a request.
×日本に来てはじめて、日本語を勉強しよう。
What follows should be a realization or change that has already happened, not “what I'm going to do”.
・Don't confuse it with verb ます-stem + はじめる (start ~): 食べはじめる means “start eating”, while 食べてはじめて means “only after eating…”. The difference is whether there's a 「て」 in the middle.
・This pattern carries a feeling of “I didn't know until then”, so it sounds odd when used for things you already knew or that are taken for granted.
Telling it apart from a similar pattern
Both express “you only know by doing it”, but compare the two:
てはじめて = looking back: you understood only after doing it: 実際に使ってみてはじめて、よさがわかった。（Only after actually using it did I see how good it was）
ないことには = a condition looking forward: without doing it first, you can't, and what follows is usually negative: 実際に使ってみないことには、よさはわからない。（Unless you actually try it, you won't know how good it is）
Quick rule of thumb: to say “it only clicked after I went through it”, use てはじめて. To say “if you don't do ~ first, you can't…”, use ないことには.
n2-63:
The idea in one line
「〜ものがある」 means “there's something ~ about it” or “it really strikes you as ~.” Say you hear a performance or look at an old photo. Something moves you, but you can't quite say what. Japanese uses this pattern for that feeling: 彼の演奏には心を打つものがある。 (There's something moving about his playing.)
The もの here isn't a physical object. It's a quality or feeling that's hard to put into words.
When to use it
Evaluating people or thingsUse it to praise works, performances and abilities. It sounds more thoughtful and measured than just saying “that's great.” You'll often hear it in film reviews, the news and feedback from a boss.
・彼の演奏には人を引き込むものがある。(There's something captivating about his playing.)
・新人だが、彼女の企画には光るものがある。(She's new, but there's something that really stands out in her proposal.)
Talking about your own feelingsSomething gives you a certain feeling, good or bad.
・この古い写真にはどこか懐かしいものがある。(There's something nostalgic about this old photo.)
・この年で徹夜するのは、つらいものがある。(At my age, pulling an all-nighter is really rough.)
How to form it
Verbs: plain dictionary form　心を打つ → 心を打つものがある
い-adjectives: attach directly　懐かしい → 懐かしいものがある
な-adjectives: add 「な」　見事 → 見事なものがある
Negatives work too: 納得できない → 納得できないものがある (it's a bit hard to accept)
The subject is often introduced with 「〜には」: この映画には, 彼の言葉には……
The phrases you'll hear most
These are nearly fixed collocations, so memorizing them as chunks is fastest:
心を打つものがある (it's moving)
胸に迫るものがある (it deeply touches you)
目を見張るものがある (it's remarkable)
光るものがある (it has something that shines)
見るべきものがある (it's worth seeing)
感慨深いものがある (it stirs deep emotion)
Common mistakes
・Not every 「ものがある」 is this grammar point: この店にはおいしいものがある。 simply means “this restaurant has some tasty things,” meaning actual food. In the grammar version, the subject is usually something abstract, like a work, a performance or an experience.
・Put the past tense on ある: to say “it moved me at the time,” use 心を打つものがあった. Don't write 心を打ったものがある.
・Don't forget the な after な-adjectives: it's 見事なものがある, not 見事ものがある, and you can't attach it directly to a noun either.
・Don't use it for objective facts: you can measure how big a room is, so just say この部屋は広い. Saying 「この部屋には広いものがある」 sounds odd. This pattern is for qualities that make you feel something.
・It's fairly formal, but it shows up in casual speech too, like それはちょっとつらいものがあるね (that's honestly kind of rough, isn't it).
Don't confuse it with look-alikes
ものだ (exclamation) = “isn't it ~!”, a remark about life or things in general:
子どもの成長は早いものだ。 (Children grow up so fast.)
ものがある = pointing at one specific person or thing and saying it has a certain quality:
彼の成長ぶりには目を見張るものがある。 (His progress is truly remarkable.)
Quick test: if you're sighing “that's just how life and the world are,” use ものだ. If you're pointing at this person or this work in front of you and saying “there's something ~ about it,” use ものがある.
n2-64:
The idea in one line
「〜抜き」 is like ordering a drink “no ice” or noodles “hold the cilantro”: you take out something that would normally be there. At a sushi restaurant in Japan, わさび抜きでお願いします means “no wasabi, please.” It always follows a noun and is usually written with the kanji 抜き, read ぬき.
The forms you'll hear most
抜きで＋actionDoing something without a certain thing.
・わさび抜きでお願いします。(No wasabi, please.)
・今朝は朝ごはん抜きで会社に行った。(I went to work this morning without breakfast.)
抜きの＋nounFollowed by a noun, it means “the ~ with that thing left out.”
・玉ねぎ抜きのハンバーガーをください。(I'd like a hamburger without onions, please.)
冗談抜きでA set phrase meaning “seriously” or “joking aside.” It's very common in casual speech.
・冗談抜きで、このラーメンは日本一だと思う。(Seriously, I think this ramen is the best in Japan.)
抜きには〜ない“Without ~, you can't ~.” It stresses how important that thing is.
・彼の協力抜きには、この仕事は終わらなかった。(Without his help, this job never would have been finished.)
・日本の夏は花火抜きには語れない。(You can't talk about Japanese summer without mentioning fireworks.)
は抜きにして“Let's skip ~” or “setting ~ aside.” You hear it a lot at the start of dinners and meetings.
・堅苦しい挨拶は抜きにして、乾杯しましょう。(Let's skip the formal greetings and have a toast.)
Common mistakes
・It only attaches to nouns. You can't say 食べ抜きで for “without eating breakfast.” Say 朝ごはん抜きで, or switch to a verb: 朝ごはんを食べないで.
・抜き carries the feeling of “it would normally be there, but it was deliberately removed.” If the thing wouldn't necessarily be there anyway, such as going out without an umbrella, 傘なしで出かけた sounds more natural.
・「抜きには」 is almost always followed by a negative or “can't do” meaning, like できない, 語れない or 考えられない. Don't follow it with an ordinary affirmative sentence.
・冗談抜きで is mostly used by the speaker to stress “I'm being serious now.” It isn't a way to tell the other person “don't joke.” You can also say 冗談抜きに, with the same meaning.
Don't confuse it with look-alikes
抜きには〜ない and ないことには (n2-19) both mean “without ~, you can't ~.” The difference is what comes before them:
・社長の許可抜きには決められない。 (We can't decide without the president's permission.): a noun before it
・社長が許可しないことには決められない。 (We can't decide unless the president approves.): a verb before it
抜きで and ことなく (n2-48) can both be translated as “without doing ~”:
・休憩抜きで働いた。 (I worked with no breaks.): the noun “break time” is taken out
・休むことなく働いた。 (I worked without resting.): a verb comes before it, and the tone is more formal
Quick test: if a noun comes before it, use 抜き. If a verb comes before it, switch to ないことには or ことなく.
What to learn next
抜き comes from the verb 抜く (to take out, to skip), and in daily life people often use the verb directly: 忙しくて昼ごはんを抜いた。 (I was so busy I skipped lunch.)
n2-65:
The idea in one line
「〜きる」means "all the way through," "completely," "to the very end": run the whole course, spend every last yen, be totally worn out.
「〜きれる」means can finish / can do it all, and 「〜きれない」means can't finish / can't do it all. The point is always "all of it, thoroughly, nothing left over."
How to form it
Take the verb's ます form, drop ます, and add きる.
走ります → drop ます → 走りきる
食べます → 食べきる使います → 使いきる
する shows up in verbs like 説明する: 説明します → 説明しきる
Once attached, きる itself conjugates as a Group 1 (godan) verb: きった (finished ~ing), きれる (can finish), きれない (can't finish).
How you'll hear it most
Doing it to the end, finishing it allYou didn't give up halfway, or nothing is left.
・フルマラソンを走りきった。(I ran the whole marathon.)
・給料を三日で使いきってしまった。(I spent my entire paycheck in three days.)
Reaching the extremeAfter state verbs like 疲れる and 困る, it means "completely ~, ~ to the limit."
・残業続きで、疲れきっている。(Overtime non-stop, and I'm completely exhausted.)
・そんな分かりきったこと、聞かないでよ。(Don't ask something that obvious, come on.)
Speaking with total certainty言いきる = to declare flatly, saying it so firmly there's no way back.
・彼は「絶対に勝つ」と言いきった。(He declared flatly, "We'll definitely win.")
きれる／きれないAsking whether you can finish it, or saying there's too much to finish.
・こんなにたくさん、一人で食べきれる？(That much food. Can you eat it all by yourself?)
・空に数えきれないほど星が出ている。(There are more stars in the sky than you could count.)
・明日からの旅行が待ちきれない。(I can't wait for the trip starting tomorrow.)
Common mistakes
・Attach it to the ます stem with ます dropped, not the dictionary form: it's 食べきる, not 「食べるきる」.
・食べきれない specifically means "there's too much to eat it all." 食べられない is broader: it can mean "can't eat it" (allergy, can't stomach it) or "can't eat any more" (もうお腹いっぱいで食べられない). To say clearly "too much, I can't finish it," 食べきれない is the safest choice.
・待ちきれない means "can't wait (too eager)," not "can't finish waiting."
・疲れきる does not mean "finished being tired" or "no longer tired." It means "tired to the extreme," so don't read きる as "finished" here.
・Writing it with the kanji 切る (食べ切る) is also fine, but it's not the 着る of wearing clothes.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
〜終わる = the action has ended; whether you did all of it isn't the point:
・もうご飯食べ終わった？(Have you finished eating yet? This asks whether the meal is over.)
〜きる = all of it, nothing left, often with a sense of "there was a lot" or "it wasn't easy":
・こんなに多いのに、全部食べきったの？(There was this much, and you ate it all?)
Quick rule: to say "I'm done, it's over," use 終わる. To stress "ate it all, stuck it out to the end, nothing left," use きる.
What to learn next
The opposite is 〜かける (halfway done): 食べかけのパン is "half-eaten bread," while 食べきる is "eat it all up." Learn them as a pair and they're easy to tell apart.
n2-66:
The idea in one line
「〜に先立って」is the formal way to say "before ~, first ~" ("prior to," "ahead of"). Think of an emcee saying "Before the ceremony begins, we'll first hear from the organizers," or a news report saying "Ahead of the product launch, a press conference was held." It's that formal kind of "before." You wouldn't use it for everyday things like washing your hands before a meal.
When to use it
Put a formal, planned major event first (a meeting, construction, a launch, a departure, a ceremony), then say what was done beforehand: a preparation, an announcement, or a ritual. It's most common in news, notices, speeches, and business documents.
・新商品の発売に先立って、記者会見が開かれた。(Ahead of the new product's launch, a press conference was held.)
・出発に先立ち、参加者に注意事項が説明された。(Before departure, the participants were briefed on the precautions.)
How to form it
Noun + に先立って／に先立ち: the most common pattern. The noun is usually one you can add する to, like 「開会、工事、発売」.
工事 → 工事に先立って
Verb dictionary form + に先立って: also possible, but less common.
留学する → 留学するに先立って
・留学するに先立って、ビザの手続きを済ませた。(Before going to study abroad, I took care of the visa procedures.)
「に先立ち」is more written and a bit stiffer than「に先立って」, but the meaning is the same.
How you'll hear it most
に先立ちましてA set phrase for opening speeches and ceremonies; it's more polite.
・開会に先立ちまして、一言ご挨拶申し上げます。(Before we open the meeting, allow me to say a few words.)
に先立つ + nounIt modifies the following noun directly, meaning "the ~ held before ~."
・試合に先立つ開会式で、選手代表が宣誓した。(At the opening ceremony before the match, the players' representative took the oath.)
Common mistakes
・Attach に directly to the noun, with no の: it's 開会に先立って, not 開会の先立って.
・The verb must be in the dictionary form, never the た form: you can't say 「決めたに先立って」.
・The reading is さきだって, not せんだって.
・Don't use it for small everyday things; it sounds absurdly grand. "Brushing your teeth before bed" is 寝る前に歯を磨く; saying 「寝るに先立って」 sounds like you're issuing a press release.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
前に = the general "before," usable in any situation: 会議の前に、資料を確認しておこう。 (Let's look over the materials before the meeting.)
に先立って = formal "in preparation for that big event, beforehand ~": 会議に先立ち、資料が配布された。 (Before the meeting began, materials were distributed.)
際に = "when ~," referring to the moment itself, not before: ご使用の際は、十分ご注意ください。 (Please be careful when using it.) / ご使用に先立ち、説明書をお読みください。 (Before use, please read the instructions.)
Quick rule: for everyday "before," use 前に. For the formal "before a major event begins, prepare first," use に先立って. For "at the moment of doing it," use 際に.
n1-8:
The idea in one line
「〜ならでは」means "only ~ could have this" or "that's ~ for you". Think "scenery you only find in Kyoto" or "the warmth only handmade things have." You use it to stress that this quality isn't found anywhere else, only here, and it's usually praise.
How to form it
Attach it directly to a noun, and most often follow it with 「の＋noun」.
職人 → 職人ならではの技術 (skill that only a craftsman has)
地元 → 地元ならではの料理 (food you can only get locally)
The noun in front is usually something with its own character: a person, a place, a shop, or a particular way of doing things.
Forms you'll see most
ならではの＋noun is the most common; about 90% of uses look like this.
・子どもならではの自由な発想に驚いた。 (I was amazed by the free thinking only children have.)
・旅館ならではのおもてなしを楽しんだ。 (I enjoyed the hospitality you only get at a Japanese inn.)
ならではだ at the end of a sentence means "this is exactly what only ~ can do."
・この味は、老舗ならではだ。 (This flavor is something only a long-established shop can produce.)
ならでは〜ない is a more formal, old-fashioned pattern meaning "you can't ~ unless it's ~." Just learn to recognize it.
・この味は、この店ならでは味わえない。 (You can't taste this flavor anywhere but this shop.)
Easy mistakes
・The 「なら」 here is not "if". Don't translate it as "if it's ~."
・The 「は」 in 「では」 is pronounced わ, so the whole thing is read ならでわ.
・Attach it directly to the noun, with no extra の: it's 日本ならではの, not 日本のならではの.
・The point is that only this has it. You can't use it for ordinary traits everyone shares. For example, "convenience stores you only find in Tokyo" would sound odd, because convenience stores are everywhere.
・It's mostly used for praise. You'll occasionally see neutral uses like 「都会ならではの悩み」 (worries unique to city life), but using it for plain flaws or failures sounds strange.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
らしい = feels very much like ~, typical of ~ (similar things may exist elsewhere):
京都らしい景色だ。 (It's a very Kyoto-like view.)
ならでは = only there, can't be found elsewhere:
京都ならではの景色だ。 (It's a view you can only see in Kyoto.)
をおいて = about choosing a person: there's no one else to pick besides them:
この役ができるのは、彼をおいてほかにいない。 (There's no one but him who can play this role.)
ならでは = about a distinctive quality: only he can do this kind of thing:
この演技は彼ならではだ。 (This kind of acting is something only he can do.)
Quick tip: use らしい for "typical of ~"; use ならでは for "a quality only ~ has"; use をおいてほかにない for "if we're choosing, only him."
n1-33:
The idea in one line
「〜とはいうものの」means "I know that's what they say, but...". First you admit that something is true, then you add that reality didn't go that way. Think "It's supposedly spring, but it's still so cold."
Breaking it down helps you remember: と (that) + いう (say) + ものの (although), which together mean "although it's said that ~."
When to use it
In the middle of a sentence A とはいうものの、B. A is a fact, or something everyone says; B is "you'd expect it to be this way, but it isn't."
・春とはいうものの、まだ寒い日が続いている。 (Although it's supposedly spring, the cold days keep going.)
・日本に十年住んでいるとはいうものの、敬語はまだ苦手だ。 (Even though I've lived in Japan for ten years, I'm still bad at honorifics.)
・便利になったとはいうものの、失われたものも少なくない。 (Things have become more convenient, but we've lost quite a lot too.)
At the start of a sentence After finishing one sentence, you can open the next with 「とはいうものの、」 to mean "that said, ..."
・今月から節約すると決めた。とはいうものの、コンビニに行くとつい買ってしまう。 (I decided to save money starting this month. That said, whenever I go into a convenience store I end up buying something.)
How to form it
Use the plain form before it, meaning the form without です・ます.
Verb: 習った → 習ったとはいうものの
い-adjective: 安い → 安いとはいうものの
な-adjective: 便利だ → 便利だとはいうものの; you can also drop だ: 便利とはいうものの
Noun: 春だ → 春とはいうものの; keeping だ is also fine: 春だとはいうものの
Easy mistakes
・What follows must be something that goes against expectations. 春とはいうものの、暖かい。 sounds odd: spring is naturally warm, so there's no contrast.
・The tone is formal and written, common in essays, news and speeches. With friends, 「けど」 or 「とはいっても」 sounds more natural; 「とはいうものの」 would sound like you're reading a script.
・What follows usually describes the situation or your own feelings. It rarely takes requests or invitations like "please ~" or "let's ~."
・いう is actually pronounced 「ゆう」, but in writing it's still spelled いう, not ゆう.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Same situation, "It's supposedly spring, but it's still cold":
とはいえ (N2): 春とはいえ、まだ寒い。 Almost the same meaning, shorter, equally formal, and it can also open a sentence.
とはいうものの: 春とはいうものの、まだ寒い。 Same meaning as とはいえ, just longer.
とはいっても: 春とはいっても、まだ寒いね。 The version used most in speech.
ものの (N2): 春になったものの、まだ寒い。 It attaches straight to a fact, without the "it's said that ~" layer.
とは言い条 (N1): 春とは言い条、まだ寒い。 Same meaning, but very archaic, and now you'll almost only see it in writing.
Quick tip: in speech, use 「とはいっても」; in writing, use 「とはいえ」 or 「とはいうものの」; 「とは言い条」 you only need to recognize, not use yourself.
n1-15:
The idea in one line
「〜が早いか」 means “the instant ~, immediately…”, and it's so fast that you can't tell which thing happened first. Literally it asks, “Was (the first thing) faster?” The first action has barely started and the second one has already happened. Think of a school bell that has only just rung, and the students are already out in the hallway.
When to use it
Describing a scene you seeUse it for things that have already happened, so the sentence usually ends in the past tense. It's common in novels, articles and news writing, and you'll almost never hear it in casual conversation.
・チャイムが鳴るが早いか、子供たちは教室を飛び出した。(The moment the bell rang, the children rushed out of the classroom.)
・彼は家に帰るが早いか、ベッドに倒れ込んだ。(The second he got home, he collapsed onto the bed.)
・新商品は発売されるが早いか、売り切れてしまった。(The new product sold out the instant it went on sale.)
How to form it
Add 「が早いか」 directly to the dictionary form of the verb (the base form you find in a dictionary). No conjugation needed.
鳴る → 鳴るが早いか帰る → 帰るが早いか発売される → 発売されるが早いか
Even when the whole sentence is about the past, the verb before it stays in the dictionary form, and the tense is left to the end of the sentence. You'll occasionally see the た form, as in 言ったが早いか, but just remember the dictionary form for now. That's enough.
Common mistakes
・It can't be followed by a command, a request, or your own intention: ×家に着くが早いか、電話してください。 To say “Call me as soon as you get home,” use 家に着いたら、すぐ電話してください。
・English “as soon as” and “whenever” cover a lot of ground. A general rule or condition like “When spring comes, the flowers bloom” can't use が早いか. That's 春になると、花が咲く。
・The tone is stiff. To a friend you'd just say 家に帰って、すぐ寝ちゃった。 (“I got home and went straight to sleep”). Using が早いか would sound like you're reading from a novel.
・Don't put ます before it: ×鳴りますが早いか.
・「早い」 is read はやい.
Telling similar patterns apart
In the same scene, all three versions are correct:
息子は帰ってくるが早いか、かばんを置いて遊びに行った。
息子は帰ってくるなり、かばんを置いて遊びに行った。
息子は帰ってくるや否や、かばんを置いて遊びに行った。
(The moment my son got back, he dropped his bag and went out to play.)
なり: The actions before and after must be done by the same person, and the second one is often a slightly surprising move. So “The bell rang and the students rushed out” can't use なり: ×チャイムが鳴るなり、生徒が飛び出した。
や否や: The two parts can involve different people or things. The tone is the most written and most formal, and news reports love it: ドアが開くや否や、客が店内になだれ込んだ。 (The moment the door opened, customers flooded into the store.)
が早いか: The subjects can also differ, and the focus is on being so fast you can't tell the order. It often paints a picture of someone eager, rushing to do something.
Quick rule of thumb: same person and a somewhat unexpected follow-up action, use なり. To stress “almost simultaneous,” use が早いか. For formal written reporting, use や否や. None of the three can be followed by a command, a request, or your own intention.
What to learn next
「〜そばから」 also looks like “as soon as ~,” but it describes something repeated again and again, “no sooner have I done ~ than…”: 覚えるそばから忘れてしまう。 (No sooner do I memorize it than I forget it.) It means “this happens every time,” not the speed of a single event.
n1-16:
The idea in one line
「〜や否や」 means “as soon as ~, …”, with the speed of one thing finishing and the next happening right away. It's a very formal written expression, common in novels, news and essays. You can think of it as the written version of 〜たとたん.
Understand this word first
It's read やいなや. 「否」 means “no / not.” The original sense of the whole phrase is “it's not even clear yet whether it was done or not,” in other words the first action has only just happened and the next one follows right on its heels. Keep that picture in mind and you'll remember that it stresses speed.
How to form it
Verb dictionary form + や否や
目を覚ます → 目を覚ますや否や(as soon as someone opens their eyes, ~)
ドアが開く → ドアが開くや否や(as soon as the door opens, ~)
In writing you'll sometimes see just 「や」, with the same meaning: 家に着くや (as soon as someone gets home, ~).
When to use it
Describing something that already happenedUse it when telling a story or reporting that “A happened, and B happened immediately.” The end of the sentence is usually in the past tense.
・ドアが開くや否や、子どもたちが飛び出してきた。(The moment the door opened, the children came rushing out.)
・新商品は発売されるや否や、売り切れた。(The new product sold out as soon as it went on sale.)
・社長が現れるや否や、会場は静まり返った。(The moment the president appeared, the hall fell silent.)
The two parts can involve different people or things. In the examples above, “the door opened” and “the children rushed out” have different subjects, and that's perfectly fine.
Common mistakes
・Use the dictionary form before it, not the た form: it's 帰るや否や, not 「帰ったや否や」. In English we say “as soon as he came back,” so many learners instinctively reach for the past tense.
・「否」 is read いな, not ひ.
・It can't be followed by a request or an intention like “I'll ~,” “Please ~,” or “Let's ~.”
　× 駅に着くや否や、電話してください。
　○ 駅に着いたら、すぐ電話してください。(Please call me right away when you get to the station.)
・It's stiff and bookish. When chatting with a friend and saying “I fell asleep as soon as I got home,” just say 家に着いたとたん、寝ちゃった or 帰ってすぐ寝た.
Telling similar patterns apart
The same situation, “As soon as he entered the room, he burst into tears”:
や否や彼は部屋に入るや否や、泣き出した。
The most formal and written. The two parts can have different subjects.
なり彼は部屋に入るなり、泣き出した。
Both parts must have the same subject, and it often carries a feeling of “why did he suddenly do that?”
が早いか彼は部屋に入るが早いか、泣き出した。
Stresses “so fast it's almost simultaneous,” with a strong novel-like flavor. The た form can also appear before it.
たとたん彼は部屋に入ったとたん、泣き出した。
The everyday version, usable in both speech and writing, and it follows the た form.
Two more are often confused with these:
次第 can be followed by a request or an intention: 着き次第、連絡します。 (I'll contact you as soon as I arrive.) This sentence doesn't work with や否や.
そばから means “as soon as you do it, it's undone again, and this keeps repeating”: 覚えるそばから忘れてしまう。 (No sooner do I memorize it than I forget it, every time.) This isn't a one-time “as soon as ~.”
Quick rule of thumb: to ask the other person to do something, use 「次第」. For wasted effort that keeps repeating, use 「そばから」. To describe a single event that already happened, use 「たとたん」 in conversation and 「や否や」 in writing.
What to learn next
Look at 〜なり, 〜が早いか and 〜そばから together. This “as soon as ~” group often shows up side by side in N1 exam questions.
n2-67:
The idea in one line
All three of these mean something like "so ... I can't stand it" or "I'm dying to ...". Use them when a feeling, emotional or physical, is too strong to hold down. The meanings are almost the same. The main difference is how formal they sound.
・合格の知らせを聞いて、嬉しくてたまらない。(Hearing that I passed, I'm unbelievably happy.)
How to form it
First put the word into its「て」form, then add たまらない / ならない / しょうがない.
Verbs: use the て-form　気になる → 気になってしょうがない
い-adjectives: replace the final「い」with「くて」　嬉しい → 嬉しくてたまらない
な-adjectives: add「で」　心配 → 心配でたまらない
Wanting to do something: たい also changes「い」to「くて」　会いたい → 会いたくてたまらない
Choosing among the three
たまらないThe most standard one. It works with emotions, physical sensations and wants, and you can use it in everyday speech.
・国の家族に会いたくてたまらない。(I miss my family back home so much.)
・今日は暑くてたまらない。(It's unbearably hot today.)
しょうがないThe most colloquial one, and the one you'll hear most when chatting with friends. A slightly more formal version is しかたがない.
・昨日あまり寝てないから、眠くてしょうがない。(I barely slept last night, so I'm dead tired.)
ならないMore written and formal. It carries the sense of a feeling that keeps welling up in you on its own. It's most often paired with expressions where a feeling "arises by itself", such as 気がする, 思われる and 思い出される.
・彼が何か隠している気がしてならない。(I can't shake the feeling that he's hiding something.)
・故郷のことが思い出されてならない。(I can't stop thinking about my hometown.)
Common mistakes
・This describes your own feelings. To talk about someone else, add ようだ or らしい: 妹は寂しくてたまらないようだ。(My little sister seems to be terribly lonely.)
・Only feelings and emotions can go before it, not an action you decide to do. You can't say "I'm studying like crazy" with 勉強してたまらない. To say you want to do something, use 〜たくて.
・Don't confuse てならない with てはならない. With an extra「は」it means "must not": 嘘をついてはならない。(You must not lie.) なくてはならない, on the other hand, means "must / have to".
・Don't confuse てしょうがない with てもしょうがない. With an extra「も」it means "it's no use even if ...": 今さら後悔してもしょうがない。(It's no use regretting it now.)
・In formal writing or speeches, しょうがない is too casual. Use ならない or しかたがない instead.
Don't confuse it with look-alikes
English often renders these as "can't help ...", so it's easy to mix them up with ずにはいられない.
てたまらない = a feeling so strong you can't stand it. The focus is on the feeling itself: 母の病気が心配でたまらない。(I'm worried sick about my mother's illness.)
ずにはいられない = you can't help doing an action: 心配で、母に電話せずにはいられなかった。(I was so worried that I couldn't help calling my mother.)
Quick test: if what you can't hold back is a feeling, use てたまらない. If it's doing something, use ずにはいられない.
n1-40:
The idea in one line
「〜にひきかえ」 works like English "in contrast to ~" or "whereas ~". You describe one side, then the completely opposite side. Usually one side is good and the other is not, and the speaker has feelings about it. For example: "Look how hardworking his older brother is, whereas the younger one..."
How to connect it
Nouns attach directly: 去年 → 去年にひきかえ
A full clause first needs 「の」 to turn it into a noun, then add にひきかえ:
兄はよく勉強する → 兄がよく勉強するのにひきかえ
姉は明るい → 姉が明るいのにひきかえ
Words like 「社交的」 need な before の: 社交的 → 社交的なのにひきかえ
When to use it
A big gap between two sidesYou set two people, two periods or two places side by side to stress how different they are.
・去年の猛暑にひきかえ、今年の夏は過ごしやすい。(Compared with last year's scorching heat, this summer is much more comfortable.)
・前の部長にひきかえ、今度の部長はとても話しやすい。(Compared with the previous department head, the new one is very easy to talk to.)
・兄が社交的なのにひきかえ、弟は人見知りだ。(My older brother is outgoing, whereas my younger brother is shy around new people.)
それにひきかえPlaced at the start of a sentence, it means "in contrast..." or "by comparison...". First you talk about how good someone else is, then you turn to yourself or your own family, often with a complaint or a self-deprecating tone.
・隣の子は毎日勉強している。それにひきかえ、うちの子はゲームばかりだ。(The kid next door studies every day. By contrast, my kid does nothing but play video games.)
Common mistakes
・You can't drop the 「の」 when attaching a clause: say 社交的なのにひきかえ, not 社交的にひきかえ. The 「のに」 here is 「の＋に」, not the "even though..." のに.
・It carries the speaker's judgment, so it is not suited to comparing plain data. For a sentence that just states numbers, like "men are 30%, women are 50%", にひきかえ would sound odd.
・It sounds written and formal. In everyday conversation, you're more likely to hear the sentence-initial それにひきかえ.
・Don't confuse it with 〜と引き換えに, which means "in exchange for ~": 代金と引き換えに商品を渡す。 (Goods are handed over in exchange for payment.) The meaning is completely different.
Telling similar patterns apart
Take the same idea, an outgoing older brother and an introverted younger one:
に対して = objectively lists how the two sides differ, with no emotion: 兄は社交的なのに対して、弟は内向的だ。 (My older brother is outgoing, while my younger brother is introverted.)
にひきかえ = carries a feeling of "what a difference!" or dissatisfaction: 兄が社交的なのにひきかえ、弟は内向的だ。 (My older brother is so outgoing, yet my younger brother is so introverted.)
に比べて = simply compares degree: 去年に比べて、今年は暑い。 (This year is hotter than last year.)
Quick rule of thumb: if you feel "look at him, and then look at you...", use にひきかえ. If you're just neutrally saying two sides differ, use に対して. If you're just comparing who has more or less, use に比べて.
n1-2:
The idea in one line
「〜をもって」 is like the formal English "by ~" / "with ~" you see in official documents. One meaning is "do something by means of ~" (notify in writing, handle with sincerity). The other is "with ~ as the cutoff point" (as of today, up to today). You'll mostly see it in announcements, notices and ceremony speeches. It almost never shows up in casual conversation.
How to connect it
Put a noun in front, then add をもって: 書面 → 書面をもって
The noun in front is usually formal or abstract, such as 書面, 誠意 or 拍手, or a time expression like 本日 or 3月.
To sound more polite when speaking, you say をもちまして, which means the same thing.
When to use it
By what means"Do something by means of ~", like a formal version of 「で」.
・合否は書面をもってお知らせします。(We will notify you of the result in writing.)
・誠意をもって対応いたします。(We will handle this with sincerity.)
・盛大な拍手をもってお迎えください。(Please welcome them with a big round of applause.)
A time boundaryA certain point in time acts as the dividing line. Most often it means "up to this day, then it ends", but it can also mean "takes effect from this day".
・本日をもって、閉店いたします。(This store will close as of today.)
・以上をもちまして、本日の会議を終了いたします。(With that, today's meeting is adjourned.)
・4月1日をもって、社名を変更いたします。(The company name will change effective April 1.)
Common mistakes
・本日をもって閉店 means the shop is still open today, and today is the last day. It doesn't mean it's already closed today. Translating it as "closed from today" easily causes confusion.
・This is a very stiff, written expression, so don't use it in daily life. To tell a friend "I write with a pen", say ペンで書く. Saying ペンをもって書く would sound odd.
・It is a different word from 持って, meaning "holding". 傘を持って出かける really means going out with an umbrella in your hand. 書面をもって means "by way of a written document", and nobody is holding anything. That's why the grammar form is usually written in hiragana.
・以上をもちまして is the standard line for wrapping up an event or ceremony. When you hear it, you know it's about to end.
Telling similar patterns apart
で = the everyday "by/with ~": 結果はメールで知らせるね。 (I'll let you know the result by email.)
をもって = the formal "by ~" of official notices: 結果は書面をもってお知らせします。 (The result will be communicated in writing.)
The two sentences mean about the same. The difference is the setting: one is casual talk between people, the other is a formal notice from a company or school.
を限りに can also mean "up to ~", but it stresses "this is the last time, and I won't do it anymore", often with a sense of personal resolve: 今日を限りにタバコをやめる。 (I'm quitting smoking, starting today.)
をもって is more like a formal announcement from an organization or company. It can also mean "takes effect from this day", a use that を限りに doesn't have: 本日をもって受付を締め切ります。 (Applications close as of today.)
Quick rule of thumb: for everyday "by/with ~", use で. For the "by ~" of announcements, notices and ceremonies, use をもって. For your own resolution, "as of today I won't ~ anymore", use を限りに.
What to learn next
をもってしても = "even with ~...", followed by something that can't be done: 最新の技術をもってしても、完全には防げない。 (Even with the latest technology, it can't be completely prevented.)
n1-3:
The idea in one line
「〜をものともせず」 means "undaunted by ~" or "in defiance of ~". Put a difficulty, danger or obstacle before it, and what follows is "and yet they did it anyway." You use it to praise someone as brave and determined. It has the tone of a news story like "braving wind and rain, he stayed at his post."
How to attach it
Noun + をものともせず (you can also add に: をものともせずに, same meaning)
病気 → 病気をものともせず (undaunted by illness)
周囲の反対 → 周囲の反対をものともせず (undaunted by opposition from those around them)
Breaking it down, もの is "thing" and せず is "not doing," so literally it means "not even treating it as a thing worth caring about."
When to use it
What goes before it: a difficultyThings that stand in the way: illness, injury, bad weather, danger, failure, opposition, pressure.
・彼は度重なる失敗をものともせず、挑戦し続けた。 (Undaunted by repeated failures, he kept taking on challenges.)
・救助隊は激しい雨をものともせず、山へ向かった。 (Undaunted by the heavy rain, the rescue team headed up the mountain.)
What goes after it: what got doneThis is usually something that actually happened, said with admiration or praise.
・彼女は周囲の反対をものともせず、自分の店を開いた。 (Ignoring the opposition around her, she opened her own shop.)
・その選手は怪我をものともせず、最後まで走り抜いた。 (Undaunted by his injury, that athlete ran all the way to the finish.)
Easy mistakes
・It praises someone else and is generally not used about yourself. 私は寒さをものともせず sounds like bragging, which is odd.
・Don't follow it with "please do ~" or "let's ~." Something like "Don't be afraid of difficulties, let's do our best!" doesn't work here. It is for describing something already accomplished.
・What comes before it must be an obstacle. You can't put in something good like "support" or "an opportunity," because there's nothing to be undaunted by.
・The particle is を, not が.
・It's stiff, formal language for writing, news and speeches. You'll almost never hear it in chat with friends.
Don't confuse it with similar patterns
をよそに = disregarding other people's worry or expectations and doing your own thing. 心配 and 期待 often come before it, with a hint of "not listening to advice."
・親の心配をよそに、彼は一人で海外へ行った。 (Paying no heed to his parents' worry, he went abroad alone.)
をものともせず = not afraid of difficulty; bravely pushing through. It is praise.
・言葉の壁をものともせず、彼は海外で成功した。 (Undaunted by the language barrier, he succeeded abroad.)
Your parents' worry isn't a hurdle to overcome, so 親の心配をものともせず sounds unnatural.
にもかかわらず = a plain "even though ~, still ~." It carries no praise or blame and works for good and bad things alike.
・雨にもかかわらず、たくさんの人が来た。 (Despite the rain, a lot of people came.)
Switch to 雨をものともせず only when you want to stress how impressive those people are.
Quick rule of thumb: if what comes before is a "hurdle" and you want to praise the person's courage, use をものともせず. If it's "other people's feelings" that the person ignores, use をよそに. If you simply mean "despite," use にもかかわらず.
n1-9:
The idea in one line
「AはおろかB」 means "let alone A, not even B" ("never mind A, even B ~"). A is the thing that goes without saying, so it's not worth mentioning. B is the more surprising thing, and it stresses how extreme the situation is. Watch the order: English usually says "B, let alone A," while Japanese puts A first and B second. So the order is flipped compared with the English "let alone."
How to attach it
Basically noun + はおろか: 漢字 → 漢字はおろか
If A is an action, first add 「こと」 after the verb to turn it into a noun: 走る → 走ることはおろか
The second half usually pairs with も、さえ、すら、まで, which work like the English "even."
How to arrange A and B
How to decide: put in A the thing that is already taken for granted, and in B the more extreme, more surprising thing.
Negative sentences (most common)A is the harder thing and B is the more basic thing. It only has force because "not being able to do the hard thing is normal, but not even the easy thing" is striking.
・漢字はおろか、ひらがなさえまだ読めない。 (I can't even read hiragana yet, let alone kanji.)
・忙しくて、休みはおろか、昼ご飯を食べる時間もない。 (I'm so busy I don't even have time to eat lunch, let alone take a day off.)
・足をけがして、走ることはおろか、歩くこともできない。 (I hurt my leg, so I can't even walk, let alone run.)
Affirmative sentencesThe other way around: A is the more ordinary thing, and B is wider in scope or more impressive.
・この歌は国内はおろか、海外でも人気がある。 (This song is popular even overseas, never mind at home.)
Don't reverse the order: ひらがなはおろか、漢字も読めない。 is illogical. If someone can't even read hiragana, of course they can't read kanji, so there's no point stressing it.
It works the same in negative and affirmative sentences: A is "naturally so," and B is "even this is so."
Easy mistakes
・The second half can't contain commands, requests or your own intentions. 漢字はおろか、ひらがなも覚えなさい。 is wrong. Use はもちろん there instead.
・は is already built in, so don't add を or が before it. And it can't attach directly to a verb, so remember to add 「こと」 first.
・The おろか here has nothing to do with 「愚か」 (foolish). Don't read it as "stupid."
・The tone is stiff and often carries a note of complaint or surprise, like "how outrageous" or "how awful." It's mostly used in writing or fairly formal situations. In casual talk with friends, Japanese people more often say どころか.
Don't confuse it with similar patterns
Compare them in the same situation:
はおろか = stresses "not even B" with a tone of amazement or dissatisfaction; the second half can only be a statement: 漢字はおろか、ひらがなも書けない。 (I can't even write hiragana, let alone kanji.)
はもちろん = a plain "A of course, and B too"; neutral in tone, and a request can follow: 漢字はもちろん、ひらがなもちゃんと書いてください。 (Kanji, of course, but please write hiragana properly too.)
どころか = close in meaning to はおろか but more colloquial. It can also mean "not only not A, but rather B": 安いどころか、すごく高かった。 (Far from cheap, it was incredibly expensive.) はおろか doesn't have this "on the contrary" use.
Quick rule of thumb: to tell someone to do something, use はもちろん. When chatting with friends, use どころか. For writing, or when you want the "it's so extreme that even this…" feeling, use はおろか.
What to learn next
Next, look at すら ("even ~"), which often appears in the second half.
n1-10:
The idea in one line
「〜ないまでも」 means "if not X, then at least Y". First you set aside a high standard (a perfect score, every day, sounding like a native speaker). Then you state a fallback, minimum goal. It's the tone of telling yourself, "I won't exercise every day, but at least once a week."
How to attach it
Verb ない-form + までも. The first half holds the "high standard" and the second half holds "the least I'll accept".
取れない → 取れないまでも
・ネイティブのようには話せないまでも、日常会話はこなしたい。(Even if I can't speak like a native, I at least want to handle everyday conversation.)
In practice, the two fixed combinations below are more common. A noun goes directly before them, so I suggest memorizing each whole phrase:
とは言わないまでも "I'm not asking for X." It's often used to express hopes or demands.
・毎日とは言わないまでも、週に一度は運動したい。(I'm not saying every day, but I'd like to exercise at least once a week.)
とはいかないまでも "Although it didn't reach X." It's often used for results that already exist.
・満点とはいかないまでも、合格点は取れた。(I didn't get a perfect score, but I at least got a passing mark.)
What the second half looks like
The second half is usually "I want to…", "I should…", "I want the other person to…", or a result you've already achieved. It's often paired with 「は」「くらいは」「せめて」 to stress "at least this much".
・謝罪とは言わないまでも、せめて一言説明してほしい。(I'm not asking for an apology, but I'd at least like a word of explanation.)
Common pitfalls
・The two halves must be high and low on the same scale: perfect score vs. passing, every day vs. once a week. The first is high and the second is low. If the second half is higher than the first, or the two things are unrelated, you can't use this pattern.
・The second half is affirmative: "at least I did it / at least I want to do it." To say "I didn't even reach the minimum," you need a different pattern (see はおろか below).
・Don't confuse it with 「〜までもない」: 言うまでもない means "it goes without saying." It attaches to the dictionary form and means "there's no need to." 言わないまでも means "even if I don't go as far as saying it." One ない makes the meaning completely different.
・It feels fairly written and formal overall, though 「とは言わないまでも」 is also quite common in everyday conversation.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
The one most easily confused with it is 〜はおろか. Both say "the high standard wasn't met," but what follows points in opposite directions. Using the same exam example:
満点とはいかないまでも、合格点は取れた。(I didn't get a perfect score, but I at least passed.) → The minimum was met, so it ends on a positive note.
満点はおろか、合格点も取れなかった。(Never mind a perfect score, I didn't even pass.) → Even the minimum was not met, so it stresses the negative.
Quick test: "Not the high one, but the low one yes" → ないまでも. "Not the high one, and not even the low one" → はおろか.
n1-22:
The idea in one line
「〜べく」means "in order to…", but it's written, formal language, much like "with a view to" or "in an effort to" in news reports or official documents. Its meaning is close to 「ために」, only stiffer and more formal, and you'll almost never use it in casual chat.
When to use it
News and reports Explaining what goal someone acted for.
・真相を確かめるべく、記者は現地へ向かった。(In order to find out the truth, the reporter headed to the site.)
・試験に合格すべく、毎日10時間勉強した。(To pass the exam, I studied 10 hours every day.)
Expressing resolve in formal settings Speeches, press conferences and company announcements saying "to do X, we will do our best."
・皆様のご期待に応えるべく、全力を尽くします。(To live up to your expectations, we will give it our all.)
How to attach it
Add 「べく」directly to the verb's dictionary form (the base form you'd look up):
確かめる → 確かめるべく
なる → なるべく
応える → 応えるべく
する is special: both forms work, but すべく is more common:
達成する → 達成すべく (you can also say 達成するべく)
Common pitfalls
・It can't follow a negative: there's no such thing as 「遅刻しないべく」. To say "in order not to…", use 遅刻しないように.
・What follows can't be a request to someone else (a request, command or invitation): 合格すべく、毎日勉強してください is wrong. Change it to 合格するために、毎日勉強してください.
・It can't attach directly to a noun: you can say 健康のために, but there's no 「健康のべく」. To use べく you need a verb: 健康を維持すべく.
・The subject of both halves is usually the same person, and the action is something done on purpose. Things people can't control, like rain, can't go before べく.
・Watch out for the adverb なるべく (as much as possible), which looks the same: なるべく早く来てください means "Please come as early as you can," while 医者になるべく is the one meaning "in order to become a doctor." Check whether something comes before it and you can tell them apart.
・Saying 「〜べく」to a friend in chat sounds like reading an official notice aloud. In speech, use ために.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
All of these say "I'm working hard in order to pass":
ために = the general form, fine in both speech and writing: 合格するために、毎日勉強している。 (I study every day in order to pass.)
べく = written and formal: 合格すべく、毎日勉強した。 (I studied hard every day in an effort to pass.)
んがため（に） = even older and stiffer, with a strong "at all costs" feel, and it attaches differently (する → せんがため): 合格せんがため、寝る間も惜しんで勉強した。 (To pass, I begrudged even the time for sleeping and studied like mad.)
Quick test: use ために for everyday language, べく for news, speeches and formal writing, and んがため only when you want to stress "I'll achieve this no matter what."
What to learn next
・べくして: "was bound to happen", a different meaning from "in order to". 起こるべくして起こった事故だ。 (It was an accident waiting to happen.)
・The related forms べき (should) and べからず (must not) don't mean "in order to" either, so don't mix them up.
n1-30:
The idea in one line
「〜と思いきや」 means "I thought ~, but it turned out…". First you state what you expected, then what actually happened, and the result is the complete opposite of the expectation. It carries a sense of surprise, like being proven wrong.
・晴れると思いきや、午後から急に雨が降り出した。（I thought it would clear up, but in the afternoon it suddenly started raining）
How to form it
Put the plain form (the form without ます or です) before it, then add 「と思いきや」 directly.
合格した → 合格したと思いきや
簡単だ → 簡単だと思いきや
かと思いきやVery often a 「か」 is added in the middle, giving a feel of "I wondered whether ~". It's extremely common. Watch how you add 「か」:
Verbs and い-adjectives: add か directly.
終わった → 終わったかと思いきや高い → 高いかと思いきや
Nouns and な-adjectives: drop 「だ」 first, then add か.
簡単だ → drop だ → 簡単かと思いきや雨だ → drop だ → 雨かと思いきや
・もう帰ったかと思いきや、まだ会社にいた。（I figured he had already gone home, but he was still at the office）
・高いかと思いきや、意外と安かった。（I thought it would be expensive, but it was surprisingly cheap）
・彼は怒るかと思いきや、笑って許してくれた。（I thought he would get angry, but he smiled and forgave me）
When to use it
It mostly shows up in storytelling contexts like articles, news, TV narration and social media posts, with a touch of surprise or humor. Online, people sometimes write just 「〜と思いきや…」 and stop there, deliberately teasing the reader until the next line reveals the twist.
Common mistakes
・When adding か to nouns and な-adjectives, don't keep だ: it's 簡単かと思いきや, not 「簡単だかと思いきや」.
・「思いきや」 is a fixed chunk and can't be conjugated. There's no such thing as 「思いましたきや」.
・Read it as おもいきや, and don't mix it up with 思い切り (with full force, to one's heart's content) or 思い切って (making up your mind and going for it). They look alike but are unrelated in meaning.
・The second half is a fact that has already happened, usually in the past tense. You can't follow it with an intention, command or invitation: 「雨だと思いきや、傘を持っていこう」 is wrong.
・The result must be the opposite of the expectation. If things turn out as you expected, you can't use it.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
In everyday conversation, と思ったら is more common. It can also mean "I thought ~, but…", and in that sense it's interchangeable with と思いきや, just more conversational:
簡単かと思ったら、意外と難しかった。（I thought it would be easy, but it was surprisingly hard）
But と思ったら has another meaning: "no sooner had ~ than…", describing things following each other quickly. と思いきや doesn't have this meaning:
子どもは泣いたと思ったら、もう笑っている。（The kid was crying just a moment ago, and now he's already laughing）
Swapping in と思いきや here would be wrong, because the point is how fast things change, not an expectation being broken.
Quick tip: if it's "expectation proven wrong", both work. Use と思いきや in writing and と思ったら in conversation. If it's "no sooner ~ than…", only と思ったら works.
n1-31:
The idea in one line
「〜ものを」 has the feel of "If only you had just said so!" Doing one simple thing would have been enough, but you didn't, and now things have gone wrong. It carries regret, resentment and blame, sometimes aimed at someone else, sometimes at yourself.
How to form it
