Put an ordinary plain form (the dictionary-style form without ます) before it. It most often follows 「〜ばいい」 or 「〜ばよかった」:
言えばいい → 言えばいいものを
聞けばよかった → 聞けばよかったものを
な-adjectives connect with 「な」: 便利だ → 便利なものを. You don't say 「便利だものを」.
The three most common forms
〜ばいいものをYou could have just done that, but you didn't. Most often used to scold someone else.
・謝ればすむものを、意地を張るから話がややこしくなる。（A simple apology would have settled it, but he's being stubborn, so it's getting complicated）
・黙っていればいいものを、余計な一言で彼を怒らせてしまった。（All you had to do was keep quiet, but one needless remark made him angry）
〜ば〜たものを"If you had ~, I would have ~", but it didn't happen, and that's a pity.
・言ってくれれば手伝ったものを。（If you had told me, I would have helped!）
・もう少し早く家を出ていれば間に合ったものを。（If you had left home just a little earlier, you'd have made it）
Left hanging at the endThe follow-up "but you didn't" is swallowed and left unsaid, leaving only a sigh. The two examples just above end this way, and it's very common in TV dramas and novels.
Common mistakes
・Don't confuse it with もの ("thing") + を: in おいしいものを食べた, もの means "thing" and a verb follows right after. With 「〜ものを」, there is usually a comma after it, followed by "but in the end…", or nothing at all.
・It talks about something that has already happened and can't be changed, so you can't follow it with a request or command. You wouldn't say 「早く言えばいいものを、言ってください」.
・The tone is written-style and somewhat literary, with blame in it. In everyday conversation people mostly say 「〜ばよかったのに」. Scolding your boss or a customer with 「ものを」 would sound very rude.
・The second half is a sigh or complaint, not a plain statement of fact, so what comes before it is almost always a hypothetical like "it would have been fine if…".
Telling it apart from similar patterns
のに: The closest in meaning and the most common in everyday speech.
早く言えばよかったのに。（You should have just said so）
ものを: Also a complaint, but more formal and with stronger feeling.
早く言えばよかったものを。（If only you had said so earlier, sigh）
Also, のに can simply state a fact meaning "even though ~, …" (雨なのに出かけた。 He went out even though it was raining), whereas ものを is rarely used that way.
ものの (N2): Just one letter different, it means "although ~, …". It calmly reports facts, with no intent to blame anyone.
先生に相談しようと思ったものの、言い出せなかった。（I thought about talking to my teacher, but I couldn't bring myself to say it）
先生に相談すればよかったものを、一人で悩んでいた。（Talking to the teacher would have been enough, but he agonized over it alone）
Quick tip: if 「〜ばいい／〜ばよかった」 comes before it and there's a "I wish I had…" sigh, it's ものを. If you're just saying "although… but…" in a flat way, it's ものの.
n1-43:
The idea in one line
「〜とは」 is like English "I can't believe…" or "to think that…". When something happens that you completely didn't expect, and you're shocked, moved, or even a bit stunned or let down, you put that thing right before とは. It's the same feeling as saying, "Wait, he was the culprit?!"
When to use it
Surprise・the unexpectedThings turned out completely differently from what you expected.
・こんな所で君に会うとは。(To think I'd run into you in a place like this)
・まさか一回で合格するとは思わなかった。(I never thought I'd actually pass on the first try)
Stunned・disappointedIt's more than surprise. There's also a sense of "how could this happen?"
・大人がこんな簡単なルールも守れないとは、情けない。(Adults who can't even follow a rule this simple. How embarrassing)
Trailing offThe 「驚いた」 or 「思わなかった」 that would follow is often dropped, leaving just the lingering "to think that…"
・彼が犯人だったとは……。(To think he was the culprit…)
How to attach it
Use the plain form (the form without です・ます) and add とは.
Verbs: 会う → 会うとは負けた → 負けたとは
い-adjectives: 高い → こんなに高いとは
な-adjectives: 簡単 → こんなに簡単だとは
Nouns: 犯人 → 犯人だとは. The だ is sometimes dropped, giving 犯人とは.
What you'll hear most often
It often pairs with まさか ("never in a million years") before it, and is often followed by 思わなかった, 思いもよらなかった, 夢にも思わなかった, 信じられない, or 驚きだ.
・自分が日本で働くことになるとは、夢にも思わなかった。(I never even dreamed I'd end up working in Japan)
Common mistakes
・The は in とは is pronounced 「わ」, so the whole thing is read とわ.
・Use the plain form before it. The ます form doesn't work: 会いますとは is wrong.
・You can't use とは for a mere hypothetical or something still uncertain (for example, 「もし合格するとは」 is wrong). But you can use it for news that hasn't happened yet but is already settled: 彼女が来月結婚するとは、驚いた。 (I'm surprised she's getting married next month)
・とは sounds fairly formal and bookish. In casual chat with friends, Japanese people more often say なんて. You can still use とは, but it sounds a bit exaggerated and dramatic.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
なんて: It means the same "to think that…", just more colloquial.
こんな所で会うなんて！ (Can't believe we met here! Among friends)
こんな所でお会いするとは。 (What a surprise to meet you here. More formal)
The とは meaning "what is ~": It's written the same way, but here it defines a word, followed by an explanation or a question. There's no surprise at all.
幸せとは何だろう。 (What is happiness, anyway?)
彼が幸せだったとは。 (To think he was happy)
と思いきや: It means "I thought ~, but then…", and what follows has to state the actual outcome.
晴れると思いきや、雨が降ってきた。 (I thought it would clear up, but it started raining)
こんなに雨が降るとは。 (To think it would rain this hard)
Quick test: if what comes before とは is a whole event that surprised you and a reaction follows, it's "to think that…". If it's just one noun and what follows explains it, it's "what is ~". If you first state what you expected and then the real result, it's と思いきや.
n1-47:
The idea in one line
「〜ともなると」 means "once you reach the level of ~, naturally…". Once your status rises, you reach a certain age, or a special period arrives, things naturally differ from usual. In English you'd say "Once you're a department head, of course the responsibility gets heavier," and in Japanese that's 部長ともなると、責任も重くなる。
When to use it
Status・positionWhen you reach a higher position, certain situations come with it.
・部長ともなると、毎日会議ばかりだ。(Once you're a department head, it's nothing but meetings every day)
Age・life stageWhen a person reaches a certain stage, they naturally change.
・高校生ともなると、親とあまり話さなくなる。(Once they're in high school, they stop talking much with their parents)
Time of yearWhenever a special period arrives, it happens every time.
・年末ともなると、どこの店も人でいっぱいだ。(Once the end of the year comes, every shop is packed with people)
Scale of an undertakingWhen you take on something big and weighty, what follows grows in scale too.
・家を建てるともなると、決めることが山ほどある。(When it comes to actually building a house, there are mountains of things to decide)
How to attach it
Noun + ともなると: 社長 → 社長ともなると
Verb dictionary form (the basic form you'd look up) + ともなると: 留学する → 留学するともなると
What goes before it is usually a status, age, period, or undertaking that is a step above the ordinary and carries weight. What follows is a situation or judgment that naturally arises at that stage.
Common mistakes
・It carries the nuance of "once you've reached that point." For a plain, general change, like "flowers bloom when spring comes," 春になると sounds more natural.
・What follows is usually a general situation or judgment, such as heavy responsibility, crowds, or lots to prepare. It rarely takes your own intentions ("I'll ~") or requests to others ("please ~").
・The とも here doesn't mean "also" or "even." It's also completely unrelated to ともなく ("without really ~ing"), so don't mix them up just because both contain とも.
・It's formal and bookish. When chatting with friends, 部長になると or 部長にもなると sounds more relaxed.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
ともなれば: The meaning is almost the same, and in most cases you can swap them directly.
部長ともなれば、責任も重くなる。 (Once you're a department head, of course the responsibility gets heavier)
とあって: It says "because of this special situation, ~ is happening right now," describing something you can actually see happening. ともなると states a general tendency: "once you reach this point, it always happens."
・連休とあって、高速道路はどこも渋滞している。(Because it's a long holiday weekend, the expressways are jammed everywhere right now)
・連休ともなると、高速道路はどこも渋滞する。(Whenever a long holiday weekend comes, the expressways get jammed everywhere)
Quick test: for "this time, because of ~, so ~," use とあって. For "once you reach ~, it naturally always ~," use ともなると.
What to learn next
〜たる also often appears with status, but it means "since you hold this status, you should act the part": 教師たる者、生徒の手本でなければならない。 (Anyone who is a teacher must be a role model for their students). ともなると describes the natural result that comes with a status, while たる describes the expected conduct of that status. Remember them side by side.
n1-28:
The idea in one line
「〜ようが／〜ようと」means "no matter what… I'll do it anyway." Whatever happens in the first part, and whatever other people do, the conclusion in the second part doesn't change. It sounds stiffer and stronger than the ordinary「〜ても」, with an attitude of "my mind is made up, and I'm not afraid."
When to use it
With question wordsPut 「何・どこ・誰・どんなに・いくら」 before it to mean "no matter what / where / who / how much…"
・何を言われようが、気にしない。(No matter what people say to me, I don't care.)
・どこへ行こうと、あなたの自由です。(Wherever you go, that's your choice.)
・誰が反対しようと、私はやる。(No matter who objects, I'm going to do it.)
On its ownWith no question word, it means "even if…, I'll still…"
・雨が降ろうが行く。(Even if it rains, I'm going anyway.)
Two side by side「AようがBようが」 = whether A or B; 「Aようが Aまいが」 = whether or not you do it. Here 「まい」 means "not do". Group 1 (godan) verbs take the dictionary form: 行くまい; する is often said as しまい.
・雨が降ろうが風が吹こうが、試合は行われる。(Rain or wind, the match will go ahead.)
・参加しようがしまいが、あなたの自由だ。(Whether you take part or not is up to you.)
The second half very often has 「自由だ」「関係ない」「構わない」「気にしない」, or a statement of determination like "I'm doing it regardless."
How to form it
Verbs: first turn the verb into the volitional form (the 「行こう」「食べよう」 shape), then add が or と.
Group 1 (godan): 行く → swap く for こ → 行こうが言う → 言おうが
Group 2 (ichidan): drop る and add よう　食べる → 食べようが. Passive forms change the same way: 言われる → 言われようが
Group 3 (する・来る): する → しようが来る → 来ようが
い-adjectives: drop the final 「い」 and add 「かろう」.
暑い → 暑かろうが高い → 高かろうと
「いい」 conjugates from 「よい」: いい → よかろうが
・どんなに暑かろうと、毎朝のランニングは欠かさない。(No matter how hot it is, I never skip my morning run.)
な-adjectives and nouns: add 「だろう」 or the more formal 「であろう」.
不便だ → 不便だろうが子ども → 子どもであろうと
・相手が子どもだろうが、ルールはルールだ。(Even if the other person is a child, rules are rules.)
Common mistakes
・The volitional form here does not mean "let's…" or "I'll…". It just borrows the shape to mean "no matter what."
・Group 1 verbs can't attach directly: it's 行こうが, not 「行くようが」.
・来ようが is read 「こようが」, not 「きようが」.
・降ろうが alone only means "even if it rains"; to say "whether it rains or not," use 降ろうが降るまいが.
・「ようが」 and 「ようと」 mean basically the same thing and are interchangeable.
・The tone is hard and forceful. In everyday chat, 「暑くても」 sounds more natural; the かろう form like 「暑かろうが」 is for writing or emphasis.
Telling similar patterns apart
Same situation: no matter how much you hurry.
ても = the plain "even if…", the most neutral: いくら急いでも、間に合わない。(No matter how much I hurry, I won't make it.)
ようが = what follows is "I'll do it anyway / it makes no difference," with a strong attitude: いくら急がされようが、手は抜かない。(No matter how much they rush me, I won't cut corners.)
たところで = what follows is "it's pointless / it won't turn out well": いくら急いだところで、もう間に合わない。(No matter how much we hurry now, it's already too late.)
Also, with nouns you can use 「であれ」 to say the same "no matter what it is": 理由が何であれ、遅刻はだめだ。 and 理由が何であろうと、遅刻はだめだ。 mean almost the same thing (whatever the reason, being late is not okay).
Quick rule of thumb: if what follows is "I'll do it anyway / do as you like / it doesn't matter," use ようが. If it's "it's pointless even if you do," use たところで. For casual speech, or when you don't want to sound so blunt, use ても.
What to learn next
For another "whether A or B" pattern, look at 「〜にせよ〜にせよ」: 行くにせよ行かないにせよ、連絡してください。(Whether you go or not, please let me know.)
n1-29:
The idea in one line
「AにせよBにせよ」 means "whether A or B, …" in English. You throw out two possibilities, then say: either way, it's the same, and the conclusion doesn't change. The tone is fairly formal and often appears in articles, news and meeting remarks.
How to form it
Verbs and い-adjectives: attach directly to the plain form (the form without ます or です).
行く → 行くにせよ行かないにせよ
高い → 高いにせよ安いにせよ
Nouns and な-adjectives: attach directly, and in the present tense don't add だ. For a more formal feel, you can add 「である」.
大人 → 大人にせよ子どもにせよ
好き → 好きにせよ嫌いにせよ
学生 → 学生であるにせよ
When to use it
A pair of oppositesGo / don't go, agree / disagree: it's the same either way.
・行くにせよ行かないにせよ、早めに連絡してください。(Whether you go or not, please let me know early.)
・好きにせよ嫌いにせよ、この仕事は誰かがやらなければならない。(Whether you like it or not, someone has to do this job.)
Two items of the same kindYou give two examples that stand for "this whole category is the same."
・大人にせよ子どもにせよ、ルールは守らなければならない。(Whether adults or children, everyone has to follow the rules.)
The second half is usually a judgment like "should…", "must…" or "no difference" that is true for both sides.
The forms you'll hear most
Set expressionsNo examples listed; one word covers every possibility. Very common in both speech and writing.
・いずれにせよ、結果が出たら連絡します。(Either way, I'll contact you once the results are in.)
・何にせよ、無事でよかった。(Anyway, I'm just glad you're safe.)
Used only onceA single 「にせよ」 = "even if…"
・冗談にせよ、そんなことを言ってはいけない。(Even as a joke, you shouldn't say something like that.)
Common mistakes
・Nouns and な-adjectives take no だ in the present tense: not 学生だにせよ, but 学生にせよ or 学生であるにせよ.
・「せよ」 looks like a command ("do it!"), but here it's just a fixed expression with no command meaning.
・The second half must be true for both cases. If the conclusion fits only one side, you can't use this pattern.
・It's very bookish. Chatting with a friend, 行っても行かなくても sounds more natural; にせよ can sound like you're reading an official document.
Telling similar patterns apart
にしろ…にしろ: exactly the same meaning, a little softer, and still usable in speech.
行くにしろ行かないにしろ、連絡してください。(Whether you go or not, please contact me.)
であれ…であれ: mainly used with nouns, and stiffer and more formal than にせよ.
大人であれ子どもであれ、ルールは守るべきだ。(Adults and children alike should follow the rules.)
ようが…まいが: carries a strong "do what you like, it's all the same to me" feeling.
行こうが行くまいが、私には関係ない。(Whether you go or not has nothing to do with me.)
Quick rule of thumb: for a calm "whether A or B," use にせよ／にしろ. For nouns only and a more formal tone, use であれ. For a "whatever, it won't change anyway" attitude, use ようが.
What to learn next
For "regardless of the content, …", learn いかんにかかわらず: 理由のいかんにかかわらず、遅刻は認めません。(Whatever the reason, we do not accept lateness.)
n1-67:
The idea in one line
「〜をよそに」means "disregarding ~" or "paying no attention to ~". よそ means "someone else's home, somewhere else," so 〜をよそに treats other people's worries or objections, or the surrounding situation, as somebody else's business while the subject carries on in their own way.
When to use it
Ignoring other people's feelingsThis is the most common use. Put other people's worry, opposition, expectations or criticism first, then say that the subject goes on doing their own thing anyway. It often carries a feeling of "how could they?", but it isn't necessarily a scolding. It can also be a neutral description.
・親の心配をよそに、息子は毎晩遅くまで遊んでいる。(Despite his parents' worry, their son plays out until late every night.)
・周囲の反対をよそに、彼女は会社を辞めて留学した。(Ignoring the objections of those around her, she quit her job and went to study abroad.)
Unaffected by the surroundingsPut a situation that you would expect to have an effect, such as the economy or a public uproar, first. Then say that the subject wasn't affected at all.
・不景気をよそに、この店はいつも行列ができている。(Despite the bad economy, this shop always has a line out the door.)
・世間の騒ぎをよそに、本人はのんびり旅行を楽しんでいた。(While the public was in an uproar, the person involved was calmly enjoying a trip.)
How to form it
It attaches directly to a noun: noun + をよそに
家族の心配 → 家族の心配をよそにファンの期待 → ファンの期待をよそに
Nouns that most often go with it: 心配, 反対, 期待, 批判, 不安, 騒ぎ.
Common mistakes
・It needs a noun before it. Don't say 「心配するをよそに」. Change the verb to the noun 心配 first.
・What comes before it is other people's reactions or the surrounding situation, not something you yourself are supposed to do. For "skipping homework to go play," don't say 「宿題をよそに」. 宿題そっちのけで遊ぶ sounds more natural.
・It mostly describes other people's behavior. It's a written-style expression common in news and articles, and you'll rarely hear it in casual conversation with friends.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
をものともせず = not letting difficulties or danger bother you, with a tone of praise:
けがをものともせず、彼は最後まで走った。(Undeterred by his injury, he ran all the way to the end: admirable.)
をよそに = ignoring other people's feelings or the surrounding situation and doing what you want:
家族の心配をよそに、彼は最後まで走った。(Despite his family's worry, he ran all the way to the end: the point is that he ignored his family.)
にもかかわらず = a plain "although ~, still ~":
雨にもかかわらず、たくさんの人が来た。(Although it was raining, a lot of people came.)
This sentence simply states "it rained, yet many people came," so にもかかわらず is the most natural choice. The point of をよそに is that the subject shrugs off something they should have cared about or been affected by, and carries on in their own way. That's why it's mostly used with other people's worry or opposition, or with surrounding conditions like the economy that should have had an effect.
Quick rule of thumb: overcoming difficulty and deserving admiration → をものともせず; ignoring what others think and being unaffected by the surroundings → をよそに; a plain "although ~, still ~" → にもかかわらず.
n1-70:
The idea in one line
「〜ずにはおかない」means "is bound to make someone ~" or "won't rest until ~". It has two uses. In one, something is so powerful that it inevitably produces a certain feeling in people. In the other, a person is determined and won't stop until they've done it. It's a hard-edged N1 expression, mostly found in film reviews, book reviews, news and novels.
It's easier to remember if you break it down: おく means "to leave something be." So "won't leave it alone without doing ~" means "will definitely do ~."
When to use it
Something inevitably triggers a reactionThis is the most common use. The subject is a film, a work, a phrase or an event, and you say it is bound to move, surprise or make people think.
The person affected is marked with を or に (人を～させる／人に～させる), so the verb is usually in the causative form, the "make someone ~" form: 感動する → 感動させる (to move someone emotionally).
・この映画は、観客を感動させずにはおかない。(This film is bound to move the audience.)
・この小説の結末は、読者を驚かせずにはおかないだろう。(The ending of this novel is sure to astonish readers.)
・彼の言葉は、聞く人の心を動かさずにはおかない。(His words are bound to touch the hearts of those who hear them.)
Won't stop until it's doneThe subject is a person, and it expresses strong determination, with a fierce "I will make this happen" feel.
・今度こそ、真相を明らかにせずにはおかない。(This time I won't rest until I've uncovered the truth.)
・あんな失礼なことを言われたんだ。必ず謝らせずにはおかない。(He said something that rude to me. I'll make him apologize, no matter what.)
How to form it
First turn the verb into its ない form, then drop the ない and add ずにはおかない.
感動させる → 感動させない → 感動させずにはおかない
動かす → 動かさない → 動かさずにはおかない
Remember the irregular verbs specially: する → せずにはおかない来る → 来ずにはおかない（こず）
Another form attaches ではおかない directly to the ない form. You don't drop the ない, and the meaning is the same:
感動させない → 感動させないではおかない
「ずには」 is the more common one, and it sounds more formal and written.
Common mistakes
・する becomes せず, not しず: 明らかにせずにはおかない.
・In the first use, the person affected is the object marked with を／に, not the subject. 観客は感動せずにはおかない is wrong. To say "the film moves the audience," use 映画は観客を感動させずにはおかない.
・The tone is heavy and very written. In everyday conversation, to say "it'll definitely make you cry," just say 絶対泣けるよ. Using ずにはおかない would sound like you're reading out a review.
・The second use expresses a "do it at all costs" determination, so don't use it for small things like "finishing this bowl of ramen."
Telling it apart from look-alikes
ずにはいられない (N2) = a person can't help themselves: この映画を見て、泣かずにはいられなかった。(Watching this film, I couldn't help crying.)
ずにはおかない = something is bound to make people react that way: この映画は、見る人を泣かせずにはおかない。(This film is bound to make viewers cry.)
ずにはすまない (n1-71) = given the reason or situation, you can't get away without doing it: 失礼なことを言ってしまったから、謝らずにはすまない。(I said something rude, so I can't get away without apologizing.)
ずにはおかない = I insist on making it happen: 失礼なことを言われたから、謝らせずにはおかない。(He said something rude to me, so I'll make him apologize.)
Quick rule of thumb: "can't help oneself" is ずにはいられない; "something is bound to make people ~" or "I must make it happen" is ずにはおかない; "can't get away without doing it" is ずにはすまない.
What to study next
Next, look at 〜ずにはすまない・ないではすまない (n1-71). The two are often tested together, and comparing them side by side makes the difference clearest.
n1-72:
The idea in one line
「〜を余儀なくされる」 is the phrase the news uses for “be forced to ~.” Think “the event was forced to be canceled because of the typhoon.” It isn't something you chose. The situation or the wider circumstances left you no other way out. 余儀 means “another option,” so 余儀ない means “there's no other option.”
When to use it
News and reportsBig events such as natural disasters, pandemics or economic shocks that leave a person or organization with no choice but to do something.
・大雨で、試合は中止を余儀なくされた。(Because of the heavy rain, the match was forced to be canceled.)
・地震で、多くの住民が避難生活を余儀なくされている。(Because of the earthquake, many residents are forced to live in shelters.)
Describing your own situation in formal settingsYou'll also use it in reports, or when explaining your background in an interview.
・会社の倒産で、退職を余儀なくされました。(Because the company went bankrupt, I had no choice but to leave my job.)
How to form it
Put a noun before it, specifically a noun that expresses an action. The most common are 中止, 延期, 変更, 撤退, 入院 and 移転, words that can take する after them.
If you start from a verb, drop the する and keep the noun: 延期する → 延期を余儀なくされた
The subject of the sentence (the part before は／が) is the side that is affected and forced: the match, the old shop, the residents, me.
Forms you'll hear most
余儀なくされたSomething that already happened. This is the most common form.
余儀なくされているBeing forced to do it right now, still ongoing, like the shelter life above.
余儀なくさせるThe reverse, from the side of the cause. The subject is often the event itself:
・円安が、計画の見直しを余儀なくさせた。(The weak yen forced a rethink of the plan.)
Easy mistakes
・Read it よぎなく, not よぎむなく.
・You can't put a verb directly before it. Say 中止を余儀なくされた, not 「中止するを余儀なくされた」.
・Don't use it for things you chose or wanted to do. If you changed jobs because you wanted a new challenge, you weren't “forced.”
・It's heavy and very formal, so using it for trivial matters sounds exaggerated. 「宿題を余儀なくされた」 sounds like a joke.
・English “be forced to” maps onto both させられる and を余儀なくされる, so many learners reach for させられる by instinct. The two mean different things, so see below.
Telling it apart from similar forms
Take “leaving a job” as the example:
を余儀なくされる = forced by circumstances. Nobody in particular is pushing you. Formal and mostly written:
会社の倒産で、退職を余儀なくされた。(Because the company went bankrupt, I was forced to leave.)
させられる = a specific person makes you do it, often with some resentment. Common in speech too:
上司に無理やり退職させられた。(My boss forced me to quit.)
ざるを得ない = you yourself weigh it up and conclude you have no choice. The focus is on your own judgment:
体調が悪くて、退職せざるを得なかった。(I was in poor health, so I had no choice but to quit.)
Quick test: if a person is pushing you, use させられる. If you thought it over and had no choice, use ざるを得ない. If big circumstances like a disaster, the economy or the times left you no way out, and the setting is formal, use を余儀なくされる.
n1-77:
The idea in one line
「〜んばかりに」 means “as if about to ~” or “looking like one is about to ~.” It's an exaggerated way to describe how intense something is: it's close to doing that action, but usually it hasn't actually done it. Compare English “she looked like she was about to cry.” The point is how upset she was, not that she actually cried.
How to form it
Turn the verb into its ない form, remove 「ない」, then add 「んばかり」.
泣く → 泣かない → 泣かんばかり
言う → 言わない → 言わんばかり
あふれる → あふれない → あふれんばかり
する is an exception: it's not しんばかり, but the classical form する → せんばかり
Forms you'll hear most
んばかりに + actionDescribes how someone does an action.
・彼女は泣かんばかりに頼んできた。(She begged me, almost in tears.)
・犬が飛びつかんばかりに喜んで走ってきた。(The dog came running, so happy it seemed about to jump on me.)
んばかりの + nounModifies the noun that follows.
・会場は割れんばかりの拍手に包まれた。(The hall was filled with deafening applause.)
・彼は「お前のせいだ」と言わんばかりの顔で私を見た。(He looked at me as if to say “it's your fault.”)
んばかりだPlaced at the end of the sentence.
・彼の喜びようは、今にも踊り出さんばかりだった。(He was so happy he looked ready to burst into dance.)
Four combinations come up especially often: 言わんばかり, 割れんばかり, あふれんばかり and 泣かんばかり. Memorize them as set phrases. The overall tone is written and literary, though 「〜と言わんばかりの顔」 is also common in everyday speech.
Easy mistakes
・The 「ん」 here is not a negative. 泣かん looks like the Kansai-style “won't cry,” but in this grammar it's the classical ん meaning “about to ~.” 泣かんばかり means “on the verge of tears,” not “not crying.”
・する becomes せんばかり. Writing しんばかり is wrong.
・It's an exaggerated description of appearance or degree. If you just want to say “looks like they're about to cry,” everyday conversation is fine with 泣きそうな顔. Using 泣かんばかり sounds very dramatic.
・It usually means “close to doing it,” not that it actually happened. あふれんばかり means “full to the brim,” and the water hasn't actually spilled over.
Telling it apart from similar forms
とばかりに follows a line of “dialogue,” and means “as if saying ~.” It means almost the same as と言わんばかりに:
・店長は「早く帰れ」と言わんばかりに時計を見た。(The manager looked at the clock as if to say “go home already.”)
・店長は「早く帰れ」とばかりに時計を見た。(Same as above.)
The difference is what can go before it. Before んばかりに goes an action that was nearly carried out, such as crying, overflowing or jumping up. Before とばかりに goes words in someone's mind. So “almost in tears” can only be 泣かんばかりに, never 泣くとばかりに.
Quick test: if what comes before is a “line of speech,” either とばかりに or と言わんばかりに works. If it's an “action about to happen,” you can only use the ない form + んばかりに.
n1-89:
The idea in one line
This pair works like English "without ~" and "not ... without ~". There are two uses:
なしに: "He took it without saying anything." Someone skipped the step they should have taken and just did it.
なしには: "Without you, we couldn't have succeeded." Without A, B is simply impossible.
The two differ by just one は, but they are used very differently.
When to use it
なしにSomething that should have been there was missing, and the person went ahead anyway. It often carries a hint of disapproval, like "that's not right, is it?"
・彼は連絡なしに会社を休んだ。(He took the day off without telling anyone.)
・断りなしに、人の物を使ってはいけない。(You must not use other people's things without asking.)
・彼は一言の断りもなしに帰ってしまった。(He went home without so much as a word.)
Add も in the middle to get もなしに. It is stronger and feels like "not even ~".
なしにはA is an indispensable condition. Without A, B can't be done.
・この映画は、涙なしには見られない。(You can't watch this movie without crying.)
・皆さんの協力なしには、成功できなかった。(Without everyone's help, I couldn't have succeeded.)
・皆さんの協力なしには、成功しなかったでしょう。(Without everyone's help, it probably wouldn't have succeeded.)
How to attach it
Nouns attach directly: 許可 → 許可なしに努力 → 努力なしには
Verbs need こと first, giving 「dictionary form + ことなしに(は)」. This is the more formal, written form:
・彼は休むことなしに働き続けた。(He kept working without a moment's rest.)
・努力することなしには、夢はかなわない。(Without effort, dreams don't come true.)
The second half after なしには must be negative. Common endings are 〜できない, 〜られない and 〜ありえない, but 〜ない and 〜なかった（でしょう） also work.
Common mistakes
・What follows なしに doesn't have to be negative: 連絡なしに休んだ is an affirmative sentence. Only なしには must be followed by a negative.
・なしには can't be followed by an affirmative: ×協力なしには成功した doesn't make sense.
・Verbs can't attach directly: ×連絡しなしに. Write 連絡なしに (as a noun) or 連絡することなしに.
・This is a formal, written style. In everyday speech people mostly say なしで: 予約なしで入れますか。(Can I go in without a reservation?)
Don't confuse with similar forms
Both of these talk about "no reservation":
予約なしに店に入った。(He went into the shop without a reservation: this describes how he did it.)
予約なしには入れない。(You can't get in without a reservation: this states a necessary condition.)
なくして（は）: nearly the same meaning as なしには, but stiffer, and mostly used in speeches and writing.
皆さんの協力なくしては、成功はありえなかった。(Without your cooperation, success would have been impossible.)
あっての: the same idea from the opposite direction: "B exists only because of A."
お客様あっての店だ。(A shop exists only because of its customers.)
＝お客様なしには、店は成り立たない。(Without customers, a shop can't survive.)
Quick rule of thumb: for "did it without ~", use なしに. For "impossible without ~", use なしには (always followed by a negative). For a more formal tone, switch to なくしては. To say it from the "B exists only because of A" angle, use あっての.
n1-91:
The idea in one line
「〜に足る」 means "worthy of ~" or "enough to ~": a person or thing is good enough to be trusted, respected or found satisfying. The reverse, 「〜に足りない」, is like "nothing to fear" or "not worth mentioning": not worth it, no need to bother. 「足る」 is read たる. It is a stiff, written expression that often appears in news, commentary and novels.
How to attach it
Verb dictionary form + に足る: 信頼する → 信頼するに足る満足する → 満足するに足る
For 「〜する」 verbs, drop する and attach the noun directly: 信頼 → 信頼に足る尊敬 → 尊敬に足る
It is mostly placed before a noun as a modifier, as in 「信頼に足る人物」, but it can also end a sentence as a conclusion.
When to use it
に足るA formal way to judge a person, document, reason or result as "good enough, up to standard." It often goes with verbs of evaluation such as 信頼する・尊敬する・満足する・納得する・信じる.
・彼女は尊敬に足る先輩だ。(She is a senior colleague worthy of respect.)
・彼の説明は、納得するに足るものだった。(His explanation was convincing enough.)
・この報告書には、信頼に足るデータがない。(This report contains no data worth trusting.)
に足りないSays something is not important at all, nothing to be afraid of. It is mostly used in a few fixed expressions. に足らない is also common and means the same.
・そんなのは取るに足りない問題だ。(That's just a trivial problem.)
・相手は新人ばかりだ。恐れるに足りない。(The opponents are all rookies. There's nothing to fear.)
Common mistakes
・取るに足りない doesn't mean "not enough to pick up." It is a set phrase to memorize as a whole: "trivial, insignificant." It has nothing to do with the "not enough" of お金が足りない (not enough money).
・Only the dictionary form or the noun of a する verb can come before it, not the た form or ます form: 信頼したに足る is wrong. You also can't attach ordinary nouns freely: 彼に足る makes no sense.
・The negative に足りない is mainly used in fixed phrases like 取るに足りない and 恐れるに足りない. To say "not trustworthy" in general, 信頼できない or 信頼に値しない sounds more natural.
・This is written language. When chatting with a friend and saying "that person is reliable," あの人は信頼できる is enough. Using に足る would sound like reading out an official document.
Don't confuse with similar forms
Here are three ways to judge a book:
に足る = up to standard, good enough: これは読むに足る本だ。(This is a book worth reading.)
に値する = has that kind of value. The meaning is very close, and in many cases they are interchangeable. The difference is that its negative に値しない can be used freely: この本は一読に値しない。(This book isn't worth reading even once.)
に堪えない (n1-36) = so bad that it's unbearable, with strong emotion: 読むに堪えない文章だ。(It's writing too awful to read.)
So 「取るに足りない」 means "unimportant, not worth minding," while 「見るに堪えない」 means "so bad I can't stand to look at it." The two point in completely different directions.
Quick rule of thumb: for "enough to ~ / not worth mentioning," use に足る・に足りない. To freely say "not worth ~," use に値しない. For "so bad it's unbearable," use に堪えない.
n1-19:
The idea in one line
「〜に至るまで」 is like English "from A all the way down to B" or "right down to B". Take "from the boss to the part-timers, everyone joined." The point isn't where the range stops. It stresses that even something that far out, or that small, is included, so the range is very wide.
How to attach it
Noun + に至るまで. It most often pairs with 「から」:
A から B に至るまで = from A all the way to (even) B
子供から高齢者 → 子供から高齢者に至るまで (from children to the elderly)
B usually sits at the other end of the range, and it's often the end you wouldn't expect to be counted. It's often followed by "all"-type words such as 全員, すべて, 誰もが, 細かく.
Where you'll hear it most
Range of peopleFrom top to bottom, from old to young: everyone is included.
・社長から新入社員に至るまで、全員が会議に参加した。 (From the company president to the newest hires, everyone took part in the meeting.)
・子供から高齢者に至るまで、誰もが楽しめるイベントだ。 (It's an event that everyone, from children to the elderly, can enjoy.)
Range of detailsFrom the big picture down to the smallest detail, everything is covered.
・服装から髪型に至るまで、細かく決められている。 (From clothing down to hairstyle, even the details are specified.)
・部屋の隅々に至るまで、きれいに掃除した。 (I cleaned the room spotless, right down to every corner.)
Range of timeFrom long ago all the way to the present, stressing a long stretch of time.
・創業から現在に至るまで、この味を守り続けている。 (From the founding to the present day, we have kept protecting this flavor.)
Easy mistakes
・English "up to" or "until" can make it sound like drawing a line or setting a limit. It's actually the opposite: it doesn't mean "only as far as here" but "even this is included". The point is the wide range.
・A and B must be the two ends of the same kind of thing: people with people, things with things, time with time.
・For an ordinary endpoint, like "wait until what time" or "walk to the station", plain まで is enough. Using に至るまで there sounds odd.
・This is formal, written language, common in news, announcements and company profiles. With friends, おじいちゃんまでみんなスマホ持ってるよ (even grandpa has a smartphone!) is all you need.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
N1 has three easily confused 「至る」 patterns. Let's compare them in one situation, "a family and their smartphones":
に至るまで = a very wide range, everything included:
祖父母から孫に至るまで、家族全員がスマホを持っている。 (From the grandparents to the grandchildren, the whole family has a smartphone.)
に至っては = picks out the most extreme case from a group, usually with a hint of criticism:
うちの家族は機械に弱い。祖母に至っては、電話のかけ方も知らない。 (My family is bad with machines. As for my grandmother, she doesn't even know how to make a phone call.)
に至る = things develop step by step until they finally reach a result:
何度も話し合って、ようやく祖母もスマホを買うに至った。 (After talking it over many times, my grandmother finally ended up buying a smartphone too.)
Quick test: for "from ~ to ~, all of it", use に至るまで. For "the most extreme one is ~", use に至っては. For "it ended up as ~", use に至る.
n1-20:
The idea in one line
「〜を経て」 is like English "after going through ~", "through ~" or "via ~". The point is that you pass through a process, a stage, or a place along the way, and only then reach the result that follows. It's formal and common in news, reports, profiles and speeches, but less so in chats with friends.
How to attach it
Noun + を経て　長い議論 → 長い議論を経て (after a long discussion)
Only a noun goes before it, never a verb directly. To talk about "preparing", write 準備を経て, not 「準備するを経て」.
「経て」 is read へて. Its base form is 経る (へる), meaning "to pass through".
When it needs to modify a noun, change it to を経た + noun:
厳しい訓練 → 厳しい訓練を経た選手 (an athlete who has gone through strict training)
When to use it
Going through a processThings that take time and effort, like discussion, review, negotiation or preparation. The result comes only after they're done.
・長い議論を経て、ようやく結論が出た。 (After a long discussion, a conclusion was finally reached.)
・厳しい審査を経て、新しい薬が発売された。 (After a strict review, the new drug went on sale.)
Time passingOften used with 「歳月」 or 「年月」, giving a feeling of "after so many years".
・10年の歳月を経て、橋が完成した。 (After ten years, the bridge was finally completed.)
Going through a roleVery common in profiles, describing the stages a person has been through.
・彼は会社員を経て、作家になった。 (After working as an office worker, he became a writer.)
Passing through a placeA place you pass through along the way.
・香港を経て、日本に着いた。 (Via Hong Kong, I arrived in Japan.)
・台北から台中を経て、高雄へ向かう。 (From Taipei, via Taichung, we head to Kaohsiung.)
Easy mistakes
・「経て」 is read へて, not けいて or たって.
・The same 「経」 also appears in 経つ (たつ), meaning "time passes". 3年経って is read さんねんたって and is the everyday spoken "three years went by". The two look alike, but the reading and the tone are different.
・This is formal. If you tell a friend "I changed planes via Hong Kong", 香港経由で or 香港で乗り換えて sounds more natural. Using 「を経て」 for small everyday things sounds like reading a press release.
・What goes before it should be a process worth mentioning. For small things like eating a meal or taking a bath, just use 「〜てから」, not 「を経て」.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
を経て vs 経って: both can express "a period of time passed".
3年経って、やっと仕事に慣れた。 (After three years, I finally got used to the job.): Casual. 「経って」 follows the time expression directly, with no を.
3年の歳月を経て、作品が完成した。 (After three years, the work was completed.): Formal, and it usually carries the feeling that "a lot of effort went into the result".
を経て vs に至る: they often appear together, but they play different roles.
何度もの交渉を経て、合意に至った。 (After many rounds of negotiation, they finally reached an agreement.)
「を経て」 describes the road passed along the way, while 「に至る」 describes the final destination reached.
Quick test: to say what you went through in the middle, use 「を経て」. To say where you ended up, use 「に至る」. For a casual "a few years passed", use 「経って」.
What to learn next
The same-level 〜に至る and 〜に至るまで are worth memorizing together with 「を経て」. They're very useful when writing about a process leading to a result.
n1-38:
The gist
「〜に難くない」 means "it's not hard to imagine", "it's easy to understand", "it goes without saying". You use a small clue to work out the situation or feeling behind it. It's read かたくない. It's formal and written in tone, and very common in news, commentary, and essays.
How to form it
What comes before it is almost always a word for "working something out in your head". The set is small, so it's fastest to memorize each chunk whole:
想像に難くない (not hard to imagine)
理解に難くない (not hard to understand)
予想に難くない (not hard to predict)
推測に難くない (not hard to infer)
察するに難くない (not hard to sense or guess)
Nouns like 想像 and 理解 attach directly with 「に」. 察する is a verb itself, so it takes the dictionary form.
The content you're inferring goes in front. It usually takes one of three shapes: 「〜は」, 「〜ことは」, or 「〜のは」.
・親を亡くした彼の悲しみは想像に難くない。 (It's not hard to imagine how sad he is after losing his parents.)
・この計画に反対の声が上がることは予想に難くない。 (It's easy to predict that opposition to this plan will arise.)
・物価がこれだけ上がれば、生活が苦しくなるのは想像に難くない。 (With prices rising this much, it's easy to imagine that life will get harder.)
・彼女の表情から、何があったかは察するに難くない。 (From her expression, it's not hard to guess what happened.)
Common mistakes
・「難くない」 is read かたくない, not むずかしくない.
・It means "not hard to imagine", not "easy to do". To say "this problem is easy to solve", say この問題は簡単だ. You can't use に難くない there.
・Don't put just any verb in front. Stick to 想像, 理解, 予想, 推測, and 察する.
・It's stiff, and you won't hear it in everyday chat. With a friend, for "you can imagine", 想像できる or 想像がつく sounds natural.
・Don't read the 「ない」 as a negative meaning. 「難くない」 = not hard = easy, so the whole sentence is affirmative in tone.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
N1 has several 「〜に＋negative」 patterns that look alike but mean very different things. Let's compare them in one situation: a friend was laid off.
に難くない = not hard to imagine: 彼のショックは想像に難くない。 (It's not hard to imagine how shocked he is.)
には当たらない = no need to react that way: この不景気だから、リストラされても驚くには当たらない。 (With the economy this bad, there's no need to be surprised at being laid off.)
に堪えない = so bad you can't bear to watch or listen: 会社の説明は聞くに堪えない言い訳ばかりだった。 (The company's explanation was nothing but excuses too awful to listen to.)
Quick test: "you can well imagine" is に難くない; "no need to bother with ~" is には当たらない; "too awful to bear" is に堪えない.
n1-37:
The gist
「〜を禁じ得ない」 means "can't help feeling ~", "can't help but ~". When you see or hear something, an emotion like sympathy, surprise, or anger wells up on its own, and you can't suppress it. It's very formal and mostly appears in news commentary, essays, and speeches. You'll almost never say it in casual conversation.
Break it down
禁じる means "to forbid", and 得ない means "can't ~". Put together, it's "can't hold it back even if you try": the emotion can't be stopped and just surfaces.
It's read きんじえない. Here 「得」 is read 「え」.
How to form it
Put a noun expressing an emotion in front and add 「を禁じ得ない」. For past events, it becomes 「を禁じ得なかった」.
同情 → 同情を禁じ得ない (can't help feeling sympathy)
驚き → 驚きを禁じ得なかった (couldn't help being astonished)
Common nouns: 同情, 驚き, 怒り, 憤り, 涙, 戸惑い, 疑問.
When to use it
Being moved by something First you usually say what you saw, heard, or thought about, then say that the emotion couldn't be held back.
・その知らせを聞いて、驚きを禁じ得なかった。 (Hearing that news, I couldn't help being astonished.)
・被害者の話を聞き、涙を禁じ得なかった。 (Listening to the victim's account, I couldn't hold back my tears.)
Formal statements of opinion Very common in commentary and editorials for expressing strong views.
・政府の対応には、怒りを禁じ得ない。 (I can't help feeling anger at the government's response.)
・この計画には疑問を禁じ得ない。 (I can't help having doubts about this plan.)
Common mistakes
・A noun must come before it, not a verb directly. Say 涙を禁じ得ない or 驚きを禁じ得ない, not 「泣くを禁じ得ない」 or 「驚くを禁じ得ない」.
・It describes an emotion welling up in yourself. You don't use it to describe other people's feelings.
・The tone is very stiff. Saying 「感動を禁じ得なかった」 to a friend sounds like reading from a script. In speech, 思わず泣いちゃった (I couldn't help crying) is enough.
・「得ない」 is read えない, not うない.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Same situation: you heard what happened to him and feel sorry for him.
を禁じ得ない = the emotion wells up and can't be held back. Very formal, and it takes a noun:
彼の話を聞いて、同情を禁じ得なかった。 (Hearing his story, I couldn't help feeling sympathy for him.)
ずにはいられない (N2) = "can't help doing ~". It takes a verb, can describe actions, and is more common and less stiff:
彼の話を聞いて、同情せずにはいられなかった。 (Hearing his story, I couldn't help feeling sorry for him.)
あまりにおかしくて、笑わずにはいられなかった。 (It was so funny that I couldn't help laughing.)
When に堪えない follows an emotion noun, it means "extremely ~" or "~ beyond measure". Common ones are 感謝に堪えない (deeply grateful), 遺憾に堪えない, 同情に堪えない, and 憤慨に堪えない. They're mostly used in formal speeches and writing. The feel is "the emotion is so intense you can hardly bear it":
被災された方々のことを思うと、同情に堪えない。 (When I think of those affected by the disaster, I feel deep sympathy.)
Also, when に堪えない follows a verb, it means something different: 見るに堪えない means "too awful to watch". That has nothing to do with を禁じ得ない, so don't mix them up.
Quick test: an emotion that "wells up and can't be held back" takes を禁じ得ない; an emotion "so intense you can hardly bear it, or ~ to the extreme" takes に堪えない; the general "can't help doing it" takes ずにはいられない.
What to learn next
Another N1 pattern from the same group of strong emotions is 〜て止まない (keep ~ from the bottom of one's heart). For example: 皆様のご健康を願って止みません。 (I sincerely wish everyone good health.) It often appears at the end of speeches and letters.
n1-93:
The idea in one line
「〜たが最後」 means "once you do that, it's all over" or "there's no going back once you start". As soon as the first thing happens, things inevitably turn bad, become irreversible, or can't be stopped. Think of "once you open a bag of chips, that's it, you'll finish the whole bag." That's the feeling.
How to form it
Put the verb in the た-form (the past form ending in 「〜た」), then add 「が最後」 directly.
言う → 言った → 言ったが最後
寝る → 寝た → 寝たが最後
見つかる → 見つかった → 見つかったが最後
「最後」 is read さいご.
When to use it
Describing someone's habitsOnce a certain person does a certain thing, the same result always follows.
・彼は一度寝たが最後、朝まで何をしても起きない。(Once he falls asleep, that's it. Nothing you do will wake him until morning.)
Can't stopOnce you start, you can't pull back.
・このドラマは見始めたが最後、止まらなくなる。(Once you start watching this drama, you can't stop.)
Warning about consequencesA reminder: "Whatever you do, don't do this, or you'll be in big trouble."
・部長に見つかったが最後、一時間は説教される。(If the department head catches you, you're done. You'll get lectured for at least an hour.)
In speech it's often replaced by 「〜たら最後」. The meaning is the same, but the tone is more casual:
・そんなこと言ったら最後、絶交されるよ。(Once you say something like that, it's over. They'll cut you off, you know.)
Common mistakes
・What follows can only be a bad result. You can't use が最後 for good things like "once I win the lottery, I'll live well."
・The verb before it is always in the た-form, even when you're talking about something that hasn't happened yet. You can't say 「食べるが最後」.
・Here 「最後」 doesn't mean "last" or "finally" in the English sense. It means "that's the end, it's over." Don't translate it as "after eating, finally...".
・What follows is usually a description or judgment ("this will definitely happen"). It rarely takes a request ("please...") or a statement of resolve ("I will...").
・It often pairs with "no way back" expressions like 二度と〜ない, 止まらない, and 終わりだ.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
〜が早いか: also often translated "as soon as ~", but it only says that something happens very quickly, whether good or bad.
・彼は布団に入るが早いか、眠ってしまった。(As soon as he got under the covers, he fell asleep.)
・彼は布団に入ったが最後、昼まで出てこない。(Once he gets under the covers, that's it. He won't come out until noon.)
The first sentence is about speed. The second is about "no way back afterward."
〜たところで: it also follows the た-form, but it means "even if you do it, it's no use."
・彼に話したが最後、みんなに知られてしまう。(Once you tell him, that's it. Everyone will find out.)
・今さら彼に話したところで、何も変わらない。(Telling him now won't change anything.)
Quick test: "once it's done there's no going back, and the result is bad" is が最後. "As soon as X, immediately Y" is が早いか. "Even if you do it, it's pointless" is たところで.
n1-18:
The idea in one line
「〜に至る」 is the phrase you often hear in the news for "it developed into ~" or "it ended up reaching the point of ~". Over time, through a series of developments, things arrive at a certain outcome. That outcome is usually something weighty: a lawsuit, bankruptcy, a settlement, a conclusion. It's very written and formal, and appears most in news, reports, press conferences, and company announcements.
How to form it
Nouns: add に至る directly, with no の in between.
訴訟 → 訴訟に至る和解 → 和解に至る
Verbs: use the dictionary form (the base form you find in the dictionary) plus に至る.
中止する → 中止するに至る考える → 考えるに至る
至る itself is a Group 1 (godan) verb and conjugates like 帰る:
至る → 至った至る → 至っていない至る → 至らなかった
How you'll most often hear it
Ending up at a resultIt's most common in the past tense 「〜に至った」. It's often preceded by ついに, 〜の末, or 〜結果, signaling "after a process."
・長い話し合いの末、両社は合併に至った。(After lengthy negotiations, the two companies ended up merging.)
・留学を通して、日本で働きたいと考えるに至った。(Through studying abroad, I gradually came to want to work in Japan.)
Not there yetThe negative is usually written 「〜には至っていない」, meaning things haven't developed to that stage yet.
・この技術は、まだ実用化には至っていない。(This technology hasn't reached the stage of practical use yet.)
Set phrasesThese three are very common. Memorize them as whole sentences.
・幸い、大事には至らなかった。(Fortunately, it didn't turn into anything serious.)
・中止に至った経緯をご説明します。(I will explain how we came to the decision to cancel.)
・1990年に創業し、現在に至る。(Founded in 1990 and operating up to the present.)
Common mistakes
・Verbs take the dictionary form, not the た-form: it's 中止するに至った, not 「中止したに至った」. The past meaning goes on 至った alone.
・It's very written. If you're telling a friend "we ended up breaking up," 結局別れることになった is enough. Saying 「別れるに至った」 would sound like you're reading out a press release.
・The outcome has to be weighty, usually after a process. For small things like buying bread because you're hungry, you can't say 「パンを買うに至った」.
・Although it literally means "reach," for everyday "arriving at a place" you need 着く.
・On its own, 至らない often has a different meaning, "lacking / falling short": 至らない点もありますが、よろしくお願いします。(There may be areas where I fall short, but I look forward to working with you.)
Telling it apart from look-alikes
N1 has three look-alike 「至る」 patterns. Let's compare them in one scenario, "a company in bad shape":
に至る = things end up becoming a certain result:
赤字が続き、ついに倒産に至った。(Losses continued, and it finally ended in bankruptcy.)
に至るまで = a range from A all the way to B, even B:
社長から新入社員に至るまで、全員が毎日残業している。(From the president down to the newest employees, everyone works overtime every day.)
に至っては = as for B, it's even more extreme, singling out the most extreme example:
どの部署も業績が悪いが、営業部に至っては目標の半分にも届いていない。(Every department is performing badly, but the sales department hasn't even reached half its target.)
Quick test: at the end of a sentence, saying "it finally became ~", it's に至る. With "from A to B" before it, describing a range, it's に至るまで. In the middle of a sentence as a topic, introducing "the even worse one," it's に至っては.
What to learn next
Next, study 〜に至るまで and 〜に至っては. Memorizing all three together is the best way to avoid mixing them up. You can also learn 〜を経て ("after going through ~"), which often appears together with に至る: 何度もの議論を経て、合意に至った。(After many rounds of discussion, they finally reached an agreement.)
n1-34:
The idea in one line
「〜極まりない」 means "utterly ~" or "~ in the extreme", as in "utterly rude" or "dangerous in the extreme." You use it to criticize something harshly. The tone is as stiff as a news report, an editorial or a formal letter of protest. 「〜極まる」 means the same thing but sounds a bit more literary.
When to use it
Harsh criticismYou pass a very strong verdict on someone's attitude or behavior.
・あの店員の対応は失礼極まりない。(That clerk's service was utterly rude.)
・夜中に大声で騒ぐなんて、迷惑極まりない。(Making loud noise in the middle of the night is a nuisance in the extreme.)
Describing a very bad situationNews and reports use it for dangerous or troublesome things.
・雨の夜に無灯火で走るのは危険極まりない。(Riding without a light on a rainy night is extremely dangerous.)
Before a nounYou can use it directly to describe the noun that follows.
・退屈極まりない会議が三時間も続いた。(The meeting was unbelievably boring and went on for a full three hours.)
How to connect it
With な-adjectives, drop 「な」 and attach it directly:
失礼な → 失礼極まりない危険な → 危険極まる
The most common partners: 失礼、無礼、危険、迷惑、不快、不愉快、退屈、非常識、無責任. Almost all are words of two or more kanji that are already negative.

Since 「極まりない」 ends in 「ない」, it can go into the past tense like an い-adjective: 失礼極まりない → 失礼極まりなかった
い-adjectives can't attach directly. Add 「こと」 first: 情けない → 情けないこと極まりない (pathetic in the extreme)
Common mistakes
・The 「ない」 in 「極まりない」 is not a negation. 「極まり」 means "limit" or "end," so 「極まりない」 means "there is no limit," that is, "extremely ~." 失礼極まりない means "utterly rude," not "not rude."
・Don't add な in the middle. It's 失礼極まりない, not 「失礼な極まりない」.
・It's used almost only for bad things. To say food is delicious or something is handy, use another expression. Don't force this one.
・The tone is heavy and stiff. When complaining to a friend, 本当に失礼だよね is enough. Saying 「失礼極まりない」 to someone's face is basically a formal break in the relationship.
・Readings: 極まりない is read きわまりない, and 極まる is read きわまる.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Take the same case of being treated rudely by a clerk:
極まりない = a calm, very heavy verdict: あの店員の態度は失礼極まりない。 (That clerk's attitude is utterly rude.)
といったらない = an exclamation where your emotions overflow. It's more colloquial, and い-adjectives attach directly: あの店員の態度、腹が立つといったらない。 (That clerk's attitude made me so angry, you can't imagine.)
の至り also means "the utmost ~," but it points the other way. It talks about your own feelings, mostly good ones like honor or gratitude, and it's used in speeches and polite settings.
このような賞をいただき、光栄の至りです。 (Receiving an award like this is the utmost honor.)
Quick rule of thumb: to criticize something bad, use 「極まりない」. To politely say you feel very honored or grateful, use 「の至り」. For an outburst of anger, embarrassment or joy, use 「といったらない」.
What to learn next
The same kanji appears in two other common expressions:
Noun + の極み: こんな料理を毎日食べるなんて、贅沢の極みだ。 (Eating food like this every day is the height of luxury.)
The set phrase 「感極まる」: 優勝が決まった瞬間、感極まって泣き出した。 (The moment the win was decided, I was overcome with emotion and burst into tears.)
n1-52:
The idea in one line
「〜まじき」 means "How could you do that, as a ~!" You use it to scold someone for doing something unbecoming of their position, like "conduct unbecoming of…" in the news. The tone is very heavy and formal, and you mostly see it in news, editorials and formal statements.
How to connect it
Verb dictionary form (the base form you'd look up) + まじき + noun
ある → あるまじき行為 (conduct that should not exist)
許す → 許すまじき犯罪 (an unforgivable crime)
言う → 言うまじきこと (something that should never be said)
Besides するまじき, you'll also see the older form すまじき for 「する」.
The form you'll hear most
Position + にあるまじきOver 90% of uses are this fixed combination: 「person or position + に (or として) + あるまじき + noun」, meaning "a ~ that should never appear, given that position."
・医者にあるまじき行為だ。(That's conduct unbecoming of a doctor.)
・プロにあるまじきミスだ。(That's a mistake a professional should never make.)
・社会人としてあるまじき態度だと叱られた。(I was scolded for an attitude unbecoming of a working adult.)
許すまじきWithout mentioning any position, it says directly, "This must never be forgiven."
・子どもを狙った許すまじき犯罪だ。(It's an unforgivable crime that targeted children.)
Common mistakes
・まじき must be followed by a noun. It can't end the sentence:
　×教師にあるまじきだ。
　○教師にあるまじき発言だ。
・It means "should not," not "cannot / is unable to." It's a moral judgment and has nothing to do with ability.
・The 「許す」 in 「許すまじき」 is about whether others forgive, so 「政治家として許すまじき発言」 can easily be misread as "a statement we can't forgive as politicians." To say "that politician shouldn't have said that," 政治家としてあるまじき発言 is the clearest.
・It's very stiff and sounds odd in everyday conversation. In casual speech, 先生なのに、ありえない。 (They're a teacher, and yet… unbelievable.) is enough.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Take the same case of scolding a teacher for corporal punishment:
べきではない = the general "shouldn't." It works in any setting and can end a sentence: 教師は体罰をするべきではない。 (Teachers shouldn't use corporal punishment.)
まじき = also "shouldn't," but heavier and more written, and it can only go before a noun: 体罰は教師にあるまじき行為だ。 (Corporal punishment is conduct unbecoming of a teacher.)
べからざる = the focus is "must not / indispensable." It often talks about rules or necessity and doesn't have to involve a position: 水は生活に欠くべからざるものだ。 (Water is indispensable to life.)
Quick rule of thumb: if there's 「position + に／として」 in front and you're calling someone unfit, it's まじき. If you're talking about rules or something "indispensable," it's べからざる.
What to learn next
「〜たる」 = "being the kind of person who is a ~." It often appears together with まじき in meaning: 教師たる者、生徒の手本でなければならない。 (One who is a teacher must be a model for their students.)
n1-53:
The idea in one line
「〜べからず」is what you see on a sign: "Do not ~", "~ prohibited", "Please do not ~". It's classical Japanese, and it feels like English signs such as "No trespassing" or "Keep out": stiff and formal. You'll almost never hear it in everyday speech. You'll mostly see it on notices, slogans and proverbs.
When to use it
SignsA prohibition written for everyone to read, placed at the end of the sentence.
・ここに入るべからず。(No entry here.)
・ここにごみを捨てるべからず。(No dumping trash here.)
Proverbs and slogansMany old sayings and famous quotes use this form. Just memorize the whole sentence.
・働かざる者食うべからず。(Those who don't work shall not eat.)
・初心忘るべからず。(Never forget your original resolve.)
べからざる + nounWhen a noun follows, switch to べからざる. It means "a ~ that must not be done" or "a ~ that cannot be ~ed", and it shows up in essays and news.
・水は生活に欠くべからざるものだ。(Water is something indispensable to life.)
・それは許すべからざる行為だ。(That is an unforgivable act.)
How to form it
Verbs use the dictionary form (the base form you find in a dictionary). Just add it directly:
入る → 入るべからず捨てる → 捨てるべからず
する usually becomes す before it: 駐車する → 駐車すべからず (You'll also see するべからず, but すべからず sounds more authentic.)
To modify a noun, change ず to ざる: 欠くべからず → 欠くべからざるもの
Common mistakes
・Use べからず at the end of a sentence and べからざる before a noun. Don't write「べからずもの」.
・It belongs on signs and in writing, so you can't use it to tell someone face to face not to do something. Saying「吸うべからず」to a friend would sound very odd. In conversation, use 吸わないで or 吸っちゃだめ.
・Don't attach it to the ない form. 「行かないべからず」is wrong, because it already means "must not" by itself.
・The 「忘る」 in 初心忘るべからず is the classical base form of 忘れる. It's a fixed phrase, so memorize it as is and don't change it.
・すべからく looks similar but is a different word. It means "by all means; ought to", and it is not negative.
Telling it apart from similar forms
Take the same situation, smoking:
べからず = a prohibition on a sign: ここでたばこを吸うべからず。 (No smoking here.)
べきではない = advice that someone "shouldn't". You can use it in ordinary speech or writing: ここでたばこを吸うべきではない。 (You shouldn't smoke here.)
まじき = something that shouldn't be done by someone in that position: 患者の前でたばこを吸うなんて、医者にあるまじき行為だ。 (Smoking in front of patients is conduct unbecoming of a doctor.)
Also, べく only looks similar. It means something completely different, "in order to ~": 合格すべく、毎日勉強している。 (I study every day in order to pass.)
Quick rule of thumb: for a "prohibition" on a notice or in a proverb, use べからず. For advice that someone "shouldn't", use べきではない. When it's about "as a ~" (someone's role), use まじき. And "in order to ~" is べく.
n1-55:
The idea in one line
「〜たる」means "as a ~" or "being a ~", with the same tone as "as a teacher" or "those who are parents". You first bring up a weighty role, then say what someone in that role ought to do.
たる is a very old form meaning the same as である. It goes only before a noun, so it sounds formal and lofty, and you mostly see it in writing, speeches and lectures.
How to form it
Noun + たる + noun. The most common pattern is followed by 者 (often written もの, which also means "person"):
医者 → 医者たる者 (someone who is a doctor)
親 → 親たるもの (someone who is a parent)
How you'll usually hear it
Saying what one should doThis is the biggest use. It's often followed by べきだ, なければならない or てはならない.
・医者たる者、患者の話をよく聞くべきだ。(As a doctor, you should listen carefully to your patients.)
・プロたる者、言い訳はしない。(As a professional, you don't make excuses.)
Criticizing a failureYou first state the role, then point out that the person did something unworthy of it.
・教師たる者が生徒にうそをつくなんて、許されることではない。(For a teacher to lie to students is unforgivable.)
With other nounsWhat follows doesn't have to be 者. It can also be a noun like「資格」.
・彼に代表たる資格はない。(He isn't qualified to be a representative.)
Common mistakes
・Only a noun goes before it, usually a role, position or standing that carries responsibilities. You can't attach it to a verb or adjective.
・It is not the past-tense 「た」 plus 「る」. たる is a single word, so don't split it up.
・It's very stiff, and using it in casual chat sounds like you're lecturing. For "as a ~, you should ~" in conversation, 〜なんだから is enough: 先生なんだから、ちゃんとしてよ。 (You're a teacher, so act like one!)
・Don't mix it up with the homophone 足る (to be worthy of, to be enough). They're compared below.
Telling it apart from similar forms
Take the same topic, teachers:
たる者 = state the role first, then say what one should do (or criticize a failure to do it): 教師たる者、生徒の手本であるべきだ。 (As a teacher, you should be a role model for your students.)
にあるまじき = directly judge a specific act or remark as "unbecoming of that role". It's followed by nouns like 行為 or 発言: 教師にあるまじき発言だ。 (That's a remark unbecoming of a teacher.)
ともなれば = once you reach that level, naturally ~. It describes an expected result, not an obligation: ベテラン教師ともなれば、生徒の顔を見ただけで悩みに気づく。 (A veteran teacher can tell a student is worried just by looking at their face.)
に足る = worthy of ~. It follows words like 信頼 or 尊敬, and note the extra に: 彼は信頼に足る教師だ。 (He is a teacher worthy of trust.)
Quick rule of thumb: to say "as a ~, one should…" or "as a ~, how could you…", state the role first with たる(者). To judge a specific act as "unbecoming of a ~", use「～にあるまじき + 行為／発言」. For "at that level, naturally ~", use ともなれば. For "worthy of ~", use に足る.
What to learn next
Two more related forms are worth learning together: 〜まじき (unbecoming of ~), which also judges someone's role, and 〜ともなれば, which talks about "once you reach that level".
n1-36:
The idea in one line
「〜に堪えない」 has two meanings that point in opposite directions, and English has a match for each:
①“Unbearable to see / hear”: something so bad or so tragic that you can't stand to look at it or listen to it.
②“Deeply grateful, deeply moved”: feelings so full they can't be contained, which means “extremely ～”.
Both are very written and formal. You'll almost never hear them in everyday chat.
How to attach it
①Verb dictionary form + に堪えない: almost only the three verbs “see, hear, read” go in front.
見る → 見るに堪えない聞く → 聞くに堪えない読む → 読むに堪えない
②Emotion noun + に堪えない: the most common words are 感謝, 感激, 感慨, 遺憾 and 痛恨.
感謝 → 感謝に堪えません遺憾 → 遺憾に堪えない
「堪えない」 is read たえない, and it's often written directly in hiragana as 「たえない」.
Usage ①: so bad you can't stand it
Criticism, disgustThis says the content is too poor, too ugly or too tragic to be worth seeing, hearing or reading. It often connects directly to a noun, as in 「聞くに堪えない悪口」.
・聞くに堪えない悪口だった。（Those insults were unbearable to listen to）
・この翻訳はひどくて、読むに堪えない。（This translation is so awful it's unreadable）
・事故の現場は見るに堪えない状態だった。（The accident scene was too horrific to look at）
Usage ②: feelings too full to hold
Formal speechesCommon in speeches, thank-you letters, apology statements and eulogies, and it expresses your own strong feelings. When you say it to someone's face, it usually becomes 「〜に堪えません」.
・皆様の温かいご支援に、感謝の念に堪えません。（We are deeply grateful for your warm support）
・このような事態となり、誠に遺憾に堪えません。（It has come to this, and we deeply regret it）
・二十年ぶりに母校を訪れ、感慨に堪えない。（Visiting my old school for the first time in twenty years, I'm overcome with emotion）
Common mistakes
・②is not negative. 「感謝に堪えない」 doesn't mean “so thankful it's unbearable / annoying”. It means “so grateful my heart can't hold it”, which is the same as “extremely grateful”.
・Don't use it for physical endurance. For “I can't stand this heat”, say 暑くてたまらない or 暑さに耐えられない, not 暑さに堪えない.
・①criticizes the thing itself as too awful or too tragic. It doesn't mean “I don't have time to watch” or “I don't want to watch”.
・②is very formal. Saying 「感謝に堪えない」 to a friend sounds like you're giving a speech. In daily life, 本当にありがとう is enough.
・②needs a kanji emotion noun like 「感謝」 or 「遺憾」 in front. It can't attach directly to an adjective, so you can't say 悲しいに堪えない.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Take the same “accident”. The three patterns feel different:
に堪えない = expressing your own very deep feeling in a formal setting, like an official statement:
このような事故が起きたことは、誠に遺憾に堪えません。（That such an accident happened is deeply regrettable）
を禁じ得ない = something makes an emotion well up involuntarily, with the focus on “can't hold it back”:
遺族の話を聞いて、涙を禁じ得なかった。（Hearing the bereaved family's story, I couldn't hold back my tears）
てたまらない = the colloquial “so ～ I can't stand it”, for personal feelings or physical sensations:
あの映像を思い出すと、つらくてたまらない。（When I remember that footage, it hurts so much I can't bear it）
Quick rule: for “deeply ～” in a statement or speech, use に堪えない. For “can't help ～ing”, use を禁じ得ない. For “so ～ I could die” with a friend, use てたまらない.
What to learn next
In the affirmative form 「〜に堪える」, the meaning becomes “withstand ～, be worth ～”: 大人の鑑賞に堪える作品だ。（This is a work worthy of adult appreciation）. 「〜に足る」 is close in meaning, so it's worth studying together.
n1-39:
The idea in one line
「〜てやまない」 is like English “sincerely hope ～” or “never cease to ～”. やむ means “stop”, as in 雨がやむ (the rain stops). So 願ってやまない literally means “the wish won't stop”, that is, a deep, intense feeling you keep in your heart all the time. It's a formal, written expression, common in speeches, congratulatory messages and essays.
How to attach it
Verb て-form + やまない. It's usually written in hiragana as やまない, and rarely in kanji.
願う → 願って → 願ってやまない
期待する → 期待して → 期待してやまない
In formal settings, when speaking to someone, use the polite form やみません. For past feelings, use やまなかった.
Almost always it follows a verb of feeling: 願う, 祈る, 望む, 期待する, 愛する, 尊敬する, 信じる, 憧れる.
How you'll most often see it
Speeches, congratulationsWishing someone well. This is the most typical use.
・皆様のご健康を祈ってやみません。（I sincerely wish you all good health）
Your own convictionUsed in writing to express a long-held belief.
・私は彼の才能を信じてやまない。（I have always believed in his talent）
CaptivatingThe subject is a thing, and it means the thing keeps drawing people in deeply.
・この町の景色は、今も多くの人を魅了してやまない。（The scenery of this town still captivates so many people）
Modifying a nounWhen talking about someone else's feelings, it often goes before a noun as a modifier.
・祖父が愛してやまなかった海（The sea my grandfather loved all his life）
Common mistakes
・It may be glossed as “nonstop”, but it is not for an action that keeps going. 雨が降ってやまない and 走ってやまない are both wrong. For rain that keeps falling, just say 雨がやまない. It's only for feelings and wishes.
・It attaches only to verbs, not adjectives. “So happy I can't stand it” can't be 嬉しくてやまない. Say 嬉しくてたまらない.
・It's very formal. Saying 君を愛してやまない to a friend in casual chat would sound like you're reading from a script.
・In formal settings, when speaking to someone, use 願ってやみません. Don't say 願ってやまないです.
・At the end of a sentence, the subject is usually “I”. Other people's feelings mostly appear in writing, or before a noun as in the example above.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Take the same topic, “hometown”. The three feelings differ:
てやまない = a deep feeling held in the heart for a long time, written style: 故郷を愛してやまない。（I love my hometown dearly）
てたまらない (N2) = a feeling right now that's so strong you can't stand it, and it works in speech too: 故郷に帰りたくてたまらない。（I'm dying to go back to my hometown）
を禁じ得ない = a feeling that wells up involuntarily when you see something: 故郷の変わりように驚きを禁じ得ない。（Seeing how my hometown has changed, I can't help but be surprised）
Quick rule: for long-held wishes, love and beliefs, use てやまない. For a feeling that is intense right now, such as distress or a strong craving, use てたまらない. For a reaction you can't help when something moves you, use を禁じ得ない.
n1-56:
The idea in one line
「〜なくして（は）」means "without ~, there's no way…". You put something very important in front, then say "without it, this simply can't happen" to stress that this thing is absolutely indispensable. The tone is very formal, and you'll mostly see it in essays, speeches and award acceptance remarks.
How to connect it
Attach なくして directly to a noun, with no 「が」 or 「を」 in between:
努力 → 努力なくして協力 → 協力なくしては
What follows is always an "impossible / can't be done" expression. The most common are あり得ない (can't exist), できない, and 語れない (can't be talked about).
To put an action in front, use "dictionary form + ことなくして": 苦労する → 苦労することなくして
When to use it
Making an argumentExplaining the conditions you can't do without behind a success or result.
・日々の努力なくして成功はあり得ない。(Without daily effort, success is impossible.)
・信頼関係なくして、いいチームは作れない。(Without mutual trust, you can't build a good team.)
・苦労することなくして、本当の喜びは味わえない。(Without hardship, you can't taste true joy.)
Thank-you speechesLooking back and saying "it wouldn't have been possible without you." The ending is often in the past tense.
・皆様のご協力なくしては、このプロジェクトは成功しませんでした。(Without everyone's cooperation, this project would not have succeeded.)
EvaluationSaying that a person or thing is so important you can't leave them out.
・彼の存在なくして、日本のサッカーの歴史は語れない。(You can't tell the history of Japanese soccer without mentioning him.)
Common mistakes
・What follows must be "impossible / can't be done." You can't say 「努力なくして成功した」, because that contradicts itself.
・Don't add 「を」: 財布をなくして困った means "I lost my wallet and was in trouble." That's the verb なくす (to lose), which has nothing to do with this grammar.
・Put something truly important in front, like effort, love, cooperation or trust. With something trivial like an umbrella it sounds exaggerated; in daily life just say 傘がないと出かけられない.
・It's stiff, so you won't use it when chatting with friends. In casual speech, 「〜がなかったら、〜できない」 is enough.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
All three can thank people for their help:
なくしては = without ~, it can't be done (most formal): 皆様の協力なくしては、成功できませんでした。
なしには = almost the same meaning, a little less stiff: 皆様の協力なしには、成功できませんでした。
あっての = the reverse angle, "B exists only because of A": 皆様の協力あっての成功でした。 (This success was thanks to everyone's help.)
Note that 「なしに」 without は can also simply mean "did ~ without doing ~ first": 連絡なしに休んだ。 (I took the day off without telling anyone.)
なくして has no such use; it's only for "it's impossible without it."
Quick test: if what follows is "impossible / can't be done," both なくして and なしには work, and なくして is more formal. If it's "just did it without ~," only なしに works. If you want to talk from the "having it" side, use あっての.
What to learn next
「〜あっての」 (B exists thanks to A) is the flip side of なくして, so it's best to learn the two together: お客様あっての商売だ。 (Business exists because of customers.)
n1-57:
The idea in one line
「にして」 is a very stiff written-style expression, a bit like literary English: "only at fifty did he…", "in a single night", "at once a doctor and a writer." It has three common meanings: "only when/at ~" (including "only ~ can"), "in an instant", and "both ~ and ~". The first two often carry a sense of "that's quite something / I never expected that." "Both ~ and ~" simply lines up two roles or qualities; it's formal and dignified and doesn't necessarily imply surprise.
How to connect it
Basically it follows a noun: 50歳 → 50歳にして
The "both ~ and ~" use also often follows na-adjectives (adjectives that take な, like 簡潔な). Drop the な and attach it: 簡潔な → 簡潔にして
When to use it
Only when ~Put a "stage" in front, such as an age, an attempt number, or a year. It's often followed by 初めて or ようやく, meaning "only after getting this far did it finally…".
・三度目の挑戦にして、ようやく合格した。(It took until my third attempt to finally pass.)
・50歳にして初めて海外に行った。(He went abroad for the first time at 50.)
Followed by なお, it becomes "even at this stage, still…":
・彼は90歳にしてなお現役の医者だ。(Even at 90, he is still an active doctor.)
Only ~ canPut a person in front to mean "only this kind of person could do it." It's often written 「〜にして初めて」.
・これは彼にして初めてできる仕事だ。(This is work that only he could do.)
・この親にしてこの子あり。(Like father, like son.)
In an instantIt follows very short spans of time like 一瞬 and 一夜, meaning "in the blink of an eye…". In speech, people just say 一瞬で.
・町は一瞬にして炎に包まれた。(The whole town was engulfed in flames in an instant.)
・彼女は一夜にしてスターになった。(She became a star overnight.)
Both ~ and ~「AにしてB」 = having both A and B at once. It means the same as 「で」: 医者で作家 is the everyday way to say it, while 医者にして作家 is the formal, written way.
・彼は医者にして作家でもある。(He is both a doctor and a writer.)
・説明は簡潔にして明快だった。(The explanation was concise and clear.)
Also, 幸いにして (fortunately) and 不幸にして (unfortunately) are fixed phrases; just memorize them as single words:
幸いにして、けが人はいなかった。(Fortunately, no one was injured.)
Common mistakes
・For "only when ~," put a life stage or a count in front (an age, which attempt, which year). You can't just drop in a clock time; 「3時にして」 is wrong.
・This is the language of writing, speeches and news. Using it with friends sounds affected; in speech, 「で」 or 「〜歳で初めて」 is enough.
・With na-adjectives, drop the な: it's 簡潔にして, not 「簡潔なにして」.
・Don't confuse it with the te-form of 「〜にする」: ジュースにして飲む means "make it into juice and drink it," which has nothing to do with this grammar. Judge by context.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
にして = something happens only at this stage:
50歳にして初めてパソコンを買った。(I bought a computer for the first time at 50.)
にしては = "for ~, it's rather…", a comment that differs from the usual expectation:
50歳にしては体力がある。(For a 50-year-old, he has good stamina.)
Quick test: if 「初めて／ようやく／なお」 follows and says something finally happened or is still true, it's にして. If what follows evaluates "how it compares with the norm," it's にしては. One extra 「は」 changes the meaning a lot.
n1-59:
The idea in one line
「〜には当たらない」means "there's no need to ～" or "no reason to ～". You use it to comment calmly: this isn't that big a deal, and that kind of reaction is overblown. For example, no need to be surprised, no need to be sad, no need to scold anyone. It's close to saying "What's the big deal?" in English, but the tone is more formal, so you'll see it mostly in essays, commentary, and formal speech.
How to attach it
Verb dictionary form (the base form you look up in a dictionary) + には当たらない
驚く → 驚くには当たらない (no need to be surprised)
悲観する → 悲観するには当たらない (no need to be pessimistic)
For a politer tone, say 〜には当たりません. The 「は」 is sometimes dropped, as in 驚くに当たらない, with the same meaning.
When to use it
Commenting on an overblown reactionUsually the reason comes first, like "because that's just how it is" or "it's only this much", and then the conclusion follows: "so there's no need to ～".
・彼はずっと努力してきたのだから、合格したのも驚くには当たらない。 (He's been working hard all along, so it's no surprise that he passed.)
・一度失敗したくらいで、悲観するには当たらない。 (You've only failed once, so there's no need to be pessimistic.)
・子どもが言ったことだから、そんなに責めるには当たらない。 (It's just something a child said, so there's no need to blame them that much.)
What you'll hear most often
The verb in front is often a "reaction" verb: 驚く, 嘆く, 悲観する, 責める, 非難する, 褒める, 感心する.
The reason part often pairs with 〜くらいで (just because of something this small), 〜からといって (even if it's because of ～), and 〜のだから (since ～).
Easy mistakes
・The 当たる here has nothing to do with "winning a prize" or "hitting a target". Learn the whole phrase as one fixed expression.
・What comes before it is a reaction to something, or a judgment of it. For "no need to make a special trip", meaning "you don't have to go out of your way to do something", Japanese usually uses 〜には及ばない, not this one (compared below).
・With a noun, に当たらない often means something else: "doesn't count as ～, doesn't amount to ～". For example, これは違反には当たらない。 (This doesn't count as a violation.) As a beginner, just remember verb dictionary form + には当たらない = no need to ～.
・Translating it as "not worth ～" can mislead you into thinking "this thing has no value". What it really means is "that reaction is unnecessary and unreasonable", so "no need to ～" is more accurate.
Telling it apart from similar-looking phrases
には及ばない = no need to go to the trouble of doing (often caring, said to the other person)
Situation: a subordinate made a small mistake.
The boss says to the subordinate: わざわざ謝りに来るには及ばないよ。 (No need to come all the way to apologize.)
A colleague comments on the matter: 一度のミスで、そこまで彼を責めるには当たらない。 (It was just one mistake, so there's no need to blame him that much.)
に足りない = the target itself isn't significant enough to ～, not worth ～
Situation: there's a match tomorrow.
あんな相手は恐れるに足りない。 (An opponent like that is nothing to fear: the point is that the opponent is weak.)
初めての試合だからといって、恐れるには当たらない。 (Even though it's your first match, there's no need to be afraid: the point is that the fear is unnecessary.)
Quick tip: to say "that reaction isn't called for", use には当たらない. To say "no need to go to the trouble of doing it", use には及ばない. To say "the target itself has little weight", use に足りない.
n1-62:
The idea in one line
「〜がてら」means "while ～" or "on the side of ～". You head out once and take care of two things in one go: buying bread on a walk, or chatting while seeing a friend off at the station. The key is that one action serves two purposes, like killing two birds with one stone.
How to attach it
Noun + がてらThis is the most common pattern. The noun in front is an "action" noun, such as 散歩, 買い物, 見物 (sightseeing), 運動, ドライブ.
散歩 → 散歩がてら (while taking a walk)
・散歩がてら、パンを買ってきた。 (I went for a walk and bought some bread on the way back.)
・花見がてら、久しぶりに実家に帰った。 (I went back to my family home for the first time in a while, and saw the cherry blossoms while I was at it.)
ます-stem + がてらWith verbs, drop 「ます」 and add がてら directly.
送ります → drop ます → 送りがてら
・駅まで送りがてら、ちょっと話そうか。 (I'll walk you to the station, so let's chat a bit on the way.)
When to use it
The second half usually involves moving or going out, such as 行く, 来る, 寄る (to drop by), 歩く, 出かける. That's because "on the side" really means "since I'm going out anyway, I'll do this too".
・運動がてら、一駅歩いて帰った。 (For the exercise, I walked one extra station on the way home.)
Easy mistakes
・What comes before it must be an action. 散歩がてら works, but words that aren't actions, like 「雨がてら」 or 「休みがてら」, can't be used.
・The two things must be done by the same person.
・It isn't strictly written language. You'll hear it often in everyday conversation, and it's only slightly more mature-sounding than ついでに.
・It describes doing something on the side this one time, not doing two things in parallel over the long term. For long-term, use かたわら.
Telling it apart from similar-looking phrases
Take "going shopping and stopping by the post office":
ついでに = the most casual and handy one. The main trip is shopping, and the post office is incidental: 買い物のついでに、郵便局に寄った。
がてら = one trip out with two purposes: 買い物がてら、郵便局に寄った。
かたがた = very formal, mostly used for visits and greetings, often in business settings or letters: お礼かたがた、ご挨拶に伺いました。 (I came to thank you, and to pay my respects as well.)
かたわら = long-term, doing one thing as your main job while also doing another: 会社に勤めるかたわら、小説を書いている。 (I write novels while working at a company.)
ながら = doing two actions at the same time: 歩きながら電話する。 (I talk on the phone while walking.)
Quick tip: for everyday "while I'm at it", use ついでに or がてら. For visits and greetings to clients or elders, use かたがた. For doing both over the long term, use かたわら. For two simultaneous physical actions, use ながら.
What to learn next
Next, look at 〜かたがた and 〜かたわら. Memorize all three together, and multiple-choice questions on the exam will be easy to sort out.
n1-64:
The idea in one line
「〜ずくめ」is like English "all in black," "nothing but ~," "~ from start to finish". Looking at the whole picture, it's all one kind of thing: dressed head to toe in black, a whole year of one good thing after another, or rules everywhere you turn.
How to attach it
Just add ずくめ to a noun. It's that simple.
黒 → 黒ずくめいいこと → いいことずくめ規則 → 規則ずくめ
Once attached, it behaves like an ordinary noun:
Before a noun, add「の」：黒ずくめの男 (a man dressed all in black)
At the end of a sentence, add「だ」：いいことずくめだ
When the sentence continues, use「で」：規則ずくめで、疲れる
The patterns you'll hear most
ずくめ doesn't attach to just any noun. Japanese speakers mostly use a handful of set combinations, so the most practical thing is to memorize the ones below first.
Colors, clothingThe whole outfit is one color.
・黒ずくめの男が店に入ってきた。 (A man dressed all in black walked into the shop.)
Good thingsOne good thing after another.
・今年は結婚に昇進に、いいことずくめだった。 (This year I got married and promoted. Nothing but good news.)
・旅行中はごちそうずくめで、3キロも太った。 (Every meal on the trip was a feast, and I gained a full 3 kg.)
Rules, restrictionsBeing controlled at every turn, usually with a complaint about feeling tied down.
