・うちの会社は規則ずくめで、息が詰まる。 (My company is full of rules. It's suffocating.)
Common in the newsDescribing an event with many things that differ from the usual.
・今回の大会は異例ずくめだった。 (This tournament was unusual in every respect.)
As you can see, ずくめ is neither good nor bad in itself. The point is simply "uniformly the same throughout." 黒ずくめ is neutral, いいことずくめ is positive, and 規則ずくめ leans negative.
Easy mistakes
・It attaches only to nouns. To say "all delicious things," say 美味しいものずくめ or ごちそうずくめ. You can't attach it straight to an adjective, as in 美味しいずくめ.
・Dirt stuck on you doesn't take ずくめ: "covered in mud" is 泥まみれ, not 泥ずくめ; "drenched in sweat" is 汗まみれ.
・結構ずくめ (conditions so good you can't find fault) often carries a hint of suspicion: 結構ずくめの話には気をつけたほうがいい。 (You should be careful about deals that sound too good to be true.)
・You'll occasionally see it written「づくめ」. It's the same thing, but the usual spelling today is ずくめ.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Take the same piece of clothing and see how the three expressions differ:
ずくめ = uniformly one thing throughout: 黒ずくめの服 (an outfit that's black from head to toe)
まみれ = the surface is coated with liquid or powdery stuff, almost always negative: 泥まみれの服 (clothes covered in mud)
だらけ = so much of something that it's everywhere, mostly something undesirable: しわだらけの服 (clothes full of wrinkles)
Quick rule of thumb: uniformly one thing (outfits, good things, rules, and other set combinations) → ずくめ; stuck on the surface, coated all over → まみれ; so many that they're everywhere → だらけ.
n1-63:
The idea in one line
「〜まみれ」is like English "covered in mud," "drenched in sweat," "soaked in blood". The key is that things like mud, sweat, blood, or dust stick to the surface and coat it all over, and they're usually dirty or unpleasant.
When to use it
Body or object covered in something dirtyThe most basic use. Words that often go with it: 泥, 汗, 血, ほこり (dust), 油.
・泥まみれになって、子供と遊んだ。 (I played with the kids and got covered in mud.)
・汗まみれで家に帰ってきた。 (I came home drenched in sweat.)
・倉庫からほこりまみれのアルバムが出てきた。 (A dust-covered photo album turned up from the storeroom.)
Figurative: tangled up in something badYou can also use it for abstract things, as if you're wrapped up in debt or lies and can't shake them off.
・彼は借金まみれだ。 (He's up to his neck in debt.)
・あの人の話は嘘まみれだ。 (Everything that person says is a pack of lies.)
How to attach it
Simple: add まみれ directly to a noun: 泥 → 泥まみれ
After that, treat it as a noun. The most common forms are:
・〜まみれになる: to end up covered in ~
・〜まみれだ: (right now) covered in ~
・〜まみれで: while covered in ~ (doing something)
・〜まみれの＋名詞: (something) covered in ~　Example: 血まみれのシャツ (a blood-soaked shirt)
Easy mistakes
・まみれ gives the feeling of something stuck on, clinging to the surface, so don't use it for things that are merely "many." For a crowd, say 人でいっぱい or 人だらけ, not 人まみれ.
・For things that aren't "stuck on," like wounds or typos, use だらけ: 傷だらけ, 間違いだらけ.
・It's negative. Good or pretty things don't normally take まみれ, so for positive ideas like "covered in flowers" or "full of happiness," use another expression.
・Add「の」before a noun: it's 血まみれのシャツ, not 血まみれシャツ.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
だらけ = lots of, all over the place (the focus is on large quantity, scattered everywhere): この作文は間違いだらけだ。 (This essay is riddled with mistakes.)
まみれ = coated, stuck all over the surface (the focus is on being covered by liquid or powdery stuff): 顔が汗まみれだ。 (His face is drenched in sweat.)
For things like mud, sweat, and blood, both work: 泥だらけ and 泥まみれ are both fine, but まみれ paints a stronger picture of being thickly coated.
ずくめ = uniformly one thing from start to finish (not necessarily negative; it can be good things too): 黒ずくめの服 (an all-black outfit), いいことずくめ (nothing but good things)
まみれ, on the other hand, means being coated in something dirty: 泥まみれの服 (clothes covered in mud)
Quick rule of thumb: stuck on you, coated all over → まみれ; large quantity, everywhere → だらけ; uniformly one thing, all of it → ずくめ.
What to learn next
The pattern most often compared with this one is 〜ずくめ (uniformly ~, nothing but ~). Take a look at it next. Memorizing the two together is the best way to avoid mixing them up.
n1-69:
The idea in one line
「〜を皮切りに」means "starting with ~" or "kicking off with ~". Think of a concert: "We're starting with the Taipei show, then touring the whole country." The Taipei show is the 「皮切り」, the first leg. What matters is that a whole series of things follows.
「皮切り」originally meant the first moxibustion burn, the hottest and most painful one. It later came to mean "the first in a series of events."
When to use it
Events, toursThe first stop starts things off, and the rest follow one by one.
・東京公演を皮切りに、全国ツアーが始まった。(Starting with the Tokyo show, the nationwide tour got under way.)
Business expansionIt starts with the first store or the first product, then grows from there.
・この店は渋谷店を皮切りに、各地に店舗を増やしている。(Starting with its Shibuya store, this chain has been opening branches around the country.)
One person leads, others followSomeone speaks up first, and then everyone else chimes in.
・彼の発言を皮切りに、次々と意見が出た。(Once he spoke up, opinions came out one after another.)
The second half of the sentence often includes words like 次々と (one after another), 相次いで (in succession) or 各地で (in various places), to show that "a lot more is coming."
How to connect it
It attaches directly to a noun: 東京公演 → 東京公演を皮切りに
If you mean an action, you usually use its noun form: 発売 (release), 開店 (store opening), 発言 (remark).
Adding 「して」 means the same thing, so both forms work. 「を皮切りに」 without 「して」 is more concise and more common in writing: 東京公演を皮切りにして.
You will also see を皮切りとして, which means the same.
Common mistakes
・There must be a "series" afterward. If only one thing happens, you can't use it. 入学を皮切りに、一人暮らしを始めた is wrong because only one thing follows. Change it to 入学をきっかけに.
・It isn't simply "starting from ~". For a starting point in time, 「から」 is enough: 月曜日から仕事が始まる. Don't say 月曜日を皮切りに.
・It's rarely used for chains of bad events. For earthquakes, accidents and the like happening one after another, Japanese speakers generally don't use 皮切り. It's mostly used for events, business, competitions and other things that "unfold step by step."
・It sounds fairly formal and is common in news, reports and introductions. You'll rarely hear it in chats with friends.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Take the same concert: with different grammar, the meaning changes a lot.
を皮切りに = this show is the first stop, with many more to come:
・そのライブを皮切りに、彼らは全国を回った。(Starting with that concert, they toured the whole country.)
をきっかけに = because of this event, some change happened (not necessarily a series):
・そのライブをきっかけに、彼らは有名になった。(Thanks to that concert, they became famous.)
を限りに = the exact opposite: it's the last time, the end of the line:
・今日のライブを限りに、活動を休止する。(Today's concert is the last one; after it, they'll go on hiatus.)
Quick tip: use を皮切りに for "first stop, with a string of more to come"; use をきっかけに for "changed because of that event"; use を限りに for "the last time, ending here."
n1-75:
The idea in one line
「〜きらいがある」means "has a tendency to ~" or "is prone to ~", and it is always a negative tendency. The tone is like a teacher writing in a report card, "This student has a tendency to be hasty." It points out a flaw, but politely and indirectly. You'll mostly see it in writing, in commentary, or in fairly formal speech.
How to connect it
Verb dictionary form + きらいがある　抱え込む → 抱え込むきらいがある
Verb ない-form + きらいがある　聞かない → 聞かないきらいがある
Noun + の + きらいがある　独断 → 独断のきらいがある
・彼は何でも一人で抱え込むきらいがある。(He tends to take everything on by himself.)
・彼女は人の話を最後まで聞かないきらいがある。(She tends not to listen to people until the end.)
・彼のやり方は独断のきらいがある。(His way of doing things is a bit high-handed.)
How you'll hear it most often
〜すぎるきらいがあるEspecially common when criticizing "going too far."
・うちの部長は細かいことを気にしすぎるきらいがある。(Our department head tends to worry too much about small details.)
Talking about a groupUsed to comment on the overall style of a group, an organization or society.
・最近のニュースは話題性を重視しすぎるきらいがある。(Recent news tends to put too much emphasis on being talked about.)
Common mistakes
・It's written with the kanji 「嫌い」, but here it has nothing to do with "dislike". It means "tendency, flaw." Today it's mostly written in hiragana as きらい.
・It only works for negative tendencies. You can't use it to say someone is considerate. Say 優しいところがある instead.
・It describes a person's (or group's) usual style or personality, not something that happened once. You can't use きらいがある for "He was late yesterday."
・With a noun you must add 「の」: it's 独断のきらいがある, not 「独断きらいがある」.
・It sounds stiff. When chatting with friends and saying "He tends to overthink," 考えすぎるところがある or 考えすぎがちだ sounds more natural.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
All of these describe a person who easily leans toward the negative:
がち = "often ~, tends to ~". The focus is on frequency, and you can use it in everyday conversation: 彼は物事を悲観的に考えがちだ。 (He often looks at things pessimistically.)
きらいがある = "has a tendency to ~". It carries a flavor of gently commenting on someone's character, and it's more of a written style: 彼は物事を悲観的に考えるきらいがある。 (He has a tendency to look at things pessimistically.)
気味 = "a slight feeling of ~". It describes a mild state right now, not a personality trait: 最近、ちょっと疲れ気味だ。 (I've been feeling a bit tired lately.)
Also, がち can describe weather and natural phenomena (冬は空気が乾燥しがちだ, the air tends to be dry in winter), while きらいがある is basically only used to comment on the style of people or groups.
Quick tip: in conversation, use がち for "often ~" and 気味 for "a bit ~". Use きらいがある when you're writing a commentary or politely pointing out a person's or group's "bad habit."
What to learn next
It often appears together with 「ともすると・ともすれば」 (before you know it, ~): 人はともすると、楽な方を選ぶきらいがある。 (People tend to pick the easier path before they know it.)
n1-80:
The idea in one line
「〜にとどまらず」is the news-style “not limited to ~, but extending to ~.” とどまる means “to stay where you are,” so とどまらず means “it doesn't stop there.” You first name a smaller scope, then follow with a bigger one, like ripples spreading outward on water.
When to use it
Widening scopeIt's most often used for things that “spread”: influence, damage, popularity, events. You'll see it a lot in news, reports and speeches. It's written and formal.
・彼女の人気は日本にとどまらず、アジア全体に広がっている。(Her popularity isn't limited to Japan. It has spread across all of Asia.)
・この問題は一つの会社にとどまらず、業界全体に関わる。(This problem doesn't involve just one company. It affects the whole industry.)
Going a step further with an actionYou can also put an action before it, meaning “not only did ~, but went even further and ~.”
・ボランティアたちは物資を届けるにとどまらず、被災者の話にも耳を傾けた。(The volunteers didn't just deliver supplies. They also listened to the survivors' stories.)
How to attach it
Noun ＋ にとどまらず: 国内 → 国内にとどまらず
Verb dictionary form (the base form you'd look up in a dictionary) ＋ にとどまらず: 届ける → 届けるにとどまらず
You'll also often see 国内だけにとどまらず with 「だけ」 added. The meaning is the same, just a bit more emphatic.
At the end of a sentence or when modifying a noun, it becomes にとどまらない:
・彼の才能は音楽にとどまらない。(His talent isn't limited to music.)
Easy mistakes
・It's とどまる, not とまる. 涙が止まらない means “the tears won't stop,” which has nothing to do with this grammar. Don't drop the 「とど」.
・You must follow it with a bigger scope, often with 「も」「まで」「へと」: 海外にも、全国へと. If you say only the first half, the sentence feels unfinished.
・It's very formal, so don't use it for small everyday things. For “I didn't just eat ramen, I had sushi too,” just say ラーメンだけじゃなくて、寿司も食べた. Using にとどまらず there would sound like you're reading a press release.
・The affirmative にとどまる (without the negative) is also common, with the opposite meaning: “stay limited to ~.” 今回の値上げは一部の商品にとどまる。(This price increase is limited to some products.)
Telling similar patterns apart
Let's say an anime is popular:
だけでなく = the most ordinary “not only ~ but also ~,” usable in any situation: このアニメは子どもだけでなく、大人にも人気だ。(This anime is popular not only with kids but with adults too.)
に限らず = not limited to one category, and the same goes for others: このアニメは子どもに限らず、大人にも人気だ。(It's not just kids. Adults like it too, so basically everyone does.)
にとどまらず = the scope spreads outward: このアニメの人気は日本にとどまらず、世界中に広がっている。(Its popularity isn't limited to Japan. It has spread all over the world.)
はおろか = the first item goes without saying, and even the most extreme case is true too: このアニメは、子どもはおろか、お年寄りまで知っている。(Never mind kids, even elderly people know this anime.)
Quick rule of thumb: use にとどまらず when influence or scope keeps growing; に限らず for “not limited to any one type”; はおろか for “even the most extreme case”; and when in doubt, だけでなく is the safest.
n1-81:
The idea in one line
「〜すら」means “even ~…”. You pick the most basic example, the one least likely to be a problem, to show how extreme the situation is: 名前すら知らない means you don't even know the name, so you certainly don't know anything else. The meaning is close to 「さえ」, but the tone is harder and more literary, and it often appears in articles, news and commentary.
How to attach it
Noun ＋ すらThe most basic pattern. The original 「が」「を」 is simply replaced by すら.
時間がない → 時間すらない (there isn't even time)
・忙しくて、食事する時間すらない。(I'm so busy I don't even have time to eat.)
Noun ＋ ですらVery common when the noun is a person who is performing the action. The 「で」 here doesn't mean “at/in,” so just memorize 「ですら」 as a set.
・専門家ですら答えられない問題だ。(This is a question even experts can't answer.)
・子どもですら知っていることだ。(This is something even children know.)
Noun ＋ に・と etc. ＋ すらParticles like 「に」「と」 stay, and すら goes after them.
・このことは親にすら話していない。(I haven't even told my parents about this.)
て-form ＋ すらいないThis emphasizes the action itself: they haven't even gotten as far as doing it.
・彼はメールを読んですらいない。(He hasn't even read the email.)
Easy mistakes
・すら is not only for negatives. Most of the time it's followed by 「ない」, but an affirmative sentence like 子どもですら知っている is perfectly natural.
・You can't drop 「に」「と」: say 親にすら, not 親すら話していない.
・メールすら読んでいない means “hasn't even read the email” (the focus is the email), while メールを読んですらいない means “hasn't even read it” (the focus is the act of reading). Where you put すら changes what you emphasize.
・すら sounds stiff. In casual conversation with friends, 名前も知らない or 名前さえ知らない is more natural.
・すら often carries a feeling of surprise, disbelief or criticism, so it's rarely used to praise someone.
Telling similar patterns apart
すら and さえ are almost interchangeable in the “even ~” sense:
名前すら知らない。／名前さえ知らない。 (I don't even know the name.)
The difference is that すら is more literary, and さえ also has a use that すら doesn't have: 「〜さえ〜ば」 = “as long as ~.”
時間さえあれば行ける。 (As long as I have time, I can go.)
You can't replace さえ with すら in this sentence.
Quick rule of thumb: for “even ~,” either works, and すら gives more punch in writing. For “as long as ~,” only さえ works.
What to learn next
すら is often paired with 「〜はおろか」 (let alone ~), with the hard thing first and the easy thing after:
漢字はおろか、ひらがなすら書けない。 (Let alone kanji, I can't even write hiragana.)
n1-1:
The idea in one line
「〜に至っては」 means “as for ~, it's even worse…” or “and ~ is the extreme case, where…”. First you say how things are for everyone or overall, then you pick out the single most extreme case and talk about that.
It's like complaining: “Everyone in my family is terrible at getting up in the morning, and my dad is the worst. He doesn't get out of bed until noon.”
How to connect it
Noun + に至っては.
父 → 父に至っては数学 → 数学に至っては
The whole sentence usually goes: general situation → 〇〇に至っては → the most extreme thing.
・うちの家族はみんな朝が弱い。父に至っては、昼まで起きてこない。(Everyone in my family struggles in the morning. My dad is the worst: he doesn't get up until noon.)
・成績が悪く、数学に至っては赤点だ。(My grades are bad, and in math I actually failed.)
・会議では誰も意見を言わなかった。部長に至っては、最初から最後まで寝ていた。(Nobody gave an opinion in the meeting. The department head was the worst: he slept from start to finish.)
The second half often includes emphatic expressions like 「さえ」「まで」「一度も〜ない」 to make the sense of extremity even stronger.
Common mistakes
・You must first have a whole group (a group of people, several subjects, a whole situation) before you can “pick out the most extreme one.” If you suddenly say 「父に至っては…」 with nothing before it, a Japanese listener won't know what you're comparing against.
・It's almost always used for bad or jaw-dropping things. Using it to praise someone, like “he's even better, he got a perfect score,” sounds odd.
・What follows has to be the truly extreme case. If it's only an ordinary level, this pattern sounds like making a big fuss over nothing.
・This is a written, formal expression. When chatting with friends, people more often say 「父なんか、昼まで寝てるよ」.
・It's read いたっては; 「至」 is read いた.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
に至っては = picks out the most extreme one from the whole (mostly negative):
・部屋はどこも汚かった。台所に至っては、足の踏み場もなかった。(Every room was dirty. The kitchen was the worst: there was nowhere to even put your feet.)
に至るまで = from A to B, everything included; it stresses a wide range and works for good or bad:
・リビングから台所に至るまで、全部きれいに掃除した。(From the living room to the kitchen, I cleaned everything until it was spotless.)
ときたら = simply singles out one person to complain about. You don't need to mention a group first, and the tone is more casual and carries dissatisfaction:
・うちの父ときたら、毎晩飲んで帰ってくる。(Speaking of my dad, he comes home drunk every night.)
・家族はみんなお酒好きだが、父に至っては毎晩飲んで帰ってくる。(Everyone in my family loves drinking, but my dad is the extreme case: he comes home drunk every night.)
Quick rule of thumb: first “everyone is ~,” then “and so-and-so is even worse” → に至っては; “everything from A to B” → に至るまで; just “honestly, I can't stand so-and-so” → ときたら.
n1-4:
The idea in one line
「〜たりとも…ない」 means “not even one ~”, in a more emphatic version. Think of someone slamming the table and saying “Not a single cent!” or “Not one minute is to be wasted!” That firm, no-compromise tone is what たりとも gives in Japanese.
How to connect it
The formula is fixed: 「一」 + counter + たりとも + negative.
一日 → 一日たりとも (not even one day)
一円 → 一円たりとも (not even one yen)
一人 → 一人たりとも (not even one person)
What follows must be negative: things like 〜ない, 〜ません, 〜できない, 許されない, 〜するな.
The most common combinations: 一秒, 一瞬, 一日, 一円, 一人, 一歩, 一滴, 一度. These are all “smallest units,” stressing that not even that tiny amount is acceptable.
When to use it
Strong resolveYou absolutely won't or don't want to do something.
・残り時間、一秒たりとも無駄にしたくない。(I don't want to waste even one second of the time left.)
Rules and orders“Not allowed,” “not permitted.” Very common with bosses, coaches and public notices.
・試合が終わるまで、一瞬たりとも気を抜くな。(Until the match is over, don't let your guard down for even a moment.)
・医療ミスは一件たりとも許されない。(Not a single medical error can be tolerated.)
Strong emotionOften paired with 「〜たことはない」 to express “never once.”
・君のことを一日たりとも忘れたことはない。(There hasn't been a single day when I forgot you.)
One special fixed expression
何人たりとも = “no one, whoever they are, is allowed to ~.” Here 何人 is read なんぴと. It's very stiff, written language, often seen in notices, novels and anime lines.
・何人たりとも、ここに立ち入ることは許さない。(No one, whoever they are, is allowed to set foot here.)
Common mistakes
・Only 「一」 can come before it: 二日たりとも and 三人たりとも are both wrong. The whole point is the “smallest amount.”
・What follows is always negative. You can't say something positive like 「一日たりとも休む」.
・Attach たりとも directly after the counter. Don't add 「も」 or 「の」: 「一日もたりとも」 is wrong.
・The tone is heavy and bookish. In everyday chat, 一円も払わない is enough; switching to たりとも would sound like you're swearing an oath or making a declaration.
・To simply describe a fact (for example, “there wasn't a single student in the classroom”), 一人もいなかった is more natural. たりとも suits resolve, rules and strong emotion.
・The 何人 in 何人たりとも is read なんぴと, not なんにん.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Let's compare three ways of talking about money:
一〜も…ない = simply “there isn't even one,” neutral and everyday: 財布には一円もない。 (There isn't a single yen in my wallet.)
一〜たりとも…ない = a strong stance, no compromise: 税金は一円たりとも無駄にできない。 (Not even one yen of tax money can be wasted.)
すら = names one “most basic thing” for emphasis, and doesn't need “一 + counter” before it: 今月は電車代すらない。 (This month I don't even have money for the train.)
Quick rule of thumb: just stating “there isn't even one” → も; “一 + counter” with a tone of resolve, prohibition or absolute refusal → たりとも; pointing to “even something this basic ~” → すら.
n1-5:
The idea in one line
「〜であれ」 means "no matter who/what it is, ..." or "even if it's ~, ...". For example, "Everyone has to wait in line, no matter who they are" or "Even the company president has to follow the rules." Whatever you put in front, the conclusion that follows doesn't change. It's very formal and mostly shows up in news, speeches and writing.
How to form it
Put a noun in front and add であれ directly: 社長 → 社長であれ
For na-adjectives, drop 「な」 and add であれ: 有名な → 有名であれ
You can also use question words like 「誰、何、どんな～」: 誰 → 誰であれどう → どうであれ
「であれ」 is actually the imperative form of 「である」 (the written-style version of 「だ」, common in prose). But here it is not telling anyone to do something. It's a concessive use meaning "it doesn't matter what it is", i.e. "even if it's ~".
The three most common patterns
たとえ＋noun＋であれEven if it's some special status or situation, the result is the same. 「たとえ」 (even if) is often added to strengthen it.
・たとえ子供であれ、自分のしたことには責任がある。(Even a child is responsible for what they've done.)
誰／何／どんな～＋であれNo matter who or what it is, it's all the same.
・誰であれ、許可なく入ることはできない。(No matter who you are, you can't enter without permission.)
・理由はどうであれ、約束を破ったのは事実だ。(Whatever the reason, the fact is that you broke the promise.)
AであれBであれWhether it's A or B, the result is the same.
・男であれ女であれ、能力があれば評価される。(Whether you're a man or a woman, you'll be recognized if you have ability.)
・晴れであれ雨であれ、試合は予定どおり行う。(Rain or shine, the match will go ahead as planned.)
The second half is usually a conclusion that won't change because of this. Common endings are 「〜できない」, 「許されない」, 「〜べきだ」 and 「変わりはない」.
Common mistakes
・What comes before must be a noun or the stem of a na-adjective. A verb can't connect directly: you can't say 「行くであれ」. If you want a verb there, use 「〜ようが」 or 「〜にせよ」 instead.
・It's stiff, and sounds odd in everyday conversation. In speech, use 「でも」 instead, for example: 誰でも許可が必要だよ。 (Everyone needs permission, you know.)
・To say "nobody can get in", use 誰も入れない, not 誰でも入れない (which sounds very unnatural). To say "not just anyone can get in", say 誰でも入れるわけではない.
・であれ and であれば differ by only one syllable, but the meanings are completely different. であれば means "if it's ~": 社長であれば決められる。 (If it's the president, he can decide.) であれ means "even if it's ~": 社長であれ、勝手には決められない。 (Even the president can't decide on his own.)
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Here are three ways to say "Whatever the reason, being late is not OK":
であれ: a noun or na-adjective stem comes before it; the most formal.
どんな理由であれ、遅刻は許されない。
にせよ: can follow a noun or a verb; a little less stiff.
どんな理由にせよ、遅刻はよくない。
行くにせよ行かないにせよ、連絡してください。 (Whether you go or not, please let me know.)
ようが／ようと: attaches to the volitional form of a verb (the 〜う／〜よう form), with the feel of "no matter how much ~, it makes no difference".
どんな理由があろうと、遅刻は許されない。
Quick rule of thumb: if a noun comes before it and the situation is very formal, use であれ. If you want a verb there, use にせよ or ようが.
What to learn next
Other "whether A or B" patterns include 「〜にせよ…にせよ」 and the set phrases with 「〜かれ〜かれ」: 多かれ少なかれ (more or less) and 遅かれ早かれ (sooner or later).
n1-6:
The idea in one line
「〜とあれば」 means "if it's ~, then (I'll) ...". What comes before it is a special, weighty reason, such as "for the kids," "the boss's order," or "a close friend's request." What follows is "then I'm willing to do it" or "then I have no choice but to do it." It has the feel of "If it's for my children, no hardship is too much."
How to form it
Nouns attach directly: 子供のため → 子供のためとあれば
Na-adjectives also attach directly: 必要 → 必要とあれば
Verbs use the plain form (dictionary form, ない form or た form): 社長が来る → 社長が来るとあれば
When to use it
Willing to sacrificeFor an important person or cause, you'll do anything. It most often appears together with 「のため」.
・子供のためとあれば、親はどんな苦労も厭わない。(If it's for their children, parents will gladly endure any hardship.)
・家族のためとあれば、どんな仕事でもする。(If it's for my family, I'll do any kind of work.)
Having to acceptThe person or situation is special enough that refusing wouldn't be right.
・親友の頼みとあれば、断るわけにはいかない。(If it's a close friend asking, I can't very well refuse.)
・社長の命令とあれば、従うしかない。(If it's the president's order, we have no choice but to obey.)
Where you'll hear it most
You'll hear these two set phrases a lot in business settings:
・必要とあれば、いつでもご連絡ください。(If necessary, please contact me at any time.)
・お客様のご希望とあれば、できる限り対応いたします。(If it's the customer's wish, we'll accommodate it as far as we can.)
Common mistakes
・What comes before must be a weighty reason. Don't use it for ordinary everyday conditions: for "If it rains, I'll take an umbrella", say 雨なら傘を持っていく. 「雨とあれば」 sounds strange.
・What follows is usually a resolve or judgment, such as 何でもする, 喜んで, しかない or わけにはいかない, not a plain description of something that happened.
・After a noun, attach とあれば directly; you don't add だ.
・The tone is formal and bookish. With friends, just say 子供のためなら, which means about the same and is more relaxed.
・The "for" meaning comes from the のため before it. とあれば itself only means "if it's ~", so not every sentence has a "for" sense.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
「とあれば」 and 「とあって」 both start with 「と＋あ…」 and differ only slightly at the end. 「ともなれば」 also starts with と and looks similar. Let's compare them using the same "president" situation:
とあれば = if it is ~, then... (hypothetical; followed by resolve): 社長の命令とあれば、従うしかない。 (If it's the president's order, we have no choice but to obey.)
とあって = because it is ~, so... (a fact that has already happened; followed by a description of the situation): 社長の命令とあって、みんな必死に働いている。 (Because it's the president's order, everyone is working frantically.)
ともなれば = once you reach the status or level of ~, naturally...: 社長ともなれば、責任も重くなる。 (Once you become president, the responsibility naturally gets heavier.)
Quick rule of thumb: for "if it's ~, I'm willing / I have no choice", use とあれば. For "because it's ~, things are like this now", use とあって. For "once you reach the level of ~, naturally...", use ともなれば.
n1-17:
The idea in one line
「〜そばから」means "no sooner have you done X than Y undoes it again". You're working on something here, and over there it's immediately undone, and it happens every time, so the effort is wasted. Picture yourself mopping the floor, and your kid walks straight over it in slippers. You mop, they stomp, over and over. That helpless feeling is そばから.
How to form it
Add そばから directly after the dictionary form or the た form of a verb.
片付ける → 片付けるそばから (just as I tidy up)
覚えた → 覚えたそばから (just after memorizing)
The two forms mean about the same. If you really want to split hairs, the dictionary form feels more like "as I'm doing it, it's being ruined," and the た form feels more like "the moment I finish, it's ruined."
When to use it
Effort cancelled outYou do something, and it's immediately undone.
・覚えたそばから忘れてしまう。 (I forget things the moment I memorize them.)
・雪かきしたそばから、また積もっていく。 (The moment I finish shoveling snow, it piles up again.)
In one end, out the otherSomething arrives and is gone right away, so you can't hold on to it.
・稼ぐそばから使ってしまうので、全然貯金できない。 (I spend money as fast as I earn it, so I can't save anything.)
・掃除するそばから、犬が毛を落としていく。 (As soon as I clean, the dog sheds hair all over again.)
The second half often pairs with 〜てしまう or 〜ていく, or uses the passive 〜される (e.g. 子供に散らかされる). This conveys the feeling that "things are out of my control and I can't do anything about it."
Common mistakes
・そばから is about things that happen repeatedly. You can't use it for a one-time event. For example, you can't say 「家に着いたそばから雨が降り出した」 for "It started raining the moment I got home." For that, use とたん or や否や.
・It's almost always used in situations of complaint, resignation, or wasted effort. When good things keep coming, you normally wouldn't use そばから.
・The second half describes "how things just are," so it can't take expressions of will or command like 「I'll ～」 or 「Please ～」.
・The そば here isn't 「蕎麦」 (buckwheat noodles). It means 「旁邊」, "beside." Think of it as "I've just done it, and right beside me it's already ～."
Telling it apart from similar patterns
〜が早いか and 〜や否や also mean "as soon as ～, ～," but they describe one particular occasion, where two things happen back to back, with no sense of wasted effort.
Take the same topic, getting paid:
そばから: 給料が入るそばから使ってしまう。 (My pay gets spent the moment it comes in, every month.)
や否や: 給料が入るや否や、新しいスマホを買った。 (The moment my pay came in that one time, I bought a new phone.)
Quick test: use そばから for "it happens every time, and what I did is wasted." Use が早いか or や否や for "on that one occasion, the next thing followed right after the first."
n1-21:
The idea in one line
「〜んがため（に）」means "in order to ～, at all costs". It means "for the purpose of" just like 「ために」, but the tone is much stronger, with a drive of "I have to achieve this." It's very old-fashioned. You almost never hear it in everyday conversation, and you're more likely to see it in novels, speeches, and opinion pieces.
What is this 「ん」?
The 「ん」 here is not a negative. It's a classical-Japanese form meaning "want to ～" or "intend to ～," close to modern 「〜う／〜よう」. 「が」 works like 「の」. So 勝たんがため is roughly "the purpose of wanting to win," in other words "in order to win."
How to form it
Put the verb in its ない form, drop ない, then add 「んがため（に）」.
Group 1 (godan verbs):
勝つ → 勝たない → 勝たんがため
守る → 守らんがため
売る → 売らんがため
言う → 言わんがため (verbs ending in う change to わ, same as in the ない form)
Group 2 (ichidan verbs):
生きる → 生きない → 生きんがため
逃れる → 逃れんがため
Group 3: する becomes せ, not し.
する → せんがため
優勝する → 優勝せんがため
「来る」 almost never appears in this pattern, so don't worry about memorizing it.
How you'll most often see it
んがためにGoes in the first half of the sentence, followed by what was done to achieve it.
・勝たんがために、彼は必死に練習した。 (To win, he practiced desperately.)
・生きんがために、どんな仕事でもした。 (To stay alive, I took any job.)
んがための＋nounModifies the noun that follows. 売らんがため often has a negative nuance, meaning "thinking only of making a sale."
・売らんがための広告には、もううんざりだ。 (I'm fed up with ads that only care about selling.)
んがためだGoes at the end of the sentence, explaining "the reason for doing that was ～."
・彼が嘘をついたのは、自分を守らんがためだった。 (He lied in order to protect himself.)
Common mistakes
・The form for する is せんがため. 「しんがため」 is wrong.
・「ん」 is not a negative: 勝たんがため means "in order to win," not "in order not to win."
・The second half must be something a person does deliberately, usually a goal the same person wants to achieve. You can't use it for the weather or natural phenomena.
・The second half can't be a request or command like 「please ～」 or 「go and ～」: 合格せんがため、勉強しなさい sounds unnatural. Say 合格するために、勉強しなさい instead.
・Used for small things, it sounds exaggerated and funny. If you're going to the convenience store for bread, パンを買うために is plenty.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Take one situation: "To pass, I studied late every night."
ために = the ordinary "in order to," usable anywhere: 合格するために、毎晩遅くまで勉強した。
べく = the written-style "in order to." It attaches directly to the dictionary form, and する can become すべく: 合格すべく、毎晩遅くまで勉強した。
んがため = even more old-fashioned, with a "even at the risk of my life" feel: 合格せんがため、毎晩遅くまで勉強した。
Another one to watch out for is んばかりに. The form before it is exactly the same, but the meaning is completely different: "looking as if ～ were about to happen."
泣かんばかりに頼んだ。 (I begged so hard I was almost in tears.)
Quick test: 「ん」 followed by がため means "in order to"; followed by ばかり it means "almost ～." To say "in order to," use ために in everyday speech and べく in writing. Save んがため for when you want to convey "at all costs."
n1-7:
The idea in one line
「〜をおいて」 means "no one but ~" or "who else but ~?". The speaker runs through all the possible people or things in their head and concludes that only this one is truly the right fit. It's not just saying "only." It also carries a very high opinion of that one choice.
How to connect it
Noun + をおいて + ほかに〜ない／いない
Use いない when you're talking about people, and ない for things, times and places.
彼 → 彼をおいてほかにいない (no one but him)
今 → 今をおいてほかにない (no other time but now)
How you'll hear it most
PeopleMost common when recommending someone, or praising them as the one and only choice.
・次のリーダーにふさわしいのは、山田さんをおいてほかにいない。 (For our next leader, nobody fits but Yamada.)
Timing今をおいてほかにない is a set phrase meaning "it's now or never."
・留学するなら、今をおいてほかにない。 (If you're going to study abroad, now is the time.)
Rhetorical questionThe ending doesn't have to be 「ない」. You can also use a "who else?" rhetorical question, which means the same thing: "only him."
・この役を演じられるのは、彼をおいて誰がいるだろうか。 (Who else but him could play this role?)
Where people go wrong
・You can't use it for plain facts. "There was no one in the room but him" is just an objective situation. Say 部屋には彼以外誰もいなかった, not をおいて.
・It's normally used for positive evaluations, like "the best fit," "the greatest," or "only he can do it." Using it for bad things sounds odd.
・をおいて and において differ by only one character but mean completely different things. 会議室において means "in the meeting room," marking a place or occasion.
・This is fairly formal, written-style language, common in articles, speeches and the news. When chatting with friends, just say 彼しかいないよ.
・何をおいても is a different idiom meaning "above all else, whatever happens": 何をおいても駆けつける (I'll rush over no matter what). Don't mix it up with the "nothing other than ~" meaning.
Telling similar-looking patterns apart
Say you're talking about one really excellent old shop:
をおいて = picks out the single one from a field of candidates: この味を出せるのは、あの店をおいてほかにない。 (No place but that shop can produce this flavor.)
ならでは = a characteristic that only it has: これはあの店ならではの味だ。 (This is a flavor unique to that shop.)
以外 = simply says "other than ~", with no evaluation: あの店以外で食べたことがない。 (I've never eaten anywhere other than that shop.)
Quick test: if you're saying "in choosing who or which, this is the only answer," use をおいて. If you're saying "this trait belongs exclusively to it," use ならでは. If you're just stating "other than ~" objectively, use 以外.
n1-11:
The idea in one line
「〜ならまだしも」 means "~ would be one thing, but…". You first take a step back and say, "if it were only this, I could accept it," then point out, "but at the level it's actually at, it's not okay." The weight of the sentence is in the second half: you're complaining and saying you can't accept it.
・一度ならまだしも、三度も遅刻するなんて。 (Once would be one thing, but being late three times!)
Breaking it down
You can think of まだしも as "まだ (still) + しも (adds emphasis)," meaning "still passable." So the sentence structure is always:
a milder, tolerable situation + ならまだしも, a more serious, unacceptable situation.
The mild situation in the first half is often not what actually happened and is only there for contrast. With 冗談ならまだしも, the implication is "you're clearly not joking."
How to connect it
Nouns: attach directly. 冗談 → 冗談ならまだしも
な-adjectives: attach directly, without だ. 下手 → 下手ならまだしも
Verbs and い-adjectives: use the plain form (the casual form, without ます or です). 知らない → 知らないならまだしも
When to use it
Dissatisfaction with something that already happened
・知らないならまだしも、知っていて黙っていたのは許せない。 (Not knowing would be one thing, but I can't forgive that you knew and kept quiet.)
Judging a situation that hasn't happened yetThe second half doesn't have to be about the past. It can also be a judgment about a hypothetical or the future.
・夏はまだしも、冬はこの部屋じゃ無理だ。 (Summer might be fine, but there's no way I could live in this room in winter.)
Asking someone to stopThe second half can also be a request or a prohibition.
・一日ならまだしも、毎日来るのはやめてほしい。 (One day would be fine, but I really wish you'd stop coming every day.)
How you'll hear it most
After a noun you'll also often hear はまだしも used directly, like 夏はまだしも above, with the same meaning.
Another pattern with a very close meaning is ならともかく, and in many cases the two are interchangeable.
Where people go wrong
・The order can't be reversed: put the mild case first and the serious one second. Saying 三度ならまだしも、一度遅刻するなんて makes no logical sense.
・Don't add だ after nouns and な-adjectives: it's 冗談ならまだしも, not 冗談だならまだしも.
・The second half must be a negative evaluation (things like ありえない, 許せない, 無理だ, やめてほしい). You can't use it to praise or talk about good things.
・The tone is complaining or scolding. Saying it directly to a superior or a customer can sound accusatory, so be careful about the setting.
Telling similar-looking patterns apart
Say you see a grown adult crying over something trivial:
ならまだしも: 子どもならまだしも、大人がこんなことで泣くなんて。 (A child would be one thing, but a grown adult crying over something like this!)
ではあるまいし: 子どもではあるまいし、こんなことで泣かないで。 (You're not a child, so don't cry over something like this.)
The point of ならまだしも is the gap between "the first part I could accept" and "this level is not okay," and it's often used to complain or say you can't accept something. The point of ではあるまいし is "it's not like you're ~," which denies the premise before telling the other person what they should do or giving a judgment.
Quick test: if you want to say "A would be fine, but B is too much," use ならまだしも. If you want to say "it's not like you're A, so you should…," use ではあるまいし.
n1-24:
The idea in one line
「〜とあって」is a favorite in news and reports. It means "because it's such a special occasion, naturally…". Think of English news lines like "With the holiday weekend just starting, the airport was packed with travelers." That "with…" feeling is what it captures. First you name a special day or occasion, then you describe the scene or reaction that followed.
When to use it
Special days and occasionsLong weekends, big sales, fireworks festivals: things that don't happen every day, so there are more people and more excitement than usual.
・連休初日とあって、空港は大混雑だった。(It was the first day of the long weekend, so the airport was incredibly crowded.)
・年に一度のセールとあって、店の前には朝から長い列ができていた。(It was the once-a-year sale, so a long line had formed in front of the store since early morning.)
People's reactionsBecause the situation is rare, the people involved are nervous, excited, or extra serious.
・初めての海外旅行とあって、娘はずいぶん張り切っている。(It's her first trip abroad, so my daughter is really fired up.)
・人気歌手が来るとあって、会場には若い人が大勢集まった。(A popular singer was coming, so tons of young people gathered at the venue.)
How to attach it
Nouns: attach directly, usually without 「だ」.
連休 → 連休とあって花火大会 → 花火大会とあって
Verbs and い-adjectives: use the plain form (no ます or です; past tense is fine too).
来る → 来るとあって優勝した → 優勝したとあって安い → 安いとあって
Common mistakes
・The second half can only describe an actual result or situation you can observe. You can't put your own intentions, invitations, or requests there.
×連休とあって、旅行に行こう。
○連休だから、旅行に行こう。 (It's a long weekend, so let's go on a trip.)
・The first half needs to be something special or rare. An everyday reason sounds odd. For something like "I was hungry, so I bought bread," just use 「から」or「ので」.
・Nouns usually don't take だ: say 連休とあって, not 連休だとあって.
・This is a written, news-style tone. When chatting with friends, 「〜から」or「〜ので」sounds more natural.
Telling similar patterns apart
Here's the same "company president" situation with three patterns:
とあって = because it's ~, this is the result we see (something that has already happened)
社長が来るとあって、社員はみんな緊張している。 (The president is coming, so all the employees are nervous.)
とあれば = if it's ~, then (I'm willing to)… (hypothetical, conditional)
社長の頼みとあれば、断るわけにはいかない。 (If it's a request from the president, I can't very well refuse.)
にあって = being in the position or situation of ~
社長という立場にあって、そんな発言は許されない。 (In the position of president, a remark like that is not acceptable.)
Quick tip: "Because it's ~, (everyone) naturally…" is とあって; "if it's ~" is とあれば; "being in the midst of ~" is にあって.
n1-25:
The idea in one line
「〜ばこそ」means "precisely because ~, …". It's close to「からこそ」but more formal, the kind of phrasing you'd see in essays or speeches. It's often used when something that looks bad actually has a good reason behind it, like "I scold you precisely because I love you."
When to use it
Stating the real reasonOthers may misunderstand your behavior, and you want to stress "I'm doing this because ~."
・あなたを思えばこそ、厳しく言うのです。(It's precisely because I care about you that I speak harshly.)
・信頼していればこそ、この仕事を任せたのです。(It's precisely because I trust you that I entrusted this job to you.)
Only possible with this conditionEmphasizes that a certain good condition is the key.
・若ければこそ、失敗を恐れずに挑戦できる。(Only because you're young can you take on challenges without fearing failure.)
・健康であればこそ、好きなことに挑戦できる。(Only because you're healthy can you take on what you love.)
How to attach it
First put the preceding word into its 「〜ば」form, then add こそ.
Group 1 (godan verbs): change the last sound to the え-row sound of the same row, then add ば.
思う → う becomes え → 思えばこそ
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): drop る and add れば.
信じる → 信じればこそ
Group 3 (する・来る): する → すればこそ来る → 来ればこそ (くればこそ)
For 「〜ている」, change いる to いれば: 案じている → 案じていればこそ
い-adjectives: change い to ければ. 若い → 若ければこそ
Nouns and な-adjectives: add であれば. 親 → 親であればこそ健康 → 健康であればこそ
・親であればこそ、子どもの幸せを願うのだ。(It's precisely because we're parents that we wish for our children's happiness.)
Common mistakes
・The 「ば」here is not "if"; it means "because." 思えばこそ doesn't mean "if you think of (them)" but "precisely because I think of (you)." This is a holdover from classical Japanese, which is why it looks identical to the conditional form.
・Nouns and な-adjectives can't attach directly: say 健康であればこそ, not 「健康ばこそ」.
・The tone is very formal and rarely used in conversation. With friends, just use からこそ; ばこそ would sound like you're reading a script.
・The reason in the first half is usually positive and sincere (love, trust, health, effort). It's not really used for bad luck or negative causes.
・The second half often ends with のだ／のです, giving a "this is actually the reason" feel. Watch for that in the examples.
Telling similar patterns apart
からこそ = precisely because ~, …; works in both speech and writing: 好きだからこそ、厳しく言うんだよ。 (It's precisely because I like you that I'm being tough.)
ばこそ = same meaning, but more formal, mostly in essays and speeches: 愛すればこそ、厳しく言うのである。 (It is precisely because I love them that I speak sternly.)
あっての = "~ exists only thanks to…"; attaches to a noun and stresses "without it, it doesn't hold up": 健康あっての人生だ。 (Life exists only with health.)
Quick tip: use からこそ in everyday speech; use ばこそ when writing or giving a speech and you want a solemn tone; use あっての when you mean "without it, there's nothing."
What to learn next
Among other N1 ways to express reasons, take a look at 〜ゆえ（に） (because of ~; even more formal, written style) and 〜あっての.
n1-12:
The idea in one line
「AこそあれB（ない）」means “there is A, but there's no B”, or more plainly, “only A, no B.” Think of “I feel only gratitude toward him, no resentment.” It's stiff written language. In everyday conversation, just say 「Aはあっても、Bはない」.
When to use it
Only A, no BPut a pair of opposite or contrasting things on either side, such as gratitude and resentment, or criticism and praise. First you admit that A really exists, then the point is to stress that B is “simply not there.”
・彼には感謝こそあれ、恨みは少しもない。(I feel only gratitude toward him, not the slightest resentment.)
・彼の行動には批判こそあれ、賞賛の声はほとんど聞かれない。(His actions draw only criticism; you hardly hear any words of praise.)
Set phrases程度の差こそあれ、多少の違いこそあれ＝“there may be a difference in degree, but…” Here the second half is not necessarily negative. It's often used to say “everyone is actually the same.”
・程度の差こそあれ、誰にでも悩みはある。(The degree may differ, but everyone has worries.)
How to form it
Noun + こそあれ directly: 感謝 → 感謝こそあれ批判 → 批判こそあれ
The second half usually ends with 「〜はない」, 「ほとんど〜ない」 or 「〜ことはない」.
Common mistakes
・What comes before it must be a noun. You can't attach a dictionary-form verb directly; 「批判するこそあれ」 is wrong. To use a verb, switch to「こそすれ」 below, and attach it to the ます-stem (the ます form with ます removed).
・It does not mean “precisely because there is ~.” That's a common misunderstanding from older textbooks; “precisely because” is a different grammar point.
・The two sides must be a contrasting pair within the same topic. If they're unrelated, for example “the festival has a simple feel, but shows no signs of decline,” a Japanese person will find it odd.
・The tone is very formal and it mostly shows up in essays, commentary and speeches. Say it to a friend and you'll sound like you're reading an official notice.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
こそすれ also means “only A, no B,” but what comes before it is an action.
Formation: verb ます-stem (drop ます) + こそすれ
上がります → drop ます → 上がりこそすれ
褒められます → drop ます → 褒められこそすれ
For する verbs you can use either 「noun + こそすれ」 or 「し + こそすれ」: 感謝します → 感謝こそすれ／感謝しこそすれ
・物価は上がりこそすれ、下がることはないだろう。(Prices will only go up, never down, I think.)
・褒められこそすれ、叱られる理由はない。(He should be praised; there's no reason to scold him.)
Compare them in the same situation:
彼女には感謝こそあれ、恨みはない。(What I have in my heart is gratitude: this talks about “existence.”)
彼女には感謝こそすれ、恨むことはない。(What I do is thank her: this talks about an “action.”)
The two sentences mean almost the same thing in English.
Also, “precisely because ~” is 〜ばこそ, and “only by ~ can you ~” is 〜てこそ, as in 努力してこそ成功できる (only through effort can you succeed). Don't mix them up with こそあれ just because they all contain こそ.
Quick test: if a noun comes before it (感謝, 批判, 差), use こそあれ. If a verb comes before it, use こそすれ, and first turn the verb into the ます form and drop ます, as in 「上がり（こそすれ）」「褒められ（こそすれ）」「感謝し（こそすれ）」. Never write 「褒められるこそすれ」.
n1-13:
The idea in one line
「〜まで（のこと）だ」is like English “worst case, I'll just ~” and “I only ~, that's all.” まで originally means “up to,” and here you can think of it as “things only go as far as this point, no big deal.” The meaning changes depending on whether a dictionary form or a た form comes before it, so let's take them separately.
When to use it
Dictionary form: worst case, I'll just ~When a plan doesn't work out, you've already thought of a fallback, and your attitude is “fine, I'll just do this.” It's very often preceded by 「〜なら」「〜ば」「〜ても」, first stating “if things go badly.”
・だめなら、また一からやり直すまでだ。(If it doesn't work, I'll just start over from scratch.)
・誰も手伝ってくれないなら、一人でやるまでだ。(If nobody will help, I'll just do it by myself.)
・電車が動かなければ、歩いて帰るまでのことだ。(If the trains aren't running, I'll just walk home.)
た form: I only ~, that's allYou use it to explain something you did, meaning “I had no other intention” or “it's nothing special.” It's very common when someone thanks you, and it sounds modest.
・当然のことをしたまでです。(I only did what anyone should do.)
・念のため、確認したまでです。(I just checked to be on the safe side, that's all.)
・思ったことを言ったまでだ。(I merely said what I was thinking.)
How to form it
Verb dictionary form + までだ／までのことだ: やり直す → やり直すまでだ
Verb た form + までだ／までのことだ: した → したまでです
With or without 「のこと」 the meaning is the same, but adding it gives more of a “that's all there is to it” feel. To be polite, just replace だ with です.
Common mistakes
・The まで here is not “until.” 帰るまで on its own means “until I go home,” so check whether it's closed off with だ.
・Don't mix up the dictionary form and the た form: やり直すまでだ means “I'll just redo it” (not done yet), while やり直したまでだ means “I only redid it” (already done).
・The dictionary-form usage carries a “do or die” tone and normally expresses your own resolve; you don't use it to tell someone else what to do.
・What comes before it is usually a backup plan that wasn't your first choice but is fine anyway, not something happy and good.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
〜までだ = I'll just do it if I have to: 聞かれたら、説明するまでだ。(If I'm asked, I'll just explain.)
〜までもない = there's simply no need to do it: 簡単だから、説明するまでもない。(It's simple, so there's no need to explain.)
〜までだ = there's still a way out, optimistic: 失敗したら、またやるまでだ。(If I fail, I'll just try again.)
〜ばそれまでだ = once that happens, it's all over, pessimistic: 一度失敗すれば、それまでだ。(Fail once and it's over.)
Quick test: “verb + までだ” means there's still a path ahead; 「それまでだ」means the path is cut off; 「までもない」means there's no need to take that path at all.
n1-26:
The idea in one line
「〜手前」 is like English "I said I'd do it, so I can't back out now…" or "With everyone watching, I can't lose face…". Because of something you already said or did, or because people are watching, you have to protect your own face and standing. So you end up doing something, or not being able to do something.
When to use it
You already said itA verb comes before it, usually something you already said or did. Since you said it, you can't now make yourself look bad by going back on it.
・引き受けた手前、途中でやめるわけにはいかない。(Since I took the job on, I can't just quit halfway.)
・「絶対合格する」と言った手前、遊んでいられない。(After boasting "I'll definitely pass," I can't be out having fun.)
People are watchingA person comes before it, meaning "in front of ～" or "considering how ～ will see me." What you're protecting is your own image in those people's eyes.
・みんなの手前、そんなことは言えない。(In front of everyone, I can't say something like that.)
・子どもの手前、夫婦げんかはしないようにしている。(For the kids' sake, we try not to argue in front of them.)
Your own positionUse 「〜である手前」 to talk about your own role. It means "as a ～, I can't possibly…"
・教師である手前、生徒の前でたばこは吸えない。(As a teacher, I can't smoke in front of my students.)
How to attach it
Verbs: attach directly to the plain form (the form without ます). The た-form is the most common; the dictionary form and the ている-form also work.
約束した → 約束した手前言っている → 言っている手前
Nouns: add 「の」 first.部下 → 部下の手前
The second half usually expresses "have to" or "can't," for example 〜わけにはいかない, 〜しかない, 〜られない, 〜ないといけない.
Common mistakes
・It's about the face and standing of yourself (or the subject of the sentence), not about protecting the other person's face. 部長は部下の手前、ミスを認めにくかった。 means the department head couldn't bring himself to admit a mistake in front of his subordinates. What he's protecting is his own image, not his subordinates' pride.
・The second half almost always has a forced feeling, like "have no choice but to ～" or "can't ～." It doesn't go with happy or exciting things. Something like 「約束した手前、楽しみだ」 sounds odd.
・手前 is read てまえ. Originally it means "this side, just before something," as in 駅の手前で降りる (get off just before the station). When you see 「noun + の手前」, check the context: if a person comes before it and what follows is something you can't do or have to do, it's this grammar point, not a location.
・It's fairly formal and bookish. In everyday conversation you're more likely to hear something like 「言っちゃったし…」.
Don't confuse it with similar patterns
〜からには and 〜以上 also translate as "now that ～," but the focus is different:
からには／以上 = now that ～ has happened, you should and must see it through. The focus is on logic and resolve.
手前 = now that ～ has happened, not doing this would be embarrassing. The focus is on how others see me.
・約束したからには、必ず行く。(Since I promised, I'll definitely go: resolve.)
・約束した手前、行かないわけにはいかない。(I promised them, so I can't very well not go: saving face.)
After からには and 以上 you can put something you want to do, but not after 手前:
日本に来たからには、富士山に登りたい。(Now that I'm in Japan, I want to climb Mt. Fuji.)
Swapping in 手前 here doesn't work, because climbing Mt. Fuji has nothing to do with saving face.
Quick test: if you can add "or else it'd be embarrassing / I couldn't justify it" after the clause, use 手前. If it's just "now that ～, I should ～," use からには or 以上.
n1-32:
The idea in one line
「〜ところを」 is most commonly like English "Thank you for taking the time out of your busy schedule" or "Sorry to disturb you while you're resting." You first name the state the other person is in (busy, resting, tired), then follow with thanks or an apology. It's a very formal, polite set phrase. It can also mean "you would normally ～, but…"
When to use it
Politeness: disturbing someonePut the other person's situation before it, then "thank you," "sorry," or what they did for you. It shows up constantly in business calls, speeches, and emails.
・お忙しいところをありがとうございます。(Thank you, even though you're so busy.)
・お休みのところ、申し訳ありません。(I'm sorry to disturb you while you're off.)
・お疲れのところ、すみません。少しだけいいですか。(Sorry to bother you when you're tired. Do you have a moment?)
Should have been ～, butThe first part says what would normally happen, and the second says that something else actually happened, usually something in your favor.
・本来ならこちらから伺うべきところを、わざわざお越しいただきました。(We should have been the ones to visit you, but you kindly made the trip yourself.)
・普通なら罰金のところを、今回は注意だけで済んだ。(Normally it would have been a fine, but this time I got off with just a warning.)
How to attach it
Verbs: attach directly.
休んでいる → 休んでいるところを
伺うべき → 伺うべきところを
い-adjectives: attach directly; in polite speech お is often added in front.
忙しい → お忙しいところを
な-adjectives: add な first.
大変 → 大変なところを
Nouns: add の first.
お休み → お休みのところを
ご多忙 → ご多忙のところを
In speech 「を」 is often dropped, so お忙しいところ is perfectly fine.
Common mistakes
・Don't add の after an い-adjective: it's お忙しいところ, not お忙しいのところ. Only nouns take の.
・This is very formal. Saying 「お忙しいところを」 to a friend sounds stiff and distant. Between friends, 忙しいのにごめんね is enough.
・In the polite usage, what comes before it is the other person's state, not your own. If you're busy yourself but still helping, you wouldn't say 「私の忙しいところを」.
・What follows usually affects the other person: disturbing them, troubling them, or something they did for you. You can't follow it with something unrelated to them.
Don't confuse it with similar patterns
ところを＋見る／見つかる = the scene in which someone got caught. This is the N3 ところ plus the object marker を, not a polite phrase: タバコを吸っているところを先生に見られた。 (I got seen by my teacher while I was smoking.)
ところを (should have been ～, but) = it would normally go one way, but it actually had a good result: 普通なら怒られるところを、許してもらった。 (I would normally have been scolded, but I was forgiven.)
ものを = "if only you had ～," with a tone of complaint or regret, often at the end of a sentence: 一言言ってくれればよかったものを。 (If you'd just said a word, it would have been fine.)
Quick test: if what follows is 「見られた、見つかった」 → a caught-in-the-act scene. If it's thanks, an apology, or a benefit → the polite use or "should have been ～, but." If the whole sentence is a complaint like "I wish you had ～" → ものを.
What to learn next
A very similar pattern, also common in polite speech, uses 「中」: お足元の悪い中、お越しいただきありがとうございます。 (Thank you all for coming despite the bad weather.)
n1-42:
The idea in one line
「Aと言わずBと言わず」means "whether it's A or B, all of it is ～". You name two representative parts so the listener feels that the whole thing is like this. It's like saying in English "mud on his hands, mud on his feet" when you really mean he's filthy from head to toe.
・手と言わず足と言わず、泥だらけになった。(Hands and feet alike, everything was covered in mud.)
How to form it
Noun + と言わず + noun + と言わず. Each of the two nouns takes its own 「と言わず」.
「言わず」is a more literary form of「言わない」. Literally it means "not saying A, not saying B", i.e. "making no distinction between A and B". It's also often written in hiragana: といわず.
When to use it
BodyFrom head to toe, the whole body.
・顔と言わず腕と言わず、蚊に刺されてしまった。(Face, arms, everywhere, I got bitten by mosquitoes.)
PlaceThe whole space, the whole area.
・壁と言わず床と言わず、部屋中に落書きがしてあった。(Walls and floor alike, the whole room was covered in graffiti.)
TimeNo matter the time of day, it's constant.
・昼と言わず夜と言わず、工事の音が響いている。(Day and night, the sound of construction never stops.)
・平日と言わず週末と言わず、この店はいつも行列ができている。(Weekdays or weekends, this shop always has a line.)
You'll notice the second half often contains "all of it" words like 部屋中, 町中, いつも and だらけ. They echo the "A and B alike" in the first half.
Common mistakes
・You need 「と言わず」 twice. 手と足と言わず is wrong; say 手と言わず足と言わず.
・A and B should be the same kind of thing, and parts of one whole (hands and feet = the whole body, day and night = all day). Pairing two unrelated things sounds odd.
・It describes what you actually see, and usually something surprising or not so good (covered in mud, wounds everywhere, nonstop noise).
・It's written, fairly stiff language, more common in novels and news reports. In everyday conversation Japanese people usually say 手も足も or どこもかしこも.
・Don't confuse it with a standalone 「と言わず」: 明日と言わず、今すぐ行こう。 (Not tomorrow, let's go right now.) That means "no need to wait for A", which is a different pattern.
・In 何も言わずに帰った (left without saying anything), 「言わず」 really means "not speaking". It has nothing to do with this pattern.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Both mean "whether A or B", but Aであれ Bであれ feels different:
と言わず = describes the actual situation in front of you, it's like this everywhere:
駅前と言わず住宅街と言わず、どこも観光客であふれている。 (Whether in front of the station or in residential areas, tourists are everywhere.)
であれ = the same rule or judgment applies no matter which one:
駅前であれ住宅街であれ、ごみを捨ててはいけない。 (Whether in front of the station or in a residential area, you must not litter.)
The second sentence states a rule, so switching to と言わず would sound unnatural.
Quick test: if you're describing "everywhere you look, it's like this", use と言わず. If you're stating a rule or judgment that holds "whichever one it is", use であれ.
n1-44:
The idea in one line
「名詞＋ったら」is like the English "Honestly, my brother…!" or "Oh, that mother of mine…". You first single out someone close to you, then talk about something they did that's both annoying and funny. The point is exasperation and complaint, but with affection. You're not really scolding.
How to form it
Just add 「ったら」 right after the noun. No conjugation needed.
弟 → 弟ったらお母さん → お母さんったらあなた → あなたったら
When to use it
Complaining to someone elseWhen chatting with a friend about family, coworkers or pets, it introduces the topic of "there they go again".
・うちの猫ったら、また私の椅子で寝てる。(Honestly, my cat is sleeping on my chair again.)
・父ったら、また眼鏡をなくしたの。(Honestly, my dad lost his glasses again.)
Scolding someone to their faceYou address the person directly to mean "Oh, you!" It's often paired with「もう」.
・もう、お母さんったら！その話はしないでって言ったでしょ。(Oh, Mom! I told you not to talk about that.)
・田中さんったら、冗談ばっかり。(Honestly, Tanaka, you're always joking around.)
The rest of the sentence often trails off, as in 弟ったら、また忘れ物して…。 (My brother, honestly, he forgot something again…). The unspoken part is that little sigh.
Common mistakes
・It is not "if". The たら in 雨が降ったら means "if ～", while noun + ったら means "speaking of ～, honestly…". They're completely different.
・The tone is casual and familiar, used for family, friends and pets. It's not suitable to say to a boss or customer's face, or in formal settings.
・What follows is usually something that leaves you speechless, exasperated or a little embarrassed. To simply praise or thank someone, a plain「は」is enough. Even with something good, the feeling is a shy or exasperated "oh, they're too polite, honestly".
・The small っ before たら takes a one-beat pause: say「ったら」, not「たら」.
・You'll also hear お母さんってば, which has a very similar tone to ったら and is also colloquial.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
ったら = exasperation mixed with affection, and you can also use it to address the person directly:
うちの子ったら、またゲームばっかり。 (Honestly, my kid is playing video games again.)
ときたら = a more serious telling-off with a stronger negative feeling. It's mostly said to someone else, not used to address the person to their face:
うちの子ときたら、毎日ゲームばっかりで全然勉強しない。 (As for my kid, he does nothing but play video games every day and never studies.)
ったらない = usually follows an adjective and means "extremely ～". It has nothing to do with complaining about a person:
あの時は恥ずかしいったらなかった。 (I was so embarrassed back then, you have no idea.)
Quick test: if you say "honestly!" with a smile, it's ったら. If you say it with a frown while listing grievances, it's ときたら. If ったら is followed by「ない」and comes after an adjective, it means "extremely ～".
What to learn next
Next, study ～ときたら to tell apart the two tones: affectionate complaint and serious scolding.
n1-35:
The idea in one line
「〜の至り」 means “extremely ~” or “~ beyond words”, as in “I’m deeply honored” or “I’m utterly grateful.” 光栄の至りです means “I am honored to the very highest degree.” It’s very formal. You’ll hear it in ceremony speeches, award acceptance remarks, and business letters, but you wouldn’t say it when chatting with friends.
What is 「至り」?
至り is a noun made from the verb 至る (to reach), and it means “reaching the very peak.” So 光栄の至り = honor at its peak = honored beyond measure.
How to form it
Noun + の至り, and the sentence usually ends with です or でございます.
光栄 → 光栄の至りです
感激 → 感激の至りでございます
Note that the nouns that go in front are almost always the same few. You can’t plug in just any noun.
The forms you’ll hear most
Gratitude and honorThe most common are 光栄の至り and 感激の至り.
・このような賞をいただき、光栄の至りです。(To receive an award like this is an honor beyond words.)
・皆様から温かいお言葉をいただき、感激の至りです。(I’m deeply moved to receive such warm words from all of you.)
Apology and embarrassmentCommon ones are 恐縮の至り (I feel terribly sorry / deeply obliged) and 赤面の至り (so embarrassed my face turns red).
・お忙しいところお越しいただき、恐縮の至りでございます。(I’m deeply grateful, and sorry, that you took the trouble to come when you’re so busy.)
・こんな初歩的なミスをしてしまい、赤面の至りです。(Making such a basic mistake is utterly embarrassing.)
The odd one out若気の至り works a little differently. It refers to “mistakes made out of youthful naivety.” Here 至り is closer to “the result of.” People often use it to look back on foolish things they did in the past, with a touch of self-mockery, so it isn’t necessarily formal.
・学生時代は若気の至りで、ずいぶん無茶をした。(In my student days I did a lot of reckless things out of youthful folly.)
Where learners slip up
・What goes in front is noun + の. You can’t attach it directly to an adjective. 嬉しいの至り and ありがたいの至り are both wrong. To express happiness or thanks, use the fixed pairings 光栄 and 感激.
・Don’t swap in nouns on your own. Memorizing 光栄・感激・恐縮・赤面・若気 is the safest approach.
・This phrase is mainly about your own feelings, and it carries a humble tone. Using it for someone else’s feelings, such as saying “the department head is extremely honored,” sounds very odd.
・The tone is extremely formal. If you say ケーキありがとう、感激の至り！ to a friend, it sounds like you’re joking and putting on airs.
・若気 is read わかげ, not わかき.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
の至り = your own gratitude or embarrassment reaching its peak, in a humble tone: お招きいただき、光栄の至りです。 (Being invited is an honor beyond words.)
極まりない = something or someone’s attitude is “extremely ~”, mostly used to criticize or complain: 連絡もなく欠席するなんて、失礼極まりない。 (Being absent without even a word is extremely rude.)
に至る = a verb meaning that things “develop to a certain result or point”: 何度も話し合った結果、ようやく合意に至った。 (After talking it over many times, we finally reached an agreement.)
Quick test: use の至り for your own “extremely ~” feelings, 極まりない to scold or complain that something is “extremely ~”, and に至る for things that “end up reaching ~”.
What to learn next
〜に堪えない is another way to express strong feelings on formal occasions: 皆様のご支援には感謝に堪えません。 (I can’t thank you enough for everyone’s support.)
n1-41:
The idea in one line
「〜といったらない」 means “incredibly ~,” “so ~ you can’t describe it,” “~ beyond words”. Literally it’s “if you talk about how ~ it is, there are simply no words to describe it.” You use it to emphasize that a feeling is intense to the extreme. It works for both good and bad things: incredibly happy, freezing cold, mortifyingly embarrassed, and so on.
How to form it
Noun + といったらない (most often an adjective turned into a 「～さ」 noun)
寒い → change い to さ → 寒さといったらない
い-adjective: attach directly
うれしい → うれしいといったらない
な-adjective: drop な and attach directly
退屈 → 退屈といったらない
When talking about something in the past, change it to 「といったらなかった」.
・初めて富士山を見た時の感動といったらなかった。(The emotion I felt when I first saw Mt. Fuji was beyond words.)
・毎日同じ作業ばかりで、退屈といったらない。(It’s the same task every day, so boring I can’t stand it.)
The forms you’ll hear most
ったらないA shortened, spoken version of 「といったらない」. You hear it a lot when chatting with friends or venting, and it’s mostly attached directly to an い-adjective.
・隣の工事、うるさいったらないよ。(The construction next door is unbelievably loud.)
ったらありゃしないAn even more colloquial and emotional version, mostly used for complaints, embarrassment, and anger.
・みんなの前で転ぶなんて、恥ずかしいったらありゃしない。(Falling in front of everyone was so embarrassing I wanted to die.)
Where learners slip up
・The 「ない」 here is not a negation. うれしいといったらない means “I’m overjoyed,” not “I’m not happy.”
・Don’t add な to な-adjectives: say 退屈といったらない, not 退屈なといったらない.
・If it’s already over, use 「といったらなかった」. Otherwise it sounds like it’s still happening.
・What goes in front is usually an adjective or a noun, especially a 「～さ」 noun. Verbs are rarely attached directly.
・「ったらない」 and 「ったらありゃしない」 are very colloquial. Don’t use them in formal situations or with your boss.
・Don’t confuse it with 「といったら (speaking of ~)」: 日本といったら、やっぱり寿司だ。 (Speaking of Japan, it’s sushi, of course.) There’s no ない afterward, and the meaning is completely different.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
〜ったら（n1-44）: attached to a person, it means “honestly, that ~,” with a tone of exasperation or complaint, followed by a full sentence.
うちの母ったら、また夜中に電話してきた。 (Honestly, my mom called in the middle of the night again.)
うちの母、心配性ったらない。 (My mom is unbelievably anxious.)
Quick test: if 「ったら」 is followed right away by 「ない」 and what comes before is an adjective or a 「～さ」 noun, it’s about degree. If what comes before is a person and a full sentence follows, you’re complaining about that person.
〜極まりない（n1-34）: also means “extremely ~,” but it’s stiffer and more written, and mostly used for negative judgments, as in news reports or complaint letters. 「といったらない」 is more about your own firsthand feelings and works for both positive and negative things.
あの店員の態度は失礼極まりない。 (That clerk’s attitude is extremely rude: like a formal complaint.)
あの店員の態度の悪さといったらなかった。 (That clerk’s attitude was unbelievably bad: like telling a friend about what happened.)
Quick test: use 「極まりない」 for formal writing and harsh criticism, and 「といったらない」 for your own feelings with a bit of emotional exaggeration.
n1-45:
The idea in one line
「〜ときたら」 works like an English complaint such as "Honestly, my son…" or "Don't even get me started on…". You name a person or thing that drives you up the wall, then rattle off what's wrong with it. The core feeling is dissatisfaction, exasperation, and "what can you do?"
How to connect it
Add ときたら directly to a noun, usually a person or a thing.
うちの息子 → うちの息子ときたら（talk about my son…）
このパソコン → このパソコンときたら（this computer, honestly…）
When to use it
Complaining about people around youMost often used for family, coworkers, and bosses: people close to you who give you headaches.
・うちの息子ときたら、ゲームばかりしている。（My son, honestly, does nothing but play video games all day）
・うちの部長ときたら、会議のたびに話が長い。（Our department head, honestly, talks forever at every meeting）
Complaining about thingsIt works for things that don't work well, too.
・このパソコンときたら、すぐ固まるんだから。（This computer, honestly, freezes all the time）
Scolding yourselfIt's perfectly natural to aim it at yourself, too.
・私ときたら、また傘を電車に忘れてきた。（Honestly, me… I left my umbrella on the train again）
Leaving it unfinishedIn speech, people often skip the actual complaint and stop at ときたら, letting their tone show the annoyance.
・まったく、うちの主人ときたら……（Honestly, my husband…）
Common mistakes
・It's for complaining to a third party about someone or something. You can't use it to address the person directly. Saying 「お母さんときたら！」 to your mom's face is wrong.
・What follows is a description or a complaint. Don't follow it with a request or decision like "please do ~" or "let's ~". Something like うちの部長ときたら、早く帰ってください, with a request attached, is wrong.
・It's basically negative, so don't use it to praise someone. うちの息子ときたら、頭がいい would sound odd.
・It's casual and chatty, and rarely used in formal writing or reports.
・In speech you'll sometimes hear 夏ときたら、やっぱりビールでしょ。（Speaking of summer, it's got to be beer, right?）This "talking about A, you think of B" use is a different usage, not a complaint, so don't mix them up when you hear it.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
ったら: It can also complain, but the tone is lighter, often with an affectionate "what am I going to do with you?" feel, and you can say it to the person's face.
もう、お母さんったら！（Oh, Mom, honestly!）: said to your mom, which is fine
ときたら: The criticism is harsher, and you can only use it when talking to others about that person.
うちの母ときたら、人の話を全然聞かない。（My mom, honestly, never listens to anything anyone says）: complaining to a friend
に至っては: You first mention a group of people or a bunch of things, then pick out the most extreme one.
みんな遅刻したが、田中さんに至っては来なかった。（Everyone was late, but Tanaka was even worse: he didn't show up at all）
ときたら doesn't need a comparison. You just single someone out and complain about them.
Quick rule of thumb: to say "honestly, you!" to someone's face, use ったら; to complain to others about a specific person, use ときたら; to pick the worst case out of a group, use に至っては.
What to learn next
It often appears together with 「まったく」 and 「〜んだから」, which make the complaint even stronger: うちの夫ときたら、まったく何もしないんだから。（My husband, honestly, does absolutely nothing）
n1-46:
The idea in one line
「〜にあって」 is the formal, written-style "in the midst of ~" or "as ~". You put a special era, situation, or status in front, and then describe the state, behavior, or what should be done in that environment. It's common in news, speeches, and essays, and almost never used in everyday chat.
How to connect it
It attaches only to nouns: noun + にあって
非常時 → 非常時にあって（in this kind of emergency）
現代 → 現代にあって（in the modern age）
When to use it
Special eras and situationsEmergencies, recessions, the age of information overload, and the like.
・この非常時にあって、リーダーは冷静であるべきだ。（In this kind of emergency, a leader should stay calm）
・情報があふれる現代にあって、正しい情報を選ぶ力が必要だ。（In a modern age overflowing with information, we need the ability to pick out accurate information）
Status and positionOften written as 「〜という立場にあって」.
・社長という立場にあって、軽率な発言は許されない。（As company president, you can't afford to say careless things）
Being in a certain placeUsually an unusual place such as a foreign country or a battlefield, with a literary flavor.
・異国にあって、家族からの手紙が何よりの支えだった。（Living in a foreign land, letters from my family were my greatest support）
Two common variations
にあってもAdding 「も」 gives "even in ~, still…", followed by things like "still didn't give up" or "still stayed strong".
・どんな苦境にあっても、彼女は笑顔を忘れなかった。（No matter how difficult her situation was, she never forgot to smile）
にあってはAdding 「は」 emphasizes "in this situation, one has no choice but to…".
・この不況下にあっては、どの会社も節約せざるを得ない。（Under this recession, every company has no choice but to cut costs）
Common mistakes
・It attaches only to nouns. If you want to use a verb, first turn it into a noun, or say 「〜という状況にあって」 instead.
・What comes before it should be a special environment or status worth mentioning. Ordinary times like 「月曜日にあって」 or 「普通の日にあって」 sound strange.
・It's very stiff written language. When chatting with friends, just say 「忙しい中」 or 「〜なのに」; using にあって would sound like reading a press release.
・Don't confuse it with the plain "is located at": その店は駅前にあって便利だ。（That shop is in front of the station, so it's convenient）Here あって just means "being located", and it isn't this grammar point.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
にあたって (just one letter different, and the one most often misread) = right before or at the moment of doing something, and it can attach to verbs.
社長に就任するにあたって、一言ご挨拶申し上げます。（On the occasion of taking up the post of president, I'd like to say a few words）
社長という立場にあって、軽率な発言は許されない。（As company president, you can't afford to say careless things）
The first sentence focuses on the point in time of taking office; the second is about continuously being in the president's position.
とあって = because it's ~, so… (giving a reason).
不況とあって、就職が厳しい。（Because of the recession, finding a job is hard）
不況にあって、この会社は売り上げを伸ばしている。（Even amid the recession, this company is increasing its sales）
とあって means "because of this, that happens"; にあって means "being in this environment, how someone behaves".
Quick rule of thumb: use にあって for "in the midst of ~ / as ~", にあたって for "on the occasion of doing ~", and とあって for "because it's ~".
n1-48:
The idea in one line
「～ともなれば」means "once you're at the level of ~, of course…". You put a status, age, or period that is a step above the ordinary in front, and the second half says "at that level, this naturally follows." It's the tone of English like: "Well, he's company president now, so of course he takes work calls on his days off."
When to use it
Moving up in status or ageWhen someone reaches a certain position or age, their responsibilities and other people's expectations change with it.
・プロともなれば、これくらいは当然できる。 (When you're a professional, of course you can do this much.)
・社長ともなれば、休みの日も仕事の電話が来る。 (When you're the company president, work calls come even on your days off.)
When the time comesWhen a special season or day arrives, the surroundings naturally change.
・12月ともなれば、街はクリスマス一色になる。 (Once December comes, the streets are all about Christmas.)
When it's a really big undertakingAfter a verb, it means "if you're really going to go that far," and the sense of "if" is stronger here.
・海外に引っ越すともなれば、準備することが山ほどある。 (If you're really moving overseas, there's a mountain of things to prepare.)
How to form it
Noun + ともなれば: 大学生 → 大学生ともなれば
Verb dictionary form + ともなれば: 結婚する → 結婚するともなれば
The second half often uses expressions like 当然, ～なければならない, and ～ものだ, which say "of course" or "naturally should."
Common mistakes
・The first half has to give the feeling that you've reached a different level. 小学生ともなれば works because, compared with kindergarten, you've moved up a step. Drop in just any ordinary word and the sentence sounds odd.
・The second half says "this is what naturally happens," so don't put your own will or a request there. To say "if I become president, I want to try harder," you can't say 社長ともなれば、もっと頑張りたい. Say 社長になったら、もっと頑張りたい。
・The tone is fairly formal, more common in news, writing, and speeches. In everyday conversation people usually say ～になると or ～となると.
・Don't mix it up with となれば: without the も, it's just a plain "if that's the case," with no emphasis on "now that you're at this level." Example: 明日も雨となれば、試合は中止だ。 (If it rains tomorrow too, the game is cancelled.)
Telling it apart from look-alikes
ともなると: almost the same meaning, and on exams you can usually swap the two.
12月ともなると、街はクリスマス一色になる。
12月ともなれば、街はクリスマス一色になる。
Both are correct. If you have to split hairs, ともなれば has the ば, so it carries slightly more of a "if it really gets to that point" feel.
とあれば: it looks similar but points the opposite way. It means "if it's for ~ / if it's a request for ~," and what follows is often something you're willing to do or have no choice but to do.
社長の命令とあれば、従うしかない。 (If it's the president's order, we have no choice but to obey.)
社長ともなれば、責任も重くなる。 (When you're the president, your responsibility naturally gets heavier too.)
Quick test: if the first half is "moved up a level" and the second half says "this naturally follows," use ともなれば／ともなると. If the first half is "a special reason" and the second half says "then I'll do it," use とあれば.
n1-49:
The idea in one line
ともなく has two uses, and both are about something being vague.
One is an action with no particular purpose, like "half-watching" in English: the TV is on and your eyes are on it, but you're not really watching anything.
The other is not being able to say the source: "from somewhere," "nobody knows who started it."
When to use it
Doing something absent-mindedlyYou didn't plan to do it, but you find yourself doing it. The biggest giveaway is that the same verb appears before and after, or two verbs with very close meanings.
・見るともなく窓の外を見ていた。 (I wasn't looking at anything in particular, just gazing out the window.)
・聞くともなく隣の席の話を聞いていた。 (I wasn't trying to listen, but the conversation at the next table reached my ears anyway.)
・見るともなくテレビを眺めていたら、見覚えのある街が映った。 (I was half-watching TV when a familiar street appeared on the screen.)
Can't say who or wherePut a question word like 「どこ、誰、いつ」 in front. It's often followed by から, へ, or に.
・どこからともなく、いい匂いがしてきた。 (A nice smell drifted in from somewhere.)
・誰からともなく拍手が起こった。 (Nobody knows who started it, but applause broke out.)
・男はどこへともなく歩いていった。 (The man walked off to who knows where.)
・誰にともなく「ありがとう」とつぶやいた。 (Not addressing anyone in particular, I murmured "thank you.")
How to form it
Verbs: take the dictionary form, add ともなく, then repeat the same verb.
見る → 見るともなく見る聞く → 聞くともなく聞く
Question words: take 「どこ、誰、いつ」 plus a particle, then add ともなく.
どこから → どこからともなく誰から → 誰からともなく
Common mistakes
・Use the dictionary form of the verb: 見るともなく. You can't drop ます and attach it as 「見ともなく」, and you can't use the past form 「見たともなく」.
・Only a limited set of verbs work here, almost all things the eyes, ears, mouth, or mind do naturally: 見る, 聞く, 言う, 考える, 待つ. Don't apply it to other verbs at random.
・どこからともなく and どことなく look almost the same but mean different things. どことなく means "somehow, in some way, a little ~" and is about a feeling: 彼はどことなく父に似ている。 (I can't say where exactly, but he somehow resembles my father.) To say "from somewhere," use どこからともなく.
・"Absent-mindedly" doesn't mean "not doing it." With 見るともなく見る you are still looking, just without any purpose.
・This is a written-style expression, common in novels and essays. In everyday conversation people usually say なんとなく or どこからか.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
The same-level ともなると (same meaning as ともなれば) differs by only a few characters but means something completely different. It means that once you reach a certain level or position, ~ naturally follows. What comes before it is mostly a noun, but it can also take the verb dictionary form.
Compare them in the same "living alone" setting:
ともなく (absent-minded): 一人の部屋で、見るともなくテレビを見ていた。 (Alone in my room, I was half-watching TV.)
ともなく (unknown source): 夜中、どこからともなく猫の鳴き声が聞こえてきた。 (In the middle of the night, a cat's meowing came from somewhere.)
ともなると (noun): 夜中ともなると、この辺りはすっかり静かになる。 (Once it's the middle of the night, this area gets completely quiet.)
ともなると (verb): 一人暮らしをするともなると、家事も全部自分でやらなければならない。 (Once you're actually living alone, you have to do all the housework yourself.)
Quick test:
・ともなく usually takes the shape "same verb + ともなく + same verb" or "どこから／誰から + ともなく," and means absent-mindedly, or not being able to say who or where.
・ともなると is followed by "then naturally ~ / of course ~," meaning that once you reach that level or position, a certain situation naturally arises.
Don't just look at whether a noun or a verb comes before it; look at the form and meaning of the whole sentence.
n1-50:
The idea in one line
「AともBともつかない」 means “you can't tell whether it's A or B”, as in “neither quite A nor quite B.” Think of a smile that isn't quite a smile, or a color that's not really blue and not really green. What's in front of you sits between the two, and you can't say which side it belongs to.
How to form it
Put a noun or a plain-form verb (dictionary form, ている form, ない form, anything without ます) in A and B. Add とも after each one, then finish with つかない.
本気＋冗談 → 本気とも冗談ともつかない
笑っている＋泣いている → 笑っているとも泣いているともつかない
Here 「つかない」 means “can't be pinned down, can't settle on one,” and it's usually written in hiragana. Most often a noun follows directly, such as an expression, voice, tone, answer or color.
The two patterns you'll hear most
