ともつかないThe thing itself is ambiguous. Even when you look at it or listen to it, you can't tell which it is.
・本気とも冗談ともつかない言い方だった。(The way he said it, you couldn't tell if he was serious or joking)
・ため息ともあくびともつかない声が聞こえた。(I heard a sound that could have been a sigh or a yawn)
・彼女は笑っているとも泣いているともつかない顔をしていた。(She had an expression that was neither quite a smile nor quite crying)
とも言わないA and B are usually a positive/negative pair. It means the other person won't commit, so they stay noncommittal.
・彼は行くとも行かないとも言わない。(He doesn't say he'll go, and he doesn't say he won't)
・部長はいいとも悪いとも言わなかった。(The manager said neither that it was good nor that it was bad)
Easy mistakes
・「つかない」 means the thing itself can't be told apart, so use it for things right in front of you, like expressions, voices and answers. Don't use it for a plain “I don't know the answer.” To say “I don't know whether he'll come,” say 彼が来るか来ないか分からない.
・Both A and B need とも. Only one, or 「AかBともつかない」, is wrong.
・A verb connects straight to とも with no extra 「の」. Just write 笑っているとも, not 笑っているのとも.
・This is a written, novel-style pattern. In everyday conversation, 冗談か本気か分からない is enough.
Don't mix it up with look-alikes
AともBとも言わない: neither is said, so the attitude is unclear.
彼は賛成とも反対とも言わなかった。(He said neither that he agreed nor that he objected)
Aと言わずBと言わず: whether it's A or B, all of it is like that.
手と言わず足と言わず泥だらけになった。(Hands, feet, everything was covered in mud)
Both have “A… B…” plus 「言わ」, so they look alike, but the meanings are completely different. One means “neither side is stated,” the other means “it's the same everywhere.”
〜ともなく also has とも, but only one slot, often after a question word, and it means “from somewhere, someone, you can't say where or who.”
どこからともなく音楽が聞こえてきた。(Music came drifting in from somewhere)
Quick test: two options and you can't tell which one, use ともつかない. Neither side is stated and the person won't commit, use とも言わない. Both are included and everything is the same, use と言わず. Just one question word, “from somewhere, someone,” use ともなく.
n1-51:
The idea in one line
「〜てまで」 means “go as far as ~ to do…” or “even ~ in order to…”. To reach some goal, you do something you normally wouldn't, something that costs you a lot. When Japanese speakers say it, it often carries a tone of “is it really necessary to go that far?”
How to form it
Put the verb in the て form, add 「まで」, then follow with the goal you really want.
借金する → 借金して → 借金してまで
無理をする → 無理をしてまで
嘘をつく → 嘘をついてまで
The skeleton of the sentence is 「Aてまで、B」 = to get B, go as far as doing A. A is the price you pay, and B is what you want.
The patterns you'll hear most
Not worth itIt's followed by 「〜必要はない」 or 「〜たくない」, meaning “going that far for this isn't worth it.” This is the most common use.
・借金してまで、ブランド品を買う必要はない。(There's no need to go into debt to buy designer goods)
・体を壊してまで働きたくない。(I don't want to work if it means ruining my health)
Disbelief, doubtWhen you think the price someone is paying is over the top, you express it as a question.
・そこまでして行きたいの？(You want to go that badly, even after all that?)
・友達を裏切ってまで、出世したかったのか。(You wanted a promotion so badly that you'd betray your friends?)
Just describing the effortIt isn't always criticism. It can simply describe how much someone gave up, sometimes with a bit of admiration.
・徹夜してまで並んで、限定スイーツを手に入れた。(He stayed up all night in line and finally got the limited-edition sweets)
・社長は自分の給料を減らしてまで、社員を守った。(The president even cut his own salary to protect his employees)
Easy mistakes
・Don't flip the order. Before てまで comes the “price,” and the “goal” comes after. 借金してまで買う means “borrow money in order to buy.” If you wrote 「買ってまで借金する」, it would mean “buy in order to borrow money,” which makes no sense.
・Put something unusual and costly before it. If you put in something easy that you'd do anyway, the sentence loses the “go as far as” feel and sounds odd.
・そこまでして is a very common set phrase in speech meaning “going that far,” and it has the same feel as てまで. Note that it's about the price being too high, not “given that things are already like this.”
・A noun must first become a verb with 「する」 or 「をする」 before it can take てまで: 借金してまで, 無理をしてまで, 家族を犠牲にしてまで. You can't write 「借金まで」 directly. That would mean “even borrowing money…,” which is a different meaning.
Don't mix it up with look-alikes
In all of these, 「まで」 follows a verb, and the meaning changes completely depending on the verb form:
Dictionary form + まで = until ~
・彼が来るまで待った。(I waited until he came)
て form + まで = go as far as ~ to do
・3時間も待ってまで、彼に会いたかった。(I wanted to see him so badly that I even waited three hours)
Dictionary form + までだ (at the end of a sentence) = at worst, I'll just ~
・彼が来ないなら、一人で行くまでだ。(If he doesn't come, I'll just go by myself)
Quick test: if まで follows the て form, it's “go as far as.” If it follows the dictionary form and the sentence isn't over, it's “until.” If までだ sits at the end of the sentence, it's “at worst I'll just / that's all.”
n1-60:
The idea in one line
「Aかたがた」 means "and also, as a way of thanking/greeting you", the kind of phrasing you see in formal letters. You visit or write to someone and use the occasion for a second purpose too, such as thanking them, updating them, or saying hello. It's very formal and shows up when visiting seniors or clients, or in business letters.
How to attach it
Put a noun before it, usually a noun for an action, such as お礼 (thanks), ご挨拶 (greeting), ご報告 (report), お見舞い (visiting someone who is ill), 散歩 (a walk).
お礼 → お礼かたがたご報告 → ご報告かたがた
What follows is usually an action like visiting, or writing or speaking. The most common ones are 伺う, お邪魔する, and 申し上げる.
How you'll usually hear it
Visiting in personYou explain why you've come today.
・先日のお礼かたがた、ご挨拶に伺いました。(I've come to say hello, and also to thank you for the other day.)
・近くまで来ましたので、ご挨拶かたがたお邪魔しました。(I happened to be nearby, so I dropped in to say hello.)
LettersVery common in business and greeting letters, almost a set phrase.
・略儀ながら書中をもちまして、お礼かたがたご挨拶申し上げます。(Please forgive me for doing this by letter; I write to thank you and to send my greetings.)
・転勤のご報告かたがた、お手紙を差し上げます。(I'm writing this letter to let you know about my transfer, too.)
Common mistakes
・It attaches to a noun, not a dictionary-form verb: say お礼かたがた, not お礼を言うかたがた.
・English "while I'm at it" or "by the way" can sound like the second thing doesn't matter much. かたがた doesn't mean that. Both the thanks and the greeting are sincere purposes. Using お礼かたがた isn't rude; it sounds polished.
・It's very formal and often pairs with humble verbs like 伺う and 申し上げる. You wouldn't use it to tell a friend "I'm popping into the convenience store."
・The 「方々（かたがた）」 in ご来場の方々 and 関係者の方々 means "everyone, all of you." It's only pronounced the same and has nothing to do with this grammar.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
かたがた = formal; when visiting or writing, you combine a second purpose:
お礼かたがた、先生のお宅に伺いました。 (I visited my teacher's home, also to thank them.)
がてら = everyday speech; you go out to do A and do B on the way:
散歩がてら、パンを買ってきた。 (I went for a walk and picked up some bread while I was at it.)
かたわら = over a long period, you do your main job and also another thing; it has nothing to do with "while you're at it":
会社に勤めるかたわら、小説を書いている。 (He works at a company and writes novels on the side.)
Quick rule of thumb: for a formal visit or letter that adds thanks or a greeting, use かたがた. For doing a small errand on a trip out, use がてら. For long-term double duty, use かたわら.
n1-61:
The idea in one line
「AかたわらB」 means "besides doing A (your main job), you also do B", a bit like having a side hustle. かたわら originally means "beside": the main thing sits in the middle, and another activity runs alongside it.
When to use it
Doing something on the side long-termYou describe someone's life or work: what their main job is, and what else they keep doing over time. It often appears in profiles, news articles, and self-introductions.
・会社に勤めるかたわら、週末は小説を書いている。(Besides working at a company, he writes novels on weekends.)
・彼女は大学で教えるかたわら、翻訳の仕事もしている。(Besides teaching at a university, she also does translation work.)
・仕事のかたわら、日本語の勉強を続けている。(Alongside work, I keep studying Japanese.)
How to attach it
Verb: dictionary form (the base form in the dictionary) + かたわら
働く → 働くかたわら店を経営する → 店を経営するかたわら
Noun: noun + の + かたわら
仕事 → 仕事のかたわら育児 → 育児のかたわら
The noun is usually a word like "work," "research," or "child-rearing" that stands for a whole ongoing activity.
Common mistakes
・It does not mean doing two things with your hands at the same moment. 音楽を聞くかたわら勉強する is wrong; for that, use 聞きながら.
・Both activities continue over a period of time, so 「〜ている」 often follows. It doesn't suit something that happens only once.
・Put the main activity first and the side activity second. Don't swap them.
・It doesn't attach to the た-form: 勤めたかたわら is wrong. Always use the dictionary form.
・It's written-style language and rarely used in chat with friends. In speech people usually say 仕事しながら or 本業のほかに.
・When you see 「名詞のかたわらで」 as in 母のかたわらで, it's mostly the literal "beside ~," not this grammar.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
ながら = doing two things with your hands at the same moment:
音楽を聞きながら勉強する。 (I study while listening to music.)
かたわら = two long-term roles or jobs:
会社で働くかたわら、夜間の大学に通っている。 (Besides working at a company during the day, I attend a night university.)
がてら = on this one outing, you also take care of another thing; it's short-term and one-off:
散歩がてら、パンを買ってきた。 (I went out for a walk and bought some bread while I was at it.)
かたがた = close in meaning to がてら but more formal, mostly used for visits, thanks, and greetings. What follows is the actual action, and what comes before it is the extra purpose:
先日のお礼かたがた、ご挨拶に伺いました。 (I've come to visit and greet you, and also to thank you for the other day.)
Quick rule of thumb: for someone juggling two roles long-term, use かたわら. For one trip out that covers two things, use がてら (or かたがた in formal situations). For two things done at the same moment, use ながら.
n1-54:
The idea in one line
「〜かろう」 is the old-fashioned, written version of 「〜いだろう」. It means "probably ~" or "surely ~." 難しいだろう becomes 難しかろう with the same meaning. It just sounds like an editorial, a novel, or an old man in a period drama.
How to form it
It attaches only to い-adjectives: drop the final 「い」 and add 「かろう」.
難しい → drop い → 難しかろう
寒い → 寒かろう高い → 高かろう
Two to memorize:
いい → よかろう (it comes from よい)
ない → なかろう
「〜たい」 conjugates like an い-adjective, so it works too: 帰りたい → 帰りたかろう ("probably wants to go home badly")
When to use it
Written conjectureUsed in articles and commentary to guess at a situation. It often appears with さぞ ("surely").
・山の上はさぞ寒かろう。 (It must be freezing at the top of the mountain.)
・最初は苦しかろうが、すぐに慣れる。 (It'll probably be hard at first, but you'll get used to it quickly.)
Forms you'll hear most
ではなかろうか= "Isn't it that ~?" Very common in papers and editorials, and a softer way to state an opinion.
・この計画には無理があるのではなかろうか。 (Isn't this plan a bit of a stretch?)
よかろうAn elder or boss saying "Fine, all right," with a top-down, grudgingly-granting feel.
・まあ、よかろう。今回だけは許してやる。 (Well, fine. I'll let you off just this once.)
Set phrase安かろう悪かろう = cheap means poor quality (you get what you pay for).
・安かろう悪かろうの時代は終わった。 (The era of "cheap means poor quality" is over.)
Common mistakes
・な-adjectives and nouns cannot take かろう: 静かかろう is wrong. Say 静かだろう or 静かであろう. Nouns work the same way: use 学生だろう or 学生であろう.
・Verbs can't take it either. Say 行くだろう or 行くであろう.
・いい must become よかろう. There is no 「いかろう」.
・「ろう」 is pronounced with a long vowel, like ろー.
・Saying 暑かろう to a friend sounds like you're acting in a period drama. In everyday talk, just say 暑いだろう.
・よかろう talks down to the listener, so it's very rude to say to a boss or teacher.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
「〜かろうが／〜かろうと」 has two meanings, depending on the sentence:
"Probably ~, but…" (conjecture, then contrast): その試験は難しかろうが、準備すれば突破できる。 (That exam is probably hard, but you can pass if you prepare.)
"Whether ~ or not…" (the い-adjective version of 〜ようが／〜ようと): 高かろうが安かろうが、必要なものは買う。 (Whether it's expensive or cheap, I'll buy what I need.)
どんなに辛かろうと、最後までやり抜く。 (No matter how hard it is, I'll see it through to the end.)
Quick test: if 「どんなに」 or 「いくら」 comes before it, or two forms appear as a pair (高かろうが安かろうが) → "no matter ~." If there's just one and it's followed by "but…" → "probably ~, but."
What to learn next
The verb and noun version of "no matter ~" is 〜ようが／〜ようと: 雨が降ろうが、試合は行われる。 (Even if it rains, the match will go ahead.)
n1-58:
The idea in one line
「〜とばかりに」 means "as if to say '~'". The person doesn't say anything out loud, but their actions or expression clearly say something. You put that unspoken line in front, and then the action they take.
For example, your section chief keeps glancing at his watch. He says nothing, but everyone can tell he's saying "Let's call it a day." That's when you use this.
When to use it
Describing how someone looks or actsYou spell out the "line" behind the person's action. It's most common in novels, news reports, and scene descriptions.
・「早く帰れ」とばかりに、課長は時計をちらちら見た。 (The section chief kept glancing at his watch, as if to say "Hurry up and go home.")
・「遊ぼう」とばかりに、犬がボールをくわえて走ってきた。 (The dog ran over with a ball in its mouth, as if to say "Let's play!")
・「待ってました」とばかりに、彼は勢いよく手を挙げた。 (He shot his hand up, as if to say "I've been waiting for this!")
How to form it
What goes in front is a line of dialogue, so it can take almost any form: a command (帰れ), an invitation (遊ぼう), the ます form (待ってました), or even a single word or exclamation. It's often put in 「」 so you can see at a glance that it's a line.
Before a noun, it becomes とばかりの:
・「もう帰れ」とばかりの冷たい態度だった。 (He had a cold attitude, as if to say "Just go home already.")
Forms you'll hear most
ここぞとばかりにここぞ = "this is the place, this is the moment." The whole phrase means "seizing the chance, going all out," and it's very common.
・会議で、彼はここぞとばかりに不満を言い始めた。 (At the meeting, he seized the chance and started airing all his complaints.)
今だとばかりに"Now's the time!" Spotting the moment and acting right away.
・相手が転んだ瞬間、今だとばかりに走り出した。 (The moment his opponent fell, he bolted, as if to say "Now!")
Common mistakes
・This is a way of watching someone from the outside, so you don't normally use it about yourself. You know exactly what you're thinking, so there's no need for "looks like I'm saying."
・The line in front was never actually spoken. If the person really said it, use 「〜と言って」 instead.
・The ばかり here doesn't mean "only." Don't translate it as "just ~."
・It isn't limited to the plain form. Commands, ます forms, and single words all work, because it's simply quoting a line.
・It's mostly used in writing and scene description, and is less common in everyday conversation.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
とばかりに = a line of dialogue in front: "as if to say '~'"
んばかりに = an action about to happen in front: "so much that one almost ~"
Same situation: a child is overjoyed to get a present.
・「やった」とばかりに、子どもは両手を上げた。 (The child threw both hands up, as if to say "Yes!")
・子どもは飛び上がらんばかりに喜んだ。 (The child was so happy he almost jumped up.)
How to form んばかりに: change the verb to the ない form, drop 「ない」, and add 「ん」.
飛び上がる → 飛び上がらない → 飛び上がらんばかりに
泣き出す → 泣き出さない → 泣き出さんばかりに
※する becomes 「せん」, not 「しん」: する → せんばかりに (e.g. 今にも爆発せんばかりに)
Also, 「帰れ」と言わんばかりに ("as if about to say 'Go home'") means almost the same as 「帰れ」とばかりに, so the two are interchangeable.
Quick test: if what's in front is a line of dialogue, use とばかりに. If it's an action that someone almost carries out, use んばかりに.
What to learn next
Since this is also about describing how someone looks or acts, move on to 〜んばかりに ("almost ~"). Learn the two together and you're least likely to mix them up.
n1-68:
The idea in one line
「〜をもってしても」 means “even with ～, still…”. You put something impressive up front, something that should work (the latest technology, someone's ability), and then say “it still doesn't work” or “it's still hard.” The point is “even something this strong can't do it,” which shows how difficult the matter is.
How to connect it
It attaches directly to a noun: noun + をもってしても
最新の技術 → 最新の技術をもってしても (even with the latest technology)
彼の実力 → 彼の実力をもってしても (even with his ability)
You can also put a person directly before it, meaning “even someone as capable as him”: 彼をもってしても
When to use it
Technology, science, methods Even the best method available can't do it.
・今の科学をもってしても、地震を正確に予知することはできない。 (Even with today's science, we can't predict earthquakes accurately.)
Human ability Even a very capable person finds it hard.
・彼の実力をもってしても、優勝は難しいだろう。 (Even with his ability, winning the championship will probably be difficult.)
・天才と呼ばれた彼をもってしても、この問題は解けなかった。 (Even he, who was called a genius, couldn't solve this problem.)
Language, expression A common phrase in speeches and formal remarks, meaning your feelings are too strong to put into words.
・どんな言葉をもってしても、この感謝の気持ちは伝えきれません。 (No words, whatever they may be, can fully express my gratitude.)
Common mistakes
・What follows is almost always a result like “can't do it, it's hard, it's still not enough”, for example できない, 難しい, 無理だ. If you follow it with “and it succeeded,” the whole sentence sounds odd.
・What comes before it should be something that was expected to be very useful. If you put in something ordinary, like “with my pencil,” there's no “even this doesn't work” tension.
・This is a very formal, written expression, common in news, papers and speeches. In everyday speech, just say 最新の技術でも (even the latest technology…).
・Its focus is “using this power to do something,” not “from the viewpoint of ～.” Don't translate it as “judging by ～.”
Telling it apart from similar forms
With the same “technology,” three forms give completely different results:
をもって = with, by means of (simply stating the means): この技術をもって、問題を解決した。 (We solved the problem with this technology.)
をもってすれば = if you have ～, you can do it: この技術をもってすれば、問題は解決できる。 (With this technology, the problem can be solved.)
をもってしても = even with ～, you can't do it: この技術をもってしても、問題は解決できない。 (Even with this technology, the problem can't be solved.)
Also, をもって has a use meaning “as a cutoff point,” as in 本日をもって閉店します。 (This shop closes as of today.). That has nothing to do with をもってしても, so don't mix them up.
Quick tip: look at the short part in the middle. 「すれば」 means having it is enough; 「しても」 means even having it isn't enough.
n1-71:
The idea in one line
「〜ずにはすまない」 means “it won't do not to ～” or “you can't get away without ～ing.” すむ (済む) means “a matter is settled, it's acceptable,” so すまない means “it can't be settled.” The whole phrase says: given what's reasonable and the current situation, you can't wrap this up without doing it.
When to use it
Morally obliged You made a mistake or caused trouble. Not apologizing, compensating or taking responsibility simply wouldn't be acceptable.
・人の車に傷をつけたのだから、弁償せずにはすまない。 (Since you scratched someone's car, you can't get away without paying for it.)
Forced by circumstances The matter has blown up, and there's no way to close it without dealing with it.
・ここまで問題が大きくなれば、社長も記者会見をせずにはすまないだろう。 (With the problem this big, the president probably can't avoid holding a press conference.)
A reason often comes first, such as 〜のだから, 〜以上 or 〜たら, and だろう is often added at the end, meaning “as things stand, it looks unavoidable.”
How to connect it
ずにはすまない: take the ない-form, remove 「ない」, then add 「ずにはすまない」.
謝る → 謝らない → 謝らずにはすまない
払う → 払わない → 払わずにはすまない
認める → 認めない → 認めずにはすまない
Remember the irregular verbs: する → せずにはすまない来る → 来ずにはすまない（こずに）
ないではすまない: add 「ではすまない」 directly to the ない-form without removing anything. The meaning is the same, but the tone is a little less stiff.
・会議を無断で休んだのだから、部長に説明しないではすまない。 (You skipped the meeting without notice, so you can't get away without explaining to the department head.)
There is also 〜ではすまない after a noun or 「〜だけ」, meaning “that alone won't settle it”:
・冗談ではすまない。 (This can't be brushed off as a joke.)
・謝るだけではすまない。 (Just apologizing won't settle it.)
Common mistakes
・する becomes せずに, not 「しずに」. The correct form is 説明せずにはすまない.
・The すまない here doesn't mean “sorry.” It means “the matter can't be settled.”
・This is a written, formal expression, more common in news, commentary and formal settings. When chatting with friends and saying “you should apologize,” Japanese people usually say 謝らないとまずいよ or use 謝らないわけにはいかない.
・The point is that “external reason or circumstances push you to do it.” It isn't that you badly want to do it, nor that you can't help it emotionally.
Telling it apart from similar forms
Take the same act of “apologizing.” Three similar-looking forms mean very different things:
ずにはすまない = it wouldn't be acceptable not to do it (forced by the situation)
・ミスをしたのは私だから、謝らずにはすまない。 (I'm the one who made the mistake, so I can't get away without apologizing.)
ずにはいられない = you can't help it emotionally (covered at N2)
・彼の涙を見て、謝らずにはいられなかった。 (Seeing his tears, I couldn't help apologizing.)
ずにはおかない = I'll make it happen, I won't rest until it's done (strong will)
・今度こそ、彼に謝らせずにはおかない。 (This time, I will definitely make him apologize.)
Quick tip: “it wouldn't be acceptable not to” is すまない, “can't help it” is いられない, and “won't rest until it's done” is おかない.
n1-66:
The idea in one line
「〜いかんによらず／いかんにかかわらず」 means "regardless of how ~ is, always ...", the kind of phrase you'd see in official documents. You put something that can vary (a reason, a result, the weather) up front, and the conclusion that follows doesn't change because of it. You'll see it most on notices, contracts, and ticket refund rules, and almost never in everyday chat.
Breaking it down
いかん is written 如何 in kanji and means "how the content or situation is."
によらず = not depending on, not determined by; にかかわらず = having no bearing on ~.
The two mean the same thing: "no matter how ~ is." There's another common variant too: いかんを問わず (regardless of ~).
How to connect it
Noun + の + いかんによらず／いかんにかかわらず
理由 → 理由のいかんによらず天候 → 天候のいかんにかかわらず
The noun before it should be something that has several possibilities, such as 理由, 結果, 事情, 国籍, 天候.
In formal documents, the の is sometimes dropped, giving 理由いかんにかかわらず. It's enough to recognize it; when you write your own sentences, stick with the version with の.
The forms you'll see most
Rules and notices A shop or company is saying "no exceptions."
・理由のいかんを問わず、購入後のキャンセルはできません。 (Regardless of the reason, purchases cannot be canceled.)
・天候のいかんにかかわらず、イベントは予定通り開催されます。 (Regardless of the weather, the event will be held as scheduled.)
Eligibility and conditions Everyone is treated equally.
・国籍のいかんによらず、どなたでも応募できます。 (Regardless of nationality, anyone can apply.)
Where people slip up
・Only nouns can come before it, not verbs or adjectives directly: 行くいかんによらず is wrong.
・Put a word that has "various situations" in front. 雨のいかんにかかわらず doesn't work, because "rain" has no "how it is" to speak of. Say 天候のいかん instead.
・Here 如何 is read いかん. The same kanji is read いかが in 如何ですか, so don't confuse them.
・It's very stiff, and sounds odd with friends. In conversation, just say どんな理由でも (for whatever reason).
Telling it apart from look-alikes
〜いかんで／いかんによっては (N1, the "depends on" pattern) means exactly the opposite: the outcome depends on how the preceding thing is.
・面接の結果いかんで、採用が決まります。 (Whether you're hired depends on the interview result.)
・面接の結果のいかんにかかわらず、交通費は支給します。 (Regardless of the interview result, we will pay your travel expenses.)
〜にかかわらず (N2) is the more general "regardless." It doesn't need いかん, and you can put words like 天気 and 年齢 in front: 天気にかかわらず、試合は行われます。 (Regardless of the weather, the match will be held.)
Adding 「のいかん」 makes it more formal, with the tone of an official document.
Quick test: if いかん is followed by 「によらず／にかかわらず／を問わず」, it means "regardless." If it's followed by 「で／によっては」, it means "depends on."
n1-73:
The idea in one line
「ただ～のみ」 means "only ~" or "all that's left is ~". It's the formal, literary version of 「だけ」. Its most common use is to express resolve: you've done everything you can, and only one road is left in front of you. For example, あとはただ待つのみだ (All that's left now is to wait). The tone is firm, as if you're saying "I won't think about anything else. I'll just focus on this."
When to use it
Only thisStresses that the range is just this one thing and nothing else.
・合格したのは、ただ一人のみだった。(Only one person passed.)
The only thing left to doAt the end of a sentence it becomes 「～のみだ」, meaning you can stop worrying about anything else and just do this one thing. It's common in speeches, statements before a match, and news reports.
・やるべきことはすべてやった。あとはただ結果を待つのみだ。(I've done everything I should. All that's left is to wait for the result.)
・今はただ無事を祈るのみです。(All we can do now is pray they're safe.)
How to form it
Noun: ただ + noun + のみ　一人 → ただ一人のみ
Verb: ただ + dictionary form + のみ　前進する → ただ前進するのみだ
To be more polite, change the final だ to です: 祈るのみです.
You can drop 「ただ」 and use only 「のみ」 with the same meaning. Adding ただ just adds emphasis.
The form you'll hear most
Noun + あるのみTo say "the only thing left is to do this," 「ある」 is often added after the noun. It's practically a set phrase: 努力あるのみ, 前進あるのみ, 練習あるのみ.
・試合まであと一週間。練習あるのみだ。(One week until the match. All we can do is practice.)
SignsOn the streets of Japan you'll often see 「のみ」 on its own, meaning "only ~" or "~ only."
・この席は会員のみご利用いただけます。(This seat is for members only.)
・関係者のみ(Authorized personnel only)
Common mistakes
・It's very formal and dramatic. Saying 「ただ食べるのみ」 to a friend while chatting about lunch would sound like you're acting in a play. In everyday speech, just use だけ: あとは待つだけだ.
・Verbs take the dictionary form, never the ます form. Say 前進するのみです, not 「前進しますのみ」.
・のみならず looks similar, but it means "not only ~", which is the opposite: ただ日本のみならず、世界中で人気がある。 (It's popular not only in Japan but all over the world.) When you see ならず after のみ, switch your reading to "not only."
Telling it apart from similar patterns
～のみだ = this is the only road in front of you, so you focus and push forward: ここまで来たら、ただ前進するのみだ。 (Now that we've come this far, all that's left is to move forward.)
～まで（のこと）だ = "the worst that can happen is ~". It's a fallback you've already thought out, and it's often preceded by 「だめなら」 or 「失敗したら」: だめなら、もう一度挑戦するまでだ。 (If it doesn't work, I'll just try again.)
Quick test: if you could say "all that's left is to ~" or "the only thing to do is ~" in English, use のみ. If it's "if that fails, I'll just ~" with an "if it doesn't work" before it, use までだ.
n1-74:
The idea in one line
「〜ないものでもない」 means "it's not that I won't ~" or "I suppose I could ~". Say a friend asks you to help them move, and you answer, "Well, depends on whether you buy me dinner. I wouldn't say no." It means it's possible, but you're not exactly eager, and you're not agreeing outright.
How to form it
Change the verb to its negative ない form, then add ものでもない directly.
引き受ける → 引き受けない → 引き受けないものでもない
許す → 許さない → 許さないものでもない
間に合う → 間に合わない → 間に合わないものでもない
Two negatives ("not" + "not the case that") cancel out and become a reserved "yes, it's possible."
When to use it
Agreeing with conditionsThe most common use. It often comes after 「〜ば」, 「〜なら」, or 「〜次第では」 (depending on ~). You set the condition first, then say "I wouldn't say no."
・条件次第では、引き受けないものでもない。(Depending on the terms, I might not turn it down.)
・ちゃんと謝るなら、許さないものでもない。(If you apologize properly, I might not refuse to forgive you.)
Still possibleYou judge that something isn't completely hopeless.
・あと一週間あれば、間に合わないものでもない。(With one more week, we might not miss the deadline.)
Grudging understandingYou say you "kind of get" someone else's way of thinking.
・彼の気持ちも分からないものでもない。(I can't say I don't understand how he feels.)
Common mistakes
・Don't drop 「ない」. If you write 引き受けるものでもない, it means "it's not something you should take on," which is the opposite. Likewise, お金で買えるものでもない means "it's not something money can buy," which has nothing to do with this grammar.
・It only means "it's possible." It doesn't mean "I definitely will" or "I really want to." Translating it as "I'm happy to" or "no problem" goes too far.
・The tone is stiff and written-style, and it often carries a slightly superior "I'll grudgingly agree" or "I'll think about it" attitude. Saying 「手伝わないものでもないです」 to your boss or a customer would be rude, so avoid it when you need to be polite.
・What comes before it is usually your own action or judgment, such as taking something on, considering it, or understanding it. It's rarely used to talk about other people's actions.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Several patterns mean almost the same thing: ないこともない, ないでもない, and なくもない. The difference is the setting:
ないものでもない: written and stiff. Often found in articles, negotiations, and fairly formal statements.
条件が合えば、協力しないものでもない。 (If the terms fit, I wouldn't rule out cooperating.)
ないこともない／ないでもない: the most common in everyday conversation.
時間があれば、行けないこともないよ。 (If I have time, I could go, I guess.)
なくもない: more casual and offhand.
まあ、分からなくもないけど。 (Well, I can't say I don't get it.)
Quick tip: they all mean "it's not that I can't ~." Use 「ないこともない」 when chatting. Save 「ないものでもない」 for writing, negotiating terms, or when you want to sound a bit lofty.
n1-79:
The idea in one line
「ともすると／ともすれば」means "all too easily," "before you know it," "tends to ~". It describes an undesirable tendency: it doesn't happen every time, but the moment you let your guard down, things drift in that direction. Think of how, once you have free time, you easily end up scrolling your phone until midnight.
How to use it
It's a standalone word. It doesn't attach to anything. Just put it at the start of the sentence, or right before the bad thing you're talking about.
The second half usually has an expression meaning "easy to ~", and the two together sound most natural:
Common pairings〜がちだ (tends to ~), 〜やすい (easy to ~), 〜てしまう (end up ~ing)
・人はともすると、楽なほうへ流れがちだ。 (People tend to drift toward the easier option.)
・忙しいと、ともすれば食事を抜いてしまう。 (When I'm busy, I often end up skipping meals.)
・一人暮らしだと、ともすると生活が不規則になりやすい。 (When you live alone, your lifestyle easily becomes irregular.)
「ともすると」and「ともすれば」mean the same thing and are interchangeable. Just pick whichever sounds better to you.
Common mistakes
・It isn't a grammar pattern that attaches to the word before it, so you can't write「忙しいともすると」. Keep it separate: 忙しいと、ともすると〜.
・It describes a bad tendency. You wouldn't use it for good habits, e.g. to say "I often find myself exercising without noticing," ともすると doesn't fit.
・It describes a "recurring tendency," not a one-time event. "I accidentally came late yesterday" is just a one-off slip, so skip ともすると and simply say うっかり遅刻した.
・The tone is written and formal, and it's common in essays, speeches, and commentary. In casual chat with friends, people more often say つい or すぐ, for example ついスマホを見ちゃう (I can't help checking my phone).
Telling it apart from look-alikes
ともすると／ともすれば: stands alone in the sentence and describes a bad tendency you easily fall into. It's often paired with がち or やすい.
ともなると／ともなれば: attaches to a noun (mostly a status, position, time, or degree), and can also attach to the dictionary form of a verb. It means "once you reach a certain status, period, or situation, naturally ~".
Here's a comparison, both about being so busy you skip meals:
・忙しいと、ともすると食事を抜きがちだ。 (When busy, I tend to skip meals: a bad habit.)
・年末ともなると、食事をする時間もない。 (Once it's year-end, there isn't even time to eat: that's just how it is at that time of year.)
More examples of ともなると: 社長ともなると、なかなか休めない。 (Once you're a company president, it's hard to take time off.)
海外に住むともなると、準備が大変だ。 (When it comes to actually living abroad, the preparation is a lot of work.)
Quick tip: if there's a noun or verb before it and the meaning is "once you get to that stage, naturally ~", it's ともなると. If it stands alone and means "tends to ~ (something bad)", it's ともすると.
What to learn next
For another way to talk about a bad tendency, look at 〜嫌いがある, which goes at the end of the sentence: 彼は物事を悲観的に考える嫌いがある。 (He has a tendency to look at things pessimistically.) The two are often used together: 人はともすると、自分に甘くなる嫌いがある。 (People tend to have a flaw of going too easy on themselves.)
n1-82:
The idea in one line
「〜を限りに」means "up to ~ and no more after that". It's like saying in English "today is the last day" or "this is my last job, then I'm done": you draw a line, and what's before it exists but what's after it doesn't.
How to use it
Put a noun for a point in time directly before it, then add「を限りに」:
今日 → 今日を限りに今回 → 今回を限りに本日 → 本日を限りに
The most common are words for "this present point in time", such as 今日・本日・今回・今月・今年度.
When to use it
Resolving to stopYou cut ties with your past self, often with a sense of determination.
・今日を限りに、お酒はやめる。 (Today is my last drink. I'm quitting alcohol.)
Announcing an endingA shop closing, an athlete retiring, a system being abolished, often with a touch of emotion.
・今回の試合を限りに、引退します。 (I'll retire after this match.)
・この路線は今年度を限りに廃止される。 (This line will be discontinued at the end of this fiscal year.)
Another meaning「声を限りに」is a fixed phrase meaning "with all one's might, at the top of one's voice". It has nothing to do with time, but you should recognize it when you see it.
・声を限りに助けを呼んだ。 (I shouted for help at the top of my lungs.)
Common mistakes
・It isn't a "deadline." For a submission deadline, use までに: 金曜日までに出してください。 (Please submit it by Friday.) You can't say「金曜日を限りに出してください」.
・What follows is mostly something that ends, stops, or won't be done anymore, such as やめる・引退する・閉店する・解散する. If you just want to say "I'll start trying hard from today," Japanese usually uses 今日から.
・This is a formal, written-style expression. In everyday talk with friends, 今日でやめる or 今日限りでやめる is enough.
・Don't confuse it with "verb + 限り": 生きている限り means "as long as I'm alive", which is a completely different meaning.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
をもって can also mean "ending with ~". Both can be used in the same store-closing notice, but they feel different:
本日をもって閉店いたします。 (This store will close as of today.)
→ A formal, businesslike announcement that simply notifies people that things end on this date.
本日を限りに閉店いたします。 (Today is our last day of business.)
→ The focus is "up to today and never again", which feels more emotional, like a curtain falling.
Also, をもって can express a start too: 4月1日をもって新制度を実施します。 (The new system will be implemented starting April 1.) を限りに can only be used for the "last" point, never for a start.
Quick tip: use を限りに when you want to stress "the last time, never again after this"; use をもって for formal notices of a start or end on a given day.
What to learn next
The exact opposite is「〜を皮切りに」, meaning "starting with ~, and then things unfold one after another": 東京公演を皮切りに、全国ツアーが始まる。 (Starting with the Tokyo show, a nationwide tour begins.)
n1-83:
The idea in one line
めく means "has a touch of ~" or "gives off a hint of ~". It hasn't fully become that thing yet, but you can already feel it. Say it suddenly turns warm one day in late February and you'd say "It's starting to feel like spring." In Japanese, that's 春めいてきた.
When to use it
Seasons slowly changingThis is the most common use, usually paired with 〜めいてきた, meaning "it's gradually starting to feel like ~."
・一気に春めいてきた。(It suddenly started to feel like spring.)
・風が少し秋めいてきた。(The wind is starting to feel a bit like autumn.)
Describing people or ways of speakingUse 〜めいた before a noun to mean "with a touch of ~."
・彼女はどこか謎めいた人だ。(She's a somewhat mysterious person.)
・皮肉めいた言い方はやめてよ。(Stop talking in that sarcastic way.)
・言い訳めいたことは言いたくない。(I don't want to say anything that sounds like an excuse.)
How to attach it and conjugate it
Add めく straight onto a noun and the whole thing becomes a verb, specifically a Group 1 (godan) verb that conjugates like 書く.
Before て and た, く changes to い:
春めく → 春めいて → 春めいてきた
謎めく → 謎めいた → 謎めいた事件 (a mysterious incident)
Common pitfalls
・Not every noun works. めく only pairs with a small set of fixed words. Common ones are 春めく, 秋めく, 謎めく, 皮肉めく, 冗談めく, 言い訳めく and 説教めく. Something like 「学生めく」 or 「先生めく」 sounds unnatural. Say 学生らしい or 学生っぽい instead.
・Before a noun, you almost always use めいた: say 謎めいた人, not 謎めく人.
・The て-form is めいて, not めくて or めきて.
・春めいてきた means "it's starting to feel like spring," which is not the same as 春になった (it's already spring).
・It has a written, literary feel and is very common in weather reports and novels. In casual chat with friends, っぽい is more common.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Here are three ways to talk about "spring":
だんだん春めいてきた。 (It's gradually starting to feel like spring.): the focus is on the first signs appearing.
今日は春らしい天気だ。 (Today is typical spring weather.): the focus is on being a true, textbook example.
春っぽい服を買った。 (I bought some spring-looking clothes.): casual speech, a loose "kind of like ~."
Quick rule of thumb: use めく for "starting to give off a hint of ~"; use らしい for "truly has the qualities ~ should have"; use っぽい for a casual "it feels kind of ~" in conversation.
What to learn next
めく has a sibling, めかす, meaning "to deliberately make it seem like ~": 冗談めかして本音を言った。 (He said what he really felt in a joking tone.)
n1-84:
The idea in one line
This grammar group means "a good ~ of it" or "as much as ~". Put a number in front, and the speaker is stressing "that's a big number!", and it may even be more than that. Picture seeing a 30 kg bag and saying "That's a good 30 kilos, easily!" That's when you use this in Japanese.
How to attach it
What comes before must be a number + a unit (100キロ、1万人、50万円), followed directly by からある / からする / からの. Which of the three you pick depends on what you're talking about.
からあるWeight, length, height, distance, size.
Japanese naturally says 「重さがある」 and 「長さがある」, so for "how heavy / how long it is" you use ある.
・30キロからある荷物を一人で運んだ。(I carried a good 30 kg of luggage all by myself.)
・2メートルからある魚が釣れた。(I caught a fish a good two meters long.)
・片道100キロからある道のりを毎日車で通っている。(He commutes by car every day, a full hundred kilometers each way.)
からするPrices.
Japanese naturally uses する for "how much something costs": この時計は100万円する。 (This watch costs 1 million yen.) So prices go with からする.
・一泊10万円からするホテルに泊まった。(I stayed at a hotel that costs a good 100,000 yen a night.)
・あのバッグは50万円からするらしい。(I hear that bag costs as much as 500,000 yen.)
からのMost often used for numbers of people, and it must be followed by a noun (の works like a possessive "of"). Amounts like money or debt can also take からの + noun.
・会場には1万人からの人が集まった。(As many as 10,000 people gathered at the venue.)
・彼には1000万円からの借金がある。(He has debts of as much as 10 million yen.)
Common pitfalls
・Only use it with big numbers. 1キロからある荷物 sounds odd, because one kilo isn't worth stressing.
・からする only covers prices. For weight, say 100キロからある, not 100キロからする.
・からの always needs a noun after it: 1万人からの人 is fine, but ending a sentence on 「1万人からの。」 is not.
・This pattern is somewhat written and formal, and very common in news, reports and articles. You can say it to friends, but the more casual way is to use 「も」 (covered below).
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Ordinary 「から」 = starting from ~ (the lowest price in a range):
この店の時計は1万円からあります。 (Watches at this shop start from 10,000 yen.)
からする = a full ~ in cost (stressing that it's expensive):
この時計は100万円からする。 (This watch costs a good 1 million yen.)
The first tells you where the cheapest option begins; the second says this one item is seriously expensive.
Number + も = the casual "wow, as many as ~": この荷物、30キロもあるよ。 (This bag is a whole 30 kilos, you know.)
からある = more written, with the feel of "at least this much, maybe even more": 30キロからある荷物 (luggage of a good 30 kg)
Quick rule of thumb: when a shop writes 「～円から」, it's stating the lowest price. When からある / からする / からの follows a number, the speaker is marveling at how big that number is. Use ある for weight and length, する for prices, and からの when a noun follows.
n1-85:
The idea in one line
「〜ようにも〜ない」 means "I'd like to ~, but I can't" or "even if I wanted to ~, I couldn't", as in "I'd run away if I could, but I can't" or "I'd forget it if I could, but I can't." You really want to do something, but the situation blocks you, so you simply can't. There's a note of helplessness in it.
・逃げようにも逃げられない状況だった。(It was a situation where I couldn't have escaped even if I'd wanted to.)
When to use it
Blocked by circumstancesAn injury, no car, no way to contact someone... It's not that you don't want to; the conditions don't allow it.
・終電がなくて、帰ろうにも帰れない。(The last train is gone, so I can't get home even if I want to.)
・足をけがしていて、歩こうにも歩けない。(I've hurt my leg, so I can't walk even if I want to.)
Blocked emotionallySometimes what holds you back is a feeling or a memory.
・忘れようにも忘れられない思い出だ。(It's a memory I can't forget, however much I'd like to.)
・状況が深刻すぎて、笑おうにも笑えなかった。(The situation was so serious that I couldn't even laugh if I'd wanted to.)
How to connect it
Volitional form of the verb (「〜う／〜よう」, the "let's ~" form) + にも + the same verb in its "can't do" form (negative potential).
A reason is often slipped in between: 帰ろうにも、終電がなくて帰れない。
The second half doesn't have to repeat the verb. You can just state what is blocking you:
・電話しようにも、番号が分からない。(I'd call, but I don't know the number.)
How to conjugate: check the verb group first
Group 1 (godan verbs): In the first half, change the final sound to the 「お」-row sound of the same row and add 「う」. In the second half, change the final sound to the 「え」-row sound of the same row and add 「ない」.
書く → change く to こ → 書こう書く → change く to け → 書けない
Put together: 書こうにも書けない
帰る → 帰ろうにも帰れない
話す → 話そうにも話せない
会う → 会おうにも会えない
Group 2 (ichidan verbs): In the first half, drop 「る」 and add 「よう」. In the second half, drop 「る」 and add 「られない」.
逃げる → 逃げようにも逃げられない
忘れる → 忘れようにも忘れられない
Group 3 (only two verbs, just memorize them):
する → しようにもできない, for example: 予約しようにも予約できない
来る → 来ようにも来られない (こようにもこられない)
Easy mistakes
・The first half must be in the volitional form: it's 帰ろうにも, not 帰るようにも. It has nothing to do with the N4 「〜ように」 (so that ~), so don't attach the dictionary form just because you see 「よう」.
・The second half must mean "can't do it", not "won't do it". Writing 帰らない would mean "I choose not to go home", which contradicts the "want to go home" in the first half.
・It assumes the speaker really wants to do it. If you're just too lazy or not interested, you can't use this pattern.
・For Group 2 "can't do", write 逃げられない in formal writing and on exams. The spoken form 「逃げれない」 is common in conversation, but avoid it in writing.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Here are three ways to talk about "escaping" and how they differ:
ようにも = you want to, but simply can't: 逃げようにも、ドアに鍵がかかっていて逃げられない。 (I'd like to escape, but the door is locked, so I can't.)
たところで = even if you did it, it's pointless: 今さら逃げたところで、すぐに見つかるだろう。 (Even if you run now, you'll be found right away.)
ようと／ようが = no matter how you do it, the result is the same: どこへ逃げようと、必ず見つけ出す。 (No matter where you run, I'll find you.)
Quick tip: use ようにも for "want to but can't", たところで for "doing it is pointless", and ようと／ようが for "no matter how you do it".
n1-86:
The idea in one line
「〜とは言い条」 means "although it's said to be ~, but..." or "~ in name, but actually...". You first acknowledge a claim, then immediately say that the real situation isn't that simple. The meaning is close to 「とはいえ」, but it's more old-fashioned and bookish, and you almost never hear it in everyday speech.
First, understand the word 「言い条」
言い条 is read いいじょう and originally meant "what someone says, a claim". So 「Aとは言い条」 literally means "it's said to be A, but that's just one way of putting it". The implication is: that's what people say, but reality is another matter.
How to connect it
Nouns attach directly: プロ → プロとは言い条
Verbs and adjectives attach in the plain form (the form without ます or です): 分かっている → 分かっているとは言い条安い → 安いとは言い条
In practice, you'll see nouns attached directly most often.
When to use it
Name doesn't match realityThe first part is a commonly accepted claim or name, and the second part points out that reality isn't like that.
・春とは言い条、朝晩はまだ冷える。(Although it's supposedly spring, mornings and evenings are still cold.)
・自由とは言い条、実際には多くの制約がある。(It's called freedom in name, but in reality there are many restrictions.)
Understand it, but can't do itYou admit the first part is true, but the result is still not what you'd hope.
・頭では分かっているとは言い条、なかなか実行に移せない。(Although I understand it in my head, I can't seem to put it into action.)
・プロとは言い条、ミスを犯すこともある。(Even though they're professionals, they sometimes make mistakes.)
Easy mistakes
・The reading is いいじょう. 「条」 is read じょう (long vowel), so don't read it as 「いうじょう」 or a short 「じょ」.
・It goes in the middle of a sentence, and a "but..." clause must follow. You can't just end the sentence with it.
・It's very stiff written language, used in commentary, novels, and essays. Saying 「春とは言い条」 to a friend would sound like you're reading an old book; in conversation, 春だけど is enough.
・On exams, it's enough to recognize it as "although ~, but...". In your own writing, 「とはいえ」 is less likely to sound odd.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
All three mean "although ~, but...". The difference is how formal and how old-fashioned they are. Let's compare them in the same situation:
とはいうものの: Used in writing, and also in speech on formal occasions.
・春とはいうものの、まだ寒い。(Although it's spring, it's still cold.)
とはいえ: Mainly written; very common in news and essays, and you'll also hear it in somewhat formal speech.
・春とはいえ、まだ寒い。(Although it's spring, it's still cold.)
とは言い条: The most archaic; today you'll see it almost only in essays and literature.
・春とは言い条、まだ寒い。(Although it's spring, it's still cold.)
Quick tip: they all mean "although ~, but...". The more archaic and literary it sounds, the more likely it's 「とは言い条」. For your own writing, 「とはいえ」 is the safest choice.
n1-90:
The idea in one line
「〜にかこつけて」means "using ~ as a pretext" or "under the guise of ~". On the surface you're doing A, but what you really want to do is B. Say you announce "I'm going on a business trip," then spend most of it shopping and eating out. That's the feeling of this phrase.
How to attach it
Noun + にかこつけて, followed by the thing you really want to do.
出張 → 出張にかこつけて (under the guise of a business trip)
仕事 → 仕事にかこつけて (using work as an excuse)
The part before it is the "respectable reason you can say out loud." The part after it is "what you actually wanted to do."
When to use it
Calling someone outThis is the most common use. You're annoyed that someone is hiding behind a legitimate reason, so there's a hint of criticism.
・部長は視察にかこつけて、毎年ハワイに行っている。 (The department head goes to Hawaii every year under the guise of an inspection.)
・彼は仕事にかこつけて、毎晩飲みに行っている。 (He uses work as an excuse to go out drinking every night.)
Self-mockeryYou can also use it about yourself. It's like admitting "okay, I really just wanted to do that," with a slightly sheepish, funny tone.
・子どもの誕生日にかこつけて、自分が食べたいケーキを買った。 (Using my kid's birthday as a pretext, I bought the cake I wanted to eat.)
・雨にかこつけて、ジムをサボった。 (I used the rain as an excuse to skip the gym.)
Common mistakes
・The particle is に, not を. The similar everyday expression 「〜を口実に」 is the one that takes を. Don't mix the two up. 「出張をかこつけて」 is wrong.
・It always carries the sense that "the stated reason and the real purpose are different." If you really did go on a business trip and just happened to see some sights, using this phrase would make it sound like a fake business trip and a real holiday.
・Because it carries criticism or self-mockery, it's not suitable for explaining your own schedule in formal situations. If you tell your boss 「出張にかこつけて…」, you're basically admitting you're slacking off.
・It's usually written in hiragana. The kanji form is 「託けて」, which you rarely see. Just be able to recognize it.
Don't confuse it with look-alikes
Same situation: you went sightseeing in Kyoto during a business trip.
がてら = "while at it". Both things are genuine and above board:
出張がてら、京都を観光した。 (I did some sightseeing in Kyoto while I was there on business.)
かたがた = also "while at it, and also," but more formal, often used for visits and thank-yous:
お礼かたがた、先生のお宅に伺った。 (I visited my teacher's home, also to express my thanks.)
にかこつけて = the reason in front is just a front, and the real purpose is the thing that follows:
出張にかこつけて、京都を観光した。 (Under the guise of a business trip, I actually went sightseeing in Kyoto.)
Quick test: if you genuinely meant to do both things, use 「がてら」, or 「かたがた」 in formal situations. If the first reason is just an excuse and the second thing is what you really wanted, use 「にかこつけて」.
What to learn next
In everyday conversation you'll hear 「〜を口実に」 more often. The meaning is almost the same, but the tone is more direct: 風邪を口実に、会社を休んだ。 (I used a cold as an excuse to take the day off work.)
n1-92:
The idea in one line
「AとBが相まって」means "A and B come together and amplify each other." It's like English "a perfect storm" or "good weather on top of a long weekend": either factor alone might be fine, but stacked together the result really stands out. You can use it for good or bad things, and it shows up a lot in news, commentary and essays.
How to attach it
It follows a noun. There are three common patterns:
AはBと相まってThe main subject A combines with another factor B.
・彼の才能は努力と相まって、大きな成果を生んだ。 (His talent, combined with his effort, produced great results.)
AとBが相まってTwo factors are placed side by side, and together they cause the result that follows.
・この店は料理の味と雰囲気の良さが相まって、いつも予約でいっぱいだ。 (The food and the great atmosphere together keep this restaurant fully booked.)
Bも相まってThe most common form in news. 「も」 signals "there were already other causes, and on top of that there's B."
・円安も相まって、外国人観光客が急増している。 (With the weak yen on top of that, the number of foreign tourists is soaring.)
If what comes before it is a whole clause, add 「こと」 first to turn it into a noun:
駅から近い → 駅から近いことも相まって (on top of being close to the station)
Common mistakes
・Read it あいまって, not 「そうまって」.
・You need two or more factors. You can't use it with a single cause. If rain canceled a game, just say 雨で試合が中止になった. You can't say 「雨と相まって中止になった」.
・It isn't limited to good things. Bad things work too: 寝不足と疲れが相まって、熱を出してしまった。 (Lack of sleep combined with fatigue, and I ended up with a fever.) So don't think of it as "complementing each other," which only suits positive things.
・This is a fairly formal, written-style expression. When chatting with friends, 〜もあって or 〜も重なって sounds more natural.
Don't confuse it with look-alikes
に加えて = simply "besides A, there's also B." It just lists things one by one:
円安に加えて、物価も上がっている。 (Besides the weak yen, prices are also rising.)
と相まって = two factors work together to produce a result:
円安と物価高が相まって、生活が苦しくなっている。 (The weak yen and high prices combine to make life harder.)
とあって (it differs by just one character, so it's easy to misread) = "because it's such a special situation as ~, ...". There is only one cause:
連休とあって、どこも混んでいる。 (Since it's a long holiday weekend, everywhere is crowded.)
と相まって = two causes stacked together:
連休と好天が相まって、どこも混んでいる。 (The long weekend and the good weather together make everywhere crowded.)
Quick test: for just "there's also ~," use に加えて. For "because it's ~," use とあって. Use と相まって only when "two factors stack up and amplify the effect."
n1-87:
The idea in one line
「〜かれ〜かれ」 gives you English phrases like "sooner or later," "more or less," and "for better or worse." It isn't a pattern where you can swap in any words. It's three fixed expressions, so just memorize each set as a whole.
Where it comes from
「かれ」 is a classical imperative form, roughly "be it ~, so be it."
多かれ少なかれ originally meant something like "be it many, be it few," and later became "many or few, it's there either way."
You don't need to study classical Japanese. Just know this: it puts two adjectives with opposite meanings side by side to say "it's the same whichever way, and the outcome won't change."
The three you'll hear most
遅かれ早かれRead it 「おそかれはやかれ」. It means "sooner or later." It usually goes with something that's bound to happen, with a feeling of "you can't avoid it," and it's common in everyday conversation too.
・嘘は遅かれ早かればれるよ。(Sooner or later, a lie gets exposed.)
・遅かれ早かれ、決めなきゃいけないことだ。(Sooner or later, this is something you have to decide.)
多かれ少なかれRead it 「おおかれすくなかれ」. It means "more or less." It often goes with 「誰でも」 or 「みんな」, saying that everyone has it, just to different degrees.
・多かれ少なかれ、誰にでも悩みはある。(Everyone has worries, more or less.)
善かれ悪しかれRead it 「よかれあしかれ」. It means "for better or worse." It's more formal than the other two and is mostly used in writing and commentary.
・善かれ悪しかれ、スマホは私たちの生活を大きく変えた。(For better or worse, smartphones have changed our lives enormously.)
Easy mistakes
・You can't make your own: when you see "adjective + かれ," don't try plugging in 高い or 大きい. That doesn't work. It really is just these three.
・It's 悪しかれ, not 「悪かれ」. This uses the classical 「悪し」, not the modern 「悪い」.
・The order is fixed: say 遅かれ早かれ and 多かれ少なかれ, and don't flip them around.
・よかれと思って on its own is a different expression. It means "meaning well, thinking it would be good for the other person," and has nothing to do with "for better or worse."
　よかれと思って言ったのに、怒られた。(I said it meaning well, and still got scolded.)
Telling it apart from similar patterns
All of these mean "whether A or B," but with 〜にせよ〜にせよ and 〜であれ〜であれ you can swap in your own words, while with 〜かれ〜かれ you can't.
・行くにせよ行かないにせよ、早めに連絡してね。(Whether you go or not, let me know early.)
・雨であれ雪であれ、試合は行われる。(Rain or snow, the game will be held.)
・遅かれ早かれ、ばれるよ。(Sooner or later, it'll come out.)
Conversely, you wouldn't say "sooner or later" as 遅いにせよ早いにせよ. It isn't grammatically wrong, but it sounds like you're discussing two cases, "slow" and "fast," rather than using the set phrase for "sooner or later." Japanese speakers simply say 遅かれ早かれ.
One more note: であれ attaches to nouns or na-adjectives and not to i-adjectives, so 「遅いであれ」 is wrong in itself.
Quick rule of thumb: for "sooner or later / more or less / for better or worse," use the three fixed かれ sets. For any other "whether A or B," use にせよ or であれ.
n1-88:
The idea in one line
「〜始末だ」 means "it got to the point where, of all things, ~" or "it ended with ~". You describe a string of outrageous things, then drop an even worse ending, with a tone of disbelief, exasperation, and reproach. It's like complaining to a friend: "He was late, fine, and he forgot his stuff too, and then what? He even got yelled at by his boss."
When to use it
Criticizing someoneThis is the classic use. You describe someone who keeps getting more ridiculous until they reach an extreme.
・息子は毎晩ゲームばかりして、ついには学校を休む始末だ。(My son plays video games every night, and it's gotten to the point where he even skips school.)
・彼は何度注意しても聞かず、最近は返事もしない始末だ。(No matter how many times I warn him he won't listen, and lately he doesn't even answer.)
Self-deprecationYou can use it about yourself too, with a "I'm hopeless" kind of self-mockery.
・寝坊して駅まで走ったのに、財布を家に忘れる始末だ。(I overslept and ran all the way to the station, and then I even forgot my wallet at home.)
How to attach it
Verb dictionary form + 始末だ: 休む → 休む始末だ
Verb ない form + 始末だ: しない → 返事もしない始末だ
Demonstrative + 始末だ: この始末だ, あの始末だ ("look at the mess it's ended up in")
・あれほど言ったのに、この始末だ。(I told you so many times, and look how it turned out.)
What it usually looks like
It often comes with "in the end" words in front, which build up the feeling of things getting worse and worse: ついには, とうとう, 最後には, 挙句の果てには.
・借金を重ね、挙句の果てには夜逃げする始末だ。(He piled up debt, and in the end he even ended up skipping town in the night.)
When talking about the past, the verb in front stays in dictionary form, and you can end the sentence with 始末だった.
Easy mistakes
・Use the dictionary form or ない form in front, not the た form: it's 叱られる始末だ, not 叱られた始末だ.
・It's for bad outcomes only. You can't use 始末だ for "I studied hard and finally got in."
・You need the buildup beforehand. Tacking 始末だ onto a single line saying only that he showed up late sounds odd. First explain how things went downhill step by step.
・The tone is reproachful and complaining, so saying this about your boss or a customer to their face is very rude. It shows up more in complaints, writing, and commentary.
・始末 on its own also means "dealing with, cleaning up," as in 後始末 (cleaning up afterward) and 始末書 (a written apology). That's a separate matter from this pattern.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
For "ending up ~," there are also 「末に」 and 「羽目になる」 from N2. They differ in whether the result is good, who it's about, and how the speaker feels.
末に = a conclusion after a process, neutral, and a good result is fine:
何度も話し合った末に、ゲームは一日一時間と決めた。(After talking it over many times, we finally decided on one hour of games a day.)
羽目になる = you yourself get forced into some troublesome task, with a sense of regret:
息子のゲームの課金を、私が払う羽目になった。(I ended up having to pay for my son's in-game purchases.)
始末だ = the speaker is exasperated and reproaching someone, as in "it actually got to this point":
息子はゲームに夢中で、ついには学校を休む始末だ。(My son is so hooked on games that he's even skipping school now.)
Quick rule of thumb: for a neutral "in the end we decided ~," use 末に. For "I got stuck having to ~," use 羽目になる. When you want to roll your eyes and say "it ended with him actually ~," use 始末だ.
What to learn next
It often appears together with 「〜あげく」: さんざん迷ったあげく、何も買わずに帰ってくる始末だ。(After dithering forever, he actually came home without buying anything.)
n5-25:
The short version
「から」means “from”. Use it for a starting time, a starting place, or the person something comes from. It often appears with 「まで」(until / to), and AからBまで means “from A to B.”
How to attach it
Easy: just add から right after the noun. Nothing changes.
9時 → 9時から(from 9 o'clock)駅 → 駅から(from the station)友達 → 友達から(from a friend)
When to use it
Starting point in timeSomething starts at a certain time.
・仕事は9時からです。(Work starts at 9.)
・明日から夏休みです。(Summer vacation starts tomorrow.)
Starting point in placeWhere you set out from or come from.
・どこから来ましたか。(Where are you from? / Where did you come from?)
・台湾から来ました。(I'm from Taiwan.)
From a personWho gave you something or who the news came from.
・友達から電話がありました。(I got a call from a friend.)
What you'll hear most: AからBまで
When you talk about a range, 「から」and 「まで」usually go together, for both time and place.
・月曜日から金曜日まで働きます。(I work from Monday to Friday.)
・家から駅まで歩きます。(I walk from home to the station.)
・何時から何時までですか。(From what time to what time?)
That last one is super handy for asking about a shop's opening hours or an event's schedule, and you'll definitely use it in Japan. When you don't need a range, 「から」on its own is perfectly fine too.
Common mistakes
・The position is the opposite of English: English puts “from” before the noun, but Japanese puts 「から」after the noun. “From the station” is 駅から, not から駅.
・In English you might say “starting tomorrow.” In Japanese, 明日から夏休みです is enough. 「から」already carries the meaning “starting from,” so don't try to translate “start” separately.
・To say “at what time you do something,” use 「に」, not 「から」. More on that below.
Don't mix it up with look-alikes
① から (starting point) vs に (point in time)
9時に起きます。(I get up at 9: just that one moment)
9時から勉強します。(I study from 9: it continues for a while afterward)
“Getting up” is an instant action, so saying 9時から起きます would sound odd.
Quick tip: if you only say “at what time” something happens, use に. If you mean “starting then and continuing after,” use から.
② から (starting point) vs から (reason)
At N5 you'll also learn another 「から」meaning “because.” They look exactly the same, so check what comes before it.
Starting point: a noun plus から directly, such as 駅から (from the station).
Reason: it follows a whole clause. A noun needs だ or です first (雨だから, 雨ですから), or it's a verb or い-adjective in plain or polite form (行くから, 行きますから, 高いから, 高いですから).
Compare them with the same “tomorrow's test”:
明日からテストです。(The tests start tomorrow.)
明日テストだから、勉強します。(I have a test tomorrow, so I'll study.)
Quick tip: if only a noun like a time, place, or person comes before から, it means “from.” If it follows だ／です, or a verb or adjective in plain or polite form (行くから, 行きますから, 高いから), it means “because.” (“Verb て-form + から” is a different grammar point meaning “after doing ~.” Don't mix them up.)
What to learn next
Its partner 「まで」(until / to) is a good one to study alongside. Later you'll also learn “verb て-form + から” = “after doing ~, then ~”: ご飯を食べてから、出かけます。(I'll go out after eating.)
n5-26:
The short version
「まで」means “until ~” or “up to ~”. It marks where something ends. The endpoint can be a time (until 5 o'clock) or a place (as far as the station). It often pairs with 「から」(from ~): から is the starting point and まで is the endpoint.
When to use it
TimeYou keep doing something until that point in time, and then you stop.
・5時まで待ちます。(I'll wait until 5.)
・昨日は11時まで寝ました。(Yesterday I slept until 11.)
PlaceHow far you go.
・駅まで歩きます。(I'll walk to the station.)
・空港までバスで行きます。(I'll take the bus to the airport.)
How to attach it
Easy: just add まで right after the noun. Nothing changes.
6時 → 6時まで金曜日 → 金曜日まで東京 → 東京まで
What you'll hear most
から～までFrom where to where, or from what time to what time. It states the whole range at once.
・9時から5時まで働きます。(I work from 9 to 5.)
・東京から大阪まで新幹線で行きます。(I'll take the Shinkansen from Tokyo to Osaka.)
～までですYou can follow it directly with です. This is very common for opening hours and class times.
・この店は夜10時までです。(This shop is open until 10 p.m.)
いつまで・どこまでAsking “until when” and “how far.”
・いつまで日本にいますか。(How long will you be in Japan? / Until when will you be in Japan?)
Common mistakes
・まで means the action keeps going up to that point. So you can't translate “Be here by 5” as 「5時まで来てください」. That would come across as “keep coming until 5,” which is very odd. To say “come at 5,” use 5時に来てください.
・「金曜日まで休みです」usually includes Friday, so it means “off through Friday.”
・まで only marks the endpoint. It doesn't carry the idea of “going” by itself, so you still need a verb after it, as in 駅まで歩きます and 駅まで行きます.
Don't mix it up with look-alikes
に (point in time) = at that time, something happens once: 11時に寝ました。(I went to bed at 11.)
まで = keep doing something until that time: 11時まで寝ました。(I slept until 11.)
One small particle makes the difference: in one you go to bed at 11, in the other you don't get up until 11.
までに = finish before that time (a deadline): 5時までに帰ります。(I'll be back by 5.)
まで = keep going until that time: 5時まで待ちます。(I'll wait until 5.)
Quick tip: “keep doing something until X” takes まで. “Get it done by X” takes までに. “Do it at X” takes に.
What to learn next
Add に after まで and you get までに, which expresses a deadline: 金曜日までに出してください。(Please hand it in by Friday.)
n5-68:
The idea in one line
「AというB」means "a B called A". Say you tell a friend, "There's a shop called Shunsuidō in Taichung." In Japanese you use「という」to link the shop's name to the word for "shop." Use it when the listener may not know the name.
How to connect it
Name (noun A) + という + what kind of thing it is (noun B)
村田 ＋ 人 → 村田という人 (a person named Murata)
さくら ＋ 店 → さくらという店 (a shop called Sakura)
B is usually a word like「人、店、町、食べ物、ドラマ、本」, which tells the listener what kind of thing the name refers to.
When to use it
Introducing a nameUse it for a person, shop, work or food the listener may not have heard of.
・駅の前に「さくら」という喫茶店があります。 (There's a café called "Sakura" in front of the station.)
・山田という人から電話がありました。 (There was a phone call from someone named Yamada.)
・小籠包という食べ物を知っていますか。 (Do you know a food called xiaolongbao?)
Asking a nameWhen you don't know what something is called, ask with 何という. Here 「何」 is read なん.
・これは何という花ですか。 (What is this flower called?)
Common mistakes
・というmust be followed by a noun. You can't say「さくらというです」. Say the whole thing: さくらという店です.
・Don't use it for things everyone knows. Saying「富士山という山」to a Japanese person sounds like "there's a mountain called Mt. Fuji, you've probably never heard of it," which is odd.
・「いう」is often pronounced ゆう, but you still write「いう」. Don't write「とゆう」.
・This「いう」is normally written in hiragana, not with the kanji「言う」.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
という = called / named ～: 村田という人 (a person whose name is Murata)
の = belonging to ～ / from ～: 村田さんの友達 (Mr. Murata's friend)
In English, "a person named Murata" and "Murata's friend" are clearly different phrases, but learners often grab「の」for both because it feels like the easy "link" word. 「村田の人」would mean "someone from the Murata family / Murata's side," not "someone called Murata."
Also, the 林といいます。 (My name is Hayashi.) you hear in self-introductions puts "called" at the end of the sentence, with no noun after it.
林といいます。 (My name is Hayashi.)
林という人がいます。 (There's a person named Hayashi.)
When you give your own name, don't add さん. 「林さんといいます」is wrong.
Quick test: if English would say "called / named ～", use という. If it's just "whose" or "from where," use の.
What to learn next
Asking "How do you say this in Japanese?": これは日本語で何といいますか。 (What is this called in Japanese?)
n4-30:
The idea in one line
These three all mean "do something for someone." Use てあげる when you do something for someone else, てくれる when someone does something for you, and てもらう when you receive someone's help. The directions are exactly the same as the gift verbs あげる・くれる・もらう. The only difference is that what's passed along isn't a present but "a favor."
How to connect it
Change the verb to the て-form, then add あげる／くれる／もらう.
貸す → 貸して → 貸してあげる
作る → 作って → 作ってくれる
撮る → 撮って → 撮ってもらう
For the polite form, use あげます、くれます、もらいます.
When to use it
I do it for someoneてあげる. The pattern is "I は (person) に ～てあげる."
・妹に本を読んであげました。 (I read a book to my little sister.)
・友だちに傘を貸してあげた。 (I lent my umbrella to a friend.)
Someone does it for meてくれる. The pattern is "(person) が ～てくれる." You usually don't say "for me," because くれる itself already means "toward me." Family counts as "my side" too.
・母がお弁当を作ってくれた。 (My mom made me a packed lunch.)
・友だちが駅まで送ってくれました。 (My friend took me to the station.)
I receive helpてもらう. The pattern is "I は (person) に ～てもらう." Here「に」means "from whom" you receive the help.
・友だちに写真を撮ってもらいました。 (I had a friend take a photo of me.)
・美容院で髪を切ってもらいました。 (I got my hair cut at the salon.)
The stylist cut your hair, not you, so Japanese naturally uses てもらう.
Forms you'll hear most
Asking for a favorTo ask for help, you can simply ask "Could you ～ for me?"
・ちょっと手伝ってくれない？ (Can you give me a hand? — to a friend)
・このペンを貸してもらえませんか。 (Could I borrow this pen? — polite)
Common mistakes
・くれる can only point toward "me (my side)." When I help someone else, it's always あげる. You can't say「私が友だちに貸してくれた」.
・The「に」with もらう doesn't mean "to": 友だちに手伝ってもらった means "my friend helped me," not "I helped my friend." If you read に as "to," it's easy to flip the meaning.
・Which particle marks the other person depends on the original verb, not always に. "I carried my mom's bags for her" is 母の荷物を持ってあげた. Saying「母に持ってあげた」sounds unnatural.
・In English, "My friend taught me Japanese" already shows who benefited through "me." In Japanese, if you only say 友だちが日本語を教えた, it sounds like you're talking about someone else's business, and the gratitude is missing. When someone does something for you, Japanese people almost always add てくれる: 友だちが日本語を教えてくれた.
・てあげる carries a nuance of "I'm doing you a favor." Saying「持ってあげましょうか」to a teacher or boss is rude. Say お持ちしましょうか instead. Be careful when telling others "I did X for him," too, since it can sound like you're taking credit.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
てくれる and てもらう often describe the same event. Only the focus changes:
友だちが手伝ってくれた。 (My friend helped me.) The focus is on the friend: "how kind of them."
友だちに手伝ってもらった。 (I got my friend to help.) The focus is on me: "I received help."
In most situations either works. But when the other person offers help on their own initiative, くれる is the most natural: 頼んでいないのに、友だちが手伝ってくれた。 (I hadn't even asked, but my friend came and helped me.)
When you asked for it or paid for the service, もらう is more common: 店の人に包んでもらいました。 (I had the shop staff wrap it for me.)
Quick test: if I help someone else, use あげる. If the other person is the subject and is marked with が, use くれる. If I'm the subject and the other person is marked with に, use もらう.
What to learn next
With teachers and elders, switch to the honorific versions:
先生が教えてくださいました。 (The teacher taught me.)
先生に教えていただきました。 (I was taught by the teacher.)
When asking a favor, 「〜てもらえませんか」becomes even more polite as「〜ていただけませんか」. You can learn these together with honorific (尊敬語) and humble (謙譲語) forms.
n4-2:
The idea in one line
「〜つもりです」means "I plan to ~" or "I'm going to ~". You've already made up your mind to do something, and you use it to tell someone your plan.
For example, a friend asks what you're doing over summer break, and you say "I'm planning to go to Japan". That's 日本へ行くつもりです.
How to form it
Plan to doVerb dictionary form (the base form you'd look up in a dictionary) + つもりです
行く → 行くつもりです買う → 買うつもりです勉強する → 勉強するつもりです
・来年、日本へ留学するつもりです。(I plan to study abroad in Japan next year.)
・週末は家でゆっくりするつもりです。(I plan to relax at home this weekend.)
Plan not to doVerb ない form + つもりです
吸う → 吸わない → 吸わないつもりです
・もうタバコは吸わないつもりです。(I don't plan to smoke anymore.)
When you're talking with friends, swap です for だ, or just stop at つもり: 夏休み、どうするつもり？ (What are you planning to do over summer break?)
Forms you'll hear most
つもりはありません"I have no intention at all." It's more firm than 「〜ないつもりです」 and is often used to refuse.
・会社をやめるつもりはありません。(I have no intention of quitting my job.)
つもりでした"I was planning to ~." It's usually followed by "but it didn't work out."
・早く寝るつもりでしたが、ゲームをしてしまいました。(I was planning to go to bed early, but I ended up playing video games.)
Common mistakes
・Put the dictionary form before つもり, not the ます form: it's 行くつもりです, not 「行きますつもりです」.
・It expresses a person's intention, so you can't use it for things outside your control. Japanese doesn't use つもり for something like "it's going to clear up tomorrow."
・It's mainly for talking about your own plans. For someone else's plans, you usually add 「そうです」 or 「と言っていました」: 田中さんは留学するつもりだそうです。 (I hear Tanaka plans to study abroad.)
・Asking a teacher or boss directly 「どうするつもりですか」 sounds like you're demanding "What on earth do you intend to do?" To ask an older or senior person about their plans, ご予定は？ is more polite.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Take "going to Japan next year". Different phrasings show how settled the plan is:
ようと思っています = you have the idea in mind and are thinking it over (N4-42)
来年、日本へ行こうと思っています。 (I'm thinking of going to Japan next year.)
つもりです = a plan you've firmly decided on, stronger than the sentence above
来年、日本へ行くつもりです。 (I plan to go to Japan next year.)
予定です = already scheduled, with concrete arrangements, like a booked flight and a set date
来年3月に日本へ行く予定です。 (I'm scheduled to go to Japan in March next year.)
Quick rule of thumb: use ようと思う for "still thinking about it", つもり for "my mind is made up", and 予定 for "it's already on the calendar".
What to learn next
To say "I've decided to ~", learn 〜ことにします (N4-47) next: 来年留学することにしました。 (I've decided to study abroad next year.)
n4-3:
The idea in one line
「〜かもしれません」means "maybe ~" or "might ~". You're not sure, and you think something is possible, but it may not happen. Like saying "It might rain tomorrow," which in Japanese is 明日は雨が降るかもしれません.
When to use it
GuessingYou're not sure about something, and you state what you think is possible.
・明日は雨が降るかもしれません。(It might rain tomorrow.)
・あの店、今日は休みかもしれない。(That shop might be closed today.)
・彼はもう帰ったかもしれない。(He might have already gone home.)
Giving a heads-upIt's also very common when talking about yourself. It softens what you say and prepares the other person.
・すみません、少し遅れるかもしれません。(Sorry, I might be a little late.)
・土曜日はちょっと行けないかもしれない。(I might not be able to make it on Saturday.)
How to form it
Verbs: no change needed, just attach it directly. The same goes for negative and past forms.
行く → 行くかもしれない行かない → 行かないかもしれない行った → 行ったかもしれない
い-adjectives: attach directly.
高い → 高いかもしれない
な-adjectives and nouns: drop 「だ」 before attaching.
静かだ → drop だ → 静かかもしれない
雨だ → drop だ → 雨かもしれない
But keep the past 「だった」: 雨だった → 雨だったかもしれない
Forms you'll hear most
かもしれませんThe polite version, for teachers, coworkers and customers.
かもしれないUsed among friends and family.
かもAn even more casual shortened form, heard all the time when young people and friends chat.
・あ、財布忘れたかも。(Oh, I think I forgot my wallet.)
Common mistakes
・Don't keep 「だ」 after nouns or な-adjectives: say 雨かもしれない, not 「雨だかもしれない」.
・The final 「ない」 in 「かもしれない」 is not a negative. 来るかもしれない means "might come". To say "might not come", make the verb before it negative: 来ないかもしれない.
・It expresses low certainty, around 50-50 or even lower. Don't use it for things you're sure about, or you'll sound irresponsible. For example, if you've made plans with someone and say 行くかもしれません, they'll think you might not show up.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
Say you're guessing whether Suzuki will come. The level of certainty differs:
かもしれない = might or might not, you have no real idea: 鈴木さんは来るかもしれません。 (Suzuki might come.)
でしょう = probably, it seems quite likely: 鈴木さんは来るでしょう。 (Suzuki will probably come.)
はず = should, based on solid grounds, like him saying himself yesterday that he'd come: 鈴木さんは来るはずです。 (Suzuki should be coming.)
Quick rule of thumb: from low to high certainty, it's かもしれない ＜ でしょう ＜ はず. If you have no real idea and it's just "maybe", use かもしれない. If you have a reason and think "it should happen", use はず.
n5-30:
The idea in one line
「に」 goes after a person and shows who the action is directed at. English changes the wording every time: "give to mom," "call a friend," "ask the teacher," "tell mom." Japanese is simpler: you just add 「に」 after the person.
How to attach it
The basic order is: person + に　thing + を　verb.
Say who first, then what, and put the action last:
母に (to mom) + 花を (flowers) + あげます (give) → 母に花をあげます。
If there is no "thing," go straight to "person + に + verb": 友達に電話します。 (I call a friend.)
Patterns you'll hear most
Giving something to someoneGiving, lending, showing.
・母に花をあげます。 (I give flowers to my mom.)
・妹に本を貸しました。 (I lent a book to my younger sister.)
・友達に写真を見せます。 (I show photos to a friend.)
Speaking to / contacting someoneCalling, writing letters, asking questions.
・友達に電話します。 (I call a friend.)
・先生に聞きます。 (I ask the teacher.)
・田中さんに手紙を書きました。 (I wrote a letter to Mr. Tanaka.)
Teaching someone
・弟に英語を教えます。 (I teach English to my younger brother.)
Easy mistakes
・In English you "ask the teacher" and "meet a friend," with the person right after the verb as a direct object, so many learners reach for を. 先生を聞きます is wrong; say 先生に聞きます. 友達を会います is also wrong; say 友達に会います. Some verbs do take を with a person, though, for example 友達を待きます. Learn each verb together with an example sentence instead of guessing from English.
・The person after に is not always the one who receives something. With actions like "borrow" and "learn," the に person is the source: 友達に本を借りました。 (I borrowed a book from a friend.) 先生に日本語を習います。 (I learn Japanese from my teacher.)
・「に」 has other uses too, such as time (7時に) and destination (東京に). Look at what comes before it: if it's a person, it's usually the usage on this card.
Telling look-alikes apart
English "talk to" and "talk with" are a good way to feel the difference between に and と:
友達に話します。 (I tell my friend something: I speak, they listen. It's one-way.)
友達と話します。 (I chat with my friend: you go back and forth, doing it together.)
Both are "talking to a friend," but with に it's me addressing them, and with と it's the two of us chatting together.
Quick test: if you can say "with ～" or "together with ～" in English, use と; if it can only be "to," "for," or "at," use に.
What to learn next
Expressions for "who gives what to whom," such as あげます, もらいます, and くれます, rely on this 「に」 all the time, so giving-and-receiving verbs are a good next step.
n4-39:
The idea in one line
「〜でいちばん」 means “the most ~ in/of …”. First use 「で」 to mark the range (the class, Japan, your family), then use 「いちばん」 to say “most”. In English you'd say “the tallest in the class is Tanaka”, and in Japanese that's クラスでいちばん背が高いのは田中さんです.
How to build it
range ＋ で ＋ いちばん ＋ adjective
高い山 → 日本でいちばん高い山(the tallest mountain in Japan)
・富士山は日本でいちばん高い山です。(Mt. Fuji is the tallest mountain in Japan.)
・クラスで田中さんがいちばん背が高いです。(Tanaka is the tallest in the class.)
「いちばん」 isn't limited to adjectives. It can also go before a verb, meaning “do ~ the most / the earliest”:
・家族で父がいちばん早く起きます。(In my family, my dad gets up the earliest.)
If the range is “a category of things” or you've just listed some options, の中で (“among ~”) is common:
・スポーツの中で、サッカーがいちばん好きです。(Among sports, I like soccer the most.)
How you'll hear it most
Asking “which is the most ~?”range ＋ で ＋ question word ＋ が ＋ いちばん～ですか。 Pick the question word to fit what you're asking about: things use 何 (use どれ when you've listed options), people use だれ, places use どこ, and times use いつ.
・一年でいつがいちばん好きですか。(What time of year do you like the most?)
・夏がいちばん好きです。(I like summer the most.)
・日本でどこがいちばんよかったですか。(Where was your favorite place in Japan?)
“The most ~ is X”Put the answer at the very end for more emphasis:
・家族でいちばん料理が上手なのは母です。(The best cook in my family is my mom.)
Common mistakes
・Use で for the range, not に: it's 日本でいちばん, not 日本にいちばん.
・In questions, put が after the question word, not は: it's 何がいちばん好きですか, not 何はいちばん. Answers usually use が too: 夏がいちばん好きです.
・The object of 「好き」 and 「上手」 also takes が: 料理がいちばん上手です, not 料理をいちばん上手.
・「いちばん」 already means “the most”, so don't add とても before it.
・You can also write it in kanji as 一番. It's the same word with the same reading.
Don't confuse it with similar patterns
The key is how many things you're comparing. Say you're asking what someone likes to drink:
Comparing two uses 「どちら」 ＋ 「ほうが」 (〜より…ほうが):
コーヒーと紅茶とどちらが好きですか。(Which do you prefer, coffee or tea?)
コーヒーのほうが好きです。(I prefer coffee.)
Comparing three or more uses 「どれ／何」 ＋ 「いちばん」:
コーヒーと紅茶とジュースの中で、どれがいちばん好きですか。(Among coffee, tea and juice, which do you like the most?)
コーヒーがいちばん好きです。(I like coffee the most.)
Quick test: if English would use “-er / more / prefer”, you're comparing two, so use ほうが. If it would use “-est / most”, you're comparing three or more (or a whole range), so use いちばん.
What to learn next
「今まで～た中で、いちばん…」 = “the most … I've ever ~”: 今まで食べた中で、これがいちばんおいしいです。(This is the most delicious thing I've ever eaten.)
n3-26:
The idea in one line
「きり」 has two faces.
① After a noun it means “only ~”, like “just the two of us” or “just this once”.
② After a verb's た-form it means “~ and never again”, like “went out and never came back” or “haven't heard from him since”.
How to build it
Only ~noun ＋ きり. The noun is usually a number of people, a number of times, or 「これ」.
二人 → 二人きり(just the two of us)一度 → 一度きり(just once)これ → これきり(only this much)
Note: あれきり and それきり usually don't mean “only that one”. They mean “nothing since that time”, which belongs to the second use below.
・二人きりで話したい。(I want to talk, just the two of us.)
・チャンスは一度きりだ。(You only get one chance.)
・お金はこれきりしかない。(This is all the money I have left.)
Never again after ~verb た-form ＋ きり. First put the verb in the た-form, then add きり.
出かける → 出かけた → 出かけたきり
What follows is something that should have happened but never did, so the sentence is often negative. You can also put 「〜たきりだ」 right at the end of a sentence.
・父は朝出かけたきり、まだ帰ってこない。(My dad left this morning and still hasn't come back.)
・彼女とは卒業式で会ったきりだ。(I saw her at the graduation ceremony and haven't seen her since.)
・あれきり、彼から連絡はない。(I haven't heard from him since then.)
One very common word is 寝たきり = lay down and never got up again = bedridden.
祖母は去年から寝たきりだ。(My grandmother has been bedridden since last year.)
Common mistakes
・In casual speech it's often pronounced っきり: 二人っきり, これっきり. The meaning is the same, so don't mistake it for a different word.
