・「たきり」 can't be followed by “started doing something new”. To say “since joining the company I've been busy every day”, use てから: 会社に入ってから、毎日忙しい。 You can't say 「会社に入ったきり、毎日忙しい」.
・きり already means “since then”, so don't stack it with 以来.
・When 「○○きり」 points to a moment in time, that moment was the last time. It doesn't mean it never happened before. 卒業式で会ったきり means “the graduation ceremony was the last time we met”, not “we only met that once”.
Don't confuse it with similar patterns
きり vs だけ: Both can be translated as “only”, but きり attaches only to words like numbers of people, counts, and これ, and it often carries a feel of “no one else, that's all”.
一人だけ来た。／一人きりだ。(Only one person came. / It's just me alone.) Both are fine here.
りんごだけ食べた。(I ate only an apple.) With ordinary things like this, you can't swap in きり.
たきり vs っぱなし: Both carry a feel of “nothing more after that”, but the focus differs.
テレビをつけっぱなしで寝てしまった。(I fell asleep with the TV left on.): The finishing step (turning it off) wasn't done, so the state just stays as it is.
兄は東京へ行ったきり、帰ってこない。(My older brother went to Tokyo and never came back.): After that event, nothing that should have followed ever happened.
Quick test: “only these people / these few times” → noun ＋ きり; “after that time, never again ~” → た-form ＋ きり; “left on, left as it is” → っぱなし.
n1-14:
The short version
「〜なり」means "the moment ~, (they) immediately…", with a hint of "Whoa, that fast?" surprise. It's like telling a friend: "He walked in and ran straight into his room without even taking his shoes off." You use it to describe someone else who had just finished one action and right away did a second one that was a bit unexpected.
How to form it
Add「なり」directly to the dictionary form of the verb (the base form you'd look up in a dictionary). No conjugation needed.
帰る → 帰るなり聞く → 聞くなり見る → 見るなり
When to use it
Describing someone else's reactionOne action has only just finished, and the same person immediately does something else, and that something is a bit sudden.
・彼は家に帰るなり、部屋にこもってしまった。(The moment he got home, he shut himself in his room.)
・その知らせを聞くなり、彼女は泣き出した。(As soon as she heard the news, she burst into tears.)
・息子は私の顔を見るなり、走って逃げた。(The moment my son saw my face, he ran away.)
Storytelling toneYou'll mostly see it in novels and articles, or when you're "telling someone about" something that happened. In everyday chat, the「〜たとたん」you learned at N3 is more common for "as soon as ~".
Common mistakes
・The subject must be the same before and after. "The moment he got home, he shut himself in his room" works. "The moment the bell rang, the students rushed out" changes the subject, so なり sounds off.
・It's usually not used for yourself. なり feels like an onlooker describing events. For "I went to bed as soon as I got home," saying 家に帰ってすぐ寝た。 is more natural.
・What follows must be something that has already happened. You can't follow it with commands, invitations, or intentions:
×家に帰るなり、宿題をしなさい。 (You can't use it to tell someone to do something.)
・The verb before it must be in dictionary form. Switching to the た-form,「〜たなり」, gives a different meaning: "has stayed that way ever since," as in 出かけたなり、帰ってこない。 (He went out and hasn't come back since.)
・「〜なり〜なり」(either ~ or ~ is fine) and「私なりに」(in my own way) look the same but are completely different grammar. Don't mix them up.
Telling it apart from similar patterns
N1 has several "as soon as ~" patterns. They all attach to the dictionary form and are followed by something that already happened. The differences are in who does it, what's emphasized, and where it's used.

なり: the same person does a slightly unexpected action.
部長は会議室に入るなり、大声で怒鳴り始めた。(The moment the department head walked into the meeting room, he started shouting.)

や否や: very formal and written. The subjects before and after can differ.
ベルが鳴るや否や、学生たちは教室を飛び出した。(The instant the bell rang, the students rushed out of the classroom.)

が早いか: the focus is on speed. The second action happens almost at the same moment the first ends.
子どもたちは「いただきます」と言うが早いか、料理に手を伸ばした。(The kids had barely finished saying "Let's eat" before they reached for the food.)

たとたん (N3): everyday spoken style. You can use it about yourself too, and what follows is often something you can't control.
立ち上がったとたん、めまいがした。(The moment I stood up, I felt dizzy.)
Quick rule of thumb: the same person suddenly does something → なり. Two different events follow each other, and it's written style → や否や. You want to stress lightning speed → が早いか. About yourself, or in everyday conversation → たとたん.
What to learn next
Next, look at the others in the same group,「〜が早いか」and「〜や否や」. Then compare them with「〜そばから」(no sooner has ~ than ~ again, for things that keep repeating). Memorizing these together is the best way to avoid mixing them up.
n1-23:
The short version
「〜ゆえ（に）」is the formal, written-style "owing to ~" / "because of ~". It means "because," just like「から」and「ので」, but it has put on a suit and talks in a stiff, literary way. You'll often see it in news commentary, novels, and speeches, and almost never in casual chat with friends.
How to form it
NounsThe most common pattern is attaching it directly. You can also put「の」in between.
若さ → 若さゆえ貧しさ → 貧しさのゆえに
Verbs and い-adjectivesUse the plain form (the dictionary-style form without ます), then add either「がゆえ」or「ゆえ」.「がゆえ」sounds more formal.
人気がある → 人気があるがゆえに若い → 若いがゆえに
な-adjectives and nouns used as predicatesReplace「だ」with である before attaching.
真面目だ → 真面目であるがゆえに学生だ → 学生であるがゆえに
How you'll usually see it
ゆえに、〜A full clause stating the result follows.
・人気があるがゆえに、予約がなかなか取れない。(Because it's so popular, it's hard to get a reservation.)
・責任ある立場ゆえに、軽率な発言は許されない。(Because of his responsible position, careless remarks are not allowed.)
ゆえの＋nounIt modifies the following noun directly, meaning "a ~ that comes from ~".
・経験不足ゆえの失敗だった。(It was a failure caused by lack of experience.)
・優しさゆえの嘘もある。(There are also lies told out of kindness.)
ゆえに at the start of a sentenceOn its own at the start of a sentence, it means "therefore" or "thus." It's common in mathematical proofs and philosophical writing.
・我思う、ゆえに我あり。(I think, therefore I am.)
Common mistakes
・Nouns and な-adjectives can't take「だ」. It's not「学生だがゆえに」, you say 学生であるがゆえに.
・In everyday conversation it sounds like you're acting in a period drama or reciting lines. To a friend, "because I'm busy" is just 忙しいから. Saying「忙しいがゆえに」would make people laugh.
・It can be written with the kanji「故」. When you see 若さ故に, don't think it's some other grammar. It's still read ゆえに.
・What follows is often a rather negative result, or a "on the contrary ~" outcome, with a sense of "it's precisely because of this trait that it turns out this way," as in 真面目であるがゆえに、かえって批判されることもある。 (Precisely because he's serious, he is sometimes criticized for it.)
Telling it apart from similar patterns
から／ので = the ordinary "because," fine in both speech and writing: 子どもを愛しているから、厳しくする。 (I'm strict because I love my child.)
がゆえに = the same meaning in a written style, stating the reason objectively: 子どもを愛するがゆえに、厳しくする。 (Owing to my love for my child, I am strict with him.)
ばこそ = strongly emphasizes "it's precisely because of this and nothing else." The speaker is often defending their own approach, and the sentence often ends in のだ: 子どもを愛すればこそ、厳しくするのだ。 (It's precisely because I love my child that I'm strict with him.)
Quick rule of thumb: if you're just stating "because" in a more formal way, use ゆえに. If you want to stress "this is exactly the reason, and I want you to understand me," use ばこそ.
What to learn next
Another N1 grammar point for giving reasons is 〜とあって (because of a special situation like ~). Try memorizing it alongside ゆえに so you can compare them.
n1-76:
The idea in one line
「〜ではあるまいし」means “It's not like you're ~, so (why… / you should…)”. Picture your mom seeing you cry and saying, “You're not a little kid, so stop crying.” That's the tone. You first state something that is obviously not true, then use it to scold or advise the other person.
Where it comes from
Break it down and it makes sense: ではあるまい is a slightly literary “it probably isn't ~”, and し means “since ~”. Together: “It's not like it's ~, so…”
In speech people almost always say じゃあるまいし. ではあるまいし shows up more in writing or in somewhat formal settings.
How to attach it
NounAttaches directly: 子供 → 子供じゃあるまいし
・子供じゃあるまいし、自分のことは自分でやりなさい。(You're not a kid, so take care of your own things.)
・神様じゃあるまいし、明日のことなんて分からないよ。(I'm not a god, so how would I know what happens tomorrow?)
VerbYou must put の (ん in speech) or わけ in between. You can't attach it directly.
遊びに行く → 遊びに行くんじゃあるまいし
会えない → 会えないわけじゃあるまいし
・遊びに行くんじゃあるまいし、もっとちゃんとした服を着ていきなさい。(You're not going out to hang around, so wear something more proper.)
・一生会えないわけじゃあるまいし、そんなに泣かないで。(It's not like you'll never see each other again, so don't cry so much.)
What usually follows
The second half is what you really want to say. It's almost always a command, prohibition, advice, criticism, or your own judgment: “don't ~ anymore,” “do it yourself,” “this shouldn't happen.” The first half usually uses something so exaggerated that everyone knows it's not true, like 子供, 神様, or 素人.
・素人じゃあるまいし、こんなミスは許されないよ。(You're not an amateur, so a mistake like this is unacceptable.)
Spoken inversionIn conversation people often tack it on at the end as an afterthought.
・いちいち説明しなくても分かるよ。子供じゃあるまいし。(You don't have to explain every little thing. I get it. I'm not a kid.)
Common mistakes
・A verb must be preceded by の／ん／わけ. It's 死ぬわけじゃあるまいし, not 「死ぬじゃあるまいし」. Nouns are the opposite: don't add の. You won't hear 「子供のじゃあるまいし」.
・The first half must be something everyone knows is “obviously not the case”. If you're just stating a plain reason, like “I'm not a student, so I pay the full fare,” this pattern sounds odd. Use 〜ではないので instead.
・The tone is scolding or snapping back, with a hint of impatience. Saying it directly to a boss or a customer would be very rude.
・It is not a “probably not ~” guess. The point is the scolding or advice in the second half.
Don't confuse it with similar forms
〜じゃないんだから: Almost the same meaning, “it's not like you're ~, you know,” but more everyday and much more common. Even learners below N1 use it.
・子供じゃないんだから、泣かないで。(You're not a kid, so stop crying.)
・子供じゃあるまいし、泣かないで。(Same as above, but a bit old-fashioned, with more of a scolding flavor.)
〜ではあるまいか: Only the last syllable differs, but the meaning is completely different. It's a literary “could it be ~? / it's probably ~,” used for conjecture.
・子供ではあるまいし、一人で行けるだろう。(You're not a kid, so you can surely go by yourself.)
・彼は何か隠しているのではあるまいか。(Could it be that he's hiding something?)
Quick tip: if it ends in 「し」 followed by a scolding line, it means “it's not like you're ~.” If it ends in 「か」, it's a guess: “could it be ~?”
n1-27:
The idea in one line
「〜たところで」 means "even if you do X, it won't help" or "so what if you do X?". It's the tone of English lines like "What's the use of crying now?" or "No matter how you explain it, he won't believe you." It sounds a bit resigned and a bit of a cold shower: whatever you do in the first part will be wasted effort.
・今さら謝ったところで、関係は戻らないだろう。(Even if you apologize now, the relationship won't go back to how it was.)
How to form it
Put the verb in the た-form (the past-tense form), then add 「ところで」 directly.
Group 1 (godan verbs):
急ぐ → 急いだ → 急いだところで
言う → 言った → 言ったところで
Group 2 (ichidan verbs):
慌てる → 慌てた → 慌てたところで
Group 3 (する・来る):
する → した → したところで
来る → 来た → 来たところで
How you'll hear it most
Doing it is pointlessThis is the most common use. The first part often has 「いくら」, 「どんなに」 or 「今さら」, and the ending is a futile result such as 「～ない」, 「無駄だ」 or 「仕方がない」.
・どんなに急いだところで、最終便には間に合わない。(No matter how much you hurry, you won't make the last service.)
・いくら説明したところで、わかってもらえないだろう。(No matter how much I explain, he probably won't understand.)
At best, only ~With 「せいぜい」 in the second part, it means "even if you do it, the result won't amount to much."
・今から急いだところで、せいぜい5分早く着くくらいだ。(Even if we hurry now, we'll arrive 5 minutes earlier at best.)
Easy mistakes
・It uses the た-form, but it talks about a hypothetical, not something that already happened. 「謝ったところで」 means "even if (you) apologize," not "you apologized."
・The second part must be a useless or underwhelming result. For a good result like "if you try hard, you'll pass," you can't say 頑張ったところで合格できる. Use 頑張れば合格できる.
・The second part is your own judgment or guess, often ending in 「～だろう」 or 「～わけではない」. It doesn't take requests like 「～てください」.
・The same 「たところで」 has another meaning: "at the point when ~, just as ~ wraps up," followed by the next action: 話が一段落したところで、休憩しましょう。 (Now that the discussion has reached a stopping point, let's take a break.) Check what follows: if it's "pointless," it's the meaning in this lesson; if it's "then do something," it's the timing meaning.
・The tone is cold and resigned. Telling someone directly "it's no use doing that" can feel like a cold shower, so be careful with context.
Telling it apart from similar forms
ても = the ordinary "even if." It's neutral, and the result can be good or bad: 彼に説明しても、わかってもらえないだろう。 (Even if I explain it to him, he probably won't understand.)
たところで = strongly stresses "it'll be wasted effort," and sounds more resigned than ても: 彼に説明したところで、わかってもらえないだろう。 (Even if I explain it to him, it's no use. He won't understand.)
ようと = "no matter what ~, I'll still ~." The focus is on the second part being unaffected, so it can carry your own determination: みんなが反対しようと、私はこの計画を進める。 (No matter how much everyone objects, I'm going ahead with this plan.)
Say the same thing about opposition with たところで and it becomes: みんなが反対したところで、社長の考えは変わらない。 (Even if everyone objects, it's no use. The president won't change his mind.)
Quick rule: use たところで for "it's pointless to do it," ようと for "no matter what, I'll do it," and ても for a plain "even if."
n1-65:
The idea in one line
「〜いかん」 means "depending on ~" or "it all comes down to ~", in the stiff register of official English like "contingent upon" or "hinges on." It's written with the kanji 如何, but today it's mostly written in hiragana as いかん. The meaning: how things turn out depends on the state of the first thing. It's very stiff and formal, found in news, notices, contracts and managers' speeches.
How to form it
It attaches only to a noun. The 「の」 in between is optional, and leaving it out is more common.
努力 → 努力いかん (depends on the level of effort)
試験の結果 → 試験の結果いかん (depends on the exam result)
The noun must be something that can be good or bad, high or low, for example: 結果, 努力, 態度, 対応, 天候, 返答, 内容.
How you'll hear it most
いかんだ／いかんにかかっているAt the end of a sentence: "it's up to ~."
・合格できるかどうかは、本人の努力いかんだ。(Whether you pass or not depends on the person's own effort.)
・今期の業績は、チームの努力いかんにかかっている。(This quarter's results depend on the team's efforts.)
いかんで／いかんによってIn the middle of a sentence: "decided by, or changing according to, ~."
・参加費は人数いかんで変わります。(The participation fee varies depending on the number of people.)
いかんでは／いかんによってはWith the extra 「は」, the meaning becomes "depending on the situation, it's even possible that ~." The second part usually describes a special, often unwelcome outcome.
・天候いかんでは、試合が中止になることもあります。(Depending on the weather, the match may even be cancelled.)
・会社の対応いかんでは、訴訟も考えています。(Depending on how the company responds, we are also considering a lawsuit.)
Easy mistakes
・Read it いかん. The same kanji 如何 is read いか in 如何ですか (read いかが), so don't mix them up.
・It can't attach directly to a verb or adjective. To say "depending on whether you try hard," write 努力いかんで, not 「頑張るいかんで」.
・The noun must be a variable one. A word like 「明日」, which has no good or bad, high or low, can't be used.
・It's too formal. Saying 「天気いかんで決めよう」 to a friend sounds very odd. In casual speech, use 天気次第で決めよう or 天気によって決めよう.
・In casual speech, the standalone phrase それはいかん means "that won't do." It's a different word and has nothing to do with this grammar.
Telling it apart from similar forms
次第 (N2) = almost the same meaning, but it works in both spoken and written Japanese and feels more relaxed:
結果次第で、計画を変えるかもしれない。 (Depending on the result, we may change the plan.)
いかん = the same meaning in the tone of official notices and reports:
結果いかんでは、計画を変更することもあり得る。 (Depending on the result, the plan may also be changed.)
いかんによらず／いかんにかかわらず (n1-66) = the opposite meaning: "regardless of ~, it's the same."
理由のいかんにかかわらず、返金はいたしません。 (Regardless of the reason, we do not offer refunds.)
Quick rule: if いかん is followed by 「で・によって・だ・にかかっている」, it means "it depends on it"; if it's followed by 「によらず・にかかわらず・を問わず」, it means "regardless of it." To sound more casual, swap いかん for 次第.
What to learn next
Next, learn いかんによらず and いかんにかかわらず in n1-66, as well as 理由のいかんを問わず (regardless of the reason), which you often see in notices.
n4-4:
The idea in one line
「AはBより～」 means "A is more ~ than B". 東京は大阪より人が多い。 means "Tokyo has more people than Osaka."
The biggest difference is word order. English puts "than" before B, but Japanese より goes after B, like a "than" stuck onto the end of B: "B-than."
How to build it
Add は to the subject A, add より to B (the thing you compare against), and put the adjective last.
い-adjectives just take です after them.
・今日は昨日より暑いです。(Today is hotter than yesterday.)
な-adjectives also just take です. Among friends, use だ or nothing at all.
・電車はバスより便利です。(Trains are more convenient than buses.)
Comparing one aspect To say which aspect you are comparing, use 「～が＋adjective」.
・兄は私より背が高いです。(My older brother is taller than me.)
・姉は私より料理が上手です。(My older sister is a better cook than me.)
Works with actions too What comes last doesn't have to be an adjective. It can also describe how you do something.
・弟は私よりよく食べます。(My younger brother eats more than me.)
You'll also hear よりも. The meaning is the same, just a bit more emphatic.
Easy mistakes
・Whatever より attaches to is the one being compared against (the "lower" one). If you translate straight from English word order, it's easy to misplace it: 東京より大阪は人が多い becomes "Osaka has more people than Tokyo," so the meaning flips completely.
・The adjective doesn't change form, and you don't need to force in a "more." English builds the comparison into the word ("taller"), but in Japanese plain 高いです is enough. Adding もっと actually changes the meaning to "both are tall, and A is even taller."
・To name the aspect you're comparing, use が: 背が高い, 気温が高い. Don't write を.
・To say "A isn't as ~ as B," Japanese people usually use ほど…ない. 「より～くない」 is less common.
Telling look-alikes apart
Same situation, comparing the populations of Tokyo and Osaka:
AはBより = you're talking about A as the subject and bring in B for comparison: 東京は大阪より人が多いです。 (Tokyo has more people than Osaka.)
BよりAのほうが = you put the two side by side and pick A. It's often used to answer "Which one is more ~?": 大阪より東京のほうが人が多いです。 (Compared to Osaka, Tokyo has more people.)
BほどAない = the reverse, "not as ~": 大阪は東京ほど人が多くないです。 (Osaka doesn't have as many people as Tokyo.)
Quick rule of thumb: to simply describe "A is more ~ than B," use AはBより. To pick one of two, use のほうが. To say "not as ~," use ほど…ない.
What to learn next
To ask "Which one is more ~?": 電車とバスとどちらが便利ですか。 (Which is more convenient, the train or the bus?) You answer with ～より…ほうが. To pick the top one out of three or more, learn ～でいちばん next.
n4-38:
The idea in one line
「AはBほど～ない」 means "A is not as ~ as B". The order is almost the same as in English: 京都は東京ほど人が多くない = Kyoto does not have as many people as Tokyo. ほど means "to that extent," and it must always be followed by a negative.
How to build it
A (the subject) は B (the thing compared) ほど + negative form
Get the negative form ready first:
い-adjectives Replace the final 「い」 with 「くない」.
高い → replace い with くない → 高くない寒い → 寒くない
Exception: いい → よくない (you can't say いくない)
・この店の料理は前ほどよくない。(The food at this restaurant isn't as good as it used to be.)
な-adjectives Add 「じゃない」 after them, or 「ではない」 for a more formal tone.
便利 → 便利じゃない
・このアプリは前のほど便利じゃない。(This app isn't as convenient as the previous one.)
Verbs Just use the ない form.
食べる → 食べない
・私は兄ほど食べない。(I don't eat as much as my older brother.)
To sound polite, just add です after it: 寒くない → 寒くないです
Forms you'll hear most
思ったほど～ない "Not as ~ as I thought." Extremely common in daily conversation.
・テストは思ったほど難しくなかった。(The test wasn't as hard as I thought.)
前ほど～ない "Not as ~ as before."
・最近は前ほど忙しくないです。(I'm not as busy as I used to be lately.)
それほど～ない Leave out B and just say "not that ~." It's handy for answering someone.
・日本語、難しい？(Is Japanese hard?)
・いや、それほど難しくないよ。(Nah, it's not that hard.)
Easy mistakes
・This pattern is always followed by a negative. 京都は東京ほど人が多いです is wrong. To say "more," use より instead.
・What goes before ほど is the stronger side. 今日は昨日ほど暑くない means yesterday was hotter, so don't read it backwards.
・The negative of いい is よくない. Writing いくない is wrong.
・The tone is softer. 私の部屋は田中さんの部屋ほど広くない (My room isn't as big as Tanaka's) sounds more polite than bluntly saying "mine is smaller."
Telling look-alikes apart
Same situation: yesterday was hot, and today is a bit cooler.
より（～ほうが） = directly says who is "more" something, and can take an affirmative:
昨日より今日のほうが涼しい。 (Today is cooler than yesterday.)
今日は昨日より涼しい。 (Today is cooler than yesterday.)
ほど～ない = says A "doesn't reach B's level," and is always followed by a negative:
今日は昨日ほど暑くない。 (Today isn't as hot as yesterday.)
Quick rule of thumb: if you'd say "-er than" in English, use より. If you'd say "not as ... as," use ほど + negative.
What to learn next
After comparing two things, learn "the most ~ in a group": クラスでいちばん背が高い。 (He's the tallest in the class.)
n5-64:
The idea in one line
English has "this" and "that". Japanese has four series: こ = this (near me), そ = that (near you), あ = that over there (far from both of us), ど = which. Memorize these four starting sounds, then swap in different endings to point to things, places, and directions.
Picture it first
You and a friend are standing on the street. You're holding a phone, your friend is holding a cup of coffee, and far away across the road there's a big building.
The phone is near you, so use こ. The coffee is near your friend, so use そ. The building is far from both of you, so use あ. If you don't know which one, use ど.
All four series together
Pointing to thingsこれ・それ・あれ・どれ
These words can stand alone as the subject, followed directly by 「は」 or 「が」.
・これは私の傘です。(This is my umbrella.)
・それ、何ですか。(What's that you're holding?)
・あれは東京タワーです。(That's Tokyo Tower.)
Followed by a nounこの・その・あの・どの
These words can't be used alone. A noun must always follow.
・この本、おもしろいですよ。(This book is really good, you know.)
・そのかばん、かわいいですね。(That bag of yours is so cute.)
・あの人はだれですか。(Who is that person?)
Pointing to placesここ・そこ・あそこ・どこ
・トイレはどこですか。(Where is the restroom?)
・あそこにコンビニがあります。(There's a convenience store over there.)
Polite versionこちら・そちら・あちら・どちら
These can point to directions or places, and can also politely introduce people. Shop staff and receptionists use them a lot. When talking with friends, they become こっち・そっち・あっち・どっち.
・受付はあちらです。(The reception desk is over there.)
・こちらは田中さんです。(This is Mr. Tanaka.)
Easy mistakes
・この・その・あの・どの can't be used alone. "This is mine" is これは私のです, not このは私のです.
・The word for "over there" (place) is あそこ, not あこ. It doesn't follow the pattern of the others in its set, so memorize it specially.
・English uses "that" for both, but Japanese keeps them apart: if the thing is next to the other person or in their hands, use それ. Only when it's far from both of you do you use あれ.
・When you change position, the word changes too. If the other person points at something in their own hand and asks これは何ですか, you answer それは～です, because the thing is on their side.
・Something the other person just mentioned is also referred to with a 「そ」 word: それ、いいですね。(That sounds good!)
・Use こちら to introduce people. Pointing at a person with これ treats them like an object, which is very rude.
Telling similar words apart
これ and この: both mean "this"; the difference is what follows.
これは私の本です。(This is my book.)
この本は私のです。(This book is mine.)
In the first sentence, これ is followed by 「は」. In the second, この is followed by 「本」.
どれ and どちら: both mean "which one"; the difference is how many choices there are.
この三つの中で、どれがいいですか。(Of these three, which is best?)
コーヒーと紅茶、どちらがいいですか。(Coffee or tea, which would you like?)
Use どれ when choosing among three or more things; use どちら when choosing between just two.
Quick rule: if a noun comes right after, use この; if 「は」 or 「が」 follows, use これ. Pick one of three or more: どれ. Pick one of two: どちら.
What to learn next
The 「ど」 series is really a set of question words, so a good next step is "question words". Learn だれ, なに, and いつ together.
n1-78:
The idea in one line
「AあってのB」 means "no A, no B" or "B exists only because of A". A is the precondition for B to exist; without A, B can't exist. Shop owners often say "customers are our lifeblood"; in Japanese that's: お客様あっての商売だ。(No customers, no business.)
How to form it
Noun + あっての + noun. A noun goes before it, and a noun must always follow.
「あって」 is the te-form of 「ある」 (to exist), and adding 「の」 gives "the … that exists thanks to ～".
お客様 → お客様あっての商売 (a business that exists thanks to customers)
Common patterns
AあってのBだStates a principle or a value: B is held up by A.
・選手はファンあっての存在だ。(Athletes exist because of their fans.)
・命あっての物種だ。無理はするな。(Life comes first; everything else depends on it. Don't push yourself too hard.)
〜あってのことだThe following noun becomes 「こと」, meaning "this is all thanks to ～". It's very common in award speeches and thank-yous.
・合格できたのは、先生のご指導あってのことです。(I passed only thanks to my teacher's guidance.)
・皆さんの応援あっての優勝です。(This championship exists thanks to everyone's support.)
あってこそのAdding 「こそ」 in the middle makes it stronger: 家族あってこその私です。(It's precisely because of my family that I am who I am.)
Easy mistakes
・A noun (or こと) must always follow. You can't say 「お客様あっての売れる」; say お客様あっての商売.
・The form is fixed as 「あっての」. Don't write 「あるの」.
・It isn't a plain "because". For "it was canceled because of rain", you can't say 「雨あっての中止」; say 雨で中止になった. A must be something essential and indispensable to B, usually something positive and important such as customers, health, support, or effort.
・The tone is fairly formal and a bit heartfelt, used mostly in speeches, interviews, and writing. With friends, just say お客さんがいるから.
Telling similar patterns apart
The same idea can be said positively or negatively:
あっての = the positive "B exists because of A", followed by a noun: お客様あっての商売だ。(No customers, no business.)
なくしては = the negative "without A, B is impossible", followed by a negative: お客様なくしては商売は成り立たない。(Without customers, the business can't survive.)
ばこそ = "precisely because ～", giving the reason for doing something, attached to the ば form: お客様のことを思えばこそ、品質にこだわるのだ。(It's precisely because we care about our customers that we're particular about quality.)
Quick rule: for "B exists thanks to A", use あっての with a noun after it; for "it can't be done without A", use なくしては with a negative after it; for "precisely because I think or act this way", use ばこそ.
n5-29:
The idea in one line
This 「で」 is the English "with / by / in" for tools, languages and methods. Eat with chopsticks, speak in Japanese, get in touch by phone: in Japanese you add 「で」 after the thing you use: はしで食べます (I eat with chopsticks).
When to use it
ToolSomething you hold or handle to do the action.
・はしで食べます。 (I eat with chopsticks.)
・ボールペンで書いてください。 (Please write with a ballpoint pen.)
LanguageThe language you speak or write in.
・日本語で話しましょう。 (Let's talk in Japanese.)
・これは英語で何と言いますか。 (How do you say this in English?)
MethodThe means by which you do something.
・母と電話で話しました。 (I talked with my mom by phone.)
・ネットでチケットを買いました。 (I bought a ticket online.)
MaterialWhat something is made from, when you can still see the original material in the finished product.
・紙で花を作りました。 (I made a flower out of paper.)
How to attach it
Easy: just add 「で」 right after the noun. Nothing changes.
スプーン → スプーンで英語 → 英語で
The thing being done still takes 「を」 before the verb, as usual: スプーンでスープを飲みます。 (I drink soup with a spoon.)
Easy mistakes
・English puts "with" before the noun, but Japanese puts 「で」 after it. English says "with chopsticks"; Japanese says 「はしで」. The order is reversed.
・Beginners often treat the tool as the object and say 「はしを食べます」, which means "I eat the chopsticks." After a tool, use で.
・To ask "with what?", say 何で, read なにで: 何で書きますか。 (What will you write with?) If you read it as なんで, in casual speech it is often heard as "why?"
Telling it apart from look-alikes
で (place): where you do something: 教室で書きます。 (I write in the classroom.)
で (tool): what you do it with: ペンで書きます。 (I write with a pen.)
You can put both in one sentence: 教室でペンで書きます。 (I write with a pen in the classroom.)
By the way, the 「で」 in バスで行きます (I go by bus) also means "by what means," so it's the same idea as this card.
Quick test: if what comes before is a place, it means "at / in ～"; if it's a thing you use, a language or a method, it means "with / by ～".
日本語を話します: you can speak Japanese. Japanese is something you know.
日本語で話します: you speak using Japanese. Japanese is the means of communication.
・私は日本語を話します。 (I speak Japanese.)
・店員と日本語で話しました。 (I talked with the shop clerk in Japanese.)
Quick test: to say which language you speak, use を; to say which language you used this time to communicate, use で.
n5-63:
The idea in one line
Question words are the words you use to ask things: "what, who, where, when, which, how much, how." They work much like English: put the question word where the answer would go, and add か at the end. Also, adding 「も」 or 「か」 after a question word changes the meaning completely. That's the key point of this lesson.
The seven most common ones
・これは何ですか。 (What is this?)
・あの人は誰ですか。 (Who is that person?)
・トイレはどこですか。 (Where is the restroom?)
・誕生日はいつですか。 (When is your birthday?)
・どれがいいですか。 (Which one is good?)
・これはいくらですか。 (How much is this?)
・日本はどうでしたか。 (How was Japan?)
To be more polite with customers or elders: 誰 becomes どなた, and どう becomes いかが. Shop staff often say コーヒーはいかがですか。 (Would you like some coffee?)
Is 「何」 read なに or なん?
Before です and の, or before a counter such as "o'clock" or "people," it's read なん: 何ですか, 何の本, 何時, 何人, 何曜日.
Before を, が, も and か, it's read なに: 何を食べますか, 何も, 何か.
Adding 「も」: none at all
Question word + も + negativeThis means "not anything, not anyone, not anywhere."
・何も飲みませんでした。 (I didn't drink anything.)
・誰も来ませんでした。 (Nobody came.)
・日曜日はどこへも行きませんでした。 (I didn't go anywhere on Sunday.)
Watch the particles: the original を and が are replaced by も (何を → 何も), but へ and に stay, placed before も: どこへも, どこにも, 誰にも.
Adding 「か」: some, unspecified
Question word + かThis means "something, someone, somewhere, some day." There is one, but you can't say which.
・何か食べたいです。 (I want to eat something.)
・誰かいますか。 (Is anyone there?)
・どこか静かな場所へ行きたいです。 (I want to go somewhere quiet.)
・いつか日本に住みたいです。 (Someday I want to live in Japan.)
Easy mistakes
・When the question word is the subject, use が, not は: 誰が来ましたか。 You can't say 誰は来ましたか.
・いつも does not mean "never." It means "always." It can take a positive or a negative: いつも朝ご飯を食べます。 (I always eat breakfast.) / いつも朝ご飯を食べません。 (I never eat breakfast. Literally, "I always don't eat it.")
・何も is read なにも, not なんも.
・どれ is for choosing one out of three or more; for just two, use どちら.
Telling it apart from look-alikes
Say you're asking a friend what they drank. Changing one syllable changes the meaning:
何を = asks "what," so the answer is a thing: 何を飲みましたか。 (What did you drink?) → お茶です。
何か = asks "did you or didn't you," so the answer starts with はい or いいえ: 何か飲みましたか。 (Did you drink anything?) → はい、お茶を飲みました。
何も + negative = "nothing at all": いいえ、何も飲みませんでした。 (No, I didn't drink anything.)
Quick test: to find out "what," use 何を; to find out "whether there was any," use 何か; to say "none at all," use 何も + negative.
What to learn next
"This, that, which" is easier to remember as a set, so go on to the demonstratives (こそあど): どの本ですか。 (Which book is it?)
